author: claude-opus-4-5
title: The Condensate Client Grammar: Predicting Biomolecular Condensate Composition from Scaffold Sequence
abstract: Biomolecular condensates organize cellular biochemistry through selective recruitment of client proteins, yet the rules governing client selection remain poorly understood. Existing predictive models address phase-separation propensity of scaffolds but stop short of predicting which proteins are recruited as clients—the question that matters most for understanding condensate function. This Working Group will synthesize publicly available condensate proteomics datasets (CD-CODE, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, and condensate-specific APEX/BioID studies) with intrinsically disordered region (IDR) feature databases (MobiDB, IDEAL) and full proteome sequence resources to develop the first proteome-scale model of condensate client recruitment. The team will integrate biophysicists specializing in IDR sequence-function relationships, machine learning researchers expert in protein language models, and cell biologists with deep expertise in specific condensate systems (stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, transcriptional condensates). The synthesis will harmonize ~50 published condensate proteomes into a single annotated resource with controlled vocabularies for cellular context, stress condition, and confidence level. We will train sequence-to-client models using transformer architectures pretrained on protein sequences and fine-tuned on condensate membership data, then validate predictions against held-out condensate types and orthogonal in-cell localization datasets from OpenCell and the Human Protein Atlas. The project will yield (1) a unified, openly accessible condensate-client database, (2) predictive models released as a community web tool, (3) a quantitative grammar relating IDR sequence features to client identity, and (4) testable hypotheses about previously uncharacterized condensates. This work requires NCEMS support because no single lab possesses the combined biophysical, machine-learning, and cell-biological expertise, nor the resources to harmonize fragmented condensate datasets that currently exist in inconsistent formats across publications. The training plan will support four graduate students and three postdocs through a structured rotation across participating labs, with formal training modules in protein language modeling, condensate biology, and FAIR data practices. Trainees will lead sub-projects targeting specific condensate classes and present jointly at an annual workshop. All datasets, code, and trained models will be released under permissive licenses with versioned DOIs through Zenodo and the project's GitHub organization, following community standards for reproducible ML research. Beyond its immediate scientific contribution, this Working Group will establish a template for synthesis-driven hypothesis generation in condensate biology, enabling downstream experimental groups to prioritize targets for mechanistic study. The broader impact extends to disease biology, since aberrant condensate composition underlies neurodegenerative conditions including ALS and FTD; predictive models of client recruitment will accelerate the identification of disease-relevant mis-recruitment events. By moving beyond phase-separation prediction to client-composition prediction, this project addresses a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale biology and provides infrastructure that the broader community can build upon for years.
background_and_significance:
Biomolecular condensates represent a paradigm shift in our understanding of cellular organization. These membraneless compartments, formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), concentrate specific proteins and nucleic acids to regulate biochemical reactions with spatiotemporal precision. Since the landmark discovery that P granules exhibit liquid-like properties, the field has expanded dramatically, revealing that condensates govern processes ranging from transcriptional regulation to stress responses and signal transduction. However, a fundamental gap persists: while we can increasingly predict which proteins drive phase separation (scaffolds), we lack systematic understanding of which proteins are selectively recruited into condensates as clients.

This distinction between scaffolds and clients is biologically critical. Scaffolds provide the structural framework for condensate formation, but clients execute the functional outputs—enzymatic activities, regulatory interactions, and signaling cascades that determine cellular phenotypes. The selective recruitment of clients transforms condensates from simple concentration devices into sophisticated biochemical reactors with emergent properties. Understanding the molecular grammar that dictates client recruitment represents a central challenge in mesoscale biology, directly aligned with NCEMS's mission to illuminate emergent properties at scales between biomolecules and organelles.

Current computational approaches have made significant strides in predicting phase-separation propensity. Tools like catGRANULE, PSPredictor, and FuzDrop identify sequence features associated with LLPS, primarily focusing on intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) enriched in specific amino acid compositions. More recent efforts leverage protein language models to capture complex sequence patterns. However, these tools answer a different question than the one most relevant to cellular function: they predict whether a protein can phase-separate, not which condensate it will join or what clients it will recruit.

The timing for addressing this gap is optimal. The community has generated substantial publicly available data that, when synthesized, can reveal client recruitment principles. Databases including CD-CODE, PhaSepDB, and DrLLPS catalog condensate-associated proteins across organisms and conditions. Proximity labeling studies (APEX, BioID) have mapped condensate proteomes with unprecedented resolution. Meanwhile, resources like MobiDB and IDEAL provide comprehensive IDR annotations, and large-scale localization atlases (OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas) offer orthogonal validation data. These resources exist in fragmented, inconsistent formats, preventing systematic analysis.

The significance of solving this problem extends beyond basic biology. Aberrant condensate composition underlies numerous diseases. In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), mutations in scaffold proteins like FUS and TDP-43 alter client recruitment, disrupting RNA metabolism. Cancer cells exploit condensate dysregulation to rewire transcriptional programs. Predictive models of client recruitment would transform disease research by identifying mis-recruitment events as therapeutic targets.

This Working Group addresses a long-standing puzzle that no single laboratory can solve. The challenge requires integration of biophysical expertise in IDR sequence-function relationships, machine learning capabilities for protein language model development, and deep biological knowledge of specific condensate systems. Furthermore, harmonizing heterogeneous datasets demands coordinated effort exceeding individual lab capacity. NCEMS support provides the essential infrastructure for this transdisciplinary synthesis, positioning this project to deliver foundational resources for the condensate biology community while training the next generation of data-savvy scientists.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses one overarching question: Can we predict which proteins are recruited as clients into specific biomolecular condensates based on sequence features, and what molecular grammar governs this selectivity? We decompose this central question into four interconnected research questions, each with testable hypotheses.

Research Question 1: What sequence features distinguish clients of different condensate types?

Hypothesis 1a: Client proteins recruited to the same condensate type share IDR sequence signatures that are distinct from clients of other condensate types, even when controlling for overall disorder content. We hypothesize that beyond simple amino acid composition, higher-order sequence patterns—including charge patterning, aromatic residue spacing, and short linear motifs (SLiMs)—encode condensate-specific recruitment signals.

Hypothesis 1b: The specificity of client recruitment correlates with the presence of multivalent interaction motifs that complement scaffold IDR features. Specifically, we predict that stress granule clients will be enriched for RGG motifs and arginine-rich sequences that interact with G3BP1/2 scaffolds, while nucleolar clients will display distinct patterns reflecting NPM1 and fibrillarin interactions.

Research Question 2: Can transformer-based protein language models learn client recruitment rules from condensate proteomics data?

Hypothesis 2a: Fine-tuning pretrained protein language models (ESM-2, ProtTrans) on condensate membership data will outperform traditional feature-based classifiers in predicting client identity. We hypothesize that language models capture evolutionary and structural information relevant to condensate recruitment that hand-crafted features miss.

Hypothesis 2b: Attention patterns in fine-tuned models will highlight biologically meaningful sequence regions, including known interaction motifs and previously uncharacterized recruitment determinants. These attention maps will provide interpretable insights into the learned grammar.

Research Question 3: How does cellular context modulate client recruitment rules?

Hypothesis 3a: Stress-induced condensates (stress granules, heat shock granules) recruit overlapping but distinct client sets compared to constitutive condensates (nucleoli, Cajal bodies), and these differences are predictable from sequence features combined with contextual annotations. We hypothesize that stress-responsive clients contain sequence elements that are masked or modified under basal conditions.

Hypothesis 3b: Post-translational modification sites within IDRs serve as context-dependent switches for client recruitment. Proteins with phosphorylation sites in condensate-targeting regions will show condition-dependent localization patterns in validation datasets.

Research Question 4: Can synthesis of heterogeneous condensate proteomics data reveal universal versus condensate-specific recruitment principles?

Hypothesis 4a: A subset of sequence features constitutes a universal recruitment grammar shared across condensate types, while additional features provide type-specific selectivity. We predict that general features include overall IDR length and net charge, while specificity arises from motif composition and patterning.

Hypothesis 4b: Harmonization of ~50 published condensate proteomes will reveal previously unrecognized client proteins shared across condensate types, suggesting functional connections between apparently distinct membraneless organelles. These multi-condensate clients will be enriched for hub proteins in protein-protein interaction networks.

Validation Strategy: Each hypothesis generates specific predictions testable against held-out data. We will reserve entire condensate types (e.g., paraspeckles, PML bodies) for validation, ensuring models generalize beyond training data. Predictions will be cross-validated against OpenCell localization data and Human Protein Atlas subcellular annotations. For interpretability hypotheses, we will compare attention-highlighted regions against experimentally validated interaction motifs from the Eukaryotic Linear Motif (ELM) database. This rigorous validation framework ensures that our synthesis generates robust, generalizable insights rather than dataset-specific artifacts.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises four integrated phases: data harmonization, feature engineering, model development, and validation. Each phase involves specific computational strategies designed for synthesis research using exclusively publicly available data.

Phase 1: Data Harmonization and Database Construction (Months 1-8)

We will systematically collect condensate proteomics data from CD-CODE, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, and primary literature describing APEX/BioID proximity labeling experiments. Our team will develop a standardized schema capturing: protein identifiers (UniProt), condensate type (controlled vocabulary), organism, cell type, experimental method, stress condition, and confidence score. We will implement automated pipelines using Python and R to parse heterogeneous source formats, with manual curation for ambiguous entries. Protein identifiers will be mapped to canonical UniProt accessions using the UniProt ID mapping service. We anticipate harmonizing approximately 50 condensate proteomes encompassing stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, Cajal bodies, paraspeckles, nuclear speckles, PML bodies, and transcriptional condensates. Quality control will include cross-referencing against Gene Ontology cellular component annotations and flagging inconsistencies for expert review. The resulting database will include approximately 15,000-20,000 unique protein-condensate associations.

Phase 2: Feature Engineering and IDR Characterization (Months 4-12)

We will extract comprehensive sequence features for all proteins in our harmonized database. IDR annotations will be obtained from MobiDB and IDEAL, supplemented by disorder predictions from IUPred3 for proteins lacking experimental annotations. Feature categories include: (1) Compositional features—amino acid frequencies, charge distribution, hydropathy; (2) Patterning features—charge segregation (kappa parameter), aromatic clustering, proline spacing; (3) Motif features—SLiM occurrences from ELM database, RGG/RG motifs, [G/S]Y[G/S] motifs; (4) Evolutionary features—conservation scores from ConSurf, phylogenetic distribution; (5) Structural features—predicted secondary structure propensities, AlphaFold2 predicted disorder. We will compute features using established bioinformatics tools (localCIDER, CIDER, IUPred3) integrated into reproducible Snakemake workflows.

Phase 3: Model Development and Training (Months 8-20)

We will develop two complementary modeling approaches. First, interpretable feature-based models using gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) will establish baseline performance and identify predictive features through SHAP analysis. Second, we will fine-tune pretrained protein language models (ESM-2 with 650M parameters) for condensate client classification. Fine-tuning will employ a multi-label classification head predicting membership across condensate types. We will implement curriculum learning, starting with binary client/non-client classification before progressing to multi-class condensate-type prediction. Training will use cross-validation with condensate-type-aware splits ensuring no data leakage. Hyperparameter optimization will employ Optuna with early stopping. For interpretability, we will extract attention weights and apply integrated gradients to identify sequence regions driving predictions. All model development will occur on GPU clusters available through institutional resources and NCEMS computational allocations.

Phase 4: Validation and Hypothesis Generation (Months 16-24)

Validation will proceed at multiple levels. Internal validation uses held-out condensate types never seen during training. External validation compares predictions against OpenCell (1,310 proteins with subcellular localization) and Human Protein Atlas immunofluorescence data. We will compute precision, recall, F1-score, and area under precision-recall curves. For biological validation, we will assess whether predicted clients for understudied condensates are enriched for relevant Gene Ontology terms and protein-protein interactions with known scaffolds (STRING database). Finally, we will generate ranked predictions for uncharacterized condensates, providing the community with testable hypotheses prioritized by model confidence.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will deliver four major outcomes with lasting impact on molecular and cellular sciences.

Outcome 1: Unified Condensate-Client Database. We will release the first harmonized, openly accessible database of condensate-protein associations, encompassing ~50 proteomes with standardized annotations. This resource will serve as the foundation for future condensate research, eliminating redundant curation efforts across laboratories and enabling systematic comparative analyses currently impossible with fragmented data.

Outcome 2: Predictive Models and Community Tools. Our trained models will be released as a user-friendly web server allowing researchers to query any protein sequence for predicted condensate recruitment. The tool will return ranked predictions across condensate types with confidence scores and highlighted sequence features. All model weights, training code, and inference pipelines will be publicly available, enabling community extension and improvement.

Outcome 3: Quantitative Grammar of Client Recruitment. Through systematic feature analysis and model interpretation, we will define the sequence rules governing client selectivity. This grammar will formalize relationships between IDR sequence properties and condensate targeting, providing mechanistic hypotheses testable through mutagenesis and in vitro reconstitution by experimental groups.

Outcome 4: Testable Hypotheses for Uncharacterized Condensates. Model predictions will generate prioritized lists of candidate clients for understudied condensates, accelerating discovery in systems lacking comprehensive proteomics data.

Broader Impact: The disease relevance of this work is substantial. By predicting normal client recruitment patterns, our models enable identification of aberrant recruitment in disease states. For ALS/FTD, we will specifically analyze how disease-associated mutations in FUS and TDP-43 alter predicted client profiles, generating hypotheses about pathological mis-recruitment. This framework extends to cancer biology, where condensate dysregulation drives oncogenic transcription programs.

The Working Group will train seven early-career scientists (four graduate students, three postdocs) in transdisciplinary synthesis research, creating a cohort of data-savvy researchers equipped to tackle future challenges at the intersection of computational biology and cell biology. This training impact multiplies as trainees establish independent research programs applying synthesis approaches to new biological questions.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
This Working Group is committed to exemplary open science practices aligned with NCEMS principles and FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data standards.

Data Sharing: All harmonized datasets will be deposited in Zenodo with versioned DOIs upon major milestones and final release. The condensate-client database will be available in multiple formats (CSV, JSON, SQLite) with comprehensive documentation including data dictionaries, provenance information, and quality metrics. We will register our database with FAIRsharing.org and pursue integration with established resources (UniProt, Gene Ontology) to maximize discoverability.

Code and Workflow Transparency: All analysis code will be maintained in a public GitHub organization (github.com/condensate-client-grammar) from project initiation. We will use Snakemake for workflow management, ensuring computational reproducibility. Docker containers will encapsulate software environments, enabling exact replication of analyses. Jupyter notebooks will provide interactive documentation of key analyses. Code will be released under MIT license; workflows under CC-BY 4.0.

Model Sharing: Trained model weights will be deposited in Hugging Face Model Hub with model cards documenting training data, hyperparameters, performance metrics, and intended use cases. We will follow emerging standards for ML model documentation (Model Cards, Datasheets for Datasets) to ensure responsible AI practices.

Reproducibility Verification: Prior to publication, we will conduct internal reproducibility audits where team members unfamiliar with specific analyses reproduce results from documented workflows. We will pursue external verification through NCEMS reproducibility initiatives.

Community Engagement: We will present preliminary findings at annual NCEMS workshops and relevant conferences (ASCB, Biophysical Society). Preprints will be posted on bioRxiv prior to peer review. We will establish a project website with tutorials, FAQs, and community forums for user feedback. All publications will be submitted to journals with open-access options, with preprints ensuring immediate availability regardless of publication timeline.

Training Integration: Trainees will receive formal instruction in FAIR data practices, version control, and reproducible research as part of their professional development, embedding open science principles in the next generation of researchers.
budget_and_resources:
The requested budget supports personnel, computation, meetings, and training activities essential for this synthesis project. Total request: $450,000 over 24 months.

Personnel (60%, $270,000): Partial salary support for three postdoctoral researchers ($45,000 each annually, covering 50% effort) and four graduate student stipend supplements ($15,000 each annually). Postdocs will lead computational development across the three core expertise areas (IDR biophysics, machine learning, cell biology). Graduate students will execute sub-projects on specific condensate classes while rotating across labs for cross-training.

Computational Resources (20%, $90,000): Cloud computing allocations (AWS/Google Cloud) for GPU-intensive model training and large-scale data processing. While participating institutions provide baseline computational resources, the scale of protein language model fine-tuning and hyperparameter optimization requires dedicated GPU clusters beyond typical lab allocations. Budget includes storage costs for large datasets and model checkpoints.

Meetings and Workshops (12%, $54,000): Two in-person Working Group meetings annually ($20,000 each) bringing all participants together for intensive collaboration, data harmonization sprints, and training workshops. Additional funds support trainee travel to present at conferences ($14,000 total).

Training and Professional Development (8%, $36,000): Development of formal training modules in protein language modeling, condensate biology fundamentals, and FAIR data practices. Includes materials development, guest speaker honoraria, and trainee workshop registration fees.

Justification for NCEMS Support: This project requires NCEMS because: (1) No single lab possesses the required combination of biophysical, ML, and cell biology expertise; (2) Data harmonization demands coordinated effort across multiple groups with dedicated personnel time; (3) Computational requirements for language model training exceed typical lab resources; (4) NCEMS provides the collaborative infrastructure and community connections essential for broad adoption of resulting tools. The synthesis nature of this work—integrating existing public data rather than generating new experimental data—aligns precisely with NCEMS's mission and capabilities.

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Membrane Contact-Site Composition Rules Across the Cell-Type Landscape
abstract: Inter-organelle membrane contact sites (MCSs) coordinate lipid transfer, calcium signaling, and organelle dynamics, yet whether their molecular composition follows universal rules or varies systematically with cell type remains unknown. This question has resisted resolution because relevant data—electron tomography reconstructions, organelle-proximity proteomes, and lipidomic atlases—live in disconnected archives with incompatible annotations. This Working Group will synthesize EMPIAR cryo-electron tomography datasets, organelle-targeted proximity proteomics studies (Mito-IP, ER-IP, lipid-droplet-IP, peroxisome-IP), and tissue/cell-type lipidomic atlases to derive the first cross-cellular rulebook for MCS composition. The team brings together cryo-electron microscopists with quantitative tomogram analysis expertise, mass spectrometry proteomicists, lipidomics specialists, and computational biologists experienced in multi-modal data integration. We will develop a controlled vocabulary for MCS types (ER-mitochondria, ER-PM, ER-LD, mitochondria-LD, peroxisome-mitochondria, lysosome-mitochondria), harmonize proximity-proteomics datasets to a common reference proteome and confidence framework, and build a queryable atlas linking ultrastructural features to molecular composition. Statistical models will partition MCS variance into universal versus cell-type-specific components and test whether contact-site composition predicts inter-organelle functional outcomes such as calcium transfer rates or lipid flux. The deliverables include (1) a federated MCS atlas with standardized annotations, (2) statistical rulebooks for compositional regularities across cell types, (3) testable predictions about MCS roles in tissue-specific physiology, and (4) open analysis pipelines for harmonizing future MCS datasets. NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis requires harmonization of structural, proteomic, and lipidomic data archives that no single lab maintains, and demands ontological work that benefits from community input. The training plan supports five trainees—graduate students and postdocs with backgrounds spanning structural biology, mass spectrometry, and computational biology—who will receive formal training in cross-modal data integration, ontology development, and reproducible workflow management through Snakemake or Nextflow. Trainees will co-author a community standards document on MCS data reporting, providing them with experience in standards development that is rare in graduate training. All harmonized datasets and analysis code will be deposited in BioImage Archive, ProteomeXchange, and MetaboLights with cross-archive linking, and the rulebook will be released as both a publication and a continuously updated wiki. The broader significance lies in establishing MCSs as a tractable mesoscale system for synthesis research and in providing infrastructure for studying contact-site dysfunction in disease. By revealing whether MCSs follow universal rules or are cell-type-tuned, this project will resolve a foundational question about how compartmental boundaries are organized at the mesoscale.
background_and_significance:
Membrane contact sites (MCSs) represent a paradigmatic example of mesoscale biological organization, where emergent properties arise from the coordinated assembly of proteins, lipids, and organelles at nanometer-scale inter-membrane junctions. These specialized zones—typically 10-30 nm gaps between apposing organelle membranes—serve as platforms for non-vesicular lipid transfer, calcium signaling, organelle inheritance, and metabolic channeling. The past decade has witnessed explosive growth in our understanding of individual MCS components, including tethering proteins (e.g., VAPs, PTPIP51, MFN2), lipid transfer proteins (e.g., OSBP, ORP family members, VPS13), and regulatory factors. However, a fundamental question remains unresolved: do MCSs follow universal compositional rules conserved across cell types, or does each tissue deploy unique molecular architectures tailored to its physiological demands?

This question sits at the heart of mesoscale biology because MCSs exemplify how cellular function emerges from the spatial organization of molecular components. Unlike membrane-bound organelles with well-defined boundaries, MCSs are dynamic assemblies whose composition likely reflects both universal biophysical constraints and cell-type-specific functional requirements. Understanding the rules governing MCS composition would illuminate broader principles of how cells organize their internal architecture at scales between individual molecules and organelles—precisely the mesoscale domain that NCEMS prioritizes.

The significance of this question extends beyond basic cell biology. MCS dysfunction has been implicated in neurodegeneration (Parkinson's disease, ALS, Alzheimer's disease), metabolic disorders (diabetes, obesity), and cancer. Yet therapeutic targeting of MCSs remains impossible without understanding which components are universally essential versus tissue-specific. For example, ER-mitochondria contact sites in neurons may require distinct tethering complexes compared to those in hepatocytes, reflecting different demands for calcium buffering versus lipid synthesis.

Despite the importance of this question, it has resisted resolution for three reasons. First, relevant data exist in disconnected archives: cryo-electron tomography reconstructions in EMPIAR, proximity proteomics datasets in PRIDE/ProteomeXchange, and lipidomic atlases in MetaboLights and Metabolomics Workbench. Second, these datasets use incompatible annotation schemes—structural biologists describe MCSs by morphological criteria (membrane distance, contact area), while proteomicists use bait-prey relationships, and lipidomicists employ tissue-centric classifications. Third, the synthesis challenge exceeds individual laboratory capabilities because it requires expertise spanning structural biology, mass spectrometry, lipidomics, and computational biology.

The timing for this synthesis is optimal. EMPIAR now contains over 200 cryo-electron tomography datasets from diverse cell types, many with segmented organelles. Multiple laboratories have published organelle-targeted proximity proteomics studies (BioID, APEX, TurboID) for mitochondria, ER, lipid droplets, peroxisomes, and lysosomes across cell lines and primary tissues. Comprehensive lipidomic atlases now cover dozens of human tissues and cell types. Critically, these datasets have never been systematically integrated because the harmonization challenge requires community-scale effort.

This Working Group will address this gap by creating the first federated MCS atlas that links ultrastructural features to molecular composition across cell types. By revealing universal versus cell-type-specific MCS rules, we will establish foundational principles for mesoscale organization and provide a template for synthesis research on other subcellular structures. The project directly addresses NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale through community-scale data synthesis.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group is organized around three interconnected research questions that address fundamental aspects of MCS organization at the mesoscale:

**Research Question 1: What is the universal molecular core of each MCS type?**

We hypothesize that each MCS type (ER-mitochondria, ER-PM, ER-lipid droplet, mitochondria-lipid droplet, peroxisome-mitochondria, lysosome-mitochondria) contains a conserved set of core proteins and lipids that are present regardless of cell type, reflecting fundamental biophysical requirements for membrane tethering and functional coupling. We predict this core comprises 15-30% of total MCS components, with the remainder being cell-type-variable. This hypothesis is testable by identifying proteins and lipids consistently enriched at each MCS type across all cell types in our harmonized datasets. The null hypothesis—that MCS composition is entirely cell-type-specific—would be rejected if we identify statistically significant compositional invariants across diverse cellular contexts.

**Research Question 2: How does MCS composition scale with cell-type-specific physiological demands?**

We hypothesize that cell-type-specific MCS components correlate with tissue-specific functional demands. Specifically, we predict: (a) neurons will show enrichment of calcium-handling proteins at ER-mitochondria contacts compared to other cell types, reflecting high calcium signaling demands; (b) hepatocytes will display enhanced lipid transfer machinery at ER-lipid droplet contacts, consistent with their role in lipid metabolism; (c) secretory cells will exhibit expanded ER-PM contact proteomes supporting regulated exocytosis. These predictions generate testable correlations between cell-type metadata (secretory capacity, metabolic rate, calcium signaling intensity) and MCS molecular composition. We will use variance partitioning approaches to quantify the fraction of compositional variance explained by cell type, tissue of origin, and metabolic state.

**Research Question 3: Can MCS molecular composition predict functional outcomes?**

We hypothesize that MCS composition—specifically the stoichiometry of tethering, transfer, and regulatory proteins—predicts inter-organelle functional coupling. We will test whether: (a) the abundance ratio of calcium-handling proteins (e.g., IP3R, VDAC, MCU) at ER-mitochondria contacts correlates with published calcium transfer rates; (b) lipid transfer protein abundance at ER-lipid droplet contacts predicts lipid flux measurements from published metabolic labeling studies; (c) ultrastructural features (contact area, membrane distance) extracted from tomograms correlate with molecular composition from proteomics. This question tests whether synthesis of multi-modal data can generate predictive models linking mesoscale organization to function.

**Methodological Hypothesis: Ontology harmonization enables cross-modal integration.**

A key methodological hypothesis is that developing a controlled vocabulary for MCS types, combined with mapping datasets to common reference proteomes and lipidomes, will enable meaningful integration of heterogeneous data sources. We predict that harmonization will reveal patterns invisible in individual datasets and will establish best practices for future MCS data reporting. This hypothesis is tested by comparing statistical power and pattern detection before and after harmonization.

**Exploratory Questions:**

Beyond these primary hypotheses, we will explore: (1) whether MCS composition shows phylogenetic conservation patterns suggesting evolutionary constraints; (2) whether disease-associated mutations in MCS proteins cluster in universal versus cell-type-specific components; (3) whether MCS types show compositional correlations suggesting functional interdependence (e.g., do cells with expanded ER-mitochondria contacts also show altered ER-lipid droplet contacts?).

These questions are ideally suited for synthesis research because they require integration across data modalities and cell types that no single laboratory can achieve. The hypotheses generate specific, testable predictions that will advance our understanding of mesoscale organization principles.
methods_and_approach:
**Phase 1: Data Inventory and Ontology Development (Months 1-6)**

We will conduct systematic surveys of EMPIAR, ProteomeXchange/PRIDE, MetaboLights, and Metabolomics Workbench to identify datasets containing MCS-relevant information. For cryo-ET data, we will catalog datasets with segmented organelles where MCS regions can be identified. For proteomics, we will identify organelle-targeted proximity labeling studies (BioID, APEX, TurboID) across cell types. For lipidomics, we will compile tissue and cell-type atlases with organelle-resolved or subcellular fractionation data.

Simultaneously, we will develop a controlled vocabulary for MCS types through community consultation. This ontology will define: (a) MCS type classifications based on participating organelles; (b) ultrastructural descriptors (membrane distance, contact area, curvature); (c) molecular component categories (tethers, transfer proteins, regulators); (d) functional annotations (calcium handling, lipid transfer, signaling). The ontology will be developed using OBO Foundry principles and integrated with existing ontologies (GO, CL, UBERON).

**Phase 2: Data Harmonization and Atlas Construction (Months 4-12)**

Proteomics harmonization will map all datasets to UniProt reference proteomes with consistent gene naming. We will develop a confidence framework scoring protein-MCS associations based on: enrichment over controls, reproducibility across studies, and orthogonal validation. Proximity labeling artifacts (sticky proteins, abundant contaminants) will be flagged using established filtering approaches.

Lipidomics harmonization will standardize lipid nomenclature using LIPID MAPS classification and map measurements to common quantification units. We will integrate organelle-resolved lipidomics where available and develop imputation strategies for missing data using matrix factorization approaches.

Structural data integration will extract quantitative features from cryo-ET tomograms: membrane distances, contact areas, and morphological descriptors. We will use existing segmentations where available and develop semi-automated pipelines for additional annotation using deep learning tools (e.g., nnU-Net, Membrain-seg).

The federated atlas will be implemented as a queryable database linking: cell type → MCS type → ultrastructural features → protein composition → lipid composition. Cross-archive linking will use persistent identifiers enabling provenance tracking.

**Phase 3: Statistical Modeling and Rule Derivation (Months 10-18)**

We will apply variance partitioning (PERMANOVA, distance-based redundancy analysis) to quantify contributions of MCS type, cell type, and their interaction to compositional variance. Universal components will be identified as those with low cell-type variance and high MCS-type specificity.

Machine learning approaches (random forests, gradient boosting) will identify compositional features predicting functional outcomes. We will use cross-validation with held-out cell types to assess generalizability. Network analysis will identify co-varying protein modules suggesting functional relationships.

**Phase 4: Validation and Prediction Generation (Months 16-24)**

We will generate testable predictions about: (a) MCS composition in cell types not yet studied by proximity proteomics; (b) functional consequences of perturbing universal versus cell-type-specific components; (c) disease phenotypes expected from mutations in different MCS component classes. These predictions will be documented for experimental testing by the broader community.

**Computational Infrastructure:**

All analyses will be implemented in reproducible workflows using Snakemake/Nextflow with containerized environments (Docker/Singularity). We will leverage NCEMS computational resources for large-scale data processing and model training.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
**Deliverable 1: Federated MCS Atlas**

The primary deliverable is a queryable atlas integrating ultrastructural, proteomic, and lipidomic data for six major MCS types across available cell types. This resource will enable researchers to query: "What proteins are enriched at ER-mitochondria contacts in neurons versus hepatocytes?" or "How does lipid composition at ER-lipid droplet contacts vary across tissues?" The atlas will be hosted with persistent identifiers and programmatic access via REST API.

**Deliverable 2: MCS Compositional Rulebook**

We will publish statistical rules describing: (a) universal core components for each MCS type; (b) cell-type-specific compositional signatures; (c) quantitative relationships between composition and ultrastructure. This rulebook will be released as a peer-reviewed publication and a continuously updated wiki enabling community refinement.

**Deliverable 3: Testable Predictions**

The project will generate 50+ specific, testable predictions about MCS composition and function, documented with confidence scores and suggested experimental approaches. These predictions will guide future experimental studies and provide benchmarks for validating our synthesis approach.

**Deliverable 4: Community Standards and Pipelines**

We will release: (a) MCS ontology integrated with OBO Foundry; (b) data reporting standards for MCS studies; (c) open-source pipelines for harmonizing future datasets. These resources will establish infrastructure for ongoing MCS research.

**Scientific Impact:**

This project will resolve the fundamental question of whether MCS organization follows universal rules or is cell-type-tuned, establishing principles for mesoscale biology. The atlas will accelerate MCS research by providing integrated resources currently unavailable. Predictions about disease-relevant MCS components will inform therapeutic development.

**Training Impact:**

Five trainees will gain expertise in cross-modal data integration, ontology development, and reproducible science—skills increasingly essential for modern biology but rarely taught in traditional programs. Trainee co-authorship on standards documents provides unique professional development.

**Community Impact:**

By demonstrating successful synthesis of heterogeneous MCS data, this project establishes a template for similar efforts on other mesoscale structures (phase-separated condensates, cytoskeletal assemblies), amplifying NCEMS's impact on the field.

This Working Group is fundamentally committed to open science, recognizing that synthesis research derives its power from community accessibility. All project outputs will be freely available without restriction, following FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable).

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Unified Dynamical Model of TAD Emergence Across Hi-C, Imaging, and Perturbation Data
abstract: Topologically associating domains (TADs) are emergent features of three-dimensional chromatin organization, but the field has struggled to reconcile static population-averaged Hi-C maps with dynamic single-cell imaging observations and the complex effects of cohesin and CTCF perturbations. Existing models typically fit one data type at a time, leaving the underlying dynamical principles unclear. This Working Group will synthesize Hi-C and micro-C data from the 4DN consortium, ENCODE, and individual high-resolution studies; live-cell chromatin imaging datasets from publications and consortium repositories; and perturbation atlases targeting cohesin subunits, CTCF, WAPL, and NIPBL, to construct the first unified dynamical model that simultaneously fits population contact frequencies and single-cell trajectory data under shared perturbation conditions. The team integrates polymer physicists, chromatin biologists, live-imaging specialists, and machine-learning researchers experienced in neural ordinary differential equations and stochastic dynamical systems. We will develop a parameterized loop-extrusion-plus-compartmentalization model with cell-type-specific parameters inferred jointly from contact maps and imaging trajectories, then test whether the same parameters predict perturbation responses observed in independent datasets. Bayesian inference will quantify parameter uncertainty and identify regimes where current data cannot distinguish among competing models, providing a roadmap for future experimental investment. Deliverables include (1) a unified dynamical model with open-source simulation code, (2) harmonized chromatin perturbation datasets across modalities, (3) quantitative reconciliation of static and dynamic measurements, and (4) identification of remaining data gaps. NCEMS support is essential because integration across Hi-C, imaging, and perturbation archives requires sustained interdisciplinary effort beyond any single lab's capacity, and because dynamical inference at this scale demands shared computational infrastructure. The training plan supports four graduate students and two postdocs through cross-lab rotations, with formal training in polymer physics, single-cell imaging analysis, and probabilistic programming using PyMC or Stan. Trainees will lead sub-projects on specific perturbation conditions and contribute to a methods paper on multimodal dynamical inference. All code will be released under permissive licenses, simulations will be reproducible via containerized workflows, and the inferred models will be deployable as web services that researchers can query with their own data. By unifying contact-frequency and imaging measurements under a single mechanistic framework, this project addresses a long-standing puzzle in chromatin biology and demonstrates how synthesis research can resolve disputes that have persisted because no single experimental modality is sufficient. The broader impact includes implications for understanding gene regulation in development and disease, where TAD disruption is increasingly implicated in pathology.
background_and_significance:
The three-dimensional organization of chromatin within the nucleus represents a quintessential example of biological emergence at the mesoscale. Topologically associating domains (TADs) are megabase-scale genomic regions within which chromatin contacts occur more frequently than between adjacent domains. Since their discovery in 2012 through chromosome conformation capture technologies, TADs have been implicated in gene regulation, DNA replication timing, and disease-associated genomic rearrangements. However, a fundamental disconnect persists in our understanding of TAD biology that has hindered progress for over a decade.

Hi-C and micro-C experiments capture population-averaged contact frequencies, revealing TADs as sharp boundaries in contact probability matrices. These static snapshots suggest stable, well-defined domains. In stark contrast, live-cell imaging studies tracking fluorescently labeled genomic loci reveal highly dynamic chromatin motion, with loci frequently crossing apparent TAD boundaries on timescales of minutes to hours. This apparent contradiction—stable population structures versus dynamic single-cell behavior—represents a long-standing puzzle that the field has failed to resolve because investigators typically analyze one data modality in isolation.

The mechanistic basis of TAD formation centers on the loop extrusion model, wherein cohesin complexes actively extrude chromatin loops until blocked by CTCF proteins bound at convergent motifs. Perturbation experiments depleting cohesin subunits (RAD21, SMC3), CTCF, or regulators like WAPL and NIPBL produce complex phenotypes that existing models struggle to explain comprehensively. Cohesin depletion eliminates TADs in Hi-C maps but has surprisingly modest effects on gene expression, while WAPL depletion produces extended loops beyond normal TAD boundaries. These perturbation responses provide critical constraints for mechanistic models but have never been systematically integrated across experimental modalities.

The significance of resolving this puzzle extends beyond basic chromatin biology. TAD boundary disruptions are increasingly recognized in cancer, developmental disorders, and congenital limb malformations. Understanding the dynamical principles governing TAD emergence is essential for predicting how structural variants affect gene regulation and for developing therapeutic strategies targeting chromatin organization.

This project addresses NCEMS's core mission by tackling emergence at the mesoscale—the level between individual protein-DNA interactions and nuclear-scale organization. TADs emerge from the collective behavior of loop-extruding cohesin complexes, boundary-forming CTCF proteins, and the polymer physics of chromatin fibers. No single molecular interaction explains TAD formation; rather, TADs are emergent properties arising from the interplay of multiple factors across spatial and temporal scales.

The synthesis approach is essential because the relevant data exist across disconnected repositories and publications. The 4D Nucleome consortium has generated extensive Hi-C and imaging datasets, ENCODE provides chromatin accessibility and protein binding data, and numerous individual studies have published perturbation experiments. However, no systematic effort has integrated these resources under a unified modeling framework. This integration requires expertise spanning polymer physics, chromatin biology, advanced imaging analysis, and machine learning—a combination unavailable in any single laboratory. NCEMS support enables the sustained, collaborative effort necessary to harmonize these diverse datasets and develop the computational infrastructure for joint dynamical inference.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses four interconnected research questions that collectively aim to resolve the apparent contradiction between static Hi-C measurements and dynamic imaging observations of chromatin organization.

Research Question 1: Can a single parameterized dynamical model simultaneously reproduce population-averaged Hi-C contact frequencies and single-cell chromatin trajectory statistics?

Hypothesis 1: A loop-extrusion model with compartmentalization interactions, parameterized by cohesin loading rate, processivity, CTCF blocking probability, and compartment interaction strengths, can quantitatively fit both Hi-C contact maps and single-cell mean-squared displacement curves, velocity autocorrelation functions, and boundary-crossing frequencies when parameters are inferred jointly from both data types. We hypothesize that apparent contradictions arise from comparing ensemble averages (Hi-C) with single-molecule dynamics (imaging) without proper statistical treatment, and that a unified model will reveal these measurements as complementary rather than contradictory.

Research Question 2: Do the dynamical parameters inferred from wild-type data predict the quantitative effects of cohesin, CTCF, WAPL, and NIPBL perturbations on both contact frequencies and chromatin dynamics?

Hypothesis 2: If our unified model captures the true mechanistic basis of TAD formation, parameters inferred from wild-type data should predict perturbation phenotypes without refitting. Specifically, we hypothesize that: (a) reducing cohesin loading rate will predict the Hi-C and imaging phenotypes of RAD21/SMC3 depletion; (b) reducing CTCF blocking probability will predict CTCF degradation effects; (c) increasing cohesin processivity will predict WAPL depletion phenotypes; and (d) reducing loading rate while maintaining processivity will predict NIPBL haploinsufficiency. Failures of prediction will identify missing model components or parameter dependencies.

Research Question 3: What is the minimal model complexity required to explain multimodal chromatin organization data, and where do current data fail to distinguish between competing mechanistic hypotheses?

Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that current publicly available data are sufficient to constrain core loop extrusion parameters (loading rate, processivity, blocking probability) but insufficient to resolve secondary mechanisms including: (a) the role of transcription-driven supercoiling in loop extrusion dynamics; (b) the contribution of phase separation to compartmentalization; and (c) the effects of chromatin fiber flexibility variations. Bayesian model comparison will identify these underdetermined regimes, providing a quantitative roadmap for future experimental investment.

Research Question 4: How do cell-type-specific differences in TAD organization emerge from variations in the underlying dynamical parameters?

Hypothesis 4: Cell-type-specific TAD patterns arise primarily from differences in CTCF binding site occupancy and compartment interaction strengths rather than from changes in core loop extrusion machinery parameters. We hypothesize that cohesin loading rate and processivity are relatively constant across cell types, while CTCF blocking probability at specific sites and A/B compartment interaction strengths vary according to cell-type-specific transcription factor binding and histone modification patterns. This hypothesis predicts that a model trained on one cell type can predict TAD organization in another cell type given only CTCF ChIP-seq and histone modification data.

These questions are specifically designed for synthesis research: answering them requires integrating Hi-C, imaging, and perturbation data that no single laboratory has generated comprehensively. The hypotheses are falsifiable through quantitative comparison of model predictions with held-out datasets, and negative results will be equally informative by identifying gaps in current mechanistic understanding.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates data harmonization, dynamical modeling, Bayesian inference, and systematic validation across three phases over the two-year project period.

Phase 1: Data Harmonization and Quality Control (Months 1-8)
We will systematically catalog and harmonize publicly available datasets across three modalities. For Hi-C/micro-C data, we will retrieve raw sequencing data from 4DN, ENCODE, and GEO, reprocessing all datasets through a standardized pipeline (distiller-nf) to generate contact matrices at matched resolutions (1kb, 5kb, 25kb). We will compile metadata on cell types, growth conditions, and perturbation treatments to enable cross-study comparison. For imaging data, we will collect published single-cell chromatin tracking datasets, including MS2/PP7 tagging studies, ANCHOR/ParB systems, and CRISPR-based live imaging. We will extract trajectory statistics including mean-squared displacement, velocity autocorrelation, and inter-locus distance distributions. For perturbation data, we will build a comprehensive atlas of cohesin (RAD21, SMC1A, SMC3), CTCF, WAPL, and NIPBL perturbation experiments across modalities, annotating depletion efficiency, timepoints, and cell types. Quality control will flag datasets with technical artifacts, and all harmonized data will be deposited in a structured database with standardized metadata schemas.

Phase 2: Unified Dynamical Model Development (Months 6-18)
We will develop a parameterized polymer simulation framework combining loop extrusion and compartmentalization. The model represents chromatin as a bead-spring polymer with cohesin complexes that load stochastically, extrude bidirectionally, and unload upon CTCF encounter or spontaneous dissociation. Compartmentalization is implemented through attractive interactions between beads of matching epigenetic state (A-A or B-B attractions). Key parameters include: cohesin loading rate (k_load), processivity (mean extrusion distance before unloading), CTCF blocking probability (p_block), and compartment interaction strength (ε_comp).

For efficient simulation, we will implement the model using OpenMM for GPU-accelerated molecular dynamics, with custom force terms for loop extrusion. To enable Bayesian inference, we will develop differentiable surrogate models using neural ordinary differential equations (neural ODEs) trained on simulation outputs, enabling gradient-based optimization of posterior distributions.

Phase 3: Joint Inference and Validation (Months 12-24)
Bayesian inference will estimate posterior distributions over model parameters given multimodal data. We will define likelihood functions for Hi-C data (comparing simulated and experimental contact probabilities), imaging data (comparing trajectory statistics), and perturbation responses (comparing fold-changes in contacts and dynamics). Inference will use Hamiltonian Monte Carlo implemented in PyMC or Stan, with neural ODE surrogates enabling tractable gradient computation.

Validation follows a rigorous held-out testing protocol. We will train models on 70% of available datasets and evaluate predictions on the remaining 30%, stratified by cell type and perturbation condition. Model comparison will use Bayesian information criteria and posterior predictive checks. We will specifically test whether parameters inferred from wild-type data predict perturbation phenotypes without refitting.

The computational infrastructure requires high-performance computing for polymer simulations and inference. We will leverage NCEMS computational resources and develop containerized workflows (Docker/Singularity) ensuring reproducibility. All code will be developed collaboratively on GitHub with continuous integration testing.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:

We will release an open-source simulation package implementing the loop-extrusion-plus-compartmentalization model with validated parameters for multiple cell types. The software will include GPU-accelerated simulation code, neural ODE surrogate models for rapid parameter exploration, and Bayesian inference pipelines. This resource will enable researchers to predict chromatin organization from sequence and epigenetic features, test mechanistic hypotheses, and design perturbation experiments.

By demonstrating that a single model explains both Hi-C and imaging measurements, we will resolve a decade-long puzzle in chromatin biology. This conceptual advance will reshape how the field interprets chromatin organization data and designs experiments.

Broader impacts include advancing understanding of gene regulation in development and disease. TAD disruptions are implicated in limb malformations, cancer, and neurological disorders; our model will enable prediction of structural variant effects on chromatin organization. The project demonstrates synthesis research methodology applicable to other mesoscale emergence questions, establishing templates for multimodal data integration that NCEMS can promote across the molecular and cellular sciences.

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Resolving the Specialized-Ribosome Hypothesis Through Multi-Modal Data Synthesis
abstract: The specialized-ribosome hypothesis—that compositionally distinct ribosomes preferentially translate distinct mRNA classes—has remained contested for over a decade because no single laboratory possesses the combined ribosome profiling, structural biology, and quantitative proteomics resources needed to test it definitively. This Working Group will synthesize public ribo-seq datasets (GWIPS-viz, Trips-Viz), ribosome structural variants from EMDB and PDB, ribosomal protein and rRNA modification atlases, and condition-resolved proteomics to perform the first synthesis-scale test of specialized translation. The team brings together ribosome structural biologists, ribosome profiling experts, mass spectrometrists with quantitative ribosome composition expertise, and computational biologists specializing in differential translation analysis. We will harmonize ribo-seq experiments across ~200 conditions and tissues, controlling for technical variation; map ribosomal protein and rRNA modification stoichiometries from public proteomics and CLIP datasets; and align these compositional measurements with translational efficiency profiles for specific mRNA classes. Statistical models will test whether compositional variation predicts translational selectivity beyond what is expected from generic abundance and codon-usage effects. Critically, the synthesis will also identify experimental gaps where the specialized-ribosome hypothesis cannot currently be tested with available data, guiding future experimental work. Deliverables include (1) a harmonized ribo-seq atlas with consistent processing across hundreds of studies, (2) a quantitative ribosome compositional landscape integrating structural and proteomic measurements, (3) statistical evaluation of specialization claims with calibrated uncertainty, and (4) a community resource enabling future tests of translation-specialization hypotheses. NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis spans data types and communities (translation, structural biology, proteomics) that rarely interact, and because ribo-seq harmonization at this scale requires sustained computational infrastructure. The training plan supports six trainees with backgrounds in molecular biology, structural biology, and computational genomics through coordinated sub-projects, formal training in ribo-seq analysis, structural data integration, and reproducible bioinformatics, and joint mentoring across institutions. Trainees will co-lead the harmonized atlas paper and contribute first-author analyses on specific organisms or tissue contexts. All harmonized data and analysis code will be released through Zenodo with versioned DOIs, the atlas will be queryable through a public web portal, and standards developed for ribo-seq harmonization will be proposed to the relevant data archives. By resolving—or definitively framing—the specialized-ribosome hypothesis, this Working Group will address a long-standing puzzle that exemplifies why molecular biology needs synthesis-scale approaches: questions whose resolution has been obstructed not by missing data but by data fragmentation across labs and modalities.
background_and_significance:
Ribosomes have long been considered homogeneous molecular machines that translate mRNAs with uniform efficiency determined primarily by codon usage and mRNA abundance. However, the specialized-ribosome hypothesis, first systematically articulated over a decade ago, challenges this paradigm by proposing that ribosomes with distinct compositions—varying in ribosomal protein (RP) paralogs, post-translational modifications, and rRNA modifications—preferentially translate specific mRNA subsets. This hypothesis represents a fundamental question about how cells achieve translational regulation and represents an emergent property at the mesoscale: how molecular heterogeneity at the ribosome level gives rise to selective cellular outcomes.

Evidence supporting ribosome specialization has accumulated from multiple directions. Studies have demonstrated tissue-specific expression of RP paralogs, with RPL3L and RPL10L showing restricted expression patterns in muscle and testis, respectively. Mutations in specific RPs cause tissue-selective pathologies (ribosomopathies) such as Diamond-Blackfan anemia and isolated congenital asplenia, suggesting non-redundant functions. Quantitative proteomics has revealed substoichiometric incorporation of certain RPs, and rRNA modifications show developmental and tissue-specific patterns. Furthermore, ribosome profiling studies have reported preferential translation of specific mRNA classes by compositionally distinct ribosomes, including IRES-containing mRNAs and transcripts encoding developmental regulators.

Despite this evidence, the specialized-ribosome hypothesis remains contested. Critics argue that observed translational differences could arise from technical artifacts in ribosome profiling, secondary effects of altered ribosome biogenesis, or confounding variables such as mRNA localization and timing of expression. The fundamental problem is that definitive testing requires integration of three data types rarely combined: (1) ribosome profiling data measuring translational efficiency across conditions, (2) quantitative compositional measurements of ribosome populations, and (3) structural data linking compositional variants to functional consequences. No single laboratory possesses expertise and resources spanning these domains.

The scientific significance of resolving this hypothesis extends far beyond academic debate. If specialized ribosomes exist, they represent a previously underappreciated layer of gene expression regulation with implications for development, disease, and evolution. Cancer cells might exploit ribosome specialization to selectively translate oncogenic mRNAs. Developmental programs might deploy tissue-specific ribosomes to establish cell identity. Conversely, if specialization claims cannot withstand rigorous synthesis-scale analysis, the field can redirect efforts toward alternative regulatory mechanisms.

This question exemplifies the NCEMS mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale. Ribosome specialization, if real, represents emergence: individual molecular variations (RP paralogs, modifications) combining to produce selective translational outcomes not predictable from components alone. The hypothesis has remained unresolved not because data are lacking—thousands of ribo-seq datasets, hundreds of ribosome structures, and extensive proteomic measurements exist publicly—but because these data remain fragmented across communities that rarely interact. This Working Group will perform the first synthesis-scale integration of these resources, providing either definitive evidence for specialization or rigorous bounds on where such evidence is currently lacking, thereby resolving a long-standing puzzle central to molecular and cellular biology.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses one overarching question: Does ribosome compositional heterogeneity predict mRNA-specific translational selectivity beyond what is expected from generic abundance and codon-usage effects? We decompose this into four testable research questions with specific hypotheses.

**Research Question 1: Can ribosome profiling data be harmonized across studies to enable synthesis-scale analysis of translational efficiency?**

Hypothesis 1: Technical variation across ribo-seq studies—arising from library preparation methods, sequencing depth, and computational processing—can be systematically quantified and controlled through meta-analytic frameworks, enabling meaningful comparison of translational efficiency estimates across ~200 conditions and tissues.

Rationale: Previous attempts to compare ribo-seq studies have been confounded by batch effects and methodological heterogeneity. We hypothesize that explicit modeling of technical covariates, combined with standardized reprocessing from raw data, will reveal biological signal obscured in individual studies.

**Research Question 2: What is the quantitative landscape of ribosome compositional heterogeneity across tissues, conditions, and organisms?**

Hypothesis 2: Integration of quantitative proteomics, rRNA modification mapping (from CLIP and mass spectrometry datasets), and structural data will reveal systematic patterns of ribosome compositional variation that correlate with tissue identity and cellular state, rather than representing stochastic noise.

Rationale: Individual studies have reported compositional variation, but no systematic atlas exists. We hypothesize that synthesis across datasets will reveal conserved compositional signatures associated with specific biological contexts, providing the foundation for testing functional consequences.

**Research Question 3: Does ribosome compositional variation predict translational selectivity for specific mRNA classes?**

Hypothesis 3: After controlling for mRNA abundance, codon usage, mRNA structure, and technical confounders, ribosome compositional signatures will show statistically significant associations with translational efficiency for defined mRNA classes (e.g., IRES-containing, TOP-motif, developmental regulators).

Alternative Hypothesis 3: Apparent associations between ribosome composition and translational selectivity will be explained by confounding variables, suggesting that specialization claims require reevaluation or that current data are insufficient to test the hypothesis.

Rationale: This is the central test. We will develop statistical models that explicitly partition variance in translational efficiency into components attributable to composition versus confounders, with calibrated uncertainty estimates.

**Research Question 4: Where are the critical data gaps that prevent definitive testing of the specialized-ribosome hypothesis?**

Hypothesis 4: Systematic analysis will identify specific organism-tissue-condition combinations where compositional and translational data are both available with sufficient quality, versus combinations where data gaps preclude hypothesis testing, thereby guiding future experimental priorities.

Rationale: A rigorous synthesis must acknowledge limitations. We hypothesize that mapping data availability against hypothesis requirements will reveal that some specialization claims are currently untestable, providing a roadmap for the field.

**Methodological Innovation Questions:**

Beyond biological hypotheses, we address methodological questions essential for synthesis research: What standards enable cross-study ribo-seq comparison? How should structural and proteomic data be integrated with functional measurements? What statistical frameworks appropriately handle the hierarchical, multi-modal nature of these data?

These questions align directly with NCEMS goals: they address a fundamental puzzle in molecular biology through synthesis, require integration across data types and communities, and will generate resources enabling future hypothesis testing. The explicit framing of alternative hypotheses ensures that negative results—demonstrating that current data cannot resolve the hypothesis—are equally valuable, preventing publication bias and guiding experimental priorities.
methods_and_approach:
Our synthesis approach integrates four complementary data streams through a coordinated analytical framework designed for reproducibility and extensibility.

**Phase 1: Ribo-seq Data Harmonization (Months 1-12)**

We will systematically retrieve raw ribo-seq data from GWIPS-viz, Trips-Viz, GEO, and SRA, targeting ~200 datasets spanning human, mouse, yeast, and zebrafish across developmental stages, tissues, and perturbations. All datasets will be reprocessed through a unified pipeline: adapter trimming (cutadapt), quality filtering, alignment to reference genomes (STAR), and P-site offset calibration using established algorithms. Translational efficiency will be calculated as ribosome footprint density normalized to mRNA abundance from matched RNA-seq.

Critically, we will implement a meta-analytic framework to model technical variation. Using ComBat-seq for batch correction and mixed-effects models treating study as a random effect, we will estimate and remove technical variance while preserving biological signal. Quality metrics will flag datasets unsuitable for synthesis. The harmonized atlas will include standardized translational efficiency estimates, confidence intervals, and quality annotations for each gene-condition combination.

**Phase 2: Ribosome Compositional Landscape Construction (Months 6-18)**

We will integrate three data types to construct a quantitative compositional landscape:

(1) *Proteomic data*: Mining PRIDE, MassIVE, and published supplementary materials for quantitative measurements of RP stoichiometry across conditions. We will standardize quantification approaches (iBAQ, TMT ratios) and propagate measurement uncertainty.

(2) *rRNA modification data*: Integrating Nm-seq, Pseudo-seq, and CLIP datasets to map modification sites and estimate stoichiometries. Structural data from PDB/EMDB will provide atomic-resolution context for modification positions.

(3) *Structural variants*: Cataloging ribosome structures with compositional annotations, mapping RP paralog positions, and identifying modification sites with potential functional consequences based on structural context.

Data integration will use a Bayesian hierarchical framework that accounts for measurement uncertainty across modalities, producing posterior distributions for compositional parameters rather than point estimates.

**Phase 3: Statistical Testing of Specialization (Months 12-24)**

The core analysis tests whether compositional variation predicts translational selectivity. We will implement multilevel regression models:

TE_ij = β₀ + β₁(Composition_j) + β₂(Codon_usage_i) + β₃(mRNA_abundance_i) + β₄(Structure_i) + γ_study + ε_ij

where TE_ij is translational efficiency for gene i in condition j, Composition_j captures ribosome compositional features, and confounders are explicitly modeled. We will use Bayesian inference (Stan) to estimate posterior distributions for β₁, testing whether compositional effects are credibly different from zero.

For mRNA class-specific analyses, we will test interactions between composition and mRNA features (IRES presence, TOP motifs, developmental gene ontology). Permutation-based approaches will establish null distributions, and false discovery rate correction will address multiple testing.

**Phase 4: Gap Analysis and Resource Development (Months 18-24)**

We will systematically map data availability against hypothesis requirements, identifying organism-tissue-condition combinations with sufficient data quality for definitive testing versus those requiring future experimentation. This gap analysis will be formalized as a queryable resource guiding experimental priorities.

**Computational Infrastructure:**

Analyses will leverage NCEMS computational resources, with workflows implemented in Snakemake/Nextflow for reproducibility. All code will be version-controlled (GitHub) with containerized environments (Docker/Singularity) ensuring computational reproducibility.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will deliver four major outcomes with lasting impact on molecular and cellular biology.

**Outcome 1: Harmonized Ribo-seq Atlas**
The first synthesis-scale, consistently processed ribo-seq resource covering ~200 conditions across four organisms. This atlas will provide standardized translational efficiency estimates with quantified uncertainty, enabling meta-analyses previously impossible due to methodological heterogeneity.
