author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Allometric Scaling Laws of Subcellular Organelles Across Cell Types and Species
abstract: Metabolic scaling laws relate organism size to physiology with remarkable cross-species generality, but whether analogous laws govern subcellular organelle size, count, and connectivity remains untested at synthesis scale. Existing data on organelle morphometrics are scattered across electron microscopy archives, the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, cell atlases, and individual publications, with no harmonized resource for comparative analysis. This Working Group will synthesize quantitative organelle morphometric data across cell types, tissues, and species to derive empirical scaling laws relating organelle features to cell volume, ploidy, metabolic rate, and developmental stage. The team unites cell biologists with deep organelle expertise, electron microscopists experienced in segmentation of large volumes, comparative biologists with organism-spanning perspectives, and statistical modelers expert in allometric analysis. We will harmonize segmentation outputs from public EM volumes (OpenOrganelle, EMPIAR, CellMap), integrate them with HPA imaging-derived morphometrics and OpenCell organelle measurements, and add comparative data from non-model organisms where available. Phylogenetically informed regression will test for universal scaling exponents and identify cell types or organelles that systematically deviate. Deliverables include (1) the first cross-cellular, cross-species organelle morphometric database, (2) quantitative scaling laws for major organelles, (3) identification of outlier cell types where mesoscale architecture violates universal trends, and (4) testable hypotheses about why specific organelles scale as they do. NCEMS support is critical because the synthesis requires segmentation-tool harmonization, ontology development, and phylogenetic analysis spanning communities that rarely collaborate, and because the comparative scope demands archive-spanning infrastructure no single lab can maintain. The training plan supports five graduate students and postdocs through coordinated rotations, formal training in EM segmentation, allometric statistics, and phylogenetic comparative methods, and a cross-lab capstone project where each trainee leads scaling analysis for one organelle class. Trainees will participate in a journal club exposing them to scaling theory across biological scales and will co-author the resulting papers. All harmonized morphometric data will be released through Zenodo and the BioImage Archive with cross-references to source datasets, segmentation pipelines will be containerized and reproducible, and the scaling-law database will be available through a queryable web interface. The broader impact is foundational: establishing whether mesoscale architecture obeys universal scaling principles—or whether such principles even exist at this scale—will inform theoretical cell biology for decades. By demonstrating that cell biology can be approached with the comparative quantitative rigor of organismal allometry, this project will catalyze a new style of synthesis research at the mesoscale.
background_and_significance:
Allometric scaling laws represent one of biology's most profound organizing principles. Since Kleiber's discovery that metabolic rate scales with body mass raised to the three-quarter power across organisms spanning twenty orders of magnitude, scaling relationships have provided deep insights into the physical and evolutionary constraints shaping life. West, Brown, and Enquist's metabolic theory of ecology extended these principles to explain phenomena from forest structure to population dynamics, demonstrating that scaling laws emerge from fundamental constraints on resource distribution networks. Yet despite the transformative impact of organismal allometry, we lack equivalent understanding at the subcellular scale. Do organelles scale predictably with cell size? Are there universal exponents governing mitochondrial volume, endoplasmic reticulum surface area, or nuclear size across cell types and species? These questions address fundamental aspects of cellular organization but remain unanswered because the necessary comparative data have never been systematically synthesized.

The mesoscale—the organizational level between individual biomolecules and whole organelles—represents a critical frontier in cell biology and aligns directly with NCEMS's scientific vision. Emergent properties at this scale determine how cells allocate resources, maintain homeostasis, and respond to environmental challenges. Understanding whether universal scaling principles govern mesoscale architecture would transform our conceptual framework for cell biology, potentially revealing deep physical or evolutionary constraints analogous to those operating at organismal scales. Conversely, discovering that no such universal laws exist would itself be profound, suggesting that cellular organization is fundamentally more plastic or historically contingent than organismal form.

The significance of this synthesis project lies in its unprecedented scope and the maturation of publicly available data resources that make it feasible. Over the past decade, advances in volume electron microscopy have generated thousands of high-resolution cellular reconstructions deposited in archives including EMPIAR, OpenOrganelle, and CellMap. The Human Protein Atlas provides subcellular localization and morphometric data across human tissues. OpenCell offers systematic organelle measurements in human cells. Single-cell atlases increasingly include morphological parameters. Individually, these resources have advanced understanding of specific cell types or organelles. Collectively, they constitute an untapped resource for comparative cell biology—but only if harmonized through coordinated synthesis efforts.

No single laboratory possesses the expertise to execute this synthesis. The project requires deep knowledge of organelle biology, expertise in electron microscopy segmentation algorithms, familiarity with phylogenetic comparative methods, and statistical modeling skills for allometric analysis. Moreover, the data span archives maintained by different communities with distinct conventions for annotation, measurement, and metadata. NCEMS provides the unique infrastructure and collaborative framework necessary to bridge these communities and harmonize these resources.

The broader significance extends beyond establishing scaling laws per se. This project will demonstrate that cell biology can be approached with the same comparative quantitative rigor that transformed organismal biology. By creating the first cross-species organelle morphometric database and analytical framework, we will enable future synthesis research addressing questions we cannot yet anticipate. The identification of cell types or organelles that violate universal trends will generate testable hypotheses about the functional significance of mesoscale architecture, catalyzing new experimental investigations across the field.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses four interconnected research questions that together will establish whether universal scaling principles govern subcellular organization:

Research Question 1: Do organelle volumes scale predictably with cell volume, and if so, what are the scaling exponents?

Hypothesis 1a: Mitochondrial volume scales with cell volume with an exponent less than one (negative allometry), reflecting the decreased surface-area-to-volume ratio of larger cells and consequent reduced metabolic demand per unit volume. We predict an exponent of approximately 0.75, analogous to Kleiber's law, if similar network-based constraints operate at the subcellular scale.

Hypothesis 1b: Nuclear volume scales with cell volume with an exponent close to one (isometry), maintaining constant nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio as required for genome function. Deviations from isometry will correlate with ploidy changes.

Hypothesis 1c: Endoplasmic reticulum surface area scales with cell volume with an exponent greater than 0.67, reflecting the functional requirement for membrane surface area to exceed geometric expectations in secretory cells.

Research Question 2: Are scaling relationships conserved across species, or do lineage-specific patterns predominate?

Hypothesis 2a: Core metabolic organelles (mitochondria, peroxisomes) exhibit conserved scaling exponents across metazoans, reflecting fundamental biophysical constraints on energy metabolism that predate major phylogenetic divergences.

Hypothesis 2b: Secretory pathway organelles (ER, Golgi) show lineage-specific scaling relationships, reflecting adaptation to different secretory demands across taxa.

Hypothesis 2c: Phylogenetic signal in scaling residuals will identify clades where organelle architecture has undergone adaptive evolution, generating hypotheses about selective pressures shaping mesoscale organization.

Research Question 3: How do organelle number, size, and connectivity trade off within cells?

Hypothesis 3a: Cells maintain constant total organelle function through compensatory relationships between organelle number and individual organelle size. Specifically, mitochondrial number and mean mitochondrial volume will show negative covariation at constant cell volume.

Hypothesis 3b: Organelle network connectivity (measured through contact site frequency and morphological complexity) increases with cell volume, compensating for diffusion limitations in larger cells.

Hypothesis 3c: The transition between fragmented and networked organelle morphologies follows predictable thresholds related to cell volume and metabolic state.

Research Question 4: Which cell types systematically deviate from universal scaling relationships, and what biological factors explain these deviations?

Hypothesis 4a: Highly specialized cells (neurons, cardiomyocytes, adipocytes) will show systematic deviations from scaling relationships established in generic cell types, with deviation magnitude correlating with specialization degree.

Hypothesis 4b: Cells with extreme metabolic demands will show positive residuals for mitochondrial scaling; cells with extreme secretory demands will show positive residuals for ER/Golgi scaling.

Hypothesis 4c: Cancer cells will show disrupted scaling relationships compared to matched normal cells, potentially providing new morphometric biomarkers.

These hypotheses generate specific, testable predictions that will be evaluated through phylogenetically informed statistical analysis. The hierarchical structure—from individual organelles to cross-species comparisons—ensures that findings at each level inform interpretation at other levels. Importantly, rejection of these hypotheses would be equally informative, demonstrating that subcellular organization is not governed by the universal principles that characterize organismal allometry and requiring alternative theoretical frameworks for understanding mesoscale architecture.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises four integrated phases: data acquisition and harmonization, morphometric standardization, statistical analysis, and validation.

Phase 1: Data Acquisition and Harmonization (Months 1-8)
We will systematically survey and acquire organelle morphometric data from publicly available sources. Primary sources include: (1) Volume EM archives—OpenOrganelle (Janelia), EMPIAR, and CellMap datasets with existing segmentations for mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, and nuclei; (2) Human Protein Atlas subcellular imaging data with morphometric annotations; (3) OpenCell systematic organelle measurements; (4) Published datasets from comparative studies in non-model organisms identified through systematic literature review. We estimate accessing morphometric data from >50,000 cells across >20 species.

Data harmonization presents the central technical challenge. Different sources use different segmentation algorithms, resolution levels, and annotation conventions. We will develop a harmonization pipeline that: (a) standardizes morphometric measurements to common units and definitions using an organelle morphometry ontology we will create; (b) implements quality control filters based on segmentation confidence scores and image resolution; (c) propagates uncertainty estimates through all downstream analyses; (d) cross-validates measurements where the same cell types appear in multiple sources.

Phase 2: Morphometric Standardization (Months 4-12)
For each organelle class, we will extract standardized morphometric features including: volume, surface area, number per cell, sphericity, network connectivity indices, and contact site frequencies with other organelles. Cell-level covariates will include total cell volume, nuclear volume, estimated ploidy, tissue of origin, species, and available metabolic annotations.

Where existing segmentations are incomplete, we will apply validated deep learning segmentation tools (e.g., Cellpose, StarDist for nuclei; MitoNet for mitochondria) to raw EM volumes, containerizing all pipelines for reproducibility. We will not generate new experimental data but will apply computational methods to extract additional measurements from existing public datasets.

Phase 3: Statistical Analysis (Months 8-18)
Allometric analysis will employ phylogenetically informed regression methods that account for non-independence among species. We will use phylogenetic generalized least squares (PGLS) with phylogenies from TimeTree and Open Tree of Life. For within-species analysis across cell types, we will employ mixed-effects models with tissue and individual as random effects.

Scaling relationships will be modeled as: log(Y) = α + β·log(X) + ε, where Y is the organelle metric, X is cell volume (or other predictor), β is the scaling exponent, and ε includes phylogenetic error structure. We will test whether β differs significantly from isometry (β=1), surface-area scaling (β=0.67), and metabolic scaling (β=0.75). Model selection will compare alternative predictors (cell volume, metabolic rate proxies, ploidy) using AIC and cross-validation.

Outlier analysis will identify cell types with residuals exceeding two standard deviations, followed by enrichment analysis to identify biological features associated with deviation.

Phase 4: Validation and Robustness (Months 15-20)
We will validate findings through: (1) cross-validation across data sources—relationships identified in EM data should replicate in fluorescence-based measurements; (2) sensitivity analysis varying quality control thresholds and harmonization parameters; (3) comparison with published single-study findings to ensure consistency; (4) expert review by Working Group members with deep organelle-specific knowledge.

All analyses will be implemented in reproducible workflows using Snakemake, with code versioned in GitHub and archived in Zenodo. The Working Group will meet biweekly virtually and quarterly in person at NCEMS to ensure coordination across analysis teams.

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Cytoskeletal Coordination as a Distributed Control System: Synthesis of Live-Cell Imaging Data
abstract: The actin and microtubule cytoskeletons coordinate diverse cellular behaviors—migration, division, polarization—through dynamics that have traditionally been modeled with reaction-diffusion frameworks. Engineering control theory, which formally analyzes how distributed systems regulate variables despite noise, has rarely been applied to cytoskeletal coordination, yet cells appear to solve control problems remarkably similar to those addressed in robotic swarms and distributed sensor networks. This Working Group will synthesize live-cell imaging datasets of cytoskeletal dynamics from the Image Data Resource (IDR), Cell Image Library, and individual publications to identify control-law signatures—evidence that cells regulate specific physical variables (cortical tension, polymer flux, leading-edge curvature) through feedback. The team unites cell biologists studying cytoskeletal dynamics, control theorists from engineering departments, computer-vision researchers expert in cell tracking, and biophysicists experienced in active-matter modeling. We will harmonize quantitative cytoskeletal time-series from ~30 published imaging studies into a unified format, develop control-theoretic identification methods that infer regulated variables from observed trajectories, and test whether identified control laws transfer across cell types and perturbation conditions. Deliverables include (1) a harmonized cytoskeletal dynamics dataset with consistent quantification, (2) inferred control architectures for major cytoskeletal coordination tasks, (3) open-source software bringing engineering control identification methods to cell biology, and (4) testable predictions about how cells respond to perturbations of inferred control variables. NCEMS support is essential because the project requires deep collaboration between cell biology and engineering communities that rarely co-author work, and because harmonizing live-imaging datasets across labs demands sustained quantitative-imaging expertise. The training plan supports four trainees from cell biology and engineering programs through co-mentoring across disciplines, formal training in control theory and quantitative imaging, and joint work on shared sub-problems that demand bridging both fields. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary seminars and co-author the methods paper introducing control identification to cell biology. All harmonized datasets and analysis code will be released through IDR and GitHub with reproducible Jupyter notebooks, control-identification software will be packaged as installable Python libraries, and a web tool will allow researchers to upload their own time-series data for control analysis. By recasting cytoskeletal coordination as a control problem, this project introduces a new analytical lens that may resolve why cytoskeletal dynamics appear robust to many perturbations but fragile to specific ones. The broader impact extends to synthetic biology and tissue engineering, where designing cells with desired dynamic behaviors will require the very kind of control framework this synthesis aims to establish.
background_and_significance:
The cytoskeleton represents one of biology's most sophisticated examples of emergent coordination, where actin filaments and microtubules orchestrate cellular behaviors spanning migration, division, polarization, and morphogenesis. These dynamic polymer networks operate at the mesoscale—precisely the scale between individual biomolecules and organelles that NCEMS has identified as ripe for synthesis-driven discovery. Despite decades of research, fundamental questions remain about how cells achieve robust coordination of cytoskeletal dynamics across spatial scales ranging from nanometer-scale filament assembly to micrometer-scale cellular morphology.

Traditionally, cytoskeletal dynamics have been understood through reaction-diffusion frameworks that describe how biochemical concentrations evolve through local reactions and molecular diffusion. While these models have provided valuable insights into pattern formation and self-organization, they fundamentally describe open-loop dynamics—systems evolving according to intrinsic rules without explicit reference to regulated output variables. This perspective struggles to explain several puzzling observations: how cells maintain stable morphologies despite continuous cytoskeletal turnover, why certain perturbations cause catastrophic failures while others are readily compensated, and how the same molecular machinery produces dramatically different behaviors across cell types and contexts.

Engineering control theory offers a complementary analytical framework that has transformed understanding of complex distributed systems in robotics, aerospace, and networked infrastructure. Control theory formally addresses how systems regulate specific variables (controlled outputs) through feedback mechanisms that sense deviations and adjust inputs accordingly. Critically, control-theoretic analysis can identify what variables a system regulates from observed trajectories alone—a methodology called system identification that has never been systematically applied to cytoskeletal dynamics.

The significance of applying control theory to cytoskeletal coordination extends beyond analytical novelty. Control frameworks naturally explain robustness and fragility: systems are robust to disturbances that feedback mechanisms can counteract but fragile to perturbations that disrupt the feedback itself. This distinction may resolve long-standing puzzles about why cytoskeletal dynamics tolerate some drug treatments while collapsing under others. Furthermore, control architectures can be hierarchical, with fast local loops nested within slower global regulation—a structure that may explain how cells coordinate across scales.

The timing for this synthesis is opportune because publicly available live-cell imaging datasets have reached sufficient volume and quality to enable systematic analysis. The Image Data Resource, Cell Image Library, and supplementary data from individual publications collectively contain thousands of time-series capturing cytoskeletal dynamics across cell types, perturbations, and imaging modalities. However, these datasets remain siloed, with inconsistent quantification methods preventing cross-study comparison. No individual laboratory possesses the combined expertise in cell biology, control theory, computer vision, and biophysics required to harmonize these data and develop appropriate analytical methods.

This project directly addresses NCEMS priorities by synthesizing existing data to answer fundamental questions about emergent cellular properties. The cytoskeleton exemplifies mesoscale emergence: molecular-scale polymer dynamics give rise to cellular-scale behaviors through mechanisms that remain incompletely understood. By introducing control-theoretic analysis, we aim to reveal organizing principles that have eluded traditional approaches, potentially transforming how the field conceptualizes cytoskeletal coordination.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses three interconnected research questions that progressively build from data harmonization through methodological development to biological insight. Each question is paired with testable hypotheses derived from control-theoretic principles and preliminary observations from cytoskeletal biology.

**Research Question 1: What physical variables do cells regulate during cytoskeletal coordination tasks?**

Cells performing migration, division, or polarization must coordinate cytoskeletal dynamics across space and time. Control theory predicts that regulated systems maintain specific output variables near setpoints despite disturbances. We hypothesize that cytoskeletal coordination involves regulation of distinct physical variables for different cellular tasks: (H1a) During cell migration, cells regulate leading-edge curvature and retrograde actin flow rate as primary controlled variables, with protrusion velocity emerging as a downstream consequence rather than a directly regulated quantity. (H1b) During cytokinesis, cells regulate cortical tension at the cleavage furrow and the ratio of contractile ring circumference to cell diameter, explaining the remarkable precision of division plane positioning. (H1c) During polarization, cells regulate the spatial gradient of active Rho-family GTPases rather than absolute concentrations, enabling scale-invariant polarity establishment.

These hypotheses are testable through system identification methods that distinguish regulated variables (showing reduced variance and rapid return to setpoints after perturbation) from unregulated variables (showing drift or perturbation-dependent steady states).

**Research Question 2: What feedback architectures implement cytoskeletal control, and do they exhibit hierarchical organization?**

Engineered control systems often employ hierarchical architectures with fast inner loops handling local disturbance rejection and slower outer loops coordinating global behavior. We hypothesize that cytoskeletal control exhibits analogous hierarchical structure: (H2a) Local feedback loops operating on timescales of seconds regulate individual filament dynamics and local cortical properties through mechanochemical coupling between membrane tension and actin polymerization. (H2b) Global feedback loops operating on timescales of minutes coordinate spatial patterns through reaction-diffusion of regulatory proteins, with the regulated variable being the spatial distribution rather than local concentrations. (H2c) The hierarchy is organized such that inner loops are conditionally stable—they require outer loop supervision to prevent runaway dynamics, explaining why certain signaling perturbations cause catastrophic cytoskeletal collapse.

These hypotheses predict specific signatures in frequency-domain analysis of cytoskeletal time-series: hierarchical control produces characteristic transfer functions with distinct frequency bands corresponding to different control loops.

**Research Question 3: Do inferred control laws generalize across cell types and predict responses to novel perturbations?**

A stringent test of whether identified control architectures capture genuine biological organization is their transferability. We hypothesize that: (H3a) Core control architectures for fundamental tasks (migration, division) are conserved across cell types, with cell-type-specific differences appearing primarily in control gains (feedback strengths) rather than control structure. (H3b) Perturbations that disrupt inferred feedback pathways will produce qualitatively different responses than perturbations affecting feedforward elements—specifically, feedback disruption will cause increased variance and loss of setpoint tracking, while feedforward disruption will shift setpoints without affecting variance. (H3c) Control architectures identified from wild-type cells will predict the specific failure modes observed in published perturbation experiments, providing retrospective validation.

These hypotheses enable quantitative predictions that can be tested against held-out datasets and published perturbation studies not used in model identification. The transferability tests are particularly powerful because they require the control framework to capture generalizable principles rather than dataset-specific patterns.

Collectively, these research questions address the fundamental problem of how cells achieve robust coordination through distributed molecular machinery—a quintessential emergence problem at the mesoscale that synthesis of existing data is uniquely positioned to address.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises three integrated phases: data harmonization, control-theoretic analysis development, and validation through cross-dataset testing. Each phase involves specific techniques adapted from engineering and computer vision to the unique challenges of live-cell imaging data.

**Phase 1: Data Harmonization and Quantification Pipeline (Months 1-8)**

We will systematically curate live-cell imaging datasets from the Image Data Resource (IDR), Cell Image Library, and supplementary materials from approximately 30 published studies selected based on temporal resolution (≥0.5 Hz), spatial resolution (≤500 nm), and documentation quality. Our computer vision team will develop a unified quantification pipeline using established tools (CellProfiler, TrackMate, FIESTA) augmented with custom algorithms for cytoskeletal-specific features.

Quantified variables will include: filament orientation fields, polymer density maps, flow velocities from optical flow analysis, cell boundary curvature, and fluorescence intensity profiles for labeled cytoskeletal components. Critical to harmonization is uncertainty quantification—each measurement will carry associated confidence intervals derived from image noise characteristics and tracking algorithm validation. We will employ standardized metadata schemas (OME-NGFF format) and develop automated quality control metrics to flag problematic time-series.

The harmonized dataset will be structured as multivariate time-series with consistent temporal sampling (achieved through interpolation with uncertainty propagation) and spatial registration to cell-centric coordinate systems. This structure enables direct application of time-series analysis methods across studies.

**Phase 2: Control-Theoretic Identification Methods (Months 4-14)**

We will adapt system identification techniques from control engineering to infer regulated variables and feedback architectures from observed trajectories. The core methodology involves three complementary approaches:

*Variance-based regulation detection*: Regulated variables exhibit reduced variance compared to unregulated quantities. We will apply principal component analysis to identify low-variance directions in the space of measured variables, hypothesizing these correspond to regulated combinations. Statistical tests will distinguish genuine regulation from measurement artifacts.

*Perturbation response analysis*: Published datasets including drug treatments, optogenetic perturbations, or mechanical interventions provide natural experiments for identifying feedback. We will fit autoregressive models with exogenous inputs (ARX models) to characterize how perturbations propagate through the system, identifying feedback loops as pathways showing compensatory responses.

*Frequency-domain decomposition*: Hierarchical control produces characteristic spectral signatures. We will compute power spectral densities and coherence functions between measured variables, using techniques from control theory (Bode plots, Nyquist analysis) to identify feedback loop structures and estimate loop gains.

Our control theory team will develop methods to handle challenges specific to biological data: non-stationarity (cells change behavior over time), nonlinearity (cytoskeletal dynamics are inherently nonlinear), and partial observability (not all relevant variables are measured). We will employ state-space models with hidden variables and develop identifiability criteria to determine when data suffice for reliable inference.

**Phase 3: Validation and Generalization Testing (Months 12-18)**

Validation proceeds through three strategies: cross-validation within datasets (training on subsets, testing on held-out cells), cross-dataset transfer (training on one study, testing on others), and retrospective prediction of published perturbation outcomes. We will quantify prediction accuracy using metrics appropriate for dynamical systems: trajectory prediction error, variance explanation, and perturbation response fidelity.

The biophysics team will assess whether inferred control laws are physically plausible given known cytoskeletal biochemistry and mechanics. This constraint-based validation ensures identified architectures are not merely statistical artifacts but correspond to implementable biological mechanisms.

Throughout all phases, the team will meet biweekly via videoconference, with quarterly in-person workshops at NCEMS facilities for intensive collaborative analysis sessions.

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: A Renormalization-Group Framework for Multiscale Modeling of Mesoscale Biological Assemblies
abstract: Renormalization-group (RG) theory provides a principled framework for coarse-graining systems across scales, yet its application in biology has been largely confined to neural and tissue dynamics. The mesoscale—where biomolecular complexes give rise to organelle-scale phenomena—is precisely the regime where RG approaches should yield predictive multiscale models, but the requisite synthesis of structural, dynamical, and functional data has not been undertaken. This Working Group will develop and validate RG-style coarse-graining methods for mesoscale assemblies by synthesizing structural data from PDB and AlphaFold-DB, cryo-electron tomography from EMPIAR, dynamical data from molecular dynamics archives (MoDEL, BIGNASim) and live-cell imaging, and functional data from perturbation atlases. The team brings together statistical physicists with RG expertise, structural biologists, computational biophysicists experienced in coarse-grained modeling, and machine-learning researchers expert in neural-network coarse-graining methods. We will develop coarse-graining schemes that systematically integrate molecular-scale information into mesoscale effective models, test their predictive accuracy against held-out functional data, and identify which mesoscale phenomena admit RG-style treatment versus which require fundamentally different approaches. Deliverables include (1) RG-coarse-graining methods released as open-source software with clear documentation, (2) validated multiscale models for several mesoscale systems (a condensate, a membrane assembly, a chromatin domain), (3) a theoretical framework distinguishing tractable from intractable mesoscale phenomena, and (4) a benchmark dataset enabling future methods development. NCEMS support is essential because the project bridges statistical physics and cell biology in ways no single lab supports, and because validation across mesoscale systems requires archive-spanning data integration. The training plan supports five trainees from physics and biology programs through formal training in statistical mechanics, coarse-grained modeling, and biological data integration, complemented by cross-disciplinary seminars and joint sub-projects requiring physics-biology collaboration. Trainees will lead system-specific applications and contribute to the methods paper introducing the framework. All software will be released under permissive licenses, models will be containerized for reproducibility, and the benchmark will be hosted on Zenodo with clear evaluation protocols. By bringing rigorous multiscale theory to mesoscale biology, this project addresses an innovative analytical strategy explicitly sought by the call. The broader impact lies in establishing whether biological mesoscale phenomena can be understood with the kind of universal frameworks that physics has provided for other multiscale systems, or whether biology demands fundamentally different theoretical foundations—either answer would reshape how the field approaches mesoscale phenomena.
background_and_significance:
The mesoscale represents one of the most challenging frontiers in molecular and cellular biology. Spanning approximately 10-1000 nanometers, this regime encompasses biomolecular condensates, membrane protein assemblies, chromatin domains, and cytoskeletal networks—structures that emerge from molecular interactions yet exhibit collective behaviors that cannot be predicted from individual components alone. Understanding how molecular-level information propagates to generate organelle-scale function remains a fundamental unsolved problem that lies at the heart of NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale.

Renormalization-group (RG) theory, developed in statistical physics to understand phase transitions and critical phenomena, provides a mathematically rigorous framework for relating descriptions of systems at different scales. The core insight of RG is that coarse-graining—systematically integrating out microscopic degrees of freedom—can reveal which features of a system are relevant at larger scales and which become irrelevant. This approach has revolutionized our understanding of phenomena ranging from magnetism to turbulence, and more recently has been applied to neural networks and tissue mechanics. However, its systematic application to mesoscale biological assemblies remains unexplored despite the obvious conceptual fit.

The timing for this synthesis is unprecedented. The explosion of publicly available structural data—over 200,000 experimental structures in the Protein Data Bank, 200 million predicted structures in AlphaFold-DB, and thousands of cryo-electron tomograms in EMPIAR—provides molecular-resolution information at a scale unimaginable a decade ago. Simultaneously, molecular dynamics archives including MoDEL and BIGNASim contain trajectories capturing dynamics across timescales from picoseconds to microseconds. Live-cell imaging databases document mesoscale dynamics in cellular contexts, while perturbation atlases from CRISPR screens and proteomics studies link molecular changes to functional outcomes. No single laboratory possesses the expertise to integrate these disparate data types within a unified theoretical framework.

The significance of this project extends beyond methodology development. A central question in biology is whether the emergent complexity of living systems admits universal organizing principles analogous to those physics has discovered for other complex systems, or whether biological evolution has produced irreducibly diverse solutions that resist theoretical unification. The mesoscale is the critical testing ground for this question: if RG-style approaches can capture mesoscale emergence, this suggests deep universality; if they systematically fail, this reveals something fundamental about biological organization that demands new theoretical frameworks.

Current coarse-graining approaches in biology are largely ad hoc, developed for specific systems without systematic connection to microscopic physics or rigorous validation against functional data. Machine learning methods for coarse-graining, while powerful, often function as black boxes without interpretable parameters. Our approach uniquely combines the theoretical rigor of RG with data-driven validation, creating methods that are both principled and practically useful. This synthesis directly addresses NCEMS's goal of developing innovative analytical strategies through transdisciplinary collaboration, bringing together statistical physics, structural biology, computational biophysics, and machine learning in ways that no existing center or collaboration currently supports.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses four interconnected research questions that span fundamental theory to practical methodology, each with testable hypotheses derived from RG principles and biological considerations.

**Research Question 1: Can RG-style coarse-graining schemes be systematically constructed for mesoscale biological assemblies using existing structural and dynamical data?**

Hypothesis 1a: Mesoscale assemblies exhibit scale separation that permits systematic coarse-graining, with effective degrees of freedom at the 10-100 nm scale that capture essential physics while reducing computational complexity by 2-3 orders of magnitude.

Hypothesis 1b: Neural network architectures trained on molecular dynamics trajectories can learn coarse-graining transformations that preserve the mathematical structure of RG flows, specifically the semi-group property and fixed-point structure.

We will test these hypotheses by constructing coarse-grained representations from all-atom structures and dynamics, then quantifying information loss and predictive accuracy as functions of coarse-graining level. Success criteria include achieving sub-angstrom accuracy in back-mapped structures and sub-kcal/mol accuracy in free energy surfaces.

**Research Question 2: Do mesoscale phenomena exhibit universality classes analogous to those observed in physical systems near critical points?**

Hypothesis 2a: Biomolecular condensates formed through liquid-liquid phase separation belong to universality classes determined by symmetry and dimensionality rather than molecular details, predicting that condensates with similar phase diagrams share scaling exponents despite different compositions.

Hypothesis 2b: Membrane protein assemblies exhibit distinct universality classes from three-dimensional condensates due to the reduced dimensionality and curvature coupling inherent to membrane systems.

We will test universality by computing critical exponents and scaling functions for multiple systems within each category (condensates, membrane assemblies, chromatin domains) and comparing across systems. Universality predicts collapse of scaling functions onto master curves; failure would indicate system-specific physics dominating collective behavior.

**Research Question 3: Which mesoscale phenomena are amenable to RG treatment, and what features distinguish tractable from intractable cases?**

Hypothesis 3a: Systems with continuous symmetries and equilibrium-like dynamics will admit standard RG treatment, while systems with strong non-equilibrium driving or broken ergodicity will require extended frameworks.

Hypothesis 3b: The tractability of RG approaches correlates with the ratio of relaxation timescales at different spatial scales—systems with clear timescale separation are tractable, while those with entangled timescales resist coarse-graining.

We will systematically classify mesoscale phenomena by applying RG methods and quantifying prediction accuracy against held-out functional data. This will generate a decision framework for future applications.

**Research Question 4: Can RG-derived effective models predict functional outcomes from structural and dynamical inputs?**

Hypothesis 4a: Coarse-grained models parameterized from structural databases can predict perturbation responses measured in functional screens with accuracy exceeding molecular-detail simulations at equivalent computational cost.

Hypothesis 4b: The effective parameters of coarse-grained models (analogous to coupling constants in physics) correlate with disease-associated mutations and evolutionary conservation, suggesting these parameters capture functionally relevant features.

Validation will use held-out perturbation data from CRISPR screens and proteomics studies, comparing predictions from our RG-derived models against both detailed simulations and purely statistical approaches.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates four interconnected workflows: data synthesis and curation, RG-based coarse-graining development, machine learning augmentation, and systematic validation. The Working Group structure ensures each workflow benefits from transdisciplinary expertise.

**Data Synthesis Pipeline (Months 1-6, continuing throughout)**

We will construct integrated datasets for three model systems: (1) FUS-family condensates, (2) BAR-domain membrane assemblies, and (3) HP1-mediated heterochromatin domains. For each system, we synthesize: structural data from PDB (experimental structures) and AlphaFold-DB (predicted structures for full proteomes); tomographic data from EMPIAR providing in-situ mesoscale organization; dynamical data from MoDEL and BIGNASim molecular dynamics repositories plus published trajectories; and functional data from DepMap CRISPR screens, proteomics atlases, and curated literature. Data harmonization will address format inconsistencies, resolution differences, and metadata standardization. We estimate integrating approximately 500 structures, 50 tomograms, 100 microseconds of simulation time, and 10,000 perturbation measurements per system.

**RG Coarse-Graining Development (Months 3-18)**

We implement three complementary coarse-graining strategies. First, real-space RG methods adapted from polymer physics will define block-spin transformations for protein complexes, grouping atoms into effective beads with systematically derived interaction potentials. Second, momentum-space RG methods will identify relevant operators by analyzing fluctuation spectra from molecular dynamics, determining which collective modes dominate mesoscale behavior. Third, functional RG approaches will track how effective Hamiltonians flow under coarse-graining, identifying fixed points corresponding to universal behavior. Each method will be implemented as modular Python code interfacing with standard simulation packages (OpenMM, GROMACS) and analysis tools (MDAnalysis, PyEMMA).

**Machine Learning Integration (Months 6-18)**

We will develop neural network coarse-graining methods that respect RG structure. Graph neural networks will learn coarse-graining maps from fine-grained to coarse-grained representations, with architecture constraints ensuring the learned transformations satisfy semi-group properties. Normalizing flows will parameterize the distribution of fine-grained configurations consistent with coarse-grained states, enabling thermodynamically consistent back-mapping. We will benchmark neural approaches against analytical RG methods to understand when machine learning adds value versus introducing unnecessary complexity.

**Validation Framework (Months 12-24)**

Validation proceeds hierarchically. Structural validation tests whether coarse-grained models reproduce experimentally observed mesoscale organization in tomograms. Dynamical validation compares predicted relaxation times and fluctuation spectra against live-cell imaging data. Functional validation—the most stringent test—evaluates whether models predict perturbation responses in held-out data. We will implement cross-validation protocols holding out 20% of functional data for final testing, with separate validation sets for each model system.

**Integration and Synthesis (Months 18-24)**

The final phase synthesizes results across systems to address the theoretical questions: identifying universality classes, delineating tractable versus intractable phenomena, and establishing best practices for mesoscale modeling. Working Group meetings (quarterly in-person, monthly virtual) ensure continuous integration of insights across sub-projects.

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Condensate Composition as Community Ecology: Neutral and Niche-Based Assembly Models
abstract: Community ecology has developed sophisticated null models and theoretical frameworks—neutral theory, niche partitioning, environmental filtering—to explain why specific species co-occur in specific environments. Biomolecular condensates pose a strikingly analogous question: why do specific proteins co-occur in specific condensates? Yet ecological frameworks have not been applied to condensate composition at synthesis scale, leaving the field reliant on ad hoc explanations for client recruitment. This Working Group will synthesize public condensate proteomics data across condition, cell type, and organism with ecological community-assembly statistics to test which class of assembly model—neutral, niche-based, or hybrid—best explains condensate composition. The team unites quantitative ecologists with deep expertise in community-assembly theory, condensate biologists, computational biologists experienced in compositional data analysis, and statisticians expert in null-model testing. We will harmonize condensate proteomic datasets into species-by-site-style matrices (proteins-by-condensates), apply ecological null models including the Raup–Crick metric, joint species distribution models, and phylogenetic community ecology methods adapted for protein evolutionary relationships, and test whether condensate composition shows signatures of competitive exclusion, environmental filtering by physicochemical condition, or stochastic assembly. Deliverables include (1) condensate-as-community datasets formatted for ecological analysis, (2) statistical evaluations of competing assembly models, (3) an open-source toolkit applying ecological methods to molecular composition data, and (4) testable predictions about how condensate composition should respond to perturbation. NCEMS support is essential because the project requires sustained collaboration between ecological and molecular biology communities that rarely interact, and because the methodological transfer demands joint development of new statistical approaches. The training plan supports four trainees from ecology and molecular biology programs through cross-disciplinary co-mentoring, formal training in community ecology theory and condensate biology, and shared sub-projects requiring fluency in both fields. Trainees will participate in a joint reading group spanning the two communities and will co-author the toolkit paper. All datasets, code, and statistical pipelines will be released through GitHub with reproducible R and Python notebooks, and the toolkit will be packaged as an installable library with extensive tutorials. The broader impact lies in demonstrating that ecological frameworks can illuminate molecular-scale assembly questions and in establishing methodological infrastructure for future synthesis projects that treat molecular communities with ecological rigor. By importing tested ecological theory into condensate biology, this project addresses both a novel scientific question and an innovative analytical strategy that could transfer to other mesoscale assemblies.
background_and_significance:
Biomolecular condensates represent one of the most transformative discoveries in cell biology over the past decade. These membrane-less organelles—including stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, and nuclear speckles—form through liquid-liquid phase separation and concentrate specific sets of proteins and nucleic acids to perform specialized cellular functions. While the biophysical principles governing phase separation are increasingly understood, a fundamental question remains unanswered: why do specific proteins co-occur in specific condensates? Current explanations rely largely on identifying sequence features such as intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and specific interaction motifs, yet these features are necessary but insufficient to explain the remarkable selectivity of condensate composition observed across cellular conditions.

Community ecology has spent over a century developing theoretical frameworks to address an analogous question: why do specific species co-occur in specific habitats? Three major paradigms have emerged. Neutral theory posits that community composition reflects stochastic processes—dispersal limitation, demographic drift, and random colonization—rather than species-specific traits. Niche-based models emphasize deterministic processes including environmental filtering (abiotic conditions select for species with appropriate traits) and biotic interactions (competition and facilitation shape co-occurrence patterns). Hybrid models recognize that both stochastic and deterministic processes operate simultaneously, with their relative importance varying across scales and contexts. These frameworks have been formalized into rigorous statistical null models that distinguish random from structured assembly patterns.

The analogy between ecological communities and condensate composition is striking and underexploited. Proteins can be conceptualized as species, condensates as habitats, and the cellular environment as the regional species pool. Just as ecologists ask whether savanna tree communities reflect competitive exclusion or rainfall filtering, we can ask whether stress granule composition reflects competitive binding for scaffold sites or physicochemical filtering by the stress-induced cytoplasmic environment. Despite this conceptual parallel, ecological assembly frameworks have never been systematically applied to condensate proteomics data at synthesis scale.

This gap represents a significant missed opportunity. The condensate field has accumulated substantial public proteomics data characterizing the composition of diverse condensates across organisms, cell types, and conditions. Databases including PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, and CD-CODE aggregate thousands of protein-condensate associations. Mass spectrometry studies have quantified condensate proteomes under varying stress conditions, developmental stages, and disease states. Yet these data remain fragmented and analyzed primarily through enrichment statistics rather than community-assembly theory.

The significance of applying ecological frameworks to condensate composition extends beyond conceptual elegance. First, ecological null models provide rigorous statistical machinery for distinguishing random from structured patterns—machinery that condensate biology currently lacks. Second, ecological theory generates specific, testable predictions about how composition should respond to perturbation (e.g., environmental filtering predicts trait convergence under stress). Third, demonstrating that ecological frameworks illuminate molecular assembly would establish methodological infrastructure transferable to other mesoscale phenomena including protein complexes, metabolons, and signaling clusters. This project directly addresses NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale by asking whether condensate composition—an emergent property arising from molecular interactions—follows assembly rules analogous to those governing ecological communities.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group will address three interconnected research questions that progressively test the applicability of ecological assembly theory to biomolecular condensate composition.

Research Question 1: Does condensate composition deviate significantly from neutral assembly expectations?

Neutral theory provides the essential null model against which deterministic assembly must be evaluated. We hypothesize that condensate composition will show significant departures from neutral expectations, with co-occurrence patterns more structured than predicted by random sampling from the cellular proteome. Specifically, we predict that (H1a) protein pairs will show non-random co-occurrence frequencies across condensates, with both significant aggregation (proteins that consistently co-occur) and segregation (proteins that rarely co-occur despite similar abundances); (H1b) the magnitude of departure from neutrality will vary across condensate types, with constitutive condensates (nucleoli, Cajal bodies) showing stronger structure than stress-induced condensates; and (H1c) departure from neutrality will correlate with condensate functional specificity—condensates performing defined biochemical functions will show more structured composition than storage-oriented condensates.

Research Question 2: What ecological assembly mechanisms best explain non-random condensate composition patterns?

Having established departure from neutrality, we will discriminate among deterministic assembly mechanisms. We hypothesize that condensate composition reflects a combination of environmental filtering and competitive interactions, with their relative importance varying by condensate type. Specifically, we predict that (H2a) environmental filtering signatures will dominate stress-induced condensates, with proteins sharing physicochemical traits (IDR composition, charge patterning, aromatic content) converging under stress conditions; (H2b) competitive exclusion signatures will appear in condensates with limited scaffold capacity, where functionally redundant proteins show negative co-occurrence; (H2c) phylogenetic community structure will reveal whether closely related proteins (by sequence homology) co-occur more or less than expected, distinguishing habitat filtering (phylogenetic clustering) from competitive exclusion (phylogenetic overdispersion); and (H2d) joint species distribution models will identify latent environmental gradients structuring composition, potentially revealing previously unrecognized physicochemical axes of condensate variation.

Research Question 3: Can ecological assembly models predict condensate compositional responses to perturbation?

The ultimate test of any theoretical framework is predictive power. We hypothesize that ecological assembly models, once parameterized on existing data, will generate accurate predictions about compositional changes under novel conditions. Specifically, we predict that (H3a) if environmental filtering dominates, perturbations altering the physicochemical environment (pH, ionic strength, crowding) should shift composition toward proteins with traits matching the new conditions; (H3b) if competitive interactions dominate, removal of abundant scaffold proteins should release competitive suppression, allowing previously excluded proteins to enter; and (H3c) hybrid models incorporating both filtering and competition will outperform single-mechanism models in predicting held-out perturbation datasets.

These hypotheses are testable using existing public data. Perturbation predictions (RQ3) can be validated against published studies examining condensate composition under stress, drug treatment, or genetic manipulation—data that will be held out during model training. The hierarchical structure of our questions—from null model testing through mechanism discrimination to prediction—ensures that each stage builds logically on previous findings while generating independent insights.

Methodologically, we will adapt established ecological statistics for molecular data. The Raup-Crick metric quantifies whether observed co-occurrence deviates from null expectations given species abundances. Phylogenetic community metrics (NRI, NTI) test whether co-occurring species are more or less related than expected. Joint species distribution models (JSDMs) simultaneously estimate species responses to environmental gradients and residual species associations, distinguishing environmental filtering from biotic interactions. Each method has been extensively validated in ecological applications and requires careful adaptation—not wholesale replacement—for molecular contexts.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises four integrated phases: data harmonization, null model testing, mechanistic model fitting, and predictive validation.

Phase 1: Data Harmonization and Matrix Construction (Months 1-6)

We will aggregate condensate proteomics data from public repositories including PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE, and primary literature. Our target is comprehensive coverage of at least 50 distinct condensate types across human, mouse, yeast, and Drosophila, with condition-specific composition data (stress, developmental stage, disease state) where available. Raw data will be processed through standardized pipelines: protein identifiers mapped to UniProt accessions, abundance values normalized within studies using quantile normalization, and presence/absence matrices constructed at multiple abundance thresholds to assess sensitivity. The resulting data structure will mirror ecological species-by-site matrices, with proteins as rows (species), condensates as columns (sites), and cells containing abundance or presence/absence values. Metadata will capture condensate type, organism, cell type, experimental condition, and study source. Protein trait matrices will be constructed in parallel, including IDR content (from MobiDB), charge patterning metrics, aromatic residue frequency, molecular weight, cellular abundance (from PaxDB), and evolutionary conservation. Phylogenetic relationships among proteins will be estimated from sequence alignments using established methods, enabling phylogenetic community analyses.

Phase 2: Null Model Testing (Months 4-12)

We will implement multiple null model algorithms to test whether condensate composition deviates from neutral expectations. The Raup-Crick metric compares observed co-occurrence frequencies to null distributions generated by random sampling while preserving row and column totals (protein prevalence and condensate richness). We will implement multiple null model algorithms (fixed-fixed, fixed-equiprobable, proportional sampling) to assess robustness. Checkerboard scores and C-scores will quantify overall co-occurrence structure. For each condensate type, we will calculate standardized effect sizes comparing observed metrics to null distributions, with significance assessed through permutation testing (10,000 iterations). Results will be synthesized across condensate types to identify general patterns and condensate-specific deviations.

Phase 3: Mechanistic Model Fitting (Months 8-18)

Having established departure from neutrality, we will fit mechanistic models to discriminate assembly processes. Phylogenetic community metrics (Net Relatedness Index, Nearest Taxon Index) will test whether co-occurring proteins are phylogenetically clustered (suggesting environmental filtering) or overdispersed (suggesting competitive exclusion). We will adapt these metrics using protein sequence phylogenies rather than species phylogenies. Trait-based analyses will test whether condensate composition shows trait convergence (filtering) or divergence (competition) using community-weighted mean and functional dispersion metrics. Joint Species Distribution Models (JSDMs) will be implemented using the Hierarchical Modelling of Species Communities (HMSC) framework, modeling protein occurrence as a function of environmental covariates (condensate type, cellular condition) while estimating residual correlations reflecting unmeasured environmental variation or biotic interactions. Model comparison will use information criteria (AIC, BIC) and cross-validation to evaluate relative support for neutral, filtering, competition, and hybrid models.

Phase 4: Predictive Validation (Months 15-24)

We will partition data temporally and by study, training models on earlier/training studies and validating predictions on later/held-out studies. Perturbation datasets (stress response, drug treatment, knockdown studies) will serve as critical tests: models will predict compositional changes, and predictions will be compared to observed changes using correlation and classification metrics. Prediction accuracy will be compared across model classes to identify which assembly framework best captures condensate biology.

Computational Infrastructure: All analyses will be implemented in R and Python, leveraging existing ecological packages (vegan, picante, HMSC) with custom extensions for molecular data. Code will be version-controlled on GitHub with continuous integration testing. Computationally intensive analyses (null model permutations, JSDM fitting) will utilize NCEMS computational resources.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will generate four major deliverables with significant scientific and methodological impact.

First, we will produce harmonized condensate-as-community datasets comprising the most comprehensive, standardized compilation of condensate proteomics data formatted for ecological analysis. These datasets will be deposited in public repositories with full metadata, enabling future synthesis research and serving as a community resource extending beyond this project.

Second, we will deliver rigorous statistical evaluations of competing assembly models, providing the first systematic test of whether condensate composition follows neutral, niche-based, or hybrid assembly rules. These findings will transform how the field conceptualizes client recruitment, moving from ad hoc explanations toward principled theoretical frameworks. If environmental filtering dominates, the field should prioritize identifying the physicochemical gradients structuring composition. If competition dominates, attention should focus on scaffold-client binding competition. If hybrid models prevail, the field gains nuanced understanding of when different processes dominate.

Third, we will release an open-source toolkit (R package and Python library) enabling researchers to apply ecological community-assembly methods to any molecular composition dataset. This toolkit will include functions for null model testing, phylogenetic community analysis adapted for protein phylogenies, and JSDM implementation with molecular-specific priors. Extensive tutorials and vignettes will lower barriers to adoption.

Fourth, we will generate testable predictions about condensate compositional responses to perturbation, providing the experimental community with specific hypotheses for validation. These predictions, derived from ecological theory, will demonstrate the practical value of the conceptual framework.

The broader impact extends beyond condensates. By demonstrating that ecological frameworks illuminate molecular assembly, we establish proof-of-concept for applying community ecology to other mesoscale phenomena—protein complexes, metabolic channeling, signaling clusters. The methodological infrastructure we develop will transfer directly to these applications, amplifying impact across molecular and cellular biology. This project exemplifies NCEMS's vision of synthesis research generating insights impossible within single disciplines.
