author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Self-Organized Criticality at the Mesoscale: Avalanche Statistics in Cellular Dynamics
abstract: Self-organized criticality (SOC) describes systems that naturally evolve to critical states exhibiting power-law avalanche statistics, with examples ranging from neural dynamics to earthquakes. Whether mesoscale cellular dynamics—signaling cascades, condensate formation events, cytoskeletal rearrangements—exhibit SOC signatures has been suggested theoretically but never tested at synthesis scale, in part because doing so requires harmonizing live-imaging time-series data across many studies. This Working Group will synthesize live-cell imaging datasets capturing dynamic mesoscale events from the Image Data Resource, Allen Cell Explorer, and individual high-quality time-series studies to test for SOC signatures across multiple mesoscale phenomena. The team brings together statistical physicists with avalanche-analysis expertise, cell biologists studying signaling and condensate dynamics, quantitative-imaging specialists, and computational biologists experienced in time-series analysis. We will harmonize quantitative time-series of calcium dynamics, kinase activation, condensate nucleation events, and cytoskeletal pattern formation from ~50 published datasets, apply rigorous statistical tests for power-law distributions and finite-size scaling, and assess whether observed signatures are consistent with SOC versus alternative explanations such as multiplicative noise. Deliverables include (1) harmonized mesoscale dynamics datasets with consistent quantification, (2) rigorous statistical evaluation of SOC signatures across phenomena, (3) open-source software for SOC analysis adapted to biological time-series, and (4) a theoretical assessment of which mesoscale phenomena are candidates for criticality-based explanations. NCEMS support is essential because rigorous SOC testing requires statistical-physics expertise rare in biology, and because synthesis across imaging modalities demands sustained quantitative infrastructure. The training plan supports four graduate students and one postdoc through co-mentoring across physics and biology, formal training in statistical-physics methods and quantitative cell imaging, and joint work on system-specific sub-projects. Trainees will participate in a cross-disciplinary seminar series and co-author the methods paper introducing rigorous SOC analysis to mesoscale biology. All harmonized datasets, analysis pipelines, and statistical code will be released openly through Zenodo and GitHub, with reproducible notebooks documenting every analysis step. The broader impact lies in determining whether the unifying framework of criticality—which has illuminated diverse complex systems—applies to mesoscale cellular dynamics, or whether biology requires different theoretical foundations. Either answer would meaningfully advance mesoscale biology, and the harmonized datasets and methods will support future quantitative work regardless of the SOC outcome.
background_and_significance:
Self-organized criticality (SOC), first proposed by Bak, Tang, and Wiesenfeld in 1987, describes a class of dynamical systems that naturally evolve toward critical states without external tuning. At criticality, these systems exhibit characteristic signatures including power-law distributed avalanche sizes and durations, long-range spatiotemporal correlations, and finite-size scaling relationships. SOC has provided unifying explanations for phenomena spanning earthquakes, forest fires, solar flares, and neural avalanches in cortical networks. The discovery that neuronal activity exhibits SOC signatures revolutionized our understanding of brain function, suggesting that criticality optimizes information processing, dynamic range, and computational flexibility.

Despite theoretical predictions that mesoscale cellular dynamics may operate near criticality, this hypothesis has never been rigorously tested through systematic data synthesis. The mesoscale—the organizational level between individual biomolecules and organelles—represents a frontier where emergent properties arise from collective molecular behaviors. Phenomena at this scale include biomolecular condensate formation through liquid-liquid phase separation, signaling cascade propagation, calcium wave dynamics, and cytoskeletal network reorganization. Each involves threshold-dependent activation, cooperative interactions, and spatiotemporal propagation—hallmarks of systems potentially exhibiting SOC.

Several theoretical frameworks suggest mesoscale processes may operate near criticality. Condensate formation involves nucleation events that could exhibit avalanche-like dynamics as local concentration fluctuations trigger cooperative phase transitions. Signaling cascades feature amplification through enzymatic reactions with threshold behaviors, where small perturbations can trigger large-scale cellular responses. Calcium dynamics show regenerative wave propagation through calcium-induced calcium release, exhibiting event-size distributions that preliminary studies suggest may follow power laws. Cytoskeletal networks undergo catastrophic reorganizations driven by cooperative filament dynamics and motor protein activity.

However, claims of SOC in biological systems have historically suffered from methodological limitations. Power-law distributions can arise from multiple mechanisms beyond SOC, including multiplicative noise processes, sample-size biases, and measurement artifacts. Rigorous SOC identification requires not merely fitting power laws but demonstrating finite-size scaling, temporal correlations consistent with critical dynamics, and ruling out alternative explanations through statistical model comparison. These analyses demand expertise in statistical physics that is rarely available in cell biology laboratories.

The significance of this synthesis project extends beyond testing a specific hypothesis. Understanding whether mesoscale dynamics operate near criticality would fundamentally reshape our theoretical frameworks for cellular organization. If SOC signatures are confirmed, criticality-based models could predict how cells maintain sensitivity while avoiding pathological runaway activation. Alternatively, if mesoscale dynamics systematically deviate from SOC predictions, this would indicate that biological systems have evolved regulatory mechanisms that specifically avoid critical dynamics, perhaps because criticality's inherent unpredictability is incompatible with reliable cellular function. Either outcome would substantially advance mesoscale biology.

This project directly addresses NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale. By synthesizing diverse live-imaging datasets and applying rigorous statistical-physics methods, we will determine whether criticality represents a unifying principle of mesoscale organization or whether biology requires fundamentally different theoretical foundations. The timing is ideal: publicly available imaging datasets have reached sufficient quality and quantity to enable synthesis-scale analysis, while advances in SOC analysis methods from neuroscience provide the statistical tools necessary for rigorous testing.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses four interconnected research questions that collectively test whether self-organized criticality provides a unifying framework for understanding mesoscale cellular dynamics.

Research Question 1: Do mesoscale cellular events exhibit power-law size and duration distributions consistent with SOC predictions?

Hypothesis 1a: Biomolecular condensate nucleation events will exhibit power-law distributed sizes (number of molecules recruited) and durations (time to reach steady state), with exponents consistent across cell types and condensate systems.

Hypothesis 1b: Calcium signaling events, including sparks, puffs, and waves, will show power-law distributions in amplitude and spatial extent, with systematic relationships between size and duration exponents.

Hypothesis 1c: Cytoskeletal rearrangement events will demonstrate avalanche-like dynamics with power-law distributed magnitudes of actin or microtubule network reorganization.

Hypothesis 1d: Kinase activation cascades will exhibit power-law distributed response amplitudes when measured across populations of cells responding to varying stimulus intensities.

Research Question 2: Do mesoscale dynamics exhibit finite-size scaling relationships characteristic of critical systems?

Hypothesis 2: If mesoscale phenomena operate near criticality, avalanche statistics will show systematic dependence on system size (cell volume, observation region, or number of participating molecules) following finite-size scaling predictions. Specifically, cutoff sizes in avalanche distributions will scale with system size according to universal scaling exponents.

This question is crucial because power-law distributions alone are insufficient evidence for SOC. Finite-size scaling provides a more stringent test that distinguishes true critical dynamics from alternative mechanisms that can produce apparent power laws.

Research Question 3: Can alternative non-critical mechanisms explain observed statistical signatures?

Hypothesis 3a: Multiplicative noise processes operating on mesoscale dynamics will produce log-normal rather than power-law distributions when analyzed with appropriate statistical methods, allowing discrimination between SOC and stochastic alternatives.

Hypothesis 3b: Measurement and sampling artifacts, including limited temporal resolution and photobleaching effects, will introduce systematic biases in avalanche statistics that can be identified and corrected through simulation-based validation.

This question addresses a critical gap in existing biological SOC claims. We will apply rigorous statistical model comparison using likelihood ratio tests and Bayesian model selection to distinguish power-law distributions from alternatives including log-normal, stretched exponential, and truncated power-law models.

Research Question 4: Which mesoscale phenomena are most likely candidates for criticality-based explanations, and what mechanistic features predict SOC signatures?

Hypothesis 4a: Phenomena involving threshold-dependent activation with positive feedback (calcium-induced calcium release, kinase autophosphorylation) will show stronger SOC signatures than phenomena dominated by equilibrium thermodynamics.

Hypothesis 4b: Systems with intrinsic separation of timescales between driving and relaxation processes will exhibit more robust SOC signatures, consistent with theoretical requirements for self-organization to criticality.

Hypothesis 4c: Mesoscale phenomena under strong homeostatic regulation will show systematic deviations from criticality, suggesting that biological systems may be tuned away from critical points to ensure reliable function.

These hypotheses generate testable predictions that will be evaluated through systematic comparison across phenomena. By analyzing multiple mesoscale systems with identical statistical methods, we can identify mechanistic features that correlate with SOC signatures, providing theoretical insight beyond phenomenological classification.

Our approach explicitly acknowledges that negative results—failure to find SOC signatures—would be equally valuable. If mesoscale dynamics systematically deviate from SOC predictions, this would indicate that emergence at the mesoscale follows different organizing principles than other complex systems, motivating development of alternative theoretical frameworks specific to cellular biology.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises four integrated phases: dataset identification and curation, data harmonization and quality control, statistical analysis for SOC signatures, and theoretical synthesis.

Phase 1: Dataset Identification and Curation (Months 1-6)

We will systematically identify publicly available live-cell imaging datasets capturing dynamic mesoscale events from three primary sources: the Image Data Resource (IDR), Allen Cell Explorer, and supplementary data from high-impact publications. Our target is approximately 50 datasets spanning four mesoscale phenomena: calcium dynamics (15 datasets), condensate formation (12 datasets), cytoskeletal rearrangements (13 datasets), and kinase signaling (10 datasets).

Dataset selection criteria include: (1) temporal resolution sufficient to capture event dynamics (sub-second for calcium, sub-minute for condensates), (2) spatial resolution enabling individual event identification, (3) sufficient recording duration to capture multiple events per cell, (4) availability of raw or minimally processed image data, and (5) adequate metadata describing experimental conditions. We will create a standardized dataset registry documenting provenance, acquisition parameters, and quality metrics.

Phase 2: Data Harmonization and Quantification (Months 4-12)

Data harmonization represents the most technically challenging aspect of this synthesis project. We will develop phenomenon-specific image analysis pipelines that extract quantitative time-series from heterogeneous imaging data.

For calcium dynamics, we will implement automated detection of calcium transients using established algorithms (CaImAn, Suite2p adaptations) modified for non-neuronal cells, extracting event amplitudes, durations, rise times, and spatial extents. For condensate dynamics, we will apply particle tracking and segmentation methods to identify nucleation events, measuring initial sizes, growth rates, and steady-state volumes. Cytoskeletal analysis will employ optical flow and texture analysis methods to quantify reorganization magnitudes and spatial scales. Kinase signaling analysis will use biosensor intensity quantification with appropriate background correction and normalization.

Critically, we will develop cross-dataset normalization procedures that account for differences in fluorophore brightness, expression levels, imaging depths, and acquisition parameters. Normalization will be validated through comparison of overlapping datasets (same cell type, different laboratories) and through simulation-based assessment of how normalization affects avalanche statistics.

Phase 3: Statistical Analysis for SOC Signatures (Months 8-18)

Our statistical analysis pipeline implements rigorous methods developed in the statistical physics community for SOC identification, adapted for biological time-series data.

Power-law fitting will use maximum likelihood estimation with appropriate corrections for discrete data and bounded ranges. We will apply the Clauset-Shalizi-Newman framework for power-law detection, which provides statistically rigorous comparison against alternative distributions. For each dataset, we will compute likelihood ratios comparing power-law fits against log-normal, exponential, stretched exponential, and truncated power-law alternatives.

Finite-size scaling analysis will examine how avalanche statistics depend on system size. We will leverage natural variation in cell sizes within datasets and, where available, compare measurements from different cell types with varying volumes. Scaling collapse analysis will test whether data from different system sizes collapse onto universal curves when appropriately rescaled.

We will implement branching ratio analysis, which provides an independent test for criticality by measuring the average number of events triggered by each event. Systems at criticality exhibit branching ratios approaching unity.

Phase 4: Theoretical Synthesis (Months 15-24)

The theoretical synthesis phase integrates empirical findings with mechanistic understanding. We will develop minimal mathematical models for each mesoscale phenomenon incorporating known biochemical mechanisms, then analyze whether these models predict SOC signatures under biologically plausible parameter ranges. This bidirectional approach—testing data against SOC predictions while assessing whether known mechanisms could produce criticality—will generate mechanistic hypotheses for future experimental testing.

All analysis code will be developed collaboratively using version control, with continuous integration testing ensuring reproducibility. We will conduct blinded analyses where team members analyze datasets without knowledge of preliminary results from other phenomena, reducing confirmation bias.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will deliver four categories of outcomes with immediate and long-term impact on mesoscale biology.

First, we will produce harmonized mesoscale dynamics datasets comprising quantitative time-series extracted from approximately 50 published imaging studies. These datasets, standardized with consistent metadata and quality annotations, will constitute a unique resource for the cell biology community. Even independent of SOC analysis, these harmonized data will enable comparative studies of mesoscale dynamics across cell types, conditions, and phenomena that are currently impossible due to data fragmentation.

Second, we will provide definitive statistical evaluation of SOC signatures across four mesoscale phenomena. Our rigorous analysis will either confirm that criticality provides a unifying framework for mesoscale organization—with profound implications for theoretical cell biology—or establish that biological systems operate in distinct dynamical regimes requiring alternative theoretical foundations. We will quantify confidence intervals for all statistical conclusions and explicitly characterize the boundaries of our inference.

Third, we will release open-source software implementing rigorous SOC analysis methods adapted for biological time-series. This software, documented with tutorials and example analyses, will enable the broader community to apply these methods to new datasets. We anticipate this toolkit will become a standard resource for quantitative analysis of cellular dynamics.

Fourth, we will produce a theoretical synthesis identifying which mesoscale phenomena are candidates for criticality-based explanations and articulating mechanistic features that predict SOC signatures. This framework will generate specific hypotheses for future experimental testing and guide development of quantitative models for mesoscale organization.

The broader impact extends beyond immediate deliverables. By bringing statistical physics methods into mesoscale biology, we establish new standards for quantitative analysis of cellular dynamics. Our training program will develop five early-career scientists with rare interdisciplinary expertise spanning physics and cell biology. The open science practices we implement will serve as a model for future synthesis projects. Regardless of whether SOC signatures are confirmed, this project will substantially advance our understanding of emergent properties at the mesoscale, directly fulfilling NCEMS's scientific mission.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
This Working Group is committed to exemplary open science practices that maximize the impact and reproducibility of our work while serving as a model for future synthesis projects.

All harmonized datasets will be deposited in Zenodo with comprehensive metadata following FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable). Each dataset will include standardized documentation of provenance, processing steps, quality metrics, and known limitations. Raw extracted time-series, intermediate processed data, and final analysis-ready datasets will all be made available, enabling users to enter the analysis pipeline at any stage.

Our complete analysis codebase will be maintained in public GitHub repositories under permissive open-source licenses (MIT or Apache 2.0). Code will be organized as modular, documented packages with automated testing ensuring functionality across computing environments. We will provide containerized computing environments (Docker/Singularity) guaranteeing exact reproducibility of all computational analyses regardless of users' local software configurations.

Every figure and statistical result in our publications will be accompanied by reproducible Jupyter notebooks that regenerate results from deposited data using deposited code. These notebooks will include narrative documentation explaining analytical choices and their justifications. We will implement continuous integration testing that automatically verifies notebook reproducibility as code evolves.

We will pursue open-access publication for all manuscripts, utilizing preprint servers (bioRxiv) for rapid dissemination prior to peer review. Detailed methods papers will accompany primary research publications, providing sufficient detail for independent replication. We will maintain a project website with accessible summaries of findings for broad audiences.

Our commitment to open science extends to the research process itself. Working Group meetings will produce publicly available meeting notes documenting analytical decisions and their rationales. This transparency ensures that our conclusions can be independently evaluated and that our methods can be readily adopted by others.

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: The Compositional Grammar of Post-Translational Modifications and Emergent Regulatory States
abstract: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) regulate protein function combinatorially: phosphorylation alongside acetylation alongside ubiquitination produces emergent regulatory states irreducible to single-PTM effects. Despite vast public PTM datasets, no synthesis-scale framework has tested whether PTM combinations follow compositional rules analogous to syntactic grammars in linguistics, where small numbers of rules generate large numbers of valid combinations. This Working Group will synthesize PTM proteomics data from ProteomeXchange, PhosphoSitePlus, dbPTM, and condition-specific PTM atlases together with interaction-context databases (BioGRID, IntAct) and structural data to derive proteome-scale combinatorial PTM rules and link them to regulatory outcomes. The team integrates mass spectrometry experts in PTM identification, computational linguists with grammar-induction expertise, structural biologists, and machine-learning researchers experienced in compositional models. We will harmonize PTM datasets across ~300 conditions and tissues, control for false-discovery and stoichiometry biases, and apply grammar-induction algorithms originally developed in computational linguistics to identify combinatorial PTM rules. Statistical models will test whether identified rules predict downstream regulatory outcomes—interaction changes, localization shifts, degradation rates—better than additive PTM-effect models. Deliverables include (1) a harmonized combinatorial PTM atlas with controlled vocabulary, (2) inferred PTM grammars for major regulatory contexts, (3) open-source software bringing grammar-induction methods to PTM analysis, and (4) testable predictions about combinatorial PTM effects in unstudied contexts. NCEMS support is essential because the project bridges proteomics, computational linguistics, and structural biology in ways no single lab supports, and because PTM dataset harmonization at this scale demands sustained infrastructure. The training plan supports five trainees from proteomics, computer science, and structural biology programs through cross-disciplinary co-mentoring, formal training in grammar induction and PTM mass spectrometry, and joint sub-projects on specific PTM systems. Trainees will participate in a journal club spanning linguistics and biology and will co-author the methods paper. All harmonized data and code will be released through ProteomeXchange and GitHub, the inferred grammars will be queryable through a web interface, and the software will be packaged as an installable library. By extending the histone-code concept to a proteome-wide formal grammar, this project addresses an innovative analytical strategy that could transform how PTM combinatorics is studied, with implications for drug discovery and understanding regulatory dysfunction in disease.
background_and_significance:
Post-translational modifications (PTMs) represent one of the most powerful mechanisms by which cells expand the functional diversity of their proteomes. Over 400 distinct PTM types have been catalogued, with phosphorylation, acetylation, methylation, ubiquitination, and SUMOylation among the most extensively studied. These chemical modifications alter protein structure, activity, localization, stability, and interaction partners, collectively orchestrating cellular responses to internal and external signals. The biological significance of PTMs is underscored by their dysregulation in cancer, neurodegeneration, metabolic disorders, and infectious diseases, making them attractive therapeutic targets.

Historically, PTM research has focused on individual modifications in isolation, generating valuable insights into specific regulatory circuits. However, this reductionist approach fails to capture the combinatorial complexity that characterizes PTM-mediated regulation in living cells. The histone code hypothesis, proposed two decades ago, revolutionized epigenetics by suggesting that combinations of histone modifications constitute a regulatory language read by effector proteins. Yet this conceptual framework has not been systematically extended to the broader proteome, despite accumulating evidence that combinatorial PTM patterns govern protein function across diverse cellular contexts.

The emergence of high-throughput mass spectrometry has generated unprecedented volumes of PTM data, now deposited in public repositories including ProteomeXchange, PhosphoSitePlus, and dbPTM. These databases collectively contain millions of PTM site identifications across thousands of experimental conditions, tissues, and organisms. However, these data remain fragmented across platforms with inconsistent nomenclature, variable quality metrics, and limited integration with functional outcome data. This fragmentation represents both a challenge and an opportunity: the raw material for proteome-scale PTM synthesis exists, but requires coordinated harmonization efforts beyond individual laboratory capabilities.

The central conceptual innovation of this proposal is the application of formal grammar theory from computational linguistics to PTM combinatorics. In linguistics, grammars are rule systems that specify which combinations of elements (words, morphemes) are valid and meaningful. Remarkably, small sets of rules can generate vast numbers of valid sentences while excluding invalid combinations. We hypothesize that analogous compositional rules govern PTM combinations, where certain modifications co-occur preferentially, others are mutually exclusive, and specific combinations encode distinct regulatory meanings. This framework offers predictive power absent from current approaches: if PTM grammars exist, they should predict functional outcomes better than models treating modifications independently.

This synthesis project addresses NCEMS's core mission by investigating emergent properties at the mesoscale—the scale between individual PTM events and cellular phenotypes. Combinatorial PTM states represent precisely the type of emergent phenomenon where system properties cannot be predicted from component properties alone. The project leverages AI and data science to synthesize publicly available data, requires multidisciplinary collaboration impossible within single laboratories, and will train next-generation scientists in cross-disciplinary synthesis approaches. Success will transform our understanding of how PTM combinations encode regulatory information, with implications spanning basic biology to drug discovery.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses four interconnected research questions, each accompanied by testable hypotheses derived from our central premise that PTM combinations follow compositional grammatical rules.

Research Question 1: Do PTM combinations across the proteome exhibit non-random co-occurrence patterns consistent with compositional grammar rules?

Hypothesis 1a: PTM co-occurrence patterns will deviate significantly from null models assuming independent modification probabilities, with specific modification pairs showing strong positive or negative associations beyond what stoichiometry and detection biases predict.

Hypothesis 1b: The number of distinct PTM combination patterns observed across proteins will be substantially smaller than the theoretical combinatorial space, consistent with grammar-constrained generation where rules limit valid combinations.

Hypothesis 1c: PTM co-occurrence rules will show hierarchical organization analogous to syntactic structure, with local dependencies (adjacent residues) and long-range dependencies (distant domains) following distinct but interacting rule sets.

Research Question 2: Are PTM grammatical rules conserved across biological contexts, or do distinct regulatory grammars operate in different tissues, conditions, or protein families?

Hypothesis 2a: Core PTM grammar rules will be conserved across tissues and conditions, analogous to universal grammar principles in linguistics, while context-specific rules will modify these core patterns.

Hypothesis 2b: Protein families sharing functional domains will exhibit shared local PTM grammars within those domains, reflecting conserved regulatory mechanisms.

Hypothesis 2c: Disease states will show systematic grammar violations or grammar shifts compared to normal conditions, providing a new framework for understanding regulatory dysfunction.

Research Question 3: Do inferred PTM grammars predict regulatory outcomes better than additive single-PTM effect models?

Hypothesis 3a: Combinatorial PTM rules will predict protein-protein interaction changes with significantly higher accuracy than models summing individual PTM effects on interactions.

Hypothesis 3b: PTM grammar-based models will outperform additive models in predicting protein localization changes, degradation rates, and enzymatic activity modulation.

Hypothesis 3c: The predictive advantage of grammar-based models will be greatest for proteins with high PTM density and for regulatory outcomes involving multiple effector proteins.

Research Question 4: Can structural and biophysical constraints explain observed PTM grammatical rules?

Hypothesis 4a: Mutually exclusive PTM combinations will correlate with structural constraints including steric clash, overlapping binding surfaces, or incompatible conformational states.

Hypothesis 4b: Synergistic PTM combinations will correlate with cooperative structural effects, including allosteric networks connecting modification sites.

Hypothesis 4c: PTM grammar rules will show stronger structural explanations for ordered (folded) protein regions than for intrinsically disordered regions, where sequence context may dominate.

These hypotheses are designed to be testable through synthesis of existing data without requiring new experimental data generation. Each hypothesis generates specific quantitative predictions that can be evaluated against harmonized datasets. Importantly, negative results would also be informative: if PTM combinations prove largely random or context-independent, this would refute the grammar hypothesis and redirect the field toward alternative frameworks. The hierarchical structure of our hypotheses ensures that partial support still yields valuable insights about PTM regulatory logic.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises four integrated phases: data harmonization, grammar induction, functional validation, and structural interpretation.

Phase 1: Data Harmonization and Quality Control (Months 1-8)

We will systematically retrieve PTM datasets from ProteomeXchange (raw mass spectrometry data), PhosphoSitePlus (curated phosphorylation, acetylation, ubiquitination sites), dbPTM (comprehensive PTM annotations), and specialized atlases including the Cancer PTM Atlas and tissue-specific proteome resources. Initial scope targets approximately 300 distinct experimental conditions spanning normal tissues, disease states, and perturbation experiments in human and mouse.

Harmonization requires addressing several technical challenges. First, we will implement unified PTM site nomenclature using UniProt canonical sequences as reference, mapping all site identifications to standardized coordinates. Second, we will apply consistent false discovery rate thresholds (1% site-level FDR) and develop quality scores integrating spectral evidence, localization probability, and cross-study replication. Third, we will estimate PTM stoichiometry where quantitative data permit, distinguishing high-occupancy from low-occupancy modifications. Fourth, we will develop controlled vocabulary for experimental conditions enabling systematic comparison across studies.

The harmonized dataset will be structured as a tensor representing proteins × sites × modification types × conditions, with associated metadata and quality metrics. This structure enables both protein-centric and condition-centric analyses.

Phase 2: Grammar Induction (Months 6-18)

We will adapt grammar induction algorithms from computational linguistics to PTM data. Specifically, we will implement probabilistic context-free grammar (PCFG) induction using the inside-outside algorithm, treating PTM patterns as strings to be parsed. We will also apply more recent neural grammar induction methods including recurrent neural network grammars and transformer-based approaches that learn compositional structure without explicit rule specification.

Critical adaptations for biological data include: (1) handling variable-length proteins with different PTM site densities, (2) incorporating spatial information (residue positions, domain boundaries) as structural constraints, (3) modeling condition-dependent grammar parameters, and (4) accounting for missing data where PTMs may exist but remain undetected.

We will benchmark grammar models against null models (independent PTM probabilities), pairwise co-occurrence models (capturing only two-way interactions), and deep learning models without explicit compositional structure. Model comparison will use held-out prediction accuracy and information-theoretic criteria balancing fit and complexity.

Phase 3: Functional Outcome Prediction (Months 12-22)

We will link inferred PTM grammars to regulatory outcomes using interaction databases (BioGRID, IntAct, STRING), localization annotations (Human Protein Atlas, UniProt subcellular localization), and protein stability data (half-life measurements, ubiquitin-proteasome pathway annotations). For each outcome type, we will train predictive models using PTM grammar features and compare performance against single-PTM and additive models using cross-validation and independent test sets.

Phase 4: Structural Interpretation (Months 16-24)

We will map PTM grammar rules onto protein structures using AlphaFold2 predicted structures and experimental structures from PDB. Analysis will identify structural correlates of grammatical rules including spatial clustering, surface accessibility patterns, and proximity to functional sites. Molecular dynamics simulations from published trajectories will provide dynamic context for interpreting PTM cooperativity.

Throughout all phases, the Working Group will meet biweekly via videoconference with quarterly in-person meetings at NCEMS. Sub-teams organized around each phase will coordinate through shared computational infrastructure and documentation platforms.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will deliver four major outcomes with transformative potential for molecular and cellular biology.

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: The Exclusion Grammar: What Sequence Features Keep Proteins Out of Condensates
abstract: Research on biomolecular condensates has overwhelmingly focused on what is included—which proteins phase separate and which clients are recruited—while the equally informative question of what is systematically excluded has received little attention. Yet exclusion may be more diagnostic of condensate identity than inclusion, because excluded proteins reveal the active mechanisms of selectivity. This Working Group will synthesize public condensate proteomics datasets together with whole-cell proteomes, localization atlases (HPA, OpenCell), and IDR feature databases to derive the first proteome-scale rules of condensate exclusion. The team brings together biophysicists studying phase separation, mass spectrometrists with quantitative condensate proteomics expertise, machine-learning researchers experienced in negative-set construction, and cell biologists with deep condensate-system expertise. We will define exclusion sets carefully—proteins expressed and abundant in the relevant condition, present in the cell, but absent from condensate proteomes above defined confidence thresholds—and harmonize these sets across ~40 condensate types from public datasets. Predictive models will test whether sequence and biochemical features (charge patterning, hydrophobicity, structural rigidity, cell cycle regulation, specific PTMs) distinguish excluded from included proteins more strongly than they distinguish included from random. Deliverables include (1) carefully constructed exclusion datasets across condensate types with explicit confidence frameworks, (2) sequence-based exclusion predictors released as a community web tool, (3) a quantitative grammar of exclusion features, and (4) testable hypotheses about exclusion mechanisms for follow-up experimental work. NCEMS support is essential because constructing principled negative sets across condensate datasets requires sustained methodological work and because the synthesis demands harmonization no single lab supports. The training plan supports four trainees in biophysics, computational biology, and proteomics through coordinated sub-projects on specific condensate systems, formal training in negative-set construction and predictive modeling, and joint analyses requiring fluency across the relevant disciplines. Trainees will co-author both the methods paper and condensate-specific analyses. All datasets, code, and trained models will be released openly with versioned DOIs through Zenodo, exclusion predictors will be available as a web tool, and the project will contribute to community standards for condensate-data reporting. By inverting the standard inclusion question, this project addresses a genuinely novel scientific question and is likely to reveal selectivity mechanisms invisible to inclusion-focused studies, with implications for understanding why disease-associated proteins mis-localize to condensates they would normally be excluded from.
background_and_significance:
Biomolecular condensates represent a paradigm shift in our understanding of cellular organization. These membrane-less compartments, formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), orchestrate critical cellular processes including transcription, RNA processing, stress responses, and signal transduction. The past decade has witnessed explosive growth in condensate research, with over 50 distinct condensate types now characterized, including nucleoli, stress granules, P-bodies, and nuclear speckles. However, a striking asymmetry pervades this literature: research has overwhelmingly focused on inclusion—identifying scaffold proteins that drive phase separation and client proteins that partition into condensates—while systematically neglecting the equally fundamental question of exclusion.

This knowledge gap represents a significant missed opportunity. From a thermodynamic perspective, the selective exclusion of proteins from condensate interiors is as energetically meaningful as their recruitment. The dense, crowded environment within condensates creates distinct physicochemical conditions that actively exclude proteins lacking appropriate interaction motifs or possessing incompatible biophysical properties. Understanding exclusion is therefore essential for comprehending how condensates achieve their remarkable selectivity, maintaining distinct compositions despite the absence of membrane barriers.

The significance of exclusion extends beyond basic science to disease mechanisms. Numerous pathologies involve aberrant protein localization to condensates, including neurodegenerative diseases where proteins like TDP-43 and FUS accumulate in cytoplasmic stress granules rather than maintaining nuclear localization. These disease-associated proteins may represent failures of normal exclusion mechanisms. Without understanding the rules governing exclusion, we cannot fully explain why certain mutations cause proteins to mis-localize or why aging cells lose compartmentalization fidelity.

The timing for this synthesis project is optimal. Public repositories now contain quantitative proteomics data for dozens of condensate types, generated using proximity labeling, immunopurification, and fluorescence-based sorting approaches. The Human Protein Atlas (HPA) and OpenCell projects provide comprehensive subcellular localization data, while databases like DisProt and MobiDB catalog intrinsically disordered region (IDR) features across proteomes. Critically, these resources have never been systematically integrated to address exclusion.

This project directly addresses NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale. Condensates represent quintessential mesoscale phenomena—emergent structures arising from collective molecular interactions that exhibit properties unpredictable from individual components. The selectivity of condensates, including both inclusion and exclusion, emerges from the interplay of multivalent interactions, sequence features, and cellular context. By deriving proteome-scale exclusion rules, we will illuminate fundamental principles governing mesoscale organization.

The synthesis approach is essential because no single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in condensate biology, quantitative proteomics, machine learning, and biophysics required for this undertaking. Furthermore, constructing rigorous negative sets—defining what is truly excluded versus simply undetected—demands methodological sophistication that benefits from sustained collaborative development. This project exemplifies the community-scale synthesis that NCEMS was designed to catalyze, promising insights unattainable through conventional single-laboratory approaches.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses a central scientific question: What sequence and biochemical features systematically exclude proteins from biomolecular condensates? This overarching question decomposes into four specific research questions, each with testable hypotheses derived from current understanding of phase separation biophysics.

Research Question 1: Can we define rigorous, proteome-scale exclusion sets for diverse condensate types?

Hypothesis 1: Proteins that are highly expressed, cytoplasmically or nucleoplasmically localized, yet consistently absent from condensate proteomes across multiple studies represent genuinely excluded species rather than technical false negatives. We predict that 15-30% of the expressed proteome will meet stringent exclusion criteria for any given condensate type, and that exclusion sets will show partial overlap across condensate types sharing physicochemical properties.

Research Question 2: Do sequence features distinguish excluded proteins from included proteins more effectively than they distinguish included proteins from random proteome samples?

Hypothesis 2: Exclusion is an active, feature-driven process rather than merely the absence of inclusion motifs. We hypothesize that machine learning classifiers trained on excluded versus included proteins will achieve higher discriminative performance (measured by AUROC and precision-recall metrics) than classifiers trained on included versus random proteins. This would demonstrate that exclusion carries distinct informational content beyond the inverse of inclusion.

Research Question 3: What specific sequence and biochemical features constitute the exclusion grammar?

Hypothesis 3a: Proteins with high net charge density, particularly those with unbalanced charge distributions, will be systematically excluded from condensates whose scaffolds have matching charge character, reflecting electrostatic repulsion mechanisms.

Hypothesis 3b: Proteins with high predicted structural rigidity (low disorder content, high beta-sheet propensity, abundant disulfide bonds) will show elevated exclusion from condensates dependent on flexible, multivalent IDR interactions.

Hypothesis 3c: Specific post-translational modifications, particularly extensive glycosylation and certain phosphorylation patterns, will correlate with exclusion from specific condensate types, suggesting PTM-based exclusion mechanisms.

Hypothesis 3d: Proteins with hydrophobic surface patches exceeding threshold values will be excluded from hydrophilic condensate cores while potentially enriching at condensate interfaces.

Research Question 4: Is exclusion condensate-specific or are there universal exclusion features?

Hypothesis 4: We predict a hierarchical organization of exclusion features, with some features conferring universal exclusion across most condensate types (e.g., extreme structural rigidity) while other features drive condensate-specific exclusion (e.g., charge patterning matching specific scaffold proteins). This hierarchy will enable classification of condensates based on their exclusion profiles, potentially revealing functional relationships invisible to inclusion-based analyses.

Research Question 5: Do disease-associated mutations alter exclusion feature profiles?

Hypothesis 5: Pathogenic mutations in proteins that mis-localize to condensates in disease states will systematically alter exclusion-associated features, converting excluded proteins into included ones. Analysis of ClinVar pathogenic variants in normally-excluded proteins will reveal enrichment for mutations that reduce exclusion scores, providing mechanistic insight into disease pathophysiology.

These hypotheses are designed to be falsifiable through our synthesis approach. Negative results—for example, finding that exclusion features are no more predictive than inclusion features—would themselves be informative, suggesting that exclusion represents passive failure of recruitment rather than active selectivity. Our analysis framework will quantify confidence intervals and effect sizes to distinguish meaningful biological signals from noise inherent in proteomics datasets.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises four integrated phases: data acquisition and harmonization, exclusion set construction, predictive modeling, and validation and interpretation.

Phase 1: Data Acquisition and Harmonization (Months 1-6)

We will systematically compile condensate proteomics datasets from public repositories including PRIDE, MassIVE, and supplementary materials from published studies. Our preliminary survey identifies quantitative proteomics data for approximately 40 condensate types, including stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, nuclear speckles, Cajal bodies, PML bodies, and various signaling condensates. For each dataset, we will extract protein identifications, quantitative metrics (spectral counts, intensity values, enrichment ratios), and experimental metadata.

Critically, we will integrate these condensate-specific datasets with whole-cell proteome references (PaxDB, ProteomicsDB), subcellular localization atlases (Human Protein Atlas subcellular section, OpenCell), and protein feature databases (UniProt, DisProt, MobiDB, D2P2). This integration enables the key analytical innovation: distinguishing truly excluded proteins from those simply not expressed or localized elsewhere in the cell.

Harmonization will address cross-study technical variation through established proteomics normalization approaches. We will develop a unified confidence scoring framework incorporating factors including number of supporting studies, quantitative stringency, and experimental methodology.

Phase 2: Exclusion Set Construction (Months 4-10)

Defining rigorous negative sets represents the methodological core of this project. A protein qualifies as excluded from a specific condensate only if it meets all criteria: (1) expressed above threshold in the relevant cell type and condition based on transcriptomic and proteomic data; (2) localized to the same subcellular compartment as the condensate (e.g., cytoplasmic proteins for stress granules); (3) absent from condensate proteomes across multiple independent studies with defined confidence thresholds.

We will implement a tiered confidence framework: high-confidence exclusion requires absence across all available studies for a condensate type; medium-confidence requires absence from majority of studies; provisional exclusion applies to single-study absences. This framework explicitly acknowledges uncertainty inherent in negative set construction.

The machine learning team members will contribute expertise in principled negative set construction, drawing on methodologies developed for protein-protein interaction prediction and drug-target identification where similar challenges arise.

Phase 3: Predictive Modeling (Months 8-16)

We will compute comprehensive sequence and biochemical features for all proteins, including: amino acid composition and physicochemical properties; charge patterning metrics (kappa, NCPR, FCR); hydrophobicity distributions; disorder predictions (IUPred, PONDR); secondary structure propensities; predicted post-translational modification sites; domain annotations; and structural features from AlphaFold predictions.

Predictive models will employ gradient boosting frameworks (XGBoost, LightGBM) and neural network architectures, with rigorous cross-validation preventing overfitting. Crucially, we will compare three classification tasks: excluded versus included; included versus random; and excluded versus random. Superior performance on the first task would validate our central hypothesis that exclusion carries distinct information.

Feature importance analysis using SHAP values will identify the most predictive exclusion features, enabling construction of the quantitative exclusion grammar.

Phase 4: Validation and Interpretation (Months 14-20)

We will validate exclusion predictors through held-out test sets from independent studies and through analysis of proteins with known condensate localization from orthogonal imaging-based methods. Disease variant analysis will test whether pathogenic mutations alter exclusion scores for mis-localizing proteins.

The team will convene for three in-person working meetings at NCEMS facilities, supplemented by monthly virtual meetings, to ensure integration across sub-projects and collective interpretation of results.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will deliver four major outcomes with lasting impact on the condensate biology field and broader molecular cell biology.

First, we will generate the first comprehensive exclusion datasets covering approximately 40 condensate types, with explicit confidence frameworks and full methodological documentation. These datasets will serve as foundational resources for the condensate community, enabling researchers to ask not only "what is in this condensate?" but "what is actively kept out?" We anticipate these resources will catalyze new research directions examining exclusion mechanisms.

Second, we will release sequence-based exclusion predictors as freely accessible web tools and downloadable models. Researchers will be able to query whether candidate proteins are predicted to be excluded from specific condensate types, informing experimental design and hypothesis generation. These tools will be particularly valuable for interpreting disease mutations and designing synthetic proteins with controlled condensate localization.

Third, we will publish a quantitative grammar of exclusion features—the specific sequence and biochemical properties that drive exclusion from different condensate classes. This grammar will provide mechanistic insight into how condensates achieve selectivity without membrane barriers, advancing fundamental understanding of mesoscale cellular organization.

Fourth, we will generate testable hypotheses about exclusion mechanisms suitable for experimental follow-up. These hypotheses, derived from computational predictions, will be explicitly formulated with suggested experimental approaches, bridging synthesis research to future laboratory investigations.

The broader impact extends to disease understanding. By identifying features that normally exclude proteins from condensates, we provide a framework for understanding why disease-associated proteins mis-localize. This has implications for neurodegenerative diseases, cancer, and viral infections where condensate dysregulation plays pathogenic roles.

Finally, this project establishes methodological precedents for negative-set construction in proteomics that will benefit fields beyond condensate biology, contributing analytical innovations applicable wherever defining what is absent is as important as defining what is present.

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Disease as Failure of Emergence: Cross-Disease Synthesis of Mesoscale Disruption
abstract: Many diseases that affect cellular function—ALS, frontotemporal dementia, ribosomopathies, laminopathies, ciliopathies—involve disruption of mesoscale assemblies, yet the field treats each disease in isolation, obscuring potentially shared signatures of emergence failure. This Working Group will synthesize disease-relevant mesoscale datasets across multiple disease classes through a unified framework: emergence integrity. The team brings together cell biologists from each disease area, condensate biologists, structural biologists, computational biologists experienced in cross-disease integration, and machine-learning researchers expert in transfer learning. We will assemble harmonized disease-relevant datasets including patient-derived cell imaging, disease-relevant proteomics and interactomes, mesoscale-relevant variant catalogs (gnomAD, ClinVar, disease-specific databases), and cellular phenotyping screens from JUMP and other repositories. The synthesis will define quantitative metrics for mesoscale emergence integrity—stoichiometric fidelity, spatial organization, dynamic responsiveness—and test whether disease states share signatures of emergence failure across disease classes. Cross-disease comparison will identify shared molecular vulnerabilities and disease-specific signatures, and machine-learning models will test whether features learned on one disease transfer to others. Deliverables include (1) cross-disease harmonized datasets with shared annotation framework, (2) quantitative emergence-integrity metrics with open-source implementations, (3) a cross-disease atlas of mesoscale disruption, and (4) testable hypotheses about shared therapeutic targets. NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis spans disease communities that rarely collaborate and because cross-disease harmonization demands sustained ontological and computational work. The training plan supports six trainees from diverse disease and computational backgrounds through coordinated sub-projects on specific diseases, formal training in cross-disease data integration and reproducible analysis, and joint work on the cross-disease atlas. Trainees will participate in a cross-disciplinary seminar series, present at disease-area meetings as well as cell-biology venues, and co-author the resulting papers. All harmonized data, code, and metrics will be released through appropriate disease and general repositories with cross-references, and the cross-disease atlas will be queryable through a public web interface. The broader impact is substantial: identifying shared signatures of mesoscale emergence failure across diseases could illuminate therapeutic strategies that benefit multiple patient populations and would establish emergence integrity as a clinically meaningful concept. By treating diverse diseases under a shared mesoscale framework, this project demonstrates how synthesis can produce insights invisible to single-disease research.
background_and_significance:
The mesoscale—the organizational level between individual biomolecules and membrane-bound organelles—represents a frontier in cellular biology where emergent properties arise from collective molecular behaviors. At this scale, biomolecular condensates, cytoskeletal networks, nuclear lamina assemblies, and ciliary structures form through principles of self-organization, phase separation, and cooperative interactions. These mesoscale assemblies exhibit emergent properties that cannot be predicted from their individual components: they sense cellular signals, buffer stochastic fluctuations, organize biochemical reactions spatiotemporally, and respond dynamically to stress. When these emergent properties fail, disease ensues.

Remarkably, diverse human diseases share a common feature: disruption of mesoscale organization. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) involve pathological aggregation of RNA-binding proteins like TDP-43 and FUS, which normally participate in stress granules and other condensates. Ribosomopathies—including Diamond-Blackfan anemia and Shwachman-Diamond syndrome—result from perturbations in ribosome biogenesis, a process requiring precise stoichiometric assembly of dozens of proteins and RNAs. Laminopathies, caused by mutations in nuclear lamina components, disrupt the mechanical and organizational properties of the nuclear envelope. Ciliopathies affect the highly organized ciliary axoneme and transition zone, structures requiring exquisite spatial coordination of hundreds of proteins.

Despite these mechanistic parallels, each disease community operates largely in isolation. ALS researchers focus on prion-like propagation and stress granule dynamics; ribosomopathy researchers emphasize ribosome assembly checkpoints; laminopathy researchers study nuclear mechanics. This siloed approach has generated deep disease-specific knowledge but has obscured potentially unifying principles. We hypothesize that these diseases share quantifiable signatures of "emergence failure"—breakdowns in the collective properties that normally arise from mesoscale organization.

The significance of this synthesis project is threefold. First, it addresses a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biology: what are the organizational principles that enable emergence at the mesoscale, and how do these principles fail in disease? This question cannot be answered by studying single diseases because emergence failure may manifest differently across biological contexts while sharing underlying quantitative signatures. Second, the project leverages an unprecedented wealth of publicly available data that has never been integrated across disease boundaries. Patient-derived cell imaging datasets, disease-relevant proteomics, comprehensive variant catalogs (gnomAD, ClinVar), and large-scale cellular phenotyping screens (JUMP-CP) provide complementary views of mesoscale disruption. Third, the project has direct translational implications: identifying shared molecular vulnerabilities across diseases could reveal therapeutic strategies applicable to multiple patient populations, transforming how we approach diseases of mesoscale dysfunction.

This synthesis is timely because the data resources and computational methods required have only recently matured. Machine learning approaches for cross-domain transfer learning, advances in image-based profiling, and comprehensive variant effect prediction now enable rigorous cross-disease comparison. NCEMS provides the unique infrastructure to bring together disease communities that have never systematically collaborated, creating a new paradigm for understanding cellular pathology through the lens of emergence.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses three interconnected research questions that probe the fundamental nature of mesoscale emergence and its failure in disease.

**Research Question 1: Can mesoscale emergence integrity be quantified through universal metrics applicable across diverse biological assemblies?**

We hypothesize that mesoscale emergence integrity can be captured through three quantifiable dimensions: (1) stoichiometric fidelity—the precision with which component ratios are maintained; (2) spatial organization—the accuracy of component localization and assembly geometry; and (3) dynamic responsiveness—the capacity to appropriately assemble, disassemble, or reorganize in response to cellular signals. We predict that these metrics, while manifesting through different molecular players in different assemblies, will provide a common quantitative framework for assessing emergence across condensates, nuclear lamina, ribosomes, and cilia. This hypothesis is testable through systematic analysis of imaging, proteomic, and phenotypic data across disease classes.

**Research Question 2: Do diseases of mesoscale dysfunction share quantitative signatures of emergence failure that transcend disease-specific molecular mechanisms?**

We hypothesize that diseases affecting different mesoscale assemblies will exhibit convergent signatures when analyzed through emergence-integrity metrics. Specifically, we predict that: (a) disease-associated variants across all five disease classes will disproportionately affect residues critical for stoichiometric interactions, spatial localization signals, or dynamic regulatory sites; (b) cellular phenotypes in patient-derived cells will show correlated patterns of emergence failure detectable through high-content imaging; and (c) protein-protein interaction network perturbations will reveal shared "emergence hubs"—proteins whose disruption compromises emergence across multiple assembly types. This hypothesis challenges the prevailing view that each disease class requires entirely distinct mechanistic understanding.

**Research Question 3: Can machine learning models trained on emergence failure in one disease class transfer predictive power to other disease classes?**

We hypothesize that emergence failure follows generalizable rules that machine learning can capture and transfer across diseases. We will test whether: (a) variant effect predictors trained on one disease class (e.g., ALS-associated condensate mutations) improve prediction of pathogenic variants in other classes (e.g., ciliopathy mutations); (b) cellular phenotype classifiers trained to detect emergence failure in one context generalize to others; and (c) multi-task learning across diseases improves prediction accuracy compared to single-disease models. Successful transfer would demonstrate that emergence failure has learnable, disease-agnostic features.

**Secondary Hypotheses:**

We further hypothesize that: (1) emergence failure signatures will correlate with disease severity and progression across disease classes; (2) certain protein families—particularly those involved in phase separation, scaffolding, and mechanotransduction—will emerge as recurrent vulnerability points; (3) post-translational modification sites regulating assembly dynamics will be enriched among disease-associated variants across classes; and (4) compensatory mechanisms that preserve emergence integrity will be identifiable through analysis of benign variants in emergence-critical proteins.

These hypotheses generate specific, testable predictions that will be evaluated through systematic data synthesis. Negative results would be equally informative, suggesting that emergence failure is more context-dependent than hypothesized and requiring disease-specific frameworks. Our analytical approach is designed to rigorously distinguish between shared emergence principles and disease-specific mechanisms.
methods_and_approach:
**Phase 1: Data Assembly and Harmonization (Months 1-8)**

We will systematically compile publicly available datasets across five disease classes. For variant data, we will integrate ClinVar pathogenic/benign annotations, gnomAD population frequencies, disease-specific mutation databases (ALSoD, LOVD for laminopathies, Ciliopathy databases), and functional scores (AlphaMissense, EVE, ESM-1v). For proteomics and interactomics, we will leverage BioPlex, OpenCell localization data, and disease-specific interaction studies deposited in BioGRID and IntAct. For cellular imaging, we will access JUMP-CP morphological profiles, the Allen Cell Collection, and disease-specific patient-derived cell imaging from repositories including BioImage Archive and IDR. We will develop a unified ontology mapping disease-relevant proteins to mesoscale assembly types, functional roles (scaffold, client, regulator), and emergence-relevant features.

Harmonization will address critical challenges: nomenclature standardization across databases, batch effect correction for imaging data using ComBat and Harmony algorithms, and consistent variant annotation using VEP and custom pipelines. We will create a metadata schema capturing experimental conditions, cell types, and data provenance. All harmonization code will be version-controlled and documented.

**Phase 2: Emergence Integrity Metric Development (Months 4-14)**

We will operationalize three emergence-integrity dimensions through quantitative metrics:

*Stoichiometric Fidelity:* Using proteomic data, we will compute stoichiometric deviation scores comparing disease versus healthy states. We will analyze protein complex stoichiometry using CORUM annotations and calculate assembly completeness indices.

*Spatial Organization:* From imaging data, we will extract features capturing assembly morphology, localization precision, and spatial relationships using CellProfiler and custom deep learning feature extractors. We will develop metrics for condensate circularity, size distribution, and colocalization patterns.

*Dynamic Responsiveness:* Where time-series or perturbation data exist, we will quantify assembly/disassembly kinetics and stress response capacity. We will leverage JUMP-CP perturbation profiles to assess how disease-relevant genetic perturbations alter dynamic cellular responses.

Metric validation will use known pathogenic variants as positive controls and common benign variants as negative controls.

**Phase 3: Cross-Disease Analysis and Machine Learning (Months 10-20)**

We will perform systematic cross-disease comparisons at three levels:

*Variant-level:* We will test whether emergence-integrity-relevant features (interface residues, PTM sites, intrinsically disordered regions) are enriched among pathogenic variants across all disease classes using logistic regression and random forest classifiers.

*Protein-level:* Network analysis will identify shared vulnerability hubs using PageRank centrality and disease-association enrichment across the integrated interactome.

*Cellular phenotype-level:* We will apply transfer learning using domain adaptation techniques (CORAL, adversarial training) to test whether image-based classifiers trained on one disease transfer to others.

We will develop multi-task neural networks that jointly predict pathogenicity across diseases, testing whether shared representations improve performance.

**Phase 4: Atlas Construction and Validation (Months 16-24)**

The Cross-Disease Atlas of Mesoscale Disruption will integrate all findings into a queryable resource. For each disease-relevant protein, the atlas will display emergence-integrity metrics, variant effects, interaction partners, and cross-disease comparisons. Validation will assess whether atlas-derived predictions correlate with independent clinical severity measures and published functional studies.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will deliver four major outcomes with transformative potential for molecular and cellular biology and disease research.

**Outcome 1: Cross-Disease Harmonized Datasets**
We will produce the first systematically harmonized collection of mesoscale-relevant data spanning five disease classes, including standardized variant annotations for >5,000 disease-associated mutations, harmonized imaging features from >100,000 cellular profiles, and integrated interactome data covering >2,000 mesoscale-relevant proteins. This resource will enable future cross-disease research impossible with current fragmented data.

**Outcome 2: Quantitative Emergence-Integrity Metrics**
We will deliver validated, open-source computational tools implementing stoichiometric fidelity, spatial organization, and dynamic responsiveness metrics. These metrics will establish a new quantitative vocabulary for describing mesoscale biology and enable systematic comparison across biological contexts.

**Outcome 3: Cross-Disease Atlas of Mesoscale Disruption**
The publicly accessible atlas will provide researchers and clinicians with an integrated view of how mesoscale emergence fails across diseases. The atlas will support hypothesis generation for therapeutic development and variant interpretation.

**Outcome 4: Testable Therapeutic Hypotheses**
By identifying shared molecular vulnerabilities, we will generate specific hypotheses about intervention points that could benefit multiple patient populations. These hypotheses will be disseminated to disease-specific research communities for experimental validation.

**Scientific Impact:**
This project will establish "emergence integrity" as a quantifiable, clinically meaningful concept, transforming how the field conceptualizes diseases of cellular organization. By demonstrating that synthesis across disease boundaries reveals insights invisible to single-disease research, we will create a template for future cross-disease initiatives.

Six trainees will gain unique expertise in cross-disease data integration, positioning them as leaders in an emerging field. Their diverse backgrounds will seed future collaborations across disease communities.

**Broader Impact:**
Identifying shared therapeutic targets across rare diseases could accelerate drug development by enabling larger patient populations for clinical trials and repurposing of existing therapeutics.
