author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Cellular Invariants: What Mesoscale Features Are Conserved Across Single Cells
abstract: Single-cell biology has overwhelmingly focused on heterogeneity—how cells differ—yet identifying what is conserved across all cells of a type may be equally illuminating, since cellular invariants likely correspond to functional necessities. The recent abundance of single-cell omics, imaging, and multimodal datasets makes this question newly tractable, but no synthesis project has addressed it systematically. This Working Group will synthesize single-cell omics atlases (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens), single-cell imaging datasets (HPA, OpenCell), and multimodal single-cell measurements to identify mesoscale invariants—features that vary minimally across cells of a defined type—and test whether these invariants define the functional core of cell-type identity. The team brings together single-cell genomicists, quantitative imaging specialists, statisticians expert in low-variance signal detection, and cell biologists with deep cell-type expertise. We will harmonize single-cell datasets across modalities, develop statistical methods for invariance detection that account for technical noise differently than for biological variation, and identify mesoscale features (organelle counts, condensate properties, nuclear organization metrics) that are conserved within cell types but vary across cell types. Deliverables include (1) harmonized multimodal single-cell datasets with consistent cell-type annotation, (2) statistical methods for invariance detection released as open-source software, (3) a catalog of mesoscale invariants across major cell types, and (4) testable hypotheses about why specific features are conserved. NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis spans single-cell modalities (omics, imaging) treated by separate communities and because invariance detection at this scale requires methodological development beyond any single lab's capacity. The training plan supports five trainees from genomics, imaging, and statistics backgrounds through cross-disciplinary co-mentoring, formal training in single-cell methods and invariance statistics, and joint work on cell-type-specific sub-projects. Trainees will participate in a journal club spanning the relevant communities and co-author the methods paper. All harmonized data, code, and the invariant catalog will be released openly through cellxgene, BioImage Archive, and Zenodo with cross-references, and the catalog will be queryable through a public interface. By inverting the field's focus from heterogeneity to invariance, this project addresses a genuinely novel scientific question. The broader impact lies in providing a complementary lens on cell-type identity that could reveal functional necessities currently obscured by emphasis on variation, with implications for cell engineering and disease, where loss of invariants may be more diagnostic than gain of variability.
background_and_significance:
The single-cell revolution has transformed our understanding of cellular biology by revealing remarkable heterogeneity within seemingly homogeneous cell populations. Technologies including single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), single-cell ATAC-seq, mass cytometry, and high-content imaging have cataloged millions of individual cells, demonstrating that no two cells are identical. This focus on heterogeneity has yielded profound insights into developmental trajectories, disease progression, and cellular plasticity. However, this emphasis on variation has created a significant blind spot: we have systematically overlooked what is conserved across cells of the same type.

Cellular invariants—features that remain constant across all cells of a defined type—represent a fundamentally different and complementary perspective on cell biology. From an evolutionary and functional standpoint, invariance is likely more informative than variation for understanding cellular identity. Features that are tightly conserved despite stochastic gene expression, environmental fluctuations, and cell cycle dynamics must be under strong selective pressure, suggesting they represent functional necessities. These invariants may define the irreducible core of cell-type identity—the minimal set of features a cell must maintain to perform its essential functions.

The mesoscale—the organizational level between individual biomolecules and whole organelles—is particularly relevant for investigating cellular invariants. Mesoscale features include biomolecular condensates, protein complex stoichiometries, organelle numbers and spatial arrangements, chromatin organization patterns, and membrane domain compositions. These emergent properties arise from the collective behavior of thousands of molecules and represent a scale where cellular function is organized but not yet compartmentalized into discrete organelles. Importantly, mesoscale organization may buffer molecular noise while enabling functional robustness, making it a prime candidate for harboring cellular invariants.

The timing for this synthesis project is optimal. The Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens, and related initiatives have generated comprehensive single-cell transcriptomic atlases spanning dozens of human tissues and hundreds of cell types. Simultaneously, the Human Protein Atlas (HPA) and OpenCell projects have systematically imaged protein localization in millions of cells, while emerging multimodal technologies (CITE-seq, spatial transcriptomics, 4i imaging) link molecular and spatial information within single cells. These datasets collectively represent an unprecedented resource for cross-modal synthesis, yet they remain siloed within their respective communities.

Critically, no existing framework addresses invariance detection. Standard single-cell analysis pipelines are optimized for identifying differentially expressed genes, variable features, and heterogeneous subpopulations. Statistical methods for detecting low-variance signals while accounting for technical noise are underdeveloped. This methodological gap, combined with the community fragmentation between omics and imaging approaches, makes this synthesis project ideally suited for NCEMS support.

The significance of identifying mesoscale invariants extends beyond basic biology. In regenerative medicine and cell engineering, knowing which features must be preserved could guide quality control for stem cell differentiation and cellular reprogramming. In disease biology, loss of invariants may represent an earlier and more fundamental signature of cellular dysfunction than gain of aberrant features. Cancer cells, for instance, may be characterized not only by what they gain but by which normally invariant features they lose. This project will establish invariance as a complementary analytical framework with broad implications across molecular and cellular sciences.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses a central scientific question: What mesoscale features are conserved across all cells of a defined type, and do these invariants define the functional core of cell-type identity? We decompose this overarching question into four specific research questions with associated testable hypotheses.

Research Question 1: Can we develop robust statistical methods to distinguish true biological invariance from technical artifacts in single-cell data?

Hypothesis 1: Technical noise and biological variation have distinguishable statistical signatures that can be leveraged to identify genuinely invariant features. We hypothesize that technical noise follows characteristic distributions dependent on measurement platform and feature type (e.g., Poisson-like for count data, multiplicative for imaging intensities), while biological variation reflects regulatory constraints and will show feature-specific patterns. By modeling these noise sources explicitly, we can develop statistical tests that identify features with lower-than-expected biological variation—true invariants—while controlling for measurement artifacts.

Research Question 2: Which mesoscale features exhibit invariance within cell types, and how does the invariant feature set differ across cell types?

Hypothesis 2: Different cell types maintain distinct sets of mesoscale invariants reflecting their specialized functions. We predict that highly specialized cells (neurons, cardiomyocytes) will exhibit more invariants than multipotent progenitors, and that invariant features will be enriched for functions central to cell-type-specific roles. For example, secretory cells may show invariant ER-Golgi organization, while immune cells may maintain invariant surface receptor stoichiometries. We further hypothesize that some invariants will be universal across cell types (e.g., nuclear envelope integrity metrics), representing fundamental requirements for cellular viability.

Research Question 3: Do invariant features at the transcriptomic level correspond to invariant features at the protein and spatial organization levels?

Hypothesis 3: Mesoscale invariants emerge from coordinated constraints across molecular scales, creating cross-modal invariant signatures. We hypothesize that genes showing invariant expression will encode proteins with invariant localization patterns and that these proteins will participate in structurally conserved complexes or condensates. This cross-modal correspondence would suggest that invariance reflects deep functional constraints rather than measurement artifacts of any single technology. Conversely, features invariant in one modality but variable in another may reveal post-transcriptional buffering mechanisms or context-dependent regulation.

Research Question 4: Can mesoscale invariants predict cell-type identity and functional capacity better than variable features?

Hypothesis 4: Invariant features carry higher information content for cell-type classification than highly variable features. Current cell-type annotation relies heavily on marker genes selected for their differential expression. We hypothesize that invariant features, by defining what a cell type must be rather than how it differs from others, will provide superior classification performance, particularly for distinguishing closely related cell types or identifying dysfunctional cells that have lost type-specific invariants.

These hypotheses are testable using existing publicly available data and will generate concrete predictions for future experimental validation. Importantly, rejection of any hypothesis would itself be informative—for example, if invariants do not correspond across modalities, this would suggest that cellular identity is maintained through independent, modality-specific mechanisms rather than integrated mesoscale organization.

Our methodological development questions are equally specific: Can we create harmonized cell-type ontologies that enable cross-dataset comparison? Can we develop scalable algorithms for invariance detection across millions of cells? Can we build interpretable models that explain why specific features are invariant? These questions drive our technical approach while serving the broader scientific goals.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises four integrated phases: data harmonization, statistical method development, invariance detection and validation, and catalog construction with hypothesis generation.

Phase 1: Multimodal Data Harmonization (Months 1-8)
We will systematically compile and harmonize single-cell datasets across three modalities. For transcriptomics, we will integrate Human Cell Atlas (>50 million cells), Tabula Sapiens (>500,000 cells across 24 tissues), and CZ CELLxGENE collections, standardizing to common gene annotations (Ensembl) and applying consistent quality control filters. For imaging, we will process Human Protein Atlas subcellular localization images (>13,000 proteins) and OpenCell endogenously-tagged protein datasets, extracting quantitative features including organelle morphometrics, protein localization patterns, and spatial statistics. For multimodal data, we will incorporate CITE-seq, ECCITE-seq, and spatial transcriptomics datasets that link molecular and spatial information.

Critical to harmonization is establishing consistent cell-type annotations across datasets. We will develop a unified ontology mapping framework that reconciles Cell Ontology terms with dataset-specific annotations, using automated label transfer validated by expert curation. Our team's cell biologists will lead manual review of ambiguous mappings for priority cell types (hepatocytes, T cell subsets, neurons, fibroblasts).

Phase 2: Statistical Method Development (Months 4-14)
We will develop novel statistical frameworks for invariance detection. The core challenge is distinguishing low biological variance from high technical noise. Our approach involves:

(a) Technical noise modeling: We will characterize platform-specific noise distributions using spike-in controls, replicate measurements, and computational benchmarks. For scRNA-seq, we will extend existing negative binomial models to explicitly separate technical overdispersion from biological variation. For imaging, we will model point spread function effects, segmentation errors, and illumination variation.

(b) Invariance test statistics: We will develop hypothesis tests for invariance, defining the null hypothesis as expected variance given technical noise and the alternative as lower-than-expected variance indicating biological constraint. We will implement both parametric approaches (variance ratio tests) and non-parametric methods (permutation-based) to ensure robustness.

(c) Cross-modal integration: We will develop methods to test whether invariance in one modality predicts invariance in another, using canonical correlation analysis variants adapted for variance rather than mean relationships.

Phase 3: Invariance Detection and Validation (Months 10-20)
We will apply our methods systematically across cell types, beginning with well-characterized types (hepatocytes, CD4+ T cells, neurons) before expanding to comprehensive analysis. For each cell type, we will identify invariant features across modalities and compute invariance scores enabling ranking and comparison.

Validation will employ multiple strategies: (1) cross-dataset replication—invariants detected in one dataset should replicate in independent datasets; (2) cross-platform consistency—invariants should be robust to measurement technology; (3) biological coherence—invariant gene sets should show functional enrichment; (4) perturbation sensitivity—using existing CRISPR screen data, we will test whether disrupting invariant features causes greater phenotypic consequences than disrupting variable features.

Phase 4: Catalog Construction and Hypothesis Generation (Months 16-24)
We will construct a queryable catalog of mesoscale invariants organized by cell type, feature class, and confidence level. The catalog will include: invariant feature identities, statistical confidence metrics, cross-modal correspondence annotations, and functional annotations. We will generate testable hypotheses about invariance mechanisms, prioritizing predictions amenable to experimental validation by the broader community.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will deliver four major outcomes with transformative potential for molecular and cellular biology.

First, we will produce harmonized multimodal single-cell datasets with consistent cell-type annotations spanning transcriptomic and imaging modalities. This resource alone addresses a significant barrier in the field—the inability to integrate insights across single-cell communities—and will enable future synthesis projects beyond our specific scientific questions.

Second, we will release open-source statistical software for invariance detection, including R and Python packages implementing our noise-modeling frameworks, invariance test statistics, and cross-modal integration methods. These tools will establish invariance analysis as a standard component of single-cell workflows, complementing existing pipelines focused on heterogeneity.

Third, we will publish a comprehensive catalog of mesoscale invariants across major human cell types. This catalog will be queryable through a public web interface, enabling researchers to identify invariant features for their cell types of interest and access supporting statistical evidence. We anticipate cataloging invariants for >50 cell types with high confidence.

Fourth, we will generate testable hypotheses about why specific features are invariant, providing a roadmap for experimental follow-up. These hypotheses will be published alongside the catalog with explicit predictions for validation.

The broader impact extends across multiple domains. For basic cell biology, invariants provide a complementary framework for understanding cell-type identity, potentially revealing functional requirements obscured by focus on variation. For cell engineering, knowing which features must be preserved guides quality control for stem cell differentiation and cellular reprogramming. For disease biology, loss of invariants may represent early signatures of cellular dysfunction—we hypothesize that cancer cells may be characterized by which invariants they lose as much as what aberrant features they gain.

Finally, by training five graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary synthesis research, we contribute to NCEMS's mission of developing the next-generation data-savvy workforce capable of integrating diverse data types to address fundamental biological questions.

The interface will display statistical evidence, cross-modal correspondence, and links to underlying data. We will implement programmatic API access for computational users.

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Multi-Component Condensates: Synthesizing Protein, RNA, Lipid, and Metabolite Contributions
abstract: Most condensate research treats condensates as protein-based assemblies, but biological condensates contain RNA, lipids, and small metabolites that contribute to composition, material properties, and function. The fragmentation of relevant data—condensate proteomes from one literature, condensate RNA content from another, lipid composition from a third—has prevented integrated multi-component analysis at synthesis scale. This Working Group will synthesize public condensate proteomics, condensate-resident RNA datasets (CLIP, condensate-RNA-seq), condensate lipidomics where available, and metabolite-condensate interaction studies to develop the first integrated multi-component framework for condensate composition. The team brings together condensate biologists, RNA biochemists, lipidomics specialists, metabolomics experts, and computational biologists experienced in multi-modal integration. We will harmonize multi-component datasets across condensate types and conditions, develop integrated representations capturing all four molecular classes, and test whether multi-component models predict condensate properties (composition, dynamics, response to perturbation) better than protein-only models. Deliverables include (1) the first multi-component condensate dataset with consistent annotation across molecular classes, (2) integrated computational models predicting multi-component composition, (3) testable hypotheses about RNA, lipid, and metabolite contributions to specific condensates, and (4) open-source tools for multi-component analysis. NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis spans biochemistry communities (proteins, RNA, lipids, metabolites) that operate independently and because integration at this scale demands sustained interdisciplinary infrastructure. The training plan supports six trainees from each relevant biochemistry community through cross-community co-mentoring, formal training in multi-modal integration and condensate biology, and joint sub-projects on specific condensate systems. Trainees will participate in a cross-community seminar series and co-author the integrative paper introducing multi-component condensate analysis. All datasets, code, and integrated models will be released through ProteomeXchange, MetaboLights, and GitHub with cross-references, and the multi-component condensate database will be queryable through a public web interface. The broader impact lies in moving the condensate field beyond its protein-centric framing toward a more complete biochemical picture, with implications for understanding how condensates function in real cellular contexts where all four molecular classes co-exist. By integrating molecular classes typically studied in isolation, this project demonstrates how synthesis can produce qualitatively new pictures of mesoscale assemblies.
background_and_significance:
Biomolecular condensates represent a paradigm shift in our understanding of cellular organization, revealing that membraneless organelles formed through liquid-liquid phase separation orchestrate critical cellular functions including transcription, RNA processing, stress responses, and signal transduction. Since the seminal discoveries linking phase separation to P granules, nucleoli, and stress granules, the condensate field has expanded exponentially, generating vast datasets characterizing these mesoscale assemblies. However, a critical limitation pervades current understanding: the overwhelming focus on protein components while neglecting the substantial contributions of RNA, lipids, and small metabolites that constitute integral condensate components.

The protein-centric view of condensates emerged naturally from the discovery that intrinsically disordered protein regions drive phase separation through multivalent interactions. Consequently, proteomics approaches have dominated condensate characterization, yielding comprehensive catalogs of protein constituents across dozens of condensate types. Yet mounting evidence demonstrates that non-protein molecules fundamentally shape condensate biology. RNA species, including mRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and small RNAs, serve as scaffolds that nucleate condensate formation, modulate material properties from liquid to gel states, and confer specificity to condensate function. Lipids, particularly phosphoinositides and cholesterol, interact with condensate proteins to influence membrane associations and regulate condensate dynamics at organelle interfaces. Small metabolites including ATP, amino acids, and polyamines dramatically affect phase separation thresholds and condensate stability, linking metabolic state to condensate behavior.

Despite this recognized importance, no systematic effort has integrated data across these molecular classes. The fragmentation stems from disciplinary boundaries: protein biochemists publish condensate proteomes in proteomics journals, RNA biologists characterize condensate transcriptomes using CLIP and RNA-seq methodologies published in RNA-focused venues, lipidomics specialists examine lipid-protein interactions in lipid-centric publications, and metabolomics researchers study small molecule effects independently. This siloed literature creates a fundamental barrier to understanding how molecular components collectively generate emergent condensate properties—precisely the mesoscale phenomena central to NCEMS's scientific mission.

The significance of overcoming this fragmentation extends beyond academic completeness. Disease-associated condensate dysfunction, implicated in neurodegeneration, cancer, and viral infection, likely involves perturbations across multiple molecular classes. Understanding therapeutic intervention requires multi-component models. Furthermore, synthetic biology efforts to engineer condensates for biotechnology applications demand comprehensive compositional knowledge. The current inability to predict how RNA content affects protein-driven phase separation, or how metabolic changes alter condensate material properties, reflects the absence of integrated multi-component frameworks.

This synthesis project addresses a compelling scientific question ideally suited to NCEMS: How do proteins, RNAs, lipids, and metabolites collectively determine condensate composition, material properties, and function? Answering this question requires integrating datasets spanning four biochemistry communities that rarely interact, harmonizing data generated using disparate methodologies, and developing computational approaches for multi-modal analysis. No single laboratory possesses the expertise, resources, or community connections to accomplish this synthesis. The project exemplifies community-scale synthesis by leveraging publicly available data from hundreds of studies, requiring collaboration across disciplinary boundaries, and promising insights unattainable through traditional single-laboratory approaches. Success will establish the first integrated multi-component view of condensates, transforming understanding of these fundamental mesoscale assemblies.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses four interconnected research questions designed to systematically build multi-component understanding of biomolecular condensates, moving from data integration through predictive modeling to mechanistic hypothesis generation.

Research Question 1: What is the comprehensive multi-component composition of characterized condensate types, and how does composition vary across cellular conditions and perturbations?

Hypothesis 1a: Condensate types exhibit characteristic multi-component signatures that distinguish them more effectively than protein composition alone. We predict that integrating RNA, lipid, and metabolite data will reveal compositional fingerprints unique to specific condensates (stress granules versus P-bodies versus nucleoli) that protein-only analysis obscures.

Hypothesis 1b: Cellular stress conditions systematically alter the RNA and metabolite components of condensates while protein composition remains relatively stable. This hypothesis emerges from observations that stress rapidly changes metabolite pools and RNA localization, potentially explaining functional changes in condensates during stress without requiring new protein synthesis.

Research Question 2: Can multi-component models predict condensate properties—including assembly thresholds, material states, and dynamics—better than protein-centric models?

Hypothesis 2a: RNA content quantitatively predicts condensate material properties (viscosity, surface tension, aging behavior) independently of protein composition. Published studies demonstrate RNA dramatically affects condensate biophysics, but no systematic analysis has tested whether RNA abundance or identity predicts material state across condensate types.

Hypothesis 2b: Metabolite concentrations, particularly ATP and polyamine levels, predict condensate assembly thresholds with higher accuracy than protein concentration alone. ATP depletion and polyamine supplementation profoundly affect phase separation in vitro, suggesting metabolite data will improve predictive models of cellular condensate formation.

Hypothesis 2c: Lipid composition at condensate-membrane interfaces predicts condensate localization and membrane association patterns. Specific phosphoinositide species recruit condensate proteins to membranes; integrating lipidomics data should improve predictions of condensate subcellular distribution.

Research Question 3: What molecular features determine whether specific RNAs, lipids, or metabolites partition into particular condensates?

Hypothesis 3a: RNA structural features (secondary structure stability, repeat elements, modification patterns) predict condensate partitioning independently of sequence-specific protein binding motifs. This hypothesis tests whether RNA biophysical properties drive condensate localization beyond characterized protein-RNA interactions.

Hypothesis 3b: Metabolite physicochemical properties (charge, hydrophobicity, molecular weight) combined with condensate protein composition predict metabolite enrichment in specific condensates. If validated, this would enable prediction of condensate-metabolite interactions without requiring direct experimental measurement.

Research Question 4: How do perturbations to one molecular class propagate to affect other components and overall condensate behavior?

Hypothesis 4a: RNA depletion or modification systematically alters condensate protein composition beyond direct RNA-binding proteins, indicating network-level dependencies between molecular classes. Published RNA knockdown studies with proteomic readouts will test whether RNA changes propagate to protein composition.

Hypothesis 4b: Disease-associated mutations in condensate proteins alter RNA and metabolite partitioning patterns, suggesting multi-component disruption underlies pathology. Integrating mutation data with multi-component composition will reveal whether disease mutations affect non-protein components.

These hypotheses are testable through synthesis of existing public data and will generate specific predictions for experimental validation by the broader community. Each hypothesis addresses fundamental questions about mesoscale organization while remaining grounded in available datasets. The hierarchical structure—from compositional characterization through predictive modeling to mechanistic understanding—ensures systematic progress toward integrated multi-component condensate biology. Importantly, hypothesis testing will reveal both confirmatory results and unexpected findings, as synthesis often uncovers patterns invisible to individual studies. Negative results will be equally valuable, delimiting the predictive power of multi-component models and identifying gaps requiring future experimental investigation.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises four integrated phases: systematic data acquisition and harmonization, multi-modal data integration, predictive model development, and hypothesis testing with community validation.

Phase 1: Systematic Data Acquisition and Harmonization (Months 1-8)

We will conduct comprehensive literature mining and database queries to identify publicly available datasets across four molecular classes. For proteins, we will retrieve condensate proteomics from ProteomeXchange, PRIDE, and MassIVE, encompassing proximity labeling (BioID, APEX), immunoprecipitation, and biochemical fractionation studies. We estimate over 200 relevant proteomic datasets across 30+ condensate types. For RNA, we will compile CLIP-seq datasets from ENCODE and GEO identifying condensate protein-RNA interactions, condensate-specific RNA-seq from purified condensates, and RNA localization studies. For lipids, we will extract lipid-protein interaction data from published lipidomics studies, lipid droplet proteomics (which overlap with condensate biology), and membrane-condensate interface characterization. For metabolites, we will gather metabolite-condensate interaction studies from MetaboLights and Metabolomics Workbench, ATP/metabolite perturbation experiments with condensate readouts, and metabolomics of purified condensate fractions.

Data harmonization presents significant challenges given disparate experimental methodologies and annotation standards. We will develop a unified ontology mapping condensate names across studies (resolving synonyms and hierarchical relationships), standardize molecular identifiers (UniProt for proteins, Ensembl for RNAs, LIPID MAPS for lipids, HMDB for metabolites), implement quality metrics for each dataset enabling confidence-weighted integration, and create metadata schemas capturing experimental conditions, cell types, and perturbations.

Phase 2: Multi-Modal Data Integration (Months 6-14)

Integration will employ multiple complementary computational strategies. We will construct knowledge graphs representing molecules as nodes with edges encoding co-occurrence in condensates, physical interactions, and functional relationships. Graph neural network approaches will learn embeddings capturing multi-component relationships. We will develop tensor factorization methods to decompose the four-dimensional molecular space (proteins × RNAs × lipids × metabolites × condensate types) into interpretable components. Bayesian integration frameworks will combine datasets with different coverage and reliability, propagating uncertainty through downstream analyses. Multi-view learning algorithms will identify shared and distinct signals across molecular classes.

The computational infrastructure will leverage NCEMS resources for large-scale computation. We will implement scalable data processing pipelines using Apache Spark for dataset harmonization, deploy machine learning workflows on cloud computing resources, and establish version-controlled analysis environments ensuring reproducibility.

Phase 3: Predictive Model Development (Months 12-20)

We will develop and benchmark predictive models addressing our core hypotheses. Condensate composition predictors will use molecular features to predict condensate membership across all four classes. Material property predictors will integrate multi-component data to predict biophysical properties where published measurements exist. Perturbation response models will predict compositional changes following molecular perturbations using transfer learning from perturbation datasets.

Model evaluation will employ rigorous cross-validation, held-out test sets, and comparison against protein-only baselines. We will quantify the marginal predictive value of each molecular class.

Phase 4: Hypothesis Testing and Community Validation (Months 18-24)

Systematic hypothesis testing will apply statistical frameworks appropriate for each hypothesis. We will generate ranked predictions for experimental validation, prioritizing testable hypotheses for communication to experimental collaborators. Community validation workshops will present findings to condensate researchers for feedback and experimental follow-up.

Team Coordination and Expertise Integration

Monthly virtual meetings will coordinate activities across five core expertise areas. Working sub-groups will focus on specific condensate systems (stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies) enabling deep integration. Annual in-person workshops at NCEMS will facilitate intensive collaborative analysis sessions. The diverse team spanning condensate biology, RNA biochemistry, lipidomics, metabolomics, and computational biology ensures appropriate expertise for each methodological challenge.

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: The Dynamic Conditional Interactome: How Protein Networks Rewire Across Cellular Contexts
abstract: Protein-protein interaction networks underpin cellular function, but most published interactomes are static snapshots of single conditions, obscuring how networks rewire across cell-cycle phases, stress responses, differentiation states, and disease contexts. The fragmented landscape of condition-specific interactome data—BioPlex, OpenCell, condition-resolved AP-MS studies, proximity labeling experiments under specific perturbations—has prevented unified analysis of how interaction networks change with cellular context. This Working Group will synthesize condition-resolved interactome data into a unified tensor representation (proteins × proteins × conditions) and develop methods to analyze how networks rewire across conditions. The team brings together proteomicists with deep AP-MS and proximity-labeling expertise, network biologists, machine-learning researchers experienced in tensor decomposition, and cell biologists with expertise in specific conditions. We will harmonize condition-specific interactome datasets across ~100 conditions, develop tensor-decomposition methods that identify conditional interaction modules, and test whether identified modules predict cellular phenotypes under perturbation. Deliverables include (1) a harmonized conditional-interactome resource queryable by condition, (2) open-source tensor-decomposition methods adapted for conditional networks, (3) identification of context-specific interaction modules underlying major cellular processes, and (4) testable predictions about interactome rewiring in disease. NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis spans interactome communities (AP-MS, proximity labeling, Y2H) with different conventions and because tensor methods at this scale require sustained methodological development. The training plan supports five trainees in proteomics, network biology, and machine learning through cross-disciplinary co-mentoring, formal training in tensor methods and interactome data analysis, and joint sub-projects on specific cellular contexts. Trainees will co-author the methods paper introducing the tensor framework and contribute condition-specific analyses. All harmonized data, code, and the conditional-interactome resource will be released through ProteomeXchange and GitHub with reproducible workflows, and the resource will be queryable through a public web interface. The broader impact lies in demonstrating that interactome biology is fundamentally conditional, not static, and providing infrastructure for condition-aware network analysis that the broader community can build upon. By moving from static to dynamic-conditional interactomes, this project addresses an innovative analytical strategy with broad implications for systems biology, drug discovery, and understanding network dysfunction in disease.
background_and_significance:
Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) constitute the fundamental operational language of cellular function, mediating virtually every biological process from signal transduction to metabolic regulation. Over the past two decades, systematic efforts including the Human Interactome Project, BioPlex, and OpenCell have generated comprehensive catalogs of human PPIs, collectively documenting over 500,000 unique interactions. These landmark achievements have transformed our understanding of cellular organization, revealing modular network architectures and enabling systematic functional annotation of poorly characterized proteins. However, a critical limitation pervades current interactome biology: the vast majority of published interaction data represents static snapshots acquired under single experimental conditions, typically asynchronous cell populations grown in standard culture media.

This static perspective fundamentally misrepresents biological reality. Cells continuously rewire their interaction networks in response to environmental cues, developmental signals, and pathological perturbations. During cell cycle progression, hundreds of interactions dynamically assemble and disassemble as cells transition through G1, S, G2, and mitosis. Stress responses trigger rapid reorganization of protein complexes, with heat shock, oxidative stress, and DNA damage each inducing distinct rewiring patterns. Differentiation programs involve wholesale remodeling of interaction networks as cells acquire specialized identities. Disease states, particularly cancer, exhibit aberrant interaction patterns that drive pathological phenotypes. Despite the biological centrality of network dynamics, we lack systematic understanding of how interactomes rewire across cellular contexts.

The data required to address this knowledge gap already exists but remains fragmented across disparate resources. Condition-specific interactome studies have proliferated, examining interactions during specific cell cycle phases, under various stress conditions, across differentiation trajectories, and in disease models. Proximity labeling methods (BioID, APEX, TurboID) have enabled temporal resolution of interaction dynamics. Quantitative AP-MS approaches have revealed stoichiometric changes in protein complexes across conditions. Yet these datasets remain siloed within individual publications, generated using incompatible experimental protocols, analyzed with different computational pipelines, and reported using inconsistent nomenclature and confidence metrics.

This fragmentation represents a missed opportunity of substantial scientific significance. The emergence of context-dependent network properties represents a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon—individual molecular interactions combine to produce system-level behaviors that cannot be predicted from component properties alone. Understanding how networks rewire across conditions addresses fundamental questions about cellular information processing: How do cells encode and transmit contextual information through network topology? What principles govern the emergence of condition-specific functional modules? How does network dysfunction contribute to disease pathology?

The synthesis proposed here directly addresses NCEMS priorities by leveraging existing public data to investigate emergent properties at the mesoscale. By unifying condition-specific interactome data into a coherent analytical framework, we will enable systematic investigation of how molecular interactions combine to produce context-dependent cellular behaviors. This represents precisely the type of community-scale synthesis that requires collaboration across multiple laboratories with distinct expertise—proteomicists, network biologists, machine learning researchers, and cell biologists—working together to harmonize data conventions, develop appropriate analytical methods, and interpret findings across biological contexts. The significance extends beyond basic science to translational applications, as understanding condition-specific network rewiring has direct implications for identifying disease mechanisms and therapeutic targets.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group will address four interconnected research questions that collectively advance our understanding of conditional interactome dynamics:

Research Question 1: What is the global landscape of protein interaction rewiring across cellular contexts?

Hypothesis 1a: Protein interactions exhibit a spectrum of condition-dependence, with a core set of constitutive interactions (~30-40% of the interactome) that remain stable across conditions, and a larger set of conditional interactions that are activated or repressed in specific contexts.

Hypothesis 1b: Condition-dependent interactions are enriched for regulatory proteins (kinases, transcription factors, signaling adaptors) relative to constitutive interactions, which are enriched for structural and housekeeping functions.

Rationale: Individual studies have identified condition-specific interactions, but no systematic analysis has quantified the global prevalence of interaction rewiring or characterized the functional properties distinguishing constitutive from conditional interactions. Our tensor representation will enable direct quantification of interaction stability across conditions.

Research Question 2: What modular structures underlie conditional interactome organization?

Hypothesis 2a: Tensor decomposition will reveal condition-specific interaction modules—coherent sets of proteins whose mutual interactions are coordinately regulated across conditions—that correspond to functional units such as stress-response complexes, cell-cycle-dependent assemblies, and differentiation-associated networks.

Hypothesis 2b: Condition-specific modules exhibit hierarchical organization, with smaller functional units combining into larger context-dependent assemblies, reflecting the emergent nature of mesoscale cellular organization.

Rationale: Classical network clustering identifies static modules, but cannot capture conditional modularity. Tensor decomposition methods can identify multi-way associations that reveal how protein groups interact specifically under certain conditions. We hypothesize that this analysis will uncover previously unrecognized functional relationships.

Research Question 3: Can conditional interaction modules predict cellular phenotypes under perturbation?

Hypothesis 3a: The activity state of condition-specific modules, inferred from expression data, will predict cellular responses to perturbations better than static network features or individual gene expression levels.

Hypothesis 3b: Perturbations targeting hub proteins within condition-specific modules will produce context-dependent phenotypes that can be predicted from module structure.

Rationale: If conditional modules represent genuine functional units, their activity should have phenotypic consequences. We will test this by integrating our conditional interactome with publicly available perturbation datasets (DepMap, CRISPR screens, drug response data) to assess predictive power.

Research Question 4: How does interactome rewiring contribute to disease states?

Hypothesis 4a: Disease-associated proteins are enriched in condition-specific interactions relative to constitutive interactions, reflecting the context-dependent nature of disease pathology.

Hypothesis 4b: Cancer subtypes exhibit distinct patterns of interactome rewiring that correlate with clinical outcomes and therapeutic vulnerabilities.

Rationale: Disease often manifests in specific cellular contexts, suggesting that pathological mechanisms involve conditional network properties. By mapping disease-associated proteins onto our conditional interactome, we can generate testable hypotheses about context-dependent disease mechanisms.

Methodological Question: What computational approaches optimally capture conditional interactome structure?

Hypothesis M1: Non-negative tensor decomposition methods, adapted to handle missing data and varying confidence scores across conditions, will outperform matrix-based approaches in identifying biologically meaningful conditional modules.

Hypothesis M2: Incorporating prior knowledge about condition relationships (e.g., temporal ordering of cell cycle phases, hierarchical organization of stress responses) as constraints in tensor decomposition will improve module detection accuracy.

These questions and hypotheses are specifically designed to leverage the unique capabilities of synthesis research. Addressing them requires integrating data across multiple experimental platforms, biological conditions, and research communities—a scope beyond any individual laboratory. The hypotheses generate testable predictions that can be validated against independent datasets, ensuring scientific rigor.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises four integrated phases spanning data harmonization, method development, biological analysis, and validation.

Phase 1: Data Harmonization and Tensor Construction (Months 1-12)

We will systematically identify, curate, and harmonize condition-specific interactome datasets from public repositories including IntAct, BioGRID, STRING, ProteomeXchange, and MassIVE. Our initial survey identifies approximately 150 studies containing condition-resolved interaction data spanning cell cycle phases (15 studies), stress responses (35 studies), differentiation states (25 studies), disease models (40 studies), and drug treatments (35 studies). We will apply standardized quality filters including reproducibility requirements, confidence score thresholds, and bait coverage criteria.

Harmonization will address three major challenges: (1) Nomenclature standardization using UniProt accessions as canonical identifiers with systematic mapping from gene symbols and legacy identifiers; (2) Confidence score calibration using a Bayesian framework that integrates method-specific false discovery rates, enabling cross-platform comparison; (3) Condition ontology development using a hierarchical classification system that captures relationships between conditions (e.g., oxidative stress as a subtype of cellular stress).

The harmonized data will be organized into a three-dimensional tensor T(i,j,k) where dimensions represent bait proteins (i), prey proteins (j), and conditions (k). Tensor entries will encode calibrated confidence scores. We will implement sparse tensor representations to efficiently handle the expected ~80% missing data rate while preserving information about measurement absence versus true negative interactions.

Phase 2: Tensor Decomposition Method Development (Months 6-18)

We will develop novel tensor decomposition methods optimized for conditional interactome analysis. Standard approaches (CP decomposition, Tucker decomposition) assume complete data and uniform noise, assumptions violated by interactome tensors. Our methodological innovations include:

Missing-data-aware decomposition: We will extend probabilistic tensor factorization to model missing entries explicitly, distinguishing unmeasured interactions from true negatives using auxiliary information about experimental coverage.

Confidence-weighted factorization: Rather than binary interaction calls, our methods will propagate uncertainty from confidence scores through the decomposition, yielding uncertainty estimates for inferred modules.

Constrained decomposition: We will incorporate biological priors as soft constraints, including known protein complex membership, condition temporal ordering, and functional annotations, using regularization terms that encourage biologically coherent solutions.

Scalability optimization: We will implement stochastic optimization algorithms enabling analysis of tensors with millions of entries, with distributed computing support for NCEMS computational resources.

Phase 3: Biological Analysis and Module Characterization (Months 12-24)

Applying our methods to the harmonized tensor, we will identify condition-specific interaction modules and characterize their biological properties. Analysis components include:

Module functional annotation: Systematic enrichment analysis against Gene Ontology, pathway databases (KEGG, Reactome), and disease ontologies to assign biological functions to identified modules.

Module conservation analysis: Assessment of module conservation across species using ortholog mapping to yeast and mouse interactome data, identifying evolutionarily ancient versus recently evolved conditional modules.

Hub protein characterization: Identification of proteins serving as hubs within condition-specific modules, with analysis of their structural features, post-translational modification sites, and intrinsic disorder content.

Phase 4: Validation and Prediction Testing (Months 18-30)

We will validate identified modules and test phenotypic predictions using independent public datasets:

Expression-based validation: Module activity scores computed from TCGA, GTEx, and single-cell RNA-seq datasets will be correlated with phenotypic annotations to assess functional relevance.

Perturbation prediction testing: We will predict phenotypic consequences of gene knockouts based on module membership and test predictions against DepMap and published CRISPR screen data.

Disease association validation: Predicted disease-relevant modules will be validated against GWAS data, testing whether module members are enriched for disease-associated variants.

All methods will be implemented in Python and R with comprehensive documentation, unit testing, and containerized workflows ensuring reproducibility.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will deliver four major outcomes with transformative impact on molecular and cellular biology:

Outcome 1: The Conditional Interactome Resource
We will release a comprehensive, harmonized database of condition-specific protein interactions spanning approximately 100 cellular conditions, representing the first unified resource for conditional interactome analysis. The resource will include standardized confidence scores, condition ontology annotations, and comprehensive metadata. A web interface will enable researchers to query interactions by protein, condition, or module, visualize condition-specific networks, and download data in standard formats. We anticipate this resource will become a foundational tool for the interactome community, analogous to how STRING transformed static network analysis.

Outcome 2: Open-Source Analytical Methods
Our tensor decomposition methods, implemented as documented software packages with tutorials and example analyses, will provide the community with tools for conditional network analysis applicable beyond interactomes to any multi-condition molecular data. We will generate a systematic catalog of condition-specific interaction modules with functional annotations, providing mechanistic insights into how cells rewire their molecular networks across contexts. We anticipate identifying novel functional relationships invisible to static network analysis, including unexpected connections between cellular processes that share conditional interaction patterns.

Outcome 4: Testable Disease Hypotheses
Our analysis will generate specific, testable predictions about interactome rewiring in disease, including candidate therapeutic targets within disease-specific modules. These predictions will be released as a structured dataset enabling experimental follow-up by the broader community.

Broader Impact: By establishing the paradigm of conditional interactomics, this project will shift community perspective from static to dynamic network biology. The infrastructure we create—data resources, analytical methods, and conceptual frameworks—will enable future investigations into network dynamics across biological contexts, with applications spanning basic research, drug discovery, and precision medicine.

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Missing Heritability of Cellular Phenotypes: Does Mesoscale State Explain the Residuals
abstract: In human genetics, the term missing heritability refers to phenotypic variance unexplained by identified genetic variants. An analogous puzzle exists in cell biology: large-scale morphological and transcriptomic screens reveal substantial cell-to-cell phenotypic variance unexplained by genetic perturbations alone. Whether mesoscale state—condensate composition, organelle architecture, network configuration—explains these residuals has not been tested at synthesis scale. This Working Group will synthesize Cell Painting (JUMP), Perturb-seq, DepMap, and complementary perturbation atlases to partition cellular phenotypic variance and test whether mesoscale covariates explain residual variance beyond genetic and stochastic sources. The team brings together cell-painting and Perturb-seq experts, statistical geneticists with variance-partitioning expertise, mesoscale-imaging specialists, and machine-learning researchers experienced in residual modeling. We will harmonize perturbation datasets across the relevant archives, integrate them with mesoscale measurements where available (organelle morphometrics, condensate features), partition variance using methods adapted from human genetics, and test whether mesoscale covariates explain residual phenotypic variance better than alternative explanations. Deliverables include (1) a harmonized cellular-phenotype variance-partitioning resource, (2) statistical methods adapted from human genetics for cellular-phenotype residual analysis, (3) quantitative estimates of mesoscale variance contributions across phenotype classes, and (4) testable predictions about which mesoscale features matter most for which phenotypes. NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis bridges human-genetics methodology and cell biology in ways no single lab supports, and because variance partitioning at this scale demands sustained statistical and computational infrastructure. The training plan supports five trainees from human genetics, cell biology, and statistics backgrounds through cross-disciplinary co-mentoring, formal training in variance-partitioning methods and large-scale screen analysis, and joint sub-projects on specific phenotype classes. Trainees will co-author the methods paper introducing residual analysis to cell biology and contribute phenotype-specific analyses. All harmonized data, code, and analysis pipelines will be released through Cell Painting Gallery, cellxgene, and GitHub with reproducible workflows. The broader impact lies in importing the conceptual framework of missing heritability into cell biology, providing tools for systematically asking what mesoscale state contributes to cellular phenotypes beyond genetics. By framing cell biology with concepts from human genetics, this project addresses a genuinely novel question and could reshape how cellular variability is interpreted across the field.
background_and_significance:
The concept of missing heritability has profoundly shaped human genetics over the past two decades. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) consistently explain only a fraction of the heritable variance in complex traits, prompting systematic investigation into rare variants, epistasis, gene-environment interactions, and epigenetic modifications. This conceptual framework has driven methodological innovation and reshaped our understanding of genetic architecture. Remarkably, an analogous puzzle exists in cell biology that has received far less systematic attention.

Large-scale perturbation screens, including the JUMP-Cell Painting consortium, Perturb-seq atlases, and the Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap), have generated unprecedented datasets characterizing cellular responses to genetic and chemical perturbations. These resources reveal a striking observation: substantial cell-to-cell phenotypic variance remains unexplained by the perturbation itself. Even genetically identical cells exposed to identical perturbations exhibit diverse morphological and transcriptional responses. This residual variance is typically attributed to stochastic noise or technical artifacts, yet emerging evidence suggests it may contain biologically meaningful signal.

The mesoscale—the organizational level between individual biomolecules and organelles—represents a compelling candidate for explaining this residual variance. Biomolecular condensates, phase-separated compartments, organelle contact sites, cytoskeletal networks, and spatial organization of protein complexes all operate at this scale. These mesoscale features exhibit substantial cell-to-cell variation, respond dynamically to perturbations, and influence downstream cellular outcomes. However, whether mesoscale state systematically explains phenotypic variance beyond genetic and stochastic sources has never been tested at synthesis scale.

This gap exists for three reasons. First, mesoscale biology and quantitative genetics have developed as largely separate fields with distinct methodological traditions. Statistical geneticists have sophisticated variance-partitioning methods but rarely apply them to cellular phenotypes. Cell biologists generate massive perturbation datasets but lack frameworks for systematic residual analysis. Second, the relevant datasets exist in disparate repositories with incompatible formats, identifiers, and quality metrics. Synthesizing Cell Painting morphological profiles with Perturb-seq transcriptional readouts and mesoscale measurements requires substantial harmonization infrastructure. Third, the computational and statistical demands of variance partitioning across millions of cells and thousands of perturbations exceed the capabilities of individual laboratories.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to address this challenge. The Center's focus on mesoscale emergence aligns precisely with our hypothesis that mesoscale organization explains cellular phenotypic variance. The synthesis mandate enables integration of datasets that have never been jointly analyzed. The collaborative infrastructure supports the sustained cross-disciplinary effort required for methodological translation from human genetics to cell biology.

The significance of this work extends beyond explaining residual variance. If mesoscale state contributes substantially to cellular phenotypes, it implies that genetic perturbations operate through mesoscale intermediates—a fundamentally different model than direct genotype-to-phenotype mapping. This would reshape interpretation of perturbation screens, drug response studies, and disease modeling. Furthermore, identifying which mesoscale features matter most for which phenotypes would prioritize targets for mechanistic investigation and therapeutic intervention. By importing the missing heritability framework into cell biology, this project addresses a genuinely novel question with transformative potential.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses a central scientific question: Does mesoscale cellular state explain phenotypic variance that remains after accounting for genetic perturbations and stochastic noise? We decompose this overarching question into four specific research questions with testable hypotheses.

Research Question 1: What fraction of cellular phenotypic variance is unexplained by genetic perturbations across large-scale screens?

Hypothesis 1: Across Cell Painting and Perturb-seq datasets, at least 30-50% of phenotypic variance remains unexplained after accounting for perturbation identity and known technical covariates. This hypothesis is grounded in preliminary analyses of JUMP-Cell Painting data showing substantial within-perturbation variance and in analogous observations from single-cell transcriptomics. We will quantify this residual variance systematically across perturbation types (genetic knockouts, knockdowns, overexpression, chemical), cell lines, and phenotypic readouts (morphological features, transcriptional programs, functional dependencies).

Research Question 2: Do mesoscale covariates explain residual phenotypic variance beyond stochastic and technical sources?

Hypothesis 2: Mesoscale features—including organelle morphometrics, condensate properties, and spatial organization metrics extractable from Cell Painting images—explain at least 10-20% of residual variance, significantly exceeding what would be expected from technical artifacts or measurement noise alone. We will test this hypothesis using variance-partitioning methods adapted from human genetics, comparing models with and without mesoscale covariates. The critical comparison is whether mesoscale features explain variance beyond cell cycle state, cell size, and other known confounders.

Research Question 3: Which mesoscale features contribute most to explaining residual variance, and does this vary by phenotype class?

Hypothesis 3: Different mesoscale features will show phenotype-specific variance contributions. We hypothesize that organelle contact site metrics will preferentially explain metabolic phenotype variance, condensate features will explain stress response variance, and cytoskeletal organization will explain morphological phenotype variance. This hypothesis derives from known functional relationships between mesoscale structures and cellular processes. We will test it by partitioning variance separately for phenotype classes defined by gene ontology annotations and pathway memberships.

Research Question 4: Can variance-partitioning methods from human genetics be successfully adapted to cellular phenotype analysis?

Hypothesis 4: Methods including GREML (genomic-relatedness-based restricted maximum likelihood), LD score regression, and Haseman-Elston regression can be reformulated for cellular phenotypes by substituting genetic relatedness matrices with perturbation similarity matrices and mesoscale covariance structures. We hypothesize these adapted methods will provide stable, interpretable variance estimates with appropriate uncertainty quantification. This methodological hypothesis will be tested through simulation studies and comparison with alternative approaches including mixed-effects models and machine learning residual analysis.

Secondary Questions: Beyond these primary questions, we will explore whether residual variance structure predicts drug response heterogeneity, whether mesoscale variance contributions differ between cancer and non-cancer cell lines, and whether perturbation-induced changes in mesoscale state mediate phenotypic effects. These secondary analyses will generate testable predictions for future experimental validation.

Null Hypotheses and Alternative Explanations: We explicitly consider alternatives to our mesoscale hypothesis. Residual variance might reflect purely technical noise, cell cycle heterogeneity, or cryptic genetic variation in cell lines. Our analytical framework includes explicit tests distinguishing mesoscale contributions from these alternatives through appropriate controls and comparative modeling.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises four integrated phases: data harmonization, variance partitioning framework development, mesoscale feature integration, and systematic hypothesis testing.

Phase 1: Data Harmonization and Quality Control (Months 1-8)
We will synthesize four primary data resources: (1) JUMP-Cell Painting consortium data comprising over 100 million cellular morphological profiles across 116,000 chemical and genetic perturbations; (2) Perturb-seq atlases including the Replogle et al. genome-wide CRISPRi dataset with single-cell transcriptomes for 2.5 million cells; (3) DepMap functional dependency data across 1,000+ cancer cell lines; and (4) complementary perturbation atlases from the Connectivity Map and OpenTargets. Harmonization will establish common perturbation identifiers mapping gene symbols, compound identifiers, and perturbation mechanisms across datasets. We will implement batch correction using ComBat and Harmony algorithms validated for cross-dataset integration. Quality control pipelines will filter cells based on established morphological and transcriptional quality metrics. The harmonized resource will be structured using standardized schemas compatible with Cell Painting Gallery and cellxgene.

Phase 2: Variance Partitioning Framework Development (Months 4-14)
We will adapt statistical methods from human genetics for cellular phenotype analysis. The core approach uses restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation to partition phenotypic variance into components attributable to perturbation effects, mesoscale covariates, and residual sources. We will construct perturbation similarity matrices analogous to genetic relatedness matrices, capturing shared targets, pathway memberships, and mechanism similarities. Mixed-effects models will estimate variance components with appropriate random effects structures. For computational tractability with millions of cells, we will implement stochastic gradient descent approaches and leverage GPU acceleration. Method validation will use simulation studies with known variance structures and comparison with alternative approaches including Bayesian variance decomposition and machine learning residual modeling. We will develop software packages implementing these methods with comprehensive documentation.

Phase 3: Mesoscale Feature Integration (Months 6-16)
Mesoscale features will be extracted from Cell Painting images using established and novel computational approaches. Organelle morphometrics including mitochondrial network topology, ER distribution, and Golgi fragmentation will be quantified using CellProfiler pipelines. Condensate-associated features will be extracted using texture analysis and puncta detection algorithms sensitive to phase-separated structures. We will implement deep learning approaches trained on annotated mesoscale structures to extract latent representations capturing organizational features not captured by handcrafted metrics. Spatial organization metrics including protein localization entropy and organelle contact frequencies will be computed. These features will be integrated with perturbation response data, creating matched datasets where cells have both phenotypic readouts and mesoscale characterization.

Phase 4: Systematic Hypothesis Testing (Months 12-24)
We will execute systematic variance partitioning analyses testing our core hypotheses. For each phenotype class, we will estimate total variance, perturbation-explained variance, mesoscale-explained variance, and residual variance. Statistical significance will be assessed through permutation testing and bootstrap confidence intervals. We will compare nested models with and without mesoscale covariates using likelihood ratio tests. Phenotype-specific analyses will identify which mesoscale features matter most for morphological, transcriptional, and functional phenotypes. Cross-validation across cell lines will assess generalizability. All analyses will be implemented as reproducible workflows using Snakemake with containerized environments.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will deliver four primary outcomes with significant impact on molecular and cellular sciences.

Outcome 1: Harmonized Cellular Phenotype Variance-Partitioning Resource
We will produce the first integrated resource enabling systematic variance analysis across major perturbation datasets. This resource will include harmonized perturbation identifiers, quality-controlled cellular profiles, extracted mesoscale features, and pre-computed variance estimates. The resource will be deposited in Cell Painting Gallery and cellxgene with comprehensive metadata and documentation, enabling reuse by the broader community.

Outcome 2: Statistical Methods for Cellular Residual Analysis
We will release validated software implementing variance-partitioning methods adapted for cellular phenotypes. These tools will enable any researcher to decompose phenotypic variance in their own datasets, extending the impact beyond our specific analyses. Methods papers will introduce these approaches to the cell biology community with tutorials and worked examples.

Outcome 3: Quantitative Estimates of Mesoscale Variance Contributions
We will provide the first systematic quantification of how much mesoscale state contributes to cellular phenotypic variance. These estimates will establish whether mesoscale organization represents a major or minor source of cellular heterogeneity, directly testing our central hypothesis. Results stratified by phenotype class will reveal which cellular processes are most influenced by mesoscale state.

Outcome 4: Testable Predictions for Experimental Validation
Our analyses will generate specific predictions about which mesoscale features matter most for which phenotypes. These predictions will prioritize targets for mechanistic follow-up studies, providing a roadmap for experimental validation beyond this synthesis project.

Broader Impact: By importing the missing heritability framework into cell biology, this project establishes a new paradigm for interpreting cellular variability. Rather than dismissing residual variance as noise, researchers will have tools to systematically investigate its sources. This conceptual shift could transform how perturbation screens are analyzed, how drug response heterogeneity is understood, and how cellular models of disease are developed. The cross-disciplinary training of five trainees will seed future collaborations bridging quantitative genetics and cell biology.
