author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Cryo-EM Detection Bias: What Mesoscale Assemblies Are Systematically Missed
abstract: Cryo-electron microscopy has transformed structural biology, but EMDB and EMPIAR depositions disproportionately represent assemblies amenable to current methods—well-defined, homogeneous, abundant complexes with stable interfaces. Mesoscale assemblies that are heterogeneous, transient, low-abundance, or membrane-associated may be systematically underrepresented, biasing the structural-biology view of mesoscale organization. No prior project has quantified this bias at synthesis scale or developed correction strategies. This Working Group will synthesize EMDB and EMPIAR depositions against AlphaFold-Multimer predictions, complexome profiling data, and cellular fractionation proteomes to quantify which mesoscale assemblies are over- and under-represented in cryo-EM, and to develop methods that correct for this bias when drawing inferences about cellular architecture. The team brings together cryo-EM specialists, computational structural biologists, mass spectrometrists with complexome expertise, and statisticians expert in selection-bias modeling. We will harmonize cryo-EM depositions with consistent metadata, integrate with complexome profiling and AlphaFold-Multimer predictions, develop bias-correction methods analogous to those used in observational epidemiology, and produce a calibrated picture of which assemblies are detectable versus systematically missed. Deliverables include (1) a harmonized cryo-EM-deposition resource with consistent metadata, (2) quantitative bias estimates across assembly classes, (3) bias-correction methods released as open-source software, and (4) prioritized targets for future cryo-EM experimental campaigns. NCEMS support is essential because rigorous bias analysis spans structural and statistical communities that rarely collaborate and because the synthesis demands harmonization across multiple structural archives. The training plan supports four trainees in structural biology, mass spectrometry, and statistics through cross-disciplinary co-mentoring, formal training in cryo-EM analysis, complexome profiling, and selection-bias methodology, and joint sub-projects on specific bias classes. Trainees will co-author the methods paper introducing bias-correction to structural biology. All harmonized data, code, and bias-correction methods will be released through EMDB, ProteomeXchange, and GitHub with reproducible workflows. The broader impact is methodological: by quantifying and correcting representation bias in structural biology, this project will improve how the field interprets the structural record and could reshape strategic priorities for cryo-EM experimental campaigns. By treating cryo-EM data as observational rather than complete, this project introduces selection-bias frameworks—standard in epidemiology—to structural biology, with implications well beyond the specific assemblies analyzed.
background_and_significance:
Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has revolutionized structural biology over the past decade, enabling near-atomic resolution visualization of macromolecular complexes without crystallization. The Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) now contains over 40,000 depositions, and the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR) provides access to raw imaging data. These resources have fundamentally advanced our understanding of molecular machines, from ribosomes to membrane channels. However, the structural biology community has largely treated these archives as representative samples of cellular complexity—an assumption that may profoundly distort our understanding of mesoscale organization.

Mesoscale assemblies—molecular structures intermediate between individual proteins and organelles—represent a critical frontier in cellular biology and a core focus of NCEMS. These assemblies, ranging from 10 to 1000 nanometers, include phase-separated condensates, transient signaling complexes, cytoskeletal networks, and membrane-associated platforms. Understanding emergence at the mesoscale requires accurate structural information about these assemblies. Yet cryo-EM methodology inherently favors certain assembly types: abundant, stable, homogeneous complexes with well-defined stoichiometry and rigid interfaces. Assemblies that are heterogeneous, dynamic, low-abundance, or membrane-embedded present substantial technical challenges that may lead to systematic underrepresentation in structural databases.

This detection bias has profound implications for how we understand cellular architecture. If our structural knowledge systematically excludes certain assembly classes, computational models of cellular organization, drug target identification, and evolutionary analyses will inherit these biases. The problem parallels challenges in observational epidemiology, where selection bias in cohort studies can lead to incorrect causal inferences. Epidemiologists have developed sophisticated statistical frameworks—inverse probability weighting, propensity score methods, and sensitivity analyses—to quantify and correct such biases. Structural biology has no equivalent framework.

The significance of this project lies in three dimensions. First, it addresses a fundamental methodological gap: no systematic analysis has quantified which mesoscale assemblies are over- or under-represented in cryo-EM databases relative to their cellular abundance and functional importance. Second, it directly serves NCEMS's mission by synthesizing multiple publicly available data sources—structural archives, complexome profiling datasets, AlphaFold-Multimer predictions, and cellular fractionation proteomes—to generate insights unattainable from any single source. Third, it introduces analytical frameworks from epidemiology and statistics into structural biology, exemplifying the cross-disciplinary synthesis that NCEMS seeks to catalyze.

Preliminary observations suggest substantial bias. Membrane protein complexes constitute approximately 30% of the proteome but represent a smaller fraction of EMDB depositions. Transient signaling complexes, despite their biological importance, are rarely captured. Phase-separated condensates, central to mesoscale organization, have minimal structural representation. These patterns suggest systematic gaps, but rigorous quantification requires the synthesis approach proposed here.

This project is timely because the necessary data resources have recently matured. AlphaFold-Multimer now provides predictions for protein complexes, enabling comparison between predicted and experimentally determined structures. Complexome profiling datasets in ProteomeXchange catalog native protein assemblies across organisms. Cellular fractionation proteomes provide abundance estimates. Integrating these resources with EMDB and EMPIAR depositions will reveal the true landscape of detection bias and enable correction strategies essential for accurate understanding of mesoscale emergence.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses four interconnected research questions that together provide a comprehensive framework for understanding and correcting cryo-EM detection bias at the mesoscale.

Research Question 1: What is the magnitude and structure of representation bias in cryo-EM databases relative to the predicted and observed landscape of mesoscale assemblies?

Hypothesis 1a: Mesoscale assemblies in EMDB are systematically biased toward high-abundance, high-stability complexes, with representation probability correlating positively with cellular abundance (r > 0.5) and negatively with predicted conformational heterogeneity (r < -0.3).

Hypothesis 1b: Specific assembly classes—including membrane-associated complexes, phase-separated condensates, and transient signaling assemblies—are underrepresented by factors of 3-10x relative to their frequency in complexome profiling datasets.

Hypothesis 1c: The bias structure varies systematically across organisms, with model organisms (E. coli, yeast, human) showing different bias profiles reflecting community research priorities and methodological accessibility.

Research Question 2: Can we develop quantitative bias-correction methods that enable accurate inference about mesoscale organization from biased structural data?

Hypothesis 2a: Inverse probability weighting methods, adapted from epidemiological selection-bias frameworks, can effectively correct representation bias when propensity scores are estimated from assembly features (size, stability, abundance, membrane association).

Hypothesis 2b: Sensitivity analysis frameworks can bound the range of possible conclusions about mesoscale organization under varying assumptions about unmeasured confounders affecting detection probability.

Hypothesis 2c: Bias-corrected estimates of assembly class frequencies will differ substantially (>25% for at least three major classes) from naive estimates based on raw EMDB counts.

Research Question 3: What assembly features predict cryo-EM detectability, and can these predictors inform prioritization of future experimental campaigns?

Hypothesis 3a: A machine learning model incorporating assembly size, predicted stability, subunit stoichiometry, membrane association, and cellular abundance can predict EMDB representation with AUC > 0.75.

Hypothesis 3b: Comparison of AlphaFold-Multimer predictions against EMDB depositions will reveal systematic gaps where confident computational predictions exist but experimental structures are absent, identifying high-priority targets.

Hypothesis 3c: Complexome profiling datasets will identify abundant, stable assemblies absent from EMDB, suggesting technical rather than biological barriers to structure determination.

Research Question 4: How does detection bias affect downstream biological inferences about mesoscale organization and emergence?

Hypothesis 4a: Network analyses of protein-protein interactions derived from structural data show systematic differences from interaction networks derived from complexome profiling, with structural networks underrepresenting transient and conditional interactions.

Hypothesis 4b: Evolutionary analyses based on structurally characterized complexes are biased toward ancient, conserved assemblies, potentially underestimating the evolutionary dynamics of mesoscale organization.

Hypothesis 4c: Functional enrichment analyses of structurally characterized assemblies show bias toward well-studied biological processes (translation, metabolism) relative to emerging areas (phase separation, signaling).

These hypotheses are testable through synthesis of publicly available data and will generate actionable insights for both methodological correction and experimental prioritization. The quantitative predictions (correlation coefficients, fold-differences, AUC values) provide clear benchmarks for evaluating project success.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises four integrated work packages executed over 24 months, leveraging complementary expertise across the Working Group.

Work Package 1: Data Harmonization and Integration (Months 1-8)

We will systematically extract and harmonize metadata from EMDB (>40,000 entries) and EMPIAR (>2,500 datasets) using automated parsing pipelines. Key extracted features include: molecular weight, subunit composition, resolution, sample preparation method, organism, and deposition date. We will develop standardized ontologies for assembly classification (membrane-associated, cytoplasmic, nuclear; stable versus transient; homo- versus hetero-oligomeric). This harmonized cryo-EM dataset will be integrated with: (1) AlphaFold-Multimer predictions from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, focusing on predicted complexes with high confidence scores (pTM > 0.7); (2) Complexome profiling datasets from ProteomeXchange, including blue native PAGE-mass spectrometry studies across multiple organisms; (3) Cellular fractionation proteomes providing abundance estimates. Integration will use protein identifiers (UniProt) as primary keys, with careful handling of isoforms and species-specific mappings.

Work Package 2: Bias Quantification and Modeling (Months 6-16)

We will quantify representation bias using three complementary approaches. First, we calculate representation ratios: the frequency of each assembly class in EMDB relative to its frequency in complexome profiling datasets, stratified by organism and assembly features. Second, we develop propensity score models predicting EMDB inclusion probability from assembly features (size, stability, abundance, membrane association) using logistic regression and gradient boosting methods. Third, we apply selection-bias frameworks from epidemiology, treating EMDB as a biased sample from the true population of cellular assemblies. Specifically, we will adapt inverse probability weighting methods where each EMDB entry is weighted by the inverse of its estimated inclusion probability. We will develop sensitivity analysis frameworks that bound conclusions under varying assumptions about unmeasured factors affecting detection. Statistical uncertainty will be quantified through bootstrap resampling and Bayesian credible intervals.

Work Package 3: Bias-Correction Method Development (Months 12-22)

Building on bias quantification, we will develop practical correction methods for downstream analyses. These include: (1) Weighted frequency estimators that provide unbiased estimates of assembly class frequencies in cells; (2) Calibrated network construction methods that adjust protein interaction networks for detection bias; (3) Sensitivity analysis tools that report ranges of conclusions under varying bias assumptions. Methods will be implemented as open-source Python and R packages with comprehensive documentation, unit tests, and tutorials. We will validate correction methods through simulation studies with known ground truth and through cross-validation against held-out complexome profiling data.

Work Package 4: Target Prioritization and Validation (Months 18-24)

We will generate prioritized lists of mesoscale assemblies that are: (1) predicted with high confidence by AlphaFold-Multimer; (2) observed in complexome profiling; (3) absent from EMDB; (4) biologically significant based on functional annotations. These represent high-priority targets where technical advances in cryo-EM could yield substantial biological insight. We will collaborate with cryo-EM centers to assess feasibility and identify methodological barriers. The Working Group will meet biweekly via videoconference, with two in-person workshops at NCEMS facilities for intensive collaborative analysis and trainee mentoring.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will deliver four major outcomes with transformative impact on structural biology and mesoscale research.

Outcome 1: Harmonized Cryo-EM Deposition Resource. We will produce a comprehensive, consistently annotated database of EMDB and EMPIAR depositions with standardized metadata, assembly classifications, and cross-references to UniProt, AlphaFold, and complexome profiling datasets. This resource will be deposited with EMDB and maintained as a community resource, enabling future meta-analyses of structural data.

Outcome 3: Bias-Correction Software. Our synthesis will identify high-value mesoscale assemblies currently missing from structural databases, providing a roadmap for future cryo-EM campaigns and methodological development. Broader Impact: This project introduces a paradigm shift—treating structural databases as observational samples rather than complete censuses. This framework, standard in epidemiology but novel in structural biology, has implications extending far beyond cryo-EM to crystallography, NMR, and integrative structural methods. By training four trainees in cross-disciplinary methods, we develop the data-savvy workforce essential for future synthesis science.

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Pan-Eukaryotic Comparative Architecture: Conservation and Divergence of Organelle Form
abstract: Most cell-biology synthesis is anchored in a small number of model organisms, leaving pan-eukaryotic comparative architecture largely unexplored. With expanding public structural data (AlphaFold-DB), genome-spanning orthology resources (OMA, OrthoDB), and organism-spanning electron microscopy depositions, synthesis-scale comparative organelle architecture is now feasible. This Working Group will synthesize structural and comparative genomic data across diverse eukaryotic phyla to identify which features of organelle architecture are deeply conserved and which diverge with phylogenetic distance, lifestyle, or environment. The team brings together comparative cell biologists with deep expertise across protist, fungal, plant, and animal lineages, structural biologists, evolutionary biologists with phylogenetic-comparative-methods expertise, and computational biologists experienced in cross-species integration. We will harmonize organelle structural data across ~50 eukaryotic species using AlphaFold-DB orthologs and available EM and tomography depositions, integrate with comparative genomics to identify orthologous organelle components, and apply phylogenetic comparative methods to test for architectural conservation versus lineage-specific divergence. Deliverables include (1) a pan-eukaryotic organelle architecture resource with consistent annotation across phyla, (2) phylogenetic-comparative analyses of conservation and divergence, (3) identification of lineage-specific architectural innovations, and (4) testable hypotheses about why specific architectures are conserved or divergent. NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis spans communities (model-organism cell biologists, protistologists, plant biologists, mycologists) that rarely collaborate and because comparative analysis at this phylogenetic scope demands sustained ontological and computational work. The training plan supports six trainees from diverse organismal backgrounds through cross-organism co-mentoring, formal training in comparative methods and structural biology, and joint sub-projects on specific organelle classes across phyla. Trainees will participate in a cross-organism seminar series and co-author the comparative-architecture papers. All harmonized data, code, and the comparative resource will be released through Zenodo and GitHub with cross-references to source archives, and the resource will be queryable through a phylogenetically-aware web interface. The broader impact lies in establishing pan-eukaryotic comparative architecture as a tractable synthesis-research domain and in revealing which mesoscale features are evolutionary necessities versus lineage-specific solutions. By extending comparative biology beyond sequence to architecture, this project addresses a compelling scientific question and provides infrastructure that the broader community can build upon for years.
background_and_significance:
The eukaryotic cell represents one of evolution's most consequential innovations, characterized by membrane-bound organelles that compartmentalize biochemical functions and enable unprecedented cellular complexity. Despite over a century of cell biology research, our understanding of organelle architecture remains paradoxically narrow, anchored predominantly in a handful of model organisms: yeast, Arabidopsis, Drosophila, C. elegans, and mammalian cell lines. This taxonomic bias creates a fundamental gap in our understanding of which architectural features represent universal constraints versus lineage-specific adaptations. The mesoscale—the spatial regime between individual biomolecules and complete organelles—represents a critical frontier where emergent properties arise from the collective behavior of molecular components. At this scale, protein complexes assemble into higher-order structures, membrane domains organize into functional territories, and organelle morphology emerges from the interplay of physical forces and molecular determinants. Understanding mesoscale organization across eukaryotic diversity is essential for distinguishing fundamental architectural principles from evolutionary contingencies.

Recent advances in publicly available data resources have created an unprecedented opportunity for pan-eukaryotic comparative architecture. AlphaFold-DB now provides predicted structures for over 200 million proteins across diverse organisms, enabling structural comparisons previously impossible at this scale. Orthology databases including OMA and OrthoDB offer rigorously curated evolutionary relationships spanning eukaryotic diversity. Critically, electron microscopy archives including EMDB and EMPIAR contain thousands of tomographic reconstructions and high-resolution images across diverse species, providing direct visualization of organelle architecture. The integration of these resources enables, for the first time, systematic comparison of organelle form across the eukaryotic tree of life.

The significance of this synthesis extends beyond cataloging diversity. Comparative architectural analysis can reveal evolutionary constraints that maintain specific organizational features across billion-year divergences, suggesting functional necessity. Conversely, identifying lineage-specific innovations illuminates how organisms adapt organelle architecture to distinct ecological niches, metabolic demands, or developmental programs. For example, mitochondrial cristae morphology varies dramatically across eukaryotes—from tubular structures in many protists to lamellar arrangements in animals—yet the functional consequences of these differences remain poorly understood. Similarly, the nuclear envelope shows remarkable variation in nuclear pore density, lamina composition, and envelope architecture across lineages, with implications for gene regulation and nuclear mechanics.

This project directly addresses NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale. Organelle architecture represents a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence: individual proteins assemble into complexes, complexes organize into domains, and domains collectively determine organelle morphology and function. By systematically comparing these emergent features across eukaryotic diversity, we can identify which mesoscale properties are evolutionarily robust—suggesting they represent fundamental organizational principles—versus those that vary with phylogeny, environment, or lifestyle. This comparative framework transforms organelle biology from a descriptive discipline into a predictive science capable of generating testable hypotheses about architectural constraints and adaptations. The broader impact extends to understanding how cellular organization evolves, with implications for synthetic biology, disease mechanisms, and the fundamental principles governing biological complexity.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses three interconnected research questions that collectively advance our understanding of organelle architecture evolution and mesoscale emergence across eukaryotic diversity.

Research Question 1: Which features of organelle architecture are deeply conserved across eukaryotic phyla, and what does conservation imply about functional constraints?

Hypothesis 1a: Core architectural features essential for fundamental organelle functions—such as mitochondrial cristae junction complexes, nuclear pore scaffold architecture, and ER-mitochondria contact site components—will show strong structural conservation across all major eukaryotic supergroups, reflecting irreducible functional requirements.

Hypothesis 1b: The degree of architectural conservation will correlate with the centrality of the organelle function to core cellular processes. Specifically, we predict that components involved in energy transduction (mitochondria, chloroplasts) and genetic information flow (nucleus) will show higher conservation than components involved in lineage-specific metabolic adaptations.

Hypothesis 1c: Conserved architectural features will show evidence of purifying selection at the structural level, even when sequence conservation is modest, indicating that three-dimensional organization rather than primary sequence is the target of selection.

Research Question 2: How do organelle architectural features diverge with phylogenetic distance, and can we identify predictors of divergence rate?

Hypothesis 2a: Architectural divergence will not follow a simple molecular clock but will show punctuated patterns associated with major ecological transitions, including the evolution of multicellularity, parasitism, photosynthesis loss, and adaptation to extreme environments.

Hypothesis 2b: Organelle components involved in interactions with lineage-specific cellular features (e.g., cell wall interactions in plants and fungi, cytoskeletal attachments varying across lineages) will show accelerated architectural divergence compared to organelle-intrinsic components.

Hypothesis 2c: Architectural modularity—the degree to which organelle components function as independent units—will predict divergence patterns, with highly modular components showing greater evolutionary lability than integrated architectural systems.

Research Question 3: Can we identify lineage-specific architectural innovations, and what selective pressures drive their emergence?

Hypothesis 3a: Lineage-specific architectural innovations will cluster at organelle interfaces and contact sites, reflecting the evolution of novel inter-organelle communication systems in different eukaryotic groups.

Hypothesis 3b: Parasitic and symbiotic lineages will show elevated rates of architectural innovation in organelles involved in host interaction, including secretory pathway components and mitochondrial modifications associated with metabolic integration.

Hypothesis 3c: Architectural innovations will show signatures of positive selection and will correlate with the acquisition of novel ecological capabilities, enabling us to generate testable predictions about the functional significance of structural novelties.

These hypotheses are testable through our proposed synthesis approach. For conservation analyses, we will quantify structural similarity metrics across orthologous proteins and complexes, correlating conservation scores with functional annotations and network centrality measures. For divergence analyses, we will apply phylogenetic comparative methods including phylogenetic generalized least squares and Bayesian models of trait evolution to test for clock-like versus punctuated divergence patterns. For innovation detection, we will identify lineage-restricted architectural features through phylogenetic profiling and test for associations with ecological variables using phylogenetically-informed statistical frameworks. Each hypothesis generates specific predictions that can be evaluated against our integrated dataset, and negative results will be equally informative for understanding the evolutionary dynamics of organelle architecture.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates four complementary data streams through a unified computational framework, enabling systematic comparative analysis across approximately 50 eukaryotic species spanning all major supergroups.

Data Integration and Harmonization: We will construct a harmonized pan-eukaryotic organelle architecture database integrating: (1) AlphaFold-DB predicted structures for organelle-localized proteins identified through Gene Ontology annotations and experimentally validated localization databases; (2) Orthology relationships from OMA and OrthoDB, with reconciliation procedures for conflicting assignments; (3) Electron microscopy data from EMDB and EMPIAR, including tomographic reconstructions and 2D images with organelle annotations; (4) Comparative genomics data including gene family expansions, losses, and horizontal transfers from EnsemblCompara and phylome databases. Species selection will maximize phylogenetic diversity while ensuring adequate data coverage, including representatives from Opisthokonta (animals, fungi, choanoflagellates), Amoebozoa, Archaeplastida (plants, green algae, red algae), SAR (stramenopiles, alveolates, rhizaria), Excavata, and other protist lineages. We will develop standardized ontologies for organelle components that accommodate lineage-specific terminology while enabling cross-phylum comparisons.

Structural Comparison Pipeline: For each organelle class (mitochondria, nucleus, ER, Golgi, peroxisomes, and lineage-specific organelles including chloroplasts and specialized secretory organelles), we will: (1) Identify orthologous protein sets using reciprocal best-hit approaches refined by synteny and domain architecture; (2) Compute structural similarity metrics including TM-scores, RMSD values, and contact map similarities for orthologous proteins; (3) Reconstruct ancestral structures using phylogenetically-informed methods to infer evolutionary trajectories; (4) Analyze complex architecture by modeling predicted assemblies using AlphaFold-Multimer and comparing oligomeric states across species. For EM data integration, we will develop semi-automated pipelines to extract quantitative morphological features from tomograms, including membrane curvature distributions, cristae density and morphology, and inter-organelle distances.

Phylogenetic Comparative Analysis: We will apply established phylogenetic comparative methods adapted for structural data: (1) Phylogenetic signal quantification using Blomberg's K and Pagel's lambda to assess whether architectural features show phylogenetic structure; (2) Evolutionary model fitting using Brownian motion, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck, and early-burst models to characterize evolutionary dynamics; (3) Ancestral state reconstruction using maximum likelihood and Bayesian approaches to infer ancestral organelle architectures; (4) Correlation analyses using phylogenetic generalized least squares to test associations between architectural features and ecological or physiological variables while controlling for shared ancestry. We will use established phylogenetic frameworks from recent large-scale eukaryotic phylogenomics studies, with sensitivity analyses to assess robustness to phylogenetic uncertainty.

Computational Infrastructure: Analysis will leverage NCEMS computational resources for large-scale structural comparisons and phylogenetic analyses. We will develop modular, containerized workflows using Snakemake for reproducibility, with all code maintained in version-controlled repositories. Machine learning approaches, including graph neural networks for structure comparison and transformer models for sequence-structure relationships, will augment traditional comparative methods. Regular working group meetings (monthly virtual, biannual in-person) will coordinate distributed analysis efforts across team members' expertise domains.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will deliver four major outcomes with lasting impact on molecular and cellular biology.

First, we will produce a Pan-Eukaryotic Organelle Architecture Resource (PEOAR), a comprehensive database integrating structural predictions, orthology relationships, and morphological features across approximately 50 species representing all major eukaryotic supergroups. This resource will feature standardized annotations, phylogenetically-aware query interfaces, and programmatic access through APIs, enabling researchers to explore organelle architecture evolution for any component of interest. PEOAR will serve as foundational infrastructure for future comparative cell biology research.

Second, we will generate systematic phylogenetic-comparative analyses quantifying conservation and divergence patterns for major organelle systems. These analyses will identify architectural features under strong purifying selection, revealing functional constraints, while also detecting accelerated evolution associated with ecological transitions. Results will be published in high-impact journals with all underlying data and analysis code publicly available.

Third, we will catalog lineage-specific architectural innovations with associated ecological and physiological correlates. This catalog will generate testable hypotheses for experimental validation by the broader community, transforming descriptive observations into mechanistic predictions about organelle function and adaptation.

Fourth, we will establish pan-eukaryotic comparative architecture as a tractable synthesis research domain, demonstrating methodological approaches that others can extend to additional organelles, species, and biological questions.

The broader scientific impact extends to multiple communities: evolutionary biologists gain new frameworks for studying cellular evolution; structural biologists obtain comparative context for interpreting individual structures; cell biologists working on non-model organisms gain resources connecting their systems to broader patterns. For NCEMS's mission, this project demonstrates how mesoscale emergence can be studied comparatively, revealing which emergent properties are universal versus contingent. The training program will produce six researchers equipped with cross-disciplinary skills in comparative genomics, structural biology, and phylogenetic methods, contributing to the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to develop.

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Reconstructing Ancestral Mesoscale Assemblies: Phylogenetic Inference at the Architectural Scale
abstract: Phylogenetic methods have transformed our understanding of protein evolution, but ancestral reconstruction has rarely been applied at the mesoscale—to ancestral condensates, ancestral ribosomes, ancestral organelle assemblies. With AlphaFold-Multimer predictions, ancestral sequence reconstruction methods, and pan-eukaryotic orthology resources, synthesis-scale ancestral mesoscale reconstruction is now feasible and could illuminate questions about evolvability, the emergence of complexity, and the origins of mesoscale organization. This Working Group will synthesize ancestral sequence reconstructions, AlphaFold-Multimer predictions, comparative interactome data, and pan-eukaryotic orthology to reconstruct ancestral mesoscale assemblies and test hypotheses about how mesoscale complexity arose. The team brings together evolutionary biologists with ancestral-reconstruction expertise, computational structural biologists experienced in AlphaFold-Multimer, comparative biologists with deep orthology expertise, and biophysicists experienced in assembly modeling. We will reconstruct ancestral sequences for components of major mesoscale assemblies (ribosomes, nuclear pores, condensate scaffolds, motor-protein complexes) at key phylogenetic nodes, predict ancestral assembly architectures using AlphaFold-Multimer, and test whether reconstructed ancestral architectures are consistent with predicted ancestral lifestyles and inferred environmental conditions. Deliverables include (1) reconstructed ancestral mesoscale assemblies for several systems with quantified uncertainty, (2) testable hypotheses about ancestral function and the path to modern architectures, (3) open-source pipelines bringing ancestral reconstruction to the mesoscale, and (4) a framework for assessing reconstruction reliability at the mesoscale. NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis bridges evolutionary biology and structural biology in ways no single lab supports and because the methodological development demands sustained interdisciplinary effort. The training plan supports five trainees from evolutionary, structural, and computational backgrounds through cross-disciplinary co-mentoring, formal training in ancestral reconstruction and structural prediction, and joint sub-projects on specific assemblies. Trainees will participate in a cross-disciplinary seminar series and co-author the methods paper introducing mesoscale ancestral reconstruction. All reconstructions, code, and ancestral structures will be released openly through Zenodo and AlphaFold-DB with cross-references, and the pipelines will be packaged as reproducible workflows. The broader impact lies in extending the powerful framework of ancestral reconstruction from molecules to mesoscale assemblies, opening a new evolutionary perspective on how cellular complexity arose. By treating mesoscale assemblies as evolutionary objects amenable to phylogenetic inference, this project introduces a new analytical strategy with broad implications for evolutionary cell biology.
background_and_significance:
The emergence of complex cellular organization represents one of the most profound transitions in the history of life. Between individual biomolecules and fully formed organelles lies the mesoscale—a realm of multiprotein assemblies, biomolecular condensates, and supramolecular architectures that exhibit emergent properties not predictable from their components alone. Understanding how these mesoscale assemblies evolved is fundamental to explaining cellular complexity, yet our evolutionary toolkit has remained largely focused on individual proteins rather than the architectural scale at which emergence manifests.

Ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR) has revolutionized molecular evolution by enabling researchers to resurrect ancient proteins and test hypotheses about evolutionary trajectories. Pioneering work has reconstructed ancestral enzymes, receptors, and transcription factors, revealing how molecular properties changed over billions of years. However, these powerful phylogenetic methods have rarely been extended beyond individual proteins to the mesoscale assemblies that constitute the functional units of cellular organization. This gap represents both a significant limitation in our understanding and an extraordinary opportunity for synthesis research.

The convergence of three technological and data advances now makes mesoscale ancestral reconstruction feasible at unprecedented scale. First, AlphaFold-Multimer and related deep learning approaches can predict protein complex structures with remarkable accuracy, enabling computational assembly of ancestral complexes from reconstructed sequences. Second, comprehensive pan-eukaryotic orthology databases (OrthoDB, EggNOG, OMA) provide the phylogenetic scaffolding necessary for rigorous ancestral inference across diverse lineages. Third, comparative interactome data from multiple species enables validation of predicted ancestral interactions against evolutionary patterns of protein-protein associations.

This synthesis project addresses fundamental questions about emergence that lie at the heart of NCEMS's scientific mission. How did the ribosome, nature's most complex molecular machine, acquire its elaborate architecture? When did nuclear pore complexes achieve their remarkable selectivity barrier? How did phase-separating condensates evolve their material properties? These questions cannot be answered by studying modern assemblies alone—they require reconstructing evolutionary history at the architectural scale.

The significance extends beyond specific assemblies to general principles of mesoscale evolution. Do assemblies evolve by gradual accretion of components or through rapid architectural innovations? Are certain assembly architectures more evolvable than others? How do changes in individual protein sequences propagate to emergent assembly properties? By treating mesoscale assemblies as evolutionary objects amenable to phylogenetic inference, we open new windows onto these fundamental questions.

This project is uniquely suited to NCEMS support because it requires integration across disciplines that rarely interact. Evolutionary biologists expert in ancestral reconstruction typically lack structural biology expertise, while computational structural biologists rarely engage with phylogenetic methods. Comparative biologists curating orthology databases operate independently from biophysicists modeling assembly dynamics. Only through sustained interdisciplinary synthesis can these perspectives converge to enable mesoscale ancestral reconstruction. The project leverages exclusively publicly available data—sequence databases, structural predictions, orthology resources, and interactome datasets—synthesized through novel computational workflows that no single laboratory could develop alone.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses three interconnected research questions that span evolutionary biology, structural biology, and biophysics, each generating testable hypotheses amenable to synthesis-scale investigation.

Research Question 1: How did the architectural complexity of major mesoscale assemblies evolve?

We hypothesize that mesoscale assemblies evolved through identifiable architectural transitions at specific phylogenetic nodes, with complexity increasing through both component accretion and interface elaboration. Specifically, we predict that (H1a) ancestral ribosomes at the Last Eukaryotic Common Ancestor (LECA) possessed simpler peripheral architectures than modern ribosomes while maintaining conserved core structures; (H1b) nuclear pore complex scaffolds evolved modular elaborations coinciding with the emergence of open mitosis in specific lineages; and (H1c) condensate scaffold proteins acquired intrinsically disordered regions with phase-separation capacity at nodes correlating with increased cellular compartmentalization. These hypotheses are testable through ancestral reconstruction at defined phylogenetic nodes followed by structural prediction and comparison with modern architectures.

Research Question 2: Are reconstructed ancestral assembly architectures consistent with inferred ancestral cellular environments and lifestyles?

We hypothesize that ancestral mesoscale architectures exhibit structural and biophysical properties consistent with paleoenvironmental reconstructions and inferred ancestral metabolisms. Specifically, we predict that (H2a) ancestral thermophilic assemblies will show enhanced interface stability and reduced conformational flexibility compared to mesophilic descendants; (H2b) ancestral motor protein complexes in lineages with inferred high-motility lifestyles will exhibit architectural features supporting processivity; and (H2c) ancestral condensate scaffolds in lineages experiencing environmental stress will show properties consistent with stress granule formation. Testing these hypotheses requires integrating ancestral reconstructions with paleoenvironmental data and lifestyle inferences from comparative genomics.

Research Question 3: What methodological frameworks enable reliable ancestral reconstruction at the mesoscale, and how should uncertainty be quantified?

We hypothesize that mesoscale reconstruction reliability depends on both sequence-level and architecture-level factors that can be systematically characterized. Specifically, we predict that (H3a) reconstruction confidence correlates with the number of conserved inter-subunit interfaces rather than overall sequence conservation; (H3b) assemblies with modular architectures yield more reliable reconstructions than those with highly integrated interfaces; and (H3c) uncertainty propagation from sequence reconstruction to structural prediction follows quantifiable patterns that enable reliability assessment. These methodological hypotheses will be tested through systematic benchmarking using assemblies with known evolutionary histories and through cross-validation approaches.

Our approach to hypothesis testing emphasizes synthesis across data types. For each target assembly system, we will integrate: (1) ancestral sequences reconstructed using maximum likelihood methods with posterior probability distributions; (2) AlphaFold-Multimer predictions with confidence metrics; (3) comparative interactome data validating predicted ancestral interactions; and (4) orthology relationships constraining evolutionary scenarios. This multi-layered synthesis enables robust hypothesis testing while quantifying uncertainty at each analytical stage.

The Working Group will prioritize four assembly systems representing distinct mesoscale organizational principles: ribosomes (obligate complexes with ancient origins), nuclear pore complexes (modular assemblies with lineage-specific elaborations), condensate scaffolds (dynamic assemblies with emergent material properties), and motor protein complexes (mechanochemical assemblies with functional constraints). This selection enables comparative analysis across assembly types while maintaining feasibility within the project timeline.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates four computational workflows into a unified pipeline for mesoscale ancestral reconstruction, leveraging exclusively publicly available data sources.

Workflow 1: Orthology Resolution and Phylogenetic Framework Construction

We will synthesize orthology assignments from OrthoDB, EggNOG, and OMA databases, implementing consensus approaches to resolve conflicting assignments for assembly components. For each target assembly, we will construct species trees spanning key phylogenetic nodes (LECA, major eukaryotic supergroup ancestors, crown group ancestors) using established phylogenomic frameworks. Gene trees for individual components will be reconciled with species trees using probabilistic methods (NOTUNG, ecceTERA) to infer duplication and loss events. This workflow produces curated alignments and phylogenies for all components of target assemblies, with explicit uncertainty quantification.

Workflow 2: Ancestral Sequence Reconstruction

Using curated alignments and phylogenies, we will reconstruct ancestral sequences at defined nodes using maximum likelihood methods implemented in PAML and IQ-TREE, with Bayesian approaches (PhyloBayes) for uncertainty quantification. We will implement ensemble approaches sampling from posterior distributions to generate multiple plausible ancestral sequences per component. For intrinsically disordered regions critical to condensate scaffolds, we will employ specialized reconstruction methods accounting for elevated substitution rates and compositional biases. Reconstruction quality will be assessed using posterior probabilities, gap handling metrics, and cross-validation through leave-one-out analyses.

Workflow 3: Ancestral Assembly Architecture Prediction

Reconstructed ancestral sequences will be submitted to AlphaFold-Multimer for complex structure prediction, with systematic exploration of subunit stoichiometries informed by modern assembly compositions. We will implement iterative assembly strategies for large complexes, predicting subcomplexes before integrating into larger architectures. Confidence metrics (pLDDT, PAE) will be tracked throughout, enabling reliability assessment. For condensate scaffolds, we will complement structural predictions with sequence-based predictions of phase separation propensity using established predictors (catGRANULE, PSPredictor). Predicted ancestral structures will be compared against modern structures using structural alignment tools (TM-align, FATCAT) to quantify architectural changes.

Workflow 4: Validation and Hypothesis Testing

Ancestral assembly predictions will be validated through multiple approaches: (1) consistency with comparative interactome data from STRING and IntAct databases, testing whether predicted ancestral interactions are supported by conserved interactions across extant species; (2) compatibility with paleoenvironmental reconstructions, testing whether predicted biophysical properties match inferred ancestral conditions; (3) phylogenetic congruence, testing whether architectural transitions correlate with established evolutionary events. We will implement molecular dynamics simulations for selected ancestral assemblies to assess stability and dynamics, using coarse-grained approaches (MARTINI) for computational tractability.

Integration and Pipeline Development

All workflows will be implemented as reproducible Snakemake pipelines with containerized dependencies (Docker/Singularity), enabling deployment across computational environments. The Working Group will meet biweekly for virtual coordination, with three in-person workshops at NCEMS facilities for intensive integration efforts. Each assembly system will be assigned to a trainee-mentor pair spanning disciplines, ensuring cross-training while maintaining project coherence. Quality control checkpoints will be established at workflow transitions, with explicit criteria for proceeding to subsequent stages.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will deliver four categories of outcomes with transformative potential for evolutionary cell biology and mesoscale science.

First, we will produce reconstructed ancestral mesoscale assemblies for four major systems—ribosomes, nuclear pore complexes, condensate scaffolds, and motor protein complexes—at key phylogenetic nodes spanning eukaryotic evolution. Each reconstruction will include ancestral sequences with posterior probability distributions, predicted structures with confidence metrics, and explicit uncertainty quantification. These reconstructions will be deposited in public databases with full provenance documentation, enabling community validation and extension.

Second, we will generate testable hypotheses about ancestral function and evolutionary trajectories linking ancestral to modern architectures. These hypotheses will be formulated as specific predictions amenable to experimental testing through ancestral protein resurrection, providing a roadmap for future laboratory studies. The hypotheses will address fundamental questions about the origins of mesoscale complexity and the mechanisms of architectural evolution.

Third, we will release open-source computational pipelines bringing ancestral reconstruction to the mesoscale. These pipelines will integrate orthology resolution, ancestral sequence reconstruction, structural prediction, and validation into reproducible workflows accessible to the broader community. Comprehensive documentation and tutorials will lower barriers to adoption, enabling researchers without specialized expertise to apply mesoscale ancestral reconstruction to new systems.

Fourth, we will establish a methodological framework for assessing reconstruction reliability at the mesoscale, including metrics for confidence assessment, guidelines for interpretation, and benchmarking datasets for method validation. This framework will provide essential infrastructure for the emerging field of mesoscale evolutionary biology.

The broader impact extends beyond specific deliverables to establishing a new analytical paradigm. By demonstrating that mesoscale assemblies can be treated as evolutionary objects amenable to phylogenetic inference, this project opens new research directions at the intersection of evolutionary biology, structural biology, and cell biology. The framework we develop will be applicable to any mesoscale assembly with sufficient phylogenetic sampling, enabling community-wide extension to diverse biological systems.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
This Working Group is committed to exemplary open science practices aligned with NCEMS policies and FAIR principles, ensuring that all products are findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable.

All reconstructed ancestral sequences will be deposited in Zenodo with DOIs enabling persistent citation, organized hierarchically by assembly system and phylogenetic node. author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Engineered Versus Evolved Mesoscale: Do Designed Systems Obey the Same Rules
abstract: Synthetic biology has produced an expanding repertoire of engineered mesoscale systems—designed condensates, synthetic minimal cells, de novo proteins, engineered organelles. Whether these engineered systems obey the same compositional, dynamical, and organizational rules as evolved systems is unknown, with profound implications for both fundamental biology (what is necessity vs. contingency) and applied biology (what can be engineered). This Working Group will synthesize public data from synthetic-biology repositories (Addgene-derived data, JCVI minimal-cell datasets, designed-protein databases) alongside natural mesoscale datasets to test whether engineered and evolved mesoscale systems follow the same rules. The team brings together synthetic biologists with engineered-condensate and minimal-cell expertise, cell biologists studying natural mesoscale systems, biophysicists, and machine-learning researchers experienced in transfer learning. We will harmonize engineered-system datasets with natural mesoscale datasets to enable direct comparison, develop statistical methods that test whether engineered systems sample the same parameter space as evolved systems or systematically differ, and identify rules that hold across both versus rules specific to evolved systems. Deliverables include (1) harmonized engineered-vs-evolved mesoscale datasets with consistent annotation, (2) statistical comparisons identifying shared and divergent rules, (3) testable hypotheses about why engineered systems systematically differ from evolved systems where they do, and (4) design principles for synthetic biologists derived from the comparison. NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis spans synthetic and natural biology communities that rarely collaborate at the data-integration level and because the comparison demands ontological and statistical infrastructure beyond any single lab. The training plan supports four trainees from synthetic-biology and natural-cell-biology programs through cross-community co-mentoring, formal training in synthesis-data analysis and statistical comparison methods, and joint sub-projects on specific mesoscale system pairs. Trainees will participate in a cross-community seminar series and co-author the comparative paper. All harmonized data and code will be released through Addgene-linked repositories, Zenodo, and GitHub with reproducible workflows. The broader impact is conceptual: identifying which mesoscale rules transcend the engineered-evolved divide will sharpen understanding of biological necessity, while identifying engineering-specific deviations will inform synthetic-biology design principles. By using synthetic systems as natural experiments to probe what is constrained versus contingent in evolved mesoscale biology, this project addresses both novel scientific questions and innovative analytical strategies.
background_and_significance:
The mesoscale—the organizational level between individual biomolecules and membrane-bound organelles—represents one of the most dynamic frontiers in molecular and cellular biology. At this scale, emergent properties arise from the collective behavior of proteins, nucleic acids, and other biomolecules, giving rise to biomolecular condensates, cytoskeletal networks, signaling complexes, and other functional assemblies. Understanding the rules governing mesoscale organization is fundamental to comprehending how cells achieve spatial and temporal control over biochemical reactions, maintain homeostasis, and respond to environmental perturbations.

Over the past two decades, synthetic biology has emerged as a powerful complementary approach to studying biological systems. Researchers have engineered an impressive array of mesoscale structures, including designed protein condensates with programmable properties, synthetic minimal cells derived from genome-reduction efforts at the J. Craig Venter Institute (JCVI), de novo designed proteins that self-assemble into novel architectures, and engineered organelles with customized functions. These synthetic systems offer unprecedented opportunities to test our understanding of biological principles by building systems from defined components.

However, a fundamental question remains largely unexplored: do engineered mesoscale systems obey the same compositional, dynamical, and organizational rules as their naturally evolved counterparts? This question has profound implications for both basic and applied biology. From a fundamental perspective, comparing engineered and evolved systems can distinguish between biological necessity (rules that must be followed regardless of evolutionary history) and contingency (features that reflect the particular path evolution has taken). From an applied perspective, understanding where engineered systems deviate from natural rules could reveal both limitations and opportunities for synthetic biology.

Current knowledge is fragmented across disciplines. Synthetic biologists have accumulated extensive data on engineered systems, deposited in repositories like Addgene, the Protein Data Bank (for designed proteins), and specialized databases. Cell biologists have generated vast datasets characterizing natural mesoscale assemblies through proteomics, imaging, and functional studies. However, these communities rarely integrate their data or analytical frameworks, leaving the comparative question unaddressed.

Several preliminary observations suggest that systematic differences may exist. Engineered condensates often exhibit different material properties than natural condensates, designed proteins frequently show altered dynamics compared to evolved counterparts, and minimal cells display distinct metabolic constraints. Whether these differences reflect fundamental violations of mesoscale rules or simply incomplete engineering remains unknown.

This project addresses a compelling gap at the intersection of synthetic biology, cell biology, and biophysics. By synthesizing publicly available data from both engineered and evolved mesoscale systems, we will establish the first comprehensive framework for systematic comparison. The significance extends beyond academic interest: identifying universal mesoscale rules will advance our fundamental understanding of biological organization, while characterizing engineering-specific deviations will provide actionable design principles for the synthetic biology community. This synthesis research exemplifies the NCEMS mission by leveraging existing data to address emergence phenomena at the mesoscale through collaborative, transdisciplinary approaches.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group will address three interconnected research questions, each with associated testable hypotheses that will guide our synthesis and analysis efforts.

**Research Question 1: Do engineered and evolved mesoscale systems occupy the same compositional parameter space?**

We hypothesize that engineered mesoscale systems systematically differ from evolved systems in their compositional characteristics, reflecting both design constraints and the absence of evolutionary optimization. Specifically, we predict that: (H1a) Engineered condensates will show reduced compositional complexity compared to natural condensates, with fewer protein components and simpler interaction networks. (H1b) Designed proteins incorporated into mesoscale assemblies will exhibit narrower amino acid compositional distributions than evolved proteins, particularly in intrinsically disordered regions critical for condensate formation. (H1c) Minimal cells will show systematic depletion of certain functional categories compared to naturally reduced genomes, reflecting human design biases versus evolutionary constraints.

**Research Question 2: Do engineered and evolved mesoscale systems follow the same dynamical rules?**

We hypothesize that fundamental biophysical constraints impose universal dynamical rules, but evolved systems have optimized within these constraints in ways that engineered systems have not yet achieved. Specific predictions include: (H2a) Both engineered and evolved condensates will follow similar scaling relationships between size and molecular exchange rates, reflecting universal physical principles. (H2b) However, evolved condensates will show tighter coupling between compositional changes and functional outputs, reflecting evolutionary fine-tuning. (H2c) Engineered minimal cells will exhibit greater metabolic variability and reduced homeostatic control compared to naturally minimized bacterial genomes, suggesting that dynamic stability requires evolutionary optimization.

**Research Question 3: What organizational principles are universal versus evolution-specific?**

We hypothesize that certain organizational features represent fundamental requirements for mesoscale function (biological necessities), while others reflect evolutionary contingencies that engineered systems need not replicate. We predict: (H3a) Hierarchical organization—the nesting of smaller assemblies within larger structures—will be universal, as it reflects fundamental thermodynamic and kinetic constraints. (H3b) Specific molecular grammar rules (e.g., the spacing patterns of interaction motifs) will differ between engineered and evolved systems, as multiple solutions exist to achieve similar functions. (H3c) Network topology features, such as the distribution of hub proteins within mesoscale assemblies, will show systematic differences, with evolved systems exhibiting greater robustness through redundancy.

**Analytical Framework**

To address these questions, we will develop a unified analytical framework that enables rigorous statistical comparison. This framework will incorporate: (1) Dimensionality reduction approaches to visualize the parameter spaces occupied by engineered versus evolved systems; (2) Statistical tests for distribution differences that account for the heterogeneous nature of mesoscale data; (3) Machine learning classifiers to identify features that most strongly distinguish engineered from evolved systems; (4) Transfer learning approaches to test whether models trained on evolved systems accurately predict properties of engineered systems, and vice versa.

The combination of specific hypotheses and robust analytical methods will ensure that our synthesis produces actionable insights rather than purely descriptive comparisons. Where hypotheses are confirmed, we will identify the underlying mechanistic explanations. Where hypotheses are rejected, we will revise our understanding and generate new testable predictions for the field.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises four integrated phases: data identification and acquisition, harmonization and annotation, comparative analysis, and hypothesis generation.

**Phase 1: Data Identification and Acquisition (Months 1-6)**

We will systematically identify and acquire publicly available datasets spanning engineered and evolved mesoscale systems. For engineered systems, primary sources include: (1) Addgene-associated publications and supplementary datasets describing engineered condensates and synthetic assemblies; (2) JCVI minimal cell datasets, including genome sequences, transcriptomics, proteomics, and phenotypic characterizations of JCVI-syn3.0 and related strains; (3) The Protein Data Bank and specialized databases (e.g., SCOP, CATH) for de novo designed proteins; (4) Published datasets from engineered organelle studies. For evolved systems, we will leverage: (1) PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, and other condensate databases; (2) The Human Protein Atlas and comparable resources for organelle proteomics; (3) Structural databases for naturally evolved protein assemblies; (4) Comparative genomics databases for naturally reduced bacterial genomes. Our data inventory will document dataset provenance, experimental methods, and quality metrics.

**Phase 2: Harmonization and Annotation (Months 4-12)**

Data harmonization represents a critical challenge requiring dedicated methodological development. We will establish a unified ontology for mesoscale systems that bridges synthetic and natural biology terminologies. This ontology will define consistent terms for compositional features (protein identity, stoichiometry, post-translational modifications), dynamical properties (exchange rates, material properties, response times), and organizational characteristics (size, morphology, hierarchical structure). We will develop automated and semi-automated pipelines for mapping existing annotations to our unified ontology, with manual curation for ambiguous cases. Quality control procedures will flag datasets with insufficient metadata or questionable provenance. The harmonization infrastructure will be built using established standards (e.g., OBO Foundry ontologies) to ensure interoperability with existing resources.

**Phase 3: Comparative Analysis (Months 10-20)**

Our analytical approach combines statistical methods with machine learning. For compositional comparisons, we will compute feature distributions (amino acid composition, domain architecture, interaction network metrics) for engineered versus evolved systems and apply statistical tests (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, permutation tests) to identify significant differences. For dynamical comparisons, we will extract quantitative parameters from published measurements and test scaling relationships across system types. For organizational comparisons, we will analyze network topology, hierarchical structure, and spatial organization using graph-theoretic and geometric methods.

Machine learning approaches will include: (1) Supervised classifiers (random forests, gradient boosting, neural networks) trained to distinguish engineered from evolved systems, with feature importance analysis to identify discriminating characteristics; (2) Transfer learning experiments testing whether models trained on one system type generalize to the other; (3) Dimensionality reduction (UMAP, PCA) to visualize parameter space coverage. All analyses will incorporate appropriate controls for confounding variables (e.g., study methodology, organism of origin).

**Phase 4: Hypothesis Generation and Validation Framework (Months 18-24)**

Where analyses reveal systematic differences, we will generate mechanistic hypotheses explaining the divergence. These hypotheses will be formulated as testable predictions that the broader community can address experimentally. We will develop a prioritization framework ranking hypotheses by their potential impact and testability, creating a roadmap for future research.
