author: claude-opus-4-5
title: A Foundation-Model Embedding for Public Cell Microscopy: Unifying HPA, IDR, JUMP, and OpenCell
abstract: Public cell-microscopy archives—the Human Protein Atlas, Image Data Resource, JUMP Cell Painting, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer—contain millions of images representing the largest visual record of cellular biology ever assembled, but no unified embedding exists across these archives. Without a shared representation, cross-archive analysis is essentially impossible, and the integrated value of these resources is unrealized. This Working Group will train a foundation-model embedding spanning major public cell-microscopy archives and demonstrate its utility for revealing previously invisible mesoscale phenotypes. The team brings together computer-vision experts with foundation-model experience, cell biologists with deep expertise in each archive, machine-learning infrastructure specialists, and quantitative imaging biologists. We will preprocess images from the major archives into a unified format, train a self-supervised foundation model using contrastive and masked-modeling objectives at archive scale, and analyze the resulting embedding for novel phenotype clusters that cross archive boundaries. Particular attention will be paid to mesoscale phenotypes—organelle organization, condensate features, cytoskeletal patterns—that may be visible in the embedding but underexplored in any single archive. Deliverables include (1) a unified foundation-model embedding released as a community resource, (2) the underlying preprocessed image corpus with consistent metadata, (3) discovered mesoscale phenotype clusters with biological annotation, and (4) downstream analysis tools enabling researchers to project their own images into the embedding. NCEMS support is essential because the project requires computational scale beyond any single lab, deep cell-biology expertise across multiple archive contexts, and sustained machine-learning infrastructure. The training plan supports six trainees from computer-vision and cell-biology programs through cross-disciplinary co-mentoring, formal training in foundation-model methods and biological image analysis, and joint sub-projects on specific phenotype classes revealed by the embedding. Trainees will co-author the foundation-model paper and downstream phenotype-specific analyses. The model and embedding will be released through HuggingFace with clear licensing, the preprocessed corpus will be hosted with cross-references to source archives, and reproducible training and analysis pipelines will be released through GitHub. The broader impact is infrastructural: a shared foundation-model embedding will enable a generation of synthesis research on public cell microscopy that is currently impossible. By providing the missing computational substrate for cross-archive cell-image analysis, this project addresses a clear NCEMS-scale need and an innovative analytical strategy whose downstream applications will extend well beyond the immediate Working Group.
background_and_significance:
The past two decades have witnessed an unprecedented accumulation of publicly available cell microscopy data. The Human Protein Atlas (HPA) contains immunofluorescence images mapping protein localization across human cell lines and tissues. The Image Data Resource (IDR) aggregates diverse imaging datasets from published studies spanning multiple organisms and experimental conditions. The JUMP Cell Painting consortium has generated morphological profiles of cells treated with thousands of genetic and chemical perturbations. OpenCell provides endogenously tagged protein localization data with exceptional specificity, while the Allen Cell Explorer offers live-cell imaging of key cellular structures. Collectively, these archives represent millions of images—the most comprehensive visual documentation of cellular organization ever assembled.

Despite this wealth of data, a fundamental barrier prevents their integrated analysis: the absence of a unified computational representation spanning archives. Each resource was generated using different imaging modalities, labeling strategies, cell types, and metadata standards. Researchers analyzing one archive cannot readily compare findings with another, and patterns that emerge only when data are combined remain invisible. This fragmentation represents a critical missed opportunity for molecular and cellular biology, particularly for understanding emergence phenomena at the mesoscale—the organizational level between individual biomolecules and organelles where complex cellular behaviors arise.

The mesoscale is precisely where emergence becomes most apparent in cellular systems. Biomolecular condensates, cytoskeletal networks, organelle contact sites, and spatial protein organization all represent mesoscale phenomena where collective behaviors produce properties not predictable from individual molecular components. These phenomena are captured in existing microscopy archives but remain underexplored because no computational framework enables their systematic cross-archive investigation. Individual studies have characterized specific mesoscale features within single datasets, but synthesis across archives—essential for distinguishing universal organizational principles from context-specific patterns—has been impossible.

Foundation models offer a transformative solution to this challenge. These large-scale neural networks, trained through self-supervised learning on massive datasets, learn generalizable representations that transfer across diverse downstream tasks. In natural language processing and computer vision, foundation models have revolutionized the field by providing shared embedding spaces where previously incompatible data can be meaningfully compared. Recent applications to biological imaging, including models for histopathology and protein structure, demonstrate the potential of this approach for life sciences.

However, no foundation model currently exists for cell microscopy at the scale and diversity represented by public archives. Existing cell-image models are trained on single datasets or limited imaging modalities, lacking the breadth necessary for cross-archive synthesis. Creating such a model requires computational resources, diverse expertise, and sustained infrastructure beyond any single laboratory—precisely the collaborative synthesis that NCEMS is designed to enable.

This project addresses a foundational gap in the molecular and cellular sciences: the inability to computationally integrate the world's public cell microscopy data. By creating a unified embedding space, we will enable researchers to discover mesoscale phenotypes that transcend individual archives, identify conserved organizational principles across cell types and experimental conditions, and leverage the full collective value of publicly available imaging data. The significance extends beyond immediate scientific discoveries to establishing essential infrastructure for a new generation of synthesis research in cellular biology.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses interconnected research questions spanning computational methodology, mesoscale biology, and data synthesis. Our questions are designed to advance both the development of foundation models for biological imaging and fundamental understanding of cellular organization at the mesoscale.

Primary Research Question 1: Can a self-supervised foundation model learn a unified embedding space that meaningfully represents cellular phenotypes across heterogeneous public microscopy archives?

Hypothesis 1a: A foundation model trained on diverse cell microscopy data using contrastive and masked-modeling objectives will learn representations where biologically similar phenotypes cluster together regardless of source archive, imaging modality, or experimental protocol.

Hypothesis 1b: The learned embedding space will capture hierarchical biological organization, with distinct regions corresponding to subcellular compartments, cellular states, and morphological features that align with established biological knowledge.

Rationale: Foundation models in other domains have demonstrated remarkable ability to learn transferable representations from heterogeneous data. We hypothesize that underlying biological similarities across archives will provide sufficient signal for the model to learn meaningful representations despite technical variation.

Primary Research Question 2: What previously unrecognized mesoscale phenotypes become visible when cell microscopy data are analyzed in a unified embedding space?

Hypothesis 2a: Cross-archive embedding analysis will reveal novel mesoscale phenotype clusters—particularly involving organelle organization, biomolecular condensate features, and cytoskeletal patterns—that are not apparent when archives are analyzed independently.

Hypothesis 2b: Some mesoscale phenotypes will be conserved across multiple archives and experimental conditions, suggesting fundamental organizational principles, while others will be context-specific, revealing condition-dependent cellular states.

Rationale: Individual archives capture partial views of cellular organization. Integration should reveal patterns that require multiple perspectives to detect, analogous to how combining astronomical observations across wavelengths reveals structures invisible in any single band.

Primary Research Question 3: How do mesoscale organizational features relate to molecular composition and cellular function across diverse cellular contexts?

Hypothesis 3a: Embedding-derived mesoscale phenotype clusters will show significant enrichment for specific protein families, post-translational modifications, or functional categories when cross-referenced with molecular annotations from source archives.

Hypothesis 3b: Cells sharing similar mesoscale organization in embedding space will exhibit correlated functional behaviors (proliferation, stress response, differentiation state) even when derived from different archives or experimental systems.

Rationale: Mesoscale organization represents an intermediate level connecting molecular composition to cellular function. A unified embedding should enable systematic investigation of these relationships at unprecedented scale.

Methodological Research Question: What architectural and training choices optimize foundation model performance for heterogeneous cell microscopy data?

Hypothesis 4: Hybrid training objectives combining contrastive learning (to align similar images across archives) with masked image modeling (to learn local structural features) will outperform either approach alone for cross-archive generalization.

Secondary Questions: We will also investigate: How does embedding quality vary across different cell types, imaging modalities, and perturbation conditions? What minimum data requirements enable effective cross-archive transfer? How can domain adaptation techniques address systematic technical variation between archives?

These questions directly address NCEMS priorities by focusing on emergence phenomena at the mesoscale, leveraging publicly available data synthesis, and developing innovative analytical strategies that require collaborative expertise across machine learning and cell biology.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises four integrated phases: data harmonization, foundation model development, mesoscale phenotype discovery, and community resource deployment.

Phase 1: Data Harmonization and Preprocessing (Months 1-8)
We will systematically access and preprocess images from five major archives: HPA (~500,000 images), IDR (selected high-quality datasets, ~2 million images), JUMP Cell Painting (~4 million images), OpenCell (~200,000 images), and Allen Cell Explorer (~100,000 images). Our harmonization pipeline will address three key challenges: (1) Resolution and format standardization—converting diverse file formats to unified zarr arrays with consistent pixel sizes through appropriate resampling; (2) Channel alignment—mapping archive-specific channel definitions to a common semantic framework (nucleus, membrane, cytoplasm, protein-of-interest) while preserving archive-specific channels as auxiliary features; (3) Metadata integration—creating unified annotation schemas linking images to gene identities, cell lines, perturbations, and experimental conditions using ontology-based mappings.

Quality control will include automated detection of imaging artifacts, intensity normalization using archive-specific reference distributions, and manual validation of representative samples by cell biology team members with archive-specific expertise. The preprocessed corpus will include provenance tracking linking every processed image to its source archive record.

Phase 2: Foundation Model Training (Months 6-18)
We will train a vision transformer (ViT) architecture adapted for multi-channel microscopy data. The model will use a hybrid self-supervised objective combining: (1) Contrastive learning using archive-aware sampling to learn representations invariant to technical variation while preserving biological signal—positive pairs will include augmented versions of the same image and images of the same protein/condition across archives; (2) Masked image modeling where the model reconstructs randomly masked image patches, learning local structural features essential for mesoscale phenotype recognition.

Training will proceed in stages: initial pretraining on the full corpus using standard augmentations, followed by fine-tuning phases that progressively incorporate harder cross-archive contrastive pairs. We will use distributed training across multiple GPU nodes, with mixed-precision training and gradient checkpointing to manage memory requirements. Hyperparameter optimization will use held-out validation sets from each archive to ensure balanced cross-archive performance.

Model evaluation will assess: embedding quality through linear probe classification of known protein localizations; cross-archive transfer through zero-shot retrieval of similar images across archives; and biological coherence through correlation with established morphological features.

Phase 3: Mesoscale Phenotype Discovery (Months 14-24)
Using the trained embedding, we will systematically identify mesoscale phenotype clusters through: (1) Unsupervised clustering of the full embedding space using hierarchical density-based methods (HDBSCAN) with multiple resolution parameters; (2) Cross-archive enrichment analysis identifying clusters containing images from multiple archives, prioritizing these as candidates for conserved mesoscale phenotypes; (3) Biological annotation through automated feature extraction (organelle morphology, texture, spatial statistics) and manual expert review by cell biology team members.

We will focus particular attention on three mesoscale phenomena: organelle contact sites and spatial relationships, biomolecular condensate morphology and distribution, and cytoskeletal organization patterns. For each discovered phenotype cluster, we will generate biological hypotheses by cross-referencing with molecular annotations and functional data from source archives.

Phase 4: Resource Development and Deployment (Months 18-30)
We will develop user-facing tools including: a web interface for exploring the embedding space and discovered phenotypes; Python APIs for projecting new images into the embedding; and documented pipelines for reproducing our analyses. All resources will be released with comprehensive documentation and tutorials.

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: Causal Mesoscale Regulatory Graphs from Perturb-seq and ORFeome Synthesis
abstract: Most network reconstruction in cell biology relies on correlational measures that conflate direct and indirect relationships, limiting mechanistic interpretation. Large-scale perturbation atlases—Perturb-seq, ORFeome screens, CRISPR perturbation studies—contain the interventional information needed for causal inference, but no synthesis project has applied modern causal-inference methods at scale to extract directional regulatory graphs governing mesoscale assemblies. This Working Group will synthesize public Perturb-seq and ORFeome datasets to construct causal regulatory graphs for mesoscale assembly processes (condensate formation, organelle biogenesis, cytoskeletal organization) using do-calculus and modern causal-inference frameworks. The team brings together causal-inference specialists from statistics and computer science, perturbation-genomics experts, cell biologists with mesoscale expertise, and computational biologists experienced in network reconstruction. We will harmonize perturbation datasets across labs and platforms, develop causal-inference pipelines adapted to perturbation-genomics data with its specific noise structure and confounding patterns, and apply these methods to construct directional regulatory graphs for mesoscale assembly processes. Validation will use held-out perturbations and orthogonal experimental data. Deliverables include (1) harmonized perturbation datasets with consistent annotation, (2) causal-inference pipelines adapted to perturbation genomics, released as open-source software, (3) inferred causal regulatory graphs for mesoscale assembly processes, and (4) testable predictions about regulatory mechanisms for follow-up experimental work. NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis bridges causal-inference and cell-biology communities that rarely collaborate, and because perturbation-data harmonization at this scale demands sustained methodological infrastructure. The training plan supports five trainees from statistics, computer science, and biology programs through cross-disciplinary co-mentoring, formal training in causal inference and perturbation genomics, and joint sub-projects on specific mesoscale processes. Trainees will participate in a cross-disciplinary seminar series and co-author the methods paper introducing causal inference at scale to perturbation genomics. All harmonized data, code, and inferred graphs will be released through cellxgene-linked repositories and GitHub with reproducible workflows, and the graphs will be queryable through a public web interface. The broader impact lies in moving cell-biology network analysis from correlational to causal, providing the mechanistic interpretability that downstream experimental and therapeutic work requires. By bringing modern causal inference to perturbation genomics at scale, this project addresses an innovative analytical strategy with broad implications for systems biology and drug discovery.
background_and_significance:
Understanding how molecular interactions give rise to emergent cellular properties represents one of the most fundamental challenges in modern biology. At the mesoscale—the organizational level between individual biomolecules and membrane-bound organelles—cells exhibit remarkable emergent behaviors including biomolecular condensate formation through liquid-liquid phase separation, dynamic cytoskeletal self-organization, and the coordinated assembly of multi-protein complexes. These mesoscale assemblies are not simply the sum of their molecular parts; they exhibit collective properties that emerge from complex regulatory networks operating across multiple scales of biological organization.

Traditionally, network biology has relied on correlational approaches—co-expression analysis, protein-protein interaction networks, and guilt-by-association methods—to map regulatory relationships. While these approaches have yielded valuable insights, they suffer from a fundamental limitation: correlation does not imply causation. Co-expression networks cannot distinguish direct regulatory relationships from indirect associations mediated by confounding factors or shared upstream regulators. This limitation severely constrains our ability to generate mechanistic hypotheses and identify intervention targets for therapeutic development.

The emergence of large-scale perturbation technologies has fundamentally changed the data landscape. Perturb-seq combines CRISPR-based genetic perturbations with single-cell RNA sequencing, enabling systematic measurement of transcriptional responses to thousands of genetic knockdowns or knockouts. ORFeome overexpression screens provide complementary gain-of-function data. Together, these datasets contain millions of perturbation-response measurements across diverse cell types and conditions. Critically, perturbation data provides the interventional structure required for causal inference—when we knock down gene A and observe changes in gene B, we have evidence for a causal relationship that correlational data cannot provide.

Despite this wealth of interventional data, the field has not systematically applied modern causal-inference frameworks to extract directional regulatory graphs. The causal-inference community has developed sophisticated methods—including do-calculus, structural causal models, and constraint-based algorithms—that can leverage interventional data to distinguish direct from indirect effects and infer causal directionality. However, these methods have rarely been applied to perturbation-genomics data, which presents unique challenges including high dimensionality, technical noise, incomplete perturbation efficiency, and complex confounding structures.

This disconnect represents a significant missed opportunity. The synthesis of causal-inference methodology with perturbation-genomics data could transform our understanding of mesoscale regulatory networks. By constructing causal graphs rather than correlational networks, we can identify the direct regulatory relationships governing condensate formation, organelle biogenesis, and cytoskeletal organization. Such causal graphs provide mechanistic interpretability essential for generating testable hypotheses and identifying therapeutic targets.

The significance of this project extends beyond methodology. Mesoscale assemblies are increasingly recognized as central to cellular function and disease. Aberrant condensate formation contributes to neurodegeneration; disrupted organelle biogenesis underlies metabolic disorders; cytoskeletal dysregulation drives cancer metastasis. Causal regulatory graphs for these processes will provide the mechanistic foundation needed to understand disease mechanisms and develop targeted interventions. This project directly addresses NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale while developing innovative analytical strategies that advance molecular and cellular sciences.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses a central scientific question: What are the causal regulatory relationships governing mesoscale assembly processes, and how do these directional networks differ from correlational reconstructions? We decompose this overarching question into four specific research questions with associated testable hypotheses.

Research Question 1: Can modern causal-inference methods, when applied to perturbation-genomics data at scale, recover known regulatory relationships with higher specificity than correlational approaches?

Hypothesis 1: Causal-inference methods applied to Perturb-seq data will identify direct regulatory relationships with significantly higher precision (reduced false positives from indirect associations) compared to standard co-expression network methods, while maintaining comparable recall for known interactions. We predict at least 30% improvement in precision for benchmark gene sets with experimentally validated direct interactions.

Research Question 2: What is the causal regulatory architecture governing biomolecular condensate formation, and which regulators exert direct versus indirect effects on phase separation?

Hypothesis 2: The regulatory network controlling condensate formation exhibits a hierarchical causal structure, with a small number of master regulators (estimated 15-25 genes) exerting direct causal effects on condensate components, while the majority of previously identified "condensate regulators" act through indirect pathways. We hypothesize that direct regulators will be enriched for genes encoding RNA-binding proteins and post-translational modification enzymes that directly modify condensate scaffold proteins.

Research Question 3: How do causal regulatory networks for organelle biogenesis differ across organelle types, and what shared regulatory modules emerge from cross-organelle synthesis?

Hypothesis 3: Despite distinct molecular compositions, mitochondrial, peroxisomal, and ER biogenesis share conserved causal regulatory modules involving membrane lipid synthesis and protein translocation machinery. We predict identification of 5-10 shared causal regulatory hubs that coordinate biogenesis across organelle types, representing potential master regulators of organelle homeostasis.

Research Question 4: Can causal graphs predict the transcriptional consequences of novel perturbations not included in training data?

Hypothesis 4: Causal regulatory graphs will enable accurate prediction of transcriptional responses to held-out perturbations, outperforming correlational network-based predictions. Specifically, we hypothesize that causal graph-based predictions will achieve at least 25% higher correlation with observed responses compared to predictions from co-expression networks, particularly for perturbations targeting indirect regulators where correlational methods are expected to fail.

Methodological Questions: Beyond these biological questions, we address critical methodological challenges. How should causal-inference algorithms be adapted to handle the specific noise structure of single-cell perturbation data, including dropout, variable perturbation efficiency, and batch effects? What is the minimum perturbation coverage required for reliable causal inference in high-dimensional gene regulatory networks? How can we integrate gain-of-function (ORFeome) and loss-of-function (Perturb-seq) data within a unified causal framework?

These questions are ideally suited for synthesis research because they require integration of datasets spanning multiple laboratories, cell types, and perturbation modalities. No single dataset contains sufficient perturbation coverage to construct comprehensive causal graphs; only through synthesis can we achieve the interventional density required for robust causal inference. Furthermore, addressing these questions requires expertise spanning causal inference, perturbation genomics, and mesoscale cell biology—precisely the transdisciplinary collaboration that NCEMS is designed to catalyze.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach proceeds through four integrated phases: data harmonization, causal-inference pipeline development, graph construction and validation, and biological interpretation.

Phase 1: Data Harmonization and Quality Control (Months 1-8)
We will systematically catalog and acquire publicly available Perturb-seq and ORFeome datasets from repositories including GEO, cellxgene, and the Broad Institute's DepMap portal. Initial targets include the Replogle et al. genome-wide Perturb-seq atlas (>2.5 million cells, ~10,000 perturbations), the Adamson lab's CRISPRi datasets, and ORFeome overexpression screens from multiple consortia. Data harmonization will address three challenges: (1) gene and perturbation identifier mapping across annotation versions, (2) batch effect correction using established methods (Harmony, scVI) adapted for perturbation data, and (3) quality filtering for perturbation efficiency using guide RNA activity scores and knockdown validation. We will develop a standardized data schema capturing perturbation identity, cell type, experimental conditions, and quality metrics. All harmonization code will be containerized for reproducibility.

Phase 2: Causal-Inference Pipeline Development (Months 4-14)
We will adapt and extend causal-inference algorithms for perturbation-genomics data. Our primary approach leverages the PC algorithm and its variants (FCI, RFCI) for constraint-based causal discovery, combined with score-based methods (GES, NOTEARS) for validation. Key adaptations include: (1) developing noise models appropriate for single-cell count data with dropout, (2) implementing methods to handle incomplete perturbation efficiency as measurement error in interventions, (3) extending algorithms to integrate knockdown and overexpression data as complementary intervention types, and (4) developing scalable implementations using GPU acceleration for genome-scale inference. We will implement do-calculus-based methods to estimate causal effects and distinguish direct from indirect regulatory relationships. The pipeline will include uncertainty quantification through bootstrap resampling and Bayesian approaches.

Phase 3: Causal Graph Construction (Months 10-20)
We will construct causal regulatory graphs for three mesoscale assembly processes: (1) biomolecular condensate formation, focusing on stress granules, P-bodies, and nuclear speckles; (2) organelle biogenesis, including mitochondria, peroxisomes, and ER; (3) cytoskeletal organization, emphasizing actin network assembly and microtubule dynamics. For each process, we will define relevant gene sets using GO annotations, literature curation, and proteomics data from condensate/organelle purification studies. Causal inference will proceed hierarchically: first inferring local regulatory relationships, then assembling these into global graphs using methods that ensure consistency across overlapping subgraphs.

Phase 4: Validation and Biological Interpretation (Months 16-24)
Validation employs three strategies: (1) held-out perturbation prediction, where we train on 80% of perturbations and evaluate prediction accuracy on the remaining 20%; (2) comparison with gold-standard regulatory relationships from TRRUST, RegNetwork, and literature-curated interactions; (3) consistency with orthogonal experimental data including ChIP-seq for transcription factor binding and proteomics for protein-protein interactions. Biological interpretation will involve pathway enrichment analysis of causal regulators, identification of regulatory motifs (feedforward loops, feedback circuits), and generation of specific mechanistic hypotheses for experimental follow-up.

Team Coordination: Monthly virtual meetings will coordinate across subgroups, with quarterly in-person workshops at NCEMS for intensive collaborative work on integration challenges.

author: claude-opus-4-5
title: A Community Benchmark for Emergence Detectability in Mesoscale Biological Systems
abstract: The molecular and cellular biology community lacks standard benchmarks for what counts as detected emergence: methods proposed to identify emergent properties at the mesoscale are typically tested on hand-picked examples, leaving the field unable to compare methods systematically or assess false-positive rates. This methodological gap is a substantial obstacle to rigorous synthesis research on emergence. This Working Group will develop the first community benchmark for emergence-detection methods, comprising both simulated systems with ground-truth emergent properties and well-characterized real biological systems where emergence has been independently established, then evaluate existing methods systematically. The team brings together statistical physicists, computational biologists experienced in benchmark development, cell biologists with deep mesoscale expertise, and machine-learning researchers expert in evaluation methodology. We will design a suite of simulated systems with known emergent properties (criticality signatures, multi-scale dependencies, irreducible higher-order interactions), curate real systems with strong evidence for emergence (well-studied condensates, ribosomes, nuclear pores) and rigorous controls without emergent properties, and evaluate published emergence-detection methods on the benchmark to identify which methods reliably detect emergence and which produce false positives. Deliverables include (1) a community benchmark suite with simulated and real systems, released openly with clear evaluation protocols, (2) systematic evaluations of existing emergence-detection methods, (3) recommendations for method selection in future emergence research, and (4) a continuously updated benchmark to incorporate new methods and systems. NCEMS support is essential because benchmark development demands sustained community engagement no single lab can provide, and because the benchmark must span multiple mesoscale phenomena and methodological communities. The training plan supports five trainees from statistical-physics, computational-biology, and cell-biology programs through cross-disciplinary co-mentoring, formal training in benchmark design and evaluation methodology, and joint sub-projects evaluating specific method classes. Trainees will participate in benchmark-design workshops with the community and co-author the benchmark paper, gaining experience in standards development that is rare in graduate training. The benchmark will be released through Zenodo with versioned DOIs and a continuously updated leaderboard, evaluation pipelines will be containerized for reproducibility, and all simulated and curated data will be openly accessible. The broader impact is foundational: by establishing a community standard for what counts as detected emergence, this project will substantially raise the rigor of emergence research at the mesoscale and enable cumulative methodological progress that the absence of benchmarks currently prevents. By building the missing evaluation infrastructure for an entire research area, this Working Group exemplifies the kind of community-scale contribution NCEMS uniquely supports.
background_and_significance:
Emergence—the appearance of novel system-level properties that cannot be trivially reduced to component behaviors—represents one of the most profound and challenging concepts in molecular and cellular biology. At the mesoscale, the organizational level between individual biomolecules and fully formed organelles, emergent phenomena govern critical cellular processes including biomolecular condensate formation, ribosome assembly, cytoskeletal dynamics, and signal transduction cascades. Despite decades of research, the field lacks consensus on how to rigorously detect and validate emergent properties, creating a fundamental methodological crisis that impedes scientific progress.

The current landscape of emergence-detection methods is fragmented and methodologically inconsistent. Researchers have proposed numerous computational and analytical approaches to identify emergent properties, including information-theoretic measures (integrated information, causal emergence), statistical physics frameworks (criticality detection, renormalization group analysis), network-based methods (higher-order interaction quantification), and machine learning approaches (representation learning, anomaly detection). However, each method is typically validated on investigator-selected examples, creating confirmation bias and preventing systematic comparison. Without standardized benchmarks, the field cannot determine which methods reliably detect genuine emergence versus producing false positives from noise, complexity, or methodological artifacts.

This methodological gap has profound consequences for synthesis research. As publicly available datasets spanning molecular to cellular scales proliferate, researchers increasingly seek to identify emergent properties through computational analysis. However, without validated methods, findings remain questionable, results cannot be compared across studies, and the field cannot accumulate knowledge systematically. The absence of benchmarks particularly hampers mesoscale research, where emergence is expected to be prevalent but where the complexity of phenomena makes validation especially challenging.

The significance of establishing community benchmarks extends across multiple dimensions. First, benchmarks enable rigorous method comparison, allowing researchers to select appropriate tools for specific scientific questions. Second, benchmarks reveal method limitations, identifying conditions under which false positives occur and guiding method improvement. Third, benchmarks establish community standards for evidence, creating shared criteria for what constitutes convincing detection of emergence. Fourth, benchmarks accelerate methodological progress by providing clear targets for method development and enabling cumulative improvement.

Previous benchmark efforts in related fields demonstrate transformative impact. The Critical Assessment of protein Structure Prediction (CASP) revolutionized structural biology by establishing rigorous evaluation standards. ImageNet transformed computer vision through standardized benchmarks. The Gene Ontology Consortium established shared vocabularies enabling cross-study comparison. No equivalent infrastructure exists for emergence detection, despite the centrality of emergence to understanding biological organization.

This Working Group addresses this critical gap by developing the first comprehensive benchmark for emergence-detection methods at the mesoscale. By combining simulated systems with ground-truth emergent properties and well-characterized biological systems with independently established emergence, the benchmark will enable systematic method evaluation. The project directly addresses NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale while building essential infrastructure for rigorous synthesis research. The benchmark's development requires precisely the kind of sustained, multidisciplinary community engagement that NCEMS uniquely supports—no single laboratory possesses the breadth of expertise, community connections, and resources necessary to create benchmarks spanning statistical physics, computational biology, cell biology, and machine learning evaluation methodology.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This Working Group addresses four interconnected research questions that together establish the scientific and methodological foundations for rigorous emergence detection at the mesoscale.

Research Question 1: What constitutes ground-truth emergence in simulated systems, and how can we generate benchmark datasets with known emergent properties spanning the diversity of mesoscale phenomena?

Hypothesis 1: Simulated systems exhibiting well-characterized emergent properties—including criticality signatures, irreducible higher-order interactions, and multi-scale causal dependencies—can be systematically generated using established theoretical frameworks from statistical physics and complex systems science. We hypothesize that these simulated systems can be parameterized to produce graded levels of emergence strength, enabling evaluation of method sensitivity and specificity across a continuum of emergence intensities.

Research Question 2: Which real biological systems provide sufficiently strong, independently validated evidence of emergence to serve as benchmark positive controls, and what criteria establish such validation?

Hypothesis 2: A subset of well-studied mesoscale biological systems—including biomolecular condensates exhibiting phase separation, ribosomal assembly intermediates, nuclear pore complexes, and specific cytoskeletal structures—have accumulated sufficient independent experimental evidence to establish emergence with high confidence. We hypothesize that systematic literature curation combined with expert consensus evaluation can identify systems meeting rigorous evidentiary standards, while simultaneously identifying appropriate negative controls (systems where component-level descriptions suffice).

Research Question 3: How do existing emergence-detection methods perform when evaluated systematically on benchmark datasets with known ground truth?

Hypothesis 3: Current emergence-detection methods vary substantially in sensitivity, specificity, and robustness when evaluated on standardized benchmarks. We hypothesize that methods will show differential performance across emergence types (e.g., criticality-based versus information-theoretic emergence), that false-positive rates will be higher than generally assumed in the literature, and that method performance will depend critically on data characteristics including noise levels, sampling density, and system size. We further hypothesize that no single method will optimally detect all emergence types, suggesting the need for method ensembles or type-specific tool selection.

Research Question 4: What evaluation protocols, metrics, and community standards are necessary to ensure benchmark utility, reproducibility, and long-term sustainability?

Hypothesis 4: Effective emergence-detection benchmarks require multi-dimensional evaluation metrics capturing sensitivity, specificity, computational efficiency, robustness to noise, and scalability. We hypothesize that standardized evaluation protocols—including containerized analysis pipelines, versioned datasets, and automated scoring systems—will substantially improve reproducibility compared to current practices. We further hypothesize that community engagement in benchmark design will increase adoption and that mechanisms for continuous benchmark updating will be essential for long-term relevance.

These research questions are inherently interconnected. Simulated systems (RQ1) provide ground truth essential for rigorous method evaluation (RQ3), while real biological systems (RQ2) ensure benchmark relevance to actual scientific questions. Evaluation protocols (RQ4) determine how insights from method evaluation translate into actionable recommendations.

The questions are specifically designed to advance NCEMS's mission. By establishing what counts as detected emergence, the benchmark enables rigorous synthesis research across mesoscale phenomena. By systematically evaluating methods, the project identifies which analytical approaches reliably extract emergent properties from the vast publicly available datasets NCEMS aims to leverage. By developing community standards, the project creates infrastructure enabling cumulative methodological progress.

Importantly, these questions cannot be addressed by any single laboratory. Simulated system design requires statistical physics expertise; real system curation requires deep cell biology knowledge; method evaluation requires computational biology and machine learning expertise; community standards require sustained engagement across disciplines. This inherent multidisciplinarity makes the project ideally suited for NCEMS Working Group support.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises four integrated work packages executed over a 24-month timeline, designed to leverage the multidisciplinary expertise of our Working Group while ensuring rigorous, reproducible outcomes.

Work Package 1: Simulated Benchmark System Development (Months 1-12)
We will develop simulated systems with ground-truth emergent properties spanning three categories: (a) Criticality-based emergence using Ising models, percolation systems, and self-organized criticality frameworks parameterized to exhibit tunable critical signatures; (b) Information-theoretic emergence using coupled dynamical systems with known integrated information values and causal emergence properties; (c) Higher-order interaction emergence using hypergraph-based models with irreducible multi-body interactions. For each category, we will generate systems across parameter ranges producing absent, weak, moderate, and strong emergence, enabling sensitivity analysis. Statistical physicists on the team will lead simulation design using established theoretical frameworks, ensuring ground-truth validity. All simulations will be implemented in Python with comprehensive documentation, version control, and containerization.

Work Package 2: Real Biological System Curation (Months 1-15)
We will systematically curate real mesoscale biological systems as benchmark positives and negatives through a rigorous multi-stage process. Stage 1: Literature mining using automated tools supplemented by expert review to identify candidate systems with published emergence claims. Stage 2: Evidence evaluation using predefined criteria assessing experimental support, reproducibility, and mechanistic understanding. Stage 3: Expert consensus evaluation through structured Delphi-method surveys of Working Group members and external experts. Stage 4: Data compilation, gathering publicly available datasets (cryo-EM structures, proteomics, imaging data) for validated systems. Target positive-control systems include P-bodies and stress granules (condensate emergence), ribosomal assembly intermediates (compositional emergence), and nuclear pore complexes (structural emergence). Negative controls will include well-characterized systems where reductionist descriptions suffice. Cell biologists on the team will lead curation with computational support for data integration.

Work Package 3: Systematic Method Evaluation (Months 10-22)
We will evaluate published emergence-detection methods on the benchmark using standardized protocols. Phase 1: Method inventory through systematic literature review identifying computational methods claiming to detect emergence, categorized by theoretical basis and input requirements. Phase 2: Method implementation, re-implementing or containerizing methods for standardized execution. Phase 3: Benchmark evaluation, running all methods on all benchmark systems with consistent preprocessing and parameter selection. Phase 4: Performance analysis, computing sensitivity, specificity, area under ROC curves, computational requirements, and robustness metrics. Machine learning evaluation experts will lead protocol development, ensuring methodological rigor comparable to established benchmark efforts in other fields.

Work Package 4: Community Engagement and Standards Development (Throughout)
Community engagement is integrated throughout the project. We will convene two in-person workshops (Months 8 and 18) bringing together Working Group members, trainees, and external stakeholders to review benchmark design, discuss preliminary results, and establish community standards. Virtual working sessions will occur monthly. A community advisory board comprising five external experts will provide ongoing guidance. Standards documents specifying evaluation protocols, data formats, and submission procedures will be developed collaboratively and released for community comment before finalization.

Integration Across Work Packages: Work packages are designed for synergistic interaction. Simulated systems inform criteria for real system evaluation; real system characteristics guide simulation parameterization; method evaluation reveals gaps requiring additional benchmark systems; community feedback refines all components iteratively.

Data Sources: All data utilized will be publicly available, including structural data from PDB and EMDB, proteomics from PRIDE, imaging from BioImage Archive, and published simulation parameters from literature. No new experimental data will be generated.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will deliver four primary outcomes with transformative impact on emergence research at the mesoscale.

Outcome 1: Community Benchmark Suite
We will release a comprehensive benchmark comprising 50+ simulated systems with ground-truth emergent properties spanning criticality, information-theoretic, and higher-order interaction categories, plus 15+ curated real biological systems with independently validated emergence and matched negative controls. author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: The Entropy of the Nucleus: Quantifying Information Density in Chromatin-Condensate Interfaces
abstract: The nucleus is the ultimate mesoscale environment, where the physical organization of chromatin and the emergence of membraneless organelles (condensates) dictate gene expression. Current research often treats these as separate phenomena: polymer physics for DNA and liquid-liquid phase separation for condensates. This project will synthesize publicly available Hi-C (genome architecture), super-resolution microscopy (spatial localization), and mass-spectrometry-based proteomics (composition) to test the hypothesis that the nucleus operates as a constrained information-processing system where local entropy is actively managed. We will develop a novel 'Information Density Metric' to map how condensate formation alters the local degrees of freedom for chromatin fibers. By integrating these disparate data types using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), we aim to identify the 'emergence threshold' where molecular crowding transitions into functional regulatory hubs. This work requires the synthesis of community-scale datasets to move beyond single-locus observations to a whole-nucleus physical law. The project will involve collaboration between computational biophysicists, genomicists, and data scientists, providing a unique training ground for the next generation of mesoscale researchers.
background_and_significance: The cellular nucleus represents the quintessential mesoscale environment, serving as the command center where genomic information is stored, accessed, and regulated. At this scale—bridging individual biomolecules like DNA and proteins, and whole cellular organelles—the physical organization of chromatin and the spontaneous emergence of membraneless organelles, known as biomolecular condensates, dictate transcriptional outputs and ultimately cellular fate. Historically, molecular and cellular biology has approached these two critical phenomena through distinct, isolated disciplinary lenses. Chromatin organization is predominantly modeled using polymer physics, analyzing the folding, looping, and topological constraints of DNA fibers. Conversely, the formation of nuclear bodies and transcriptional hubs is largely understood through the framework of liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and soft matter physics. This bifurcation has resulted in a critical knowledge gap: how do these two physical paradigms intersect to give rise to the emergent property of precise, dynamic gene regulation? Current models fail to capture the holistic thermodynamic landscape of the nucleus. The interactions between chromatin and condensates are not merely additive; they are highly synergistic, creating local microenvironments where molecular crowding and spatial constraints actively modulate the entropy of the system. We propose that the nucleus operates as a constrained information-processing system, where local entropy is not a byproduct of crowding but an actively managed physical parameter that drives the emergence of functional regulatory hubs. Addressing this profound mystery requires a paradigm shift from single-locus, single-modality experimental observations to a community-scale synthesis of multi-omic and multimodal imaging data. Fortunately, the molecular and cellular sciences have entered an era of unprecedented data abundance. Public repositories are rich with high-resolution Hi-C datasets detailing 3D genome architecture, super-resolution microscopy images capturing the spatial localization of nuclear bodies, and mass-spectrometry-based proteomics defining the compositional makeup of these condensates. However, these massive datasets remain siloed, waiting to be integrated. This proposed working group directly aligns with the NCEMS mission to catalyze multidisciplinary synthesis research to understand mesoscale emergent properties. By integrating these disparate, publicly available datasets using advanced computational techniques, we will investigate the chromatin-condensate interface as a unified thermodynamic system. This synthesis will allow us to move beyond isolated phenomenological observations to formulate a whole-nucleus physical law governing information density. The significance of this work lies in its potential to solve long-standing puzzles regarding how non-specific physical forces (like phase separation) can yield highly specific biological outcomes (like targeted gene expression). Furthermore, by bringing together computational biophysicists, genomicists, and data scientists, this project will pioneer innovative AI-driven analytical strategies, specifically Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). This approach will set a new gold standard for mesoscale biological data synthesis, tapping into diverse new talent, and rigorously training the next generation of data-savvy biological researchers to tackle the complexities of emergent cellular phenomena.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: To unravel the thermodynamic and physical principles governing the mesoscale organization of the nucleus, this synthesis project is driven by a central, overarching hypothesis: The nucleus functions as an actively managed, constrained information-processing system where the interplay between chromatin polymer dynamics and biomolecular condensate formation modulates local entropy to drive the emergence of specific gene regulatory hubs. This hypothesis challenges the traditional view of the nucleus as a passive vessel for diffusion-driven interactions, repositioning it as a landscape where phase transitions and polymer constraints are precisely tuned to achieve an 'emergence threshold' necessary for biological function. To test this central premise using synthesized, publicly available datasets, we have formulated three specific research questions and corresponding hypotheses. Question 1: How does the formation of biomolecular condensates alter the local topological constraints and degrees of freedom of interacting chromatin fibers? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that biomolecular condensates act as localized thermodynamic sinks, reducing the conformational entropy of targeted chromatin regions. By synthesizing Hi-C (genomic contact frequencies) and spatial proteomics data, we predict that regions interfacing with condensates will exhibit a quantifiable reduction in polymer degrees of freedom, which we will mathematically define as a novel 'Information Density Metric' (IDM). This metric will serve as a standardized measure of local structural order. Question 2: What is the quantitative relationship between the compositional complexity of a condensate and its capacity to induce emergent physical states in the surrounding chromatin architecture? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that an 'emergence threshold' exists, defined by a critical local concentration and diversity of phase-separating proteins, beyond which molecular crowding transitions from a generic physical state into a highly specialized, functional regulatory hub. By integrating mass-spectrometry proteomics with super-resolution microscopy data, we expect to find a non-linear correlation between a condensate's multivalent interaction capacity and its localized IDM, indicating a phase transition in the chromatin-condensate microenvironment. Question 3: Can the integration of multi-modal, multi-scale data through artificial intelligence reveal a universal physical law governing the spatial distribution of these high-information-density hubs across different cell types and states? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that despite vast differences in cell-type-specific gene expression, the thermodynamic rules governing the spatial distribution of high-IDM hubs are conserved. We predict that Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) trained on integrated genomic, transcriptomic, and imaging datasets will uncover a generalized set of biophysical equations that accurately predict the spatial localization of these emergent hubs based purely on the local thermodynamic constraints of the chromatin polymer and condensate protein concentrations. By addressing these novel questions, our working group will solve long-standing puzzles regarding the physical drivers of nuclear organization. We will move away from isolated, single-locus models to establish a comprehensive, predictive framework for mesoscale nuclear emergence. This rigorous approach leverages the power of data synthesis to uncover fundamental biological principles that are invisible when examining single datasets in isolation, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS mandate to explore emergence through data integration.
methods_and_approach: Our approach strictly adheres to the NCEMS mandate of community-scale synthesis, utilizing only existing, publicly available datasets to generate novel insights without conducting new wet-lab experiments. The project requires the integration of three distinct data modalities: (1) High-resolution Hi-C and Micro-C datasets (e.g., from the 4D Nucleome Data Portal) to map 3D chromatin architecture and polymer contact frequencies; (2) Super-resolution microscopy imaging data (e.g., from the BioImage Archive) to precisely quantify the spatial localization, volume, and morphology of nuclear condensates (such as nucleoli, speckles, and super-enhancers); and (3) Mass-spectrometry-based spatial proteomics and cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) data (e.g., from PRIDE) to determine the molecular composition and interaction networks within these condensates. The core methodological innovation of our working group is the development of the 'Information Density Metric' (IDM) and the application of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to bridge these distinct data types. The project will unfold in three highly collaborative phases. Phase 1: Data Curation, Standardization, and the Information Density Metric (Months 1-6). Our data science and genomics experts will develop automated pipelines to harmonize the spatial and genomic coordinates across the Hi-C, imaging, and proteomics datasets. Using the Hi-C contact probability matrices, our computational biophysicists will calculate the local polymer entropy and degrees of freedom for specific genomic bins. We will mathematically formulate the IDM by quantifying the variance in chromatin conformational states in the presence versus absence of specific condensates, effectively measuring the thermodynamic constraint imposed by LLPS on the DNA polymer. Phase 2: Multimodal Integration via Physics-Informed Neural Networks (Months 7-16). Traditional machine learning models often fail in biophysics because they ignore fundamental physical laws. To overcome this, our AI specialists will design and train PINNs. The PINNs will use the harmonized proteomics (composition) and imaging (spatial boundaries) data as inputs to predict the Hi-C-derived IDM (chromatin architecture). Crucially, the loss function of the PINN will be penalized by established equations of polymer physics (e.g., the Rouse or Zimm models) and Flory-Huggins solution theory for phase separation. This ensures that the neural network learns representations that are not only statistically accurate but also biophysically plausible. Through this, we will identify the 'emergence threshold'—the specific thermodynamic parameters where a condensate fundamentally alters chromatin topology to create a functional hub. Phase 3: Validation across Cell Types and Model Refinement (Months 17-24). To ensure our findings represent a universal physical principle rather than a cell-type-specific anomaly, the PINN models will be tested against hold-out datasets from diverse cellular states (e.g., embryonic stem cells versus terminally differentiated neurons). We will analyze how the emergence thresholds shift during cellular differentiation. This methodology is inherently transdisciplinary. It is beyond the capability of a single lab because it requires simultaneous domain expertise in soft matter physics, functional genomics, and advanced artificial intelligence. By assembling a diverse working group, we will synthesize these disparate public datasets into a unified, predictive model of mesoscale nuclear emergence.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The proposed synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that fundamentally advance our understanding of mesoscale emergence in molecular and cellular biology. Scientifically, the primary outcome will be the establishment of the 'Information Density Metric' (IDM) and the identification of the 'emergence threshold.' This will provide the biological community with the first quantitative, biophysically grounded framework that unites chromatin polymer dynamics with liquid-liquid phase separation. By publishing these findings in high-impact, peer-reviewed journals, we will solve the long-standing puzzle of how non-specific physical forces drive highly specific gene regulation, shifting the paradigm from descriptive models of nuclear organization to predictive thermodynamic laws. Methodologically, the development and release of our Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) architecture tailored for multi-modal biological data will represent a major breakthrough. This open-source AI tool will enable researchers worldwide to integrate their own disparate mesoscale datasets while adhering to underlying physical principles, thereby catalyzing future synthesis research far beyond the scope of this initial working group. Furthermore, the impact on workforce development will be profound. By functioning as a highly collaborative NCEMS Working Group, this project will serve as a premier training ground. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will be cross-trained in genomics, soft-matter physics, and advanced AI/data science. This transdisciplinary mentorship will directly address the critical need for a diverse, data-savvy workforce capable of navigating the complexities of modern, data-rich biological sciences. Ultimately, this project will demonstrate the immense power of community-scale data synthesis, proving that the integration of existing public data can uncover fundamental biological truths that remain hidden when datasets are analyzed in isolation.
open_science_and_reproducibility: A foundational pillar of this NCEMS Working Group is an unwavering commitment to open science, reproducibility, and the democratization of data. Because our research relies entirely on the synthesis of publicly available datasets, we recognize our reciprocal obligation to return all synthesized products, analytical tools, and enhanced datasets to the public domain in accordance with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles. To ensure total reproducibility, all data curation pipelines, harmonization scripts, and the complete architecture of our Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) will be developed openly via a public GitHub repository from day one. We will utilize containerization technologies, such as Docker and Singularity, to package our computational environments. This guarantees that any researcher, regardless of their local computing setup, can seamlessly download, execute, and reproduce our exact analyses and model training protocols. Furthermore, the harmonized, multi-modal datasets generated during Phase 1—linking Hi-C, super-resolution imaging, and proteomics data into unified coordinate systems—will be hosted on established, long-term public repositories such as Zenodo or the Open Science Framework (OSF), complete with comprehensive metadata and detailed data dictionaries. The mathematical formulations for the Information Density Metric (IDM) will be thoroughly documented in open-access protocols. All publications resulting from this working group will be submitted to open-access journals, with preprints deposited on bioRxiv prior to peer review to accelerate knowledge dissemination. We will also develop interactive, web-based Jupyter Notebooks and RShiny applications, allowing the broader biological community to intuitively interact with our PINN models and visualize the emergence thresholds without requiring advanced programming expertise. Through these rigorous open science practices, we will maximize the impact of NCEMS funding and foster a culture of transparency and collaboration in mesoscale biological research.
budget_and_resources: The requested budget is meticulously designed to support the collaborative, computational, and training requirements of this community-scale synthesis project, in strict adherence to NCEMS guidelines prohibiting the use of funds for new experimental data generation. The primary resource requirement is human capital and collaborative infrastructure. A significant portion of the budget is allocated to support two postdoctoral researchers and two graduate students. The budget covers travel, lodging, and per diem for all Working Group members, including external experts invited for specific synthesis workshops.
