This budget directly empowers a collaboration that vastly exceeds the capabilities of any single laboratory, providing the essential resources to synthesize existing data into groundbreaking mesoscale discoveries.

author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: Urban Traffic Dynamics of the Vesicle Transport System: A Network Flow Synthesis
abstract: Intracellular transport relies on molecular motors navigating a dense, heterogeneous cytoskeletal grid. While we understand single-motor kinetics, the emergent behavior of vesicle 'traffic'—including bottlenecks, bypasses, and multi-modal congestion—remains a mystery. This project will synthesize single-particle tracking (SPT) datasets from multiple cell types with high-resolution Cryo-ET reconstructions of the cytoskeleton. By applying analogical models from urban traffic engineering and graph theory, we will treat the cytoplasm as a logistical network. We aim to identify 'high-traffic hubs' and 'dead-zones' within the cell, determining how the density of actin filaments and microtubules emerges as a self-organizing traffic-control system. This synthesis is beyond the scope of a single lab as it requires merging biophysical movement data with large-scale structural topographies. The output will be a 'Cellular Traffic Map' and a predictive toolkit for how mutations in motor proteins lead to systemic transport failure, a key feature in neurodegenerative diseases. Trainees will gain expertise in applying civil engineering algorithms to biological systems, fostering transdisciplinary innovation.
background_and_significance: Intracellular transport is a fundamental biological process that ensures the precise spatiotemporal delivery of organelles, proteins, and mRNA across the vast and highly crowded cytoplasmic space. While decades of reductionist studies have successfully elucidated the biophysical properties and kinetics of individual molecular motors (such as kinesin, dynein, and myosin) moving along isolated cytoskeletal tracks, a critical knowledge gap remains regarding the emergent behavior of these motors when operating collectively within the dense, heterogeneous, and dynamic three-dimensional meshwork of the living cell. This transition from individual motor mechanics to systemic intracellular logistics represents a classic mesoscale phenomenon—the exact domain of emergence targeted by the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). At this mesoscale, vesicle traffic exhibits complex emergent properties such as congestion, bottlenecking, dynamic rerouting, and multi-modal cooperation that fundamentally cannot be predicted merely by studying single motors in vitro. Understanding these emergent dynamics is vital, as systemic transport failures are hallmark features of numerous severe pathologies, most notably neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and ALS, where cellular cargo gridlock precipitates neuronal death. Currently, the field is data-rich but synthesis-poor. Thousands of high-resolution single-particle tracking (SPT) datasets capture vesicle trajectories across diverse cell types, while modern Cryo-Electron Tomography (Cryo-ET) provides unprecedented 3D reconstructions of complex cytoskeletal topographies. However, these massive datasets exist in isolated silos. Individual laboratories typically lack the combined expertise in cell biology, structural topography, data science, and advanced mathematical modeling required to merge these disparate data modalities. This project proposes a paradigm-shifting synthesis: treating the cytoplasm as a complex logistical network, directly analogous to an urban traffic grid. By applying established principles from civil engineering, graph theory, and network flow dynamics to synthesized biological datasets, we will uncover how the physical architecture of the cytoskeleton dictates emergent traffic patterns. This approach transcends the capabilities of any single research group, requiring a transdisciplinary collaborative working group comprising cell biologists, biophysicists, data scientists, and urban traffic engineers. The profound significance of this synthesis lies in its potential to solve long-standing puzzles regarding how cells prevent or resolve intracellular gridlock, how cargo sorting is spatially optimized, and how the structural density of actin filaments and microtubules serves as a self-organizing traffic-control system. By leveraging only publicly available SPT and Cryo-ET data, this project directly answers the NCEMS call to synthesize existing data to acquire novel, deeper insights into mesoscale emergence. Furthermore, it establishes a highly innovative analytical strategy that bridges the biological sciences with civil engineering algorithms, tapping into diverse new talent and fostering a uniquely trained, data-savvy workforce capable of navigating transdisciplinary boundaries to solve the next generation of biological mysteries.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group aims to decode the emergent rules governing mesoscale vesicle transport by formulating and addressing three primary research questions (RQs), each accompanied by specific, testable hypotheses derived from urban traffic engineering principles and network flow dynamics.

RQ1: How does the 3D topological architecture of the cytoskeleton dictate emergent intracellular traffic patterns, such as congestion and high-throughput hubs? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the intracellular environment functions analogously to an urban road network, where microtubule intersections and actin-microtubule junctions act as critical "intersections" that either facilitate rapid cargo transfer or induce severe bottlenecking. We predict that specific spatial arrangements of these filaments—quantifiable via graph-theoretic metrics like betweenness centrality, node degree, and edge density—will reliably predict the locations of "high-traffic hubs" (efficient sorting centers) and "dead-zones" (areas highly prone to gridlock) across different cell types.

RQ2: What are the self-organizing rules of multi-modal cargo navigation when encountering cytoskeletal roadblocks or high-density traffic? Hypothesis 2: Drawing from dynamic traffic assignment models used in civil engineering, we hypothesize that vesicle transport networks exhibit emergent load-balancing behaviors. Specifically, we posit that when primary microtubule "highways" become congested or structurally compromised, multi-motor complexes utilize the denser, more randomly oriented actin network as a "local road" bypass system. We expect our synthesis of single-particle tracking (SPT) data to reveal statistical signatures of adaptive rerouting, where the probability of switching from microtubule-based to actin-based transport increases non-linearly in response to local vesicle density and localized structural damage.

RQ3: How do subtle, localized perturbations in motor protein kinetics or cytoskeletal architecture cascade into systemic cellular transport failure? Hypothesis 3: Utilizing network resilience and percolation theory, we hypothesize that the cellular transport grid contains "critical edges" (highly trafficked, non-redundant cytoskeletal tracks) whose disruption leads to a disproportionate collapse of global intracellular logistics. We predict that mapping neurodegenerative disease-associated motor mutations onto our synthesized transport model will reveal that these mutations do not merely slow down individual cargos, but rather trigger cascading traffic jams that propagate backward through the network, fundamentally altering the mesoscale distribution of organelles.

By addressing these questions, our project aligns perfectly with the NCEMS mission to investigate emergent properties at the mesoscale. The transition from single-molecule kinetics to systemic network flow requires understanding how spatial constraints, energy limitations, and structural complexities interact to produce organized cellular behavior. Testing these hypotheses relies entirely on the synthesis of publicly available, disparate datasets: overlaying the dynamic, time-resolved movement data from SPT repositories onto the static, high-resolution spatial maps provided by Cryo-ET databases. This transdisciplinary framework will establish a new paradigm for understanding biological motion, providing a predictive toolkit for diagnosing the transport failures underlying severe human pathologies.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach relies exclusively on the synthesis and integration of existing, publicly available datasets, strictly avoiding any de novo experimental data generation. We will convene a transdisciplinary Working Group comprising experts in cell biology, structural bioinformatics, data science, and civil/traffic engineering. The workflow is divided into three integrated phases: Data Aggregation, Network Construction, and Traffic Flow Modeling.

Phase 1: Data Aggregation and Harmonization. We will mine publicly available repositories for two distinct data types. First, we will extract high-resolution 3D cytoskeletal architectures from the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR) and the Protein Data Bank (PDB), focusing on Cryo-Electron Tomography (Cryo-ET) tomograms of diverse cell types (e.g., neurons, fibroblasts, macrophages). Second, we will aggregate Single-Particle Tracking (SPT) datasets of vesicle and organelle motility from repositories such as the Cell Tracking Challenge, Zenodo, and published supplementary datasets. A major data science challenge will be harmonizing these disparate modalities. We will utilize AI-driven image segmentation algorithms, specifically 3D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), to automatically trace and digitize microtubule and actin networks from the Cryo-ET tomograms into mathematically definable spatial graphs.

Phase 2: Spatial Graph Construction and Network Mapping. Once digitized, the cytoskeletal architecture will be converted into a formal mathematical graph, G = (V, E), where vertices (V) represent filament intersections or branching points, and edges (E) represent the filament segments connecting them. We will calculate topological metrics for this network, including edge density, clustering coefficients, and betweenness centrality. Concurrently, the harmonized SPT trajectory data will be spatially registered and mapped onto these representative cytoskeletal graphs. Because SPT and Cryo-ET data often originate from different individual cells, we will employ probabilistic mapping techniques and generative AI models to create "consensus cells"—statistically representative models that accurately reflect the spatial distribution of both structure and dynamic flow for a given cell type.

Phase 3: Urban Traffic Modeling and Simulation. With dynamic trajectories mapped onto static structural graphs, we will apply algorithms traditionally used in civil engineering and urban traffic management. We will utilize Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams (MFDs) to relate vesicle density, flow, and velocity within specific cellular zones. We will apply the Wardrop user equilibrium principle to determine if vesicles are utilizing the most efficient routes or if they are subject to systemic, emergent delays. To identify "high-traffic hubs" and "dead-zones," we will employ network congestion algorithms like the Cell Transmission Model (CTM). Finally, we will build a predictive computational toolkit—the "Cellular Traffic Map"—using agent-based modeling (ABM). This toolkit will simulate how in silico "roadblocks" (representing cytoskeletal damage) or "speed limit reductions" (representing motor protein mutations) propagate traffic jams across the cellular network. This synthesis of biological data with engineering algorithms requires the collaborative environment provided by NCEMS and is fundamentally beyond the scope of a traditional biology laboratory.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will yield several transformative outcomes, fundamentally advancing our understanding of emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences. The primary deliverable will be the "Cellular Traffic Map," a first-of-its-kind, open-source computational atlas that mathematically defines the mesoscale logistical networks of diverse cell types. This map will identify the universal structural motifs that serve as high-throughput hubs and the topological vulnerabilities prone to congestion. Secondly, we will deliver a predictive computational toolkit capable of simulating intracellular traffic dynamics under both healthy and pathological conditions. This toolkit will allow researchers to input specific motor protein mutations or structural alterations and predict the resulting systemic transport failures, offering unprecedented insights into the etiology of neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and ALS.

Beyond scientific discovery, the impact on workforce development will be profound. The project will serve as a premier training ground for a new breed of data-savvy scientists. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will be cross-trained in biological data curation, AI-driven image analysis, and civil engineering algorithms, bridging a critical gap between the life sciences and applied mathematics. This transdisciplinary training aligns directly with the NCEMS mandate to tap diverse new talent and train the future workforce. By introducing urban traffic engineering principles to cell biology, we will establish an entirely new analytical framework, stimulating novel questions and inspiring future research directions. Ultimately, this project will demonstrate the immense, untapped potential of synthesizing existing datasets, proving that the answers to some of biology's most complex mesoscale mysteries are already hidden within publicly available data, waiting for the right collaborative lens to reveal them.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is fundamentally committed to the highest standards of open science, transparency, and reproducibility, aligning with the core values of NCEMS and the broader scientific community. All aspects of this synthesis project—from data aggregation protocols to final predictive models—will be made publicly available and strictly adhere to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles.

First, all raw and harmonized datasets utilized in this study will be cataloged and deposited into Zenodo, assigned unique Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs), and accompanied by comprehensive, machine-readable metadata detailing data provenance and processing steps. Second, all computational code, AI segmentation models, and urban traffic algorithms adapted for biological networks will be developed openly on GitHub. We will provide extensive documentation, including Jupyter Notebooks and step-by-step tutorials, ensuring that researchers from diverse disciplines can easily understand, utilize, and adapt our analytical pipelines.

To guarantee computational reproducibility, we will containerize our entire software environment using Docker and Singularity, allowing any researcher to precisely replicate our analytical workflows regardless of their local computing infrastructure. Furthermore, the "Cellular Traffic Map" and predictive toolkit will be hosted on a dedicated, user-friendly web portal, enabling biologists without advanced programming expertise to interact with the models and run in silico simulations. We are committed to publishing all findings in open-access, peer-reviewed journals and will disseminate preprints via bioRxiv to accelerate community access to our discoveries. By integrating these open science practices into the daily operations of our Working Group, we will not only ensure the rigor of our synthesis but also empower the global scientific community.
budget_and_resources:
The proposed budget is designed to exclusively support the collaborative synthesis, data integration, and transdisciplinary training objectives of the Working Group, with no funds allocated for primary experimental data generation or wet-lab equipment. The primary resource requirement from NCEMS is logistical and financial support for convening our diverse team of experts. We request funding for four in-person Working Group meetings over the two-year project period, to be held at the NCEMS facility. These intensive, multi-day sessions are critical for overcoming the communication barriers inherent in transdisciplinary research, allowing cell biologists, data scientists, and traffic engineers to iteratively refine the analogical models and harmonize analytical approaches.

A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to workforce training and development. We request support for two full-time postdoctoral researchers and two graduate student stipends. These trainees will serve as the operational core of the project, executing the data aggregation, graph construction, and algorithmic simulations while receiving unparalleled cross-disciplinary mentorship from the Working Group's senior investigators across multiple institutions.

Additionally, we require substantial computational resources to process the massive Cryo-ET and SPT datasets and run complex network flow simulations. We request funding for cloud computing allocations (e.g., AWS or NSF ACCESS) to support the AI-driven 3D segmentation and agent-based modeling tasks, which exceed the capacity of standard institutional clusters. Finally, a modest allocation is requested for open-access publication fees and the development and hosting of the "Cellular Traffic Map" interactive web portal. This budget leverages the unique collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS to maximize the scientific return on investment from existing, publicly funded datasets, ensuring a high-impact, cost-effective synthesis project.

author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: Swarm Intelligence in Mitochondrial Networks: Deciphering the Voting Rules of Organelle Fusion
abstract: Mitochondria exist as dynamic networks that undergo frequent fusion and fission to maintain metabolic health. However, the collective 'decision-making' process—how the network 'knows' which mitochondria to fuse or degrade—is unknown. This project proposes that mitochondrial networks exhibit 'swarm intelligence,' similar to social insect colonies, where local interactions lead to global optimization of energy production. We will synthesize thousands of publicly available mitochondrial morphology images with parallel metabolic flux datasets and calcium signaling records. Using Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents, we will reverse-engineer the 'voting rules' that govern organelle behavior. We hypothesize that mitochondria integrate local energy stress signals into a consensus-based fusion response. This project leverages diverse data from various physiological states (stress vs. homeostasis) to identify universal emergent behaviors in mitochondrial networks. The collaboration between AI experts and mitochondrial biologists will result in a novel framework for understanding organelle sociality, providing postdocs with advanced skills in biological agent-based modeling.
background_and_significance:
Mitochondria are fundamentally social organelles. Rather than existing as isolated biochemical reactors, they form highly dynamic, interconnected networks that continuously undergo fusion and fission. These morphological transitions are critical for maintaining cellular metabolic homeostasis, distributing mitochondrial DNA, and isolating damaged components for mitophagy. Despite decades of research identifying the core biochemical machinery governing these processes (e.g., MFN1/2, OPA1, DRP1), a fundamental puzzle remains: how does the mitochondrial network make collective 'decisions'? Current paradigms largely treat mitochondrial encounters as stochastic events driven by random cytoskeletal transport, followed by biochemically predetermined fusion or fission outcomes. However, this reductionist view fails to explain how local organelle interactions reliably scale to produce global, network-wide optimization of energy production, especially under varying physiological stresses. 

This project posits a paradigm-shifting hypothesis: mitochondrial networks exhibit 'swarm intelligence.' Similar to social insect colonies or flocking birds, we propose that individual mitochondria act as autonomous agents that follow simple local 'voting rules'—integrating signals like calcium microdomains, localized ATP/ADP ratios, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) gradients—to generate highly complex, emergent mesoscale behaviors. This conceptual leap perfectly aligns with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). By reframing organelle dynamics as an emergent mesoscale phenomenon, we aim to bridge the critical gap between molecular signaling and cellular-level phenotypic outcomes. 

Investigating this phenomenon is beyond the capabilities of any single traditional experimental laboratory. The required data—high-resolution 3D electron microscopy, live-cell fluorescence imaging of mitochondrial dynamics, metabolic flux records, and calcium signaling datasets—already exist in abundance across various public repositories (e.g., EMPIAR, Cell Image Library, and individual lab repositories). However, these diverse datasets remain siloed. A community-scale synthesis approach is urgently needed to integrate these multimodal data streams. By assembling a transdisciplinary Working Group comprising mitochondrial biologists, artificial intelligence (AI) specialists, biophysicists, and complex systems theorists, we will leverage advanced data science techniques to extract universal principles of organelle sociality. 

This synthesis project is deeply significant for several reasons. First, it addresses a long-standing mystery in cell biology by providing a deterministic, systems-level explanation for mitochondrial network behavior. Second, it pioneers the application of multi-agent Reinforcement Learning (RL) to subcellular biology, developing innovative analytical strategies that can be generalized to other complex organelle networks (e.g., the endoplasmic reticulum). Finally, it directly supports the NCEMS goal of training a data-savvy workforce. By bringing together diverse scientific perspectives to synthesize massive, disparate datasets, we will not only uncover the fundamental rules of mesoscale emergence but also equip the next generation of scientists with the transdisciplinary skills necessary to navigate the future of computational cell biology.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This synthesis project is driven by three primary research questions (RQs) and associated hypotheses, each designed to interrogate the emergent mesoscale properties of mitochondrial networks using integrated, publicly available datasets.

Research Question 1: What are the local 'voting rules' and biochemical thresholds that govern the decision of adjacent mitochondria to fuse, divide, or bypass one another?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that mitochondrial fusion is not a stochastic collision event but a consensus-based decision driven by localized biochemical 'pheromones.' Specifically, we propose that mitochondria utilize localized calcium spikes and ATP/ADP gradients as signals of metabolic fitness. Fusion only proceeds when adjacent mitochondria mutually cross a specific signaling threshold, preventing healthy networks from integrating irreversibly damaged organelles. By synthesizing live-cell imaging data of calcium/ATP biosensors with simultaneous mitochondrial tracking, we expect to identify the precise spatiotemporal voting rules that precede fusion events.

Research Question 2: How do these local organelle interactions scale to produce emergent, network-wide metabolic optimization across varying physiological states (e.g., homeostasis vs. nutrient starvation)?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that swarm intelligence in mitochondrial networks undergoes phase transitions dependent on the global cellular environment. During nutrient abundance, the network operates in a decentralized, exploratory state characterized by high fission rates and fragmented morphologies, prioritizing spatial distribution. Under metabolic stress, the voting rules shift dynamically, driving the network into a highly connected, exploitative state (hyperfusion) to maximize ATP production and share resources. We anticipate that synthesizing topological data from electron micrographs with parallel metabolic flux (Seahorse assay) datasets will reveal universal scaling laws governing these mesoscale phase transitions.

Research Question 3: Can Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) reverse-engineer these mesoscale emergent behaviors from multimodal, publicly available datasets without prior biochemical assumptions?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that by modeling individual mitochondria as autonomous RL agents whose reward function is global cellular metabolic efficiency, we can computationally reverse-engineer the observed biological voting rules. We posit that the optimal policies learned by the MARL agents in silico will independently match the empirical topological and kinetic parameters extracted from real-world imaging data. This will demonstrate that mitochondrial dynamics are mathematically optimizable swarm behaviors.

To address these questions, our transdisciplinary Working Group will rigorously test these hypotheses strictly through the synthesis of existing data. By applying AI-driven models to massive, integrated datasets spanning diverse cell types (e.g., neurons, myocytes, hepatocytes) and stress conditions, we aim to uncover whether these voting rules are cell-type specific or represent universal principles of mesoscale biological emergence. Answering these questions will fundamentally redefine our understanding of organelle interactions, shifting the focus from single-molecule pathways to the collective intelligence of subcellular networks.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodology strictly adheres to NCEMS guidelines by generating no new experimental data. Instead, we rely entirely on the community-scale synthesis of publicly available datasets, leveraging a transdisciplinary Working Group to integrate AI, network theory, and cell biology.

Phase 1: Data Curation and Integration
We will systematically harvest and curate multimodal datasets from public repositories (e.g., EMPIAR, Cell Image Library, MitoCheck, BioImage Archive) and supplementary data from published literature. The datasets will include: (1) High-resolution 3D electron microscopy (EM) and super-resolution fluorescence images of mitochondrial networks across diverse cell types and physiological states (basal, starvation, oxidative stress). (2) Live-cell time-lapse imaging of mitochondrial dynamics coupled with biosensor data (e.g., GCaMP for calcium, PercevalHR for ATP). (3) Parallel bulk and single-cell metabolic flux data (e.g., oxygen consumption rates) matched to the imaging conditions. We will standardize these disparate data types into a unified, cloud-based relational database, mapping morphological features to metabolic outputs.

Phase 2: Topological Feature Extraction via Deep Learning
To quantify the mesoscale architecture of the networks, we will deploy pre-trained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) to segment mitochondria from the curated images. We will represent the mitochondria as spatial graphs, extracting key network topology metrics: node degree, betweenness centrality, clustering coefficients, and network diameter. For time-lapse data, we will track fusion/fission frequencies, organelle velocities, and encounter durations. This step translates qualitative biological images into rigorous, quantitative mathematical representations of swarm behavior.

Phase 3: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) Modeling
This is the core analytical innovation. We will construct a MARL environment where each mitochondrion acts as an autonomous agent. 
- State Space: Local concentration of ATP/ADP, calcium, and ROS, derived from the synthesized biosensor data.
- Action Space: Fuse with neighbor, divide (fission), move, or initiate mitophagy.
- Reward Function: The global optimization of the network's metabolic output (derived from the integrated metabolic flux datasets) minus the energetic cost of transport and fusion.
We will train the MARL system using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). The objective is to reverse-engineer the agents' 'policy' (the voting rules). We will validate the model by comparing the emergent in silico network topologies generated by the AI against the empirical topological features extracted in Phase 2. 

Phase 4: Working Group Synthesis and Collaborative Analysis
The project requires profound cross-disciplinary collaboration. The Working Group—comprising AI/ML scientists, mitochondrial biologists, biophysicists, and computational modelers—will convene bi-annually in person at NCEMS, supplemented by monthly virtual sprints. Biologists will contextualize the AI-generated policies, ensuring biological plausibility, while AI experts will refine the algorithms based on biological feedback. Postdoctoral researchers will be cross-trained in both domains, acting as the primary integrators of the analytical pipeline. This iterative, transdisciplinary synthesis will ensure that the resulting framework accurately captures the emergent mesoscale properties of mitochondrial networks.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will deliver transformative scientific, methodological, and workforce outcomes, directly advancing the NCEMS mission to illuminate mesoscale emergence in molecular and cellular biology.

Scientific Impact: We will establish a groundbreaking conceptual paradigm by redefining mitochondrial networks as intelligent, decision-making swarms rather than passive participants in stochastic biochemical reactions. By identifying the 'voting rules' of organelle fusion, we will solve a long-standing puzzle regarding how local molecular signals translate into global metabolic optimization. This will yield a universal mathematical framework for mesoscale emergent properties that can be applied across different cell types, physiological states, and even different organelle systems (e.g., the endoplasmic reticulum or Golgi apparatus).

Methodological Impact: We will develop and validate a novel, highly innovative analytical strategy: the application of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) to reverse-engineer biological behaviors from static and dynamic imaging data. This pipeline will seamlessly integrate structural, dynamic, and metabolic datasets, proving that AI can be used not just for image segmentation, but for discovering fundamental biological rules. The fully documented MARL framework will be released as an open-source tool, empowering the broader scientific community to apply agent-based modeling to other complex molecular and cellular phenomena.

Workforce Development and Broader Impacts: This project will serve as a premier training ground for the future data-savvy scientific workforce. The two funded postdoctoral researchers will receive unparalleled, cross-disciplinary training at the intersection of advanced AI (reinforcement learning, computer vision) and fundamental cell biology. Furthermore, by deliberately recruiting Working Group members from diverse geographic locations, institutional research levels (including MSIs), and career stages, we will tap into diverse new talent. This collaborative ecosystem will foster a new generation of scientists who natively think across disciplinary boundaries, equipped to leverage publicly available data to drive future discoveries in the biosciences.

The entire computational pipeline—from the Deep Learning image segmentation scripts to the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) environments—will be developed openly on a public GitHub repository. We will utilize Docker containers to package our software environments, ensuring that any researcher globally can download, execute, and reproduce our AI models and analytical workflows without facing dependency conflicts or versioning issues.

Documentation and Protocols: To facilitate community adoption of our novel MARL approach, we will publish highly detailed, step-by-step tutorials and Jupyter Notebooks. These resources will allow researchers to adapt our 'swarm intelligence' analytical framework for their own specific biological questions or different organelle systems. All data curation standards and integration methodologies will be documented and published on Protocols.io.

We will prioritize publishing in peer-reviewed, open-access journals. author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: The Logic of Cellular Noise: Emergent Robustness in Stochastic Signaling Environments
abstract: Biological systems are inherently noisy at the molecular level, yet they produce remarkably robust cellular outcomes. This project challenges the view of noise as a nuisance, proposing instead that 'stochastic resonance' is an emergent property necessary for mesoscale stability. We will synthesize single-cell transcriptomics, proteomics fluctuation data, and time-lapse live-cell imaging of signaling cascades (e.g., NF-κB or p53). By applying Information Theory and stochastic modeling, we will determine if specific 'noise signatures' are conserved across different cell types and species. We aim to find the 'Criticality Point' where molecular randomness facilitates rapid state-switching in cells. This synthesis requires integrating disparate time-series data into a unified statistical manifold. The project will bridge the gap between statistical physics and cell biology, training students in the emerging field of stochastic biological engineering. The result will be a fundamental law of how biological complexity emerges from, and is stabilized by, underlying molecular chaos.
background_and_significance: For decades, the molecular and cellular biosciences have operated under a paradigm that views biological noise—the inherent stochasticity of molecular interactions, transcription, and translation—as a fundamental nuisance. Traditional models suggest that cells expend massive amounts of energy to buffer against this chaos to maintain phenotypic stability. However, recent advances in single-cell technologies and statistical physics hint at a profound paradigm shift: molecular noise is not merely an unavoidable artifact of low-copy-number thermodynamics, but rather a functional driver of biological emergence. At the mesoscale—the critical interface between individual biomolecules and functional organelles—this stochasticity may be harnessed through 'stochastic resonance,' a phenomenon where a certain level of background noise actually enhances the detection of weak signals and promotes system robustness. Despite its potential to revolutionize our understanding of cellular signaling, the study of biological noise remains highly fragmented. Individual laboratories generate vast amounts of single-cell transcriptomic data, proteomic fluctuation profiles, and high-resolution time-lapse imaging of key signaling cascades like NF-κB and p53. Yet, these datasets are rarely integrated across temporal and spatial scales. This fragmentation leaves fundamental questions unanswered regarding how molecular chaos translates into mesoscale stability and robust cellular decision-making. The proposed synthesis project directly addresses this critical gap, aligning perfectly with the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) mission. By leveraging massive, publicly available datasets, our multidisciplinary Working Group will synthesize disparate data streams to uncover the universal laws governing stochastic signaling environments. We will move beyond the capabilities of any single laboratory by combining the expertise of computational biologists, statistical physicists, AI specialists, and molecular geneticists. The significance of this research lies in its potential to solve a long-standing puzzle: how emergent properties, such as robust cellular state-switching and mesoscale structural stability, arise from underlying molecular randomness. By identifying conserved 'noise signatures' and defining the 'Criticality Point' of cellular networks, this project will fundamentally rewrite the rules of cellular signaling. Furthermore, it will establish a new methodological framework for synthesizing multi-omics and spatiotemporal imaging data into unified statistical manifolds. Ultimately, this work will not only reveal how biological complexity is stabilized by molecular chaos but will also lay the foundation for 'stochastic biological engineering,' enabling researchers to predict and manipulate cellular behavior in health and disease by targeting the noise architecture of the cell.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our synthesis project is driven by three primary research questions that seek to decode the functional role of molecular noise in driving mesoscale emergence. 

Question 1: Are there universally conserved 'noise signatures' across different cell types, signaling pathways, and species that dictate mesoscale stability? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that stochastic resonance is a universal emergent property in biological systems. Rather than being random, unstructured interference, molecular noise possesses specific, conserved frequencies and amplitudes that act as informational carriers. We predict that pathways such as NF-κB and p53, despite their distinct biological functions, share mathematically isomorphic noise signatures that are essential for maintaining stable mesoscale signaling hubs across diverse taxa. 

Question 2: What is the thermodynamic and informational 'Criticality Point' at which molecular randomness optimizes rapid cellular state-switching without sacrificing overall phenotypic robustness? 
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that mesoscale signaling networks operate at or near a phase transition, or 'criticality.' At this Criticality Point, a specific threshold of molecular noise maximizes the system's responsiveness to environmental perturbations, allowing for rapid phenotypic state-switching (e.g., from proliferation to apoptosis, or quiescence to activation). We posit that pushing a cell's noise profile outside of this critical window—either by dampening the noise or amplifying it excessively—will result in signaling failure or pathological states. 

Question 3: How can disparate temporal and spatial scales of biological noise be mathematically integrated to predict the emergence of coherent mesoscale responses? 
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that temporal fluctuations in protein expression (captured via live-cell imaging) and spatial variations in transcript abundance (captured via single-cell RNA sequencing) are mathematically coupled. We propose that by mapping these disparate data modalities onto a unified statistical manifold using advanced topological data analysis and machine learning, we can identify hidden, low-dimensional attractors that govern the emergence of complex cellular behaviors from underlying molecular stochasticity. 

Answering these questions requires a community-scale synthesis approach. No single experimental dataset contains both the temporal resolution and the multi-omic depth required to map these noise signatures comprehensively. By bringing together experts in Information Theory, non-equilibrium thermodynamics, and molecular biology to synthesize publicly available datasets, our Working Group will rigorously test these hypotheses. This transdisciplinary approach will allow us to move beyond correlative observations to establish predictive, fundamental laws regarding the role of noise in cellular emergence, fulfilling the core mandate of NCEMS.
methods_and_approach:
To achieve our objectives, we will employ a rigorous, purely computational synthesis approach that leverages existing, publicly available datasets. Our methodology is structured into three integrated phases: Data Aggregation and Curation, Manifold Alignment and Harmonization, and Physics-Informed AI Analysis. 

Phase 1: Data Aggregation and Curation. We will source high-quality datasets from established public repositories. Single-cell transcriptomic (scRNA-seq) data will be harvested from the Human Cell Atlas and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), focusing on varied cell types under basal and perturbed conditions. Proteomics fluctuation data will be sourced from PRIDE, while high-temporal-resolution live-cell imaging datasets of NF-κB and p53 dynamics will be extracted from the Image Data Resource (IDR) and OMERO-hosted repositories. A dedicated subgroup of our Working Group will establish strict quality control pipelines to ensure data compatibility, focusing on datasets with high signal-to-noise ratios and adequate metadata. 

Phase 2: Manifold Alignment and Harmonization. The central methodological challenge is integrating static, high-dimensional multi-omics data with low-dimensional, high-temporal-resolution imaging data. We will utilize advanced Artificial Intelligence and Data Science techniques to construct a 'unified statistical manifold.' Specifically, we will employ non-linear manifold alignment algorithms and multi-modal Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). These AI models will embed the disparate datasets into a shared latent space, allowing us to map the spatial distribution of transcriptomic noise onto the temporal dynamics of protein signaling. This harmonization will create a first-of-its-kind synthetic dataset that bridges the molecular and mesoscale levels. 

Phase 3: Physics-Informed AI Analysis. Once the data is harmonized, we will apply Information Theory and stochastic modeling to extract biological laws. We will calculate the mutual information and channel capacity of signaling pathways to determine how noise signatures are conserved across species. To identify the 'Criticality Point,' we will adapt Langevin dynamics and Fokker-Planck equations, traditionally used in statistical physics, to model the mesoscale biological networks. We will use Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) trained on the latent space representations to predict cellular state-switching dynamics based on initial noise conditions. 

Working Group Structure: The project will be executed by a transdisciplinary Working Group comprising 15 members, including PIs, postdocs, and graduate students from physics, computer science, and molecular biology backgrounds. The group will meet bi-weekly virtually and hold biannual in-person hackathons at the NCEMS facility. These intensive sessions will foster deep cross-disciplinary collaboration. Trainees will be paired with mentors outside their primary discipline, ensuring that biology students gain fluency in stochastic modeling, while physics students master molecular signaling concepts. This structured approach guarantees both scientific rigor and the cultivation of a uniquely cross-trained, data-savvy workforce.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The proposed synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes across scientific discovery, methodological innovation, and workforce development. 

Scientifically, the primary outcome will be the establishment of a new fundamental law of biological emergence: the characterization of conserved 'noise signatures' and the identification of the 'Criticality Point' in mesoscale signaling networks. By proving that stochastic resonance is a universal driver of cellular stability, we will fundamentally shift the paradigm of molecular and cellular biology, moving the field away from deterministic models toward probabilistic, noise-driven frameworks. This will solve long-standing mysteries regarding how cells maintain robustness in the face of molecular chaos and how they execute rapid state-switching during differentiation or stress responses. 

Methodologically, we will produce a highly innovative, open-source computational pipeline capable of integrating asynchronous, multi-scale biological data into a unified statistical manifold. The AI models and multi-modal Variational Autoencoders developed during this project will be generalizable, providing the broader scientific community with novel tools to synthesize disparate data types—a core goal of the NCEMS mandate. 

Broadly, the impact of this work extends to translational applications. Understanding the logic of cellular noise opens new avenues for 'stochastic biological engineering,' where researchers might manipulate the noise landscape of a cell to prevent pathological state-switching, such as the transition to malignancy in cancer. 

Finally, the project will have a profound impact on workforce development. By deeply integrating graduate students and postdoctoral researchers into our multidisciplinary Working Group, we will train a new generation of 'stochastic biological engineers.' These trainees will emerge with a rare, highly sought-after skillset that bridges statistical physics, advanced AI/machine learning, and molecular biology, perfectly positioning them to lead the future of data-driven biosciences.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the highest standards of Open Science and reproducibility, aligning with the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles and NCEMS guidelines. Because our project relies entirely on synthesizing publicly available data, transparent documentation of our data provenance, harmonization pipelines, and analytical workflows is paramount. 

All code, including manifold alignment algorithms, Variational Autoencoders, and stochastic modeling scripts, will be developed openly on a public GitHub repository. To ensure strict reproducibility, all computational environments will be containerized using Docker and Singularity. This will allow any researcher globally to download our environment and replicate our findings with a single command, eliminating the 'works on my machine' barrier. 

The unified statistical manifold—our primary synthetic dataset—will be extensively annotated with standardized metadata and deposited into accessible public repositories such as Zenodo and the Open Science Framework (OSF). We will also develop interactive, web-based tools (e.g., R-Shiny applications and Jupyter Notebooks) hosted on cloud platforms to allow biologists without extensive coding expertise to explore the noise signatures and criticality points intuitively. 

Dissemination of our findings will prioritize open access. All manuscripts generated by the Working Group will be uploaded to preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv, arXiv) concurrently with submission to open-access, peer-reviewed journals. Furthermore, we will host quarterly open webinars to share our progress, methodologies, and tools with the broader scientific community, inviting feedback and fostering extended collaborative networks. By embedding these practices into the core of our project, we will ensure that our synthesis efforts catalyze further research and discovery far beyond the lifespan of the grant.
budget_and_resources:
The proposed budget is carefully structured to support the community-scale synthesis, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and extensive training required by this project, demonstrating a clear need for NCEMS support that exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory. 

Personnel costs form the core of the budget, requesting support for two Postdoctoral Researchers and three Graduate Students. These trainees will be the primary engines of data curation, AI model development, and biological interpretation, benefiting directly from the cross-disciplinary mentorship of the Working Group. We also request partial summer salary support for the PI and Co-PIs to facilitate the extensive management, coordination, and integration efforts required for a transdisciplinary team of this scale. 

Travel and collaboration funds are critical to the success of this synthesis project. We request funding to support travel, lodging, and per diem for all 15 Working Group members to attend biannual, week-long hackathons at the NCEMS headquarters. These intensive, in-person meetings are essential for overcoming disciplinary language barriers, rapidly prototyping computational models, and fostering the deep collaborative partnerships mandated by the RFP. 

Computational resources are a significant requirement due to the massive scale of the multi-omics and time-lapse imaging datasets. We request funds for cloud computing credits (e.g., AWS or GCP) and access to high-performance computing (HPC) clusters necessary for training deep learning models (VAEs, RNNs) and running complex stochastic simulations. 

Finally, we have allocated funds for Open Science costs, including article processing charges (APCs) for open-access publications, and long-term data storage fees for hosting our unified statistical manifold and interactive web tools. The requested resources are indispensable for executing this ambitious synthesis, leveraging NCEMS infrastructure to achieve transformative insights into cellular emergence.

author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: The Evolutionary Persistence of Disorder: Emergent Mesoscale Functions of Intrinsically Disordered Regions
abstract: Intrinsically Disordered Regions (IDRs) in proteins often show low sequence conservation but high functional conservation in forming phase-separated condensates. This project will synthesize phyloproteomic data across 500 species with biophysical databases of known phase-separating proteins. Using Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks, we will identify 'Hidden Conserved Motifs' within IDRs that dictate the physical properties (viscosity, surface tension) of emergent mesoscale phases. We hypothesize that the 'grammar' of disorder is a primary driver of organelle evolution. This community-scale synthesis will integrate evolutionary biology with soft-matter physics to solve the puzzle of how disordered sequences produce highly ordered mesoscale structures. The collaboration will include evolutionary biologists and computational biophysicists, fostering a transdisciplinary perspective on the origin of cellular complexity. The project will produce an open-access map of the 'IDR-Phase Space,' allowing researchers to predict the mesoscale impact of any disordered protein mutation.
background_and_significance: Proteins are traditionally understood through the structure-function paradigm, yet Intrinsically Disordered Regions (IDRs) defy this rule, representing a substantial fraction of eukaryotic proteomes. Despite their lack of a fixed three-dimensional structure, IDRs are fundamental to the emergence of membraneless organelles via biomolecular condensate formation—a classic mesoscale phenomenon. A long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular sciences is the evolutionary persistence of these regions: IDRs typically exhibit remarkably low primary sequence conservation, yet their ability to drive phase separation and dictate the physical properties of condensates is highly conserved across vast evolutionary distances. This paradox suggests the existence of a 'grammar' of disorder—hidden conserved motifs or sequence features (e.g., charge distribution, pi-pi interaction spacing) that govern emergent mesoscale properties like viscosity, surface tension, and network connectivity, rather than strict amino acid identity. Understanding this grammar is critical for deciphering how disordered sequences produce highly ordered mesoscale structures and drive cellular complexity. Currently, individual research labs lack the capacity to bridge the gap between evolutionary biology and soft-matter physics due to the isolated nature of genomic and biophysical datasets. To solve this mystery, a community-scale synthesis is urgently needed. This project directly addresses the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) mission by investigating emergent properties at the mesoscale. We will synthesize publicly available phyloproteomic data spanning over 500 species with disparate biophysical databases cataloging known phase-separating proteins and their condensate properties, including DisProt, PhaSepDB, and UniProt. By integrating these massive, previously siloed datasets, our multidisciplinary team of evolutionary biologists, computational biophysicists, and data scientists will leverage advanced artificial intelligence, specifically Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), to decode the hidden grammar of IDRs. This transdisciplinary approach is beyond the scope of any single laboratory. The synthesis will illuminate the fundamental principles of how molecular-level disorder scales to mesoscale organization and cellular function. Furthermore, by linking evolutionary trajectories with soft-matter physics, this research will redefine our understanding of organelle evolution. The significance of this work extends beyond fundamental biology; mapping the 'IDR-Phase Space' will provide researchers with the predictive power to determine how specific mutations within disordered regions alter mesoscale physical properties, offering profound implications for understanding diseases linked to aberrant phase transitions, such as neurodegeneration and cancer. Ultimately, this proposal embodies the NCEMS vision by utilizing data synthesis and AI to resolve a fundamental biological puzzle, stimulating novel questions about the origins of cellular organization, and fostering a collaborative, transdisciplinary environment essential for the next generation of data-savvy scientists.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This community-scale synthesis project is driven by three primary research questions that bridge evolutionary biology, molecular biology, and soft-matter physics, aiming to uncover the mechanisms driving mesoscale emergence from molecular disorder. Question 1: What constitutes the hidden evolutionary 'grammar' within Intrinsically Disordered Regions (IDRs) that preserves phase-separation functionality despite high primary sequence divergence? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that while exact amino acid sequences in IDRs mutate rapidly, specific higher-order sequence features—such as the patterning of charged residues, the spacing of aromatic groups (pi-pi and cation-pi interactions), and overall chain flexibility—are under strong evolutionary purifying selection. We posit that Large Language Models (LLMs) trained on diverse phyloproteomic data can identify these 'Hidden Conserved Motifs' (HCMs) as a distinct syntactic grammar that is invisible to traditional sequence alignment tools. Question 2: How do these Hidden Conserved Motifs dictate the emergent biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the identified IDR grammar acts as a programmable code that explicitly determines the soft-matter physical properties of the resulting condensates, such as viscosity, surface tension, and critical concentration for phase separation. By employing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to map the sequence syntax (identified in Q1) to mesoscale network architectures, we expect to demonstrate that specific combinations and spatial arrangements of HCMs reliably predict the material state (liquid, gel, or solid) of the emergent membraneless organelle. Question 3: How has the evolutionary tuning of IDR grammar driven the diversification and adaptation of mesoscale cellular organization across eukaryotic life? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the 'grammar' of disorder is a primary driver of organelle evolution. We predict that shifts in the environmental niches of different species (e.g., temperature extremes, desiccation stress) will correlate with systematic, predictable variations in the IDR grammar of their phase-separating proteins. This evolutionary tuning allows species to modulate the mesoscale properties of their condensates to maintain cellular fitness under varying physiological conditions. To address these questions, our multidisciplinary working group will synthesize data from over 500 species, moving beyond the traditional single-organism or single-protein focus. By answering these questions, we will solve the long-standing puzzle of how disordered sequences produce highly ordered, functional mesoscale structures. The hypotheses challenge the conventional structure-function paradigm by proposing a sequence-ensemble-phase paradigm, where the statistical properties of the sequence ensemble dictate mesoscale emergence. Validating these hypotheses will fundamentally shift our understanding of molecular evolution, proving that selection can act on the emergent physical properties of a protein collective rather than just the folded state of an individual monomer. This aligns perfectly with the NCEMS goal of understanding the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at different scales of composition and space.
methods_and_approach: The proposed research relies entirely on the synthesis and integration of existing, publicly available datasets, generating no new experimental data, in strict accordance with NCEMS guidelines. Our transdisciplinary approach integrates evolutionary biology, data science, and soft-matter physics through a collaborative Working Group structure. Data Synthesis and Integration: We will aggregate phyloproteomic data across 500 eukaryotic species using databases such as UniProt and OrthoDB, focusing on orthologous groups known to undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). This genomic data will be synthesized with curated biophysical data from PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, and DisProt, which contain empirically derived mesoscale properties of condensates (e.g., critical concentrations, viscosity, material state). The central methodological challenge is harmonizing these disparate data types—mapping evolutionary sequence variation to biophysical phase diagrams. AI and Machine Learning Framework: To discover the 'grammar' of disorder, we will utilize advanced Large Language Models (LLMs) adapted for protein sequences (e.g., ESM-2). Unlike traditional alignment algorithms (like BLAST), which fail on poorly conserved IDRs, LLMs capture deep contextual relationships between amino acids. We will fine-tune these models on our synthesized IDR dataset to extract high-dimensional embeddings. We will apply manifold learning to these embeddings to identify 'Hidden Conserved Motifs' (HCMs)—patterns of charge, hydrophobicity, and spacer lengths that are evolutionarily preserved despite sequence drift. To link molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale physics, we will employ Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Condensates will be modeled as dynamic graphs where nodes represent interacting HCMs and edges represent transient, multivalent interactions (e.g., pi-pi, cation-pi). The GNNs will be trained to predict emergent macroscopic properties (viscosity, surface tension) based on the network topology dictated by the IDR grammar. Working Group Structure and Collaboration: This project is beyond the capabilities of a single lab. The Working Group will consist of PIs, postdocs, and graduate students from four distinct institutions, bridging evolutionary genomics, computational biophysics, and AI development. We will hold bi-weekly virtual meetings and two intensive, week-long in-person synthesis hackathons at the NCEMS facility. These hackathons will serve as the primary engine for data integration and model building. Training the Next Generation: A core component of our approach is the cross-training of early-career researchers. Graduate students and postdocs will be co-mentored by PIs from different disciplines. Biologists will receive hands-on training in deep learning and graph theory, while computer scientists will be trained in evolutionary theory and soft-matter physics. Trainees will lead the development of the 'IDR-Phase Space' predictive map, ensuring they emerge as leaders in the data-savvy, transdisciplinary workforce envisioned by NCEMS. Validation: The predictive power of our LLM-GNN framework will be validated using hold-out datasets and cross-referenced with recent literature on mutant IDR phase behavior. By mapping the evolutionary trajectory of these sequences against their predicted phase behavior, we will reconstruct the evolutionary history of mesoscale organelle emergence, providing a robust, data-driven answer to our core hypotheses.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This community-scale synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission to understand mesoscale emergence. The primary deliverable will be the 'IDR-Phase Space,' a comprehensive, open-access, interactive multidimensional map. This tool will allow researchers worldwide to input any wild-type or mutated disordered protein sequence and immediately predict its emergent mesoscale physical properties, such as its propensity to phase separate and the likely material state (liquid, gel, solid) of the resulting condensate. Scientifically, this project will solve a long-standing puzzle by replacing the outdated structure-function paradigm for IDRs with a new sequence-ensemble-phase paradigm. By defining the evolutionary 'grammar' of disorder, we will reveal how nature engineers complex, highly ordered mesoscale structures from seemingly chaotic, disordered molecular building blocks. This will provide unprecedented insights into the evolutionary origins of membraneless organelles and cellular complexity. The broader impacts of this work are vast. The predictive models generated will be invaluable to biomedical researchers studying neurodegenerative diseases (e.g., ALS, Alzheimer's) and cancers, where mutations in IDRs lead to aberrant phase transitions and pathological protein aggregation. Furthermore, our methodologies will establish a new gold standard for applying Large Language Models and Graph Neural Networks to biophysical data synthesis. Finally, the project will have a profound impact on workforce development. By immersing postdocs and graduate students in a deeply collaborative, transdisciplinary Working Group, we will train a new generation of data-savvy scientists fluent in both evolutionary biology and artificial intelligence. These trainees will be uniquely equipped to tackle future challenges in the molecular and cellular biosciences, ensuring the long-term impact of NCEMS funding on the scientific community.

Because this project relies entirely on synthesizing publicly available data, ensuring transparent and reproducible data provenance is our highest priority. We will utilize FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles at every stage. The computational workflows, including the architecture, weights, and training scripts for our Large Language Models and Graph Neural Networks, will be developed openly on GitHub. This ensures that any researcher, regardless of their local computing setup, can pull our containers and reproduce our synthesis and modeling results with a single command. Jupyter Notebooks detailing step-by-step analyses, from raw data ingestion to the generation of the 'IDR-Phase Space' map, will be published alongside our manuscripts. All publications resulting from this NCEMS-supported synthesis will be submitted to open-access journals or made available via preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv) prior to peer review.
