author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: Complexity from Simplification: Identifying the 'Minimum Viable Mesoscale' in Minimal Cells
abstract: What is the simplest possible architecture required for a cell to function? By synthesizing the comprehensive datasets available for the minimal cell (JCVI-syn3.0) and comparing them to wild-type Mycoplasma and higher eukaryotes, this project aims to identify the essential emergent properties of life. We will integrate metabolic models, proteomics, and 3D structural maps of minimal cells to determine which mesoscale structures (e.g., protein clusters, membrane domains) are non-negotiable for survival. We hypothesize that even in a 'minimal' genome, complexity emerges through the physical crowding and spatial coordination of limited parts. This project addresses the fundamental question of biological scaling. It requires a massive synthesis of multiple -omics layers and biophysical simulations. The resulting 'Minimal Mesoscale Blueprint' will serve as a guide for synthetic biology and our understanding of the origins of life. Trainees will work at the cutting edge of synthetic and systems biology, learning to extract high-order principles from simplified biological models.
background_and_significance: The transition from individual biomolecules to a fully functioning, living cell is governed by emergent properties at the mesoscale—the critical spatial domain spanning nanometers to micrometers. At this scale, proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids self-assemble into higher-order functional complexes, condensates, and structural networks. Understanding how these mesoscale structures emerge and orchestrate cellular life is a fundamental challenge in the molecular and cellular biosciences. The creation of JCVI-syn3.0, a synthetic minimal cell with a genome radically reduced to its 473 essential genes, provides an unprecedented, noise-free model to study this phenomenon. While the genetic blueprint of this minimal cell is well documented, its physical and spatial organization—the minimal mesoscale—remains a profound mystery. How do a mere 473 genes translate into the spatial coordination and physical architecture necessary to sustain life and cellular division? Currently, vast amounts of disparate, publicly available data exist for JCVI-syn3.0 and its wild-type counterparts, including quantitative proteomics, transcriptomics, high-resolution cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), and genome-scale metabolic models. However, these datasets remain largely siloed within their respective sub-disciplines. By synthesizing these multi-omics and structural datasets, this project will uncover the 'Minimum Viable Mesoscale.' We will identify the non-negotiable emergent properties required for cellular life, such as essential protein clustering, macromolecular crowding thresholds, and fundamental membrane domain formations. This research addresses a long-standing puzzle: how does complexity arise from simplified biological parts without the extensive regulatory networks found in more complex organisms? The significance of this work extends far beyond basic biology; it is crucial for advancing synthetic biology, informing origin-of-life studies, and enabling the bottom-up engineering of synthetic cells for therapeutic and industrial applications. This project perfectly aligns with the U.S. National Science Foundation National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) mission. It exclusively utilizes publicly available data to catalyze multidisciplinary insights, generating no new experimental data. Furthermore, this ambitious synthesis requires a transdisciplinary Working Group spanning computational biology, biophysics, systems biology, and structural bioinformatics, a collaborative effort that far exceeds the capabilities of any single laboratory. By integrating these diverse scientific perspectives, we will bridge the gap between genetic simplicity and physical complexity, revealing the universal principles of biological scaling and mesoscale emergence.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This community-scale synthesis project is driven by three primary research questions, each paired with a testable hypothesis centered on mesoscale emergence in simplified biological systems. Question 1: What constitutes the 'Minimum Viable Mesoscale' architecture required for basic cellular viability and division? We hypothesize that even within the radically simplified context of a minimal genome, specific mesoscale structures—such as functional protein clusters (metabolons), rudimentary cytoskeletal-like networks, and localized lipid membrane domains—are strictly non-negotiable for survival. We postulate that the deliberate reduction of genetic complexity forces the cell to rely heavily on higher-order physical organization to achieve essential functions, compensating for the lack of specialized genetic regulation. Question 2: How do physical constraints, specifically macromolecular crowding and spatial coordination, drive emergent biological properties in a minimal cell? We hypothesize that in the absence of membrane-bound organelles and complex spatial compartmentalization, the minimal cell relies on fundamental biophysical phenomena, such as liquid-liquid phase separation and localized macromolecular crowding, to facilitate metabolic channeling and signal transduction. We expect our synthesis of structural tomograms and quantitative proteomic data to reveal that spatial proximity and density act as functional substitutes for the complex, specialized regulatory networks seen in higher eukaryotes. Question 3: How do the emergent mesoscale properties of a minimal cell compare to those of wild-type Mycoplasma and higher eukaryotes, and what does this reveal about biological scaling? We hypothesize that a comparative data synthesis will uncover a conserved 'core' of mesoscale organization that represents the absolute foundational physical requirements for life. We anticipate that as genomic complexity increases from minimal synthetic cells to wild-type bacteria and eventually to eukaryotes, mesoscale structures become progressively more specialized and redundant, yet the fundamental biophysical rules governing their initial assembly remain constant. By addressing these three questions, we will solve the long-standing puzzle of how basic genetic components spontaneously organize into a living, functioning physical system. This requires the massive integration of diverse, publicly available datasets, including spatial proteomics, 3D cryo-ET maps, and genome-scale metabolic models. Our approach will shift the scientific paradigm from viewing the minimal cell as merely a reduced parts list to understanding it as a highly complex, spatially organized, and emergent physical system. This transdisciplinary inquiry will yield profound insights into the physical limits of life and the universal rules of mesoscale biology, directly fulfilling the core objectives of the NCEMS funding call.
methods_and_approach: Our transdisciplinary Working Group will employ a purely computational, synthesis-driven approach, utilizing exclusively publicly available datasets. The methodology is structured into four integrated phases, leveraging advanced AI and data science techniques to merge disparate omics and structural data across multiple scales. Phase 1: Comprehensive Data Curation and Harmonization. We will aggregate diverse datasets for JCVI-syn3.0, wild-type Mycoplasma mycoides, and selected eukaryotic models. Data sources include the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) for cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) maps, PRIDE for quantitative proteomics, and GEO for transcriptomics. We will also incorporate existing whole-cell metabolic models from the wholecell.org community. A key methodological development will be the creation of an AI-driven, natural language processing harmonization pipeline to standardize metadata, ensuring interoperability across structural, spatial, and molecular scales. Phase 2: Spatial Integration and 3D Mesoscale Mapping. To identify the minimal mesoscale architecture, we will map proteomic and transcriptomic data onto 3D cryo-ET tomograms. We will utilize deep learning-based structural prediction tools (e.g., AlphaFold-Multimer) and spatial clustering algorithms to predict protein-protein interactions and macromolecular assemblies within the cellular volume. This spatial integration will allow us to construct a high-resolution, spatially resolved map of the minimal cell, identifying critical emergent structures such as metabolons and membrane-associated complexes that are invisible to single-omics approaches. Phase 3: Biophysical Simulations of Crowding and Emergence. Using the integrated spatial maps generated in Phase 2, we will perform coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and spatial stochastic simulations using platforms like Smoldyn. These simulations will rigorously test our hypotheses regarding macromolecular crowding and phase separation. By simulating the physical environment of the minimal cell, we can observe the emergent properties of spatial coordination in real-time, determining how physical constraints drive metabolic efficiency and cellular division without complex genetic regulation. Phase 4: Comparative Biological Scaling Analysis. Finally, we will apply network science and machine learning algorithms to compare the minimal mesoscale blueprint against wild-type and eukaryotic datasets. We will identify which mesoscale features are universally conserved and which scale with genomic complexity. This approach requires the combined expertise of our multi-lab Working Group, which includes distinct laboratories specializing in structural bioinformatics, whole-cell modeling, biophysics, and AI. By synthesizing these diverse data streams, we will bridge the gap between 1D genomic data and 3D cellular reality, fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to develop innovative analytical strategies.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The primary outcome of this synthesis project will be the 'Minimal Mesoscale Blueprint'—the first comprehensive, spatially resolved computational model detailing the essential physical architecture required for cellular life. This blueprint will explicitly identify the non-negotiable emergent properties, such as critical protein clusters and spatial density thresholds, that bridge the gap between a minimal genome and a functional cell. Scientifically, this project will solve a long-standing mystery regarding biological scaling, demonstrating how physical forces like macromolecular crowding compensate for reduced genetic complexity. These insights will have a profound impact on synthetic biology, providing rational, physics-based design principles for engineering robust synthetic cells, biosensors, and targeted therapeutics. Furthermore, it will inform origin-of-life studies by highlighting the absolute biophysical prerequisites for the emergence of living systems from primordial components. Methodologically, we will deliver a suite of innovative, AI-driven analytical pipelines for integrating multi-omics data with 3D structural tomograms. These open-source tools will be highly adaptable, empowering the broader scientific community to investigate mesoscale phenomena in a wide variety of other organisms and disease states. Crucially, this project will have a lasting, transformative impact on workforce development. Trainees, including graduate students and postdoctoral researchers integrated into our Working Group, will receive unparalleled cross-disciplinary training. They will become part of the next-generation, data-savvy workforce, highly proficient in structural bioinformatics, biophysical simulations, and advanced data synthesis. They will leave the project fully equipped to tackle complex, multiscale biological challenges, ensuring a lasting legacy of the NCEMS investment.
open_science_and_reproducibility: Our Working Group is fundamentally committed to the principles of open, team, and reproducible science, aligning seamlessly with the NCEMS mandate and the highest standards of the scientific community. All aspects of this synthesis project—from initial data curation and analytical pipelines to final models and simulations—will be made fully transparent and publicly accessible, strictly adhering to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles. All curated datasets, harmonized metadata, and the final 'Minimal Mesoscale Blueprint' will be deposited in recognized, open-access repositories such as Zenodo and the BioModels database under a CC-BY license. To ensure strict computational reproducibility, all analytical workflows, AI models, and simulation scripts will be collaboratively developed using version control via a public GitHub repository under an MIT open-source license. We will utilize containerization technologies, such as Docker and Singularity, alongside robust workflow managers like Nextflow. This guarantees that any researcher, regardless of their local computational environment, can perfectly replicate our analyses and seamlessly build upon our findings. Furthermore, we commit to publishing all findings in open-access, peer-reviewed journals and will utilize preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv) to rapidly disseminate our results to the community prior to formal publication. We will also develop interactive, web-based visualization tools to allow researchers, educators, and the public to seamlessly explore the minimal mesoscale models in 3D. By establishing these rigorous open science practices, we will not only ensure the integrity of our own work but provide a transparent resource that catalyzes discovery.
budget_and_resources: The proposed synthesis project requires a level of integration and diverse expertise that fundamentally exceeds the capabilities of any single laboratory, making NCEMS support absolutely critical. The budget is strategically designed to facilitate deep, cross-disciplinary collaboration and support the intensive data science requirements of the project. The primary budget allocation will fund Working Group activities, including travel, accommodation, and logistical support for intensive, biannual in-person synthesis meetings at the NCEMS facility. These gatherings are essential for fostering the transdisciplinary synergy required to merge structural biology, biophysics, and AI. Additionally, funds will support regular virtual collaborative sessions to maintain momentum. A significant portion of the budget (approximately 40%) is dedicated to training the next generation of data-savvy scientists. We request support for two postdoctoral researchers and three graduate students who will be co-mentored across the participating labs. This funding will cover their stipends and travel to NCEMS, ensuring they receive hands-on experience in community-scale synthesis, AI application, and open science practices. Finally, resources are allocated for advanced computational infrastructure. While we leverage exclusively publicly available data, the synthesis, AI-driven harmonization, and whole-cell coarse-grained biophysical simulations require substantial computational power. We request funds for cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud) to ensure scalable processing and to permanently host the interactive, open-access web portals for our final models. This budget ensures the Working Group has the precise resources needed to successfully execute this ambitious, community-scale synthesis project and deliver transformative insights into mesoscale emergence.

author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: The High-Pressure Mesoscale: Emergent Mechanical Stability in Deep-Sea Piezophiles
abstract: Deep-sea organisms thrive under pressures that would denature the proteins and collapse the organelles of surface-dwelling life. This project will synthesize the proteomics, lipidomics, and structural data of deep-sea microbes (piezophiles) versus their shallow-water relatives. We aim to identify the 'Piezophilic Emergence Rules'—the specific mesoscale adaptations, such as altered membrane packing and specialized protein scaffolds, that utilize high pressure as a stabilizing force rather than a stressor. Using multi-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and AI-driven manifold learning, we will model how these organisms maintain cellular fluidity and organelle integrity. This synthesis is only possible by leveraging global oceanographic and genomic databases. The work will clarify how extreme environmental constraints drive the emergence of novel biological architectures. This project will bring together marine biologists and biophysicists, providing trainees with a unique perspective on the physical limits of life and the adaptability of mesoscale systems.
background_and_significance: The deep ocean represents the largest habitable space on Earth, yet it is characterized by extreme environmental conditions, most notably immense hydrostatic pressure, which increases by approximately 1 atmosphere for every 10 meters of depth. For surface-dwelling organisms, high pressure is a severe stressor that induces catastrophic biological failures: lipid bilayers undergo phase transitions from fluid to gel states, disrupting cellular compartmentalization, while large macromolecular protein complexes dissociate, and individual proteins denature due to the penetration of water into internal hydrophobic cavities. Despite these thermodynamic challenges, deep-sea piezophiles (pressure-loving organisms) not only survive but thrive under conditions exceeding 1,000 atmospheres. The fundamental biological puzzle lies in understanding how these organisms achieve emergent mechanical stability at the mesoscale—the critical spatial domain between individual biomolecules and whole organelles. While previous studies have isolated single proteins or sequenced individual genomes of deep-sea microbes, a fragmented, single-lab approach has failed to explain how mesoscale properties, such as dynamic membrane fluidity and robust protein scaffolding, emerge from molecular constituents under pressure. This proposal directly addresses the NCEMS mission by shifting the paradigm from isolated experimental observations to a community-scale synthesis of existing, publicly available data. By integrating disparate multi-omics datasets—including global oceanographic metagenomics, deep-sea proteomics, and lipidomics—we aim to uncover the 'Piezophilic Emergence Rules.' We postulate that mechanical stability in piezophiles is not merely a sum of individual molecular adaptations, but an emergent mesoscale property where high hydrostatic pressure is utilized as a stabilizing force rather than a disruptive one. For instance, specific alterations in membrane lipid packing and specialized protein-protein interaction interfaces may create biological architectures that require high pressure to maintain their functional conformation. Understanding these phenomena requires a transdisciplinary approach that is beyond the scope of any single research group. By bringing together experts in marine microbiology, structural biophysics, and artificial intelligence, this Working Group will synthesize vast, untapped public datasets to bridge the gap between primary molecular sequences and emergent mesoscale architecture. This synthesis will not only solve long-standing mysteries regarding the physical limits of life on Earth but will also provide profound insights into how extreme environmental constraints drive the evolution of novel biological systems. Furthermore, uncovering how mesoscale structures resist pressure-induced unfolding has direct applications in biotechnology, including the development of hyper-stable enzymes and novel biomaterials. Crucially, this project will serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists, equipping trainees with the computational skills necessary to integrate complex biological data and model emergent phenomena at the intersection of biology, physics, and computer science.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This synthesis project is driven by the overarching objective to elucidate the 'Piezophilic Emergence Rules'—the specific biological principles that govern mesoscale stability under extreme hydrostatic pressure. To achieve this, our Working Group will address three compelling, interrelated research questions that tackle long-standing puzzles in molecular and cellular biology. Question 1: How do lipidomic profiles and membrane protein compositions co-evolve to maintain mesoscale fluidity and structural integrity under extreme pressure? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that piezophiles exhibit emergent 'interlocking' lipid-protein mesoscale domains that fundamentally differ from the fluid mosaic models of surface-dwelling organisms. Rather than simply increasing the proportion of unsaturated fatty acids—a known low-temperature adaptation—piezophiles synthesize unique lipid geometries that, when combined with specific transmembrane protein scaffolds, rely on high hydrostatic pressure to compress into a functional, fluid mesophase. We predict that removing pressure destabilizes these domains, explaining why obligate piezophiles lyse at surface pressures. Question 2: What are the structural and thermodynamic signatures of piezophilic protein scaffolds, and how do they prevent pressure-induced dissociation of mesoscale complexes? Hypothesis 2: High pressure typically forces water into the hydrophobic cores and protein-protein interfaces of macromolecular assemblies, driving dissociation due to a negative change in system volume. We hypothesize that piezophilic mesoscale complexes have evolved to minimize compressible internal cavities and maximize hydration-layer packing at interaction interfaces. Consequently, the assembled mesoscale state possesses a smaller partial molar volume than the dissociated state, leading to an emergent property governed by Le Chatelier’s principle: hydrostatic pressure actively favors and stabilizes the assembled macromolecular complex. Question 3: Can artificial intelligence and manifold learning identify universal, scale-bridging adaptive trajectories from disparate multi-omics datasets that transcend phylogenetic boundaries? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the physical constraints of the deep sea are so absolute that convergent evolution dictates a limited set of viable mesoscale architectures. By applying non-linear dimensionality reduction and manifold learning to globally distributed genomic, proteomic, and lipidomic data, we predict the emergence of conserved adaptive trajectories. These trajectories will reveal how distinct evolutionary lineages utilize different primary sequence mutations and lipid syntheses to arrive at identical emergent mesoscale properties. Addressing these questions requires the community-scale synthesis of data, as the answers lie hidden within the cross-sections of diverse datasets—ranging from the Tara Oceans metagenomes to PRIDE proteomics repositories. By answering these questions, we will uncover how biological systems leverage physical extremes to build complex, higher-order structures, directly fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to explore emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences.
methods_and_approach: To identify the 'Piezophilic Emergence Rules' and model emergent mechanical stability at the mesoscale, we will employ a purely computational, community-scale synthesis approach that requires zero new experimental data generation. Our methodology integrates massive public data mining, artificial intelligence, and multi-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, requiring the collaborative expertise of our transdisciplinary Working Group. Phase 1: Data Aggregation and Harmonization. We will systematically mine, curate, and harmonize multi-omics data from publicly available repositories. Genomic and metagenomic data will be sourced from NCBI, the Tara Oceans project, and the Malaspina Expedition, focusing on paired samples of deep-sea piezophiles and their shallow-water phylogenetic relatives. Proteomic and lipidomic datasets will be retrieved from PRIDE and MetaboLights. We will construct a unified, relational database that maps species-specific environmental metadata (depth, pressure, temperature) to their corresponding molecular profiles. Phase 2: AI-Driven Manifold Learning and Feature Extraction. To handle the high-dimensionality of the synthesized omics data, we will utilize advanced AI techniques, specifically manifold learning and topological data analysis. Using algorithms such as Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) and variational autoencoders, we will project the multi-omics data into a lower-dimensional manifold. This AI-driven approach will identify non-linear, convergent patterns—the 'Piezophilic Emergence Rules'—that distinguish high-pressure adapted mesoscale systems from surface-dwelling ones. The AI models will pinpoint specific lipid combinations and protein-protein interaction motifs that consistently co-occur in deep-sea environments, flagging them as candidates for structural simulation. Phase 3: Multi-Scale Molecular Dynamics Simulations. To bridge the gap from molecular sequence to mesoscale emergence, we will model the AI-identified candidates using multi-scale MD simulations. We will utilize AlphaFold-Multimer to predict the structures of target piezophilic protein complexes. Subsequently, we will construct highly realistic, large-scale mesoscale membrane patches incorporating the identified piezophilic lipid ratios and transmembrane protein complexes. Using GROMACS, we will perform coarse-grained (Martini force field) and all-atom MD simulations under varying simulated hydrostatic pressures ranging from 1 to 1,000 atmospheres. These simulations will allow us to calculate changes in system volume, hydration shell dynamics, and membrane phase transitions, directly testing our hypotheses regarding pressure-induced stabilization. Phase 4: Synthesis and Emergence Modeling. The final phase involves integrating the structural dynamics data back into our AI models to create a predictive framework for mesoscale emergence. By correlating the thermodynamic stability calculated from MD simulations with the evolutionary trajectories identified via manifold learning, we will build a comprehensive model of deep-sea mesoscale architecture. This methodology is heavily reliant on the collaborative infrastructure provided by NCEMS. The integration of global omics databases with high-performance biophysical simulations and machine learning pipelines is a massive undertaking that far exceeds the computational and intellectual capacity of a single laboratory, demanding the synergistic efforts of our assembled team of data scientists, biophysicists, and marine biologists.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The proposed synthesis will yield transformative outcomes that advance fundamental molecular and cellular biology while driving methodological innovations. Scientifically, the primary outcome will be the establishment of the 'Piezophilic Emergence Rules,' providing the first comprehensive, multi-scale model of how biological systems achieve mechanical stability under extreme hydrostatic pressure. By elucidating how mesoscale structures—such as lipid-protein domains and macromolecular scaffolds—utilize pressure as a stabilizing thermodynamic force, we will solve a long-standing mystery regarding the physical limits of life. This will fundamentally shift the paradigm of deep-sea biology from descriptive observation to predictive, mechanistic understanding. Methodologically, we will deliver a novel, AI-driven computational pipeline that seamlessly integrates multi-omics harmonization with multi-scale molecular dynamics simulations. This highly adaptable framework will be applicable to studying emergent phenomena in other extreme environments, thereby advancing the broader field of systems biology. Technologically, the identification of pressure-stabilized protein scaffolds and unique lipid architectures will provide a blueprint for bioengineering hyper-stable enzymes and novel biomaterials for industrial applications, such as high-pressure bioreactors and deep-sea biotechnology. Crucially, in alignment with the NCEMS mission, this project will have a profound impact on workforce development. The Working Group will train a cohort of postdoctoral researchers and graduate students in cutting-edge data science, artificial intelligence, and structural biophysics. These trainees will gain invaluable experience in transdisciplinary collaboration and open science practices, emerging as highly skilled, data-savvy leaders capable of tackling complex, community-scale synthesis projects in the future.
open_science_and_reproducibility: Our Working Group is fundamentally committed to the highest standards of Open Science, ensuring that all findings, data, and analytical workflows are transparent, reproducible, and immediately accessible to the global scientific community. In strict adherence to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles, we will not only open-source our final products but also our intermediate developmental processes. All curated and harmonized datasets—linking oceanographic metadata with multi-omics profiles—will be deposited in Zenodo with comprehensive, machine-readable metadata. To guarantee computational reproducibility, all custom scripts, AI manifold learning models, and molecular dynamics simulation parameters will be version-controlled and hosted on a public GitHub repository. Furthermore, the entire computational pipeline will be containerized using Docker and Singularity, allowing any researcher to download and execute our exact workflows on their local machines or high-performance computing clusters without encountering software dependency issues. We will actively promote open collaboration by documenting our daily progress and methodological decisions in publicly accessible Jupyter Notebooks. To ensure rapid dissemination of our discoveries, all manuscripts generated from this synthesis project will be submitted to open-access preprint servers, such as bioRxiv, concurrently with their submission to peer-reviewed, open-access journals. We will also host bi-annual, open-registration virtual webinars to share our progress, solicit feedback from the broader scientific community, and demonstrate the utility of our AI and MD pipelines. By embedding these open science principles into the core of our project, we will maximize the impact of the NCEMS funding, enabling other researchers to leverage our tools and datasets to explore new dimensions of molecular and cellular emergence.
budget_and_resources: The requested budget is exclusively dedicated to supporting community-scale data synthesis, computational infrastructure, and cross-disciplinary collaboration, strictly adhering to the NCEMS mandate of generating zero new experimental data. The primary budget allocation will support human capital, specifically the salaries and fringe benefits for two postdoctoral researchers and three graduate students. These trainees will act as the operational bridge between the marine biology, artificial intelligence, and biophysics domains, receiving unparalleled cross-training in data-savvy synthesis research. A significant portion of the budget is allocated for computational resources necessary to process massive multi-omics datasets and perform computationally expensive multi-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. We request funds for high-performance cloud computing credits (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud) to facilitate the machine learning pipelines and secure time on advanced supercomputing clusters for the extensive MD simulations. To foster the transdisciplinary synergy required for this project, funds are requested for collaborative travel and meetings. This includes support for bi-annual, intensive Working Group meetings held at the NCEMS headquarters, designed to bring together our diverse team of principal investigators and trainees for strategic planning, data integration hackathons, and collaborative writing sessions. Additional travel funds will allow trainees to present their findings at major international computational biology and marine science conferences, promoting community engagement and networking. Funds are also allocated for open-access publication fees to ensure our findings are freely available. No funds are requested for laboratory supplies, reagents, or experimental equipment, ensuring that 100% of the NCEMS investment is directed toward unlocking novel emergent insights from existing, publicly available data and training the next generation of computational biologists.

author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: The Protein-to-Phase Transition Map: Synthesis of Pathological Mesoscale Shifts
abstract: Many diseases, particularly neurodegenerative and certain cancers, are increasingly seen as 'mesoscale disorders' involving the transition of liquid-like condensates into solid-like aggregates. This project will synthesize the ClinVar database (human genetic variants) with phase-separation databases and disease-specific proteomic profiles. Using Graph Neural Networks, we will build a predictive 'Phase Transition Map' to identify which genetic mutations are most likely to disrupt mesoscale organization. We hypothesize that disease states are characterized by a 'viscosity tipping point' in the cytoplasm. This synthesis integrates clinical data with fundamental cell biology to provide a novel diagnostic toolkit for identifying early-stage mesoscale pathologies. The project requires the collaboration of clinical geneticists and computational biologists. Trainees will lead the development of an open-access diagnostic pipeline, promoting the principles of team science and reproducible research in the context of human health.
background_and_significance:
The molecular and cellular biosciences are currently undergoing a paradigm shift, recognizing that many critical cellular functions are governed not merely by individual macromolecules, but by their collective, emergent behaviors at the mesoscale. One of the most profoundly important mesoscale phenomena discovered in recent decades is biomolecular condensation driven by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). These membraneless organelles—ranging from nucleoli to stress granules—represent a highly dynamic, liquid-like state of cellular organization that bridges the gap between nanoscale protein interactions and microscale cellular architecture. 

However, this delicate mesoscale organization is highly vulnerable to perturbation. An emerging body of evidence suggests that many devastating human pathologies, particularly neurodegenerative diseases (such as ALS and Alzheimer's) and various cancers, are fundamentally 'mesoscale disorders.' In these conditions, genetic mutations or altered cellular environments cause functional, liquid-like condensates to undergo an aberrant phase transition into solid-like, pathological aggregates. Despite the rapid accumulation of data characterizing individual phase-separating proteins, a critical knowledge gap remains: we lack a predictive, systems-level understanding of how specific genetic mutations alter the biophysical properties of these condensates to trigger this pathological solidification. 

Currently, the data required to solve this puzzle exists, but it is deeply fragmented across disparate domains. Clinical geneticists curate massive databases of human genetic variants (e.g., ClinVar), while biophysicists and cell biologists compile repositories of phase-separating proteins (e.g., PhaSepDB, LLPSDB) and systems biologists generate exhaustive disease-specific proteomic profiles (e.g., PRIDE). Individual laboratories lack the computational infrastructure and cross-disciplinary expertise required to integrate these massive, heterogeneous datasets. 

This proposal directly aligns with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) by leveraging AI and data science to synthesize these publicly available datasets. We propose to build the 'Protein-to-Phase Transition Map,' a comprehensive, predictive model of pathological mesoscale shifts. By unifying clinical genomics, proteomics, and biophysics, this project will address a fundamental question regarding emergence: how do microscale alterations in primary amino acid sequences cascade into mesoscale disruptions of cellular physical states? 

Our synthesis approach will not generate new experimental data; instead, it will extract unprecedented value from existing repositories. By defining the 'viscosity tipping point'—the threshold at which a healthy liquid condensate becomes a diseased solid aggregate—we will solve a long-standing mystery regarding the etiology of proteinopathies. Furthermore, this project will stimulate cross-disciplinary collaboration by uniting clinical geneticists, computational biologists, and biophysicists, providing a rich, collaborative environment to train the next generation of data-savvy scientists in the principles of reproducible, community-scale synthesis research.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This synthesis project is driven by the overarching hypothesis that diverse genetic mutations associated with neurodegenerative diseases and cancers converge on a common biophysical mechanism: they push intracellular biomolecular condensates past a critical 'viscosity tipping point,' triggering an irreversible, pathological liquid-to-solid phase transition at the mesoscale. To interrogate this emergence phenomenon, our Working Group will address three compelling, interconnected research questions:

Research Question 1: How do specific classes of human genetic variants map to systemic alterations in the biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that pathogenic missense mutations and frameshifts are non-randomly distributed and disproportionately enriched within the intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of phase-separating proteins. Furthermore, we posit that these variants systematically alter the valency and interaction strength of the condensate network, shifting the thermodynamic phase boundaries and predisposing the system to pathological solidification. By synthesizing ClinVar data with PhaSepDB and LLPSDB, we will quantify the biophysical impact of thousands of variants simultaneously, moving beyond single-gene studies to uncover universal rules of mutation-driven phase transitions.

Research Question 2: Can artificial intelligence, specifically Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), accurately predict the emergent mesoscale state (liquid vs. solid) of a protein interaction network based solely on primary sequence variants and proteomic abundance? 
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that biomolecular condensates function as complex topological networks where proteins are nodes and multivalent interactions are edges. Because GNNs excel at capturing non-euclidean, relational data, we hypothesize that a GNN trained on synthesized genomic, proteomic, and biophysical data will accurately model the complex topological changes in these networks. The GNN will predict the 'viscosity tipping point'—the threshold of network rigidity corresponding to aggregation—with significantly higher accuracy than traditional linear sequence-based prediction algorithms.

Research Question 3: Are mesoscale phase-transition thresholds universal across different cell types, or are they highly dependent on the local, disease-specific proteomic context? 
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the 'viscosity tipping point' is highly context-dependent, driven by the emergent properties of the cell-type-specific proteome. A mutation that causes pathological aggregation in a motor neuron (e.g., in ALS) might remain benign in a fibroblast due to differences in the concentration of interacting client proteins and RNA. By integrating disease-specific proteomic profiles from the PRIDE database into our GNN models, we will test whether cellular context acts as a biophysical buffer or an accelerator for mesoscale phase transitions.

By answering these questions, we will transition the field from a descriptive understanding of phase separation to a predictive science of mesoscale emergence. This will allow researchers to input a patient's genetic profile and predict the likelihood of mesoscale organizational collapse, answering fundamental questions about the physical basis of disease while providing a novel framework for diagnostic development.
methods_and_approach:
To construct the Protein-to-Phase Transition Map and identify the 'viscosity tipping point,' our multidisciplinary Working Group will employ a purely computational, data-synthesis approach. We will generate no new experimental data, instead relying on the rigorous integration of existing, publicly available databases using advanced AI methodologies.

Data Acquisition and Integration:
Our first step is to harmonize highly heterogeneous datasets across three biological scales. 
1. Genomic/Clinical Scale: We will extract pathogenic, likely pathogenic, and variants of unknown significance (VUS) from the ClinVar database. 
2. Biophysical/Mesoscale: We will pull curated lists of phase-separating proteins, their intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), and known liquid-to-solid transition behaviors from PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, and CD-CODE. 
3. Proteomic/Cellular Scale: We will utilize the PRIDE database and ProteomicsDB to extract quantitative protein abundance data specific to healthy and diseased tissues (e.g., cortical neurons in Alzheimer's, motor neurons in ALS, and tumor microenvironments).

Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering:
Trainees, co-mentored by computational biologists and clinical geneticists, will build an automated pipeline to map ClinVar genomic coordinates to protein sequences. We will engineer biophysical features for each variant, calculating changes in charge distribution, hydrophobicity, pi-pi interaction potential, and disorder propensity using established algorithms (e.g., IUPred, PONDR). 

AI Architecture: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs):
To model mesoscale emergence, we will develop a novel GNN architecture. Traditional machine learning struggles with the fluid, multivalent nature of biomolecular condensates. By representing condensates as graphs—where nodes represent specific protein domains and edges represent transient, multivalent interactions (informed by StringDB and biophysical features)—we can capture the emergent topology of the system. 

Node features will include the engineered biophysical properties of the wild-type or mutated sequences. Edge weights will be modulated by the local protein concentrations derived from our proteomic data synthesis. We will train the GNN using a contrastive learning approach, feeding the model graphs of known healthy (liquid-like) and diseased (solid-like) condensates. The GNN will learn to output a 'Network Rigidity Score,' our computational proxy for the viscosity tipping point. 

Collaborative Workflow and Validation:
The project relies heavily on transdisciplinary collaboration. Computational biologists will lead the GNN architecture development. Clinical geneticists will ensure the biological and clinical validity of the ClinVar data parsing and interpret the disease relevance of the model's predictions. Biophysicists will validate the biophysical logic of the GNN's learned parameters, ensuring the AI does not violate known laws of thermodynamics. 

To validate the model, we will use a hold-out set of recently published, experimentally validated aggregation-prone mutations that were not included in the training databases. We will assess the model's ability to accurately classify variants that drive liquid-to-solid transitions versus those that do not, refining the algorithm iteratively based on Working Group feedback.

Scientifically, this project will catalyze a paradigm shift, moving the study of neurodegeneration and cancer beyond pure biochemical signaling and into the realm of mesoscale biophysics. It will reveal universal, emergent rules governing how microscale sequence changes propagate into macroscale cellular dysfunction. 

Crucially, the impact of this proposal extends beyond its scientific discoveries to the development of the future scientific workforce. This project is explicitly designed to tap diverse new talent and train the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will be cross-trained in AI, biophysics, and clinical genetics. They will not be siloed; instead, they will lead the data integration pipelines, gaining invaluable experience in team science, cloud computing, and advanced machine learning techniques. 

By the project's conclusion, we will deliver an open-access, web-based diagnostic pipeline where researchers and clinicians worldwide can input genetic profiles to predict mesoscale disruption. author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: The Geometry of the Metabolome: Mapping Small-Molecule Microenvironments
abstract: Metabolism is often studied as a bulk 'well-mixed' process, yet enzymes are spatially organized into mesoscale metabolons. This project will synthesize MALDI-imaging (spatial metabolomics), Cryo-ET (structural topology), and metabolic flux data to create the first 3D 'Metabolic Landscape' of the cell. We will test the hypothesis that the local geometry of organelle membranes and protein scaffolds creates 'chemical micro-pockets' where metabolic reactions are accelerated beyond bulk rates. By applying Computer Vision to spatial metabolomic data, we will map the concentration gradients of key metabolites relative to mesoscale structures. This project solves the long-standing puzzle of metabolic efficiency in the crowded cytoplasm. It requires a synthesis center approach to integrate imaging and -omics data from diverse laboratories. Trainees will gain experience in spatial statistics and high-resolution imaging analysis, preparing them for the future of 'spatial biology.'
background_and_significance: For decades, the fundamental understanding of cellular metabolism has been heavily influenced by a 'well-mixed bag' paradigm, wherein enzymes and metabolites are assumed to diffuse freely and interact stochastically within the cytoplasm. However, this classical view fundamentally fails to explain a long-standing puzzle in the molecular and cellular biosciences: how cells achieve astonishingly high metabolic flux rates and thermodynamic efficiencies in an incredibly crowded intracellular environment where bulk diffusion is severely restricted. Emerging evidence suggests that the answer lies at the mesoscale—the critical spatial domain between individual biomolecules and whole organelles. At this scale, enzymes dynamically assemble into transient, highly organized multi-protein complexes known as metabolons, which are often tethered to specific architectural features of the cell, such as the highly curved regions of the endoplasmic reticulum or mitochondrial cristae. While the existence of metabolons is increasingly recognized, the emergent properties arising from their spatial organization remain poorly understood. Specifically, the field lacks a comprehensive understanding of how the physical geometry of mesoscale cellular structures influences the local concentration and channeling of small-molecule metabolites. Historically, studying this phenomenon has been impossible due to technical limitations. However, recent explosions in publicly available datasets across two distinct domains—Cryo-Electron Tomography (Cryo-ET) for high-resolution 3D mesoscale structural topology, and Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization (MALDI) imaging for spatial metabolomics—present an unprecedented opportunity. Individually, these datasets offer isolated glimpses into either structural architecture or chemical localization. Together, they hold the key to uncovering the emergent properties of spatial metabolism. This project proposes a community-scale synthesis of these disparate, publicly available datasets to construct the first comprehensive 3D 'Metabolic Landscape' of the cell. By integrating structural topologies with spatial metabolite distributions and kinetic flux data, we aim to reveal how the mesoscale geometry of the cell actively shapes its chemical environment. This endeavor perfectly aligns with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). It relies entirely on the integration and synthesis of existing, publicly available data, generating no new experimental data. Furthermore, the sheer computational complexity and the necessity of merging structural biology, analytical chemistry, and computational modeling make this project fundamentally impossible for any single laboratory to execute. It requires the transdisciplinary, collaborative Working Group model that NCEMS provides, bringing together structural biologists, metabolomics experts, data scientists, and biophysicists. Ultimately, by elucidating how mesoscale spatial organization gives rise to emergent metabolic efficiency, this synthesis project will fundamentally rewrite our understanding of cellular bioenergetics and biochemistry, shifting the paradigm from a bulk-phase to a deeply spatial framework.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This synthesis project is driven by three primary research questions that aim to unravel the emergent properties of mesoscale metabolic organization. 

Question 1: How do specific mesoscale structural topologies, such as organelle membrane curvatures and macromolecular scaffolds, correlate with local metabolite concentration gradients? We hypothesize that the local geometry of the cell does not merely serve as a passive structural backdrop, but rather acts as an active physical trap that creates distinct 'chemical micro-pockets.' Specifically, we predict that highly curved membrane regions (e.g., mitochondrial cristae junctions, ER tubules) and dense cytoskeletal intersections restrict local diffusion, resulting in metabolite concentrations that are orders of magnitude higher than bulk cytoplasmic averages. By synthesizing spatial metabolomics data with structural topologies, we aim to map these micro-pockets and quantify the concentration differentials across varying geometric landscapes.

Question 2: Does the spatial colocalization of enzymes into mesoscale metabolons mathematically account for observed accelerations in metabolic flux? The long-standing mystery of metabolic efficiency suggests that substrate channeling within metabolons bypasses bulk diffusion limitations. We hypothesize that the emergence of enhanced metabolic flux is a direct, mathematically definable function of the 3D geometric arrangement of these metabolons. We predict that by integrating existing metabolic flux data (e.g., stable isotope tracing datasets) with our synthesized 3D spatial models, we can demonstrate that reduced inter-enzyme distances within specific geometric microenvironments are both necessary and sufficient to explain the reaction rates observed in vivo. This will be tested by applying reaction-diffusion simulations to our synthesized structural-metabolic maps.

Question 3: Can we predict the spatial distribution of the metabolome based purely on the mesoscale structural architecture of the cell? We hypothesize that the relationship between structural topology and chemical localization is highly deterministic and governed by underlying biophysical principles of emergence. Therefore, we predict that machine learning models, specifically advanced Computer Vision algorithms and 3D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), trained on our synthesized datasets will be able to accurately predict local metabolite hotspots and concentration gradients using only Cryo-ET structural data as an input. 

Addressing these questions requires a profound synthesis of diverse data types. No single dataset can answer whether a specific membrane curvature causes a specific metabolic flux; only by layering spatial metabolomics over structural maps and calibrating them with kinetic flux data can we observe this emergence. This approach will not only answer fundamental questions about metabolic efficiency but will also establish a predictive framework for understanding how structural alterations in disease states (e.g., mitochondrial deformation in neurodegeneration) inherently disrupt cellular metabolism at the mesoscale.
methods_and_approach:
To achieve our objectives, we will employ a highly collaborative, AI-driven data synthesis approach, strictly utilizing publicly available datasets without generating new experimental data. The project will be executed in four primary phases by a multidisciplinary NCEMS Working Group.

Phase 1: Data Mining and Curation. We will systematically mine massive public data repositories. For mesoscale structural data, we will utilize the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR), extracting high-resolution Cryo-ET tomograms of eukaryotic cells. For spatial metabolomics, we will query MetaboLights and GNPS (Global Natural Products Social Molecular Networking) to retrieve MALDI-imaging datasets and corresponding mass spectrometry data. Finally, metabolic flux data will be sourced from the BioModels database and published literature. A dedicated team of data scientists and domain experts will establish strict inclusion criteria ensuring metadata quality, resolution compatibility, and biological relevance across datasets.

Phase 2: AI-Driven Feature Extraction and Alignment. The core challenge of this synthesis is integrating modalities with vastly different spatial resolutions and coordinate systems. We will develop a novel Computer Vision pipeline utilizing 3D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). First, we will use segmentation algorithms (e.g., deep learning models adapted from EMAN2) to automatically identify and extract mesoscale geometric features—such as membrane curvatures, organelle contact sites, and macromolecular crowding zones—from the Cryo-ET tomograms. Concurrently, we will process the MALDI-imaging data to generate spatial point-clouds of specific metabolites. We will then employ advanced manifold learning and affine transformation algorithms to map the lower-resolution metabolic point-clouds onto the high-resolution structural topologies, creating unified, multi-modal 3D coordinate spaces.

Phase 3: Spatial Statistics and Reaction-Diffusion Modeling. With the synthesized 3D maps, we will apply rigorous spatial statistics, including 3D Ripley's K-function and point pattern analysis, to quantitatively determine if metabolite clustering significantly correlates with specific mesoscale geometries (testing Hypothesis 1). To test Hypothesis 2, we will integrate kinetic parameters from the flux datasets into these spatial maps. We will utilize Smoldyn, a spatial stochastic simulator, to run reaction-diffusion models within the exact geometric constraints extracted from the Cryo-ET data. By comparing simulated flux rates in our 'micro-pocket' geometries versus simulated 'well-mixed' geometries, we will quantify the emergent efficiency gained by mesoscale organization.

Phase 4: Predictive Modeling and Workforce Training. To test Hypothesis 3, we will partition our synthesized data to train a predictive geometric deep learning model, evaluating its ability to infer metabolic hotspots purely from structural inputs. Throughout all phases, training the next generation of data-savvy scientists is paramount. Graduate students and postdocs will not merely assist; they will be the primary drivers of the computational pipelines. We will host bi-annual 'Spatial Biology Bootcamps' within the Working Group, cross-training structural biologists in spatial statistics and computational scientists in metabolic biochemistry, thereby forging a new transdisciplinary workforce equipped to tackle complex mesoscale emergence.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that fundamentally advance the molecular and cellular biosciences. The primary deliverable will be the creation of the first high-resolution, multi-modal '3D Metabolic Landscape Atlas.' This open-source, interactive atlas will map the spatial distribution of key metabolites against the mesoscale structural architecture of the cell, providing the scientific community with an unprecedented tool to explore spatial metabolism. 

Scientifically, this project will solve the long-standing puzzle of cellular metabolic efficiency. By proving that mesoscale structural geometries create chemical micro-pockets that bypass bulk diffusion limits, we will shift the dominant paradigm of metabolism from a 'well-mixed bag' to a highly deterministic, spatially organized system. This understanding of mesoscale emergence will have broad implications, offering new frameworks for understanding how structural abnormalities in organelles lead to metabolic dysfunction in diseases such as cancer and neurodegeneration.

Methodologically, we will develop and release a novel suite of AI-driven, open-source computational tools specifically designed for the integration of structural biology (Cryo-ET) and analytical chemistry (MALDI-imaging) datasets. These algorithms will overcome current bottlenecks in multi-modal data synthesis, providing a blueprint for future transdisciplinary research. 

Finally, the impact on workforce development will be profound. By embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in a deeply collaborative, cross-disciplinary Working Group at NCEMS, we will train a new generation of 'spatial biologists.' These trainees will graduate with a unique, highly sought-after skillset encompassing advanced computer vision, spatial statistics, and multi-omics integration, perfectly positioning them to lead the future of data-driven, transdisciplinary biological research.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the highest standards of open science, reproducibility, and the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles, aligning perfectly with NCEMS mandates. Because our project relies entirely on synthesizing existing public data, ensuring that our resulting synthesized datasets and analytical pipelines are transparent and accessible is our top priority.

All code, algorithms, and machine learning models developed during this project—including the novel Computer Vision pipelines for multi-modal data alignment and spatial statistics scripts—will be developed openly on a dedicated, public GitHub repository from day one. We will utilize comprehensive version control, issue tracking, and detailed documentation. To ensure absolute computational reproducibility across different operating systems and hardware, all analytical workflows will be containerized using Docker and Singularity. 

The final synthesized '3D Metabolic Landscape Atlas,' along with all intermediate processed datasets and metadata, will be deposited in Zenodo and the Open Science Framework (OSF), assigned unique Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs) to guarantee long-term findability and citation. We will adhere strictly to community-developed metadata standards for both spatial metabolomics and structural biology to ensure interoperability. 

Furthermore, we commit to publishing all findings in open-access peer-reviewed journals. Prior to formal peer review, all manuscripts will be submitted to preprint servers such as bioRxiv to accelerate the dissemination of our insights to the broader scientific community. By providing fully containerized code, raw data pointers, and detailed protocols, any researcher in the world will be able to download our pipeline, reproduce our exact findings, and apply our tools to their own localized datasets.

To successfully execute this ambitious community-scale synthesis project, we request funding from NCEMS to support Working Group convenings, personnel, and essential computational infrastructure. Crucially, in strict adherence to the NCEMS funding guidelines, zero funds are requested for wet-lab equipment, reagents, or new experimental data generation.

Personnel Support: The core 'synthesis engine' of this project will be driven by trainees. We request full stipend and benefits support for two Postdoctoral Fellows and three Graduate Students for the duration of the project. These trainees will be intentionally recruited from diverse disciplines (one from structural biology, one from spatial metabolomics, one from computer science) to foster cross-pollination of skills.

These intensive, week-long collaborative sprints are vital for overcoming the communication barriers inherent in transdisciplinary research, developing the theoretical frameworks, and mentoring the trainees. This budget directly empowers the transdisciplinary synthesis and workforce training central to the NCEMS mission.

author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: Coordination of Mitochondrial and ER Shapes: The Mechanical 'Gear Ratio' of Organelle Interfaces
abstract: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria form extensive contact sites (MAMs) that are essential for lipid exchange and calcium signaling. However, how these two distinct organelle networks coordinate their large-scale morphologies remains unknown. This project will synthesize 3D Electron Microscopy (EM) volumes and live-cell dual-channel imaging data across multiple cell types and stress conditions. We aim to define the 'Mechanical Coupling Rules'—the physical constraints that ensure the ER 'follows' mitochondrial remodeling. Using Topology Data Analysis (TDA), we will quantify the 'gear ratio' between ER tubule density and mitochondrial branching. This synthesis addresses the emergent mechanical coordination between organelles, a problem too large for a single lab's imaging capacity. The project will bridge structural biology and mechanics, training students in the quantitative analysis of organelle dynamics and network topology.
background_and_significance:
The spatial organization of the eukaryotic cell is governed by highly dynamic, interconnected organelle networks. Among these, the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria represent two of the most expansive and morphologically complex systems. They form extensive physical contact sites known as mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs), which are critical hubs for non-vesicular lipid transport, calcium ion signaling, and the regulation of apoptosis. While decades of reductionist molecular biology have successfully identified the biochemical tethers and protein complexes residing at these interfaces, a fundamental mesoscale mystery remains: how do these two distinct, massive organelle networks coordinate their large-scale, three-dimensional morphologies in real-time? 

Emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences often manifests at the mesoscale—the critical bridge between individual biomolecules and whole-cell phenotypic outcomes. The physical coordination of ER and mitochondrial networks is a prime example of mesoscale emergence. When mitochondria undergo fission, fusion, or stress-induced hyper-branching, the ER must dynamically reconfigure its tubular density and sheet-like matrices to maintain optimal MAM coverage. This implies the existence of overarching 'Mechanical Coupling Rules' or a mechanical 'gear ratio' that dictates how the topological state of one network drives the structural remodeling of the other. 

Currently, our understanding of this mechanical coupling is severely limited by the siloed nature of cellular imaging research. Individual laboratories generate massive, high-resolution datasets—ranging from isotropic 3D Focused Ion Beam Scanning Electron Microscopy (FIB-SEM) volumes to high-speed, dual-channel live-cell lattice light-sheet microscopy. However, these datasets are typically analyzed in isolation to answer narrow, lab-specific questions. The sheer volume and complexity of these datasets make it impossible for a single research group to extract universal topological rules governing organelle coordination across diverse cell types and physiological states. 

This proposal directly aligns with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) by leveraging a community-scale synthesis of publicly available data. By integrating disparate 3D EM and live-cell imaging datasets from repositories such as EMPIAR, the Allen Cell Explorer, and the Image Data Resource (IDR), we will move beyond the limitations of single-lab experimental generation. We will apply advanced mathematical frameworks, specifically Topology Data Analysis (TDA), to quantify the spatial and mechanical relationships between the ER and mitochondria. This transdisciplinary approach will solve a long-standing puzzle in cell biology: whether organelle morphological coordination is stochastically driven or deterministically governed by emergent physical constraints. Furthermore, this project will catalyze cross-disciplinary collaboration between cell biologists, computational topologists, biophysicists, and AI specialists, ultimately revealing how mesoscale architectural rules influence higher-order cellular health and disease.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our synthesis project is driven by the overarching objective of uncovering the emergent mechanical and topological rules that govern the spatial coordination of the ER and mitochondrial networks. To achieve this, our Working Group will address three compelling, interrelated research questions, each paired with a specific, testable hypothesis derived from the synthesis of publicly available multiscale imaging data.

Question 1: What are the fundamental topological scaling laws that govern ER-mitochondria morphological coordination across different mammalian cell types and states of differentiation? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize the existence of a conserved mechanical 'gear ratio'—a predictable, mathematical relationship between mitochondrial network branching (node degree and branch length) and ER tubule density (polygonal mesh size and curvature). We propose that this gear ratio is an emergent mesoscale property that remains conserved across diverse healthy cell types, ensuring that the cumulative surface area of MAMs remains within a tightly regulated optimal range, regardless of the overall cell volume or specific metabolic niche.

Question 2: How do acute and chronic cellular stress conditions (e.g., metabolic starvation, oxidative stress, and pharmacological perturbation) alter these mechanical coupling rules and the associated organelle gear ratio? 
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that cellular stress induces a topological phase transition in organelle coupling. Under metabolic or oxidative stress, the ER-mitochondria gear ratio will shift dramatically to prioritize either hyper-fusion (to maximize bioenergetic efficiency) or fragmentation (to facilitate mitophagy). We posit that these stress-induced topological shifts are mediated by physical tether constraints, and that analyzing existing datasets of stressed cells will reveal distinct, quantifiable 'stress-state' topological signatures that are currently invisible to standard volumetric colocalization analyses.

Question 3: Can the three-dimensional topological state of one organelle network be mathematically predicted given the spatial architecture of the other? 
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the mechanical coupling between the ER and mitochondria is highly deterministic at the mesoscale. Therefore, machine learning models, when trained on robust topological features (such as Betti numbers and persistent homology metrics extracted via TDA), will be able to accurately predict the spatial distribution and network state of the ER based solely on mitochondrial morphology, and vice versa. 

By answering these questions, we will transition the field's understanding of organelle contacts from a static, biochemical perspective to a dynamic, mechanical, and topological framework. This will not only solve the long-standing mystery of how massive intracellular networks coordinate their shapes without central direction, but it will also pioneer the use of TDA as a standard analytical strategy for mesoscale cellular biology. The synthesis of static high-resolution 3D EM data with dynamic live-cell fluorescence data will allow us to correlate structural ground truth with temporal remodeling dynamics, providing a comprehensive view of emergent organelle mechanics.
methods_and_approach:
To define the mechanical 'gear ratio' of organelle interfaces, our Working Group will employ a transdisciplinary data synthesis approach, integrating advanced artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and Topology Data Analysis (TDA). Crucially, no new experimental data will be generated; all analyses will rely exclusively on the integration of existing, publicly available datasets.

Data Identification and Curation: We will source high-resolution 3D FIB-SEM datasets from the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR) and the OpenOrganelle portal (Janelia Research Campus), which provide isotropic nanometer-scale resolution of whole cells. For dynamic temporal data, we will utilize dual-channel live-cell imaging datasets (e.g., lattice light-sheet microscopy) from the Allen Cell Explorer, the Image Data Resource (IDR), and published supplementary datasets. Our curation will select diverse mammalian cell types (e.g., HeLa, U2OS, neurons, hepatocytes) under both basal and well-documented stress conditions.

AI-Driven Semantic Segmentation and Network Extraction: The sheer volume of 3D data requires automated, high-throughput processing. We will leverage state-of-the-art deep learning architectures, such as 3D nnU-Net and Cellpose, pre-trained on biological structures, to segment the ER and mitochondrial networks. For datasets lacking ground-truth annotations, we will employ transfer learning and weakly supervised learning techniques. Following segmentation, the volumetric data will be skeletonized into mathematical graphs (nodes representing branch points, edges representing tubules/tubes) to extract the foundational network geometry.

Topological Data Analysis (TDA): Standard colocalization metrics are insufficient for capturing emergent mechanical coordination. We will utilize TDA, specifically Persistent Homology, to quantify the multi-scale topological features of both networks. We will calculate Betti numbers to measure connectivity: β0 (connected components/fragmentation), β1 (loops/polygonal meshes in the ER), and β2 (enclosed voids/sheet-like structures). By analyzing the cross-persistence between the ER and mitochondrial filtrations, we will quantitatively define the 'gear ratio'—the mathematical correlation between the β1 of the ER and the branching complexity of the mitochondria.

Spatiotemporal Kinematic Modeling: To integrate static EM ground truth with dynamic live-cell imaging, we will apply optical flow and graph neural networks (GNNs) to the live-cell data. This will allow us to track the temporal derivatives of the topological features, revealing the kinematics of how the ER 'follows' mitochondrial remodeling during fission/fusion events.

Working Group Structure and Collaboration: This project requires expertise beyond a single discipline. Our NCEMS-supported Working Group will consist of cell biologists (experts in MAMs and organelle stress), computational topologists (experts in TDA and persistent homology), data scientists (experts in 3D deep learning), and biophysicists. The group will meet bi-weekly virtually and convene for intensive, week-long synthesis hackathons at the NCEMS facility. This collaborative structure ensures that the biological questions drive the computational innovation, while the mathematical rigor grounds the biological interpretations, perfectly encapsulating the transdisciplinary synthesis model championed by NCEMS.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that advance the molecular and cellular sciences while fulfilling the core mission of NCEMS. Scientifically, the primary outcome will be the establishment of the first quantitative framework defining the mechanical 'gear ratio' between the ER and mitochondria. By proving that organelle morphological coordination is governed by emergent topological scaling laws rather than stochastic proximity, we will resolve a long-standing blind spot in cell biology. The identification of stress-specific topological signatures will provide novel mesoscale biomarkers for cellular dysfunction, with profound implications for understanding neurodegenerative diseases and metabolic syndromes where MAM integrity is compromised.

Methodologically, this project will pioneer the application of Topology Data Analysis (TDA) to 3D subcellular architecture. We will develop and release an innovative, AI-driven analytical pipeline that translates raw 3D EM and live-cell imaging volumes into quantifiable topological metrics. This toolset will be highly adaptable, empowering the broader scientific community to investigate the mechanical coupling of other complex organelle systems (e.g., Golgi-ER, endosome-cytoskeleton).

Beyond scientific discovery, the broader impacts of this project are deeply rooted in workforce development and cross-disciplinary training. The Working Group will serve as a premier training environment for two postdoctoral researchers and two graduate students. These trainees will be uniquely positioned at the intersection of structural cell biology, advanced mathematics, and data science, emerging as leaders in the future data-savvy biological workforce. Furthermore, by intentionally recruiting diverse talent across geographic locations and institutional research levels (including researchers from R2 and primarily undergraduate institutions), we will democratize access to cutting-edge computational research, proving that profound biological discoveries can be made without massive experimental budgets.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is fundamentally committed to the highest standards of Open Science, FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles, and reproducibility, aligning strictly with NCEMS community-created policies. Because our project relies entirely on synthesizing publicly available data, ensuring that our downstream outputs are equally accessible is paramount.

All AI segmentation models, Topological Data Analysis (TDA) algorithms, and statistical scripts developed during this project will be written in open-source languages (Python and R). The complete codebase will be version-controlled and hosted on a public GitHub repository under an MIT License. To guarantee computational reproducibility, all analytical workflows will be containerized using Docker and Singularity. This ensures that any researcher, regardless of their local operating system, can download our containers and perfectly replicate our topological feature extraction and gear-ratio calculations.

Derived datasets—including the 3D skeletonized graphs, extracted Betti numbers, and spatiotemporal kinematic models—will be deposited in universally accessible repositories such as Zenodo and the Open Science Framework (OSF) with clear, comprehensive metadata. We will not wait until final publication to share our progress; we commit to releasing intermediate datasets and preprints via bioRxiv to accelerate community feedback and collaboration.

Finally, to foster the adoption of our TDA methodologies, we will develop interactive Jupyter Notebooks and comprehensive tutorials. We will host an open, virtual workshop at the conclusion of the funding period, aimed at training the broader cell biology community on how to apply our open-source tools to their own imaging data, thereby amplifying the impact of the NCEMS funding and cementing reproducible, team-based science as the gold standard in mesoscale biology.

author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: Giant Viruses as Mesoscale Organelles: Synthesis of Viral Factory Emergence
abstract: Giant viruses (e.g., Mimivirus) create massive 'viral factories' within host cells—structures that are as large and complex as traditional organelles but assembled within hours. This project will synthesize host-pathogen proteomic data and time-course imaging of viral factory assembly. We will treat the viral factory as a temporary cellular organelle to identify the 'Assembly Accelerators' that allow such rapid mesoscale emergence. We hypothesize that viruses exploit existing host phase-separation mechanisms to 'hijack' mesoscale organization. This synthesis will provide insights into the minimum requirements for organelle formation and the logic of host-pathogen competition at the mesoscale. The project requires a transdisciplinary team of virologists, biophysicists, and computational biologists. Trainees will explore the frontiers of viral biology and synthetic cell architecture, contributing to a deeper understanding of cellular self-assembly under extreme conditions.
background_and_significance: The emergence of complex biological structures at the mesoscale—the critical spatial domain bridging individual biomolecules and functional organelles—remains one of the most profound mysteries in cellular biology. A striking, yet underutilized, natural model for studying mesoscale emergence is the formation of 'viral factories' (VFs) by giant viruses, such as Mimivirus and other Nucleocytoplasmic Large DNA Viruses (NCLDVs). Upon infecting a host cell, these giant viruses orchestrate the rapid assembly of massive, highly organized, and compartmentalized structures in the cytoplasm. These VFs rival the size and complexity of traditional eukaryotic organelles but emerge within mere hours. Despite the availability of vast amounts of host-pathogen proteomic, transcriptomic, and time-course imaging data, a comprehensive synthesis detailing the physical and molecular rules governing this rapid mesoscale emergence is lacking. This proposed Working Group directly addresses the core mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) by leveraging publicly available datasets to decode how novel biological system properties appear at the mesoscale. We conceptualize the viral factory not merely as a pathological artifact, but as a temporary, synthetic cellular organelle. By treating VFs as model systems for de novo organelle biogenesis, we can uncover the 'Assembly Accelerators'—the molecular and biophysical rules that permit such rapid, large-scale structural emergence. We hypothesize that giant viruses do not invent entirely new biophysical paradigms from scratch; rather, they hijack and hyper-activate existing host mesoscale organizational mechanisms, particularly liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and cytoskeletal remodeling. However, proving this requires a community-scale synthesis of disparate data types—ranging from cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) and fluorescence microscopy to temporal proteomics and interactomics—which currently sit siloed across various public repositories (e.g., PRIDE, EMPIAR, PDB). The significance of this project is threefold.
