The temporal layers, utilizing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) or Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), will model the dynamic shifts in node features across different conditions of energy stress. Crucially, we will implement Graph Attention Networks (GATs). The attention weights learned by the model will serve as our primary analytical tool: nodes and edges that consistently receive high attention weights under stress conditions, but deviate from baseline FBA predictions, will be classified as 'Emergent Metabolic Hubs.' 

Working Group Collaboration: This project is beyond the scope of a single lab. We will assemble an NCEMS Working Group comprising three distinct collaborative nodes: Lab A (expertise in Deep Learning and GNN architecture), Lab B (expertise in Systems Biology and FBA), and Lab C (expertise in Structural Biology and mesoscale metabolons). The Working Group will convene through bi-weekly virtual synthesis sessions and bi-annual, intensive in-person hackathons at the NCEMS facility. 

Validation: The predictive power of the GNN will be rigorously tested. We will train the model on a subset of the harmonized data and test its ability to predict metabolic flux states on unseen conditions. The model's predictions will be benchmarked against both traditional FBA predictions and the ground-truth empirical flux measurements obtained from the synthesized 13C-MFA datasets.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:

This will fundamentally shift the paradigm of how we understand metabolic robustness, moving the field from reductionist enzyme kinetics to systems-level emergent dynamics. 

Methodologically, we will produce a first-of-its-kind Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Network (ST-GCN) framework specifically engineered for multi-omic metabolic data integration. This AI architecture will overcome the limitations of traditional Flux-Balance Analysis by successfully capturing non-linear, mesoscale interactions. open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is fundamentally committed to the principles of Open Science and the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data standards. To guarantee computational reproducibility, we will utilize Docker containers to package our entire analytical environment, ensuring that any researcher can seamlessly deploy and run our models regardless of their local operating system. 

We will not only share our final code but also the intermediate, harmonized datasets. These will be deposited into Zenodo, providing static DOIs for every version of the dataset used in our analyses. Our GNN models will be accompanied by comprehensive, interactive Jupyter Notebooks that serve as living tutorials. These notebooks will walk users through the process of loading the dynamic graphs, running the attention mechanisms, and visualizing the 'Emergent Metabolic Hubs,' thereby lowering the barrier to entry for biologists wishing to utilize AI tools. 

Furthermore, all findings generated by this NCEMS Working Group will be submitted to open-access, peer-reviewed journals, with preprints deposited on bioRxiv prior to submission. We will actively participate in community-created policies on open and team science, ensuring our collaborative workflows are transparently documented. By making our entire synthesis workflow publicly available, we aim to establish a gold standard for reproducible, AI-driven synthesis research in the molecular and cellular biosciences.

author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: Topological Data Analysis (TDA) of the Cytoskeleton: Quantifying Mesoscale Strength and Resilience
abstract: The cytoskeleton provides the cell with its mechanical integrity, yet we lack a quantitative 'metric of resilience' for these networks. This project will synthesize thousands of actin and microtubule images from diverse cell types (muscle, neurons, fibroblasts) and apply Topological Data Analysis (TDA) to quantify their connectivity, 'holes,' and 'loops.' We aim to find the 'Topological Signature of Strength'—the specific arrangement of filaments that maximizes mechanical stability while minimizing protein cost. We hypothesize that cells optimize their cytoskeletal topology to reach a 'percolation threshold' that defines their mechanical identity. This community-scale synthesis will integrate math, physics, and cell biology. Trainees will gain expertise in TDA, a cutting-edge mathematical tool, and its application to biological architecture. The output will be a 'Cytoskeletal Resilience Index' for diagnosing structural failures in aging and disease.
background_and_significance:
The cytoskeleton is a paradigmatic example of an emergent mesoscale system, where the collective interactions of nanometer-scale protein polymers (actin filaments, microtubules, and intermediate filaments) give rise to the micrometer-scale mechanical properties of the cell. This dynamic network provides the structural integrity necessary for fundamental cellular processes, including migration, division, and mechanotransduction. Despite decades of research detailing the biochemical properties of individual cytoskeletal components, a critical gap remains in our understanding of how their mesoscale spatial organization translates into macroscopic resilience and strength. Traditionally, cytoskeletal architecture has been analyzed using reductionist metrics such as filament density, length distributions, or crude branching angles. However, these localized measurements fail to capture the global topological features that dictate the network's capacity to withstand mechanical stress, adapt to environmental cues, and resist structural failure. Consequently, the field currently lacks a unified, quantitative 'metric of resilience' capable of comparing cytoskeletal architectures across diverse cell types and physiological states.

This proposal addresses this profound gap by leveraging Topological Data Analysis (TDA), a sophisticated branch of applied mathematics that studies the shape and connectivity of data. TDA is uniquely suited to quantify complex, multi-scale networks by identifying persistent topological features—such as connected components, 'holes' (loops), and voids—that are invariant under continuous deformations. By applying TDA to the cytoskeleton, we can move beyond simple density metrics to extract a 'Topological Signature of Strength.' This signature represents the specific, emergent arrangement of filaments that maximizes mechanical stability while minimizing the metabolic cost of protein synthesis and maintenance.

The significance of this project lies in its potential to solve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology: how cells optimize their architecture to achieve mechanical identity. By synthesizing thousands of publicly available high-resolution imaging datasets (e.g., super-resolution microscopy, cryo-electron tomography) across highly specialized cell types—such as force-generating muscle cells, structurally complex neurons, and mechanically adaptive fibroblasts—we will uncover the universal topological rules governing cytoskeletal emergence. This transdisciplinary approach directly aligns with the NCEMS mission to catalyze synthesis research, uniting cell biologists, physicists, and mathematicians to interrogate publicly available data.

Furthermore, understanding these mesoscale topological principles has profound implications for human health. Structural failures in the cytoskeleton are hallmarks of numerous age-related pathologies and diseases, including muscular dystrophies, neurodegeneration, and cancer metastasis. By establishing a quantitative baseline for healthy cytoskeletal topology, this research will provide a transformative framework for diagnosing and ultimately correcting structural aberrations in disease states, thereby advancing both fundamental biology and translational medicine.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This community-scale synthesis project is driven by the overarching objective to mathematically define and quantify the emergent mechanical properties of the cytoskeleton at the mesoscale. To achieve this, we have formulated three primary research questions and corresponding hypotheses that will guide our transdisciplinary investigation.

Question 1: What are the defining topological features that differentiate the cytoskeletal networks of mechanically distinct cell types? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that specialized cells possess distinct 'Topological Signatures of Strength' optimized for their specific mechanical environments. For instance, we predict that muscle cells, which undergo unidirectional contraction, will exhibit a topology dominated by high-persistence linear components with minimal cross-linking loops. Conversely, fibroblasts, which must navigate and resist multidirectional forces in the extracellular matrix, will display a highly interconnected topology characterized by a high density of persistent 2D loops and 3D voids. Neurons, requiring long-range structural support along axons, will present a hybrid topology. By quantifying these differences using TDA, we will establish the first comparative topological taxonomy of the cytoskeleton.

Question 2: Does the cytoskeleton organize itself to reach a critical 'percolation threshold' that maximizes mechanical resilience while minimizing protein expenditure? 
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that cells do not simply over-build their cytoskeletal networks to achieve strength; rather, they optimize their architecture to exist precisely at or slightly above a topological percolation threshold. In network theory, percolation represents the critical point where a system transitions from disconnected clusters to a globally connected network, suddenly acquiring systemic strength. We posit that the healthy cytoskeleton operates near this critical mesoscale phase transition, providing maximum mechanical stability (resilience against deformation) with the minimum necessary structural material (actin and tubulin). Pathological or aging cells, we hypothesize, will show topologies that fall below this critical percolation threshold, leading to structural fragility.

Question 3: Can a universal mathematical index reliably predict the mechanical resilience and health state of a cell based solely on its cytoskeletal topology? 
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the persistent homology metrics derived from TDA can be distilled into a single, standardized 'Cytoskeletal Resilience Index' (CRI). This index will serve as a universal, quantitative gauge of mesoscale structural integrity. We predict that the CRI will strongly correlate with known mechanical properties (e.g., stiffness, elasticity) previously derived from biophysical assays (like atomic force microscopy) on similar cell types. Furthermore, we hypothesize that the CRI will be significantly lower in publicly available datasets of cells subjected to mechanical stress, aging models, or cytoskeletal-associated disease states (e.g., tauopathies, actin-nemaline myopathy), proving its efficacy as a diagnostic metric.

By addressing these questions, this project will fulfill the NCEMS mandate to solve long-standing puzzles in cellular biosciences using existing data. We will transition the field from qualitative descriptions of cytoskeletal morphology to rigorous, mathematically grounded definitions of emergent mesoscale resilience.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodology leverages a community-scale synthesis of publicly available data, utilizing advanced AI and mathematical modeling to avoid generating new experimental data, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS funding call. The approach is divided into three distinct phases: Data Aggregation and Preprocessing, Topological Data Analysis, and Synthesis and Modeling.

Phase 1: Data Aggregation and AI-Driven Preprocessing. 
We will mine massive public repositories, including the Cell Image Library, EMPIAR (Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive), and the Allen Cell Explorer, to aggregate thousands of high-resolution 2D and 3D images of actin and microtubule networks. The dataset will encompass diverse cell types: myocytes, neurons, and fibroblasts, representing healthy, aged, and diseased states. Because these images originate from disparate sources (e.g., STED, STORM, Cryo-ET), we will employ state-of-the-art AI and machine learning techniques for harmonization. Specifically, we will use deep learning-based image segmentation models (such as Cellpose and specialized U-Nets) to extract standardized, binarized skeletons of the cytoskeletal networks. This AI-driven pipeline ensures that varying signal-to-noise ratios and resolutions are normalized, converting raw pixel data into mathematically rigorous graph representations suitable for topological analysis.

Phase 2: Topological Data Analysis (TDA) and Persistent Homology. 
The core of our analytical strategy relies on TDA, specifically persistent homology, to quantify the mesoscale emergence of network resilience. For each segmented cytoskeletal network, we will compute the Vietoris-Rips filtration. This process involves expanding spheres around each data point (protein node) and tracking the birth and death of topological features across multiple spatial scales. We will calculate Betti numbers: B0 (connected components/filaments), B1 (1D holes/loops), and B2 (2D voids). These features will be visualized using persistence diagrams and barcodes. By measuring the 'persistence' (lifespan) of these topological features, we can distinguish between true, load-bearing structural loops and transient, noisy connections. This step will precisely quantify the 'holes' and 'loops' abstractly referenced in traditional biology, translating them into rigorous mathematical signatures.

Phase 3: Percolation Modeling and the Cytoskeletal Resilience Index. 
To test our percolation threshold hypothesis, we will map the TDA outputs onto network percolation models from statistical physics. We will simulate structural stress (e.g., random edge removal) on the extracted cytoskeletal graphs to determine the critical point of network failure. By correlating the topological signatures (persistence landscapes) with the network's distance to the percolation threshold, we will formulate the 'Cytoskeletal Resilience Index' (CRI). The CRI will be a composite score generated via a Random Forest regression model trained on the topological features, optimized to predict network stability.

Working Group Structure: 
This transdisciplinary effort requires expertise beyond a single lab. Our NCEMS Working Group will comprise computational cell biologists (for biological context and data curation), applied mathematicians (for TDA and algorithm development), and biophysicists (for percolation theory and mechanics). Graduate students and postdocs will be cross-trained in these disciplines, fulfilling the NCEMS goal of cultivating a data-savvy, multidisciplinary workforce.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that fundamentally advance our understanding of mesoscale emergence in cellular biology. The primary deliverable will be the 'Cytoskeletal Resilience Index' (CRI), the first universal, mathematically rigorous metric for quantifying the mechanical integrity of cellular networks. By defining the 'Topological Signature of Strength,' we will solve the long-standing puzzle of how cells optimize their architecture to achieve mechanical identity without over-expending cellular resources.

Beyond conceptual breakthroughs, we will produce a suite of open-source analytical tools. We will release a comprehensive, AI-integrated TDA software pipeline specifically optimized for biological image analysis. This pipeline will empower the broader molecular and cellular biology community to apply complex topological mathematics to their own imaging data, fundamentally elevating the analytical standards of the field. Ultimately, this project establishes a new paradigm where biological architecture is understood not just through its molecular parts, but through the emergent mathematical rules that bind them together.

The impact of this work extends significantly into human health. The CRI has the potential to serve as a novel diagnostic biomarker. By comparing the topological signatures of healthy cells to those in aging models or diseases characterized by structural failure (e.g., muscular dystrophy, Alzheimer’s disease), researchers can identify precisely where and how the cytoskeletal network loses its resilience at the mesoscale.

Finally, this project will have a profound impact on workforce development. Trainees within our NCEMS Working Group will receive unparalleled cross-disciplinary training. Biologists will learn cutting-edge applied mathematics and Python-based data science, while mathematicians will gain deep insights into cellular biophysics. This transdisciplinary environment will cultivate a new generation of data-savvy scientists uniquely equipped to tackle the complex, emergent phenomena of the 21st-century biosciences.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the principles of open, team, and reproducible science, strictly adhering to the highest community standards and NCEMS guidelines. To ensure maximum transparency and utility, all aspects of this synthesis project—data, code, and workflows—will be made publicly accessible under FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles.

Data Sharing: Although we are utilizing existing public data, the curated, harmonized, and annotated datasets generated during our preprocessing phase represent significant value. These intermediate and final datasets, including the segmented cytoskeletal graphs, will be deposited in Zenodo with comprehensive metadata, ensuring they are easily discoverable and citable via persistent Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs).

Code and Workflow Transparency: All computational pipelines, AI models, and TDA algorithms will be developed openly on GitHub. We will utilize Jupyter Notebooks to document our analytical workflows step-by-step, allowing external researchers to seamlessly reproduce our derivation of the Cytoskeletal Resilience Index. The repository will include detailed readmes, dependency lists (managed via Docker containers or Conda environments to guarantee reproducibility across different operating systems), and tutorial datasets. Upon project completion, the codebase will be archived and linked to our publications.

Open Access Publishing: All findings will be disseminated through open-access, peer-reviewed journals. Prior to formal peer review, manuscripts will be uploaded to preprint servers such as bioRxiv to accelerate knowledge dissemination within the scientific community.

Community Engagement: We will actively foster community engagement by hosting virtual workshops and webinars through NCEMS, demonstrating how to utilize our TDA pipeline. By prioritizing open science, we not only ensure the rigor and reproducibility of our own findings but also democratize access to advanced mathematical tools, empowering researchers globally to explore emergent topological phenomena in their respective fields.

The proposed community-scale synthesis project requires the unique infrastructure, collaborative environment, and financial support provided by NCEMS, as the scope of this transdisciplinary integration far exceeds the capabilities and resources of any single laboratory.

Personnel and Training: The primary budget allocation will support the next generation of data-savvy scientists. We request funding for one postdoctoral researcher and two graduate students. The postdoc will serve as the technical bridge between the mathematical and biological domains, leading the TDA pipeline development. The graduate students will focus on data curation, AI preprocessing, and biological validation. Their stipends and benefits are critical investments in the future STEM workforce, directly aligning with NCEMS training objectives.

Working Group Meetings: To stimulate cross-disciplinary collaboration, we request funds to support biannual, in-person Working Group meetings at the NCEMS facility. These intensive, multi-day synthesis sessions are vital for aligning the diverse expertise of our team—comprising cell biologists, applied mathematicians, and biophysicists from distinct geographic locations and institutional tiers. These face-to-face interactions are essential for troubleshooting complex percolation models and ensuring biological relevance.

Computational Resources: While we will leverage existing data, the application of deep learning for image harmonization and the computation of persistent homology across thousands of large 3D datasets are highly computationally intensive. We request funds for cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS or equivalent) to ensure rapid, scalable processing that avoids institutional bottlenecks.

In summary, the requested NCEMS resources are meticulously aligned with the project's needs, ensuring the successful synthesis of data, the cultivation of new talent, and the rigorous execution of open science.

author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: Computer Vision for Cryo-ET Discovery: Uncovering 'Unidentified Cellular Objects' (UCOs)
abstract: Cryo-Electron Tomography (Cryo-ET) provides high-resolution views of the cellular interior, but much of the 'noise' in these images may actually be unidentified mesoscale structures. This project will use unsupervised Computer Vision and Deep Learning to scan raw Cryo-ET repositories (like EMPIAR) to identify 'Unidentified Cellular Objects' (UCOs)—recurring protein or lipid structures that have not yet been annotated. We hypothesize that the 'dark matter' of the cell contains thousands of organized mesoscale assemblies that standard analysis overlooks. This synthesis project will create an automated discovery pipeline for the entire community. It requires the integration of vast amounts of raw imaging data with existing structural databases. The collaboration between computer vision experts and structural biologists will redefine how we explore the cellular interior. Trainees will lead the effort in 'digital discovery,' training AI to see what human experts might miss.
background_and_significance:
Cryo-electron tomography (Cryo-ET) has revolutionized structural biology, offering unprecedented, near-atomic resolution landscapes of the cellular interior in a native or near-native state. However, the sheer density and complexity of the cellular milieu present a formidable analytical challenge. Currently, standard Cryo-ET analysis relies heavily on template matching or supervised subtomogram averaging, which inherently biases discovery toward known, well-characterized molecular assemblies such as ribosomes or proteasomes. Consequently, a vast proportion of the tomographic volume is dismissed as 'noise' or uninterpretable background. We posit that this cellular 'dark matter' harbors a rich tapestry of Unidentified Cellular Objects (UCOs)—novel, transient, or previously uncharacterized mesoscale structures that bridge the gap between individual biomolecules and higher-order organelles.

The National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) emphasizes the understanding of emergent properties at this exact mesoscale. Despite the exponential growth of publicly available Cryo-ET data in repositories such as the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR), the lack of scalable, unsupervised analytical tools has left these datasets severely underutilized. Single-laboratory efforts are insufficient to overcome the computational and interdisciplinary bottlenecks required to synthesize these massive, heterogeneous datasets.

This project proposes a paradigm shift: leveraging advanced, unsupervised Computer Vision and Deep Learning algorithms to systematically mine public Cryo-ET repositories for UCOs. By moving away from supervised, hypothesis-driven template matching, we can achieve true 'digital discovery.' This synthesis project addresses a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular sciences: what comprises the unannotated macromolecular space of the cell, and how do these assemblies contribute to emergent mesoscale phenomena? The significance of this work lies in its potential to uncover entirely new classes of mesoscale assemblies, mapping their spatial distribution, and correlating them with specific cellular states. 

By integrating vast amounts of raw imaging data with existing structural databases (e.g., PDB, AlphaFold Protein Structure Database), our transdisciplinary team of structural biologists, data scientists, and computer vision experts will redefine our exploration of the cellular interior. The mesoscale is where the fundamental rules of life emerge from chaotic molecular interactions. By identifying UCOs, we can begin to decipher the compositional and spatial grammar of these emergent properties. For instance, do certain UCOs only appear under specific stress conditions? Do they act as transient scaffolds for metabolic channeling? Answering these questions requires a community-scale synthesis approach, pooling computational resources, algorithmic innovations, and biological intuition. This effort aligns perfectly with the NCEMS mission to catalyze multidisciplinary synthesis, answering fundamental questions about emergence without generating new experimental data, and training a data-savvy workforce capable of navigating the intersection of AI and structural biology.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This synthesis project is driven by the overarching premise that the unannotated regions of Cryo-ET tomograms—often discarded as noise—contain recurring, biologically significant mesoscale assemblies. To systematically uncover and characterize these structures, our working group will address the following primary research questions and test their associated hypotheses.

Question 1: Can unsupervised deep learning frameworks reliably distinguish recurring, unannotated mesoscale assemblies (UCOs) from true stochastic noise in highly heterogeneous, publicly available Cryo-ET datasets?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the cellular 'dark matter' contains thousands of organized mesoscale assemblies. By deploying state-of-the-art unsupervised representation learning and 3D computer vision algorithms (such as contrastive learning and variational autoencoders) on diverse EMPIAR datasets, we can cluster structural motifs based on morphological conservation rather than prior structural knowledge. We predict that true UCOs will exhibit high intra-cluster structural similarity across multiple independent tomograms and biological replicates, distinguishing them from random noise artifacts.

Question 2: What are the morphological, spatial, and contextual characteristics of the most ubiquitous UCOs across different cell types and physiological states?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that UCOs are not randomly distributed but exhibit specific spatial associations with known cellular landmarks (e.g., tethered to the endoplasmic reticulum, localized near the nuclear pore complex, or enriched in regions of high membrane curvature). By mapping the coordinates of discovered UCOs back into their native tomographic context and cross-referencing these maps with metadata from public repositories, we anticipate identifying distinct classes of mesoscale assemblies whose emergence is strictly correlated with specific cellular states (e.g., viral infection, starvation, or cell division).

Question 3: Can the molecular identities of computationally discovered UCOs be inferred by integrating unsupervised structural clustering with existing molecular databases and AI-driven structural predictions?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that a significant fraction of UCOs correspond to transient multi-protein complexes or novel lipid-protein assemblies whose high-resolution structures are either unknown or only partially characterized in isolation. By integrating the low-to-medium resolution envelopes of our UCO clusters with structural databases (e.g., PDB, EMDB) and predictive models (e.g., AlphaFold-Multimer), we predict that we can generate high-confidence molecular hypotheses for these previously 'unseen' structures.

Question 4: How do these newly identified mesoscale structures contribute to the emergent properties of the cellular system?
Hypothesis 4: We hypothesize that UCOs represent the missing physical links in mesoscale emergence—acting as transient scaffolds, phase-separated droplets, or specialized transport vesicles that coordinate complex biochemical reactions. By cataloging these structures and making the discovery pipeline openly available, we will provide the community with the foundational data necessary to formulate and test new mechanistic models of cellular emergence.

These questions require a synthesis of computational innovation and biological interpretation. They cannot be answered by a single lab or by generating more data; they demand the transdisciplinary integration of existing global datasets to extract hidden, higher-order biological principles.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodology relies exclusively on the synthesis and integration of existing, publicly available data, strictly adhering to the NCEMS mandate. The project will be executed in four interconnected phases by a transdisciplinary working group comprising computer vision experts, structural biologists, and data scientists.

Phase 1: Data Aggregation and Preprocessing. We will systematically mine the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR), selecting a diverse array of high-quality cellular Cryo-ET datasets representing various organisms, cell types, and physiological conditions. We will standardize the metadata and preprocess the tomograms using automated denoising and missing-wedge correction algorithms to ensure uniform data quality. This phase will establish a massive, harmonized data lake of raw 3D cellular volumes, an effort that necessitates the collaborative infrastructure supported by NCEMS.

Phase 2: Unsupervised UCO Discovery via Deep Learning. Instead of traditional template matching, we will develop and deploy a novel, unsupervised 3D computer vision pipeline. We will utilize a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture integrated with Contrastive Learning (e.g., SimCLR adapted for 3D volumes). The network will extract thousands of randomly sampled subtomograms from the unannotated regions of the datasets. Through contrastive learning, the model will learn rich, rotation- and translation-invariant structural representations without any manual labels. Subsequently, clustering algorithms (e.g., HDBSCAN) will group these representations in the latent space. Clusters with high density and recurrence across independent datasets will be flagged as candidate Unidentified Cellular Objects (UCOs).

Phase 3: Structural Refinement and Contextual Mapping. For each highly populated UCO cluster, we will perform automated, reference-free subtomogram averaging to generate consensus 3D density maps of the mesoscale assemblies. Concurrently, we will map the spatial coordinates of these UCOs back into the original tomograms. Using spatial point pattern analysis, we will assess the proximity of UCOs to known organelles (annotated via existing supervised methods), uncovering potential functional relationships and emergent spatial networks.

Phase 4: Multi-modal Data Integration for Molecular Inference. To bridge the gap between UCO density maps and molecular identity, we will integrate our structural findings with existing databases. We will utilize AI-driven structural fitting algorithms to dock known high-resolution structures (from PDB) and predicted multimeric complexes (from AlphaFold) into the UCO envelopes. This synthesis of raw imaging data with structural genomics data will allow us to propose molecular identities for the UCOs.

Team Science and Training: This approach is inherently collaborative. Computer science trainees will develop the unsupervised algorithms, while structural biology trainees will evaluate the biological plausibility of the UCOs and perform the molecular docking. Regular cross-disciplinary workshops will ensure that algorithmic development is guided by biological reality, and biological interpretation is constrained by statistical rigor. This collaborative environment will foster a new generation of scientists uniquely equipped to navigate the intersection of AI and mesoscale biology.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The successful execution of this synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes for the molecular and cellular biosciences. First, we will produce the 'UCO Atlas,' the first comprehensive, publicly accessible catalog of unannotated mesoscale assemblies discovered from existing Cryo-ET data. This atlas will include 3D density maps, spatial distribution profiles, and putative molecular identities for hundreds of novel structures, directly addressing the NCEMS goal of solving long-standing puzzles regarding cellular 'dark matter.'

Second, we will deliver an open-source, unsupervised Computer Vision pipeline specifically optimized for 3D tomographic data. This automated discovery tool will be a major methodological advancement, empowering the global research community to move beyond biased, template-driven analysis and continuously mine future datasets for novel emergent structures.

The broader impacts of this work are profound. By illuminating the uncharacterized mesoscale, we will provide the foundational knowledge necessary to understand how higher-order cellular functions emerge from macromolecular interactions. This could reveal new therapeutic targets, particularly if specific UCOs are associated with disease states.

Furthermore, this project will have a lasting impact on workforce development. By deeply integrating trainees into a transdisciplinary working group, we will cultivate a cohort of 'bilingual' scientists—researchers fluent in both advanced artificial intelligence and structural biology. These trainees will be uniquely positioned to lead the next generation of data-intensive biological research, fulfilling the NCEMS mission to tap diverse new talent and train a data-savvy scientific workforce. The collaborative partnerships forged through this NCEMS Working Group will bridge the historical divide between computational sciences and wet-lab structural biology. By democratizing access to high-level data synthesis tools, we will stimulate a wave of secondary discoveries across diverse biological disciplines, firmly establishing the mesoscale as a tractable frontier for scientific exploration.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our working group is fundamentally committed to the principles of Open Science, ensuring that all findings, data, and analytical workflows are transparent, reproducible, and immediately accessible to the broader scientific community. This commitment aligns directly with NCEMS requirements and community-created policies on open, team, and reproducible science.

Data Availability: All raw data utilized in this project will be sourced from public archives (e.g., EMPIAR). The synthesized outputs—including the UCO Atlas, consensus 3D density maps, spatial coordinate files, and molecular docking models—will be deposited into recognized public repositories such as the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) and the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR) under open-access licenses.

Code and Workflow Transparency: The unsupervised computer vision and deep learning pipelines developed during this project will be fully open-source. All code, scripts, and trained model weights will be hosted on a public GitHub repository under an MIT or GNU General Public License. To guarantee reproducibility, we will package our entire analytical workflow using containerization technologies (e.g., Docker, Singularity). This ensures that any researcher, regardless of their local computing environment, can deploy our pipeline to verify our results or apply the algorithms to their own datasets.

Documentation and Protocols: We will provide comprehensive, user-friendly documentation, including Jupyter Notebooks and step-by-step tutorials, to facilitate community adoption of our tools. Detailed methodological protocols will be published on platforms like protocols.io.

Preprints and Open Access Publishing: All manuscripts resulting from this synthesis project will be submitted to preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv) concurrently with submission to peer-reviewed, open-access journals. author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: Universal Rhythms of Condensates: The Temporal Emergence of Nucleolar Oscillations
abstract: Biological condensates like the nucleolus are not static; they exhibit rhythmic fluctuations in size, density, and activity. This project will synthesize time-lapse imaging of nucleoli across diverse eukaryotes (from yeast to humans) to find 'Universal Temporal Laws' of condensate behavior. We hypothesize that nucleolar oscillations are coupled to the cell cycle and metabolic state through a conserved physical mechanism. Using signal processing and manifold learning, we will determine if these rhythms are an emergent property of the phase-separated state itself. This synthesis moves beyond descriptive 'snapshots' to a dynamic understanding of mesoscale time. It requires a collaborative effort to integrate disparate temporal datasets. Trainees will gain skills in time-series analysis and biological physics, uncovering the 'metronome' that governs mesoscale organization.
background_and_significance:
The molecular and cellular biosciences are undergoing a paradigm shift driven by the discovery of biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). The nucleolus, the largest and most prominent eukaryotic condensate, serves as the central hub for ribosome biogenesis, cellular stress sensing, and genome organization. Historically, the mesoscale organization of the nucleolus and other condensates has been studied through static, high-resolution snapshots. While these approaches have illuminated the compositional and spatial complexity of condensates, they critically ignore the dimension of time. Recent, isolated experimental observations have hinted at an unexpected phenomenon: condensates are not merely fluid, but they exhibit rhythmic, oscillatory fluctuations in size, surface boundary morphology, and internal density. 

Despite these tantalizing observations, a fundamental gap remains in our understanding of mesoscale emergence. Are these temporal fluctuations merely stochastic noise driven by Brownian motion, or do they represent highly regulated, emergent rhythms intrinsic to the non-equilibrium thermodynamic state of the living cell? Currently, the field lacks a unified, pan-eukaryotic framework to describe the temporal dynamics of condensates. Addressing this requires moving beyond the capabilities of any single laboratory. Over the past decade, a massive volume of time-lapse fluorescence microscopy data capturing nucleolar and nuclear dynamics across diverse species—from Saccharomyces cerevisiae to Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, and Homo sapiens—has been deposited into public repositories such as the Image Data Resource (IDR), the Allen Cell Explorer, and various supplementary data archives. However, these datasets remain siloed, analyzed only for their original, narrow experimental purposes. 

This proposal aligns perfectly with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). By synthesizing these disparate, publicly available time-lapse datasets using advanced AI and data science, we will investigate the unexpected appearance of temporal rhythms at the mesoscale. We propose that nucleolar oscillations represent an emergent property of the phase-separated state, acting as a critical bridge between molecular-scale biophysics and cellular-scale outcomes like cell cycle progression and metabolic adaptation. Understanding the 'metronome' of the nucleolus will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how membraneless organelles sense, integrate, and respond to global cellular states without the use of membrane-bound receptors. Furthermore, by defining the universal temporal laws of condensates, this project will pioneer a new subfield of dynamic mesoscale biology. This highly collaborative, cross-disciplinary synthesis will not only yield transformative biological insights but will also serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy biological physicists and computational cell biologists.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This synthesis project is driven by three compelling, interrelated research questions that aim to uncover the fundamental rules governing the temporal emergence of mesoscale biological structures. By leveraging vast amounts of publicly available time-lapse imaging data, we will test the following questions and hypotheses:

Question 1: Do nucleoli exhibit universal, conserved oscillatory rhythms across diverse eukaryotic species, and what are the scaling laws governing these dynamics? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that despite vast evolutionary divergence and differences in specific molecular composition, the physical constraints of mesoscale phase separation dictate a 'Universal Temporal Law' of condensate behavior. We predict that nucleoli across all examined eukaryotes (yeast, nematodes, fruit flies, and humans) will exhibit rhythmic fluctuations in volume, surface area, and internal sub-compartment boundaries. Furthermore, we hypothesize that the frequency and amplitude of these oscillations will scale predictably with nuclear volume, total cellular protein concentration, and physiological temperature, reflecting fundamental physical limits of mesoscale emergence rather than species-specific genetic programs.

Question 2: How are condensate rhythms coupled to global cellular clocks, specifically the cell cycle and metabolic state? 
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that nucleolar oscillations are not isolated phenomena but are dynamically entrained by global cellular oscillators, such as cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) activity and ATP metabolic fluxes. We predict that by synthesizing time-lapse data that includes dual-reporter imaging (e.g., nucleolar markers alongside cell cycle indicators like FUCCI), we will observe phase-locking between nucleolar rhythms and cell cycle transitions. Additionally, we hypothesize that existing datasets capturing cellular stress or metabolic inhibition (e.g., ATP depletion, mTOR inhibition) will reveal a predictable dampening or phase-shifting of nucleolar oscillations, establishing the condensate as a mesoscale integrator of the cell's energetic state.

Question 3: Are these temporal rhythms an emergent physical property of the multi-phase condensate state? 
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that nucleolar rhythms are an emergent consequence of non-equilibrium thermodynamic fluxes (e.g., active RNA transcription and ribosome assembly) occurring within a multi-phase liquid environment. We predict that advanced manifold learning applied to our synthesized spatiotemporal data will reveal low-dimensional 'attractor states' characteristic of non-linear dynamical systems. By comparing the temporal dynamics of the nucleolus (an active, multi-phase condensate) to existing data on simpler, less active nuclear bodies (e.g., Cajal bodies), we expect to demonstrate that sustained, complex oscillations are an exclusive emergent property of highly active, multi-layered phase separation. 

Answering these questions relies entirely on the synthesis of existing data. By bringing together biological physicists, computational biologists, and cell biologists, we will translate isolated observations into a predictive, quantitative framework for mesoscale temporal emergence.
methods_and_approach:
To answer our research questions without generating new experimental data, we have designed a comprehensive, AI-driven data synthesis pipeline. This approach requires the integration of diverse computational methodologies, spanning computer vision, signal processing, and dynamical systems modeling, executed by a transdisciplinary Working Group.

Phase 1: Data Scraping, Curation, and Harmonization
We will systematically mine public repositories, including the Image Data Resource (IDR), the Allen Cell Explorer, the EMBL-EBI BioImage Archive, and published supplementary materials. We will identify high-frame-rate time-lapse fluorescence microscopy datasets featuring nucleolar markers (e.g., Fibrillarin, Nucleolin, RPA194) and whole-nucleus markers across our target species (yeast, C. elegans, Drosophila, human cell lines). A critical first step is data harmonization: standardizing metadata (e.g., frame rate, pixel size, temperature, cell type) and correcting for imaging artifacts like photobleaching and drift using automated, open-source registration pipelines.

Phase 2: AI-Driven Spatiotemporal Segmentation
Extracting quantitative temporal data from thousands of hours of heterogeneous video requires robust, automated computer vision. We will deploy and fine-tune state-of-the-art deep learning segmentation models, such as Cellpose and StarDist, extending them via 3D U-Nets to handle volumetric time-series (4D data). For each tracked nucleolus, the AI pipeline will extract a rich feature set at every time point, including volume, sphericity, surface roughness, centroid displacement, and internal fluorescence intensity gradients (representing sub-nucleolar phase boundaries).

Phase 3: Signal Processing and Time-Series Analysis
To detect and quantify oscillatory behaviors, the extracted temporal feature vectors will be subjected to advanced signal processing. We will utilize Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT) and continuous wavelet transforms to identify dominant frequencies and temporal stability. Autocorrelation and cross-correlation analyses will be used to determine phase relationships between nucleolar fluctuations and other cellular signals (e.g., cell cycle reporters). We will apply rigorous statistical thresholding against simulated Brownian noise to ensure the detected rhythms represent genuine biological oscillations rather than stochastic fluctuations.

Phase 4: Manifold Learning and Dynamical Systems Modeling
To determine if these rhythms are an emergent property of the phase-separated state, we will apply non-linear dimensionality reduction techniques, specifically Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) and t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE), adapted for time-series data. This manifold learning will help us identify low-dimensional 'attractor states' in the nucleolar dynamics. Furthermore, we will use Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) to extract the dominant spatiotemporal modes of the nucleolus, allowing us to build predictive mathematical models of condensate behavior as a non-equilibrium dynamical system.

Phase 5: Synthesis and Cross-Disciplinary Integration
Our Working Group will convene bi-annually to synthesize these computational outputs. Physicists will interpret the manifold topologies in the context of non-equilibrium thermodynamics, while cell biologists will map these physical states onto known cellular functions (e.g., ribosome biogenesis rates, stress responses). This iterative feedback loop between data scientists, physicists, and biologists is essential to extract deep biological meaning from the synthesized data.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This Working Group will deliver transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission to understand mesoscale emergence. 

Scientific Outcomes: First, we will establish 'CondensateTimeDB', the first comprehensive, open-access database of temporal condensate dynamics across eukaryotic life, featuring standardized time-series data and extracted biophysical features. Second, we will publish a series of high-impact syntheses detailing the 'Universal Temporal Laws' of nucleolar oscillations, fundamentally shifting the field's perspective from static spatial models to dynamic, spatiotemporal frameworks. Third, we will provide a novel mathematical model that explains how mesoscale rhythms emerge from non-equilibrium phase separation and how they couple to cellular metabolic states, solving the long-standing mystery of how membraneless organelles act as dynamic cellular sensors.

Broader Impacts: Beyond scientific discovery, this project will catalyze a new multidisciplinary community focused on dynamic mesoscale biology. By proving that hidden temporal laws can be extracted from existing, siloed datasets, we will demonstrate the immense untapped value of public bioimaging archives, encouraging future synthesis research. 

Training the Next Generation: This project is deeply committed to workforce development. Our two postdoctoral fellows and two graduate students will be cross-trained in AI, computer vision, non-equilibrium physics, and cell biology. They will learn to navigate complex public datasets and communicate across disciplinary boundaries. Furthermore, trainees will take leadership roles in organizing our Working Group meetings and leading resulting publications, ensuring they emerge as highly competitive, data-savvy leaders in the future scientific workforce.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Adherence to open science principles is central to this proposal, ensuring that all findings, data, and workflows are transparent, reproducible, and accessible to the broader scientific community in accordance with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles.

Code and Analytical Workflows: All custom scripts, AI model architectures, and signal processing pipelines will be developed openly on a dedicated GitHub repository under an MIT License. To guarantee computational reproducibility, the entire analytical environment will be containerized using Docker and Singularity. We will utilize Jupyter Notebooks and Quarto documents to provide heavily annotated, step-by-step tutorials of our workflows, allowing external researchers to easily apply our temporal analysis methods to their own condensate datasets.

Data Sharing: While we are utilizing existing public data, the harmonized datasets, trained AI segmentation weights, and the extracted time-series feature matrices represent highly valuable new resources. These will be deposited into the BioImage Archive and Zenodo, complete with comprehensive metadata following the Recommended Metadata for Biological Images (REMBI) guidelines. The 'CondensateTimeDB' will feature an interactive web interface (built via R Shiny/Python Dash) allowing researchers to visualize nucleolar rhythms without needing advanced coding skills.

Team Science Practices: Our Working Group will adopt community-created policies for open team science. We will establish a clear authorship and data-ownership charter at the project's inception, ensuring equitable recognition for all contributors, especially trainees. Preprints of all manuscripts will be posted to bioRxiv prior to peer review, and all final publications will be strictly Open Access.

The postdocs will be strategically co-mentored by Working Group PIs from different disciplines (e.g., one bridging AI/computer vision with cell biology, the other bridging non-equilibrium physics with bioinformatics). This cross-mentorship is essential for transdisciplinary synthesis and trainee development. The graduate students will lead data curation and AI model fine-tuning.

Working Group Meetings: A core component of our budget is dedicated to travel and accommodations for our Working Group. We request support for bi-annual, four-day, in-person synthesis meetings to be held at the NCEMS headquarters. No single lab possesses this breadth of expertise or the computational infrastructure required. NCEMS provides the vital collaborative scaffolding, meeting space, and funding necessary to unite this diverse talent and solve this complex mesoscale puzzle.

author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: The Energetic Efficiency of Membrane Folding: Surface-Area Laws Across Organelles
abstract: Organelles like mitochondria and chloroplasts maximize their functional surface area through complex membrane folding (cristae and thylakoids). This project will synthesize structural data from across the tree of life to identify the 'Universal Law of Membrane Efficiency.' We will use physics-based modeling to determine the energetic 'cost' of different folding geometries and the metabolic 'benefit' they provide. We hypothesize that there is a universal 'Optimal Folding Ratio' that organelles converge upon to maximize ATP production. This community-scale synthesis integrates bioenergetics with geometry. The project will bridge plant and animal biology, training students in the comparative analysis of energy-harvesting systems. The result will be a fundamental understanding of how the mesoscale geometry of membranes emerges to optimize cellular energy flux.
background_and_significance: The mesoscale organization of cellular membranes represents a profound example of biological emergence, where the spatial arrangement of lipid bilayers dictates macroscopic cellular energy fluxes. Across the tree of life, organelles such as mitochondria and chloroplasts employ highly convoluted membrane architectures—cristae and thylakoids, respectively—to maximize the functional surface area available for the macromolecular complexes of the electron transport chain and ATP synthase. Despite decades of structural and biochemical studies, a fundamental, unified understanding of the physical and geometric principles governing these membrane folds remains elusive. Specifically, we lack a quantitative framework to explain how the energetic cost of bending lipid bilayers is balanced against the metabolic benefit of increased ATP production capacity. This knowledge gap persists because structural biology, bioenergetics, and theoretical physics have traditionally operated in silos, generating vast but disparate datasets. Recent advances in cryogenic electron tomography (cryo-ET) and 3D electron microscopy have produced an unprecedented volume of publicly available structural data, capturing membrane geometries across diverse taxa and metabolic states. Concurrently, large-scale proteomics and biochemical databases provide rich information on the density and activity of energy-transducing complexes. However, these data have never been synthesized at a community scale to extract universal geometric and thermodynamic rules. This project aligns perfectly with the NCEMS mission to catalyze transdisciplinary synthesis research. By integrating existing structural, biochemical, and biophysical data, we aim to uncover the 'Universal Law of Membrane Efficiency.' We postulate that mesoscale membrane geometry is not merely a consequence of protein crowding, but an emergent property optimized through evolution to maximize energy flux under varying physiological constraints. The significance of this work is multifold. First, it solves a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular sciences regarding the physical constraints of organelle evolution. Second, it shifts the paradigm from qualitative descriptions of organelle morphology to rigorous, physics-based quantitative models. Third, by bridging plant and animal biology, this project will reveal whether mitochondria and chloroplasts, despite their distinct evolutionary origins, converge on identical biophysical solutions for energy harvesting. The emergence of these architectures from simple lipid-protein interactions to complex, dynamic 3D networks directly influences higher-order subcellular and cellular outcomes, such as metabolic adaptability and stress resilience. Understanding these mesoscale properties is critical, as defects in membrane folding are implicated in numerous human pathologies, including neurodegenerative diseases, as well as in determining agricultural crop yields. By leveraging AI and advanced data science techniques to synthesize these myriad datasets, our working group will stimulate novel questions about the physical limits of life. This synthesis requires a collaborative effort that transcends individual laboratories, bringing together experts in structural biology, membrane biophysics, and computational data science. Through this synthesis, we will pioneer innovative analytical strategies for mining and integrating complex 3D mesoscale data, fundamentally advancing our understanding of emergent mesoscale phenomena in biological systems.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: To elucidate the emergent principles governing mesoscale membrane architecture, this synthesis project is driven by a core overarching hypothesis: Across the tree of life, energy-transducing organelles converge upon a universal 'Optimal Folding Ratio' (OFR) that maximizes ATP production by perfectly balancing the thermodynamic cost of membrane curvature with the metabolic benefit of increased functional surface area. We propose that this OFR is a fundamental emergent property of the mesoscale, dictating the physical limits of cellular bioenergetics. To rigorously test this hypothesis and uncover the 'Universal Law of Membrane Efficiency,' our Working Group will address the following four compelling research questions: Question 1: What is the quantitative relationship between membrane curvature, surface area, and the density of energy-transducing complexes across diverse evolutionary lineages? We hypothesize that despite vast differences in species and organelle types (mitochondrial cristae vs. chloroplast thylakoids), there exists a conserved mathematical scaling law relating the degree of membrane folding to the packing density of ATP synthase and electron transport chain complexes. We expect that AI-driven synthesis of publicly available cryo-ET data will reveal convergent geometric patterns across plant and animal kingdoms. Question 2: What are the energetic costs associated with generating and maintaining complex mesoscale membrane geometries? We hypothesize that the energetic penalty of extreme membrane curvature (the 'cost') places a hard biophysical constraint on organelle morphology. By applying Helfrich elastic membrane theory to synthesized 3D structural datasets, we will calculate the mechanical energy required to maintain observed cristae and thylakoid architectures, predicting that structures exceeding the OFR will be evolutionarily selected against due to diminishing metabolic returns. Question 3: How does the mesoscale geometry of folded membranes optimize proton motive force and ATP synthesis rates? We hypothesize that the specific topological features of folded membranes (e.g., cristae junctions, thylakoid grana margins) create localized proton microdomains that significantly enhance the efficiency of ATP synthesis compared to flat membranes. We will synthesize existing biochemical flux data and structural parameters to build finite element models, testing whether the observed geometries maximize the 'benefit' of energy conversion. Question 4: Does the Optimal Folding Ratio dynamically adapt to differing metabolic demands and environmental stresses? We hypothesize that the OFR is not static but represents a dynamic emergent property that shifts in predictable ways in response to cellular energy states. By synthesizing structural data from organisms under different physiological conditions (e.g., state transitions in chloroplasts, apoptotic or high-respiration states in mitochondria), we will determine how mesoscale membrane topology remodels to maintain energetic efficiency. By addressing these questions, we will transcend traditional descriptive biology, utilizing existing data to establish a predictive, physics-based framework for organelle biology. This approach directly answers the NCEMS call to solve long-standing puzzles regarding molecular and cellular emergence. The synthesis of these diverse data streams will allow us to map the entire landscape of possible membrane geometries, ultimately identifying the universal biophysical rules that govern the evolution and function of energy-harvesting systems across the biosphere.
methods_and_approach: This project relies entirely on the synthesis and integration of existing, publicly available datasets, strictly adhering to the NCEMS mandate of generating no new experimental data. Our methodological approach is divided into three integrated phases: Data Aggregation and Curation, AI-Driven Geometric Extraction, and Physics-Based Bioenergetic Modeling. Phase 1: Data Aggregation and Curation. We will comprehensively mine public repositories for structural and biochemical data. Key structural databases include the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR), the Protein Data Bank (PDB), and the Cell Image Library. We will extract 3D tomograms and serial section electron micrographs of mitochondria and chloroplasts across a broad taxonomic range, encompassing mammals, plants, fungi, and single-celled eukaryotes. Concurrently, we will aggregate biochemical and proteomic data from databases such as PRIDE and BRENDA to quantify the abundance and specific activity of ATP synthase and respiratory complexes under various physiological states corresponding to the structural data. Phase 2: AI-Driven Geometric Extraction. The sheer volume of tomographic data precludes manual segmentation. We will employ advanced Artificial Intelligence and deep learning tools, such as convolutional neural networks (e.g., modified U-Net architectures), to automate the 3D segmentation of cristae and thylakoid membranes from noisy cryo-ET datasets. Our data science team will develop custom algorithms to extract precise geometric parameters from these segmented volumes, including surface-to-volume ratios, mean and Gaussian curvatures, cristae junction widths, and inter-membrane distances. This computational pipeline will enable the high-throughput, community-scale synthesis required to analyze thousands of organelle structures, transforming qualitative images into rigorous, quantitative geometric datasets. Phase 3: Physics-Based Bioenergetic Modeling. To evaluate the 'cost' versus 'benefit' of membrane folding, we will integrate the extracted geometric data with theoretical biophysics. The energetic 'cost' of membrane bending will be calculated using the Helfrich model of membrane elasticity, incorporating known lipid compositions to estimate bending rigidities. The metabolic 'benefit' will be modeled using finite element analysis (FEA) to simulate proton diffusion and ATP synthesis rates within the constrained 3D geometries extracted in Phase 2. By coupling the Helfrich elastic energy equations with reaction-diffusion models of the proton motive force, we will identify the theoretical Optimal Folding Ratio (OFR) that maximizes net ATP production. Working Group Structure: This community-scale synthesis is beyond the scope of a single lab. We will assemble a transdisciplinary Working Group comprising experts in structural biology, computational biophysics, evolutionary biology, and AI/machine learning. The group will meet bi-weekly virtually and convene for two intensive, week-long synthesis hackathons at the NCEMS facility. Furthermore, we will actively recruit early-career researchers and data science trainees, pairing them with senior scientists to foster cross-disciplinary mentorship. Trainees will lead the development of the AI segmentation pipelines and FEA models, gaining invaluable experience in handling complex biological big data. This transdisciplinary approach will ensure that diverse scientific perspectives converge to rigorously test our hypotheses and successfully define the Universal Law of Membrane Efficiency.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The proposed synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that fundamentally advance our understanding of mesoscale emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences. The primary scientific outcome will be the establishment of the 'Universal Law of Membrane Efficiency,' providing the first quantitative, physics-based framework defining the Optimal Folding Ratio of energy-transducing organelles. This will resolve the long-standing mystery of why mitochondria and chloroplasts adopt their specific, complex architectures, demonstrating how mesoscale geometry emerges as an evolutionary optimization of cellular energy flux. Beyond the core scientific discoveries, this project will generate significant methodological advancements. We will release a robust, open-source AI pipeline specifically trained for the automated 3D segmentation and geometric analysis of highly convoluted membrane systems from cryo-ET data. This tool will be invaluable to the broader cell biology community, enabling researchers to rapidly extract quantitative metrics from their own structural datasets. Additionally, our integrated finite element models linking membrane topology to proton motive force will establish a new paradigm for computational bioenergetics. The broader impacts of this work are substantial. By elucidating the physical limits of energy production, our findings will have downstream implications for understanding metabolic dysfunctions in human aging and neurodegenerative diseases, where mitochondrial cristae morphology is often disrupted. In plant biology, understanding thylakoid optimization could inform future synthetic biology efforts aimed at enhancing photosynthetic efficiency and agricultural yields. Furthermore, by strictly utilizing existing data, we demonstrate the immense, untapped potential of community-scale synthesis. Finally, this project will cultivate a new generation of data-savvy scientists. Trainees will gain highly sought-after skills at the intersection of AI, big data, and biophysics, directly contributing to the NCEMS mission of building a diverse, transdisciplinary workforce equipped to tackle the next frontier of biological complexity.
open_science_and_reproducibility: Our Working Group is deeply committed to the principles of open, team, and reproducible science, aligning seamlessly with NCEMS mandates. We recognize that the true value of community-scale synthesis lies not only in the final discoveries but in the accessibility and transparency of the analytical processes. All project outputs, including curated datasets, AI models, and analysis workflows, will be made publicly available in accordance with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles. Data and Code Sharing: The aggregated and curated structural and biochemical datasets will be deposited in Zenodo, complete with comprehensive metadata to ensure interoperability. All custom code, including the AI-driven segmentation algorithms and the physics-based finite element models, will be developed openly on a dedicated GitHub organization repository. We will utilize Jupyter Notebooks and Docker containers to package our analysis pipelines, ensuring that any researcher can seamlessly reproduce our computational environments and verify our results. This containerized approach guarantees long-term reproducibility regardless of local hardware or software variations. Open Access and Community Engagement: All resulting manuscripts will be submitted to open-access, peer-reviewed journals, with preprints deposited on bioRxiv prior to submission. To maximize community benefit, we will host virtual workshops at the conclusion of the project to train the broader scientific community on how to deploy our AI segmentation tools and bioenergetic models. Authorship and credit will be determined using the CRediT (Contributor Roles Taxonomy) system, ensuring that all contributors—particularly early-career researchers and data scientists—receive appropriate recognition for their specific roles in data curation, software development, and conceptualization. By embedding these open science practices into the core of our Working Group, we will foster an inclusive, collaborative environment that maximizes the impact and reliability of our synthesis research.

author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: Quantum Effects in the Mesoscale: Synthesis of Biological Coherence in Signaling Complexes
abstract: While quantum biology is often associated with photosynthesis, there is emerging evidence that quantum coherence might play a role in other mesoscale signaling complexes, such as bird navigation proteins or photon-harvesting units in the retina. This project will synthesize biophysical data and spectroscopic records of these specialized complexes to test for 'Emergent Quantum Properties.' Using physics-informed neural networks, we will model how the spatial arrangement of proteins at the mesoscale supports or suppresses quantum coherence. We hypothesize that specific mesoscale architectures act as 'quantum shields' against cellular noise. This high-risk synthesis will integrate quantum physics with molecular biology. Trainees will work at the absolute frontier of science, learning to use AI to find quantum signatures in biological datasets. This could lead to a transformative understanding of the limits of biological information processing.
background_and_significance:
Classical molecular biology has long viewed the cellular environment as fundamentally incompatible with quantum mechanical phenomena. The prevailing consensus dictates that the warm, wet, and highly dynamic nature of biological systems should cause delicate quantum states to rapidly decohere, rendering them functionally irrelevant at macroscopic scales. However, the burgeoning field of quantum biology has fundamentally challenged this paradigm, most notably by demonstrating that quantum coherence plays a crucial role in the energy transfer processes of photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes. Despite these breakthroughs, a critical and long-standing puzzle remains: Can quantum coherence survive and function in other biological contexts, particularly within complex mammalian and avian sensory systems? Emerging experimental evidence suggests that quantum effects may indeed drive non-photosynthetic mesoscale signaling assemblies, such as the cryptochrome proteins mediating avian magnetoreception and the highly ordered arrays of rhodopsin in the vertebrate retina. 

The National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) emphasizes the investigation of emergent properties at the mesoscale—the critical spatial domain bridging individual biomolecules and larger organelles. It is precisely at this mesoscale that the mystery of biological quantum coherence must be resolved. We propose that quantum coherence in biological systems is not merely a molecular anomaly, but rather a profound emergent property dictated by mesoscale organization. Individual proteins may not sustain coherence, but when organized into specific, higher-order mesoscale architectures, these assemblies may act as 'quantum shields.' These shields potentially manipulate the local phononic environment to protect delicate quantum states from thermal decoherence, thereby enabling ultra-high-fidelity biological information processing. 

Investigating this phenomenon is fundamentally beyond the capabilities of any single research laboratory, as it requires the integration of disparate disciplines—quantum physics, structural biology, spectroscopy, and advanced artificial intelligence. Furthermore, vast amounts of relevant data already exist in the public domain, yet they remain siloed. High-resolution structural data from cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and X-ray crystallography are housed in the Protein Data Bank (PDB), while ultrafast transient absorption and two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy records are scattered across diverse biophysical repositories. By synthesizing these publicly available structural, dynamic, and spectroscopic datasets, this project will leverage a transdisciplinary Working Group to test for emergent quantum properties in sensory signaling complexes. This synthesis approach directly aligns with the NCEMS mission by utilizing AI and data science to solve a fundamental biological mystery without generating new experimental data. The significance of this research cannot be overstated: confirming that mesoscale architectures can engineer quantum coherence would represent a paradigm shift in the molecular and cellular biosciences, redefining our understanding of biological sensory mechanisms, cellular signaling, and the fundamental limits of biological information processing.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This synthesis project is driven by three primary research questions, each addressing a fundamental gap in our understanding of how emergent quantum phenomena manifest at the biological mesoscale. By integrating disparate datasets through advanced computational synthesis, we aim to systematically investigate the intersection of mesoscale architecture and quantum mechanics.

Question 1: How do specific mesoscale spatial arrangements of proteins correlate with the preservation of quantum coherence in biological signaling complexes? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the mesoscale architectures of sensory signaling complexes, specifically cryptochrome tetramers and retinal rhodopsin arrays, exhibit unique geometric and topological features that function as 'quantum shields.' We propose that these specific spatial arrangements are evolutionarily optimized to decouple the quantum coherent states of active chromophores from the thermal phonon noise of the surrounding cellular environment, thereby drastically extending coherence lifetimes beyond what is possible in isolated monomers.

Question 2: Can emergent quantum signatures be accurately predicted based purely on structural and biophysical mesoscale data using artificial intelligence?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) can successfully bridge the gap between classical structural biology and quantum dynamics. By constraining deep learning models with the physical laws of open quantum systems (such as the Hierarchical Equations of Motion), we predict that PINNs can learn hidden, non-linear correlations between atomistic/mesoscale structural parameters (e.g., inter-chromophore distances, dipole orientations, solvent accessibility) and experimentally observed quantum coherent lifetimes. This will allow for the predictive modeling of quantum properties across a wide range of mesoscale biological assemblies without the need for de novo experimental spectroscopy.

Question 3: Is quantum coherence a ubiquitous emergent property in high-fidelity biological sensory networks, or is it an isolated evolutionary anomaly?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that quantum coherence is a generalized, emergent evolutionary adaptation utilized across diverse biological domains to achieve ultra-high-fidelity sensory transduction. By synthesizing structural and spectroscopic data across multiple species and sensory modalities (e.g., avian magnetoreception, mammalian vision, and insect olfaction), we expect to identify a conserved set of mesoscale design principles that facilitate quantum coherence. 

Addressing these questions requires a community-scale synthesis approach. The data required to test these hypotheses—ranging from sub-angstrom structural coordinates to femtosecond spectroscopic decay rates—currently exist in separate, unlinked databases. Individual labs typically focus on either structural characterization or ultrafast spectroscopy, rarely integrating the two at the mesoscale level to hunt for emergent quantum properties. By bringing together a multidisciplinary Working Group of quantum physicists, structural biologists, and AI experts, we will synthesize these data to uncover the fundamental rules governing quantum emergence in biological systems. This collaborative effort will not only answer long-standing puzzles regarding the mechanisms of complex sensory systems like bird navigation but will also pioneer a new, data-driven methodology for investigating quantum biology.
methods_and_approach:
This project strictly adheres to the NCEMS mandate of utilizing only existing, publicly available data to drive community-scale synthesis. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, we will assemble a transdisciplinary Working Group to integrate, harmonize, and analyze disparate datasets using cutting-edge artificial intelligence, specifically Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs).

Phase 1: Data Mining and Harmonization
The first phase involves the systematic aggregation of publicly available structural, dynamic, and spectroscopic data. Structural data for mesoscale signaling complexes (e.g., cryptochromes, rhodopsins, and related scaffolding proteins) will be mined from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB). Molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories and NMR relaxation data will be sourced from the Biological Magnetic Resonance Data Bank (BMRB) and the MoDEL database to capture the conformational flexibility of these complexes at room temperature. Crucially, we will synthesize these structural datasets with ultrafast spectroscopic records—such as 2D electronic spectroscopy (2DES) and transient absorption data—mined from open-access biophysical repositories and supplementary materials of published literature. A dedicated team of data scientists within the Working Group will develop automated scraping and harmonization pipelines to standardize these multimodal datasets into a unified, machine-readable relational database, mapping structural coordinates directly to observed spectroscopic decay rates and coherence signatures.

Phase 2: Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) Development
Standard machine learning models often fail when applied to quantum systems because they ignore fundamental physical laws. To overcome this, we will develop PINNs designed specifically for open quantum systems. The neural networks will take mesoscale structural parameters (chromophore distances, dipole coupling, protein scaffold rigidity, and solvent interactions) as inputs. However, the loss function of the neural network will be heavily penalized if the outputs violate the principles of quantum dynamics, specifically utilizing the Hierarchical Equations of Motion (HEOM) and the Redfield equations as physical constraints. By training these PINNs on the harmonized dataset, the AI will learn the complex mapping between mesoscale protein architecture and the preservation of quantum coherence. This approach represents a highly innovative analytical strategy, effectively turning structural biology databases into training grounds for quantum discovery.

Phase 3: Working Group Collaboration and Trainee Development
The project is fundamentally beyond the scope of a single lab. We will convene a Working Group consisting of 12 experts: three quantum biophysicists, three structural biologists, three AI/ML data scientists, and three bioinformaticians, representing diverse geographic locations, career stages, and institutional backgrounds. The Working Group will meet bi-weekly virtually and convene for two intensive, week-long synthesis hackathons at the NCEMS facility. 

Training the next-generation workforce is a core component of this approach. We will fund three graduate students and two postdoctoral researchers who will be cross-trained across all disciplines.
