A biophysicist trainee will learn deep learning architectures, while an AI trainee will learn the fundamentals of quantum decoherence. This immersive, transdisciplinary environment will produce a uniquely equipped, data-savvy workforce capable of leading the future of emergent biological research.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The proposed synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that directly advance the molecular and cellular biosciences, specifically addressing the NCEMS goal of understanding mesoscale emergence. 

First, we will deliver a first-of-its-kind, open-access relational database that links mesoscale structural topologies with quantum spectroscopic signatures. This 'Quantum-Bio Structural Database' will serve as a foundational resource for the global scientific community, enabling researchers to explore emergent quantum properties without needing to conduct costly and complex ultrafast spectroscopy experiments. 

Second, we will release the fully trained, open-source Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) model. This innovative analytical tool will allow scientists to input any mesoscale protein structure and predict its capacity to support quantum coherence, effectively acting as an in silico screening tool for discovering novel quantum-biological phenomena. 

Third, we anticipate publishing high-impact, paradigm-shifting papers that answer long-standing puzzles, such as the exact physical mechanism of avian magnetoreception and the ultimate sensitivity limits of vertebrate vision. By proving that mesoscale architectures act as 'quantum shields,' we will fundamentally redefine how the scientific community views biological information processing, shifting the perspective from classical biochemical signaling to quantum-enhanced mechanotransduction.

Beyond scientific discoveries, the impact on human capital will be profound. This project will train a cohort of five early-career researchers (graduate students and postdocs) at the absolute frontier of science. These trainees will emerge as highly sought-after, transdisciplinary leaders fluent in structural biology, quantum physics, and advanced AI. By purposefully assembling a diverse Working Group from varied institutional research levels, we will democratize access to cutting-edge synthesis research, tapping into diverse new talent and ensuring that the future data-savvy workforce reflects a broad spectrum of scientific perspectives and backgrounds.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Adherence to Open Science principles and the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data standards is foundational to this synthesis project. We are fully committed to making all findings, synthesized datasets, and analytical workflows publicly available, aligning strictly with NCEMS community-created policies on open, team, and reproducible science.

All synthesized and harmonized datasets—linking PDB structural data with spectroscopic coherence records—will be deposited in Zenodo under a Creative Commons (CC-BY 4.0) license, ensuring they receive permanent Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs) for immediate community access. To guarantee the reproducibility of our AI models, all code related to the Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), data scraping scripts, and harmonization pipelines will be developed openly on GitHub. The final software tools will be released under an open-source MIT license. 

To ensure that our complex computational environments can be replicated by any researcher worldwide, we will containerize all analytical workflows using Docker. Jupyter Notebooks detailing step-by-step data processing, model training, and figure generation will be provided alongside the containers. 

Furthermore, we embrace the principles of open team science. The Working Group will maintain a public-facing project wiki documenting our methodologies, meeting minutes, and interim progress. All manuscripts resulting from this project will be submitted to open-access preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv or arXiv) concurrently with formal journal submission, ensuring immediate dissemination of our findings. We will also host a virtual, open-registration workshop at the conclusion of the project to train the broader scientific community on how to utilize our database and PINN models. By embedding these open science practices into the core of our daily operations, we ensure that our high-risk synthesis research remains transparent, reproducible, and maximally beneficial to the global scientific community.
budget_and_resources:
To successfully execute this community-scale synthesis project, we request NCEMS support totaling $450,000 over a two-year period. This budget is meticulously designed to support multidisciplinary collaboration, extensive computational needs, and the training of the next-generation workforce, requiring resources that go far beyond the capabilities of a single lab.

Trainee Support ($220,000): The majority of the budget is dedicated to human capital. We request funding for two postdoctoral researchers and three graduate students. These funds will cover stipends, benefits, and tuition. These trainees are the engine of the data synthesis and AI development, and this funding guarantees their immersion in a transdisciplinary, cross-institutional training environment.

Working Group Collaboration and Travel ($110,000): To foster deep integration across diverse scientific perspectives, we request support for four Working Group meetings. Two of these will be intensive, week-long, in-person 'synthesis hackathons' hosted at the NCEMS facility. The budget covers travel, lodging, and per diem for the 12 Working Group members and 5 trainees. The remaining two meetings will be major virtual summits, requiring funds for collaborative software licenses and digital whiteboard platforms.

Computational Resources ($80,000): Training Physics-Informed Neural Networks on massive structural and spectroscopic datasets requires significant computational power. We request funds for cloud computing credits (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud) to access high-performance GPU clusters necessary for deep learning and quantum dynamic simulations. 

Project Management and Open Science ($40,000): A transdisciplinary project of this scale requires dedicated logistical support. We request partial salary support for a Project Coordinator to manage data integration timelines, team communications, and adherence to open science mandates. Additionally, this covers publication costs for Gold Open Access journals and fees associated with long-term data hosting and repository maintenance. 

NCEMS support is critical; without the Center's logistical framework for transdisciplinary meetings and computational infrastructure, this trans-institutional synthesis would be impossible to coordinate.

author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: The 'Softness' of Cancer Mesoscales: Defining Malignancy Through Viscosity Metrics
abstract: Cancer cells often exhibit altered mechanical properties, but we lack a comprehensive 'Viscosity Map' of the malignant mesoscale. This project will synthesize microrheology data (cell stiffness) with proteomics and imaging of the cytoskeleton and condensates across hundreds of cancer cell lines. We aim to identify the 'Malignancy Viscosity Signature'—a specific state of mesoscale 'softness' that enables metastasis. We hypothesize that cancer emergence is driven by a physical phase-shift that allows for rapid structural remodeling. This synthesis project will provide a new physical lens for understanding cancer progression. It requires the integration of biophysical measurements with large-scale cancer-omics. Trainees will bridge oncology and biophysics, developing a 'Mechanical Biopsy' toolkit for the research community.
background_and_significance: The metastasis of cancer remains one of the most complex and lethal phenomena in human biology. Historically, oncology has sought to understand tumor progression primarily through the lenses of genomics and transcriptomics. However, metastasis is fundamentally a mechanical process. To disseminate, a cancer cell must physically deform to navigate the dense extracellular matrix, intravasate into the vasculature, and establish colonies in distant tissues. This requires a profound alteration in the cell's mechanical properties, often characterized by a distinct 'softness' or increased viscoelasticity compared to benign counterparts. Despite isolated biophysical studies confirming this phenomenon, the field lacks a comprehensive understanding of how this physical state emerges. We propose that this malignant softness is a classic example of an emergent property at the mesoscale. The mesoscale—the critical spatial domain between individual biomolecules and whole organelles—is where the dynamic interplay of the cytoskeletal network and biomolecular condensates (via liquid-liquid phase separation) dictates the physical state of the cytoplasm. Individual proteins do not possess 'viscosity'; rather, viscosity emerges from the collective, non-linear interactions of thousands of cross-linkers, motors, and phase-separating proteins. Currently, vast amounts of publicly available data exist across isolated domains: atomic force microscopy and microrheology datasets detail the stiffness of various cell lines; large-scale proteomics databases (like the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia) map protein abundances; and high-content imaging repositories (like the Image Data Resource) capture cytoskeletal architectures. However, these datasets remain siloed. There has been no community-scale synthesis to link molecular composition to emergent mesoscale physical properties across diverse cancer lineages. This gap in knowledge represents a critical bottleneck in physical oncology. By aligning with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS), this project will synthesize these disparate, publicly available datasets to map the 'Malignancy Viscosity Signature.' We will investigate how molecular alterations collectively trigger a physical phase-shift at the mesoscale, granting cancer cells the structural plasticity required for metastasis. This synthesis approach is significant because it shifts the paradigm from analyzing single genetic mutations to understanding the emergent biophysical state of the cell. It addresses a long-standing puzzle in cellular sciences: how do diverse, lineage-specific mutations converge on a common physical phenotype that drives lethality? Because answering this question requires the integration of large-scale multi-omics, advanced biophysics, and artificial intelligence, it is beyond the capability of any single laboratory. It demands a transdisciplinary Working Group to harmonize heterogeneous data, develop novel analytical strategies, and ultimately provide the broader scientific community with a unified 'Viscosity Map' of the malignant mesoscale, paving the way for novel mechanotherapeutics.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This synthesis project is driven by the overarching hypothesis that cancer metastasis is fundamentally dependent on an emergent mesoscale phenomenon: a physical phase-shift within the cytoplasm that produces a highly specific, dynamically remodelable 'soft' state. We term this the 'Malignancy Viscosity Signature.' We hypothesize that this signature emerges not from a single oncogene, but from the complex, non-linear stoichiometric alterations between cytoskeletal networks and phase-separating biomolecular condensates. To unpack this emergence, our Working Group will address three compelling, interconnected research questions using exclusively publicly available data. Research Question 1: Can we define a universal 'Malignancy Viscosity Signature' across diverse cancer lineages by integrating existing microrheology, proteomics, and imaging data? We hypothesize that despite vast genomic heterogeneity, highly metastatic cancer cell lines will converge on a narrow, identifiable range of mesoscale viscoelasticity. By synthesizing biophysical data from literature and databases with omics data, we expect to find that this 'softness' is a universal emergent requirement for metastasis, distinct from the physical states of benign or non-invasive malignant cells. Research Question 2: How do specific molecular networks—specifically the cytoskeletal interactome and condensate-forming proteins—interact to produce this emergent mesoscale softness? We hypothesize that alterations in the stoichiometric ratios of cytoskeletal cross-linkers, motor proteins, and intrinsically disordered proteins (which drive liquid-liquid phase separation) lower the energy barrier for rapid structural remodeling. We will use network analysis on public proteomic data to identify the 'hub' proteins whose relative abundances consistently correlate with the physical phase-shift observed in the biophysical datasets. We suspect that the emergent viscosity is highly sensitive to the density of biomolecular condensates that act as dynamic nodes within the actin-microtubule network. Research Question 3: Can artificial intelligence and machine learning models predict the mesoscale viscosity and metastatic potential of a cancer cell solely from its proteomic and structural imaging profiles? We hypothesize that the relationship between molecular composition, mesoscale architecture, and emergent physical properties contains predictable, high-dimensional patterns. By training deep learning models on synthesized multi-omic and imaging datasets, we can create a predictive 'Mechanical Biopsy' algorithm. This model will accurately map molecular signatures to physical phenotypes, effectively bypassing the need for low-throughput, direct mechanical testing. These questions directly align with the NCEMS mandate to address fundamental questions of emergence. By focusing on how mesoscale physical properties arise from molecular components, we are solving long-standing puzzles regarding the mechanics of cancer progression. Furthermore, these questions necessitate a community-scale synthesis; no single dataset contains both the molecular depth and the biophysical breadth required to identify this signature. By integrating these layers, we will stimulate novel questions about the physical limits of cellular life and the mechanical vulnerabilities of cancer.
methods_and_approach: To uncover the emergent 'Malignancy Viscosity Signature,' our Working Group will employ a purely computational, data-synthesis approach, rigorously avoiding the generation of new experimental data. Our methodology is structured into three integrated phases: Data Curation and Harmonization, Multi-scale Network Analysis, and AI-Driven Predictive Modeling. Phase 1: Data Curation and Harmonization. We will systematically mine, extract, and harmonize publicly available datasets across three domains. First, biophysical data (atomic force microscopy, particle tracking microrheology, and optical tweezers) will be extracted from published literature and physical oncology databases to compile viscoelastic metrics (elastic modulus, loss modulus, relaxation times) for hundreds of cancer cell lines. Second, corresponding deep proteomics and transcriptomics will be sourced from the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE), DepMap, and PRIDE. Third, high-content structural imaging of the cytoskeleton and biomolecular condensates will be retrieved from the Image Data Resource (IDR) and the Cell Image Library. The primary methodological challenge—and a key innovation of this project—is the development of a unified data ontology. We will create a standardized computational framework that maps disparate biophysical metrics to standardized molecular identifiers (e.g., UniProt IDs) across identical cell lines, accounting for varying experimental conditions. Phase 2: Multi-scale Network Analysis. To understand the emergence of mesoscale softness, we will utilize advanced dimensionality reduction (e.g., UMAP, t-SNE) and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) adapted for proteomics. We will construct bipartite networks linking the abundance of cytoskeletal cross-linkers and intrinsically disordered proteins to specific viscoelastic states. By applying graph-theoretic measures, we will identify critical molecular nodes that govern the physical phase-shift. We will specifically analyze the stoichiometric ratios of condensate-forming proteins to structural filaments, testing our hypothesis that liquid-liquid phase separation dynamics are the primary drivers of emergent mesoscale remodeling. Phase 3: AI-Driven Predictive Modeling. We will develop the 'Mechanical Biopsy' toolkit using a suite of machine learning architectures. We will train Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on the protein-protein interaction networks and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) on the high-content imaging data. These models will be integrated into a multimodal deep learning framework designed to predict the continuous variables of cell stiffness and viscosity. The models will be rigorously validated using hold-out sets and cross-lineage validation techniques to ensure generalizability. Team Structure and Training: This project requires an unprecedented level of cross-disciplinary collaboration. Our Working Group will consist of biophysicists, computational oncologists, data scientists, and machine learning experts from diverse geographic and institutional backgrounds. We will establish structured sub-teams led jointly by senior PIs and trainees. Graduate students and postdocs will be the primary drivers of the data integration pipelines, receiving intensive cross-training. A biophysicist trainee will learn advanced deep learning, while a computer science trainee will master the nuances of cellular mechanobiology, directly fulfilling the NCEMS goal of training a transdisciplinary, data-savvy workforce.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes for both the molecular biosciences and the broader scientific community, fundamentally shifting how we understand and diagnose cancer. The primary scientific outcome will be the publication of the first comprehensive 'Viscosity Map' of the malignant mesoscale. By proving that diverse molecular mutations converge on an emergent physical phase-shift, we will establish a new paradigm in oncology: metastasis as a disease of mesoscale mechanics. This will solve the long-standing puzzle of how genetically distinct cancers achieve the same physical capacity for tissue invasion. The most significant methodological deliverable will be the 'Mechanical Biopsy' toolkit. This open-source, AI-driven computational platform will allow researchers and eventually clinicians to input standard proteomic or transcriptomic data and output highly accurate predictions of a tumor's mesoscale physical state and metastatic potential. This eliminates the need for specialized, low-throughput biophysical equipment, democratizing mechanobiology and accelerating the discovery of novel mechanotherapeutics—drugs designed to artificially stiffen cancer cells to halt metastasis. Beyond the scientific deliverables, the impact on workforce development will be profound. The project will train a cohort of postdoctoral fellows and graduate students at the bleeding edge of data science, AI, and biophysics. These trainees will emerge as bilingual scientists, fully fluent in both the biological realities of the mesoscale and the computational architectures required to model them. By uniting diverse talent from multiple institutions through the NCEMS infrastructure, we will foster a new, collaborative sub-field of computational mechanobiology, ensuring that the insights gained from this synthesis project catalyze decades of future transdisciplinary research.
open_science_and_reproducibility: Our Working Group is deeply committed to the principles of Open Science and strict adherence to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data practices, aligning fully with NCEMS community standards. Because our project relies entirely on synthesizing publicly available data, ensuring the transparency and reproducibility of our integration pipelines is our highest priority. All harmonized datasets, including the unified biophysical-molecular ontology and the comprehensive 'Viscosity Map,' will be deposited into open-access repositories such as Zenodo and the Open Science Framework (OSF) under a CC-BY license. To guarantee computational reproducibility, all code for data extraction, network analysis, and the 'Mechanical Biopsy' AI models will be developed openly on GitHub. We will provide comprehensive documentation, including detailed README files, step-by-step tutorials, and fully containerized computational environments using Docker. This ensures that any researcher, regardless of their local operating system, can execute our exact workflows and reproduce our findings. Furthermore, we will utilize Jupyter and Google Colab notebooks to allow the community to interact with our AI models directly in their browsers without requiring high-performance computing infrastructure. We commit to pre-registering our primary hypotheses and analytical plans on OSF prior to executing the multi-omic integration to prevent p-hacking and analytical bias. All resulting publications will be submitted to open-access journals or made immediately available via pre-print servers such as bioRxiv. Finally, our trainees will host bi-monthly open webinars and virtual 'hackathons' to share our intermediate data harmonization tools with the broader NCEMS community, actively soliciting feedback and fostering a culture of radical transparency and collaborative, team-based science.
budget_and_resources: To successfully execute this ambitious synthesis project, we require the unique logistical, computational, and collaborative resources provided by NCEMS, which far exceed the capabilities of a single laboratory or standard grant mechanism. We are requesting support primarily for personnel, community-building Working Group meetings, and advanced computational infrastructure. Personnel: We request funding for two full-time Postdoctoral Synthesis Fellows. These fellows will be the operational engines of the project. One fellow, with a background in biophysics, will lead the data harmonization and ontology development. The second fellow, specializing in AI/ML, will lead the development of the 'Mechanical Biopsy' toolkit. We also request partial stipend support for three graduate trainees who will assist in data curation while receiving cross-disciplinary training. Working Group Meetings: The core of this synthesis effort relies on deep, transdisciplinary collaboration. We request travel and logistical support for four in-person Working Group meetings (bi-annual over two years) to be held at the NCEMS headquarters. These intensive, multi-day sessions will bring together our diverse team of oncologists, physicists, and computer scientists to brainstorm, troubleshoot integration bottlenecks, and synthesize findings. Between in-person meetings, we request support for digital collaboration tools to host monthly virtual sprints. Computational Resources: Synthesizing terabytes of high-content imaging data and training multimodal deep learning models requires significant computational power. We request funding for cloud computing credits (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud Platform) to provide the necessary GPU instances for training our Convolutional and Graph Neural Networks. NCEMS Justification: This project is uniquely suited for NCEMS because it bridges disciplines that rarely share funding streams, vocabularies, or data standards. NCEMS's infrastructure is essential to provide the collaborative scaffolding, open-science guidance, and synthesis-focused environment required to transform fragmented public data into a cohesive understanding of emergent mesoscale cancer mechanics.

author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: Evolution of the Centrosome as a Computational Hub: Logic Gates in Centrosomal Proteomes
abstract: The centrosome is the microtubule-organizing center, but it also serves as a signaling scaffold. This project will synthesize centrosomal proteomes across the eukaryotic tree to identify how its 'computational capacity' has evolved. Using Graph Theory, we will model the centrosome as a 'network router' that integrates cell-cycle signals. We hypothesize that the evolution of complex life was enabled by the emergence of specific 'Logic Gates' within the centrosome that allow for more sophisticated spatial decisions. This synthesis addresses the evolutionary origin of cellular intelligence. It requires a massive integration of phylogenetic and proteomic data. Trainees will gain expertise in evolutionary cell biology and network modeling, uncovering the 'hardware' of cellular logic.
background_and_significance: The emergence of complex cellular behaviors relies on the integration of vast arrays of molecular signals into coherent physiological responses. Central to this information processing in eukaryotic cells is the centrosome. Traditionally characterized merely as the primary microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) responsible for nucleating and anchoring microtubules, the centrosome is increasingly recognized as a highly sophisticated, mesoscale signaling scaffold. It operates exactly at the scale NCEMS targets: the critical mesoscale bridging individual biomolecules and higher-order subcellular organelles. The centrosome concentrates kinases, phosphatases, and cell-cycle regulators, facilitating dynamic protein-protein interactions (PPIs) that govern mitosis, cell polarity, and differentiation. However, a fundamental mystery remains: how do the physical interactions of proteins at this mesoscale hub give rise to the emergent property of 'cellular decision-making' or 'cellular intelligence'? We propose that the centrosome functions as a computational hub—a network router that processes biochemical inputs through structured topological motifs analogous to electronic logic gates (e.g., AND, OR, NOT gates). While individual studies have identified specific signaling cascades localized to the centrosome, no study has yet synthesized the massive, publicly available proteomic and phylogenetic datasets to understand this organelle as a cohesive, evolving computational entity. The complexity of mesoscale phenomena like centrosomal signal integration cannot be understood by examining single proteins in isolated model organisms. It requires a transdisciplinary synthesis of data across the entire eukaryotic tree of life. Over the past two decades, vast amounts of data—including mass spectrometry-based proteomics, transcriptomics, and whole-genome sequences—have been deposited into public repositories. Yet, these data remain fragmented. By integrating these disparate datasets, this project will trace the evolutionary trajectory of the centrosomal proteome from the Last Eukaryotic Common Ancestor (LECA) to modern metazoans. We will investigate how the accretion of new proteins and the rewiring of interaction networks expanded the centrosome’s computational capacity. This synthesis directly aligns with the NCEMS mission to leverage data science to uncover emergent properties at the mesoscale. By modeling the centrosome as a computational hub, we will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how cells make robust spatial and temporal decisions during division and development. Furthermore, identifying the evolutionary origins of these 'logic gates' will provide profound insights into how the transition to multicellularity and complex tissue architecture was fundamentally enabled by innovations in mesoscale cellular hardware. This project represents a paradigm shift, moving the field away from viewing the centrosome as a static structural anchor and toward understanding it as a dynamic, emergent computational engine.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This synthesis project is driven by three overarching research questions that explore the emergent computational properties of the centrosome through an evolutionary lens. 

Question 1: How has the topological complexity of the centrosomal protein-protein interaction (PPI) network evolved across the eukaryotic tree of life? We hypothesize that the centrosome evolved from a structurally simple MTOC in early eukaryotes into a highly complex signaling hub through the stepwise accretion of modular protein networks. We predict that while the core structural components (e.g., centriolar cartwheel proteins like SAS-6) remain highly conserved, the peripheral matrix (pericentriolar material, PCM) has undergone massive expansion, recruiting diverse signaling molecules that dramatically increased the network's connectivity and computational potential.

Question 2: Can we identify discrete mathematical network motifs within the centrosomal proteome that function as biochemical logic gates, and how do these motifs integrate cell-cycle signals? We hypothesize that the emergent decision-making capacity of the centrosome is physically instantiated by specific graph-theoretical motifs, such as feed-forward and feedback loops, which act as Boolean logic gates (AND, OR, NOT, XOR). For example, we predict that the simultaneous recruitment of a specific kinase and the removal of a phosphatase are required to activate a downstream effector, functioning as a strict 'AND' gate that prevents premature mitotic entry. We will systematically map these gates across different species to understand the fundamental rules of mesoscale signal routing.

Question 3: Does the emergence of novel centrosomal logic gates correlate with major evolutionary transitions in cellular complexity, such as the development of multicellularity and specialized cell types? We hypothesize that the evolution of complex, multicellular life was directly enabled by the emergence of sophisticated spatial and temporal logic gates within the centrosome. We predict that early-branching unicellular eukaryotes possess basic centrosomal networks capable of simple 'ON/OFF' cell-cycle transitions, whereas metazoans possess highly layered, multi-gate networks capable of integrating diverse inputs (e.g., DNA damage, mechanical tension, metabolic state) to dictate complex outcomes like asymmetric cell division and ciliogenesis. 

By addressing these questions, we will uncover the rules governing how molecular interactions scale up to create emergent cellular logic. We hypothesize that 'cellular intelligence' is not a nebulous concept, but a quantifiable emergent property arising from the specific, evolved topology of mesoscale protein networks. Testing these hypotheses requires a massive, community-scale integration of phylogenetic profiles, public proteomics data, and advanced network theory, which far exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory and necessitates the collaborative environment fostered by NCEMS.
methods_and_approach:
This project will employ a purely synthetic, computational approach, utilizing existing publicly available data and requiring zero new experimental data generation. Our multidisciplinary Working Group—comprising evolutionary biologists, computational cell biologists, graph theorists, and AI specialists—will execute a four-phase research strategy.

Phase 1: Community-Scale Data Integration and Curation. We will systematically harvest centrosomal proteomic data, transcriptomes, and genomic sequences from diverse public repositories, including PRIDE, UniProt, OrthoDB, and the Eukaryotic Pathogen Database (EuPathDB). We will integrate these datasets to define the 'centrosome-associated proteome' across 100 diverse eukaryotic lineages, representing all major supergroups (Obazoa, Amoebozoa, Excavata, SAR, and Archaeplastida). Data harmonization will be achieved using automated orthology mapping algorithms to ensure consistent nomenclature and functional annotation across highly divergent species.

Phase 2: Phylogenomic Reconstruction of the Centrosome. Using the curated datasets, we will perform advanced phylogenetic profiling to reconstruct the evolutionary history of every centrosomal component. We will utilize maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference models to map the gain, loss, and duplication of centrosomal proteins onto the eukaryotic tree of life. This will allow us to reconstruct the ancestral centrosomal proteome of the Last Eukaryotic Common Ancestor (LECA) and trace the chronological accretion of signaling modules at key evolutionary nodes, such as the emergence of metazoans.

Phase 3: Graph Theoretical Modeling of Mesoscale Logic Gates. For each evolutionary node, we will construct comprehensive Protein-Protein Interaction (PPI) networks using data from STRING, BioGRID, and IntAct. We will apply advanced Graph Theory to analyze the topology of these mesoscale networks. Specifically, we will utilize subgraph isomorphism algorithms to scan the networks for overrepresented structural motifs (e.g., coherent and incoherent feed-forward loops, multi-input cascades). We will translate these motifs into Boolean logic models, defining how input signals (e.g., phosphorylation events) are routed through the network to produce discrete output states (e.g., microtubule nucleation, centrosome duplication).

Phase 4: AI-Driven Simulation of Signal Routing and Emergence. To understand how these static networks produce dynamic, emergent decision-making, we will deploy Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning techniques. We will train Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on the topological features of the centrosomal networks to predict the computational capacity of different evolutionary variations. Furthermore, we will use dynamic Boolean network simulations to model how signal perturbations (analogous to genetic mutations or environmental stress) propagate through the centrosomal logic gates. 

Throughout all phases, trainees (graduate students and postdocs) will be cross-trained in phylogenomics, network theory, and machine learning, ensuring the development of a highly skilled, data-savvy workforce capable of tackling complex mesoscale biological problems.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that fundamentally alter our understanding of mesoscale biology and cellular evolution. First, it will establish a new scientific paradigm: the centrosome as an evolvable computational hub rather than a mere structural scaffold. By mapping the 'hardware' of cellular logic, we will solve long-standing mysteries regarding how cells make robust, integrated decisions during division and differentiation. 

Second, we will generate 'CentroLogicDB', a comprehensive, first-of-its-kind, open-access database and interactive web portal. This resource will provide the global scientific community with searchable, evolutionary PPI networks and mapped logic gates for centrosomes across the eukaryotic tree. CentroLogicDB will serve as a foundational tool for researchers in cancer biology (where centrosome amplification is a hallmark) and synthetic biology (guiding the design of artificial, mesoscale decision-making organelles).

Third, the project will have a profound impact on workforce development. By deeply integrating trainees into our multidisciplinary Working Group, we will train a new generation of scientists fluent in both evolutionary cell biology and advanced data science. Postdocs and graduate students will lead the AI-driven network modeling and phylogenomic analyses, gaining invaluable experience in transdisciplinary collaboration, big data synthesis, and open science practices.

Finally, this project will strongly validate the NCEMS mission by demonstrating how the synthesis of existing, siloed public data—analyzed through the lens of graph theory and AI—can reveal the unexpected emergence of complex system properties at the mesoscale. The insights gained here regarding the evolution of biochemical logic gates will provide a universal framework applicable to other mesoscale organelles and condensates, thereby catalyzing broad advancements across the molecular and cellular biosciences.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the highest standards of open, team, and reproducible science, strictly adhering to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles. Because this project relies entirely on the synthesis of publicly available data, reproducibility of our computational pipelines is paramount. 

All data curation, phylogenomic reconstruction, and graph-theoretical modeling workflows will be developed as modular, fully documented code (primarily in Python and R). This code will be maintained in a publicly accessible GitHub repository under an MIT open-source license, utilizing strict version control. To eliminate the 'it works on my machine' problem and ensure absolute reproducibility, all computational environments, dependencies, and AI models (including the Graph Neural Networks) will be containerized using Docker and Singularity. 

We will utilize Jupyter Notebooks to create interactive, step-by-step tutorials of our analytical pipelines, allowing the broader community to easily replicate our findings or apply our methods to other mesoscale organelles. The final synthesized datasets, network models, and the CentroLogicDB database will be deposited in Zenodo, ensuring long-term archiving and the assignment of permanent Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs). 

We are committed to rapid and open dissemination of our findings. All manuscripts generated by the Working Group will be posted to preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv) concurrently with submission to peer-reviewed, open-access journals. Furthermore, to foster community engagement and transparent science, we will host quarterly open webinars to share our progress, demonstrate our analytical tools, and solicit feedback from the broader molecular and cellular biology community. Our comprehensive Data Management Plan, overseen by a designated Open Science Coordinator within the team, will guarantee that every output of this NCEMS-funded project remains a permanent, accessible asset to the public.
budget_and_resources:
To successfully execute this ambitious, community-scale synthesis project, we require the unique support and collaborative infrastructure provided by NCEMS. The requested budget is specifically tailored to facilitate transdisciplinary collaboration, advanced computation, and trainee development, with no funds allocated for wet-lab experimental research.

Working Group Meetings and Collaboration: We request funding to support three intensive, in-person Working Group meetings at the NCEMS facility over the project period. These funds will cover travel, lodging, and per diem for our diverse team of 12 investigators (spanning evolutionary biology, computer science, and biochemistry) from various institutions and career stages. These face-to-face meetings are critical for synthesizing diverse scientific perspectives, brainstorming network modeling approaches, and developing the conceptual framework for centrosomal logic gates.

Training the Next Generation: A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to supporting two Postdoctoral Fellows and three Graduate Students. These trainees will be the primary drivers of the data synthesis and AI modeling. The budget covers their stipends, benefits, and travel to the Working Group meetings, directly fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to train a data-savvy scientific workforce.

Computational Resources: Given the massive scale of the phylogenetic and proteomic data integration, and the computational intensity of training Graph Neural Networks, we request funds for cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud Platform). This will ensure the team has the necessary processing power and storage capacity to execute complex graph-theoretical simulations without bottlenecking local institutional servers.

Open Science and Dissemination: Finally, we request funds to cover open-access publication fees, the hosting and maintenance costs for the 'CentroLogicDB' web portal, and long-term data archiving. 

This project is fundamentally beyond the capabilities of any single research lab. It requires the dedicated synthesis environment, computational support, and collaborative convergence that only NCEMS can provide to unlock the emergent properties of mesoscale cellular intelligence.

author: gemini-3-pro-preview
title: The Thermoelectric Cell: Temperature Gradients as Drivers of Mesoscale Organization
abstract: Active metabolism generates heat, and intracellular temperature gradients may exist at the mesoscale. This project will synthesize data from fluorescent thermometry and metabolic flux records to investigate if cells utilize 'Thermal Emergence.' We hypothesize that temperature gradients across membranes and large complexes drive the spatial organization of the cell through thermophoresis (movement in response to temperature). Using manifold learning, we will correlate local heat production with the positioning of organelles. This project explores a completely new dimension of cellular organization: the 'Thermodynamic Map' of the cell. It requires a synthesis of biophysics and high-resolution sensing data. Trainees will explore the intersections of thermodynamics and cell biology, developing models for how thermal energy is harnessed for mesoscale assembly.
background_and_significance:
The prevailing paradigm in molecular and cellular biology operates under the assumption that the interior of a cell is essentially isothermal. Traditional models of mesoscale organization—the critical spatial domain bridging individual biomolecules and intact organelles—rely heavily on chemical gradients, molecular crowding, and cytoskeletal scaffolding. However, this isothermal assumption overlooks a fundamental byproduct of active metabolism: heat. Intracellular biochemical reactions, particularly those localized to mitochondria and large macromolecular complexes, are highly exothermic. Recent breakthroughs in nanoscale thermometry, including fluorescent polymeric thermometers and nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in nanodiamonds, have provided tantalizing glimpses of transient, localized temperature spikes within living cells. Despite these observations, the broader implications of intracellular temperature gradients remain a highly debated and largely unexplored frontier.

This project introduces the concept of 'Thermal Emergence,' positing that these localized temperature gradients do not simply dissipate instantaneously but instead form stable, mesoscale thermodynamic maps that actively drive cellular organization. Through the biophysical mechanism of thermophoresis—the directed movement of particles in a temperature gradient (the Soret effect)—we propose that thermal energy is harnessed to orchestrate the spatial positioning of organelles and the assembly of mesoscale macromolecular complexes.

Understanding Thermal Emergence is fundamentally beyond the capacity of any single research laboratory. Currently, fluorescent thermometry data is siloed in biophysics labs focused on tool development, while metabolic flux and spatial organelle maps are housed in separate cell biology and systems biology databases. A critical barrier to understanding mesoscale emergence has been the inability to merge these orthogonal datasets. By overlaying the thermal output of metabolic enzymes onto the high-resolution spatial coordinates of organelles, we can begin to decode the physical rules governing cellular architecture.

By leveraging the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS), this project will synthesize publicly available high-resolution fluorescent thermometry records, comprehensive metabolic flux maps, and spatial proteomics datasets. The significance of this synthesis is twofold. First, it addresses a critical gap in our understanding of mesoscale emergence by introducing thermodynamics as a primary, active driver of spatial organization, thereby challenging decades of isothermal assumptions. Second, it answers the NCEMS call to solve long-standing puzzles in cellular biosciences by providing a novel mechanism for how cells achieve rapid, energy-efficient spatial organization without relying solely on ATP-dependent motor proteins or slow passive diffusion. By mapping the 'Thermodynamic Map' of the cell, we will uncover how emergent properties at the mesoscale are dictated by the flow of thermal energy, fundamentally reshaping our understanding of cell biology.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
To rigorously investigate the concept of Thermal Emergence and its role in mesoscale cellular organization, this synthesis project is guided by a set of interconnected, compelling scientific questions and testable hypotheses. By integrating diverse publicly available datasets, we aim to uncover the hidden thermodynamic architecture of the cell.

Research Questions:
1. Do stable, functional temperature gradients exist at the mesoscale within eukaryotic cells, and how do they map onto known metabolic and structural topologies?
2. To what extent does thermophoresis (the Soret effect) drive the spatial organization, clustering, and segregation of mesoscale assemblies, such as biomolecular condensates and ribosomes, relative to heat-producing organelles?
3. How do variations in metabolic flux—and the resulting alterations in local heat production—dynamically reshape the cellular 'Thermodynamic Map' and subsequent organelle positioning?
4. Can we develop a predictive, AI-driven model that correlates localized heat generation with the emergent spatial architecture of the cell?

Hypotheses:
Hypothesis 1: The Existence of a Mesoscale Thermodynamic Map. We hypothesize that the cell is not isothermal; rather, continuous, localized metabolic activity (e.g., mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, proteasomal degradation) generates sustained, mesoscale thermal gradients. We predict that synthesizing nanoscale thermometry data with metabolic flux records will reveal a highly structured, dynamic 'Thermodynamic Map' characterized by distinct thermal peaks and valleys that correlate with specific subcellular niches.

Hypothesis 2: Thermal Emergence via Thermophoresis. We hypothesize that these mesoscale thermal gradients act as a fundamental, non-chemical driver of spatial organization. Specifically, we predict that large macromolecular complexes and specific organelles exhibit directed thermophoretic movement, migrating toward or away from heat sources based on their biophysical properties. We further predict that the magnitude of the Soret effect at the mesoscale is heavily dependent on the localized crowding of the cytoplasm, which acts to amplify thermal gradients by reducing thermal conductivity.

Hypothesis 3: Metabolic-Spatial Coupling. We hypothesize that cellular spatial organization is intrinsically coupled to metabolic state via thermal output. We predict that datasets capturing metabolic perturbations will correlate strongly with global reorganizations of the mesoscale architecture, driven by the shifting thermodynamic landscape.

Hypothesis 4: AI-Driven Predictability of Thermal Assembly. We hypothesize that the complex, high-dimensional relationship between local heat production, molecular crowding, and organelle positioning can be accurately modeled using advanced manifold learning techniques. By leveraging these AI tools, we aim to extract fundamental biophysical constants from purely observational data, bridging the gap between theoretical thermodynamics and empirical cell biology.
methods_and_approach:
This project strictly adheres to the NCEMS mandate of conducting community-scale synthesis without generating new experimental data. Our approach relies on the integration of massive, publicly available datasets and the application of advanced artificial intelligence, specifically manifold learning, combined with rigorous biophysical modeling. The methodology is divided into three primary phases: Data Acquisition and Standardization, AI-Driven Synthesis, and Biophysical Validation.

Phase 1: Data Acquisition and Standardization
We will aggregate existing, disparate datasets from public repositories such as the Image Data Resource (IDR), EMBL-EBI, and the NIH 4D Nucleome project. The datasets will include:
1. Nanoscale Thermometry Data: Publicly available fluorescent polymeric thermometer imaging, nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center nanodiamond tracking, and genetically encoded thermocouple data.
2. Spatial Architecture Data: High-resolution 3D organelle tracking via lattice light-sheet microscopy, spatial proteomics, and transcriptomics maps.
3. Metabolic Flux Records: Spatiotemporal maps of ATP/ADP ratios, oxygen consumption rates, and localized metabolic enzyme concentrations.
The primary methodological challenge is standardization. We will develop an open-source computational pipeline to co-register these multiscale datasets into a unified 3D spatiotemporal coordinate system, effectively creating a foundational 'Thermodynamic-Spatial Data Cube.'

Phase 2: AI-Driven Synthesis via Manifold Learning
To uncover the hidden relationships between heat production and mesoscale organization, we will employ advanced AI and data science techniques. We will utilize manifold learning algorithms—specifically Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) and deep autoencoders—to reduce dimensionality and identify the underlying topological structures of the data. Specifically, we will utilize autoencoders to denoise the disparate datasets and establish a latent space representation of the cell's physical state. From this latent space, UMAP will project the data into a 3D visualization, allowing the Working Group to intuitively identify non-random spatial assortments that correlate with thermal peaks. We will train graph neural networks (GNNs) to correlate local heat production profiles with the dynamic positioning of organelles, thereby constructing the first predictive map of the cell.

Phase 3: Biophysical Modeling of Thermophoresis
AI-derived correlations require mechanistic validation. We will synthesize our manifold learning outputs with theoretical biophysics. Using continuum mechanics and stochastic thermodynamics, we will model thermophoretic drift within the crowded, viscoelastic environment of the cytoplasm. These simulations will be cross-referenced with the AI predictions to establish a causal link between heat generation and spatial organization, ensuring our models are grounded in established physical laws.

Working Group Collaboration and Training
This approach requires a transdisciplinary Working Group comprising data scientists, biophysicists, and cell biologists. Trainees will lead the development of the data integration pipelines and manifold learning models, actively participating in NCEMS-hosted synthesis hackathons, thereby building the future data-savvy workforce required to tackle complex mesoscale phenomena.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project is designed to deliver transformative outcomes that fundamentally shift our understanding of cellular biology, directly addressing the NCEMS mission to decode mesoscale emergence.

1. The First Cellular Thermodynamic Map: The primary outcome will be the creation of the first comprehensive, 3D 'Thermodynamic Map' of a eukaryotic cell. By synthesizing previously disjointed thermometry and spatial datasets, we will provide the scientific community with a dynamic atlas detailing how temperature gradients fluctuate and stabilize at the mesoscale in response to metabolic demands.

2. A New Paradigm for Mesoscale Organization: We expect to validate 'Thermal Emergence' as a core principle of cellular organization. Demonstrating that thermophoresis actively drives the spatial positioning of organelles and macromolecular complexes will solve a long-standing puzzle regarding how cells achieve rapid, energy-efficient spatial coordination without relying exclusively on cytoskeletal networks. This challenges the deeply entrenched isothermal assumption in biology.

3. Innovative Analytical Frameworks: We will produce a suite of novel, AI-driven analytical tools. The manifold learning algorithms and biophysical simulation frameworks developed to correlate heat production with spatial organization will be generalized, allowing researchers to apply these methods to other complex, emergent biological phenomena.

4. Workforce Development and Training Impact: The project will cultivate a new generation of data-savvy scientists. Postdoctoral researchers and graduate students will gain unparalleled, cross-disciplinary expertise at the intersection of AI, data science, biophysics, and cell biology. By leading the synthesis efforts within our Working Group, these trainees will be uniquely positioned to drive the future of computational systems biology.

Ultimately, this project will catalyze a new subfield—cellular thermodynamics—providing deep, broad insights into how physical forces and biological structures co-emerge at the mesoscale.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the principles of open, team, and reproducible science, fully aligning with the NCEMS mandate to make all findings, data, and analysis workflows publicly accessible. We recognize that community-scale synthesis relies heavily on transparency and collaboration.

Data and Code Availability: All standardized datasets, including the integrated 'Thermodynamic-Spatial Data Cubes,' will be deposited in recognized, open-access repositories such as Zenodo and the Image Data Resource (IDR), adhering strictly to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles. All original code, manifold learning algorithms, and biophysical models will be hosted on a public GitHub repository under an open-source license (e.g., MIT or GNU GPL).

Reproducibility: To ensure absolute reproducibility of our AI models and analytical pipelines, we will utilize containerization technologies such as Docker and Singularity. These containers will encapsulate our entire computational environment, allowing any researcher globally to download and execute our workflows with identical results. Furthermore, detailed, step-by-step computational protocols will be published on Protocols.io.

Open Access Publishing: We are committed to disseminating our findings rapidly. All manuscripts will be uploaded to preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv) concurrently with submission to peer-reviewed, open-access journals. This ensures immediate community access to our insights regarding Thermal Emergence.

Community Engagement: Beyond static data sharing, we will actively engage the scientific community. We plan to host virtual workshops and webinars through NCEMS to train external researchers on how to utilize our Thermodynamic Map software and manifold learning pipelines. By providing comprehensive Jupyter Notebooks and interactive web-based visualization tools, we will empower researchers from diverse fields to explore the thermal dimension of their own cellular data.
budget_and_resources:
This ambitious, community-scale synthesis project requires the unique infrastructure and support provided by NCEMS, as it fundamentally exceeds the financial and collaborative capabilities of any single laboratory. The requested budget is meticulously allocated to support team science, advanced computation, and the training of the next-generation workforce.

Personnel and Training (50%): The majority of the budget is dedicated to supporting two Postdoctoral Fellows and three Graduate Students. These trainees will serve as the engine of the synthesis project, bridging the gap between data science and biophysics. Funding covers their stipends, benefits, and dedicated training programs in manifold learning and open science practices, fulfilling the NCEMS goal of developing a data-savvy workforce.

Working Group Collaboration (25%): To stimulate cross-disciplinary collaboration, funds are requested to support biannual, intensive, week-long synthesis meetings (hackathons) at the NCEMS headquarters. This includes travel, lodging, and per diem for our diverse team of biophysicists, cell biologists, and data scientists across multiple institutions. These face-to-face interactions are critical for overcoming disciplinary language barriers and fostering the transdisciplinary insights required for studying mesoscale emergence.

Computational Resources (15%): Synthesizing massive, high-dimensional datasets and training complex manifold learning algorithms requires significant computational power. We request funds for cloud computing credits (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud) and access to high-performance computing (HPC) clusters. This ensures our trainees have the necessary infrastructure to process spatial transcriptomics and thermometry data without institutional bottlenecks.

Open Science and Dissemination (10%): Funds are allocated to cover open-access publication fees, data storage costs in public repositories (e.g., Zenodo), and the hosting of community training workshops.

NCEMS Justification: This project does not request funds for experimental equipment or wet-lab supplies. The entire budget is optimized for data synthesis, AI-driven analysis, and collaborative team building.

author: gpt-5.2
title: Phase transitions as cellular decision points across stress granules, P-bodies, and nucleoli
abstract:
This working group asks how phase transitions as cellular decision points across stress granules, p-bodies, and nucleoli can be understood as an emergent property that links molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcome. The scientific question is not simply whether particular molecules, organelles, or pathways are associated with a phenotype, but whether publicly available datasets can reveal rules by which many molecular parts collectively produce a new, system-level behavior at the scale between biomolecules and organelles. The project is designed for the NCEMS model because the relevant evidence is scattered across incompatible imaging repositories, omics studies, perturbation resources, structural annotations, and specialized literatures; no single laboratory is likely to have the biological breadth, data-engineering capacity, and methodological expertise to integrate them.

The group would synthesize existing public data centered on imaging + proteomics, prioritizing datasets with reusable metadata, perturbation or state annotations, and links to downstream cellular phenotypes. Depending on availability, sources could include public cell atlases, the Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, EMBL-EBI and NCBI functional genomics repositories, BioImage Archive or Image Data Resource collections, PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics datasets, public CRISPR or RNAi screens, AlphaFold/PDB-derived structural features, and curated pathway or protein-interaction resources. The core analytic strategy would be causal discovery: harmonizing measurements into a common representation; explicitly modeling uncertainty, batch effects, and missingness; and testing whether mesoscale variables explain cellular outcomes above and beyond molecular abundance alone. The biological scope would focus on cross-kingdom/cross-species while deliberately including comparison cases that prevent the group from mistaking a narrow model-system pattern for a general law.

The novel element is the unit of explanation. Instead of treating mesoscale organization as an image label, downstream readout, or anecdotal mechanism, the working group would make it the primary object of synthesis: a measurable layer where composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion combine. The expected product is a predictive atlas that is open, versioned, and reusable, with transparent workflows, community-agreed metadata standards, and tutorials for trainees. The project would bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, imaging scientists, omics researchers, statisticians, machine-learning researchers, data curators, and trainees across institution types. Training would occur through hackathon-style data sprints, reproducible workflow clinics, and rotating trainee leadership of cross-dataset validation tasks. The anticipated contribution is both scientific and infrastructural: a defensible answer to a specific emergence question, plus a generalizable synthesis strategy that helps the molecular and cellular biosciences reuse public data to discover phenomena that only become visible when datasets, disciplines, and scales are brought together.
background_and_significance:
Biomolecular condensates such as stress granules (SGs), processing bodies (P-bodies), and nucleoli are mesoscale cellular structures that arise from collective molecular interactions and can reorganize rapidly in response to environmental and developmental cues. They are widely discussed as products of liquid–liquid phase separation and related phase transitions, yet the field still lacks general, predictive rules linking (i) molecular composition (proteins, RNAs, post-translational modifications), (ii) emergent mesoscale material properties (assembly/disassembly thresholds, viscosity, internal organization, multiphase structure), and (iii) cellular outcomes (translation control, RNA decay, ribosome biogenesis, stress survival, proteostasis, and disease phenotypes). This gap persists not because of a lack of data, but because the data are fragmented across imaging repositories, proteomics and transcriptomics studies, perturbation screens, and structural/sequence annotation resources, each using different assays, metadata conventions, and model systems.

From an emergence perspective, condensates are compelling because they represent a “new level of description” that is neither reducible to individual molecule abundance nor adequately captured by organelle-level labels. Condensate formation can act as a cellular decision point: a thresholded, history-dependent transition that re-routes molecular traffic, changes reaction rates, and buffers or amplifies fluctuations. For example, SG assembly can sequester translation factors and specific mRNAs; P-bodies can concentrate decay machinery; and nucleolar reorganization can reflect changes in ribosome biogenesis and stress signaling. Across these systems, a recurring puzzle is why similar molecular components sometimes yield distinct mesoscale architectures and outcomes, and why different stressors or perturbations can lead to superficially similar granules with divergent functional consequences.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis effort aimed at extracting generalizable rules from existing public data. First, the relevant evidence is inherently multidisciplinary: cell biology (organelle identity and function), biophysics (phase behavior and material states), imaging science (segmentation and feature extraction), proteomics/transcriptomics (composition and stoichiometry), and causal/statistical modeling (inference under confounding and batch effects). Second, the necessary integration is beyond typical single-lab capacity: harmonizing heterogeneous imaging and omics datasets, aligning perturbation annotations, and building cross-study models that quantify uncertainty and generalize across species and cell types. Third, this problem aligns with NCEMS’s mesoscale focus: condensates sit between biomolecules and organelles, and their emergent properties are hypothesized to influence higher-order subcellular and cellular outcomes.

The significance of this working group is twofold. Scientifically, it will test whether phase-transition-like behaviors can be formalized as decision points with measurable mesoscale variables that causally mediate outcomes. Methodologically, it will develop a reusable synthesis framework—data standards, harmonization pipelines, and causal discovery workflows—that can be applied to other emergent mesoscale phenomena (e.g., cytoskeletal assemblies, membrane-less compartments, and chromatin domains). By committing to open science and trainee-centered collaboration, the group will also strengthen the community’s capacity to reuse public molecular and cellular data for discovery rather than only retrospective validation.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The working group will address one overarching question: Do phase transitions in condensates function as reproducible cellular decision points whose mesoscale properties mediate the relationship between molecular composition and cellular outcomes? We operationalize “decision point” as a thresholded or switch-like change in mesoscale organization that predicts downstream phenotypes better than molecular abundance alone and exhibits context-dependent hysteresis or state dependence.

RQ1: What mesoscale variables best capture condensate state across SGs, P-bodies, and nucleoli? We will define a shared representation of condensate state from imaging-derived features (e.g., number, size distribution, morphology, spatial proximity to other compartments, internal texture proxies), composition proxies (enrichment scores from proteomics and localization atlases), and sequence/structure features of constituent proteins (intrinsic disorder, low-complexity regions, multivalency, predicted interaction motifs). Hypothesis 1: A low-dimensional set of mesoscale variables—capturing concentration thresholding, heterogeneity, and multiphase organization—will be conserved across condensate types and species, despite differences in specific components.

RQ2: Do mesoscale variables causally mediate the effects of perturbations on cellular outcomes? We will connect perturbations (stressors, genetic knockdowns/knockouts, chemical treatments) to outcomes (cell viability, translation rate proxies, stress response markers, RNA turnover signatures) through condensate state. Hypothesis 2a: For many perturbations, condensate mesoscale state mediates a substantial fraction of the perturbation→outcome effect, beyond what is explained by bulk abundance of key proteins/RNAs. Hypothesis 2b: Mediation strength will differ by condensate class (SG vs P-body vs nucleolus), revealing distinct “decision architectures” (e.g., SG assembly as a rapid protective switch; nucleolar reorganization as a slower integrator of stress).

RQ3: Are there universal versus context-specific rules for condensate decision points? We will test generalization across cell types, species, and stress modalities. Hypothesis 3a: Universal rules will relate multivalency/disorder and interaction-network topology to assembly thresholds and reversibility. Hypothesis 3b: Context-specific rules will arise from baseline cellular state (cell cycle, differentiation, metabolic status) and from coupling between condensates (e.g., SG–P-body exchange, nucleolus–chromatin interactions), producing distinct outcomes even with similar apparent assembly.

RQ4: Can we predict when a condensate transition is adaptive versus maladaptive? We will integrate disease-relevant annotations (e.g., ALS/FTD-associated RBPs, cancer nucleolar phenotypes) and stress survival outcomes where available. Hypothesis 4: Maladaptive transitions will be associated with signatures of reduced reversibility, altered internal organization (solid-like proxies), and network-level trapping of specific functional modules (e.g., translation initiation, RNA decay, ribosome biogenesis).

RQ5: What are the minimal data and metadata requirements to infer condensate decision points from public datasets? Hypothesis 5: A community-agreed metadata schema (perturbation identity, time since perturbation, imaging modality, segmentation provenance, cell state covariates) will be sufficient to enable cross-dataset causal discovery with calibrated uncertainty, and missingness-aware models will outperform naive pooling.

Together, these questions and hypotheses explicitly target emergence: they test whether a mesoscale layer of organization provides explanatory and predictive power that is not accessible from molecular parts alone and whether this layer obeys discoverable rules across biological contexts.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working group structure. The project will run as an NCEMS Working Group organized into iterative “synthesis cycles” combining (i) data discovery/curation, (ii) harmonization and feature extraction, (iii) causal modeling and validation, and (iv) dissemination/training. The collaboration will include at minimum: condensate cell biologists; biophysicists; imaging analysts; proteomics/functional genomics experts; statisticians/causal inference researchers; and data curators/software engineers. No new experimental data will be generated.

Data sources and inclusion criteria. We will prioritize public datasets that (a) include SG, P-body, or nucleolus imaging/localization or compositional measurements; (b) contain perturbation or condition labels (stress type, genetic perturbation, drug); (c) provide links to downstream phenotypes (viability, growth, stress markers, translation/RNA signatures) or can be joined to such data via shared perturbations/cell lines; and (d) offer reusable metadata and licensing. Candidate sources include: Human Protein Atlas (subcellular localization), BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource (microscopy collections), cell atlas resources, PRIDE/MassIVE (proteomics), NCBI GEO/ArrayExpress (transcriptomics), DepMap/CRISPR screen portals where public, and curated interaction/pathway databases. AlphaFold/PDB-derived annotations will provide protein feature priors.

Harmonization and representation learning. We will build a common data model (CDM) that maps each observation to: biological context (species, cell type, baseline state), perturbation (type, dose, time), molecular layer (abundance/localization/composition), mesoscale layer (condensate features), and outcomes. Imaging harmonization will use standardized segmentation/feature pipelines when raw images are available; when only derived labels exist, we will encode provenance and uncertainty. Feature sets will include classical morphology metrics plus learned embeddings (self-supervised models) with strict separation between training and evaluation datasets to avoid leakage. Batch effects will be addressed via hierarchical models and domain adaptation, with explicit uncertainty propagation.

Causal discovery and mediation analysis. The central analytic goal is to test whether mesoscale variables act as mediators and decision points. We will use complementary approaches: (1) structural causal models (SCMs) with directed acyclic graphs informed by biology; (2) invariant causal prediction to identify relationships stable across environments (datasets, species); (3) causal representation learning to identify latent mesoscale states that best explain outcomes; and (4) mediation analysis (including sensitivity analyses) to quantify the perturbation→mesoscale→outcome pathway. Confounding control will leverage measured covariates (cell cycle proxies, baseline expression programs) and negative control outcomes/perturbations where possible. Missingness will be handled with multiple imputation and models that accommodate partially observed multi-omics.

Cross-system and cross-species comparisons. We will explicitly include “contrast sets” (e.g., stresses that induce SGs but not P-bodies; nucleolar stress without SG assembly) to prevent overfitting to canonical narratives. Comparative analyses will test conservation of mesoscale decision variables across yeast, fly, and human datasets when available, using orthology mappings and feature alignment.

Validation using held-out datasets and triangulation. Because new experiments are not allowed, validation will be performed by (i) out-of-dataset prediction, (ii) replication across independent studies, (iii) triangulation across modalities (imaging vs proteomics vs screens), and (iv) robustness checks (placebo perturbations, shuffled labels, alternative segmentation pipelines).

Training and team science. Trainees will lead curated “mini-projects” (e.g., SG–P-body coupling, nucleolar multiphase signatures) during data sprints and workflow clinics. Each synthesis cycle will end with a reproducible release (data package + code + report) reviewed by cross-disciplinary peers within the group.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific products. (1) A cross-condensate, cross-context “Decision Point Atlas” that quantifies mesoscale state variables for stress granules, P-bodies, and nucleoli and links them to perturbations and cellular outcomes. (2) Evidence-based answers to whether and when condensate phase transitions mediate outcomes, including estimates of mediation strength and identification of conditions where composition alone is insufficient. (3) A set of candidate universal versus context-specific rules (e.g., relationships between protein multivalency/disorder, interaction-network topology, and assembly/reversibility proxies) that can be tested by the broader community.

Methodological products. (4) A reusable common data model and metadata schema for condensate synthesis that bridges imaging, proteomics, functional genomics, and structural annotations. (5) Open-source pipelines for harmonization, feature extraction, uncertainty tracking, and causal discovery tailored to heterogeneous public molecular/cellular datasets. (6) Benchmark tasks and evaluation datasets for causal inference on mesoscale biological organization, enabling method developers to compare approaches on shared problems.

Impact on emergence science. The project will advance NCEMS’s vision by making the mesoscale the primary unit of explanation and by demonstrating how emergent organization can be treated as a measurable, modelable layer that links molecular parts to cellular phenotypes. By focusing on decision points, the work reframes condensates from descriptive compartments to dynamical regulators with testable causal roles.

Broader impacts and workforce development. The working group will train graduate students and postdocs in open, reproducible synthesis science and in cross-disciplinary communication between wet-lab biology, imaging, and data science. The atlas, standards, and tutorials will lower barriers for new entrants—including researchers at teaching-focused and resource-limited institutions—to contribute to and benefit from public data reuse. The outputs will also inform disease-focused communities by clarifying which condensate transitions are most predictive of maladaptive outcomes and by providing transparent evidence trails grounded in public data.
open_science_and_reproducibility:

Reproducible workflows. Analyses will be implemented as versioned, containerized pipelines (Docker/Singularity) orchestrated with workflow managers (e.g., Snakemake/Nextflow) to ensure portability across NCEMS compute and collaborators’ institutions. Each release will include pinned software environments, checksums for inputs, and automated end-to-end tests. We will maintain a public repository with issue tracking, code review, and continuous integration.

FAIR and provenance-rich data products. We will publish a common data model and metadata schema with clear field definitions (perturbation identity, timing, imaging modality, segmentation provenance, cell state covariates, outcome definitions) and machine-readable provenance (RO-Crate or equivalent). Uncertainty will be treated as first-class metadata (e.g., segmentation confidence, batch labels, imputation flags), enabling downstream users to propagate rather than ignore error.

Transparent causal claims. Because causal inference from observational public data can be fragile, we will pre-register key analyses within the working group (analysis plans, primary outcomes, robustness checks) and publish sensitivity analyses alongside main results. We will explicitly separate exploratory discovery from confirmatory tests using held-out datasets.

Community engagement. We will coordinate with relevant community standards efforts (bioimaging metadata, proteomics reporting, interaction databases) and will host open tutorials and office hours. Trainees will co-author “living” tutorials (Jupyter/Quarto) demonstrating how to reproduce each figure and how to extend the atlas with new public datasets, supporting long-term reuse beyond the funding period.

Public repositories and archives supply the primary data; the budget is focused on synthesis, integration, and community-ready products rather than new data generation.
