title: The mesoscale grammar of organelle contact sites in metabolic state changes
abstract:
This working group asks how the mesoscale grammar of organelle contact sites in metabolic state changes can be understood as an emergent property that links molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcome. The scientific question is not simply whether particular molecules, organelles, or pathways are associated with a phenotype, but whether publicly available datasets can reveal rules by which many molecular parts collectively produce a new, system-level behavior at the scale between biomolecules and organelles. The project is designed for the NCEMS model because the relevant evidence is scattered across incompatible imaging repositories, omics studies, perturbation resources, structural annotations, and specialized literatures; no single laboratory is likely to have the biological breadth, data-engineering capacity, and methodological expertise to integrate them.

The group would synthesize existing public data centered on imaging + proteomics, prioritizing datasets with reusable metadata, perturbation or state annotations, and links to downstream cellular phenotypes. Depending on availability, sources could include public cell atlases, the Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, EMBL-EBI and NCBI functional genomics repositories, BioImage Archive or Image Data Resource collections, PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics datasets, public CRISPR or RNAi screens, AlphaFold/PDB-derived structural features, and curated pathway or protein-interaction resources. The core analytic strategy would be foundation-model representation learning: harmonizing measurements into a common representation; explicitly modeling uncertainty, batch effects, and missingness; and testing whether mesoscale variables explain cellular outcomes above and beyond molecular abundance alone. The biological scope would focus on human disease cells while deliberately including comparison cases that prevent the group from mistaking a narrow model-system pattern for a general law.

The novel element is the unit of explanation. Instead of treating mesoscale organization as an image label, downstream readout, or anecdotal mechanism, the working group would make it the primary object of synthesis: a measurable layer where composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion combine. The expected product is a predictive atlas that is open, versioned, and reusable, with transparent workflows, community-agreed metadata standards, and tutorials for trainees. The project would bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, imaging scientists, omics researchers, statisticians, machine-learning researchers, data curators, and trainees across institution types. Training would occur through hackathon-style data sprints, reproducible workflow clinics, and rotating trainee leadership of cross-dataset validation tasks. The anticipated contribution is both scientific and infrastructural: a defensible answer to a specific emergence question, plus a generalizable synthesis strategy that helps the molecular and cellular biosciences reuse public data to discover phenomena that only become visible when datasets, disciplines, and scales are brought together.
background_and_significance:
Cells reconfigure metabolism by reorganizing molecules in space and time, not only by changing expression levels. A central but under-synthesized mechanism is organelle contact sites (OCSs): nanoscale-to-mesoscale regions where two organelles come into close proximity to exchange lipids, ions, and signals. OCSs link molecular interactions (tethers, lipid transfer proteins, channels, scaffolds) to mesoscale organization (contact frequency, area, topology, and persistence) and ultimately to cellular outcomes such as ATP production, redox balance, proteostasis, and fate decisions. Yet, despite extensive literature on individual tethers and pathways, we lack general “rules”—a mesoscale grammar—that describes how ensembles of molecular parts collectively generate robust, state-dependent contact architectures.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to address this gap because the evidence needed to infer emergent mesoscale rules is distributed across data modalities and repositories. Imaging collections capture organelle morphology and proximity but are heterogeneous in markers, resolution, and metadata. Proteomics and spatial proteomics quantify organelle-localized proteins but often lack direct measures of contact geometry. Perturbation screens reveal causal genes but rarely specify which mesoscale features mediate phenotypes. Structural resources (AlphaFold/PDB) and interaction databases encode molecular capabilities (binding, flexibility, disorder, membrane association) that may predict tethering and phase-like organization at contacts. No single lab can integrate these sources at scale, harmonize metadata, or develop robust computational methods to quantify and compare OCS features across cell types and metabolic states.

The proposed working group focuses on metabolic state changes because metabolism is a canonical domain where emergence is expected: small molecular differences can precipitate large changes in cellular organization and function. Metabolic shifts (e.g., glycolysis-to-oxidative phosphorylation balance, hypoxia, nutrient starvation, lipid overload, mitochondrial stress) are accompanied by remodeling of mitochondria–ER contacts, mitochondria–lysosome contacts, peroxisome interactions, lipid droplet contacts, and Golgi–ER trafficking interfaces. These contacts influence calcium flux, phospholipid synthesis, autophagy initiation, and organelle fission/fusion—processes that are inherently mesoscale and dynamic. Importantly, many relevant datasets are already public: cell atlases with organelle markers; BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource studies with perturbations; PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics; CRISPR screening compendia; and curated pathway/interaction resources.

The significance is twofold. Scientifically, identifying a mesoscale grammar would elevate OCSs from descriptive phenomena to predictive variables that explain metabolic phenotypes beyond molecular abundance alone. Methodologically, the project will develop synthesis strategies for integrating imaging-derived mesoscale features with omics and perturbation data under uncertainty, missingness, and batch effects—challenges that currently limit reuse of public cell biology datasets. The work aligns with NCEMS’s emphasis on mesoscale emergence by treating contact organization as the primary object of explanation and by testing whether mesoscale variables provide mechanistic and predictive leverage across diverse disease-relevant human cells. The outcome will be a community resource—an open, versioned atlas and set of reproducible workflows—that enables future studies of emergent cellular organization using only public data and that trains a data-savvy workforce to operate across disciplinary boundaries.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Overall objective: Infer and validate a “mesoscale grammar” of organelle contact sites (OCSs) that links molecular composition to contact organization and to metabolic-state-associated cellular outcomes, using only publicly available datasets.

RQ1: What are the conserved, measurable mesoscale variables of OCS organization across datasets and cell contexts?
Hypothesis 1.1: A small set of latent mesoscale factors—capturing contact extent (frequency/area), topology (which organelles pair), persistence/dynamics proxies, and spatial coupling to organelle morphology—can be consistently extracted from heterogeneous imaging and spatial datasets.
Hypothesis 1.2: These latent factors are more reproducible across laboratories than individual pixel-level features because they aggregate information at an intermediate (mesoscale) level and can be modeled with explicit uncertainty.

RQ2: Do mesoscale OCS variables explain metabolic phenotypes beyond molecular abundance and pathway activity?
Hypothesis 2.1: Models that include OCS latent factors will improve prediction of metabolic state labels (e.g., hypoxia, starvation, lipid stress) and downstream outcomes (e.g., growth, apoptosis sensitivity, ROS signatures, autophagy markers when available as public readouts) compared to models using only transcript/protein abundance or pathway scores.
Hypothesis 2.2: The added explanatory power of mesoscale variables will be strongest in contexts where multiple molecular routes converge to similar phenotypes (degeneracy), consistent with emergence: different molecular configurations produce similar system-level contact architectures that drive outcomes.

RQ3: Which molecular features and interaction patterns are sufficient to generate particular OCS organizations?
Hypothesis 3.1: Contact organization is associated with “molecular capability profiles” derived from public annotations: membrane topology, predicted disorder, multivalency, lipid-binding domains, and interaction network motifs. These features will predict OCS latent factors across cell types.
Hypothesis 3.2: Structural/biophysical annotations (e.g., coiled-coils, amphipathic helices, low-complexity regions) will be enriched among proteins whose perturbation signatures correlate with OCS remodeling, suggesting generalizable tethering principles.

RQ4: Are there universal versus context-specific grammar rules, and how do they relate to disease?
Hypothesis 4.1: Some grammar rules (e.g., coupling between mitochondrial morphology and ER contact extent under energetic stress) will generalize across many cell lines, while others will be lineage- or mutation-dependent.
Hypothesis 4.2: Disease-associated states (e.g., cancer metabolic rewiring, neurodegeneration-related stress signatures) will exhibit characteristic deviations from the conserved grammar—either “mis-parsing” (aberrant combinations of contact factors) or “overfitting” (excessive reliance on a subset of contacts).

RQ5 (methodological): Can foundation-model representations unify incompatible imaging and omics measurements for OCS inference?
Hypothesis 5.1: Self-supervised or weakly supervised representation learning on public organelle images, combined with probabilistic multi-modal integration, will yield embeddings that align with known biology (organelle identity, stress response) while revealing new OCS axes.
Hypothesis 5.2: Explicit modeling of missingness and batch effects (hierarchical Bayesian or causal/robust learning approaches) will prevent spurious grammar rules driven by dataset-specific artifacts.

Collectively, these questions test emergence directly: whether mesoscale organization constitutes an explanatory layer with predictive and mechanistic content that cannot be reduced to molecular abundance alone, and whether that layer follows discoverable, generalizable rules across biological contexts.
methods_and_approach:
Working group structure and scope: A multi-lab, transdisciplinary team will run iterative synthesis cycles (data inventory → harmonization → representation learning → hypothesis testing → cross-dataset validation). The scope centers on human disease-relevant cells while including non-disease or alternative lineages as comparison sets to test generality. Only publicly available data will be used; no new experiments will be performed.

1) Data discovery, inclusion criteria, and harmonization
We will compile a registry of candidate datasets spanning: (i) fluorescence and EM imaging with organelle markers (BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas), (ii) proteomics/spatial proteomics (PRIDE, MassIVE), (iii) perturbations (public CRISPR/RNAi screens and perturb-seq where imaging/phenotype metadata exist), (iv) structural and interaction annotations (AlphaFold/PDB features, BioGRID/IntAct/String, pathway databases). Inclusion criteria: clear cell type and condition metadata; reusable licensing; sufficient sample size; and at least one of (a) metabolic state label/perturbation, (b) organelle markers enabling contact inference, (c) linkable gene/protein identifiers.
We will create a common metadata schema (cell line, perturbation, metabolic condition, imaging modality, markers, acquisition parameters, batch identifiers) and map identifiers (HGNC/UniProt/Ensembl). Harmonization will include unit normalization, controlled vocabularies, and versioned data packages.

2) Mesoscale feature extraction from imaging
We will infer OCS proxies using two complementary routes:
(a) Classical/physics-informed features: organelle segmentation (where feasible), distance transforms, co-localization at sub-resolution thresholds, contact candidate maps, and morphology descriptors (fragmentation, tubularity, surface area proxies). For EM datasets, we will use published segmentations where available.
(b) Foundation-model embeddings: self-supervised learning (contrastive/masked-image modeling) on organelle channels to obtain embeddings sensitive to spatial organization. Where labels exist (organelle identity, condition), we will use weak supervision to align embeddings with biology.
Outputs are dataset-specific features plus a shared latent representation of OCS organization.

3) Multi-modal integration and uncertainty modeling
We will integrate imaging-derived mesoscale variables with proteomics/transcriptomics and perturbation signatures using probabilistic models that handle missing modalities (e.g., variational latent variable models, hierarchical Bayesian factor models). Batch effects will be modeled explicitly (random effects; adversarial/robust alignment), and uncertainty will be propagated to downstream tests. We will pre-register core comparisons to reduce researcher degrees of freedom.

4) Hypothesis testing: emergence and added explanatory value
We will quantify whether mesoscale variables add predictive power for metabolic state and outcomes using nested model comparisons: (i) omics-only, (ii) imaging-only, (iii) integrated, and (iv) integrated + interaction/structure features. Metrics include cross-validated accuracy, calibration, and out-of-distribution performance across datasets. We will test mediation-style hypotheses: whether perturbation effects on outcomes are mediated by changes in mesoscale OCS variables, using causal inference tools adapted to observational public data (sensitivity analyses, negative controls).

5) Grammar discovery and rule extraction
We will operationalize “grammar” as a set of compositional rules mapping molecular capability profiles and organelle identities to OCS latent factors and their transitions across metabolic states. Approaches include sparse regression/rule learning, graph neural networks on organelle-contact graphs, and interpretable latent factor transitions (state-space models). We will prioritize interpretability: identifying minimal sets of features that predict contact remodeling.

6) Cross-dataset validation and robustness
All findings must replicate across at least two independent datasets or modalities when available. We will run leave-one-dataset-out validation, perturbation-based triangulation (same gene perturbed in different resources), and artifact checks (marker swaps, imaging resolution sensitivity, label permutation).

7) Training and collaboration mechanics
NCEMS-style data sprints will pair trainees with mentors across disciplines. Trainees will lead “validation pods” responsible for reproducing a result on an independent dataset, ensuring both training and rigor. Regular working sessions will converge on shared standards and deliverables.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific products:
1) A quantitative, testable “mesoscale grammar” describing how organelle contact site (OCS) organization changes across metabolic states, including conserved latent factors (e.g., contact extent, topology, coupling to organelle morphology) and interpretable rules linking these factors to molecular capability profiles and perturbation signatures.
2) Evidence for emergence: rigorous demonstrations that mesoscale OCS variables explain metabolic-state-associated cellular outcomes beyond what is captured by molecular abundance/pathway activity alone, with replication across independent public datasets.
3) Disease-relevant insights: identification of contexts (cell lineages, stress programs, mutation backgrounds) where OCS grammar rules are conserved versus violated, generating prioritized hypotheses for the broader community about vulnerability points in metabolic rewiring.

Methodological and community products:
4) An open, versioned atlas of OCS organization in public human cell datasets, with standardized metadata, embeddings, and derived features suitable for reuse. The atlas will include uncertainty estimates and provenance links to original repositories.
5) Reproducible workflows for multi-modal synthesis (imaging + omics + perturbations + structure/interaction annotations), including reference implementations for batch correction, missing-data integration, and cross-dataset validation.
6) Community standards proposals: a practical metadata checklist for OCS-relevant imaging studies (markers, acquisition parameters, condition annotations) and recommended mappings between imaging and omics identifiers.

Broader impacts:
7) Workforce development: trainees will gain hands-on experience in open, reproducible synthesis science, multi-modal machine learning, and collaborative project management, producing publishable contributions (tutorials, pipelines, validation reports).
8) Catalysis: by lowering barriers to reuse of public cell biology data, the project will enable follow-on studies of mesoscale emergence beyond OCSs (e.g., condensate–organelle coupling, cytoskeletal–organelle organization) and promote a culture of integrative, community-scale analysis aligned with NCEMS’s mission.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-science commitments (default-open, exception-justified):
1) Data sources and licensing: We will use only publicly available datasets and will preserve original licenses and attribution. For each dataset, we will publish a machine-readable “data card” describing source, access date, license, modalities, key metadata fields, and known limitations.

2) Versioned, reproducible pipelines: All code will be developed in public repositories (e.g., GitHub/GitLab) under a permissive open-source license (e.g., BSD-3/Apache-2.0). Analyses will be executed via containerized workflows (Docker/Singularity) orchestrated by workflow managers (e.g., Nextflow/Snakemake) to ensure portability. Each release will be tagged and archived (Zenodo DOI), with changelogs and semantic versioning.

3) FAIR outputs: Derived datasets (embeddings, mesoscale features, harmonized metadata tables) will be deposited in appropriate repositories (e.g., Zenodo, Figshare, or domain repositories where required) with rich metadata, persistent identifiers, and clear provenance links to raw sources. We will not redistribute restricted data; instead we will provide scripts to re-fetch from original repositories.

4) Reproducibility and robustness practices: We will pre-register core hypotheses and primary evaluation metrics (e.g., added predictive value of mesoscale variables; cross-dataset replication criteria). We will implement automated tests, continuous integration, and “reproduction notebooks” that rebuild key figures from scratch. Robustness checks (label permutation, leave-one-dataset-out, sensitivity to preprocessing) will be required for any claimed grammar rule.

5) Transparent uncertainty: Models will output calibrated uncertainty (posterior intervals or predictive distributions) and we will publish guidance on interpreting uncertainty in embeddings and downstream predictions.

6) Inclusive and collaborative governance: The working group will adopt community-created policies on authorship, contribution tracking (CRediT taxonomy), code review, and decision-making. Trainees will be supported to lead modules and be credited for substantive contributions.

7) Training materials: Tutorials, recorded workflow clinics, and annotated example datasets will be published openly, enabling adoption by labs without specialized computational infrastructure.

Together these practices ensure that the atlas, rules, and methods are verifiable, reusable, and extensible—maximizing NCEMS’s catalytic impact and aligning with gold-standard open and team science.

Budget rationale (aligned with NCEMS working-group model; no funds for new experimental data generation):

5) NCEMS resources and why they are essential
The project requires NCEMS support to convene a multidisciplinary team, provide neutral coordination and governance, and supply the synthesis infrastructure (meeting facilitation, collaborative computing guidance, and open-science frameworks). The scale and heterogeneity of the public datasets, plus the need for cross-dataset replication and standards development, exceed what a single lab or bilateral collaboration can sustain.

Budget oversight will include milestone-based releases (registry completion, first integrated model, replication package, atlas release) and transparent reporting of expenditures tied to deliverables.

background_and_significance:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed by phase separation and related mesoscale organizing principles—are now recognized as a pervasive layer of cellular organization connecting molecular interaction networks to spatially localized biochemical function. A central unresolved issue is that condensates are not static liquids: many exhibit “aging,” a progressive change in material properties from dynamic, liquid-like droplets to gel-like or solid-like assemblies. This liquid-to-solid continuum is implicated in stress responses, gene regulation, innate immunity, and neurodegenerative disease, yet the field lacks a quantitative, generalizable framework that links molecular composition and sequence/structure features to emergent mesoscale material states and, ultimately, cellular outcomes.

Aging is an archetypal emergence problem at the mesoscale targeted by NCEMS. Individual proteins and RNAs have measurable properties (sequence motifs, disorder content, interaction valency, post-translational modification sites), but the transition to a solid-like condensate is a collective phenomenon arising from multicomponent interactions, crowding, stoichiometry, and cellular context. The same molecules can participate in condensates with distinct material states across cell types, stresses, and disease mutations. Conversely, similar phenotypes (e.g., impaired proteostasis, altered transcription, reduced viability) can arise from different molecular routes to mesoscale hardening. Understanding these transitions therefore requires synthesis across scales and modalities, not incremental single-lab experimentation.

Public data relevant to condensate aging are abundant but fragmented. Imaging repositories contain time-lapse and fixed-cell microscopy capturing puncta morphology, fusion behavior, and subcellular localization; proteomics resources report condensate-enriched fractions and interaction partners; transcriptomics and perturbation screens identify regulators of granule formation, stress granule persistence, or toxicity; structural prediction databases provide residue-level features that influence interaction networks and fibrillization propensity. However, these datasets are rarely interoperable. Metadata are inconsistent (cell type, stressor, imaging modality, time after perturbation), readouts vary (qualitative labels vs quantitative dynamics), and batch effects are substantial. The key barrier is not data scarcity but the absence of a synthesis framework that (i) harmonizes heterogeneous measurements into comparable mesoscale variables, (ii) quantifies uncertainty and missingness, and (iii) tests whether mesoscale state adds explanatory power beyond molecular abundance or single-gene effects.

This working group addresses that barrier through community-scale synthesis using only publicly available data. The project is beyond the scope of an individual lab because it requires: data engineering across imaging, omics, structural annotations, and perturbation resources; expertise in condensate biophysics and polymer/soft-matter theory; statistical modeling of multi-source bias; machine learning for representation learning and segmentation; and domain knowledge of disease contexts where aging is clinically relevant. NCEMS support is essential to convene and coordinate this transdisciplinary team, provide a shared computational environment, and enforce open, reproducible workflows.

By treating mesoscale organization as the primary object of explanation, the working group aims to reveal general “rules of aging”—predictive relationships linking molecular features and context to liquid-to-solid transitions and downstream cellular phenotypes. Such rules would resolve long-standing puzzles (why some condensates harden while others remain fluid; why certain mutations are toxic only in particular contexts) and provide a reusable blueprint for emergence-focused synthesis in molecular and cellular biosciences.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The working group will pursue a focused set of emergence-centered questions that elevate condensate material state from a qualitative descriptor to a quantitatively modeled mesoscale variable connecting molecular composition to cellular outcomes.

RQ1: Can condensate “aging state” be operationalized as a reproducible, cross-dataset latent variable derived from heterogeneous imaging, biophysical proxies, and molecular annotations? 
H1: A low-dimensional latent representation (e.g., 2–5 axes) can be learned that captures a continuum from liquid-like to solid-like behavior and is stable across imaging modalities and repositories when conditioned on minimal metadata (cell type, perturbation class, time).

RQ2: Which molecular features predict a shift toward solid-like condensates across contexts, and are these predictors conserved across condensate types? 
H2a: Sequence/structure features that increase multivalency and long-lived interactions—such as high sticker density in intrinsically disordered regions, specific aromatic/charged patterning, prion-like composition, and high predicted β-aggregation propensity—will be associated with higher inferred aging state after controlling for expression and localization. 
H2b: Contextual modifiers (post-translational modifications, RNA binding capacity, chaperone abundance, stress pathway activation) will interact with these intrinsic features, producing predictable context-dependent shifts.

RQ3: Does mesoscale aging state explain cellular phenotypes beyond what is explained by molecular abundance, single-gene perturbations, or pathway membership alone? 
H3: Models that include inferred mesoscale aging state will significantly improve prediction of phenotypes such as reduced viability, proteostasis impairment, altered transcriptional programs, or persistence of stress granules, compared to models using only gene expression/protein abundance and perturbation identity.

RQ4: Are there multiple mechanistic routes to solidification (e.g., percolated interaction networks vs amyloid-like ordering), and can public data distinguish them? 
H4: Integrating structural annotations (AlphaFold/PDB-derived features), interaction networks, and imaging-derived dynamics will support at least two separable aging modes: (i) reversible gelation dominated by network connectivity and (ii) irreversible solidification associated with aggregation-prone sequence segments and fibrillar ordering. These modes will show different associations with reversibility proxies (recovery after stress removal), chaperone dependency, and disease mutation enrichment.

RQ5: How general are inferred rules across biological settings, and what are the boundary conditions? 
H5: Rules learned from human disease-relevant cell datasets will transfer, with quantifiable degradation, to non-disease contexts and selected model systems; failures of transfer will map to explicit boundary conditions (e.g., distinct RNA repertoires, temperature, osmotic conditions, or organelle proximity) rather than idiosyncratic dataset artifacts.

RQ6 (methodological): What minimal metadata and measurement standards are required for future public datasets to be maximally reusable for mesoscale emergence questions? 
H6: A small, community-agreed metadata schema (perturbation identity and timing, cell type/state, imaging modality and calibration, condensate marker identity, and a reversibility indicator) will be sufficient to enable robust cross-study synthesis; missingness in these fields will be the dominant limiter of inference quality.

Together, these questions and hypotheses ensure the project delivers both a scientific synthesis (predictive, testable rules of condensate aging) and a methodological advance (a generalizable framework for extracting mesoscale variables from public data).
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. The project will be executed as an NCEMS-style working group with three integrated thrusts: (T1) data federation and metadata harmonization, (T2) mesoscale variable extraction and uncertainty-aware modeling, and (T3) mechanistic interpretation and cross-context validation. All analyses will use only existing publicly available datasets.

Data sources and inclusion criteria. We will assemble a registry of candidate datasets spanning: (i) imaging repositories (BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas images, selected published time-lapse datasets), (ii) transcriptomics/perturbation resources (GEO/ArrayExpress, DepMap/CRISPR screens where public, published RNAi/CRISPR screens for stress granules/P-bodies/ALS-related toxicity), (iii) proteomics (PRIDE/MassIVE condensate-enrichment, proximity labeling, interactomes), and (iv) structural/sequence annotations (AlphaFold predictions, PDB where available, disorder/low-complexity predictors, aggregation propensity scores). Inclusion will prioritize datasets with: clear perturbation or state labels, reusable licenses, sufficient metadata, and links to downstream phenotypes (viability, stress recovery, transcriptional signatures).

T1: Harmonization and common representation. We will create a unified sample-level schema mapping each observation to: biological context (cell line/type, disease relevance, stressor/perturbation, time), molecular composition proxies (expression, proteomics enrichment, interaction partners), and imaging readouts. Ontology alignment will use established vocabularies (Cell Ontology, Uberon where relevant, OBI, EFO) and controlled perturbation terms. Batch effects will be modeled explicitly rather than “corrected away” blindly, preserving true biological differences.

T2: Mesoscale aging state inference from images and proxies. For imaging, we will implement reproducible pipelines for segmentation and feature extraction (morphology, size distributions, aspect ratio, texture, coalescence signatures, spatial proximity to organelles, and—where time-lapse exists—fusion kinetics and relaxation times). When FRAP-like measurements exist in public data, they will anchor material-state interpretation; when absent, we will use validated proxies (e.g., circularity + texture + persistence across timepoints) with uncertainty quantification. Representation learning (self-supervised embeddings) will be used to derive modality-robust condensate descriptors, followed by probabilistic latent-variable models to estimate an “aging state” with credible intervals.

T3: Data assimilation and mechanistic modeling. We will integrate molecular features and inferred aging state using hierarchical Bayesian models and causal-inference-inspired designs (e.g., negative controls, perturbation stratification, and sensitivity analyses). Mechanistic hypotheses will be tested via competing models: network percolation/gelation metrics derived from interaction graphs versus aggregation/fibrillization propensity derived from sequence/structure. Model comparison will use out-of-sample prediction across datasets (leave-one-study-out) and across contexts (train on one disease/stress class, test on another).

Validation strategy using only public data. Validation will be cross-dataset (same marker/perturbation in different repositories), cross-modality (imaging vs proteomics enrichment vs transcriptomic stress signatures), and cross-context (different cell types and disease models). We will predefine success criteria: stability of latent aging state, predictive improvement for phenotypes, and interpretable feature contributions consistent across independent datasets.

Training and coordination. The group will run structured data sprints (dataset onboarding), workflow clinics (containerized pipelines), and rotating trainee-led “replication challenges” where trainees reproduce key results on held-out datasets. NCEMS resources will support shared compute, collaboration, and community engagement.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific outcomes. (1) A quantitative, cross-dataset “condensate aging state” variable (or small set of variables) that operationalizes liquid-to-solid transitions using publicly available imaging and molecular proxies, with uncertainty estimates and clear boundary conditions. (2) A set of predictive rules linking sequence/structure features, interaction-network properties, and contextual modifiers (cell state, stress class, PTM/chaperone environment) to aging trajectories. (3) Evidence for distinct mechanistic routes to solidification, with interpretable signatures that differentiate reversible gelation from irreversible aggregation-like hardening.

Methodological outcomes. (4) A generalizable synthesis framework for mesoscale emergence: harmonization of heterogeneous public datasets, probabilistic latent-variable inference for mesoscale organization, and mechanistic data assimilation that tests whether mesoscale variables add explanatory power beyond molecular abundance. (5) A curated, versioned registry of reusable public datasets relevant to condensate material properties, including standardized metadata mappings and quality flags.

Community and workforce outcomes. (6) Open tutorials and trainee-led reproducibility reports that teach image/omics integration, uncertainty-aware modeling, and open workflow practices. Trainees will gain experience in cross-lab collaboration, code review, data governance, and responsible AI use.

Impact on molecular and cellular biosciences. This project will shift condensate research from case-by-case narratives to a synthesis-driven, predictive science of mesoscale material states. By demonstrating that aging is an emergent property measurable across studies, the working group will help resolve long-standing debates about generality versus context specificity and will provide a reusable template for other mesoscale phenomena (e.g., cytoskeletal gels, membrane-less organelle interactions, chromatin domains). The outputs will enable the community to reuse existing data more effectively, improving return on investment for public repositories and accelerating discovery without generating new experimental data.
open_science_and_reproducibility:

Metadata standards and community governance. A central deliverable will be a minimal metadata schema for condensate material-state studies (perturbation identity/timing, cell type/state, marker identity, imaging modality/calibration, and reversibility proxy). We will develop this schema iteratively with data curators and repository stakeholders and publish it as a versioned community recommendation.

FAIR principles. Outputs will be Findable (DOIs via Zenodo), Accessible (public repositories), Interoperable (standard ontologies and machine-readable schemas), and Reusable (clear licenses, provenance, and tutorials). title: Collective cytoskeletal excitability as an emergent cellular computation
abstract:
This working group asks how collective cytoskeletal excitability as an emergent cellular computation can be understood as an emergent property that links molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcome. The scientific question is not simply whether particular molecules, organelles, or pathways are associated with a phenotype, but whether publicly available datasets can reveal rules by which many molecular parts collectively produce a new, system-level behavior at the scale between biomolecules and organelles. The project is designed for the NCEMS model because the relevant evidence is scattered across incompatible imaging repositories, omics studies, perturbation resources, structural annotations, and specialized literatures; no single laboratory is likely to have the biological breadth, data-engineering capacity, and methodological expertise to integrate them.

The group would synthesize existing public data centered on imaging + proteomics, prioritizing datasets with reusable metadata, perturbation or state annotations, and links to downstream cellular phenotypes. Depending on availability, sources could include public cell atlases, the Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, EMBL-EBI and NCBI functional genomics repositories, BioImage Archive or Image Data Resource collections, PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics datasets, public CRISPR or RNAi screens, AlphaFold/PDB-derived structural features, and curated pathway or protein-interaction resources. The core analytic strategy would be causal discovery: harmonizing measurements into a common representation; explicitly modeling uncertainty, batch effects, and missingness; and testing whether mesoscale variables explain cellular outcomes above and beyond molecular abundance alone. The biological scope would focus on model organisms while deliberately including comparison cases that prevent the group from mistaking a narrow model-system pattern for a general law.

The novel element is the unit of explanation. Instead of treating mesoscale organization as an image label, downstream readout, or anecdotal mechanism, the working group would make it the primary object of synthesis: a measurable layer where composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion combine. The expected product is a theory/model that is open, versioned, and reusable, with transparent workflows, community-agreed metadata standards, and tutorials for trainees. The project would bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, imaging scientists, omics researchers, statisticians, machine-learning researchers, data curators, and trainees across institution types. Training would occur through hackathon-style data sprints, reproducible workflow clinics, and rotating trainee leadership of cross-dataset validation tasks. The anticipated contribution is both scientific and infrastructural: a defensible answer to a specific emergence question, plus a generalizable synthesis strategy that helps the molecular and cellular biosciences reuse public data to discover phenomena that only become visible when datasets, disciplines, and scales are brought together.
background_and_significance:
Cells compute: they integrate signals, allocate resources, and choose actions (migration, division, differentiation) without a central controller. A key substrate of this computation is the cytoskeleton—actin networks, microtubules, intermediate filaments, and associated motors and regulators—which converts biochemical cues into force, geometry, and transport. Yet many cytoskeletal phenomena are not well explained by single-molecule mechanisms or linear pathway diagrams. Instead, they resemble excitable media and active matter: local fluctuations can trigger propagating waves, pulses, and contractile instabilities; feedback between mechanics and chemistry can create thresholds, refractoriness, and pattern selection; and collective dynamics can yield robust, adaptive behaviors. These properties—collective cytoskeletal excitability—are prime examples of emergence at the mesoscale, the regime between biomolecules and organelles emphasized by NCEMS.

Despite extensive experimental literature, the field lacks a unifying, data-grounded theory that connects molecular composition to mesoscale organization and then to cellular outcomes across contexts. Existing models often focus on a single organism, cell type, or imaging modality; they rarely integrate proteomic composition, genetic perturbations, structural constraints, and imaging-derived mesoscale descriptors in a single inferential framework. Meanwhile, public data relevant to cytoskeletal excitability has rapidly expanded: large-scale cell atlases with standardized imaging, proteomics repositories capturing condition-specific abundance and modifications, pooled CRISPR screens linking genes to morphology and fitness, and structural resources (AlphaFold/PDB) that encode interaction potentials and multivalency. However, these resources remain fragmented: imaging repositories use heterogeneous metadata and segmentation pipelines; omics studies differ in quantification and batch structures; perturbation screens vary in readouts; and cross-references between modalities are incomplete. As a result, the community cannot easily ask synthesis-level questions such as: when do actin waves emerge; what molecular and structural features predict excitability; and does excitability causally mediate higher-order outcomes like migration persistence or cytokinesis success?

This proposal addresses that gap by making mesoscale cytoskeletal organization the primary unit of explanation rather than a qualitative mechanism or a downstream label. The significance is twofold. Scientifically, it aims to identify general rules by which many molecular parts collectively generate excitable cytoskeletal dynamics, and to test whether those mesoscale variables provide explanatory power beyond molecular abundance alone. Methodologically, it develops a reusable synthesis strategy: harmonized representations that bridge imaging and omics, causal discovery that explicitly models uncertainty and missingness, and cross-dataset validation that guards against overfitting to any one model system.

The project aligns tightly with NCEMS priorities. It uses only publicly available data, requires a multidisciplinary team spanning cell biology, biophysics, imaging informatics, proteomics, statistics, and machine learning, and targets emergence at the mesoscale. It is beyond the scope of any single lab because it demands coordinated curation across repositories, development of interoperable metadata and feature standards, and careful causal inference across heterogeneous datasets. Finally, it provides a natural training ground for a data-savvy workforce: trainees will learn reproducible workflows, multimodal integration, and principled inference while contributing to community resources that persist beyond the working group.

By synthesizing scattered evidence into a coherent, testable framework, this working group will transform cytoskeletal excitability from a set of compelling case studies into a generalizable emergent computation linking composition, structure, and dynamics to cellular fate.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group is organized around a central emergence question: can collective cytoskeletal excitability be formalized as a mesoscale computational layer that causally links molecular composition to cellular outcomes across organisms and conditions? We will address this through four research questions (RQs) with explicit, falsifiable hypotheses.

RQ1: What are the minimal, measurable mesoscale descriptors of cytoskeletal excitability that are reproducible across imaging datasets and modalities? Cytoskeletal excitability is often described qualitatively (waves, pulses, ruffles, oscillations), but synthesis requires quantitative descriptors that can be extracted from heterogeneous images and time series.
H1.1: A low-dimensional set of mesoscale features—capturing spatiotemporal propagation, intermittency, anisotropy, and mechanical coupling—can classify excitable vs non-excitable regimes with high cross-dataset generalization.
H1.2: These features are more stable across batches and platforms than raw intensity-based image embeddings, enabling transportable inference.

RQ2: Which molecular and structural properties predict the emergence of excitable cytoskeletal regimes? We will integrate proteomic abundance, post-translational modification proxies where available, interaction/network context, and structural annotations (e.g., multivalency, intrinsically disordered regions, oligomerization propensity).
H2.1: Excitability is associated with specific network motifs (positive feedback plus delayed negative feedback) reflected in curated pathway graphs and interaction networks, and these motifs can be operationalized as computable features.
H2.2: Structural multivalency and disorder in key regulators (e.g., scaffolds, nucleation-promoting factors) predict excitability above and beyond expression level, consistent with mesoscale assembly and phase-like behaviors.

RQ3: Does mesoscale excitability causally mediate the relationship between molecular composition/perturbations and cellular outcomes? Outcomes include migration persistence, polarization stability, cytokinesis success, endocytosis rate proxies, morphology classes, and fitness/viability readouts from screens.
H3.1: In causal graphs learned across datasets, mesoscale excitability variables act as mediators between molecular perturbations and outcomes, improving predictive and explanatory performance relative to models that omit mesoscale variables.
H3.2: The directionality is consistent with known interventions: perturbations to core excitability regulators shift mesoscale excitability first, with downstream changes in phenotype, rather than phenotypes driving apparent excitability signals.

RQ4: How general are the inferred rules across organisms, cell types, and environmental contexts? Emergent “laws” should not be artifacts of a single model system.
H4.1: A shared core of excitability rules generalizes across at least two major model systems (e.g., human cultured cells and a genetically tractable organism), while context-specific modifiers (cell cycle stage, adhesion environment, metabolic state) explain deviations.
H4.2: Apparent contradictions across literatures can be reconciled by mapping them onto distinct regions of a common phase diagram parameterized by composition and mesoscale descriptors.

Across all RQs, we will treat hypotheses as refutable: failure to find stable mesoscale descriptors, failure of structural/network features to add explanatory power, or lack of mediation would all count as informative negative results. The working group’s goal is not to force a single narrative, but to quantify when and why collective cytoskeletal excitability emerges as a computational layer and when it does not.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and design principles. The project is a community-scale synthesis effort using only publicly available data. We will (i) assemble a multimodal corpus linking cytoskeletal imaging, proteomics, perturbations, and phenotypes; (ii) derive interoperable mesoscale excitability features; (iii) integrate modalities with explicit uncertainty; and (iv) perform causal discovery and cross-dataset validation to test the hypotheses.

Data sources and inclusion criteria. We will prioritize datasets with (a) reusable metadata (cell type, perturbation, condition, imaging modality), (b) cytoskeletal markers (actin, tubulin, regulators) and/or morphology readouts, (c) links to molecular measurements (proteomics/transcriptomics) or perturbation identities, and (d) sufficient sample size for cross-validation. Candidate sources include BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource collections, Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas imaging and localization annotations, PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics studies with condition labels, NCBI/EMBL-EBI functional genomics (RNA-seq, ATAC-seq where relevant), pooled CRISPR/RNAi screens with morphological or fitness readouts, and curated interaction/pathway resources (BioGRID, STRING, Reactome). Structural features will be drawn from AlphaFold/PDB-derived annotations (e.g., disorder predictions, domain architecture, interface propensities).

Harmonization and common representation. We will build a “cytoskeletal excitability data model” that maps each sample/condition to: (1) molecular layer (abundance, network context, structural features), (2) mesoscale layer (excitability descriptors), and (3) outcome layer (phenotypes). Harmonization steps include ontology alignment (cell types, perturbations), unit normalization, and batch/technology covariates. Missingness will be modeled explicitly (e.g., probabilistic matrix factorization or multiple imputation with uncertainty propagation), avoiding listwise deletion.

Mesoscale feature extraction. For static images, we will compute interpretable descriptors of organization (filament anisotropy, texture spectra, edge/curvature distributions, spatial autocorrelation, network density proxies). For time series where available, we will quantify excitability hallmarks: wavefront velocity, refractory periods, pulse frequency, coherence length, and propagation directionality using optical-flow-based methods and event-detection on spatiotemporal maps. Where raw images are not accessible, we will leverage published derived features/embeddings and localization annotations, with calibration checks against datasets where both raw and derived features exist.

Integration and causal discovery. We will use a multi-stage modeling strategy: (i) predictive baselines (regularized regression, gradient boosting) to quantify incremental value of mesoscale variables; (ii) hierarchical models to account for dataset-specific effects; and (iii) causal discovery constrained by biological priors (e.g., perturbations precede phenotypes; molecular composition precedes mesoscale organization) using approaches such as invariant causal prediction, causal additive models, and score-based structure learning with partial ordering. Mediation will be tested using causal mediation analysis with sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding. Robustness will be assessed via negative controls (genes unrelated to cytoskeleton), placebo perturbations, and label permutation.

Cross-system generalization and phase diagram synthesis. We will perform leave-one-dataset-out and leave-one-system-out validation to identify portable rules. Finally, we will synthesize results into a phase-diagram-like map that relates molecular/structural parameters to mesoscale excitability regimes and associated outcomes.

Working group execution. NCEMS-supported meetings will alternate between (a) curation/standards sprints, (b) analysis sprints, and (c) interpretation/theory synthesis sessions. Trainees will lead cross-dataset replication tasks, ensuring that conclusions are anchored in reproducible, independently re-run workflows.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific products. The primary outcome will be a rigorously tested, data-synthesized model of collective cytoskeletal excitability as an emergent cellular computation. Concretely, we expect to deliver: (1) a validated set of quantitative mesoscale descriptors that operationalize “excitability” across imaging datasets; (2) evidence for (or against) specific molecular, network, and structural predictors of excitable regimes; and (3) causal/mediation results quantifying when mesoscale excitability explains cellular outcomes beyond molecular abundance alone. The resulting synthesis will clarify whether excitability is a general principle, a context-dependent module, or a family of related phenomena.

Methodological and infrastructural products. We will release a reusable “cytoskeletal excitability synthesis pipeline” that ingests heterogeneous public data, harmonizes metadata, extracts mesoscale features, and performs uncertainty-aware integration and causal analysis. We will also produce a community-facing data model and minimal metadata recommendations for linking imaging, omics, and perturbation information in future deposits.

Community impact. By integrating scattered repositories and literatures, the working group will create a focal point for researchers studying actin waves, microtubule instabilities, mechanochemical feedback, and cytoskeletal patterning. The cross-system validation plan will reduce the risk of model-system parochialism and provide a principled way to reconcile conflicting findings.

Training impact. Trainees will gain hands-on experience in multimodal data reuse, reproducible computational biology, and causal inference—skills central to NCEMS’s mission of building a data-savvy workforce. Rotating trainee leadership of replication and benchmarking tasks will produce durable expertise rather than one-off analyses.

Long-term significance. More broadly, the project will demonstrate how mesoscale organization can be treated as a first-class explanatory layer in molecular and cellular biology. The synthesis strategy—mesoscale feature standards plus causal discovery across public datasets—will generalize to other emergence problems (e.g., phase-separated assemblies, membrane-less organelles, organelle contact sites), amplifying NCEMS’s catalytic role in mesoscale biology.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-by-default outputs. All code, workflows, documentation, and derived (non-restricted) data products will be released under permissive open licenses (e.g., MIT/BSD for code; CC-BY/CC0 for documentation and metadata). We will not generate new experimental data; we will only reuse publicly available datasets and will respect original licenses and access controls.

Reproducible computational workflows. Analyses will be implemented as versioned, containerized pipelines (Docker/Apptainer) orchestrated with workflow managers (e.g., Snakemake/Nextflow) to ensure portability. Each figure and table in manuscripts will have an associated executable workflow and pinned software environment. Continuous integration will re-run unit tests, data integrity checks, and small benchmark analyses on each major update.

Provenance, metadata, and audit trails. We will maintain a machine-readable data catalog (dataset identifiers, accession numbers, licenses, modalities, processing steps) and record provenance for each derived feature set. Harmonized metadata will use community ontologies where possible (cell types, perturbations, phenotypes) and will include explicit uncertainty annotations (missingness mechanisms, batch variables, imputation flags).

Transparent inference and robustness. For causal discovery and mediation, we will preregister analysis plans at the level of model classes, constraints, and validation criteria (not outcomes), and we will report sensitivity analyses, negative controls, and failure modes. Competing models will be compared using out-of-sample performance and stability metrics rather than narrative preference.

Community engagement. We will host open tutorials and “workflow clinics” during NCEMS meetings and publish step-by-step training materials (notebooks, recorded walkthroughs) aimed at graduate students and postdocs. We will solicit feedback on the mesoscale feature set and metadata recommendations via public issues and lightweight community review.

Archiving and dissemination. Final releases will be archived with DOIs (e.g., Zenodo) and mirrored to long-term repositories (e.g., GitHub/GitLab plus institutional archives). Derived features and harmonized metadata tables will be deposited in appropriate public repositories when permitted, enabling reuse beyond this project and aligning with NCEMS’s gold-standard open, team, and reproducible science practices.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support rationale. This project requires NCEMS resources because it depends on coordinated, multi-lab synthesis across heterogeneous public repositories, sustained collaboration between domain experts (cell biology/biophysics) and technical experts (imaging informatics/proteomics/statistics/ML), and structured training activities. No single lab typically has the breadth to curate multimodal datasets, implement interoperable standards, and perform rigorous cross-system causal inference with replication.

(5) Dissemination: open-access publication fees where applicable; archiving costs for DOI-backed releases; and development time for tutorials and documentation.

Team composition and partnerships. The working group will include: cytoskeleton cell biologists; biophysicists/active matter theorists; imaging scientists with expertise in segmentation and spatiotemporal analysis; proteomics and functional genomics experts; causal inference/statistics researchers; ML practitioners; and data curators familiar with BioImage Archive/IDR and omics repositories. We will intentionally recruit participants across institution types (R1s, teaching-focused institutions, and research institutes), geographic regions, and career stages.

NCEMS facilities and coordination. We will leverage NCEMS convening power, meeting space, and synthesis expertise to: (i) establish shared standards and decision logs, (ii) run structured sprints with clear deliverables, (iii) ensure open-science compliance, and (iv) support cross-lab replication and consensus building. The deliverables (data catalog, feature standards, pipelines, manuscripts, and training materials) will be produced as shared community resources maintained beyond the award period.

background_and_significance:
Cells maintain organelles—nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes/vacuoles, peroxisomes, centrosomes, chloroplasts—within characteristic size and copy-number ranges despite fluctuations in growth rate, metabolism, differentiation state, and stress. This “organelle size homeostasis” is a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon: it is not encoded by a single gene or pathway, but emerges from many interacting molecular processes (biogenesis, fusion/fission, trafficking, degradation, membrane supply, and cytoskeletal organization) acting across space and time. Yet the field lacks a unified, quantitative, cross-species description of how organelle dimensions scale with cell size, cell cycle, ploidy, and environmental state, and which scaling relationships are conserved versus lineage-specific.

Classic work established scaling ideas such as nuclear-to-cell volume ratios and mitochondrial network remodeling with demand, but most evidence remains fragmented: measured with different microscopes, segmentation conventions, cell types, and perturbations; reported as summary statistics rather than reusable single-cell measurements; and rarely connected to matched molecular profiles. Meanwhile, the public data landscape has changed dramatically. High-content imaging repositories (e.g., BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource), reference atlases (e.g., Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas), and single-cell/spatial omics resources now contain millions of cells with subcellular labels, perturbation annotations, and phenotypic readouts. Proteomics repositories (PRIDE/MassIVE) and functional genomics screens (CRISPR/RNAi) provide complementary evidence about composition and regulation. Structural predictions (AlphaFold) and curated interaction/pathway databases add mechanistic context. The opportunity—and challenge—is to synthesize these heterogeneous resources to extract generalizable laws.

NCEMS is uniquely suited to catalyze this synthesis because the question is inherently transdisciplinary and beyond any single laboratory’s scope. Addressing it requires (i) data engineering to locate, curate, and harmonize imaging and omics datasets; (ii) computer vision and measurement science to derive comparable organelle metrics; (iii) statistical and causal modeling to separate biological scaling from batch effects and missingness; (iv) phylogenetic comparative methods to test conservation and evolutionary divergence; and (v) cell biology and biophysics expertise to interpret emergent mesoscale rules and connect them to plausible mechanisms.

A cross-species atlas of organelle scaling would resolve long-standing puzzles: Are organelle size ratios actively regulated or passive consequences of growth? Do different organelles obey shared constraints (e.g., membrane economy, surface-to-volume limits, transport times) that generate universal scaling exponents? When do scaling laws break—during differentiation, stress, aneuploidy, or disease—and what molecular programs predict those breaks? Importantly, the atlas would elevate mesoscale organization to a first-class quantitative layer, enabling tests of whether organelle geometry and topology explain cellular outcomes beyond molecular abundance alone.

Finally, this project aligns with NCEMS goals to train a data-savvy workforce and build community infrastructure. By producing reusable measurements, metadata standards, and reproducible workflows, the working group will lower barriers for the broader community to reuse public data for mesoscale discovery, accelerating research on emergence across molecular-to-cellular scales.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The working group will address four tightly linked research questions that together test whether organelle size homeostasis reflects conserved emergent rules rather than idiosyncratic, dataset-specific patterns.

RQ1: What scaling laws relate organelle size and copy number to cell size, cell cycle state, and growth conditions across species and cell types? Hypothesis 1A: For major organelles, there exist conserved allometric relationships of the form O ~ C^α (organelle metric O vs. cell metric C) with α values that cluster by organelle function (information storage, energy conversion, trafficking, degradation). Hypothesis 1B: Deviations from these relationships are structured (state-dependent) rather than random noise, and can be explained by physiological axes such as proliferation, metabolic mode, and stress responses.

RQ2: Are scaling exponents and set-points evolutionarily conserved, and what is the phylogenetic pattern of divergence? Hypothesis 2A: Core organelles show partial universality: broad conservation of exponent α with lineage-specific intercept shifts reflecting cell wall presence, endomembrane complexity, or energetic strategy. Hypothesis 2B: Apparent “universal” rules will weaken when sampling expands beyond a few model systems; phylogenetically informed models will reveal both deep constraints and clade-specific innovations.

RQ3: Do mesoscale organelle features improve prediction of cellular outcomes beyond molecular abundance and pathway activity? Cellular outcomes include proliferation potential, differentiation state, stress tolerance, and, where available, viability or drug response. Hypothesis 3A: Joint models that incorporate organelle geometry/topology (e.g., mitochondrial network connectedness; nuclear shape; lysosome abundance) will explain additional variance in outcomes compared with transcript/protein abundance alone, indicating that mesoscale organization is an emergent, information-bearing layer. Hypothesis 3B: The predictive contribution of organelle features will be strongest in contexts where regulation is post-transcriptional (e.g., organelle dynamics, trafficking), revealing why omics-only models sometimes fail.

RQ4: Which molecular and structural features are associated with conserved versus divergent scaling behavior? Hypothesis 4A: Variation in scaling parameters across species and conditions will correlate with quantitative properties of organelle proteomes (e.g., membrane vs. matrix fraction, curvature-generating proteins, fission/fusion machinery abundance) and with structural features (e.g., predicted disorder, multivalency) that influence mesoscale assembly. Hypothesis 4B: Perturbation datasets (CRISPR/RNAi) will show that genes affecting membrane supply, lipid metabolism, and cytoskeletal transport disproportionately modulate scaling exponents, consistent with constraint-based, system-level control.

Across all questions, we will explicitly test an “emergence criterion”: mesoscale variables should (i) be measurable and comparable across datasets, (ii) show reproducible regularities (scaling) across biological diversity, and (iii) provide explanatory/predictive power not reducible to single-molecule effects. Competing hypotheses—purely passive scaling, dataset artifacts, or model-system-specific rules—will be evaluated through cross-dataset replication, sensitivity analyses, and phylogenetically structured comparisons.

These questions are designed to yield both scientific answers (what rules exist, where they hold, where they break) and methodological advances (how to perform rigorous, uncertainty-aware synthesis of heterogeneous imaging and omics data at the mesoscale).
methods_and_approach:
This NCEMS Working Group will execute a synthesis-only, multi-lab workflow organized into four integrated aims.

Aim 1: Public data discovery, inclusion criteria, and harmonization. We will inventory candidate datasets spanning animals, fungi, plants, and protists, prioritizing those with (i) raw or minimally processed images, (ii) organelle labels or stains, (iii) single-cell/spatial omics links or matched sample metadata, and (iv) perturbation/state annotations. Sources include BioImage Archive/IDR, Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, EMBL-EBI/NCBI functional genomics repositories, PRIDE/MassIVE, and public CRISPR/RNAi screens. We will implement a transparent inclusion rubric and create a dataset registry with provenance, licensing, and quality flags. Metadata will be mapped to a common schema (cell type, species/strain, imaging modality, segmentation method, perturbation, growth condition) using controlled vocabularies where possible.

Aim 2: Comparable organelle metrics from heterogeneous imaging. We will not generate new images; instead, we will extract standardized measurements. Where segmentations exist, we will compute harmonized features: organelle volume/area, surface proxies, count, spatial dispersion, shape descriptors, and network topology (for mitochondria/ER where feasible). Where only images exist, we will apply pretrained or openly available segmentation models, benchmarking against provided labels and reporting uncertainty. To avoid overfitting to any one dataset, we will use cross-dataset evaluation and “measurement invariance” checks (e.g., whether scaling exponents are stable across segmentation approaches). All feature extraction will be containerized.

Aim 3: Statistical synthesis and phylogenetic comparative modeling. We will fit hierarchical models that separate biological signal from technical variation: multilevel allometric regressions with dataset- and batch-specific random effects; explicit modeling of measurement error; and missing-data strategies (multiple imputation and sensitivity bounds). To compare across species, we will use phylogenetic generalized least squares and Bayesian phylogenetic mixed models, estimating conserved exponents and lineage-specific shifts while accounting for shared ancestry. We will quantify uncertainty in scaling parameters and test for regime changes across states (cell cycle, stress, differentiation) using change-point and mixture models.

Aim 4: Linking mesoscale features to molecular composition and outcomes. We will integrate organelle metrics with matched transcriptomic/proteomic signatures (when available) using multi-view learning (e.g., sparse canonical correlation, variational approaches) and interpretable predictive models. We will test incremental predictive value of organelle features over omics-only baselines via nested model comparison, cross-validation, and external dataset replication. Perturbation data will be used to map genes to shifts in scaling parameters (e.g., Δα, Δintercept), enabling mechanistic interpretation without new experiments. Structural annotations (AlphaFold/PDB-derived features) and pathway networks will support enrichment analyses for proteins associated with conserved vs. divergent scaling.

Working group execution and feasibility. The project requires NCEMS coordination: two in-person synthesis meetings plus virtual sprints. Subteams (imaging/measurement, omics integration, phylogenetics/statistics, curation/standards) will produce interoperable modules that converge into an integrated atlas. Trainees will lead cross-dataset replication tasks and documentation. Milestones include: (M1) dataset registry and schema; (M2) first release of harmonized organelle metrics; (M3) phylogenetic scaling models; (M4) predictive models and atlas v1.0 with tutorials.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific products. (1) A cross-species, single-cell–resolved atlas of organelle size, copy number, and geometry metrics harmonized across public imaging resources, linked where possible to omics, perturbations, and phenotypic outcomes. (2) Quantitative scaling laws for major organelles, including estimates of conserved exponents, lineage-specific shifts, and state-dependent breakpoints (e.g., stress, differentiation, altered ploidy). (3) Evidence-based tests of whether mesoscale organelle organization contributes predictive/explanatory power beyond molecular abundance, establishing mesoscale features as an emergent information-bearing layer.

Methodological products. (4) A generalizable synthesis pipeline for heterogeneous bioimage-derived measurements with uncertainty quantification, batch-aware modeling, and phylogenetically informed comparison. (5) Community-facing metadata recommendations and a reusable dataset registry that lowers the barrier to future mesoscale synthesis projects.

Impact on emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences. The atlas will enable the field to move from anecdotal statements (“organelle X scales with cell size”) to falsifiable, quantitative, cross-species rules and principled exceptions. By explicitly connecting composition (omics, pathways, structural features) to mesoscale organization (organelle metrics) and to outcomes (state and phenotype annotations), the project will clarify when emergent properties arise from collective constraints (membrane economy, transport limits, network dynamics) rather than single-gene effects. These insights will inform models of cellular robustness, adaptation, and failure modes relevant to development, stress biology, and disease.

Community and workforce impact. The working group will train trainees in open, reproducible synthesis science (data curation, bioimage analysis, statistical modeling, and phylogenetic methods). Deliverables—versioned data releases, tutorials, and modular code—will be designed for reuse in classrooms, workshops, and downstream research, multiplying the value of existing public datasets and aligning tightly with NCEMS’s mission to catalyze community-scale discovery without generating new experimental data.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-by-default outputs. All derived organelle metrics, harmonized metadata, and model outputs will be released under permissive terms consistent with the licenses of underlying datasets. We will not redistribute restricted raw data; instead, we will provide stable pointers, accession IDs, and automated retrieval scripts where allowed.

Reproducible workflows. The full pipeline—from dataset registry creation through feature extraction, statistical modeling, and figure generation—will be implemented as version-controlled workflows (GitHub/GitLab) using containers (Docker/Singularity) and workflow managers (e.g., Snakemake/Nextflow). Each release will be tagged, archived (Zenodo DOI), and accompanied by environment files and continuous integration tests that rerun key analyses on representative subsets.

Transparent provenance and uncertainty. Every derived measurement will retain provenance fields (source dataset, imaging modality, segmentation method/version, parameter settings) and uncertainty estimates where applicable (e.g., segmentation confidence, measurement error). Statistical models will report posterior/interval estimates, sensitivity analyses for missingness, and robustness checks across alternative preprocessing choices.

FAIR and community standards. We will publish a machine-readable metadata schema and mapping tables to controlled vocabularies (species taxonomy, cell ontology where available, perturbation identifiers). Data will be organized to be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable, with clear documentation and examples.

Team science practices. The working group will adopt written collaboration norms: code review, issue tracking, authorship/contribution taxonomy (CRediT), and decision logs for inclusion/exclusion criteria. Trainees will receive structured mentoring in reproducible research, including “workflow clinics” on literate programming (Quarto/Jupyter), data management, and responsible AI use.

Dissemination. We will produce an open methods preprint, an atlas paper, and lightweight educational materials (tutorial notebooks, recorded walkthroughs). Where feasible, we will engage repository curators and standards communities to ensure our recommendations are actionable and aligned with ongoing efforts.
