author: gpt-5.2
title: Hidden mesoscale states in drug resistance trajectories
abstract:
This working group asks how hidden mesoscale states in drug resistance trajectories can be understood as an emergent property that links molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcome. The scientific question is not simply whether particular molecules, organelles, or pathways are associated with a phenotype, but whether publicly available datasets can reveal rules by which many molecular parts collectively produce a new, system-level behavior at the scale between biomolecules and organelles. The project is designed for the NCEMS model because the relevant evidence is scattered across incompatible imaging repositories, omics studies, perturbation resources, structural annotations, and specialized literatures; no single laboratory is likely to have the biological breadth, data-engineering capacity, and methodological expertise to integrate them.

The group would synthesize existing public data centered on perturbation/genetic screens, prioritizing datasets with reusable metadata, perturbation or state annotations, and links to downstream cellular phenotypes. Depending on availability, sources could include public cell atlases, the Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, EMBL-EBI and NCBI functional genomics repositories, BioImage Archive or Image Data Resource collections, PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics datasets, public CRISPR or RNAi screens, AlphaFold/PDB-derived structural features, and curated pathway or protein-interaction resources. The core analytic strategy would be foundation-model representation learning: harmonizing measurements into a common representation; explicitly modeling uncertainty, batch effects, and missingness; and testing whether mesoscale variables explain cellular outcomes above and beyond molecular abundance alone. The biological scope would focus on human disease cells while deliberately including comparison cases that prevent the group from mistaking a narrow model-system pattern for a general law.

The novel element is the unit of explanation. Instead of treating mesoscale organization as an image label, downstream readout, or anecdotal mechanism, the working group would make it the primary object of synthesis: a measurable layer where composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion combine. The expected product is a predictive atlas that is open, versioned, and reusable, with transparent workflows, community-agreed metadata standards, and tutorials for trainees. The project would bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, imaging scientists, omics researchers, statisticians, machine-learning researchers, data curators, and trainees across institution types. Training would occur through hackathon-style data sprints, reproducible workflow clinics, and rotating trainee leadership of cross-dataset validation tasks. The anticipated contribution is both scientific and infrastructural: a defensible answer to a specific emergence question, plus a generalizable synthesis strategy that helps the molecular and cellular biosciences reuse public data to discover phenomena that only become visible when datasets, disciplines, and scales are brought together.
background_and_significance:
Drug resistance is often described as a molecular problem (mutations, expression programs, pathway rewiring) or as a population-genetic problem (selection on pre-existing variants). Yet across cancers, infectious disease, and targeted therapies, resistance trajectories repeatedly display phenotypes that are difficult to explain by single genes or linear pathways alone: reversible “drug-tolerant persister” states, heterogeneous time-to-relapse, morphology-linked tolerance, and stress-adaptation programs that appear across drugs and cell types. These observations suggest that resistance is also a problem of emergence: many molecular parts collectively giving rise to system-level behaviors that are stable enough to matter, but plastic enough to transition under perturbation.

NCEMS’s focus on mesoscale emergence is directly relevant because key determinants of tolerance and resistance plausibly reside between biomolecules and organelles: phase-separated condensates that sequester signaling proteins, reorganized endomembrane trafficking that alters receptor recycling, mitochondrial network remodeling that shifts energy and redox states, chromatin compartment changes that reshape transcriptional accessibility, and cytoskeletal reconfiguration that couples mechanics to signaling. These are not merely “cell shape” correlates; they are organizational states that integrate composition, space, time, energy, and information. If such mesoscale states exist as recurring, measurable attractors, they could explain why distinct molecular perturbations converge on similar resistance outcomes and why similar molecular profiles can diverge in fate.

Despite abundant public data, the field lacks a synthesis framework to test mesoscale-state hypotheses systematically. Imaging repositories contain rich subcellular organization information but are fragmented across modalities, cell types, and metadata conventions. Functional genomics screens identify genes whose perturbation changes drug response, but rarely connect hits to mesoscale organization. Proteomics and phosphoproteomics quantify signaling and stress pathways yet often miss spatial context. Structural and interaction resources encode physical constraints on assembly, but are not routinely integrated with phenotype trajectories. Individually, these datasets yield partial explanations; collectively, they may reveal rules of mesoscale organization that only become visible at community scale.

This working group addresses a long-standing puzzle: why drug resistance repeatedly exhibits convergent phenotypes without convergent molecular causes. We posit that a hidden layer of mesoscale state variables mediates this convergence. The significance is twofold. Scientifically, identifying recurrent mesoscale states would shift resistance from a catalog of molecular associations to a mechanistic, state-based theory that links perturbations to trajectories. Practically, mesoscale states could provide more robust biomarkers and intervention points than single genes, because they represent integrated system configurations. Methodologically, the project will develop a generalizable synthesis pipeline for learning mesoscale representations from heterogeneous public data, with explicit uncertainty quantification and cross-dataset validation.

The project is uniquely suited to the NCEMS model: it requires integrating diverse public datasets, harmonizing incompatible metadata, and combining expertise in cell biology, biophysics, imaging, omics, machine learning, and data curation. No single lab can assemble the breadth of datasets, the engineering to standardize them, and the methodological rigor to test emergence claims across systems. By convening a multidisciplinary working group, NCEMS support will catalyze a reusable, open atlas of mesoscale states relevant to resistance, while training trainees in synthesis science and reproducible, AI-enabled integration.

(Word count: ~500)
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Central question: Do drug resistance trajectories pass through a finite set of recurrent, measurable mesoscale states that mediate the mapping from molecular perturbations to cellular outcomes, and can these states be inferred from existing public data better than by molecular abundance alone?

RQ1: Existence and discreteness of mesoscale states. Are there latent mesoscale organizational states that recur across datasets, drugs, and cell types, and that are separable from simple batch or modality effects?
H1.1: Multimodal representations learned from public imaging and omics will reveal a low-dimensional latent space with clustered or manifold-structured regions corresponding to mesoscale states (e.g., “stress-granule/translation repression,” “mitochondrial fusion/oxidative shift,” “endolysosomal remodeling,” “chromatin compaction”).
H1.2: These latent states will be reproducible across independent studies when controlling for technical covariates, indicating biological rather than dataset-specific structure.

RQ2: Predictive value for resistance outcomes. Do inferred mesoscale states explain drug response phenotypes (survival, growth arrest, relapse propensity, tolerance) beyond what is explained by molecular abundance, mutations, or pathway scores?
H2.1: Models that include mesoscale latent variables will improve prediction of resistance-related outcomes compared to models using transcript/protein abundance alone, measured by cross-study generalization performance.
H2.2: Mesoscale states will be especially predictive for non-genetic resistance and early adaptive responses, where molecular signatures are transient and heterogeneous.

RQ3: Causal coherence and convergent mechanisms. Do diverse perturbations converge onto shared mesoscale states, providing an emergent explanation for convergent phenotypes?
H3.1: Genes and pathways identified in CRISPR/RNAi drug-response screens will map onto a smaller number of mesoscale states than expected by chance, consistent with many-to-one convergence.
H3.2: Structural and interaction features (e.g., propensity for multivalent interactions, subcellular localization signals, organelle contact site participation) will predict which perturbations drive transitions into specific mesoscale states.

RQ4: Trajectories and transitions. Can we infer likely state transitions over time or dose—i.e., resistance trajectories—using only existing data with partial time information?
H4.1: When integrating time-course transcriptomics/proteomics with imaging snapshots, we can reconstruct probabilistic transition graphs among mesoscale states (e.g., sensitive → acute stress → tolerant persister → proliferative resistant).
H4.2: Transition probabilities will depend on drug class and cellular context but will share conserved motifs (e.g., a common “tolerant bottleneck” state) across diseases.

RQ5: Generality versus specificity. Which mesoscale states are universal across human disease cells, and which are context-specific?
H5.1: A subset of mesoscale states will be conserved across multiple disease contexts and drugs, reflecting generic cellular adaptation modules.
H5.2: Context-specific states will correlate with lineage programs and organelle baseline architecture, detectable via cell atlas references.

Together, these questions operationalize “emergence” as: (i) a latent organizational layer, (ii) integrative predictive power, and (iii) convergent mapping from diverse molecular changes to shared system-level behavior.

(Word count: ~500)
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. The project will run as an NCEMS working group with three integrated thrusts: (A) Data assembly and harmonization, (B) Representation learning and state inference, and (C) Validation, interpretation, and dissemination. All analyses will use only publicly available data; no new experiments will be performed.

A) Data assembly and harmonization (Months 0–6; ongoing updates). We will curate a “resistance-centered” corpus anchored on perturbation and phenotype annotations.
Data types: (1) Functional genomics drug-response screens (CRISPR/RNAi; viability, proliferation, resistance scores), (2) bulk and single-cell transcriptomics (including time courses), (3) proteomics/phosphoproteomics, (4) subcellular imaging datasets (high-content microscopy, organelle markers; BioImage Archive/IDR; Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas), (5) pathway and interaction networks (Reactome, STRING/BioGRID), and (6) structure-derived protein features (AlphaFold/PDB-based disorder, multivalency proxies, interaction interfaces).
Harmonization: map genes/proteins to stable identifiers; standardize drugs (RxNorm/ChEMBL where possible), doses, time, and cell lines; encode phenotypes using controlled vocabularies; capture provenance and quality metrics. We will implement a metadata “minimum information” schema for resistance synthesis, with converters for common repositories.

B) Representation learning and mesoscale state inference (Months 4–14). The key methodological development is a multimodal foundation-model approach that learns shared representations while handling missingness.
Imaging features: use pretrained self-supervised vision models (e.g., ViT-based) to embed cell and organelle organization; where raw images are unavailable, use published feature tables.
Omics features: embed gene/protein expression using pathway-aware encoders (graph regularization) and cell-atlas references for baseline states.
Multimodal integration: apply methods such as variational autoencoders with modality-specific encoders and a shared latent space, or contrastive learning to align modalities by perturbation and phenotype labels. Missingness will be modeled explicitly (partial inference) rather than imputed naively.
Batch and uncertainty: incorporate hierarchical models with study-level random effects; propagate uncertainty from measurement noise and mapping ambiguity; evaluate robustness via sensitivity analyses.
State discovery: identify latent mesoscale states using clustering on latent embeddings, hidden Markov models for time-resolved datasets, and graph community detection on inferred transition networks.

C) Validation and interpretation (Months 10–18). Because no new experiments are allowed, validation will be cross-dataset and predictive.
Cross-study generalization: train on one subset of studies and test on held-out studies/drugs/cell types; compare to baselines (molecular-only models, pathway scores).
Convergence tests: quantify many-to-one mapping from perturbations to states; test enrichment of screen hits in state-associated modules.
Mechanistic interpretation: link states to organelle-level signatures (e.g., mitochondrial morphology embeddings), pathway activation, and structural features; produce interpretable “state cards” summarizing defining features, uncertainties, and known literature.

NCEMS-style collaboration. The working group will run two in-person meetings (kickoff; synthesis/interpretation) and monthly virtual sprints. Trainees will lead cross-dataset replication tasks and documentation. A lightweight governance model (data/analysis leads; curation lead; trainee council) will ensure progress and shared ownership.

(Word count: ~500)
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific deliverables. (1) A set of empirically supported mesoscale state variables associated with drug resistance trajectories, defined operationally as latent representations that are reproducible across independent public datasets and predictive of resistance-related outcomes. (2) A probabilistic transition model (state graph) describing common routes into tolerance and resistance, including uncertainty estimates and context dependence (drug class, lineage, baseline organelle architecture). (3) Evidence for or against the emergence hypothesis: whether mesoscale organization provides explanatory and predictive power beyond molecular abundance and canonical pathway annotations.

Data and infrastructure deliverables. (4) An open, versioned “Mesoscale Resistance Atlas” consisting of harmonized metadata tables, modality-specific embeddings (where licenses permit), learned latent representations, and state annotations (“state cards”). (5) A reusable pipeline for multimodal synthesis under missingness and batch effects, packaged as containerized workflows suitable for other NCEMS-style projects.

Community and training deliverables. (6) Tutorials and short courses (recorded notebooks) on: curating public imaging and omics for synthesis, multimodal representation learning, uncertainty-aware integration, and cross-study validation. (7) Trainee-led replication reports that document what does and does not reproduce across datasets, elevating negative results into community knowledge.

Impact on molecular and cellular biosciences. By elevating mesoscale organization to a primary object of explanation, the project will connect molecular composition to higher-level cellular behaviors through a state-based framework. If successful, it will help resolve why diverse perturbations converge on similar resistant phenotypes and provide a principled vocabulary for mesoscale adaptation modules. Even if mesoscale states prove weak or non-generalizable, the project will still deliver high-value synthesis infrastructure and rigorous benchmarks that clarify limits of current public data for mesoscale inference. The atlas and methods will be broadly applicable to other emergence problems (organelle contact dynamics, condensate-driven signaling, stress adaptation) and will accelerate data reuse by providing standards, code, and validated integration strategies.

(Word count: ~300)
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-by-design outputs. All code, documentation, and analysis notebooks will be released under a permissive open-source license (e.g., BSD-3/Apache-2.0) in a public repository with issue tracking and contribution guidelines. We will publish a frozen “release” for each milestone (v0.1 curation; v0.2 embeddings; v1.0 atlas/state cards), each with a DOI via Zenodo.

Reproducible workflows. Analyses will be implemented as containerized, workflow-managed pipelines (e.g., Snakemake/Nextflow) with pinned software versions, deterministic seeds where applicable, and automated continuous integration tests. Each figure and table will be generated by a single command from raw public inputs (or from cached, checksum-verified downloads) to final outputs. We will maintain a data provenance ledger that records source URLs/accession IDs, download dates, checksums, and any transformation steps.

FAIR and ethical reuse. We will not redistribute controlled-access human data; instead we will distribute derived, non-identifiable summaries and provide scripts that authorized users can run locally. For imaging and omics datasets with redistribution restrictions, we will store only metadata pointers and computed features when permitted. All datasets will be cited with accession IDs, licenses, and attribution to original generators.

Community standards. A key working-group product will be a community-usable metadata schema for resistance-oriented mesoscale synthesis (perturbation, dose, time, cell context, imaging markers, phenotype definitions). We will align with existing standards where possible (e.g., OME for imaging metadata; gene/drug identifier standards) and document extensions needed for mesoscale-state inference.

Transparent uncertainty and negative results. The atlas will include uncertainty estimates for state assignments and explicit “known limitations” sections. We will release replication and ablation results even when they reduce performance, to prevent overclaiming and to guide future synthesis efforts.

Training and openness. Trainees will be trained in open science practices (code review, preregistered analysis plans for key benchmarks, data management) and will co-author public technical reports.

(Word count: ~300)

This scope exceeds a single lab due to (i) breadth of repositories and modalities, (ii) need for cross-study validation and governance, and (iii) specialized expertise spanning imaging, omics, ML, statistics, and cell biology.

Budget categories (working-group level; illustrative). (2) Personnel time buyout/coordination: partial support for a project manager or synthesis coordinator to track milestones, manage curation tasks, and maintain documentation; limited support for a research software engineer to harden workflows and CI. (3) Compute and storage: cloud credits or NCEMS-provided compute for embedding large imaging datasets, training multimodal models, and maintaining artifact storage; budget includes backup and long-term archiving costs for derived products. (4) Training activities: funds for hackathon-style data sprints (virtual facilitation, tutorial development time, captioning/recording), and small trainee micro-awards for leading replication packages.

Resources and team roles. The working group will include: imaging scientists (feature extraction, OME/IDR expertise), omics analysts (single-cell/bulk integration), ML researchers (representation learning, uncertainty), statisticians (hierarchical modeling, batch correction), cell biologists/biophysicists (mesoscale interpretation), and data curators (metadata schema, FAIR compliance). NCEMS will provide meeting space, facilitation, and synthesis-center expertise in open/reproducible science.

Deliverable-linked resourcing. Budget will be tied to milestones: (M1) curated corpus and schema; (M2) baseline models and benchmarks; (M3) atlas release and tutorials. This ensures feasibility and accountability while enabling community-scale integration.

background_and_significance:
Membraneless organelles (MLOs)—including nuclear speckles, transcriptional condensates, nucleoli, stress granules, and P-bodies—are mesoscale structures formed through multivalent interactions among proteins and RNAs. They concentrate, exclude, and dynamically exchange molecules without a delimiting membrane. Because they sit between molecular interactions and whole-cell phenotypes, MLOs are prime candidates for the NCEMS scientific vision: emergent properties at the mesoscale that influence higher subcellular and cellular outcomes. Yet, despite rapid growth in the phase separation and condensate literature, the field lacks a synthesis-based, quantitative account of how MLO composition and organization shape gene expression dynamics across cell types, conditions, and species.

Transcriptional bursting—stochastic switching between active and inactive promoter states—provides a mechanistic bridge between molecular regulation and phenotypic heterogeneity. Burst frequency and burst size determine cell-to-cell variability, responsiveness to stimuli, and developmental decisions. A recurring hypothesis is that MLOs modulate bursting by locally concentrating transcription factors, polymerases, coactivators, chromatin remodelers, and RNAs, thereby altering reaction rates and noise. However, evidence is dispersed across (i) live-cell imaging studies measuring burst kinetics at select loci, (ii) single-cell and spatial transcriptomics capturing population-level burst signatures, (iii) proteomics and interactomics defining MLO components, (iv) perturbation screens implicating regulators of condensate formation, and (v) structural and sequence annotations (e.g., intrinsically disordered regions) that predict phase behavior. These data streams are rarely integrated, and each uses incompatible formats, metadata conventions, and measurement scales.

A fundamental, emergence-focused question remains unanswered: do MLOs act as information filters that transform noisy molecular inputs (factor abundance, signaling state, chromatin context) into structured transcriptional outputs (burst parameters, coordinated gene programs)? “Information filter” here means a mesoscale mechanism that (a) selectively transmits certain regulatory signals while attenuating others, (b) imposes timescale-dependent smoothing or amplification, and (c) changes the mapping from molecular composition to gene expression variability in a way that is not predictable from molecular abundance alone. If true, this would constitute an emergent property: collective molecular interactions producing system-level behavior—regulated bursting statistics—at a scale not reducible to individual components.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to enable this work because answering it requires community-scale synthesis. No single lab can simultaneously curate imaging repositories, harmonize single-cell/spatial omics, interpret condensate biophysics, and build mechanistic statistical models that respect uncertainty and missingness. The working group will integrate public datasets spanning multiple organisms (e.g., human cell lines, mouse, yeast, Drosophila) to identify generalizable rules and boundary conditions. It will also treat mesoscale organization as a first-class quantitative variable, rather than an illustrative mechanism. By doing so, the project addresses long-standing puzzles (why bursting parameters vary across contexts; why condensate perturbations have locus-specific effects), develops reusable analytical strategies (data assimilation linking imaging-derived condensate features to burst inference), recruits diverse expertise, and trains data-savvy scientists.

Beyond basic science, a synthesis-based understanding of MLO filtering has implications for disease mechanisms (e.g., neurodegeneration and cancer-associated condensate dysregulation), therapeutic strategies targeting protein–RNA interaction networks, and interpretation of single-cell atlases where variability is often dismissed as noise. The proposed working group will produce both scientific insight and infrastructure—harmonized representations, benchmarks, and open workflows—that enable the broader community to interrogate mesoscale emergence using existing public data.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The working group will address the overarching question: Can membraneless organelles be quantitatively modeled as mesoscale information filters that shape transcriptional bursting across biological contexts using only publicly available data? We define “filtering” in operational terms: a transformation from upstream molecular inputs to downstream burst parameters that is selective (gene- and context-dependent), dynamic (timescale-dependent), and partially decoupled from bulk abundance.

RQ1: What measurable mesoscale variables of MLOs best predict transcriptional bursting parameters across datasets? Candidate variables include condensate presence/absence, size distributions, density proxies, component stoichiometry, exchange dynamics (FRAP-like), spatial proximity to genomic loci, and co-localization with transcriptional machinery. Hypothesis H1: Models incorporating mesoscale variables (condensate features) explain significant additional variance in inferred burst frequency and burst size beyond models using only molecular abundance (e.g., TF/cofactor expression) and chromatin covariates.

RQ2: Do MLOs implement distinct filter types (low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, or thresholding) with respect to signaling and regulatory inputs? We will treat signaling state (e.g., stress, differentiation cues), factor abundance, and post-translational modification proxies as inputs, and bursting statistics as outputs. Hypothesis H2: Specific MLO classes correspond to characteristic filter behaviors; for example, nuclear speckle-associated genes exhibit low-pass filtering (attenuated response to fast fluctuations, stabilized bursting), whereas transient transcriptional condensates exhibit thresholding or gain control (amplified bursting upon crossing multivalency thresholds).

RQ3: Are filtering rules conserved or do they depend on organism, cell type, or genomic architecture? We will compare model organisms and human systems to identify invariants and boundary conditions. Hypothesis H3: Core relationships between predicted phase-separation propensity (e.g., IDR content, multivalency, interaction degree) and filtering strength are conserved, while locus-level outcomes depend on promoter architecture and chromatin environment.

RQ4: Which molecular features of MLO components are most associated with filtering strength and specificity? We will integrate structural predictions (AlphaFold confidence, disorder predictions), domain annotations, RNA-binding motifs, and protein–protein interaction networks. Hypothesis H4: Filtering strength increases with component multivalency and network centrality, and is modulated by RNA-binding capacity; these features predict when perturbations of a component will alter bursting noise versus mean expression.

RQ5: Can we reconcile apparently conflicting literature claims about condensates and transcription by explicitly modeling uncertainty, batch effects, and missingness across studies? Hypothesis H5: Many discrepancies are attributable to measurement timescale mismatches and unmodeled confounding (cell cycle, imaging modality, perturbation strength). A unified hierarchical model with explicit uncertainty will reduce contradictions and identify contexts where condensate–burst coupling is weak or absent.

RQ6 (methodological): What minimal metadata and representation standards are required to make mesoscale organization reusable across imaging and omics repositories? Hypothesis H6: A compact “mesoscale feature schema” (MFS) capturing condensate identity, measurement modality, spatial scale, and uncertainty will enable cross-dataset validation and improve reproducibility of emergence claims.

Together, these questions test whether mesoscale organization provides an explanatory layer linking molecular composition to transcriptional dynamics, and whether that layer can be formalized as information processing—an emergent property visible only through synthesis of heterogeneous public datasets.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and design. The working group will conduct a community-scale synthesis using only publicly available data. The approach is organized into four work packages (WPs): (WP1) data discovery and harmonization, (WP2) mesoscale feature extraction and representation, (WP3) burst inference and mechanistic data assimilation, and (WP4) cross-system generalization and validation. The group will meet in NCEMS-supported working sessions combining curation sprints, model-building hackathons, and structured cross-lab replication.

WP1: Data inventory, inclusion criteria, and harmonization. We will assemble a catalog of datasets spanning (a) imaging of MLOs and transcription (BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Allen Cell collections where applicable), (b) single-cell and spatial transcriptomics (GEO/SRA, ArrayExpress, Human Cell Atlas-derived resources), (c) perturbation screens affecting condensate components (DepMap/CRISPR screens where public; GEO-based CRISPR readouts; curated RNAi resources), (d) proteomics of condensate fractions and interactomes (PRIDE, MassIVE), and (e) structural/sequence annotations (UniProt, Pfam, PDB/AlphaFold, disorder predictors available as public tracks). Inclusion criteria: clear sample metadata, reuse-permitting license/access, mapping to gene identifiers, and at least one of (i) perturbation/state labels, (ii) phenotype linkage, or (iii) imaging features enabling mesoscale quantification. Harmonization will use standardized gene IDs, controlled vocabularies for cell type/condition, and a provenance graph tracking transformations.

WP2: Mesoscale feature extraction and schema (MFS). For imaging datasets, we will compute reproducible condensate features: number per nucleus/cell, size/shape distributions, intensity-based enrichment, co-localization metrics with Pol II or nascent RNA markers (when present), spatial distances to nuclear landmarks, and temporal persistence when time series exist. When raw images are unavailable but annotations exist, we will ingest published segmentations or summary features with uncertainty tags. We will define the Mesoscale Feature Schema (MFS): a minimal, modality-agnostic representation including (i) MLO class ontology term, (ii) measurement modality and resolution, (iii) feature values with units, (iv) uncertainty/quality flags, and (v) mapping to sample/cell identifiers. This schema will be co-developed with data curators to maximize interoperability.

WP3: Burst inference and mechanistic data assimilation. For transcriptomics, we will infer burst parameters using established statistical frameworks (e.g., two-state promoter models fit to scRNA-seq count distributions with technical-noise-aware likelihoods; where allele-resolved or nascent RNA data exist, incorporate them to constrain kinetics). For spatial data, we will incorporate neighborhood covariates and tissue structure. We will then build hierarchical models that assimilate mesoscale features (MFS) as latent or observed predictors of burst frequency/size, controlling for confounders (cell cycle, library depth, batch, chromatin accessibility proxies when available). Mechanistic components will include reaction–diffusion or effective concentration models that map condensate enrichment to kinetic rate changes; these will be fit as interpretable priors within Bayesian frameworks. Missingness will be handled via explicit missing-data models rather than ad hoc imputation.

WP4: Cross-dataset generalization, causal triangulation, and robustness. We will evaluate whether mesoscale variables improve prediction of bursting across held-out datasets, organisms, and labs using nested cross-validation. To approach causality without new experiments, we will triangulate evidence from perturbation datasets: components predicted to alter mesoscale features should show consistent shifts in burst parameters and expression noise. We will perform sensitivity analyses to timescale mismatch (imaging vs sequencing), alternative burst inference methods, and alternative condensate feature definitions. Conflicts will be documented and, when possible, resolved via model comparison and metadata stratification.

Team science and training integration. Each WP will be led by co-leads from different disciplines (cell biology/biophysics; imaging/data science; statistics/ML; omics). Trainees will lead “replication pods” tasked with reproducing a key result on an independent dataset and submitting a reproducible report. NCEMS resources are essential for coordinated data access, collaborative computing practices, and sustained cross-lab synthesis beyond typical bilateral collaborations.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific products. (1) A quantitative, cross-system model of how membraneless organelles modulate transcriptional bursting, framed as mesoscale information filtering. The model will specify which condensate features (e.g., enrichment, persistence, proximity) predict burst frequency versus burst size, and under what biological contexts these relationships hold. (2) A set of testable “filter archetypes” linking MLO classes to dynamical behaviors (e.g., stabilization/low-pass filtering in speckle-associated programs; threshold-like amplification in transient transcriptional condensates). (3) A reconciled synthesis of apparently conflicting claims in the literature, with explicit attribution to timescale, modality, and confounding factors.

Methodological and infrastructural products. (4) The Mesoscale Feature Schema (MFS) and accompanying ontology mappings, enabling standardized representation of condensate organization across imaging and omics studies. (5) Open, reusable pipelines for (a) condensate feature extraction from public images, (b) burst parameter inference from scRNA/spatial data with uncertainty, and (c) hierarchical data assimilation linking mesoscale and molecular layers. (6) Benchmark datasets and evaluation protocols for predicting bursting from integrated molecular+mesoscale features, supporting future NCEMS-style synthesis projects.

Impact on emergence research. The project advances a central NCEMS goal: identifying emergent properties at the mesoscale that cannot be inferred from molecular parts alone. By quantifying the added explanatory power of mesoscale organization beyond abundance, the working group will provide a rigorous criterion for emergence in this domain. The outputs will shift the field from anecdotal mechanistic narratives to falsifiable, cross-dataset rules.

Broader impacts and workforce development. Trainees will gain skills in data curation, reproducible workflows, Bayesian modeling, and cross-disciplinary communication—core competencies for a data-savvy workforce. The resulting standards and tools will lower barriers for the community to reuse public data, accelerating discovery while reducing redundant experimentation. The synthesis will also inform disease studies where condensate dysregulation and transcriptional noise are implicated, providing a framework for interpreting public patient-derived single-cell datasets through a mesoscale lens.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-by-default outputs. All code, derived feature tables permitted by source licenses, and analysis artifacts will be released under permissive licenses (e.g., BSD-3/Apache-2.0 for code; CC-BY/CC0 where allowed for derived metadata). We will not redistribute restricted raw data; instead we will provide scripted, documented downloaders that pull from original repositories and record exact accessions and checksums.

Reproducible workflows. Pipelines will be implemented as containerized, versioned workflows (e.g., Docker/Singularity) orchestrated with workflow managers (e.g., Snakemake/Nextflow) and executed in continuous integration (CI) on representative subsets. Every figure and table in manuscripts will be linked to an executable workflow target. We will maintain a public registry of software versions, parameter settings, and random seeds.

Provenance, uncertainty, and audit trails. We will maintain a provenance graph (dataset → preprocessing → feature extraction → modeling) using machine-readable metadata (e.g., RO-Crate or equivalent lightweight packaging). Uncertainty estimates (measurement error, model posterior intervals) will be first-class outputs, and we will publish model-check diagnostics (posterior predictive checks, calibration curves) to avoid overconfident emergence claims.

Community standards and interoperability. The Mesoscale Feature Schema (MFS) will be developed in the open via issue tracking and community review, with clear mappings to existing ontologies (cell type, subcellular location, assay type). We will provide example “MFS-ready” submissions for imaging and omics datasets and a validator tool to encourage adoption.

Training and knowledge transfer. We will run reproducibility clinics where trainees learn to (i) reproduce an analysis from scratch, (ii) write data/analysis READMEs, and (iii) contribute via pull requests and code review. All tutorials, recorded walkthroughs, and template notebooks will be public. Preprints will be posted, and manuscripts will target journals supportive of open peer review and data/code deposition.

Ethics and responsible AI. We will document potential biases (cell line overrepresentation, modality biases) and report fairness/coverage metrics across organisms and cell types. ML components will be interpretable where possible, and we will publish ablations showing which features drive conclusions.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS working group model and need. The project requires coordinated, in-person and virtual synthesis among multiple labs and disciplines, plus shared computing and curation infrastructure. These needs exceed a single lab’s capacity because they involve (i) harmonizing heterogeneous public repositories, (ii) jointly developing a community schema (MFS), and (iii) performing cross-lab replication and benchmarking.

Budget categories (300-word overview; exact amounts per NCEMS guidelines to be finalized with NCEMS). (1) Personnel support: partial support for a project coordinator/data curator (to manage dataset cataloging, provenance, and schema governance) and limited support for a research software engineer (workflow engineering, CI, packaging). Trainee support will be provided primarily through travel and dedicated working sessions rather than salary, consistent with synthesis-center norms. (2) Participant support costs: travel, lodging, and per diem for working group meetings, prioritizing trainees and participants from under-resourced institutions; accessibility accommodations as needed. (3) Meeting costs: room/AV, collaborative sprint logistics, and facilitation to ensure equitable participation and productive team science. (4) Computing: cloud/HPC credits for containerized image processing and Bayesian inference, plus storage for intermediate derived features and caches (with strict linkage to original accessions). (5) Dissemination: costs for open-access publication fees when necessary, preprint-friendly venues, and maintenance of a public documentation site.

Resources leveraged. We will leverage public repositories (GEO/SRA/ArrayExpress, BioImage Archive/IDR, PRIDE/MassIVE, Human Protein Atlas), open ontologies, and open-source software ecosystems. Institutional resources contributed by participating labs include domain expertise, existing codebases for burst inference and image segmentation, and local compute for development.

Governance and deliverables tied to budget. Funds will be tied to milestones: dataset catalog release (Month 3), MFS v1.0 and validator (Month 6), benchmark + baseline models (Month 9), cross-dataset synthesis manuscript and full reproducible compendium (Month 12).

title: A negative atlas of failed mesoscale organization
abstract:
This working group asks how a negative atlas of failed mesoscale organization can be understood as an emergent property that links molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcome. The scientific question is not simply whether particular molecules, organelles, or pathways are associated with a phenotype, but whether publicly available datasets can reveal rules by which many molecular parts collectively produce a new, system-level behavior at the scale between biomolecules and organelles. The project is designed for the NCEMS model because the relevant evidence is scattered across incompatible imaging repositories, omics studies, perturbation resources, structural annotations, and specialized literatures; no single laboratory is likely to have the biological breadth, data-engineering capacity, and methodological expertise to integrate them.

The group would synthesize existing public data centered on text/knowledge graph + repositories, prioritizing datasets with reusable metadata, perturbation or state annotations, and links to downstream cellular phenotypes. Depending on availability, sources could include public cell atlases, the Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, EMBL-EBI and NCBI functional genomics repositories, BioImage Archive or Image Data Resource collections, PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics datasets, public CRISPR or RNAi screens, AlphaFold/PDB-derived structural features, and curated pathway or protein-interaction resources. The core analytic strategy would be benchmark/standard/community resource: harmonizing measurements into a common representation; explicitly modeling uncertainty, batch effects, and missingness; and testing whether mesoscale variables explain cellular outcomes above and beyond molecular abundance alone. The biological scope would focus on cross-kingdom/cross-species while deliberately including comparison cases that prevent the group from mistaking a narrow model-system pattern for a general law.

The novel element is the unit of explanation. Instead of treating mesoscale organization as an image label, downstream readout, or anecdotal mechanism, the working group would make it the primary object of synthesis: a measurable layer where composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion combine. The expected product is a open knowledge graph that is open, versioned, and reusable, with transparent workflows, community-agreed metadata standards, and tutorials for trainees. The project would bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, imaging scientists, omics researchers, statisticians, machine-learning researchers, data curators, and trainees across institution types. Training would occur through hackathon-style data sprints, reproducible workflow clinics, and rotating trainee leadership of cross-dataset validation tasks. The anticipated contribution is both scientific and infrastructural: a defensible answer to a specific emergence question, plus a generalizable synthesis strategy that helps the molecular and cellular biosciences reuse public data to discover phenomena that only become visible when datasets, disciplines, and scales are brought together.
background_and_significance:
Mesoscale cellular organization—structures and patterns between individual macromolecules and whole organelles—includes biomolecular condensates, cytoskeletal networks, membrane contact sites, phase-separated compartments, protein clusters, and transient assemblies that reorganize with signaling, stress, cell cycle, and differentiation. These mesoscale patterns are widely believed to be central to emergent cellular behaviors (robustness, adaptability, threshold responses, and spatial memory), yet they remain difficult to formalize because they are heterogeneous, context dependent, and measured with incompatible modalities. A major barrier is that mesoscale organization is often treated as a qualitative mechanism (“puncta,” “mislocalization,” “fragmentation”) rather than a quantitative layer of explanation that can be compared across experiments, species, and perturbations.

In parallel, the last decade has produced a vast public record of cell images, omics profiles, perturbation screens, structural predictions, interaction networks, and curated pathway knowledge. However, these resources are siloed: imaging repositories frequently lack standardized phenotype ontologies and perturbation metadata; functional genomics datasets may not encode subcellular organization outcomes; proteomics and interactomes rarely connect to spatial state; and text-mined knowledge is rich but noisy and difficult to align to quantitative measurements. As a result, the field lacks a synthesis framework to ask a fundamental emergence question: when does molecular composition fail to produce the expected mesoscale organization, and how do such failures propagate to cellular outcomes?

A “negative atlas of failed mesoscale organization” addresses this gap by making failure—not success—the organizing principle. Negative evidence is abundant but underutilized: screens where perturbations do not yield expected localization changes; imaging studies reporting disrupted assemblies; datasets where predicted interactions do not manifest spatially; and conditions where known components are present yet organization collapses. Systematically integrating these “non-canonical” or “failed” states can reveal constraints and rules that are invisible when only canonical examples are studied. In emergence science, failures are especially informative because they expose boundary conditions: which combinations of components, physical properties, and cellular contexts are necessary and sufficient for mesoscale patterns to arise.

This proposal aligns with NCEMS’s mission in three ways. First, it is synthesis-only: all inputs are publicly available datasets and literature-derived knowledge, integrated into a community resource without generating new experimental data. Second, it is beyond any single laboratory: the work requires coordinated expertise in cell biology, imaging, biophysics, omics, knowledge representation, statistics, and machine learning, plus substantial data engineering to harmonize formats, ontologies, and provenance. Third, it targets mesoscale emergence directly by representing mesoscale organization as a measurable intermediate layer linking molecular composition to phenotypes.

The significance is both scientific and infrastructural. Scientifically, the atlas will enable tests of whether mesoscale variables (e.g., spatial clustering, compartment integrity, contact-site frequency, condensate material properties proxies) explain cell outcomes beyond abundance changes. Infrastructurally, the project will establish reusable standards for describing mesoscale failure modes, uncertainty, and missingness across modalities, lowering barriers for broad community participation. Ultimately, a negative atlas can transform scattered observations into a coherent map of when and why mesoscale organization breaks—an essential step toward general principles of cellular emergence.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will address the overarching question: Can publicly available data be synthesized to infer generalizable rules that govern the emergence—and failure—of mesoscale organization, and can those rules predict downstream cellular outcomes more accurately than molecular abundance alone?

RQ1: What are the recurrent “failure modes” of mesoscale organization across datasets, perturbations, and species?
Hypothesis 1A: Mesoscale failures cluster into a limited set of cross-context motifs (e.g., loss of compartment integrity, ectopic assembly, fragmentation, coalescence/over-fusion, mispartitioning, altered contact topology) that can be detected from heterogeneous evidence (images, screen annotations, text, and interaction/structure features).
Hypothesis 1B: These motifs are conserved at the level of physical/organizational descriptors even when the specific molecular players differ across taxa or cell types.

RQ2: Which molecular and biophysical features predict susceptibility to mesoscale failure?
Hypothesis 2A: Predictors of failure are combinatorial and include (i) network context (interaction degree, modularity, redundancy), (ii) structural properties (intrinsic disorder, multivalency proxies, domain architecture), and (iii) expression/stoichiometry constraints (relative abundance and co-regulation), rather than single-gene effects.
Hypothesis 2B: Failures are enriched near “constraint boundaries” where small changes in stoichiometry, post-translational modification state (as available), or crowding-related proxies shift systems between organized and disorganized regimes.

RQ3: Do mesoscale descriptors add explanatory and predictive power for cellular phenotypes beyond molecular abundance and pathway membership?
Hypothesis 3A: Models that incorporate mesoscale variables will improve prediction of downstream outcomes (fitness, viability, stress sensitivity, cell cycle defects, morphology, trafficking defects) compared with models using only transcript/protein abundance and pathway annotations.
Hypothesis 3B: Mesoscale variables will mediate a substantial fraction of the effect of perturbations on outcomes (i.e., composition → mesoscale state → phenotype), consistent with mesoscale organization as an emergent causal layer.

RQ4: How do measurement uncertainty, missingness, and dataset bias shape our inference of mesoscale emergence?
Hypothesis 4A: Apparent contradictions across datasets often reflect unmodeled uncertainty (batch effects, imaging modality differences, annotation granularity) rather than true biological disagreement.
Hypothesis 4B: Explicit probabilistic representations of evidence and provenance will reduce false generalizations and enable robust cross-dataset synthesis.

RQ5: Can we define a transferable representation and ontology for “failed mesoscale organization” that supports community-scale reuse?
Hypothesis 5A: A compact, hierarchical ontology of mesoscale failure modes linked to existing standards (Gene Ontology cellular component, Cell Ontology, phenotype ontologies, perturbation vocabularies) will enable automated integration and benchmarking.
Hypothesis 5B: A knowledge-graph-centered representation that connects entities (genes/proteins, complexes, structures, perturbations, conditions) to mesoscale states and phenotypes will allow both mechanistic querying (“what fails when X is perturbed?”) and predictive modeling (“what perturbations likely cause failure motif Y?”).

Together, these questions test a core emergence claim: that mesoscale organization is not merely a descriptive intermediate, but a quantitatively recoverable, generalizable layer where collective molecular properties produce system-level behavior, and where failures reveal the governing rules.
methods_and_approach:
Working group structure and scope: We will run an NCEMS-style synthesis working group with three integrated teams—(1) Data & Curation, (2) Representation & Knowledge Graph, (3) Modeling & Validation—plus a trainee cohort rotating through all teams. The project uses only public data and literature-derived knowledge.

Data sources (public-only) and inclusion criteria: We will prioritize datasets with reusable licensing, stable identifiers, and machine-readable metadata for perturbation/state and phenotype. Candidate sources include: Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas; BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource (IDR) collections with perturbations; EMBL-EBI/NCBI functional genomics repositories (GEO/ArrayExpress, SRA-derived processed matrices where available); PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics; public CRISPR/RNAi screens (e.g., DepMap, genome-wide screens with phenotype readouts); curated interaction/pathway resources (BioGRID, STRING, Reactome); AlphaFold/PDB-derived structural annotations; and text-mined assertions from open corpora and curated databases. We will deliberately include multiple organisms/cell systems (e.g., human, yeast, fly, plant) to test generality.

Harmonization and mesoscale feature extraction: (i) Metadata normalization: map genes/proteins to canonical IDs (HGNC/UniProt/Ensembl), compounds to ChEBI, cell types to Cell Ontology, phenotypes to appropriate phenotype ontologies, and subcellular structures to GO cellular component. (ii) Mesoscale descriptors: from imaging-derived measurements when available (object counts, size distributions, spatial clustering, colocalization/contact proxies, texture features) and from annotations/text when not (standardized “failure mode” labels with confidence scores). Where raw images are available and licensing permits, we will use containerized, reproducible pipelines (e.g., CellProfiler/napari-compatible workflows) to compute comparable descriptors; otherwise we will rely on published feature tables.

Negative atlas construction: We define “failure” as a deviation from expected mesoscale organization given context, encoded as (a) observed disruption labels, (b) statistically inferred outliers in mesoscale descriptors relative to matched controls, or (c) contradictions between expected localization/assembly and observed evidence. Each assertion will be stored with provenance, modality, and uncertainty.

Knowledge graph (KG) and ontology: We will build a versioned KG connecting: molecular entities → complexes/interactions/structure features → perturbations/conditions → mesoscale states (including failure motifs) → phenotypes. The KG will use interoperable schemas (e.g., RDF/OWL or property-graph with exported RDF), persistent identifiers, and evidence codes. We will develop a minimal ontology of mesoscale failure modes aligned to existing ontologies, enabling both human interpretation and machine reasoning.

Modeling strategy and benchmarks: (i) Predictive models: compare baseline models (abundance + pathway) to augmented models (baseline + mesoscale descriptors + network/structure features) using regularized regression, gradient boosting, and graph neural network variants where justified. (ii) Causal/mediation analyses: evaluate whether mesoscale variables mediate perturbation-to-phenotype effects using causal graphs and sensitivity analyses. (iii) Cross-dataset validation: hold out entire datasets, organisms, or modalities to test transferability. (iv) Uncertainty modeling: hierarchical models and measurement-error-aware learning; explicit missingness mechanisms; batch correction with conservative reporting.

Community process: We will run structured data sprints to ingest datasets, “workflow clinics” to standardize pipelines, and benchmarking jamborees to compare models. Decisions (ontology terms, inclusion rules, QC thresholds) will be documented and ratified by the group to ensure transparency and broad buy-in.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Primary scientific outcome: a defensible, cross-context answer to whether mesoscale organization—quantified as a set of transferable descriptors and failure motifs—explains cellular outcomes beyond molecular abundance and pathway membership. We expect to identify a small number of recurrent failure motifs and the molecular/network/structural conditions that predispose systems to each motif, yielding testable rules about emergence at the mesoscale.

Primary resource outcome: an open, versioned “Negative Atlas of Failed Mesoscale Organization,” implemented as a knowledge graph with linked evidence, uncertainty, and provenance. The atlas will support queries such as: “Which perturbations cause loss of ER–mitochondria contact topology across species?”, “Which structural features are enriched among proteins implicated in ectopic condensate formation?”, and “Which phenotypes are consistently mediated by a specific mesoscale failure motif?”

Methodological outcomes: (1) A harmonized representation for mesoscale states that bridges imaging, omics, screens, and literature; (2) benchmark datasets and evaluation protocols for predicting mesoscale failures and downstream phenotypes; (3) uncertainty-aware synthesis workflows that explicitly address missingness and batch effects, reducing overconfident claims from heterogeneous public data.

Workforce and community outcomes: trainees will gain skills in data curation, ontology/KG development, reproducible analysis, and cross-disciplinary communication. The working group will build durable collaborations among cell biologists, biophysicists, imaging scientists, data curators, and AI researchers, including participants from diverse institution types and career stages.

Broader impact: By elevating “failure” to a first-class object of analysis, the project shifts community practice from anecdotal mechanistic narratives to quantitative, falsifiable mesoscale principles. The atlas will lower barriers to reusing public data for emergence questions, enabling future NCEMS-style efforts to generalize across systems and accelerating discovery of mesoscale mechanisms relevant to disease, stress adaptation, and cellular engineering—without generating new experimental data.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
The project will follow open science principles by default, with a commitment to make all derived products publicly available, reproducible, and reusable.

Open outputs: (1) A publicly accessible knowledge graph release (with DOIs per version) containing only public-source identifiers and derived annotations/features permissible under source licenses; (2) harmonized metadata tables, ontology files, and mapping dictionaries; (3) benchmark datasets with clear data-use terms; (4) analysis notebooks and reports; (5) training materials (tutorials, recorded workflow clinics, and example queries).

Reproducible workflows: All data ingestion, transformation, and modeling will be implemented as containerized pipelines (Docker/Singularity) orchestrated with workflow managers (e.g., Snakemake/Nextflow) and executed in continuous integration where feasible. Each pipeline will produce machine-readable provenance (inputs, versions, parameters, checksums) and will be accompanied by minimal working examples.

Transparent governance: We will adopt a written collaboration agreement covering authorship, contribution tracking (CRediT taxonomy), decision-making for ontology/schema changes, and conflict resolution. All issues and decisions (dataset inclusion/exclusion, QC thresholds, term definitions) will be tracked in public repositories.

Data ethics and licensing: Because all inputs are publicly available, we will respect dataset licenses and human-subject constraints. For human-derived data, we will use only de-identified, openly accessible resources and will not attempt re-identification. Where redistribution is restricted, we will store pointers and run pipelines that fetch data from original sources, releasing only permissible derived summaries.

Quality control and auditability: We will implement automated QC checks (identifier validity, ontology consistency, outlier detection, leakage checks in benchmarking) and manual review for a subset of high-impact assertions. Uncertainty will be encoded explicitly (confidence scores, evidence codes, modality tags), avoiding “single truth” overclaiming.

Training for reproducibility: Trainees will lead reproducibility audits (rerun-from-scratch exercises), create “how-to” guides, and maintain example end-to-end workflows so that external users can reproduce key figures and KG queries without specialized infrastructure.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support is essential because the project requires sustained, in-person and virtual synthesis, neutral coordination across labs, shared compute, and professional data stewardship that exceed typical single-lab capabilities.

Requested NCEMS resources (categories):
1) Working group convenings: Support for 3–4 multi-day meetings over ~18–24 months (kickoff design meeting; two build/benchmark meetings; final synthesis and release meeting). Funds cover travel, lodging, and accessibility needs for a geographically distributed team, including trainees and participants from under-resourced institutions.

2) Personnel support (synthesis-focused): Partial support for a project coordinator/synthesis facilitator to manage timelines, documentation, and community processes; and support for a research software/data engineer embedded with the working group to implement ingestion pipelines, KG infrastructure, and CI testing. Trainee support (stipends/travel) enables participation in data sprints and reproducibility audits.

3) Compute and storage: Shared cloud/HPC allocations for workflow execution on public datasets, container registries, and hosting the KG and documentation. Resources emphasize reproducible execution (CI runners), versioned artifact storage, and scalable query endpoints.

4) Data stewardship and dissemination: Support for persistent identifiers/DOIs, long-term archiving of releases (e.g., Zenodo/OSF), documentation websites, and community training events (virtual workshops, tutorial development).

Budget rationale: The work requires (i) harmonizing heterogeneous public datasets, (ii) building and maintaining a versioned KG with provenance, (iii) benchmarking models across modalities with uncertainty-aware methods, and (iv) training and coordination across disciplines. These activities demand centralized infrastructure, facilitation, and dedicated engineering time—precisely the role of an NSF synthesis center.

Leveraged resources (in-kind): Participating labs will contribute domain expertise, existing open-source tools, and limited local compute for development. NCEMS will provide the neutral convening space, collaboration platform, and the shared infrastructure needed to deliver a community-scale, open, reusable negative atlas.
