background_and_significance:
Cell polarity—the reproducible breaking of symmetry to establish a directional axis—is a canonical example of emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences. Polarity underlies diverse outcomes including directed migration, asymmetric division, epithelial organization, neuronal wiring, immune synapse formation, and developmental patterning. Yet across systems, polarity is not “coded” by a single molecule or pathway. Instead, it arises when many molecular components (lipids, scaffolds, cytoskeletal regulators, trafficking machinery, signaling modules) collectively organize into mesoscale structures—cortical domains, actin networks, microtubule arrays, membrane microdomains, phase-separated condensates, and organelle positioning patterns—that then bias transport, force generation, and information flow. The mesoscale (between biomolecules and organelles) is therefore the natural level at which polarity becomes a system property: composition, geometry, mechanics, and dynamics interact nonlinearly to yield stable axes and robust patterning.

Despite decades of mechanistic work in individual model systems (e.g., yeast budding, C. elegans zygote, Drosophila epithelia, mammalian migration), the field lacks generalizable “rules of emergence” that predict polarity from molecular asymmetry across contexts. This gap is partly conceptual (how to define comparable mesoscale variables across organisms and imaging modalities) and partly infrastructural (relevant evidence is distributed across disparate public repositories and literatures). Large-scale perturbation resources and atlases now exist—CRISPR/RNAi screens, single-cell and spatial omics, proteomics, protein localization atlases, and rapidly expanding bioimage archives—yet they remain under-integrated. Many datasets report molecular abundance or localization, while polarity is captured as qualitative annotations, downstream phenotypes, or specialized readouts. As a result, we often know that “gene X affects polarity” without understanding whether polarity is mediated by a shared mesoscale mechanism (e.g., cortical flow organization, vesicle trafficking anisotropy, actin alignment) that could unify findings across systems.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that converts scattered public data into a coherent, testable framework. First, no single lab can integrate the required breadth: high-content imaging repositories (BioImage Archive/IDR), protein localization resources (Human Protein Atlas), functional genomics (GEO/SRA/ArrayExpress), proteomics (PRIDE/MassIVE), interaction/pathway databases, and structure-derived features (AlphaFold/PDB). Second, the methodological demands—cross-dataset harmonization, uncertainty-aware modeling, causal discovery, and domain-informed representation learning—require collaboration among cell biologists, imaging scientists, statisticians, ML researchers, and data curators. Third, polarity is an ideal emergent phenotype for NCEMS’s mesoscale focus: it is measurable, mechanistically rich, and expressed across kingdoms, enabling tests of universality versus system-specificity.

The proposed working group will deliver both scientific insight and reusable infrastructure: a shared vocabulary for mesoscale polarity variables, a harmonized set of cross-repository datasets with provenance, and validated models that quantify when and how molecular asymmetry predicts emergent polarity. By explicitly treating mesoscale organization as the primary explanatory layer, this project advances a central NCEMS goal: discovering emergent principles that are invisible within single datasets or single disciplines but become tractable through synthesis, AI, and open, reproducible collaboration.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group addresses a fundamental emergence question: under what conditions does molecular asymmetry reliably give rise to emergent cell polarity, and what mesoscale variables mediate that mapping across biological systems? We focus on prediction and explanation at the mesoscale rather than cataloging gene–phenotype associations.

RQ1: What mesoscale organizational features best mediate the relationship between molecular asymmetry and cell polarity outcomes across systems? We will define a set of candidate mesoscale variables that can be extracted or inferred from public data: (i) cortical domain number/size/contrast (e.g., polarized caps vs multiple patches), (ii) cytoskeletal alignment and anisotropy (actin/microtubule orientation fields), (iii) organelle positioning asymmetry (Golgi/centrosome/nucleus displacement), (iv) trafficking anisotropy (endocytosis/exocytosis spatial bias), and (v) condensate or cluster metrics (puncta size distributions, coalescence signatures). Hypothesis H1: Mesoscale variables provide substantial explanatory power beyond molecular abundance or single-protein localization metrics, enabling cross-system prediction of polarity states.

RQ2: Are there conserved “polarity modules” that recur across kingdoms and cell types when mapped at the mesoscale? We will compare yeast, animal, and plant datasets where polarity is annotated or inferable. Hypothesis H2: While molecular players differ, a smaller number of mesoscale regimes (e.g., single stable axis, oscillatory polarity, multi-site polarity) recur and can be captured by common latent representations learned from integrated imaging and perturbation data.

RQ3: Which molecular asymmetries are causal drivers versus consequences of polarity, and how do feedback loops differ across contexts? We will apply causal discovery and intervention-aware modeling using perturbation screens linked to polarity phenotypes. Hypothesis H3: Apparent molecular predictors often reflect downstream stabilization; true drivers will show consistent causal directionality across datasets and be mediated by specific mesoscale intermediates (e.g., actin alignment mediating Rho GTPase perturbations).

RQ4: What dataset properties and experimental contexts determine whether general rules transfer across systems? We will explicitly model context variables (cell geometry, adhesion state, developmental stage, substrate stiffness proxies, imaging modality, batch). Hypothesis H4: Transfer fails primarily when unmodeled context shifts alter mesoscale constraints (geometry/mechanics), not because molecular networks are entirely idiosyncratic; incorporating context into hierarchical models will restore predictability.

RQ5: Can we formalize a minimal, testable theory that links composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion to polarity emergence using only public data? We will operationalize these axes as measurable proxies: spatial gradients (space), temporal autocorrelation/flows (time/motion), ATP/mitochondrial proxies or metabolic state signatures (energy), signaling entropy or network controllability metrics (information), and molecular composition vectors (composition). Hypothesis H5: A joint model integrating these proxies will classify polarity regimes and identify system-level constraints (e.g., energy limitation reduces polarity stability via weakened active transport), producing a reusable emergence framework.

Collectively, these questions and hypotheses transform polarity from a system-specific phenomenon into a cross-system emergent property with measurable mesoscale mediators and causal structure, directly aligned with NCEMS’s mission and mesoscale emphasis.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. The project will be executed as an NCEMS-style working group with iterative synthesis cycles: (1) data discovery and triage, (2) harmonization and representation, (3) model building and causal inference, (4) cross-system validation, and (5) community outputs (standards, tutorials, benchmarks). Work will be distributed across collaborating labs with complementary expertise (cell polarity biology; bioimage analysis; omics integration; causal inference/ML; data curation).

Data sources (public-only). We will prioritize datasets that include perturbations or state labels and measurable polarity-related outcomes. Candidate sources include: BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource (high-content imaging with perturbations), Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas (protein localization patterns), GEO/SRA/ArrayExpress (transcriptomics, including perturbation series), PRIDE/MassIVE (proteomics and phosphoproteomics), public CRISPR/RNAi screens with morphology readouts, interaction/pathway resources (BioGRID, STRING, Reactome), and structure-derived features (AlphaFold/PDB annotations such as disorder, oligomerization propensity, domain architecture). No new experiments will be performed.

Harmonization and metadata. We will create a cross-repository “Polarity Synthesis Table” (PST): a standardized schema linking (i) biological context (species, cell type, geometry proxies), (ii) perturbation details (gene, reagent, dose/time where available), (iii) molecular measurements (omics, localization, interaction features), (iv) mesoscale features (image-derived or inferred), (v) polarity outcomes (axis presence, directionality, stability, migration persistence, asymmetric division metrics), and (vi) provenance/quality metrics. We will use controlled vocabularies/ontologies where possible (e.g., Gene Ontology, Cell Ontology) and develop minimal polarity-specific extensions.

Mesoscale feature extraction. For imaging datasets, we will apply reproducible pipelines (containerized) to compute interpretable polarity/organization descriptors: segmentation of cell boundary and key structures; intensity-gradient vectors; spatial autocorrelation; domain number/contrast; orientation fields for filamentous structures; organelle centroid displacement; and texture/cluster statistics. Where raw images are unavailable, we will use published feature tables or infer mesoscale proxies from localization categories and morphology embeddings.

Modeling strategy: predictive + causal. (1) Predictive modeling: hierarchical/multitask models that predict polarity outcomes from molecular features alone versus molecular+mesoscale features, quantifying incremental value of mesoscale organization (testing H1). We will use uncertainty-aware methods (Bayesian hierarchical models, conformal prediction) and domain adaptation to handle batch and modality shifts. (2) Representation learning: learn latent “polarity regime” embeddings from combined feature spaces while enforcing interpretability via disentanglement and feature attribution. (3) Causal discovery: apply intervention-aware causal inference using perturbation as instruments where appropriate, combining constraint-based and score-based approaches with prior biological knowledge. We will test mediation explicitly: molecular perturbation → mesoscale variable → polarity outcome, using causal mediation analysis and sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding.

Cross-system validation and robustness. We will implement leave-one-system-out evaluation (e.g., train on yeast+animal, test on plant) and stratified analyses by context variables (geometry, adhesion, cell cycle). Robustness checks will include negative controls (randomized links, permuted labels), missingness simulations, and re-analysis across alternative feature sets.

NCEMS need. The integration of heterogeneous public datasets, development of shared standards, and sustained cross-lab coordination (data engineering, modeling, validation, and training) exceed typical single-lab capacity and directly leverages NCEMS convening, cyberinfrastructure, and open-science governance.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific outcomes. (1) A cross-system, mesoscale-centered model of polarity emergence that quantifies when molecular asymmetry predicts polarity and when it fails due to contextual constraints. (2) Identification of conserved mesoscale “polarity regimes” (e.g., single-axis stable, oscillatory, multi-site) and their characteristic molecular and structural correlates. (3) A ranked set of candidate causal mediators—mesoscale variables that repeatedly explain polarity outcomes across perturbation datasets—distinguishing drivers from consequences and highlighting feedback architectures.

Methodological outcomes. (4) A generalizable synthesis workflow for emergence research: harmonization schema (PST), feature extraction pipelines, uncertainty-aware cross-dataset modeling, and causal mediation templates tailored to molecular→mesoscale→cellular outcome questions. (5) Benchmarks and evaluation protocols for cross-repository polarity prediction, including standardized train/test splits and context-aware transfer tests.

Community and infrastructural outcomes. (6) An open, versioned “Polarity Synthesis Compendium” linking curated datasets, derived features, and metadata with full provenance, enabling reuse by the broader community. (7) Recommendations for minimal metadata standards for polarity-relevant imaging and perturbation studies (what must be reported to enable synthesis), created in partnership with data curators.

Impact. By elevating mesoscale organization to the primary explanatory layer, the project will produce a defensible, quantitative answer to an emergence question that has remained largely qualitative: how collective molecular asymmetries become a new system-level behavior. The outputs will accelerate hypothesis generation in diverse subfields (development, immunology, neurobiology, plant biology), improve interpretability of high-content screens, and provide a blueprint for NCEMS-style synthesis efforts targeting other emergent cellular properties (e.g., phase separation, mechanosensing, organelle biogenesis). Training activities embedded in the working group will expand the pool of scientists fluent in open, reproducible, cross-domain data synthesis—directly advancing NCEMS workforce goals.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-by-default products. All code, documentation, and derived (non-restricted) data products will be released under permissive licenses (e.g., MIT/BSD for code; CC-BY/CC0 for documentation/metadata where feasible). The central deliverable will be a public repository hosting: (i) the Polarity Synthesis Table (PST) schema, (ii) dataset manifests with persistent identifiers, (iii) feature extraction and harmonization pipelines, (iv) modeling notebooks/scripts, and (v) figures/tables regenerated from raw inputs.

Reproducible workflows. Analyses will be executed via containerized environments (Docker/Singularity) and workflow managers (e.g., Snakemake/Nextflow) with pinned versions and automated checks. Each dataset ingestion will include a “provenance card” documenting source, access date, licensing, preprocessing steps, and known limitations. Continuous integration will run unit tests, style checks, and small-scale pipeline tests on representative samples.

FAIR data and interoperability. We will prioritize machine-readable metadata and standard identifiers (Ensembl/UniProt, ontology terms, repository accessions). Derived feature tables will include explicit coordinate systems and units, and we will provide mappings from dataset-specific labels to shared polarity and context vocabularies. When redistribution of certain data is restricted, we will provide reproducible download scripts and hashed manifests rather than mirroring the data.

Transparent modeling and uncertainty. We will publish model cards describing intended use, training data composition, performance across contexts, failure modes, and uncertainty calibration. Causal claims will be accompanied by explicit assumptions, sensitivity analyses, and robustness checks.

Team science and training. Working-group meetings will include “reproducibility clinics” where trainees lead end-to-end reruns of analyses on fresh environments, and “open peer review” of pull requests to instill best practices. Tutorials (short courses) will be released as executable notebooks and recorded sessions, enabling external learners to reproduce key results and adapt pipelines to new datasets.

Community engagement. We will solicit feedback on the PST schema and polarity metadata recommendations through public issues, lightweight workshops, and coordination with repository curators, ensuring outputs are usable beyond the immediate team.
budget_and_resources:
Budget rationale (NCEMS working-group model). The project requires sustained, in-person and virtual collaboration among multiple labs and disciplines, plus dedicated support for data engineering, curation, and training. Funds are requested to cover convening, personnel time for synthesis tasks, and computational needs, consistent with the requirement to use only publicly available data (no experimental costs).

Key cost categories. (1) Working group meetings: support for 2–3 multi-day meetings at NCEMS (or NCEMS-supported venue) plus regular virtual sprints. Costs include participant travel, lodging, and per diem, with deliberate inclusion of trainees and participants from under-resourced institutions. (2) Personnel support: partial support for a project coordinator/data steward (to manage PST schema, provenance, licensing, and releases), and limited salary/fringe for data-science staff or research software engineers across participating labs to build and maintain reproducible pipelines. (3) Trainee support: travel and subsistence for graduate students/postdocs to attend meetings; small stipends for trainee-led data validation tasks; and support for tutorial development. (4) Computing: cloud credits or allocated compute for scalable feature extraction from large imaging datasets, model training, and storage of derived feature tables and intermediate artifacts (not duplicating restricted raw data). (5) Dissemination: costs for maintaining a project website, hosting documentation, and (if needed) open-access publication fees.

NCEMS resources leveraged. We will rely on NCEMS for convening infrastructure, facilitation of cross-disciplinary team science, guidance on open-science policies, and access to shared computational and data-management expertise. NCEMS support is essential to coordinate contributions across institutions, ensure consistent standards, and maintain momentum through structured synthesis cycles.

Budget governance and feasibility. We will implement a milestone-based spending plan aligned to deliverables (schema v1, curated dataset releases, benchmark models, final compendium). A lightweight steering committee (PIs + data steward + trainee representative) will track progress, manage risks (e.g., data licensing constraints), and ensure that resources are allocated to maximize shared outputs rather than duplicative effort.

background_and_significance:
Cells are crowded. Macromolecules occupy a substantial fraction of cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic volume, altering diffusion, reaction rates, binding equilibria, phase behavior, and mechanical properties. Yet “crowding” is typically treated as a qualitative context or a single scalar (e.g., volume fraction) measured in one system with one probe. This leaves a gap between molecular composition (proteins, RNAs, lipids, metabolites), mesoscale organization (condensates, ribosome-rich regions, cytoskeletal networks, organelle contact sites), and cellular outcomes (growth, stress tolerance, differentiation, drug response). NCEMS’s focus on emergence at the mesoscale makes crowding an ideal target: it is not a property of any single molecule, but a collective thermodynamic and transport regime arising from many components interacting in space and time.

Public data now contain the ingredients to quantify and test crowding as an emergent mesoscale variable. Imaging repositories capture spatial organization at submicron resolution across many cell types and conditions; proteomics and transcriptomics quantify composition; structural resources (PDB, AlphaFold-derived features) provide estimates of size, shape, disorder, and interaction propensity; perturbation screens (CRISPR/RNAi, chemical) connect molecular changes to phenotypes. However, these resources were produced for different purposes, with inconsistent metadata, different cell lines and growth conditions, and incomparable measurement units. As a result, the field lacks a synthesis-level framework that turns heterogeneous public datasets into a coherent, testable thermodynamics of subcellular crowding.

A key conceptual challenge is that crowding is both physical and biological. Physical crowding depends on excluded volume, polymer physics, and hydrodynamic interactions; biological crowding depends on regulated localization, stoichiometry, and active processes (ATP-driven remodeling, trafficking, cytoskeletal transport). The emergent behavior of interest is therefore not merely “high density,” but a state space of mesoscale regimes—e.g., diffusion-limited vs. reaction-limited kinetics; percolated cytoskeletal networks vs. fluid-like cytoplasm; nucleoplasm with distinct viscoelastic properties; or condensate-rich vs. condensate-poor organization. A rigorous synthesis must quantify these regimes and test whether they explain outcomes beyond what can be predicted from molecular abundance alone.

The significance of this working group is threefold. First, it addresses a long-standing puzzle: why similar molecular inventories can yield different mesoscale organization and phenotypes across cell types and species. Second, it creates an integrative strategy for emergence science by combining mechanistic thermodynamic/transport models with data assimilation from public resources, explicitly propagating uncertainty and missingness. Third, it produces reusable community infrastructure—harmonized metadata, derived mesoscale “crowding state” variables, and benchmark tasks—that can be applied to other mesoscale phenomena (e.g., organelle contact thermodynamics, cytoskeletal percolation, condensate maturation). Because no single lab can curate the necessary imaging, omics, structural annotations, and perturbation evidence across organisms and platforms, NCEMS support is essential to convene the multidisciplinary team, provide synthesis-oriented project management, and enable community-scale open and reproducible outputs.

By treating crowding as a measurable emergent property linking composition to organization and outcome, this project will advance molecular and cellular biosciences from cataloging parts to discovering rules—predictive, falsifiable, and portable across biological contexts.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will answer a central emergence question: can subcellular crowding be quantified from public data as a thermodynamic/transport state variable that mediates the mapping from molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcomes? We focus on questions that are testable with existing public datasets and that require synthesis across modalities.

RQ1: Can we infer robust, comparable “crowding state variables” across cell types, conditions, and species using only publicly available measurements? We define crowding state variables as latent or derived quantities such as effective macromolecular volume fraction, viscosity/viscoelasticity proxies, anomalous diffusion exponent proxies, interaction network connectivity, and condensate propensity indices. H1: A small set of latent crowding variables can be inferred that are stable to platform differences and capture meaningful variation across biological states (e.g., cell cycle, stress, differentiation) when uncertainty and batch effects are modeled explicitly.

RQ2: Do inferred crowding state variables explain mesoscale organization beyond molecular abundance? Mesoscale organization includes spatial heterogeneity of protein localization, organelle morphology, condensate prevalence, and cytoskeletal architecture as derived from public imaging and annotation. H2: Crowding variables mediate the relationship between composition and organization; models that include crowding variables will outperform abundance-only baselines in predicting mesoscale organization metrics across datasets.

RQ3: Do crowding state variables predict cellular outcomes and phenotypes across perturbations? Outcomes include growth rate proxies, viability, stress sensitivity, drug response, and genetic interaction signatures from public screens. H3: Crowding variables provide incremental predictive power for phenotypes (above abundance and pathway membership) because they capture collective physical constraints on reaction-diffusion and assembly processes.

RQ4: Are there conserved and diverged “crowding regimes” across kingdoms and evolutionary distance? We will include bacteria/archaea, yeast, and mammalian cells where data permit, emphasizing matched perturbation classes (osmotic stress, heat shock, translation inhibition, cytoskeletal disruption). H4: Some crowding regimes are conserved (e.g., stress-induced ribosome redistribution and viscosity increase), while others are lineage-specific due to compartmentalization and cytoskeletal complexity; these differences can be quantified as shifts in the inferred state space rather than ad hoc exceptions.

RQ5: What mechanistic thermodynamic/transport models are minimally sufficient to link composition to crowding and crowding to outcome? Candidate model families include excluded-volume and polymer mixture models, effective medium diffusion models, and coarse-grained interaction network/phase-separation models. H5: Mechanistic models constrained by public structural features (size, disorder, multivalency) and localization priors can reproduce observed crowding regime transitions and identify which molecular classes (e.g., ribosomes, intrinsically disordered proteins, cytoskeletal polymers) dominate regime shifts.

RQ6: How sensitive are conclusions to measurement bias, incomplete metadata, and missing modalities? H6: Explicit uncertainty propagation and sensitivity analyses will reveal which conclusions are robust and will identify the minimal metadata required for future reusable datasets (e.g., cell line, growth medium, temperature, imaging modality, fixation state).

Together, these questions operationalize emergence: we will test whether collective physical constraints at the mesoscale form a transferable explanatory layer linking molecular parts to system-level behavior, and we will define falsifiable predictions that can be evaluated across independent public datasets.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. The project will run as an NCEMS working group with coordinated data sprints and synthesis meetings. Participants will include experts in cell biology (crowding, cytoskeleton, organelles), biophysics/thermodynamics, imaging analysis, omics integration, statistics/causal inference, machine learning, and data curation. The work is strictly synthesis-based: we will use only existing publicly available data and derived annotations.

Data sources and inclusion criteria. We will prioritize datasets with (i) reusable licenses and stable identifiers, (ii) sufficient metadata (cell type, condition, perturbation, imaging modality or omics protocol), and (iii) links to phenotypes or perturbations. Candidate sources: Human Protein Atlas (Cell Atlas), BioImage Archive/IDR imaging collections, single-cell RNA-seq atlases (NCBI GEO/SRA, EMBL-EBI ArrayExpress), PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics, DepMap/other public CRISPR screens where accessible, PDB/AlphaFold-derived structural features, STRING/BioGRID interaction networks, and curated pathway resources.

Harmonization and common representation. We will build a “Crowding Synthesis Table” keyed by (species, cell type/line, condition, perturbation, compartment). For each key, we will store: composition vectors (protein/RNA abundance with uncertainty), structural feature summaries (size, disorder, multivalency proxies), interaction network summaries, and imaging-derived organization metrics. Harmonization steps include identifier mapping (UniProt/Ensembl), compartment ontology mapping (GO/Cell Ontology), and condition/perturbation normalization using controlled vocabularies. Batch effects will be modeled rather than merely corrected, preserving uncertainty.

Imaging-derived mesoscale metrics. Using public segmentation/annotation where available (and community models where permitted), we will extract standardized metrics: spatial autocorrelation of intensity, granularity/texture measures, organelle morphology descriptors, colocalization/contact proxies, and condensate-like puncta statistics. When raw images are too heterogeneous, we will use published feature tables or reprocess a curated subset with reproducible pipelines.

Inference of crowding state variables. We will infer latent crowding variables via probabilistic factor models and hierarchical Bayesian models that integrate multiple modalities with missingness (e.g., Bayesian multi-view factor analysis). We will incorporate mechanistic priors: excluded-volume contributions from estimated macromolecular sizes; polymer/IDR contributions from disorder and multivalency; and compartment-specific priors (nucleus vs cytoplasm). Outputs will be posterior distributions over crowding variables, enabling uncertainty-aware downstream tests.

Mechanistic simulation and data assimilation. We will implement coarse-grained models (effective medium diffusion; excluded-volume mixture models; simplified phase-separation propensity models) and fit them using data assimilation techniques (approximate Bayesian computation or likelihood-free inference where necessary). The goal is not atomistic accuracy but mechanistic sufficiency: identify which physical terms are required to reproduce observed regime shifts.

Testing hypotheses and causal structure. Predictive evaluation will use cross-dataset validation: train on one repository or organism and test on another. We will compare (i) abundance-only models, (ii) abundance + pathway/network features, and (iii) abundance + inferred crowding variables. Mediation analyses and causal graphical models will test whether crowding variables plausibly mediate composition-to-phenotype links, while acknowledging limitations of observational synthesis.

Sensitivity, robustness, and benchmarks. We will run systematic sensitivity analyses to metadata omissions, modality dropout, and alternative mappings. We will define benchmark tasks (e.g., predict stress survival class; predict condensate prevalence) with fixed splits and evaluation metrics to enable community reuse.

Training integration. Trainees will lead rotating “validation pods” responsible for reproducing a published result using the shared pipeline, then extending it across datasets. Workflow clinics will teach containerization, provenance tracking, and uncertainty modeling.

This integrated approach—harmonization, latent variable inference, mechanistic modeling, and cross-dataset validation—directly targets emergent mesoscale rules and is feasible only through a coordinated, multidisciplinary synthesis team supported by NCEMS infrastructure.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific outcomes. (1) A quantitative, uncertainty-aware set of inferred subcellular “crowding state variables” across multiple organisms, cell types, compartments, and perturbations, derived solely from public data. (2) Evidence-based tests of whether crowding variables improve prediction of mesoscale organization and cellular phenotypes beyond molecular abundance and pathway annotations. (3) A minimally sufficient mechanistic model (or model family) linking composition and structural features to crowding regimes and linking those regimes to outcomes, with clear falsifiable predictions and documented failure modes. (4) A comparative map of conserved versus lineage-specific crowding regimes, identifying which molecular classes drive regime shifts in different biological contexts.

Methodological and infrastructural outcomes. (1) A reusable “Crowding Synthesis Table” with harmonized identifiers, controlled vocabularies, and provenance that can be extended by the community. (2) Reproducible pipelines for extracting mesoscale organization metrics from heterogeneous public imaging datasets, with standardized outputs and quality-control reports. (3) Benchmark tasks and evaluation suites for multi-modal mesoscale emergence modeling, enabling future methods development at NCEMS and beyond.

Impact on emergence science. The project will elevate mesoscale crowding from a qualitative explanation to a testable explanatory layer that links molecular composition to system-level behavior. By showing when and why crowding mediates phenotype, the work will clarify which cellular properties are genuinely emergent (requiring collective variables) versus reducible to individual components. The cross-kingdom synthesis will prevent overfitting to a single model system and will identify general physical principles and their biological modulations.

Workforce and community impact. Trainees will gain hands-on experience in open, reproducible synthesis science, including data curation, uncertainty modeling, and mechanistic-data integration. The open outputs will lower barriers for experimentalists and computational scientists to reuse public data for mesoscale discovery, aligning directly with NCEMS goals of catalyzing multidisciplinary teams and training a data-savvy workforce.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-by-default products. All derived datasets, code, and documentation produced by the working group will be released publicly under permissive licenses (e.g., code under BSD-3/Apache-2.0; derived data under CC-BY/CC0 where allowed by upstream terms). We will not redistribute restricted raw data; instead we will provide stable pointers, accession lists, and automated retrieval scripts that respect repository policies.

Reproducible workflows. Analyses will be implemented as versioned, containerized workflows (Docker/Singularity) orchestrated with a workflow manager (e.g., Snakemake/Nextflow) and executed in continuous integration (CI) where feasible. Each release will include: (i) environment files, (ii) deterministic seeds and configuration manifests, (iii) provenance logs for every derived artifact, and (iv) automated unit/integration tests for key steps (identifier mapping, feature extraction, model fitting).

Transparent uncertainty and QC. We will publish quality-control dashboards summarizing dataset coverage, missingness patterns, batch structure, and sensitivity results. Community metadata standards. A dedicated curation subgroup will propose minimal metadata recommendations for crowding-relevant reuse (e.g., compartment definitions, fixation/live status, temperature, osmolarity, cell cycle annotations). These will be shared as machine-readable schemas (JSON Schema) and mapped to existing ontologies (GO, Cell Ontology, OBI) to maximize interoperability.

Open collaboration practices. The working group will use transparent issue tracking, public meeting notes, and a published authorship/contribution policy (CRediT taxonomy). Trainees will be supported to contribute via well-scoped issues and code review. Preprints will be posted prior to journal submission, and we will target journals supportive of open data and methods.

Reusability and education. We will publish tutorials and “analysis recipes” (Jupyter/Quarto) demonstrating how to (i) reproduce main figures, (ii) extend the synthesis to a new dataset or organism, and (iii) run benchmark tasks. These materials will be designed for graduate and postdoctoral training and for adoption in short courses, aligning with NCEMS’s mission to train the next generation in gold-standard open and reproducible synthesis science.

title: Organelle neighborhood effects in viral infection
abstract:
This working group asks how organelle neighborhood effects in viral infection can be understood as an emergent property that links molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcome. The scientific question is not simply whether particular molecules, organelles, or pathways are associated with a phenotype, but whether publicly available datasets can reveal rules by which many molecular parts collectively produce a new, system-level behavior at the scale between biomolecules and organelles. The project is designed for the NCEMS model because the relevant evidence is scattered across incompatible imaging repositories, omics studies, perturbation resources, structural annotations, and specialized literatures; no single laboratory is likely to have the biological breadth, data-engineering capacity, and methodological expertise to integrate them.

The group would synthesize existing public data centered on single-cell/spatial omics, prioritizing datasets with reusable metadata, perturbation or state annotations, and links to downstream cellular phenotypes. Depending on availability, sources could include public cell atlases, the Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, EMBL-EBI and NCBI functional genomics repositories, BioImage Archive or Image Data Resource collections, PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics datasets, public CRISPR or RNAi screens, AlphaFold/PDB-derived structural features, and curated pathway or protein-interaction resources. The core analytic strategy would be causal discovery: harmonizing measurements into a common representation; explicitly modeling uncertainty, batch effects, and missingness; and testing whether mesoscale variables explain cellular outcomes above and beyond molecular abundance alone. The biological scope would focus on human disease cells while deliberately including comparison cases that prevent the group from mistaking a narrow model-system pattern for a general law.

The novel element is the unit of explanation. Instead of treating mesoscale organization as an image label, downstream readout, or anecdotal mechanism, the working group would make it the primary object of synthesis: a measurable layer where composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion combine. The expected product is a predictive atlas that is open, versioned, and reusable, with transparent workflows, community-agreed metadata standards, and tutorials for trainees. The project would bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, imaging scientists, omics researchers, statisticians, machine-learning researchers, data curators, and trainees across institution types. Training would occur through hackathon-style data sprints, reproducible workflow clinics, and rotating trainee leadership of cross-dataset validation tasks. The anticipated contribution is both scientific and infrastructural: a defensible answer to a specific emergence question, plus a generalizable synthesis strategy that helps the molecular and cellular biosciences reuse public data to discover phenomena that only become visible when datasets, disciplines, and scales are brought together.
background_and_significance:
Viruses remodel host cells by reorganizing membranes, organelles, and molecular traffic to create replication-permissive environments. Classic examples include coronavirus-induced double-membrane vesicles, flavivirus remodeling of endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and herpesvirus impacts on nuclear architecture. Yet across viruses and host cell types, a persistent puzzle remains: why do similar molecular perturbations sometimes yield divergent infection outcomes, and why do different viruses sometimes converge on similar cellular phenotypes? A growing body of work suggests that the answer is not solely in molecular abundance or single pathways, but in mesoscale organization—the spatial and functional “neighborhoods” formed by organelles, membrane contact sites, and local molecular assemblies.

Organelle neighborhood effects refer to the idea that the state of an organelle (e.g., mitochondrion, ER, Golgi, endosome, lysosome, lipid droplet) depends on its local context: which other organelles are nearby, the density and topology of contacts, and the local distribution of proteins and lipids that enable exchange of energy, metabolites, ions, and information. Such neighborhood organization can plausibly be an emergent property: it arises from many molecular interactions but exhibits system-level regularities (e.g., stable contact networks, coordinated trafficking routes, stereotyped spatial patterns) that are not obvious from any single component. In viral infection, these mesoscale patterns may determine whether a cell mounts an effective antiviral response, supports efficient replication, undergoes apoptosis, or transitions into persistent infection.

Despite conceptual importance, organelle neighborhoods are rarely treated as first-class quantitative variables in synthesis research. Public datasets relevant to this problem are abundant but fragmented: (i) high-content microscopy and multiplexed imaging capturing organelle morphology and colocalization; (ii) spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics that encode local molecular states; (iii) single-cell multi-omics that capture heterogeneous host responses; (iv) perturbation resources (CRISPR/RNAi screens, drug-response datasets) linking genes to viral phenotypes; and (v) structural and interaction annotations (AlphaFold/PDB features, protein–protein interaction networks) that constrain plausible mechanisms. Each data type alone provides partial evidence; integration is required to infer general rules.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze this integration. The proposed working group targets the Center’s emphasis on emergence at the mesoscale, explicitly connecting composition (molecules), organization (organelle neighborhoods), and outcomes (infection phenotypes). The work is beyond a single lab because it requires (a) harmonizing incompatible metadata and ontologies across repositories; (b) developing representations that bridge imaging-derived spatial variables and omics-derived molecular variables; (c) applying causal discovery methods robust to batch effects, missingness, and confounding; and (d) validating generality across viruses, cell types, and experimental contexts.

The significance is twofold. Scientifically, we aim to resolve whether mesoscale neighborhood variables add explanatory and predictive power beyond molecular measurements, thereby identifying emergent “rules” of infection-related organization. Methodologically, we will create reusable standards and workflows for turning public imaging and omics into interoperable mesoscale features, enabling broader community-scale synthesis. By training trainees in open, reproducible, cross-dataset analysis, the project also advances NCEMS goals of building a data-savvy workforce capable of discovering emergent phenomena from public molecular and cellular data.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will address a central emergence question: do reproducible organelle neighborhood states arise during viral infection that cannot be reduced to changes in molecular abundance alone, and do these states causally contribute to infection outcomes? We define “organelle neighborhood state” as a quantitative, multivariate description of organelle proximity, contact topology, morphology, and local molecular composition that is measurable (directly or indirectly) from public imaging and spatial/single-cell omics.

RQ1: Are there conserved organelle neighborhood states associated with viral infection across diverse viruses and host cell contexts?
Hypothesis 1A: Across multiple viral families, infection induces convergent neighborhood motifs (e.g., increased ER–mitochondria contacts, altered endosome–lysosome coupling, lipid droplet clustering near replication compartments) that appear as low-dimensional, recurrent states in integrated datasets.
Hypothesis 1B: These motifs are partially conserved but modulated by cell type and baseline organelle architecture; accounting for baseline neighborhood structure improves cross-study reproducibility.

RQ2: Do organelle neighborhood variables explain infection phenotypes beyond molecular abundance and pathway activation?
Hypothesis 2A: Mesoscale neighborhood features provide incremental predictive power for outcomes such as viral load, cytopathic effect, innate immune activation signatures, and cell survival, even after controlling for transcript/protein abundance.
Hypothesis 2B: Neighborhood features mediate the effect of molecular perturbations on outcomes (e.g., a host factor knockdown changes ER morphology and contact network, which in turn changes viral replication).

RQ3: What causal relationships link molecular drivers, neighborhood states, and cellular outcomes?
Hypothesis 3A: The directionality of influence is not purely molecular-to-mesoscale; feedback exists where neighborhood reorganization alters signaling and metabolism, reshaping molecular states (bidirectional causal edges).
Hypothesis 3B: Latent variables (e.g., cell cycle, stress, metabolic state) confound naive associations; causal discovery with explicit latent/confounding modeling will identify robust causal graphs shared across datasets.

RQ4: Which neighborhood rules generalize, and which are virus- or context-specific?
Hypothesis 4A: A “core” causal subgraph linking a small set of organelle neighborhood modules to outcomes generalizes across viruses, while peripheral edges vary by viral replication strategy (nuclear vs cytoplasmic replication, enveloped vs non-enveloped).
Hypothesis 4B: Comparison to non-viral perturbations (e.g., interferon stimulation, ER stress, mitochondrial toxins) will distinguish infection-specific neighborhood signatures from generic stress responses.

RQ5: Can we define community-reusable representations and metadata standards for organelle neighborhood synthesis?
Hypothesis 5A: A minimal, interoperable schema—linking cell type, infection/perturbation state, imaging modality, segmentation/feature provenance, and outcome labels—will enable robust cross-repository integration.
Hypothesis 5B: Standardized neighborhood feature sets (graph-based contact metrics, spatial autocorrelation, morphology descriptors) will be transferable across imaging datasets and alignable with spatial omics through shared cellular coordinates or probabilistic mapping.

Together, these questions move beyond cataloging “what changes” in infection to identifying emergent mesoscale rules that connect many molecular parts to system-level cellular behavior, using only public data and requiring a transdisciplinary synthesis approach aligned with NCEMS priorities.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will run an NCEMS-style synthesis working group organized around three integrated workstreams: (W1) data discovery and harmonization; (W2) mesoscale feature engineering and representation learning; (W3) causal discovery, validation, and generalization tests. The group will include expertise in cell biology/virology, organelle biophysics, bioimage analysis, single-cell and spatial omics, statistics/causal inference, machine learning, and data curation.

W1: Public data acquisition and harmonization (no new experiments). We will systematically curate datasets that jointly provide (a) infection or viral-protein expression labels, (b) organelle-resolved imaging or spatially resolved molecular profiles, and (c) measurable outcomes (viral load proxies, host response signatures, viability). Sources will include BioImage Archive/IDR for imaging; Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas for protein localization; GEO/SRA/ArrayExpress for transcriptomics; PRIDE/MassIVE for proteomics; DepMap and published CRISPR/RNAi screens for host factors; and curated interaction/pathway resources (STRING, BioGRID, Reactome). We will harmonize metadata using controlled vocabularies (cell line/cell type ontologies, virus taxonomy, perturbation descriptors) and create a crosswalk linking dataset identifiers, conditions, and outcome labels. Batch and study effects will be tracked explicitly.

W2: Mesoscale neighborhood feature extraction and integration. For imaging datasets, we will use reproducible pipelines (e.g., containerized Cellpose/StarDist segmentation where permissible, or author-provided masks) to derive organelle morphology metrics (size, elongation, fragmentation), spatial distributions (radial positioning, clustering), and neighborhood/contact proxies (distance distributions, co-occurrence, graph edges between organelle centroids or segmented surfaces). For multiplexed imaging, we will compute multi-organelle adjacency graphs and network statistics (degree, modularity, motif counts). For spatial omics, we will infer organelle neighborhood states indirectly by mapping organelle-localized gene/protein signatures (from HPA and curated localization sets) onto spatial coordinates, producing probabilistic organelle “fields” and co-localization measures. We will integrate modalities via a common representation: a cell-level feature table with uncertainty estimates, plus a graph representation for spatial relationships.

W3: Causal discovery and validation. We will model relationships among (i) molecular variables (expression/protein abundance, pathway scores), (ii) neighborhood variables (graph/morphology features), (iii) perturbations (gene knockouts, drugs, infection status), and (iv) outcomes. Methods will include: invariant causal prediction across datasets/contexts; causal structure learning with latent confounder allowances; mediation analysis to test whether neighborhood variables mediate perturbation effects; and counterfactual prediction to estimate outcome changes under hypothetical neighborhood shifts. Missingness will be handled with probabilistic models and sensitivity analyses. We will evaluate predictive value using nested cross-validation with dataset-held-out tests, and generalization using leave-one-virus-out and leave-one-cell-type-out protocols.

Comparative controls and robustness. To avoid mistaking generic stress for infection-specific emergence, we will include non-viral perturbation datasets (interferon, ER stress, autophagy induction) and test discriminability. We will perform robustness checks to segmentation variability, feature choices, and metadata uncertainty.

Training and sprints. Trainees will lead rotating “validation tasks” (e.g., reproduce a published organelle phenotype across datasets) and participate in workflow clinics on reproducible pipelines, causal inference, and FAIR data practices. All analyses will be conducted in shared, version-controlled environments to ensure continuity across institutions.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific products. (1) A cross-virus, cross-cell-type atlas of organelle neighborhood states during infection, represented as standardized features and interpretable modules (e.g., ER–mitochondria coupling module, endolysosomal routing module). (2) Quantitative evidence for (or against) the emergence claim that mesoscale organization explains infection outcomes beyond molecular abundance—reported as incremental predictive performance, mediation effects, and causal graph structures with uncertainty. (3) A set of candidate “neighborhood rules” (generalizable motifs and causal pathways) that distinguish infection-specific reorganization from generic stress responses.

Methodological products. (4) Reusable, containerized workflows for extracting organelle neighborhood features from public imaging and for mapping spatial omics to organelle-localization fields, including documented assumptions and uncertainty propagation. (5) A minimal metadata schema and ontology crosswalk for infection-centered organelle neighborhood synthesis, designed for reuse by repositories and future working groups.

Community and workforce impact. (6) Training materials—tutorial notebooks, recorded workflow clinics, and example datasets—enabling graduate students and postdocs to learn reproducible bioimage/omics integration and causal discovery. (7) A template for community-scale synthesis that bridges imaging and omics without generating new experimental data, directly aligned with NCEMS’s mission.

Broader impacts. By identifying mesoscale variables that are predictive and potentially causal for infection outcomes, the project can reframe how the field interprets host factors and antiviral targets: not only as molecular components, but as drivers of emergent organizational states. The atlas and workflows will lower barriers for researchers to reuse public data, accelerate hypothesis generation, and support more principled comparisons across viruses and experimental systems. Even if some hypothesized neighborhood effects do not generalize, the project will still deliver high-value negative results and a rigorous framework for testing emergence claims in molecular and cellular biology using public data.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-by-default outputs. All derived products that can be legally shared will be released publicly: curated dataset index (with source links and licenses), harmonized metadata tables, derived feature matrices, and trained models (with model cards describing intended use, limitations, and bias considerations). Sensitive or restricted datasets will be referenced with reproducible access instructions and scripts that operate on user-authorized data.

Reproducible workflows. Analyses will be implemented as version-controlled, tested pipelines using community tools (e.g., Snakemake/Nextflow) and containerization (Docker/Singularity) to pin dependencies. Each major result will have an executable “research compendium” including code, configuration files, and a provenance log capturing dataset versions, preprocessing parameters, and random seeds. Continuous integration will run unit tests for feature extraction, metadata validation, and model training.

FAIR data practices. We will follow FAIR principles by (i) assigning persistent identifiers to releases (Zenodo DOIs), (ii) providing rich metadata and data dictionaries, (iii) using interoperable formats (AnnData for single-cell-like tables, OME-NGFF pointers for imaging where possible, parquet/CSV for tabular outputs), and (iv) adopting standard ontologies (NCBI Taxonomy for viruses, Cell Ontology, UBERON where relevant, PSI-MI/GO for molecular annotations).

Transparent uncertainty and limitations. We will publish sensitivity analyses (e.g., segmentation alternatives, batch correction choices, missingness mechanisms) and explicitly report uncertainty in causal edges and effect sizes. Negative findings and non-generalizing patterns will be documented to prevent publication bias.

Team science practices. The working group will use open lab notebooks, issue tracking, and pre-registered analysis plans for key hypotheses to reduce researcher degrees of freedom. Trainees will be credited via contributorship (CRediT taxonomy) and encouraged to lead public tutorials and documentation.

Community engagement. We will host open virtual seminars and invite repository curators and external experts to review the metadata schema and recommend improvements, ensuring outputs are usable beyond the immediate team and aligned with NCEMS community standards.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support needs. This project requires NCEMS coordination and resources because it integrates heterogeneous public imaging, spatial omics, perturbation screens, and structural/interaction annotations at a scale that exceeds typical single-lab capacity. NCEMS will provide convening infrastructure, collaborative working space, and access to computational resources appropriate for large-scale feature extraction and model training.

Budget categories (illustrative, aligned with working-group model). (1) Personnel support: partial support for a project manager/data steward to coordinate dataset licensing/metadata harmonization; and limited support for trainee participation (graduate students/postdocs) to ensure sustained contributions between meetings. (2) Working group meetings: travel, lodging, and per diem for 2–3 in-person meetings at NCEMS (or an approved venue), plus support for hybrid participation to include geographically distributed and resource-limited institutions. (3) Computing: cloud/HPC credits for image processing at scale, storage for intermediate derived features, and compute for causal discovery/model evaluation; costs will be minimized by processing only necessary derivatives and by caching reusable outputs. (4) Dissemination: funds for open-access publication fees where needed, tutorial hosting, and long-term archiving (e.g., Zenodo storage is free but curation and packaging require staff time).

Resource plan and roles. Participating labs will contribute domain expertise and existing codebases: bioimage analysis specialists will lead segmentation/feature extraction; omics experts will lead normalization and pathway scoring; statisticians/ML researchers will lead causal discovery and validation; virologists/cell biologists will define biologically meaningful outcomes and interpretability constraints; data curators will lead metadata schema design and FAIR release packaging.

Feasibility and risk management. To manage scope, we will prioritize datasets with strong metadata and clear outcome labels, and we will stage work: a pilot integration on a small, diverse set of viruses/cell types in months 1–6, followed by scaling to additional datasets once pipelines and schemas are stable. This staged approach reduces risk while ensuring deliverables that justify NCEMS investment.

background_and_significance:
Cells repeatedly evolve compartment-like organization without lipid membranes: biomolecular condensates, protein microcompartments, cytoskeletal foci, ribonucleoprotein granules, and parasite-specific assemblies. These mesoscale structures (tens of nanometers to microns) concentrate reactants, filter interactions, buffer noise, and coordinate spatiotemporal programs. Yet their evolutionary origins remain poorly understood because the “parts list” (proteins/RNAs) is insufficient to explain the “system behavior” (assembly, material state, dynamics, and phenotypic consequences). This gap is central to NCEMS’s mission: emergent properties arise when many molecular components collectively generate new behaviors across scales of composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion.

A core challenge is that evidence is fragmented across data types and communities. Imaging repositories capture localization patterns and subcellular morphology but often lack standardized metadata for growth condition, perturbation, or species context. Omics datasets measure abundance, PTMs, and interactions but rarely encode mesoscale organization directly. Structural resources (PDB, AlphaFold, disorder/low-complexity predictions) characterize sequence biophysics that may predispose proteins to phase separation or scaffold formation, but these annotations are not routinely linked to cellular phenotypes. Perturbation screens (CRISPR/RNAi/chemical genetics) provide causal signals but are typically interpreted at pathway or gene levels rather than as drivers of emergent mesoscale states. As a result, the field lacks a synthesis-derived, quantitative framework to ask: under what evolutionary and cellular conditions do membrane-less compartments arise, and what general rules connect molecular composition to mesoscale organization and phenotype?

This working group targets microbes and parasites as a strategically powerful domain for synthesis. First, these lineages span deep evolutionary time and diverse ecological pressures, enabling comparative inference about invention, loss, and convergence of compartmentalization strategies. Second, many microbes and parasites display dramatic life-cycle transitions and stress responses where mesoscale reorganization is pronounced, providing natural “experiments” already captured in public datasets. Third, microbial genomes are compact and well annotated, facilitating cross-species feature extraction and phylogenetic modeling. Importantly, we will include comparison cases across eukaryotes and bacteria/archaea to avoid overfitting to any single model system.

NCEMS support is essential because the proposed work is community-scale synthesis: it uses only publicly available data; it requires integration of incompatible imaging, omics, perturbation, and structural annotations; and it demands expertise spanning cell biology, biophysics, evolutionary biology, machine learning, statistics, and data curation. No single lab typically has the breadth to (i) harmonize metadata across repositories, (ii) develop robust mesoscale feature representations, (iii) build phylogenetically informed causal models that propagate uncertainty, and (iv) produce reusable open workflows and standards.

Beyond answering a fundamental question about emergent organization, this project will create enabling infrastructure. By defining mesoscale variables as first-class, measurable entities and linking them to molecular features and phenotypes, we will provide a reusable template for future NCEMS-style synthesis projects. The outcome will be a community-vetted, open, versioned model of membrane-less compartment invention—grounded in public data, explicit about uncertainty, and designed to train a new generation of data-savvy molecular and cellular scientists.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Overall objective: derive generalizable, evolution-aware rules by which molecular composition and biophysical properties give rise to membrane-less mesoscale compartments and associated cellular outcomes.

RQ1: What measurable mesoscale “state variables” best summarize membrane-less compartmentalization across diverse organisms and conditions using public data?
H1.1: A small set of latent mesoscale variables—e.g., spatial concentration (enrichment), anisotropy/shape complexity, number/size distribution, co-localization modularity, and inferred dynamics/material state proxies—can be extracted from heterogeneous imaging and interaction data and will generalize across datasets after harmonization.
H1.2: These mesoscale variables capture information not reducible to molecular abundance alone, improving prediction of phenotypes such as stress tolerance, growth rate changes, virulence traits, or cell-cycle progression.

RQ2: Which molecular features predict the emergence of membrane-less compartments across evolution?
H2.1: Sequence-encoded biophysics (intrinsic disorder, low-complexity regions, multivalency motifs, charge patterning, prion-like composition), together with interaction-network topology (hubness, community structure), predict the probability and type of compartment formation better than expression level or essentiality alone.
H2.2: Convergent evolution will be detectable: unrelated lineages will independently acquire similar combinations of biophysical and network features when facing similar ecological pressures (e.g., heat shock, nutrient limitation, host immune environments).

RQ3: How do perturbations rewire mesoscale organization, and do mesoscale changes mediate phenotypic outcomes?
H3.1: Genetic or chemical perturbations that alter post-translational modification machinery, RNA metabolism, chaperone systems, or cytoskeletal organization will produce reproducible shifts in mesoscale variables across datasets.
H3.2: Mesoscale variables will statistically mediate the relationship between perturbations and cellular outcomes (e.g., fitness, infectivity proxies), indicating that compartmentalization is not merely correlated but part of the causal path.

RQ4: What are the evolutionary dynamics of invention, loss, and diversification of membrane-less compartments?
H4.1: Gains and losses of compartment-associated traits will follow punctuated patterns aligned with major lifestyle transitions (e.g., parasitism, multicellularity, obligate intracellular life), detectable via phylogenetic comparative models.
H4.2: Certain compartments will show “deep homology” (shared ancestral molecular modules) while others will show repeated invention using different molecules but similar mesoscale state variables (emergent equivalence classes).

RQ5 (methodological): Can we build a synthesis framework that remains robust to missingness, batch effects, and inconsistent annotations while enabling cross-repository inference?
H5.1: Hierarchical Bayesian and multi-view learning models that explicitly represent dataset-specific noise and missingness will yield stable, reproducible rules and calibrated uncertainty, outperforming naive pooling or single-dataset analyses.

These questions collectively test emergence: whether mesoscale organization constitutes an explanatory layer connecting molecular parts to cellular behavior, and whether evolution discovers recurring design principles for building compartments without membranes.
methods_and_approach:
Working group structure and scope: We will form a multi-lab team spanning (i) cell biology of condensates/microcompartments, (ii) microbial/parasite evolution, (iii) bioimage analysis, (iv) proteomics/transcriptomics integration, (v) statistical phylogenetics/causal inference, and (vi) data stewardship. The project uses only publicly available data and will proceed through iterative synthesis “sprints” hosted/organized with NCEMS.

Data sources (public): Imaging (BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas where applicable; organism-specific repositories); omics (GEO/ArrayExpress, SRA, PRIDE/MassIVE); perturbations (DepMap where relevant, published CRISPR/RNAi screens, chemical genomics datasets); structures/biophysics (AlphaFold DB, PDB, disorder/low-complexity annotations, Pfam domains); interactions/pathways (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, KEGG/Reactome where applicable). We will prioritize datasets with condition/perturbation metadata and links to phenotypes.

Aim 1: Build a harmonized “mesoscale compartment” knowledge graph.
- Extract entities: proteins/RNAs, species/strains, conditions, perturbations, phenotypes, imaging-derived compartment calls/labels, interaction edges, structural/sequence features.
- Normalize identifiers (UniProt/Ensembl/NCBI), map orthologs (OrthoDB/eggNOG), and represent provenance.
- Implement a common metadata schema (minimal required fields; controlled vocabularies for condition, life stage, microscopy modality).

Aim 2: Derive mesoscale state variables from heterogeneous data.
- Imaging: compute standardized features (enrichment ratios, puncta counts, size distributions, spatial autocorrelation, co-localization indices, texture-based proxies of material state) using reproducible pipelines (e.g., CellProfiler/napari + Python). When raw images are unavailable, use published segmentation masks/summary features.
- Omics/interaction: infer mesoscale proxies (co-expression modules, interaction-community density, stoichiometry imbalance, PTM signatures) that may correspond to assembly propensity.
- Multi-view representation learning: integrate imaging and molecular views into shared latent variables with uncertainty (e.g., variational models or Bayesian factor analysis), while preserving dataset-specific effects.

Aim 3: Comparative phylogenetic synthesis and hypothesis testing.
- Phylogenetic comparative models: model gain/loss and trait correlations of mesoscale variables across species while accounting for shared ancestry.
- Predictive modeling: test whether molecular features predict mesoscale states; evaluate out-of-domain generalization across clades and labs.
- Mediation/causal analysis: connect perturbations → mesoscale variables → phenotypes using structural equation models or Bayesian mediation, with sensitivity analyses for confounding.
- Robustness: explicitly model batch effects, missingness (MNAR/MAR scenarios), and measurement error; perform leave-dataset-out validation.

Aim 4: Community validation via cross-dataset replication.
- Define a set of “benchmark questions” (e.g., stress granule–like assemblies in parasites; bacterial microcompartment emergence) and require independent replication across at least two repositories or studies.
- Use preregistered analysis plans within the group to reduce researcher degrees of freedom.

Training and coordination: Each sprint pairs trainees with mentors to lead a module (data ingestion, image feature extraction, phylogenetic modeling, or reproducibility). NCEMS-hosted workflow clinics will ensure consistent environments (containers), code review, and documentation.

Scientific products:

This will provide an explicit answer to the emergence question: when and how does collective molecular behavior produce new mesoscale organization that matters for phenotype?
2) Identification of convergent “design principles” (e.g., combinations of disorder, multivalency, and network topology) that repeatedly enable membrane-less compartments across microbes and parasites, distinguishing deep homology from repeated invention.
3) Evidence for mediation: cases where perturbations affect phenotypes primarily through altering mesoscale organization, elevating compartments from descriptive observations to explanatory, testable mechanisms.

Synthesis infrastructure:
4) A harmonized, provenance-rich knowledge graph and curated crosswalks among imaging, omics, perturbation, and structural resources, enabling others to extend the analysis to new species, compartments, or phenotypes.
5) A reusable, validated set of mesoscale feature extraction and multi-view integration workflows that can be applied to other NCEMS problems involving mesoscale emergence.

Community and workforce impact:
6) A cross-disciplinary network of investigators and trainees trained in data synthesis, AI-enabled integration, and rigorous comparative inference. Trainees will leave with demonstrable products (reproducible pipelines, curated datasets, benchmarks) and experience in team science.

Broader significance:
By making mesoscale organization a first-class quantitative layer, the project will shift how public molecular and cellular data are reused: from single-dataset associations to integrated, evolution-grounded rules of emergence. The resulting framework will support future hypothesis generation for experimentalists (without generating new data in this project) and will accelerate discovery of mesoscale principles relevant to infection biology, stress adaptation, and cellular robustness.

Open-by-default outputs: All derived datasets (within license constraints), code, workflows, and documentation will be released under permissive open licenses (e.g., MIT/BSD for code; CC-BY/CC0 for metadata/derived features where allowed). We will not redistribute restricted raw data; instead we will publish reproducible “data recipes” (download scripts, accession lists, and checksums) that reconstruct inputs from public repositories.

- Calibrated uncertainty reporting (credible intervals, posterior predictive checks) and explicit sensitivity analyses for missingness and batch effects.
- Benchmarking and replication: leave-dataset-out and leave-clade-out validation; publication of benchmark splits and evaluation metrics.

FAIR and community standards:
