title: Benchmarking AI models for mesoscale emergence, not just molecule annotation
abstract:
This working group asks how benchmarking ai models for mesoscale emergence, not just molecule annotation can be understood as an emergent property that links molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcome. The scientific question is not simply whether particular molecules, organelles, or pathways are associated with a phenotype, but whether publicly available datasets can reveal rules by which many molecular parts collectively produce a new, system-level behavior at the scale between biomolecules and organelles. The project is designed for the NCEMS model because the relevant evidence is scattered across incompatible imaging repositories, omics studies, perturbation resources, structural annotations, and specialized literatures; no single laboratory is likely to have the biological breadth, data-engineering capacity, and methodological expertise to integrate them.

The group would synthesize existing public data centered on text/knowledge graph + repositories, prioritizing datasets with reusable metadata, perturbation or state annotations, and links to downstream cellular phenotypes. Depending on availability, sources could include public cell atlases, the Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, EMBL-EBI and NCBI functional genomics repositories, BioImage Archive or Image Data Resource collections, PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics datasets, public CRISPR or RNAi screens, AlphaFold/PDB-derived structural features, and curated pathway or protein-interaction resources. The core analytic strategy would be benchmark/standard/community resource: harmonizing measurements into a common representation; explicitly modeling uncertainty, batch effects, and missingness; and testing whether mesoscale variables explain cellular outcomes above and beyond molecular abundance alone. The biological scope would focus on cross-kingdom/cross-species while deliberately including comparison cases that prevent the group from mistaking a narrow model-system pattern for a general law.

The novel element is the unit of explanation. Instead of treating mesoscale organization as an image label, downstream readout, or anecdotal mechanism, the working group would make it the primary object of synthesis: a measurable layer where composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion combine. The expected product is a reusable benchmark/workflow that is open, versioned, and reusable, with transparent workflows, community-agreed metadata standards, and tutorials for trainees. The project would bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, imaging scientists, omics researchers, statisticians, machine-learning researchers, data curators, and trainees across institution types. Training would occur through hackathon-style data sprints, reproducible workflow clinics, and rotating trainee leadership of cross-dataset validation tasks. The anticipated contribution is both scientific and infrastructural: a defensible answer to a specific emergence question, plus a generalizable synthesis strategy that helps the molecular and cellular biosciences reuse public data to discover phenomena that only become visible when datasets, disciplines, and scales are brought together.
background_and_significance:
Mesoscale cellular organization—the spatial and temporal arrangement of macromolecular assemblies, phase-separated condensates, membrane contact sites, cytoskeletal networks, and organelle subdomains—often determines cellular behavior in ways not predictable from individual molecules alone. This “between molecules and organelles” regime is where emergent properties arise: collective phenomena such as self-organization, robustness, bistability, and adaptation that depend on composition, geometry, dynamics, and context. Yet most public molecular and cellular datasets, and most AI models trained on them, treat mesoscale organization as either (i) an image label (e.g., “mitochondria”), (ii) a proxy for gene function, or (iii) an anecdotal mechanistic story appended to molecular associations. The field lacks community benchmarks that ask a harder question aligned with NCEMS: can we infer generalizable rules of emergence linking molecular composition to mesoscale organization and then to cellular outcomes, using only existing public data?

Public data relevant to mesoscale emergence are abundant but fragmented. Imaging repositories (e.g., BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas) contain millions of images with heterogeneous metadata, variable staining and acquisition protocols, and inconsistent cell-state annotations. Functional genomics repositories (GEO, ArrayExpress, SRA, ENCODE-like resources), perturbation screens (CRISPR/RNAi, chemical screens), and proteomics databases (PRIDE, MassIVE) provide complementary molecular readouts and phenotypes, but are rarely linked in a way that supports mechanistic inference at the mesoscale. Structural resources (AlphaFold, PDB) and interaction/pathway databases add constraints on assembly formation and network topology, yet these are seldom incorporated into predictive models of cellular organization. As a result, AI efforts often optimize for annotation accuracy within a single modality rather than for cross-modal explanatory power.

This working group addresses a long-standing puzzle: why do many molecular perturbations produce similar cellular outcomes, while similar molecular profiles can yield distinct outcomes depending on spatial organization? Mesoscale variables—such as organelle morphology distributions, condensate number/size, spatial co-localization patterns, and dynamic texture features—may mediate these discrepancies. If so, models that explicitly represent mesoscale organization should explain phenotypes beyond what can be predicted from molecular abundance or gene identity alone. Demonstrating this requires synthesis across repositories, careful uncertainty modeling, and evaluation across species and cell types to avoid overfitting to a single model system.

NCEMS is uniquely suited because the project is intentionally beyond a single laboratory: it demands expertise in cell biology, imaging science, biophysics, machine learning, statistics, knowledge representation, and data curation; it requires sustained coordination to harmonize metadata and align modalities; and it benefits from community-scale governance to produce a benchmark that others trust and reuse. The significance is twofold. Scientifically, the project will test whether mesoscale organization is a quantitatively predictive layer of explanation for cellular outcomes. Infrastructurally, it will produce an open, versioned benchmark and workflows that shift the community from “AI for labeling” to “AI for emergence,” enabling more rigorous, comparable, and mechanistically grounded synthesis research across molecular and cellular biosciences.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The working group will pursue a focused set of research questions that collectively test whether mesoscale organization functions as an emergent explanatory layer and how to benchmark AI models accordingly.

RQ1: Do mesoscale organizational variables explain cellular outcomes beyond molecular abundance and gene identity? Many studies correlate transcript or protein levels with phenotypes (growth, viability, stress resistance, differentiation), but these correlations often fail across contexts. We will test whether adding mesoscale descriptors—derived from public imaging and/or inferred from multimodal data—improves prediction of cellular outcomes after controlling for molecular abundance and known pathways.

H1: Models that include mesoscale features (e.g., organelle morphology distributions, spatial co-localization metrics, condensate statistics, cytoskeletal texture features) will significantly improve out-of-dataset prediction of cellular outcomes compared to models using only molecular abundance and pathway annotations.

RQ2: Are there conserved “mesoscale motifs” that generalize across species, cell types, and perturbation classes? Emergent phenomena should exhibit partial universality: different molecular implementations can yield similar organizational states and outcomes.

H2: Unsupervised and weakly supervised representation learning across imaging datasets will identify mesoscale states (latent motifs) that recur across taxa and experimental systems and that map to similar downstream outcomes (e.g., stress adaptation, proliferation arrest), even when the underlying molecular drivers differ.

RQ3: What benchmark tasks best measure AI capability for mesoscale emergence rather than annotation? Current benchmarks emphasize classification/segmentation. We will define tasks that require linking composition → organization → outcome and that penalize shortcuts.

H3: Benchmark tasks that enforce cross-modal generalization (train on one modality/dataset, test on another) and causal/perturbational structure (predict organizational change under perturbation) will differentiate models that capture mesoscale principles from those that memorize dataset-specific cues.

RQ4: How should uncertainty, missingness, and batch effects be represented to avoid false emergence claims? Public data are noisy and biased; emergent patterns can be artifacts of acquisition or curation.

H4: Explicit probabilistic modeling of batch effects and missing data mechanisms will reduce spurious mesoscale–outcome associations and produce more stable estimates of effect sizes and generalization across datasets.

RQ5: Can knowledge graphs and literature-derived constraints improve interpretability and mechanistic plausibility of mesoscale models? Emergence claims must be biologically defensible.

H5: Integrating protein interaction networks, complex/condensate annotations, and structural features (e.g., disorder propensity, oligomeric interfaces) as priors or auxiliary objectives will yield models whose learned mesoscale representations align better with known assembly biology and produce more interpretable, testable hypotheses.

Collectively, these questions operationalize “mesoscale emergence” into measurable tasks: (i) incremental predictive value, (ii) cross-context universality, (iii) robustness to confounding, and (iv) mechanistic coherence. The working group’s deliverable will be a benchmark suite and accompanying analyses that provide clear quantitative answers: when, where, and to what extent mesoscale organization is necessary to explain cellular outcomes using existing public data.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. The project will run as an NCEMS-style working group with three integrated thrusts: (T1) data synthesis and harmonization, (T2) benchmark/task design and evaluation, and (T3) emergence-focused modeling and analysis. Participants will include imaging experts, omics analysts, ML/statistics researchers, biophysicists, and data curators, with trainees embedded in each thrust and rotating across tasks.

T1: Public data inventory, selection, and harmonization (no new data generation). We will assemble a curated “mesoscale emergence corpus” from publicly available sources with permissive reuse terms and adequate metadata. Candidate sources include BioImage Archive/IDR collections with perturbations or time series; Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas images and localization annotations; GEO/ArrayExpress expression studies paired with phenotypes; PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics with condition labels; public CRISPR/RNAi screens with morphological or fitness readouts; AlphaFold/PDB-derived features; and curated interaction/pathway resources. Inclusion criteria: (i) explicit perturbation/state labels, (ii) measurable cellular outcome (fitness, morphology score, stress marker, differentiation), (iii) traceable sample provenance, and (iv) sufficient metadata to model batch effects. We will map entities to stable identifiers (UniProt, Ensembl, OBO ontologies), standardize condition and phenotype terms, and create a crosswalk between imaging samples and molecular/perturbation records when possible.

T2: Mesoscale feature extraction and representations. For imaging, we will not attempt to re-segment every dataset uniformly; instead we will support two parallel representations: (i) lightweight, broadly applicable “mesoscale descriptors” (e.g., intensity texture, organelle shape proxies, spatial autocorrelation, co-localization statistics) computed with reproducible pipelines; and (ii) learned embeddings from foundation models (self-supervised vision models) evaluated for cross-dataset transfer. For non-imaging datasets, we will derive proxy mesoscale predictors from interaction/complex membership, predicted disorder/phase-separation propensity, subcellular localization distributions, and network topology measures. Missingness will be explicitly encoded.

T3: Benchmark task suite. We will define tasks that require emergence-relevant reasoning: (a) outcome prediction with ablation tests (molecular-only vs molecular+mesoscale), (b) perturbation-to-organization prediction (predict mesoscale shift under genetic/chemical perturbation), (c) cross-dataset generalization (train on one repository, test on another), and (d) counterfactual robustness checks (hold out cell types/species/assay batches). Metrics will include predictive performance with uncertainty (calibration), effect-size stability across datasets, and “shortcut” diagnostics (e.g., performance drop when acquisition cues are removed).

Modeling and inference. We will compare baselines (regularized regression, random forests, gradient boosting) to multimodal deep models (late fusion, graph neural networks over knowledge graphs, multimodal transformers) and causal-inspired approaches (invariant risk minimization, domain adaptation, hierarchical Bayesian models). We will quantify incremental value of mesoscale variables via nested model comparisons, permutation tests, and partial R²/ELPD improvements with cross-validation by dataset (not by sample) to prevent leakage.

Quality control and rigor. We will implement standardized data audits, batch-effect modeling (ComBat-like and hierarchical approaches), and sensitivity analyses. All results will be replicated across at least two independent dataset families (e.g., one atlas-scale imaging resource and one perturbation screen) and evaluated for cross-species generality where feasible.

NCEMS need. The approach requires coordinated multi-repository engineering, shared compute/workflows, consensus benchmark governance, and cross-domain expertise—precisely the synthesis capacity NCEMS is designed to provide.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Primary scientific outcome: a quantitative answer to whether mesoscale organization is an explanatory layer that improves prediction of cellular outcomes beyond molecular abundance alone, across diverse public datasets. We expect to identify specific classes of outcomes (e.g., stress survival, proliferation arrest, organelle dysfunction signatures) where mesoscale descriptors provide the largest incremental value and to delineate contexts where they do not, thereby sharpening the boundary conditions of mesoscale emergence.

Primary infrastructural outcome: an open, versioned benchmark suite for “AI for mesoscale emergence,” including curated crosswalked datasets (or pointers plus harmonized metadata tables where redistribution is restricted), standardized task definitions, evaluation scripts, and baselines. The benchmark will emphasize cross-dataset generalization and perturbation-aware prediction, enabling fair comparison of models and discouraging overfitting to single repositories.

Methodological outcomes: (i) practical guidance on uncertainty and batch-effect modeling for multimodal synthesis; (ii) validated emergence-oriented metrics (e.g., incremental explanatory power, invariance across domains, calibration under missingness); and (iii) reference workflows for extracting mesoscale descriptors and embeddings from heterogeneous imaging data.

Community and workforce outcomes: trainees will gain experience in reproducible data synthesis, multimodal modeling, and open-science collaboration through data sprints, workflow clinics, and leadership of benchmark components. The working group will also produce training materials (tutorial notebooks, recorded walkthroughs) usable beyond the project.

Impact: By shifting evaluation from “annotation accuracy” to “emergence explanation,” the project will reorient AI development toward mechanistic, cross-context insights in molecular and cellular biology. The benchmark will lower barriers for new teams to enter mesoscale research using public data, accelerate discovery of conserved organizational motifs, and provide NCEMS and the broader community with a reusable template for future synthesis projects targeting emergent phenomena at the mesoscale.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
The working group will follow open, team, and reproducible science practices as a core deliverable rather than an afterthought.

Open outputs and licensing. All code, documentation, and analysis workflows will be released under a permissive open-source license (e.g., BSD-3 or Apache-2.0). Derived metadata tables, feature matrices, and benchmark splits will be released under CC-BY where allowed. For datasets that cannot be redistributed, we will provide immutable accession lists, checksums, and automated download/processing scripts so others can reproduce the corpus exactly.

Reproducible workflows. All processing and analyses will be implemented as containerized, workflow-managed pipelines (e.g., Docker/Singularity with Nextflow/Snakemake). Each benchmark release will be versioned (semantic versioning), with locked dependencies and computational provenance (software versions, parameter settings, random seeds). We will provide “small” toy runs for laptops and “full” runs for HPC/cloud.

Transparent evaluation. The benchmark will include standardized evaluation scripts and reporting templates that require: (i) dataset-level cross-validation, (ii) uncertainty calibration reporting, (iii) ablation results (molecular-only vs molecular+mesoscale), and (iv) robustness checks against acquisition/metadata shortcuts. Leaderboard-style reporting will be accompanied by model cards describing training data, assumptions, and failure modes.

Data governance and documentation. We will adopt community ontologies (e.g., Gene Ontology, Cell Ontology, OBI) and publish a data dictionary describing all fields, mappings, and known limitations. Curation decisions (inclusion/exclusion, mapping rules) will be recorded in an auditable change log.

Open collaboration. Work will be coordinated in a public repository with issue tracking, contribution guidelines, and a code of conduct. Working-group meetings will produce public notes and action items. Trainees will be supported to make visible contributions (pull requests, documentation, tutorial authorship) that are citable.

FAIR and reuse. Outputs will be deposited in long-term archives (e.g., Zenodo) with DOIs for each release, enabling citation, reuse, and extension by the broader molecular and cellular community.
budget_and_resources:
This proposal is designed as an NCEMS Working Group requiring synthesis coordination, shared computational resources, and cross-disciplinary participation beyond a single lab.

Requested NCEMS support (categories). (1) Working-group convening: funds for multiple in-person meetings (kickoff, mid-project integration, final release workshop) plus virtual collaboration infrastructure. Travel support will prioritize broad participation across geographic regions, institution types (R1, PUIs, minority-serving institutions), and career stages, with dedicated trainee travel. (2) Personnel time for synthesis: partial support for a project coordinator/data steward to manage data inventories, identifier mapping, documentation, and release engineering; and limited support for trainee stipends/assistantships tied to benchmark construction and tutorial development (no experimental work). (3) Compute and storage: allocation for shared compute (HPC/cloud credits) to run standardized feature extraction, model baselines, and cross-validation at scale; and storage for intermediate derived artifacts and versioned releases. (4) Training and community building: resources for hackathon-style data sprints, reproducible workflow clinics, and external speaker sessions on benchmarking, uncertainty, and multimodal integration.

Resource justification and necessity. Integrating heterogeneous public imaging, omics, perturbation, and structural resources requires sustained engineering, governance, and compute that exceed typical single-lab capacity. NCEMS provides the neutral convening power to establish community-agreed tasks/standards and the infrastructure to host iterative benchmark releases.

Cost controls and feasibility. The project minimizes costs by using only public data, reusing existing open-source tools, and focusing on a curated subset of high-value datasets with strong metadata. Compute will be managed via standardized containers and scheduled batch runs; expensive model training will be limited to representative baselines and a small number of carefully chosen advanced models for comparison.

In-kind contributions. Participating labs will contribute domain expertise, existing open-source code where applicable, and mentoring for trainees. Data curators and repository liaisons will advise on metadata standards and redistribution constraints.

Deliverables tied to budget. Each funded convening milestone will correspond to a concrete release: v0 (corpus + task definitions), v1 (baselines + evaluation), v2 (robustness/uncertainty + final benchmark and tutorials).

background_and_significance:
Cell fate decisions—differentiation, stress adaptation, quiescence, senescence, and death—are often studied as transcriptional programs or signaling cascades. Yet across many systems, similar gene-expression states can yield divergent outcomes, and conversely distinct molecular profiles can converge on shared phenotypes. This gap motivates an emergence framing: cell fate is not only a function of molecular composition but also of how molecules are organized and transported in space and time. The mesoscale—between biomolecules and organelles—contains the logistics layer of the cell: vesicle trafficking, endomembrane organization, cargo sorting, organelle contact sites, and cytoskeletal transport. These processes determine where molecules are, when they arrive, their local concentrations, and which partners they encounter. Such logistics can create nonlinear thresholds, delays, and spatial compartmentalization that plausibly generate new system-level behaviors not predictable from abundance alone.

Trafficking networks are especially compelling as a candidate mesoscale driver of emergent fate because they integrate multiple physical and informational constraints. Cargo selection and coat assembly encode information; motor-driven transport and diffusion impose motion and energy constraints; membrane curvature, phase behavior, and organelle geometry constrain space; and feedback between trafficking, signaling, and metabolism creates time-dependent control. For example, receptor endocytosis can switch signaling from sustained to transient; lysosomal positioning can regulate mTORC1 activity; ER–mitochondria contacts can tune calcium and apoptosis sensitivity; and Golgi and endosomal maturation can gate secretion versus degradation. These examples suggest a general principle: reconfigurations of trafficking topology and organelle connectivity can act as a mesoscale “control layer” that amplifies or buffers molecular perturbations.

Despite intense study, the field lacks a cross-system, quantitative synthesis that tests whether trafficking organization explains fate outcomes across organisms, cell types, and perturbations. Existing evidence is fragmented across imaging repositories (capturing spatial organization), proteomics (capturing composition and complex membership), perturbation screens (capturing causal interventions), and pathway/interaction resources (capturing prior knowledge). These datasets are rarely interoperable: metadata standards differ, phenotypes are inconsistently annotated, and imaging-derived features are not aligned with omics measures. As a result, many conclusions remain case-specific, and it is unclear which mesoscale variables generalize.

NCEMS is uniquely suited to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that can overcome these barriers without generating new experimental data. The project requires (i) data engineering to harmonize heterogeneous public datasets; (ii) imaging science to extract reusable mesoscale features; (iii) omics expertise to model abundance, complexes, and PTM states; (iv) causal inference and machine learning to separate association from mechanism; and (v) cell biology and biophysics to interpret emergent rules. No single lab typically spans these capabilities, and the payoff scales with community participation: shared feature definitions, reusable pipelines, and a vetted set of cross-dataset benchmarks.

By focusing on subcellular logistics as the unit of explanation, this working group targets NCEMS’s core vision: emergent properties at the mesoscale that influence higher-order cellular outcomes. A successful synthesis would establish whether trafficking-network organization is a measurable, predictive, and potentially causal mediator between molecular composition and fate—providing a principled bridge between molecules and phenotypes and a template for future emergence-focused synthesis projects.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will address whether and how mesoscale trafficking organization mediates the relationship between molecular composition and cell fate across diverse biological contexts using only publicly available data. We define “subcellular logistics” as the integrated state of endomembrane compartments, vesicle flux proxies, cargo routing, organelle contact topology, and cytoskeletal transport organization. We define “cell fate” broadly to include differentiation endpoints, proliferation/quiescence, senescence, apoptosis/ferroptosis sensitivity, and stable stress-adapted states measured by established phenotypic readouts in public datasets.

RQ1: Do mesoscale trafficking variables explain fate outcomes beyond molecular abundance alone? Hypothesis H1: Models that include mesoscale logistics features (e.g., organelle spatial distributions, compartment connectivity proxies, cargo colocalization patterns, endosomal/lysosomal positioning metrics) will significantly improve prediction of fate-related phenotypes compared with models using transcript/protein abundance only, across multiple datasets and species. This hypothesis operationalizes emergence: added explanatory power arises from organization, not merely parts lists.

RQ2: Are there conserved “logistics motifs” that recur across organisms, cell types, and perturbations? Hypothesis H2: A small set of mesoscale motifs—such as perinuclear clustering of lysosomes, increased ER–mitochondria contact signatures, altered recycling-to-degradation routing, or Golgi fragmentation patterns—will appear as shared latent factors that map to similar fate outcomes (e.g., stress resistance vs apoptosis) even when upstream molecular drivers differ. We will test conservation by comparing model organisms (yeast, fly, worm, zebrafish, mouse, human cell lines) where public imaging and perturbation data are abundant, while explicitly modeling context dependence.

RQ3: Do trafficking networks act as mediators (causal intermediates) between perturbations and fate? Hypothesis H3: In perturbation datasets (CRISPR/RNAi/chemical), inferred causal graphs will place mesoscale logistics variables on directed paths from perturbation targets to fate phenotypes more often than expected by chance, consistent with mediation. We will assess mediation using multiple causal discovery approaches and sensitivity analyses for hidden confounding and measurement error.

RQ4: Which molecular features most strongly control logistics state transitions? Hypothesis H4: Structural and network properties of proteins (e.g., disordered regions, coiled-coils, membrane-binding domains, predicted oligomerization, interaction centrality) will predict whether perturbing a gene shifts the logistics latent state. This links biomolecular properties to mesoscale organization, aligning with NCEMS’s composition-to-organization-to-outcome framing.

RQ5: Under what conditions does logistics fail to generalize as an explanatory layer? Hypothesis H5: For some fate outcomes (e.g., rapid toxin-induced necrosis) or contexts with minimal trafficking involvement, mesoscale features will not add explanatory power; identifying these boundaries will refine theory and prevent overgeneralization.

Together, these questions test a coherent emergence claim: that trafficking organization constitutes a mesoscale state variable with partial autonomy from molecular abundance, capable of mediating and constraining fate outcomes. The hypotheses are designed to yield falsifiable results through cross-dataset replication, explicit uncertainty quantification, and pre-registered evaluation metrics agreed upon by the working group.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. The project will proceed through iterative synthesis cycles: (1) dataset discovery and triage; (2) harmonization and feature extraction; (3) integrative modeling and causal discovery; (4) cross-dataset validation and theory refinement. NCEMS support is essential for convening multi-lab expertise, hosting data sprints, providing neutral governance for standards, and enabling shared compute and curation.

Data sources (public only). Imaging: Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Allen Cell Explorer (where licensing permits reuse), and organism-specific atlases with subcellular markers and perturbations. Omics: PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics (including organelle proteomes and proximity labeling where available), GEO/ArrayExpress functional genomics, DepMap and other public CRISPR screen releases with phenotypic endpoints, and curated interaction/pathway resources (Reactome, STRING, BioGRID). Structural annotations: AlphaFold-derived features and PDB mappings for domain composition and predicted interfaces.

Harmonization. We will build a unified entity mapping (genes/proteins/orthologs), controlled vocabularies for compartments and phenotypes, and dataset-level provenance records. Batch effects and missingness will be modeled explicitly using hierarchical models and multiple imputation where appropriate; we will avoid “complete case” bias by propagating uncertainty into downstream analyses.

Mesoscale feature extraction from images. Using reproducible pipelines (e.g., Nextflow/Snakemake + containerized tools), we will extract interpretable logistics features: organelle size/shape distributions, radial positioning, colocalization and adjacency graphs, texture-based proxies for fragmentation, and dynamic proxies where time-lapse exists (e.g., track-based transport metrics). When raw images are unavailable, we will use published segmentation masks or derived features, prioritizing datasets with reusable intermediate products. Integrative representations. We will align imaging-derived logistics features with omics and perturbation metadata at the sample/condition level. For perturbation-linked datasets, we will infer causal graphs among perturbation targets, molecular abundance, logistics features, and phenotypes using complementary methods (constraint-based, score-based, and invariant causal prediction across environments). Performance metrics will include predictive lift over abundance-only baselines, calibration, and causal graph stability. Biological plausibility will be assessed via enrichment of known trafficking regulators and concordance with curated pathways, without circularly training on those annotations.

Training and collaboration. Trainees will lead rotating “validation pods” responsible for reproducing a result on an independent dataset. Hackathon-style sprints will focus on (i) entity mapping, (ii) feature extraction, (iii) causal modeling, and (iv) documentation and tutorials. This structure ensures deliverables, cross-training, and rigorous replication culture.

title: The mesoscale ecology of the cell: cooperation and competition among compartments
abstract:
This working group asks how the mesoscale ecology of the cell: cooperation and competition among compartments can be understood as an emergent property that links molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcome. The scientific question is not simply whether particular molecules, organelles, or pathways are associated with a phenotype, but whether publicly available datasets can reveal rules by which many molecular parts collectively produce a new, system-level behavior at the scale between biomolecules and organelles. The project is designed for the NCEMS model because the relevant evidence is scattered across incompatible imaging repositories, omics studies, perturbation resources, structural annotations, and specialized literatures; no single laboratory is likely to have the biological breadth, data-engineering capacity, and methodological expertise to integrate them.

The group would synthesize existing public data centered on text/knowledge graph + repositories, prioritizing datasets with reusable metadata, perturbation or state annotations, and links to downstream cellular phenotypes. Depending on availability, sources could include public cell atlases, the Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, EMBL-EBI and NCBI functional genomics repositories, BioImage Archive or Image Data Resource collections, PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics datasets, public CRISPR or RNAi screens, AlphaFold/PDB-derived structural features, and curated pathway or protein-interaction resources. The core analytic strategy would be foundation-model representation learning: harmonizing measurements into a common representation; explicitly modeling uncertainty, batch effects, and missingness; and testing whether mesoscale variables explain cellular outcomes above and beyond molecular abundance alone. The biological scope would focus on cross-kingdom/cross-species while deliberately including comparison cases that prevent the group from mistaking a narrow model-system pattern for a general law.

The novel element is the unit of explanation. Instead of treating mesoscale organization as an image label, downstream readout, or anecdotal mechanism, the working group would make it the primary object of synthesis: a measurable layer where composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion combine. The expected product is a open knowledge graph that is open, versioned, and reusable, with transparent workflows, community-agreed metadata standards, and tutorials for trainees. The project would bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, imaging scientists, omics researchers, statisticians, machine-learning researchers, data curators, and trainees across institution types. Training would occur through hackathon-style data sprints, reproducible workflow clinics, and rotating trainee leadership of cross-dataset validation tasks. The anticipated contribution is both scientific and infrastructural: a defensible answer to a specific emergence question, plus a generalizable synthesis strategy that helps the molecular and cellular biosciences reuse public data to discover phenomena that only become visible when datasets, disciplines, and scales are brought together.
background_and_significance:
Cells are not well-mixed bags of molecules; they are spatially and temporally organized systems in which organelles, condensates, cytoskeletal structures, and membrane contact sites interact to allocate resources, buffer fluctuations, and coordinate signaling. Many cellular phenotypes—stress resilience, growth rate, fate commitment, proteostasis, and metabolic flexibility—depend on how these compartments cooperate (e.g., handoffs of lipids, ions, and proteins) or compete (e.g., for ribosomes, ATP, membrane area, chaperones, or trafficking capacity). Yet most molecular and cellular datasets are analyzed as if the relevant explanatory units are genes, proteins, or pathways. This reductionist framing often succeeds in identifying components but struggles to explain emergence: why similar molecular inventories can yield different cellular states, why perturbations have context-dependent outcomes, and how higher-order organization modulates function.

The mesoscale—between individual biomolecules and whole organelles—is where composition, geometry, dynamics, and physical constraints combine. At this scale, “ecological” interactions among compartments become visible: competition for shared pools (e.g., translation machinery), mutualism via metabolite exchange, parasitism-like sequestration (e.g., aggregates recruiting chaperones), and facilitation through scaffolding or co-localization. A mesoscale ecology perspective predicts that cellular outcomes depend not only on abundance but on how compartments partition, exchange, and regulate resources over time. However, mesoscale organization is difficult to capture comprehensively in any single experiment. Evidence is distributed across imaging repositories (subcellular localization, morphology), omics (proteome, transcriptome, metabolome), perturbation screens (CRISPR/RNAi, chemical), structural annotations (domains, disorder, multimerization), and curated interaction/pathway databases. These resources are large, heterogeneous, and often incompatible in metadata and identifiers.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that integrates these public data to address a fundamental emergence question: do there exist general, measurable rules linking molecular composition to mesoscale organization and, in turn, to cellular phenotype? The project is beyond a single lab because it requires (i) cross-repository data engineering and harmonization; (ii) domain expertise spanning cell biology, biophysics, and comparative biology; (iii) advanced statistical and machine-learning methods to represent uncertainty, missingness, and batch effects; and (iv) community governance to produce reusable standards and open infrastructure.

Recent advances make this timely. Public cell atlases and protein localization resources provide broad coverage of compartment membership and spatial patterns across cell types. Large-scale perturbation datasets connect genetic and chemical interventions to phenotypes such as viability, morphology, and transcriptional state. Foundation models for images, sequences, and multimodal data offer a principled way to embed heterogeneous measurements into shared latent spaces while preserving uncertainty. Meanwhile, knowledge graph technology enables integration of structured databases and text-mined literature into machine-queryable networks.

By treating mesoscale organization as the primary object of explanation—rather than an annotation or afterthought—this working group will create a synthetic, comparative, and testable framework for “cellular mesoscale ecology.” The significance is twofold: scientifically, it aims to reveal emergent principles governing compartmental cooperation and competition; infrastructurally, it will deliver open, reusable representations, metadata crosswalks, and workflows that enable the broader community to ask new emergence questions using existing data. This aligns directly with NCEMS goals to catalyze multidisciplinary teams, leverage AI/data science, and train a data-savvy workforce while adhering to open and reproducible science practices.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Overall objective: infer generalizable rules by which interactions among cellular compartments at the mesoscale (cooperation, competition, buffering, and handoff) emerge from molecular properties and predict cellular outcomes across diverse organisms and contexts using only publicly available data.

RQ1: Can mesoscale variables derived from integrated public data explain cellular phenotypes beyond molecular abundance?
Hypothesis 1A: Multimodal mesoscale representations (combining localization, morphology, interaction topology, and predicted biophysical features) will improve prediction of cellular outcomes (e.g., growth, stress survival, morphology classes, transcriptional states) compared with models using only gene/protein abundance.
Hypothesis 1B: The added explanatory power will be strongest in contexts where spatial organization is known to matter (e.g., ER–mitochondria contact regulation, autophagy/lysosome flux, proteostasis stress), indicating that mesoscale organization is a distinct causal layer.

RQ2: What are the dominant “ecological interaction motifs” among compartments, and are they conserved across species and cell types?
Hypothesis 2A: A small set of recurrent motifs—resource competition, mutualistic exchange, sequestration/decoy, and buffering—will be detectable as statistically enriched patterns linking (i) compartment co-variation across perturbations and conditions, (ii) contact/co-localization signatures in imaging, and (iii) shared dependency on limiting factors inferred from genetic interaction and essentiality data.
Hypothesis 2B: Motif prevalence will show partial conservation across eukaryotes, with motif-specific adaptations (e.g., plant vacuole-mediated buffering; fungal vacuole–mitochondria crosstalk), supporting a “conserved grammar” with lineage-specific parameters.

RQ3: Which molecular features predispose proteins and pathways to mediate compartment cooperation vs competition?
Hypothesis 3A: Proteins enriched at interfaces (contact sites, condensate boundaries, trafficking hubs) will share biophysical signatures—intrinsic disorder, multivalency, specific domain architectures, and membrane-binding motifs—capturable from AlphaFold/PDB-derived features and curated annotations.
Hypothesis 3B: Interface mediators will occupy characteristic network positions (high betweenness in interaction graphs; bridging communities in knowledge graphs) and will be disproportionately represented among context-dependent genetic dependencies.

RQ4: Can we identify “mesoscale tipping points” where small compositional changes trigger qualitative reorganization?
Hypothesis 4A: Across perturbation datasets, there exist thresholds where incremental changes in key regulators (e.g., lipid synthesis enzymes, chaperone capacity, trafficking adaptors) correlate with abrupt shifts in mesoscale embeddings (morphological state transitions, relocalization events) and downstream phenotypes.
Hypothesis 4B: These tipping points will be predictable from latent variables that capture competition for shared resources (e.g., translation capacity, membrane flux), providing a quantitative handle on emergence.

RQ5: How robust are inferred rules to dataset heterogeneity, and what uncertainty is irreducible?
Hypothesis 5A: Explicit modeling of batch effects, missingness mechanisms, and label uncertainty will yield stable rules that replicate across independent repositories and labs.
Hypothesis 5B: Remaining uncertainty will concentrate in poorly annotated compartments and rare states, motivating community metadata standards and targeted re-annotation (not new experiments) as a practical path to improved synthesis.

These questions are intentionally cross-disciplinary and require NCEMS-style collaboration: cell biologists define interpretable mesoscale constructs; imaging experts curate and validate spatial features; omics and perturbation experts map phenotypes and contexts; ML/statistics experts develop multimodal representation learning with uncertainty; and data curators ensure harmonized identifiers and provenance. Together, the hypotheses operationalize “mesoscale ecology” as a testable emergent layer linking molecules to cellular outcomes.
methods_and_approach:
Working group structure and phases (24 months; synthesis-only). The project will be executed through three in-person NCEMS meetings (kickoff, mid-project integration, capstone) plus monthly virtual collaboration, with trainee-led data sprints between meetings.

Phase 1: Data inventory, selection, and harmonization. We will compile a registry of candidate public datasets spanning (i) imaging-based localization/morphology (Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas; BioImage Archive; Image Data Resource; selected Cell Painting collections), (ii) transcriptomics/proteomics (NCBI GEO/SRA, ArrayExpress, PRIDE/MassIVE), (iii) perturbations and phenotypes (public CRISPR/RNAi screens; morphological profiling; viability; stress assays; single-cell perturbation atlases when publicly available), (iv) structural/biophysical features (AlphaFold-derived disorder, surface properties; PDB where available), and (v) curated interactions/pathways (STRING, BioGRID, Reactome, GO, Complex Portal). Inclusion criteria: public access; reusable licensing; sufficient metadata for mapping (cell type/line, species, condition, perturbation); and links to phenotypes or states.

We will implement identifier crosswalks (gene/protein, cell line, compartment ontology) using established resources (e.g., UniProt, Ensembl, Cellosaurus, GO cellular component) and produce a provenance-aware data model. A key deliverable is a “mesoscale metadata schema” describing compartments, contact sites, condensates, and morphological states with controlled vocabularies.

Phase 2: Knowledge graph construction and literature synthesis. We will build an open, versioned knowledge graph (KG) connecting entities (proteins, complexes, compartments, contact sites, perturbations, phenotypes, species) with typed edges (localizes_to, interacts_with, affects, co-varies_with, part_of, at_contact_with). Edges will come from curated databases plus text-mined assertions from open-access literature, with confidence scores and provenance. The KG will enable queryable hypotheses (e.g., “proteins bridging mitochondria and ER that are essential under oxidative stress”).

Phase 3: Multimodal representation learning for mesoscale organization. We will learn shared latent representations that integrate modalities:
- Imaging embeddings: use publicly available pretrained vision foundation models (or self-supervised training on public images when permissible) to embed subcellular patterns; map to compartments and morphological states.
- Omics embeddings: reduce transcript/protein profiles with models that preserve pathway structure (e.g., graph-regularized latent factor models).
- Structural/biophysical embeddings: encode disorder, multivalency proxies, membrane association, and predicted interaction interfaces.
- KG embeddings: learn graph representations capturing network context.

These embeddings will be fused via probabilistic multimodal models that explicitly represent missingness and batch effects (hierarchical Bayesian models; domain-adversarial alignment; uncertainty-aware variational approaches). We will perform rigorous validation through (i) held-out dataset prediction, (ii) cross-lab replication where multiple datasets measure similar contexts, and (iii) negative controls (randomized mappings; species-shuffled baselines).

Phase 4: Testing hypotheses and extracting “ecological motifs.” We will operationalize cooperation/competition motifs as patterns across perturbations: e.g., competition inferred when two compartments show anti-correlated resource markers and opposing fitness effects; cooperation inferred when perturbations that disrupt one compartment induce compensatory changes in another and shared phenotype directionality. We will use causal-inference-inspired strategies feasible with observational/perturbation public data: difference-in-differences across conditions, instrumental-variable proxies (e.g., perturbations targeting compartment-specific machinery), and mediation analysis to test whether mesoscale embeddings mediate molecular-to-phenotype links.

Phase 5: Cross-species comparative synthesis. Using orthology mappings, we will test conservation of motifs and tipping points across representative taxa (e.g., yeast, human, plant where data allow). Comparisons will be designed to avoid overfitting to a single model system by requiring replication in at least two independent species or cell-type contexts.

Throughout, trainees will lead reproducible “validation notebooks” for specific claims (one claim per notebook), ensuring each conclusion is backed by executable code, data provenance, and uncertainty estimates.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific outcomes. (1) A quantitative, testable framework for “mesoscale ecology” that links molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcomes. The project will deliver evidence for (or against) the central claim that mesoscale variables explain phenotypes beyond abundance, including effect sizes, uncertainty, and contexts where the claim fails. (2) A catalog of recurrent compartment interaction motifs (cooperation, competition, buffering, sequestration) with operational definitions and cross-dataset support. (3) Identification of candidate “interface mediators”—proteins and complexes that bridge compartments—characterized by shared biophysical and network signatures, and prioritized lists of contexts where they are most predictive of phenotype. (4) Detection of candidate mesoscale tipping points and state transitions, with quantitative thresholds and conditions, providing a new lens on emergent cellular behavior.

Methodological outcomes. (1) A generalizable multimodal synthesis pipeline for integrating imaging, omics, perturbation, structural, and knowledge-graph data with explicit treatment of batch effects and missingness. (2) Benchmark tasks and evaluation metrics for mesoscale emergence (e.g., “predict phenotype improvement from mesoscale embedding,” “motif conservation score across species”). These will be packaged so other groups can extend the approach to additional compartments or phenotypes.

Community and infrastructure outcomes. (1) An open, versioned mesoscale knowledge graph with documented schema, provenance, and confidence scoring; (2) metadata crosswalks and controlled vocabularies for compartments/contact sites/morphological states; and (3) curated training materials enabling reuse by the broader molecular and cellular community.

Impact. By making mesoscale organization a first-class, measurable explanatory layer, the project will shift synthesis efforts from component lists to system-level rules. The outputs will help researchers interpret heterogeneous perturbation results, generate mechanistic hypotheses grounded in cross-dataset evidence, and identify general principles of cellular organization relevant to disease (e.g., proteostasis collapse, organelle stress crosstalk) and biotechnology (e.g., engineering compartmentalized metabolism). The project directly advances NCEMS goals by delivering a community-scale synthesis that no single lab can accomplish, while producing reusable open infrastructure and training a cohort of data-savvy scientists.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-by-default products. All code, derived data products, and documentation will be released under permissive open licenses (e.g., MIT/BSD for code; CC-BY/CC0 where allowable for derived metadata), with clear attribution and compliance with upstream dataset licenses. The working group will not redistribute controlled-access raw data; instead, we will provide reproducible “data access recipes” and pointers to original repositories.

Reproducible workflows. Analyses will be implemented as containerized, versioned workflows (Docker/Singularity) orchestrated with a workflow manager (e.g., Snakemake/Nextflow) and executed in continuous integration (CI) to ensure that figures and tables rebuild from pinned inputs. We will use environment locking (conda-lock/uv) and semantic versioning for releases. Each major claim will be accompanied by an executable notebook and a machine-readable manifest listing input datasets, checksums (when available), preprocessing steps, and parameter settings.

Provenance and uncertainty. The knowledge graph will store provenance at the edge level (source, date accessed, evidence code, confidence). For learned embeddings and motif calls, we will publish uncertainty estimates (posterior intervals, bootstrap distributions, calibration curves) and sensitivity analyses to batch correction choices, missingness assumptions, and alternative mappings.

FAIR principles and community standards. We will align compartment and phenotype annotations with established ontologies (GO cellular component, UBERON where relevant, Cellosaurus for cell lines) and will propose extensions for mesoscale constructs (contact sites, condensate classes, morphological states) when gaps exist. Outputs will include schema documentation, example queries, and validation suites.

Collaborative governance. The group will adopt an authorship and contribution policy (CRediT taxonomy), a code-of-conduct, and an issue-tracking process for decisions. Trainees will be included as first-class contributors, with rotating responsibility for release management and documentation.

Training as reproducibility. Training events (workflow clinics, data sprints) will culminate in merged pull requests and tagged releases, ensuring that learning translates into durable, reusable artifacts. All tutorials will be recorded or written as step-by-step guides and deposited in a public repository with DOI-based archiving (e.g., Zenodo).
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support is essential because the project requires sustained, structured, multi-institution collaboration; access to synthesis expertise and facilitation; and shared compute/data infrastructure for harmonizing large public datasets. A single lab typically lacks the breadth to curate multi-repository imaging and omics data, the methodological depth to build uncertainty-aware multimodal models, and the convening power to align community metadata practices.

Budget categories (illustrative, aligned to a working-group model; exact amounts to follow NCEMS guidelines):
1) Working group meetings and collaboration logistics: travel, lodging, and per diem for three in-person NCEMS meetings; accessibility support; and virtual collaboration tooling. Priority will be given to enabling participation across geography, institution types (R1, PUIs), and career stages.
2) Personnel support (time-limited, synthesis-focused): partial support for a project coordinator/data curator to manage dataset registry, identifier mapping, provenance tracking, and KG releases; and partial support for a research software engineer to maintain containers, CI, and workflow automation. These roles are critical to ensure the synthesis outputs are robust and reusable.
3) Trainee support and training: travel funds for graduate students and postdocs; stipends for trainee-led hackathon sprints; and small sub-awards for trainees at under-resourced institutions to ensure equitable participation.
4) Computing and storage: cloud credits or shared HPC allocations for embedding generation, KG construction, and cross-validation experiments; storage for intermediate derived products; and costs for long-term archiving of releases (e.g., Zenodo) and hosting documentation.
5) Community engagement: funds for an open virtual symposium and a documentation sprint with external stakeholders (repository maintainers, ontology developers) to review the mesoscale schema and KG usability.

Resource plan. NCEMS will provide convening space, facilitation, and synthesis expertise; participating labs contribute domain knowledge, existing pipelines, and mentoring capacity. Deliverables will be scheduled as quarterly releases (KG versions, benchmark tasks, tutorial modules), ensuring steady progress and accountability within the funding period.

background_and_significance:
Cells adapt to stress not only by changing gene expression, but by reorganizing molecules into mesoscale assemblies that alter reaction environments, information flow, and resource allocation. In plants and other nontraditional eukaryotes, a diverse set of stress-induced bodies—including stress granule–like assemblies, processing-body–like foci, heat-shock–associated condensates, and RNA/protein granules with species-specific components—appear rapidly, reversibly, and in cell-type-specific ways. These structures sit squarely at the NCEMS mesoscale: larger than individual macromolecules yet smaller than organelles, and capable of shaping cellular outcomes such as translational repression, mRNA storage/decay, proteostasis, signaling, and survival.

Despite intense interest in biomolecular condensates, plant stress bodies remain underused as models for emergence. The literature is fragmented across specialized subfields (plant stress physiology, RNA biology, imaging, biophysics), and evidence is scattered across publicly available but poorly interoperable data types: microscopy images with heterogeneous annotations; bulk, single-cell, and spatial transcriptomes; proteomics and phosphoproteomics; perturbation screens; interaction networks; and structural predictions. Consequently, most studies treat bodies as qualitative markers (“granules present/absent”) or focus on a few canonical components, limiting discovery of general rules. Yet emergence questions demand synthesis: How do many weakly interacting molecular parts collectively produce new mesoscale behaviors, and when do those behaviors causally improve cellular performance?

Plants are uniquely informative for mesoscale adaptation. They experience fluctuating environmental stress (heat, drought, salinity, oxidative stress, pathogens) without the option of movement, and they have evolved lineage-specific RNA-binding proteins, intrinsically disordered regions, and signaling modules that may tune assembly thresholds and material properties. Their cells also exhibit distinctive subcellular architecture (large vacuoles, cell walls, plastids) and strong spatial constraints that can influence mesoscale organization. These features create natural variation for inference: across species, tissues, and stresses, plants provide repeated “experiments” in how cells deploy mesoscale bodies.

NCEMS’s synthesis-centered model is essential because the key signal is distributed. No single lab can (i) locate and curate sufficiently diverse imaging and omics datasets, (ii) harmonize metadata to enable comparisons across species and platforms, (iii) build robust models that separate mesoscale effects from molecular abundance and batch artifacts, and (iv) validate generality with phylogenetic and cross-system comparisons. A working group can assemble complementary expertise: plant cell biology to define plausible mechanisms and phenotypes; imaging science to extract quantitative mesoscale features; data curation to standardize metadata; statistics and machine learning to model uncertainty and missingness; and biophysics to interpret emergent organization.

The significance is twofold. Scientifically, the project will test whether stress bodies constitute a predictive mesoscale layer that explains adaptation beyond transcript/protein levels alone, addressing a fundamental emergence problem: when does organization become a new explanatory variable? Methodologically, it will deliver interoperable representations and workflows that make mesoscale synthesis feasible, enabling broader reuse of public data. By centering plants and nontraditional eukaryotes while including comparison cases, the project will avoid overgeneralizing from a narrow model system and instead identify principles that are robust across evolutionary distance and cellular contexts.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will address a central emergence question: can plant stress bodies be treated as a measurable mesoscale state variable that links molecular composition to cellular outcomes, and can rules governing that state be inferred from synthesis of public datasets? We focus on questions where integration across imaging, omics, perturbations, and phylogeny is essential, and where answers cannot be obtained by any single dataset or laboratory.

RQ1: What are the conserved and lineage-specific “assembly programs” of plant stress bodies across stresses, cell types, and species?
H1.1: Across datasets, stress bodies exhibit a limited number of recurrent mesoscale phenotypes (e.g., size distributions, number per cell, subcellular localization patterns, dynamics proxies) that form discrete or low-dimensional manifolds rather than a continuum of idiosyncratic patterns.
H1.2: Conserved phenotypes correspond to conserved compositional modules enriched for RNA-binding proteins, chaperones, and post-translational modification machinery, while lineage-specific phenotypes are associated with expansions in intrinsically disordered proteins and plant-specific signaling components.

RQ2: Do mesoscale features explain cellular outcomes beyond molecular abundance alone?
H2.1: Models that include mesoscale variables derived from images (or inferred from multi-omic signatures) predict downstream outcomes—stress tolerance proxies, growth recovery, translational capacity, or cell viability—better than models using transcript/protein abundance alone, after controlling for batch effects, stress intensity, and cell type.
H2.2: The added predictive value of mesoscale variables is greatest under acute stress transitions (onset and recovery), consistent with bodies acting as rapid-response organizational states.

RQ3: What molecular and structural features bias proteins/RNAs toward participation in stress bodies, and are these rules transferable across species?
H3.1: Participation likelihood is predicted by a combination of intrinsic disorder, low-complexity regions, multivalency (interaction degree), RNA-binding domains, and phosphorylation sites; these features generalize across plant species with appropriate phylogenetic correction.
H3.2: Transfer learning from well-annotated non-plant systems (e.g., yeast/mammalian stress granules) improves prediction in plants only when models incorporate plant-specific sequence features and interaction contexts, revealing both universal and lineage-specific design principles.

RQ4: Are there detectable causal signatures of stress-body regulation in perturbation data?
H4.1: Public perturbation datasets (genetic knockouts/knockdowns, overexpression, chemical treatments) show consistent directional effects: perturbations that reduce assembly propensity (e.g., disrupting multivalency or chaperone support) associate with poorer stress recovery, whereas perturbations that tune assembly timing or dissolution correlate with improved outcomes.
H4.2: The relationship is non-monotonic: excessive persistence or hyper-assembly predicts maladaptation, implying an optimal mesoscale regime.

RQ5: Can we build a cross-dataset, cross-species “mesoscale adaptation atlas” that yields falsifiable predictions?
H5.1: A harmonized atlas will identify candidate regulators and conditions where stress bodies shift state; predictions (e.g., which proteins are likely scaffolds, which stresses induce which phenotypes) will be testable by the community using existing or future experiments, even though this project itself generates no new experimental data.

Together these questions operationalize emergence: they treat mesoscale organization as a primary explanatory layer, quantify its contribution, and seek transferable rules linking molecular parts to system-level behavior.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. The project is a community-scale synthesis effort using only publicly available data. We will organize work into four integrated tracks executed through NCEMS-facilitated meetings, virtual sprints, and shared infrastructure: (A) data discovery/curation, (B) mesoscale feature extraction, (C) integrative modeling and phylogenetic synthesis, and (D) atlas construction, validation, and dissemination. Each track will be co-led by investigators from different labs to ensure cross-disciplinary integration.

A) Data discovery, inclusion criteria, and harmonization. We will compile datasets spanning: (i) imaging repositories (BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, institutional repositories) with plant stress conditions; (ii) bulk/single-cell/spatial transcriptomics from GEO/ArrayExpress/ENA and plant atlases; (iii) proteomics/phosphoproteomics from PRIDE/MassIVE; (iv) perturbation resources (public mutant collections metadata, CRISPR/RNAi screens where available, chemical perturbation studies); (v) interaction/pathway databases (STRING, BioGRID where available, Reactome/KEGG/GO); and (vi) structural annotations (AlphaFold-derived disorder and domain features; PDB when present). Inclusion will prioritize reusable metadata: species, tissue/cell type, stressor, time point, imaging modality, and outcome proxy.

We will create a unified metadata schema (“StressBody-MESO”) with controlled vocabularies for stress type, developmental stage, and imaging/omics descriptors. Harmonization will use ontology mappings (GO, Plant Ontology, Environment Ontology) and record provenance. Missing metadata will be flagged and handled explicitly rather than imputed silently.

B) Mesoscale feature extraction from images and proxies from omics. For imaging, we will develop reproducible pipelines (containerized) for segmentation and quantification: number of bodies per cell, size/shape distributions, intensity/texture features, colocalization with markers when available, and spatial statistics (e.g., distance to nucleus, ER, plastids if labeled). Where raw images are unavailable, we will extract features from published segmentations or derived tables.

For datasets lacking imaging, we will infer “mesoscale state” proxies using multi-omic signatures: co-expression modules of known granule-associated genes, enrichment of RNA-binding/disorder features among upregulated proteins, and stress-response regulons. We will calibrate these proxies against imaging-derived states in overlapping datasets.

C) Integrative modeling, uncertainty, and comparative phylogenetic synthesis. We will use hierarchical Bayesian and mixed-effects models to quantify how mesoscale variables relate to outcomes while accounting for batch, platform, lab-of-origin, and species. Missingness will be modeled (e.g., selection models or multiple imputation with sensitivity analyses) to avoid biased conclusions.

To identify conserved vs lineage-specific rules, we will apply phylogenetically informed regression and multilevel transfer learning: species-level random effects informed by phylogenetic distances, and domain adaptation methods to align feature spaces across species and platforms. We will test incremental predictive value via nested model comparisons and out-of-distribution validation (train on some species/stresses, test on others).

D) Atlas construction and validation. Outputs will be assembled into a versioned “Plant Stress Body Mesoscale Atlas” with: (i) standardized dataset descriptors, (ii) derived mesoscale feature tables, (iii) cross-species embeddings/manifolds of stress-body phenotypes, and (iv) predictive models with documented performance. Validation will emphasize cross-dataset replication, leave-one-study-out tests, and negative controls (e.g., random gene sets, shuffled labels, non-stress conditions).

Training and coordination. Trainees will lead sprint tasks: dataset onboarding, pipeline testing, and replication analyses. NCEMS resources (compute, convening, facilitation, and data-science support) are required to coordinate multi-lab curation, run scalable workflows, and maintain shared infrastructure beyond a single lab’s capacity.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific outcomes. (1) A quantitative, cross-species typology of plant stress-body mesoscale phenotypes, identifying recurrent organizational states across stresses and cell types. (2) Evidence-based tests of whether mesoscale organization provides explanatory and predictive power for cellular outcomes beyond molecular abundance, clarifying when “organization becomes information.” (3) A set of conserved and lineage-specific design rules linking molecular/structural features (disorder, domains, interaction degree, phosphorylation propensity) to stress-body participation and dynamics proxies. (4) A ranked list of candidate regulators and conditions predicted to tune assembly/dissolution into adaptive vs maladaptive regimes, generating falsifiable hypotheses for the broader community.

Methodological outcomes. (1) A reusable metadata standard (StressBody-MESO) and crosswalks to existing ontologies, enabling interoperability between imaging and omics for mesoscale studies. (2) Containerized, documented pipelines for image-derived mesoscale feature extraction and for omics-based mesoscale-state inference, designed to run on shared NCEMS compute and portable to other environments. (3) A generalizable comparative synthesis framework that integrates heterogeneous datasets with explicit uncertainty modeling, phylogenetic structure, and robust cross-study validation.

Community and workforce outcomes. The working group will build a durable cross-disciplinary network connecting plant cell biology, imaging, biophysics, and data science. Trainees will gain hands-on experience in open, reproducible synthesis science, including data curation, workflow engineering, and statistical modeling.

Impact. By elevating plant stress bodies to first-class mesoscale variables, the project advances NCEMS’s mission to explain emergent properties at the mesoscale and their influence on cellular outcomes. The atlas and workflows will lower barriers for researchers to reuse public data, accelerating discovery in plant stress biology and offering transferable strategies for other mesoscale assemblies (e.g., centrosome satellites, ER subdomains, RNA granules) across eukaryotes. The project will also broaden the emergence canon beyond traditional model systems, increasing the diversity of biological contexts used to infer general principles.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open products by default. All derived data products, code, and documentation will be released publicly under permissive licenses (e.g., CC-BY for documentation; MIT/BSD for code), consistent with repository terms of use and respecting any restrictions on redistribution of raw data. We will not generate new experimental data; we will maximize reuse and transparency of existing public datasets.

Reproducible workflows. Analyses will be implemented as version-controlled, containerized workflows (Docker/Singularity) orchestrated with reproducible tooling (e.g., Snakemake/Nextflow) and executed with pinned software versions. Each dataset ingestion will produce a machine-readable provenance record: source accession, retrieval date, checksum, preprocessing steps, and mapping decisions to the StressBody-MESO schema. Continuous integration will run unit tests on key functions and smoke tests on representative datasets.

FAIR and interoperable metadata. We will publish the StressBody-MESO schema, controlled vocabularies, and ontology mappings, and provide templates for dataset submitters. Derived feature tables will include explicit uncertainty estimates where applicable (e.g., segmentation confidence, model posterior intervals) and clear definitions of each feature.

Transparent modeling and validation. We will preregister core evaluation metrics and validation strategies within the working group (e.g., leave-one-study-out, out-of-distribution tests) and report negative results and sensitivity analyses (batch correction choices, missingness assumptions). Model cards will document intended use, limitations, and failure modes.

Open collaboration practices. The working group will adopt community-created policies for open, team, and reproducible science: shared governance for contributions, code review norms, contributor credit via CRediT taxonomy, and a public issue tracker for requests and bug reports.

Training materials. We will release tutorials and lesson-style notebooks that walk trainees and community users through: dataset onboarding, image feature extraction, omics harmonization, phylogenetic modeling, and atlas querying. All training content will be accessible and designed for reuse in courses and workshops.
budget_and_resources:
Budget rationale aligned with NCEMS working-group support. This project requires NCEMS resources because it is beyond a single lab’s capacity: it demands coordinated multi-lab curation across repositories, scalable compute for image/omics processing, and structured convening to align standards and integrate methods. The budget emphasizes personnel time for synthesis, trainee training, and shared infrastructure rather than new data generation.

Primary cost categories (illustrative, adaptable to NCEMS guidelines):
1) Convening and collaboration (meetings, hybrid participation, facilitation). Support 2–3 in-person working meetings at NCEMS plus regular virtual sprints. Funds cover travel for a geographically diverse team (including participants from PUIs/MSIs), lodging, and accessibility needs. Structured facilitation ensures progress across disciplines and equitable participation.
2) Trainee support and training activities. Provide stipends/salary support for graduate students and postdocs to lead curation and validation tasks, plus support for hackathon-style sprints and workflow clinics. Allocate funds for trainee-led mini-projects (e.g., benchmarking segmentation methods, ontology mapping) and for professional development in reproducible research.
3) Data engineering and research software support. Partial support for a research software engineer/data curator (or buy-in from multiple labs) to implement the StressBody-MESO schema, maintain ingestion pipelines, manage provenance, and ensure robust releases.
4) Compute and storage. Use NCEMS-provided compute where possible; budget for cloud credits or supplemental storage for processing large imaging datasets and hosting derived feature tables and atlas artifacts. Emphasize efficient caching and avoidance of duplicating raw repositories.
5) Dissemination and community engagement. Support for maintaining a public atlas website/repository, documentation, and a capstone webinar/workshop to transfer methods to the community.

In-kind and leveraged resources. Participating labs contribute domain expertise, existing code, and mentoring. NCEMS provides convening infrastructure, collaborative platforms, and guidance on open science policies. No funds are requested for wet-lab experiments or new data collection; all work is synthesis and integration of public data.
