title: Public-data reconstruction of intracellular phase diagrams
abstract:
This working group asks how public-data reconstruction of intracellular phase diagrams can be understood as an emergent property that links molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcome. The scientific question is not simply whether particular molecules, organelles, or pathways are associated with a phenotype, but whether publicly available datasets can reveal rules by which many molecular parts collectively produce a new, system-level behavior at the scale between biomolecules and organelles. The project is designed for the NCEMS model because the relevant evidence is scattered across incompatible imaging repositories, omics studies, perturbation resources, structural annotations, and specialized literatures; no single laboratory is likely to have the biological breadth, data-engineering capacity, and methodological expertise to integrate them.

The group would synthesize existing public data centered on perturbation/genetic screens, prioritizing datasets with reusable metadata, perturbation or state annotations, and links to downstream cellular phenotypes. Depending on availability, sources could include public cell atlases, the Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, EMBL-EBI and NCBI functional genomics repositories, BioImage Archive or Image Data Resource collections, PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics datasets, public CRISPR or RNAi screens, AlphaFold/PDB-derived structural features, and curated pathway or protein-interaction resources. The core analytic strategy would be mechanistic simulation/data assimilation: harmonizing measurements into a common representation; explicitly modeling uncertainty, batch effects, and missingness; and testing whether mesoscale variables explain cellular outcomes above and beyond molecular abundance alone. The biological scope would focus on cross-kingdom/cross-species while deliberately including comparison cases that prevent the group from mistaking a narrow model-system pattern for a general law.

The novel element is the unit of explanation. Instead of treating mesoscale organization as an image label, downstream readout, or anecdotal mechanism, the working group would make it the primary object of synthesis: a measurable layer where composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion combine. The expected product is a reusable benchmark/workflow that is open, versioned, and reusable, with transparent workflows, community-agreed metadata standards, and tutorials for trainees. The project would bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, imaging scientists, omics researchers, statisticians, machine-learning researchers, data curators, and trainees across institution types. Training would occur through hackathon-style data sprints, reproducible workflow clinics, and rotating trainee leadership of cross-dataset validation tasks. The anticipated contribution is both scientific and infrastructural: a defensible answer to a specific emergence question, plus a generalizable synthesis strategy that helps the molecular and cellular biosciences reuse public data to discover phenomena that only become visible when datasets, disciplines, and scales are brought together.
background_and_significance:
Cells exhibit mesoscale organization—biomolecular condensates, membrane-less compartments, microdomains, and dynamic assemblies—that cannot be predicted by any single molecule’s properties yet strongly conditions gene expression, signaling, stress responses, and fate decisions. A central challenge in molecular and cellular biosciences is to connect molecular composition (proteins, RNAs, metabolites, lipids) to emergent mesoscale states and then to cellular outcomes. “Intracellular phase diagrams” offer a rigorous conceptual bridge: they describe how collective variables (concentration, stoichiometry, interaction valency, post-translational modification, ionic strength, crowding, temperature, and activity) determine whether a system is mixed, demixed, gel-like, or forms multiple coexisting phases. While phase diagrams are routine in soft matter physics, they are rarely reconstructed for living cells because the necessary measurements are distributed across experiments, platforms, and organisms.

At the same time, the public data landscape has changed. Imaging repositories (e.g., BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource), cell atlases (e.g., Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas), functional genomics archives (NCBI GEO/SRA, EMBL-EBI ArrayExpress), proteomics resources (PRIDE, MassIVE), perturbation compendia (CRISPR/RNAi screens), and structural annotations (PDB, AlphaFold-derived features) collectively contain millions of observations relevant to mesoscale organization. Yet these resources remain siloed: imaging readouts are rarely linked to matched omics; perturbation screens often lack standardized phenotype ontologies; and structural/biophysical annotations are not routinely integrated with cellular localization and morphology. The result is a long-standing puzzle: we can name many condensate-associated proteins and pathways, but we lack generalizable rules that predict when and how cells transition between mesoscale states and how those transitions shape phenotype.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that treats mesoscale organization as the primary object of explanation rather than an anecdotal mechanism. This project aligns with the NCEMS emphasis on emergence at the mesoscale and on leveraging AI and data science to integrate publicly available data. The work is inherently beyond a single lab: it requires (i) cross-repository data engineering and metadata normalization; (ii) biophysical theory to define interpretable “phase variables”; (iii) statistical and machine-learning methods that handle missingness, batch effects, and uncertainty; (iv) biological expertise spanning multiple taxa and cell types to avoid overfitting to model-system idiosyncrasies; and (v) community governance to ensure outputs are reusable.

The significance is twofold. Scientifically, reconstructing intracellular phase diagrams from public data would enable predictive, mechanistic statements such as: which combinations of abundance, interaction propensity, and cellular state variables are sufficient to trigger condensate formation; which perturbations move cells across phase boundaries; and which mesoscale states causally explain phenotypes beyond molecular abundance alone. Methodologically, the project will establish a general synthesis framework—mechanistic simulation coupled with data assimilation—that can be reused for other emergent mesoscale phenomena (e.g., cytoskeletal patterning, organelle contact sites, chromatin domains). By integrating disparate public datasets into a coherent, uncertainty-aware model, the working group will transform existing data into a community resource that advances fundamental understanding of emergence in molecular and cellular systems and trains a data-savvy workforce in reproducible synthesis science.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group addresses the overarching emergence question: can intracellular phase behavior—an emergent mesoscale property—be reconstructed as a quantitative, predictive “phase diagram” using only publicly available molecular, structural, perturbational, and imaging data, and does that reconstruction explain cellular outcomes better than molecule-centric models?

RQ1: Can we define a cross-dataset, cross-species latent representation of mesoscale “phase state” that is measurable from heterogeneous public readouts?
Hypothesis 1A: Diverse imaging phenotypes (puncta number/size, texture, colocalization, compartment morphology) and non-imaging proxies (fraction insoluble, sedimentation profiles, proximity labeling enrichments, stress granule marker expression) share a low-dimensional latent structure corresponding to canonical mesoscale states (mixed, demixed-liquid, gel/solid-like, multiphase).
Hypothesis 1B: This latent “phase state” is conserved in its geometry across taxa (e.g., yeast, fly, human) even if the specific molecules differ, enabling cross-kingdom transfer learning with appropriate covariates.

RQ2: Which molecular and structural features best predict movement across intracellular phase boundaries under perturbation?
Hypothesis 2A: Sequence- and structure-derived interaction propensities (intrinsic disorder, low-complexity content, multivalency motifs, predicted binding interfaces, charge patterning) combined with abundance/stoichiometry changes predict phase transitions better than abundance changes alone.
Hypothesis 2B: Perturbations that modify interaction strength (post-translational modification enzymes, chaperones, RNA metabolism factors, ionic homeostasis genes) produce larger shifts in inferred phase state than perturbations affecting only expression level, consistent with a “control parameter” view of phase behavior.

RQ3: Do mesoscale phase variables provide explanatory power for cellular outcomes beyond molecular composition?
Hypothesis 3A: In predictive models of downstream phenotypes (viability, stress resistance, differentiation markers, signaling outputs, organelle integrity), inclusion of inferred mesoscale phase variables yields significant out-of-sample improvements relative to models using omics and pathway annotations alone.
Hypothesis 3B: Mesoscale variables mediate the effect of perturbations on phenotype: causal mediation analyses will show that a substantial fraction of perturbation→phenotype associations are transmitted through changes in phase state rather than direct pathway effects.

RQ4: Are reconstructed phase diagrams robust to dataset heterogeneity, missingness, and batch effects, and can we quantify uncertainty in phase boundaries?
Hypothesis 4A: A hierarchical Bayesian/data-assimilation framework that explicitly models measurement noise, batch effects, and missingness will produce stable phase boundary estimates across repositories and experimental conditions.
Hypothesis 4B: Uncertainty will concentrate near inferred boundaries and in under-sampled regions of the control-parameter space, enabling principled prioritization of future community data generation (outside this project) and guiding interpretation of ambiguous phenotypes.

RQ5: Can we identify general “rules of mesoscale organization” that are not reducible to a single organelle or pathway?
Hypothesis 5A: Across systems, a small set of control parameters—effective valency, interaction anisotropy, crowding/activity proxies, and stoichiometric imbalance—will recurrently define separatrices between mesoscale regimes.
Hypothesis 5B: These rules will generalize across distinct condensate classes (stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli-associated assemblies) and across cell states, revealing emergence principles that only become visible through community-scale synthesis.

Together, these questions test whether intracellular phase diagrams can be reconstructed from public data as a rigorous, generalizable explanatory layer linking molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcomes.
methods_and_approach:
Working group structure and scope: The project will operate as an NCEMS-style synthesis working group with coordinated data engineering, modeling, and biological interpretation subteams across multiple institutions. All analyses will use only publicly available data. The biological scope will include multiple taxa (at minimum: yeast and human; optionally fly or plant) and multiple perturbation modalities (genetic perturbations, stress conditions, and chemical treatments where metadata allow).

1) Data discovery, inclusion criteria, and harmonization: We will curate a registry of candidate datasets emphasizing (i) explicit perturbation/state annotations, (ii) reusable metadata (cell type, condition, imaging modality, timepoint), and (iii) links to phenotypes. Sources include BioImage Archive/IDR imaging collections; Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas; GEO/SRA/ArrayExpress transcriptomics; PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics; DepMap/other public CRISPR screens; and curated interaction/pathway databases (STRING, BioGRID, Reactome). Inclusion will require permissive reuse licenses and sufficient metadata to map to controlled vocabularies (Cell Ontology, UBERON where relevant, Gene Ontology, OBI, and phenotype ontologies). We will implement ETL pipelines that (a) map identifiers, (b) standardize units and normalization, (c) encode perturbations (target, direction, dose/time), and (d) capture provenance.

2) Feature extraction for mesoscale organization: For imaging data, we will compute standardized morphological and texture features using reproducible pipelines (e.g., CellProfiler- or deep-embedding-based descriptors) without retraining on private data. Where segmentation labels exist, we will use them; otherwise we will apply publicly available pretrained models and report uncertainty. For non-imaging datasets, we will derive proxies of mesoscale state: solubility/partitioning measures (when available), co-fractionation profiles, proximity labeling enrichments, and co-localization scores from atlas annotations. Structural/biophysical features will be derived from AlphaFold/PDB annotations and sequence analysis (disorder, low complexity, charge/hydropathy patterning, motif counts, predicted multivalency).

3) Latent phase-state model and data assimilation: We will build a hierarchical model linking observed features to latent phase state Z and control parameters C. The model will include dataset-specific observation models to handle differing modalities and batch effects. Candidate approaches include: (i) Bayesian latent variable models with modality-specific likelihoods; (ii) multi-view representation learning with uncertainty estimation; and (iii) state-space/data-assimilation formulations for time-resolved datasets. Outputs will include posterior distributions over Z and estimated phase boundaries in C-space.

4) Reconstruction of intracellular phase diagrams: For each biological context (cell type/species/condition class), we will estimate phase diagrams as decision surfaces separating mesoscale regimes, with credible intervals. Control parameters will include molecular abundances/stoichiometries, interaction propensity summaries, and state variables (stress markers, energy proxies, crowding/activity surrogates). We will test robustness via leave-dataset-out validation and sensitivity analyses to missingness.

5) Linking phase state to cellular outcomes: We will integrate downstream phenotypes from screens and atlases (fitness/viability, stress tolerance, morphology, signaling readouts). Predictive evaluation will use strict train/test splits by dataset and by lab-of-origin. We will compare baseline models (omics-only, pathway-only) to models augmented with inferred phase variables. Mediation analyses and causal-graph sensitivity checks will assess whether Z provides explanatory power consistent with an emergent mesoscale mediator.

6) Cross-species generalization and falsification cases: We will intentionally include “hard negatives” (systems where condensates are not expected or where perturbations should not alter mesoscale state) to avoid confirmation bias. Transfer learning experiments will test whether phase-boundary structure is conserved while allowing species-specific parameterization.

7) Team-based implementation and trainee integration: Work will proceed through NCEMS-facilitated meetings, code sprints, and rotating trainee-led replication tasks. Each major claim (phase boundary, predictor importance, phenotype mediation) will require independent reproduction by a separate subteam using the shared workflow.

This approach is feasible because it leverages existing data at scale, uses uncertainty-aware modeling suited to heterogeneous public resources, and is explicitly designed for cross-lab synthesis beyond any single group’s capabilities.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific products: (1) Reconstructed intracellular phase diagrams for selected mesoscale phenomena (e.g., stress granule/P-body-like assemblies and nuclear bodies) across multiple species and cell contexts, with quantified uncertainty and explicit control parameters. (2) A validated latent “phase state” representation that integrates imaging and non-imaging evidence and can be used as a common currency for mesoscale organization. (3) Evidence-based rules identifying which molecular/structural features and perturbation classes most strongly move cells across inferred phase boundaries. (4) Demonstrations that mesoscale phase variables improve prediction and explanation of cellular outcomes beyond molecular abundance and pathway annotations alone, supporting emergence claims.

Methodological and infrastructural products: (1) A reusable, versioned benchmark dataset and evaluation suite (“public-data intracellular phase diagram benchmark”) that packages harmonized features, provenance, and phenotype links for community reuse. (2) Open-source workflows for ETL, feature extraction, and uncertainty-aware modeling, designed to be portable across repositories and organisms. (3) Community-facing metadata recommendations for linking perturbations, imaging phenotypes, and omics readouts to mesoscale constructs.

Impact on the field: The project will shift mesoscale organization from a qualitative narrative to a quantitative, testable layer of explanation. By making phase behavior reconstructable from existing public data, it will enable researchers to (i) reinterpret disparate screens through a unifying mesoscale lens, (ii) generate new mechanistic hypotheses about how cells regulate demixing/assembly, and (iii) identify conserved versus lineage-specific emergence principles. Because outputs are designed as benchmarks and workflows rather than a single bespoke analysis, the work will lower barriers for additional groups to extend the synthesis to new condensates, organelle contact phenomena, or developmental contexts.

Workforce and community impact: Trainees will gain experience in cross-disciplinary synthesis, reproducible computational biology, and collaborative science practices. The working group will also strengthen connections among data repositories, curators, and domain scientists, increasing the long-term utility of public molecular and cellular datasets and directly advancing NCEMS’s mission to catalyze AI-enabled, community-scale discovery of emergent mesoscale phenomena.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-by-default outputs: All code, documentation, and non-restricted derived data products will be released under permissive licenses (e.g., MIT/BSD for code; CC-BY/CC0 for documentation and derived metadata where allowed). The project will not redistribute controlled-access human data; instead, it will publish reproducible pointers, scripts, and containerized workflows that users can run where access is permitted.

Reproducible computational environment: Analyses will be implemented as end-to-end, automated workflows using workflow managers (e.g., Snakemake/Nextflow) with containerization (Docker/Singularity) and pinned dependencies. Each release will include: (i) executable pipelines, (ii) environment files, (iii) checksums for inputs, and (iv) provenance logs capturing dataset versions and download dates.

FAIR data practices: We will publish a harmonized metadata schema that maps to community ontologies (Cell Ontology, Gene Ontology, OBI, phenotype ontologies) and provides stable identifiers for datasets, perturbations, and features. Derived feature tables will include complete provenance (source dataset, processing parameters, QC flags) and will be deposited in an appropriate open repository (e.g., Zenodo/OSF) with DOIs.

Transparent uncertainty and validation: All phase-diagram estimates will include uncertainty quantification (credible intervals/posterior samples) and sensitivity analyses. We will predefine evaluation metrics (e.g., held-out predictive performance, calibration of uncertainty, robustness to dataset removal) and publish negative results where hypotheses fail. Major claims will require independent reproduction by a separate subteam (“two-team rule”) before inclusion in manuscripts or releases.

Open collaboration and governance: The working group will adopt a written collaboration agreement covering authorship, decision-making, code review, and conflict resolution. Meetings will include open training segments when possible, and we will maintain a public project board (issues, milestones) to enable community feedback.

Training materials: We will produce tutorials and “workflow clinics” materials (recorded walkthroughs, notebooks, example runs) targeted to graduate students and postdocs. Trainees will lead at least two public-facing training sessions and will be credited through contributorship taxonomies (CRediT) in all outputs.

This open science plan ensures that the project’s primary value—reusable synthesis workflows and benchmarks—remains accessible, auditable, and extensible, consistent with NCEMS’s gold-standard practices for open, team-based, reproducible science.
budget_and_resources:
Budget rationale (working group model): The project requires NCEMS support because it integrates multiple public repositories, modalities, and disciplinary perspectives, and because it depends on sustained coordination, shared computational infrastructure, and intensive collaborative synthesis that exceeds a typical single-lab effort.

Requested resources (categories):
1) Personnel support: Partial support for a cross-institutional project manager/data steward to coordinate dataset registry, metadata standards, and releases; limited analyst effort (e.g., part-time research software engineer) to maintain workflows, containers, and CI. Trainee participation (graduate students/postdocs) will be supported primarily through travel and focused sprint activities rather than salary, consistent with a synthesis center model.

2) Working group meetings and collaboration: Funds for 2–3 in-person meetings at NCEMS (or NCEMS-supported venue) plus regular virtual meetings. Support includes travel, lodging, and per diem with deliberate allocation to include participants from a range of institution types (R1s, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions) and career stages. Additional resources for short “data sprints” and trainee-led hack sessions.

3) Computing and data infrastructure: Cloud/HPC credits as needed for large-scale feature extraction from public imaging datasets and for probabilistic modeling/validation runs. Storage for intermediate derived features and model artifacts, with lifecycle policies to control costs. CI services for automated testing and reproducibility checks.

4) Dissemination and training: Support for producing and hosting training materials (workshop logistics, captioning for recorded tutorials), and for open-access publication fees when appropriate.

In-kind and leveraged resources: Participating labs will contribute domain expertise, existing open-source tools, and local compute where available. Data repositories and curators will be engaged as partners to align metadata practices and deposition targets.

Budget governance and feasibility: The budget will be milestone-driven, tied to (i) dataset registry and harmonized schema release, (ii) benchmark v1 with reproducible pipelines, (iii) phase-diagram reconstruction and validation report, and (iv) final public release and training workshop. This ensures efficient use of NCEMS resources while delivering durable community products.

background_and_significance:
Cells with identical genomes often display striking variability in morphology, growth, stress tolerance, differentiation propensity, and drug response. Such heterogeneity is not a nuisance but a fundamental biological feature that can enable bet-hedging, division of labor, and robust tissue function. Yet, mechanistic explanations frequently focus on molecular abundance (e.g., transcript or protein levels) or on single pathways, leaving a gap between molecular parts lists and the emergent, cell-level behaviors that arise from their collective organization. NCEMS’s emphasis on emergence at the mesoscale—the regime between biomolecules and organelles—provides a timely framework for resolving this gap.

Mesoscale organization includes properties such as biomolecular condensates, cytoskeletal architectures, membrane microdomains, organelle contact sites, chromatin domains, and spatial compartmentalization of signaling. These structures are shaped by composition but are not reducible to it: weak multivalent interactions, phase transitions, mechanical constraints, and feedback loops can create nonlinear thresholds, hysteresis, and memory. Consequently, two cells with similar molecular abundances can differ in mesoscale state (e.g., condensate number/size, mitochondrial network connectivity, ER–mitochondria contacts), leading to divergent phenotypes. Conversely, cells may converge on similar phenotypes via distinct molecular routes if they reach similar mesoscale configurations. Understanding mesoscale determinants of variability is therefore a central emergence problem: how collective organization generates new, system-level properties that influence fate and function.

Public data now make this problem tractable through synthesis. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics provide high-dimensional molecular snapshots across many conditions; proteomics and phosphoproteomics add functional layers; large-scale perturbation screens link genes to phenotypes; and expanding imaging repositories capture subcellular organization directly. However, these resources are fragmented across modalities, organisms, and metadata standards. Imaging datasets often lack harmonized annotations; omics datasets may omit spatial context; perturbation screens may report phenotypes without mechanistic intermediates. Integrating them requires community-scale coordination, robust data engineering, and methodological innovation—precisely the niche of an NCEMS working group.

This proposal is significant for three reasons. First, it targets a long-standing puzzle: why genetically identical cells diverge in behavior even in controlled environments. Second, it reframes explanation around mesoscale variables as primary causes/mediators, not post hoc descriptors. Third, it will produce reusable synthesis infrastructure: harmonized representations, causal modeling workflows, and community guidance for linking composition to organization to outcome.

The working group will unite expertise in cell biology, biophysics, imaging analysis, statistical causal inference, machine learning, and data curation. By leveraging only publicly available datasets and focusing on cross-dataset generalization, the group will aim to identify rules that are robust across experimental contexts and taxa. The outcome will advance molecular and cellular biosciences by providing a principled account of how mesoscale organization modulates variability and by establishing a template for future mesoscale-focused synthesis efforts aligned with NCEMS’s mission.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The working group will address a central emergence question: what mesoscale variables mediate and constrain cell-to-cell variability in phenotype among cells with identical genotypes, and can we infer general rules from existing public data? We define “mesoscale variables” as quantitative descriptors of subcellular organization between molecular composition and whole-cell outcomes, including spatial distributions, co-localization patterns, organelle morphology and connectivity, condensate statistics, contact-site frequency, and network-level structural features.

RQ1: Which mesoscale features explain phenotypic variability beyond what is predictable from molecular abundance alone? Hypothesis 1A: In diverse datasets, models that incorporate mesoscale descriptors (from imaging and/or spatial omics) will significantly improve prediction of cellular outcomes (e.g., growth rate proxies, stress response signatures, cell cycle state, differentiation markers, drug sensitivity) compared to abundance-only models. Hypothesis 1B: The incremental explanatory power of mesoscale features will be strongest for phenotypes known to depend on spatial organization (e.g., signaling dynamics, metabolic state, organelle stress).

RQ2: Do mesoscale states act as causal mediators between molecular perturbations and cellular outcomes? Hypothesis 2A: Perturbations (CRISPR/RNAi/chemical) influence outcomes partly through altering mesoscale organization; causal mediation models will identify mesoscale variables that lie on directed paths from perturbation to phenotype. Hypothesis 2B: Some mesoscale variables will function as “bottlenecks” (high mediation proportion) across multiple perturbations, indicating convergent organizational control points.

RQ3: Are there conserved mesoscale “modules” that recur across organisms and cell types? Hypothesis 3A: Unsupervised factorization/representation learning across harmonized datasets will reveal a limited set of mesoscale modules (e.g., cytoskeletal polarity, mitochondrial network fragmentation, nuclear speckle organization, ER–mitochondria coupling) that capture major axes of variation. Hypothesis 3B: While module prevalence varies by organism and context, module–phenotype relationships will show partial conservation (same directionality or conditional dependence) across at least two model systems.

RQ4: What are the rules governing transitions between mesoscale states, and do they exhibit emergent nonlinearities? Hypothesis 4A: State transitions inferred from time-resolved imaging collections and pseudotime-ordered single-cell/spatial omics will display threshold behavior (e.g., abrupt condensate formation) and hysteresis consistent with phase-separation or mechanical feedback mechanisms. Hypothesis 4B: Variability will be amplified near critical transition boundaries, producing increased phenotypic dispersion even when molecular variance is modest.

RQ5: How do measurement uncertainty, batch effects, and missing modalities bias inference about mesoscale determinants? Hypothesis 5A: Explicit uncertainty models and negative-control analyses will reduce spurious causal edges and reveal a subset of robust mesoscale determinants that replicate across repositories. Hypothesis 5B: Multi-modal missingness (e.g., imaging without matched omics) can be partially mitigated by shared latent representations, but causal claims will require cross-dataset triangulation rather than single-dataset discovery.

Together, these questions and hypotheses operationalize emergence: we will test whether mesoscale organization is a necessary explanatory layer linking composition to outcome, identify candidate universal organizational control points, and determine when mesoscale effects are context-specific versus generalizable.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. The project will be executed as an NCEMS-style synthesis working group with iterative, in-person and virtual meetings, interleaved with trainee-led data sprints. The workflow has four technical phases: (1) dataset selection and harmonization, (2) mesoscale feature extraction and representation learning, (3) causal discovery and mediation analysis, and (4) cross-dataset validation and synthesis into generalized rules.

1) Public dataset scope and inclusion criteria. We will use only existing public data. Candidate sources include: Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas (subcellular localization), BioImage Archive/IDR (microscopy images with perturbations), single-cell and spatial transcriptomics atlases (e.g., GEO/ArrayExpress/Single Cell Expression Atlas), proteomics/phosphoproteomics (PRIDE/MassIVE), perturbation screens (DepMap, CRISPR screens in GEO/PRISM-like resources where public), interaction/pathway databases (BioGRID, STRING, Reactome), and structural annotations (AlphaFold/PDB-derived features such as disorder, multivalency proxies). Inclusion criteria: (i) reusable licenses and accessible raw/processed data, (ii) sufficient metadata (cell type/condition/perturbation), (iii) measurable phenotype or state label, (iv) at least one modality informing mesoscale organization (imaging, spatial omics, or curated localization).

2) Harmonization and common data model. We will develop a minimal, community-oriented schema capturing: sample provenance, perturbation/condition, cell state labels, measurement modality, and mapping to standardized ontologies (Cell Ontology, UBERON where applicable, Gene Ontology cellular component). Data will be transformed into interoperable objects (e.g., AnnData for single-cell, OME-NGFF/Zarr pointers for imaging) with versioned manifests. Batch effects will be handled via hierarchical models and integration methods appropriate to modality (e.g., scVI-like latent variable models for scRNA; ComBat/linear mixed models where justified), always retaining batch indicators for causal sensitivity analyses.

3) Mesoscale feature extraction. From imaging: use pretrained/self-supervised vision models and classical morphology pipelines to quantify organelle shape, texture, spatial distribution, co-localization, contact proxies, and network connectivity (e.g., mitochondrial skeleton graphs). From spatial omics: compute spatial autocorrelation, neighborhood composition, subcellular compartment enrichment (when subcellular spatial resolution exists), and spatial co-expression modules. From localization/proteomics: derive compartmental allocation vectors and stoichiometric imbalance indicators. Features will be standardized with uncertainty estimates (segmentation confidence, dropout-aware variance).

4) Representation learning across modalities. We will learn shared latent “mesoscale state” embeddings using multi-view methods (canonical correlation variants, variational multi-modal models) that allow missing modalities. The goal is not maximal prediction but interpretable factors linked back to measurable mesoscale features and known biology.

5) Causal discovery and mediation. We will apply causal graph learning under explicit assumptions (e.g., acyclicity within defined time windows; known intervention nodes from perturbation datasets). Approaches include invariant causal prediction across environments, constrained structure learning with biological priors (e.g., perturbation → molecular changes → mesoscale → phenotype), and mediation analysis to quantify indirect effects through mesoscale variables. Confounding will be addressed via: (i) environment stratification (cell cycle, batch, cell type), (ii) negative controls (genes/markers not expected to affect target phenotypes), and (iii) sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounders.

6) Validation and generalization tests. Findings must replicate across at least two independent datasets and, when feasible, across organisms (e.g., yeast vs mammalian cultured cells) or across cell types. We will predefine replication criteria: consistent directionality, effect size thresholds, and stability under alternative integration choices. The final synthesis will produce a set of “mesoscale rules” expressed as testable statements (e.g., conditional independencies, threshold relationships) plus code to reproduce all analyses end-to-end.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific outcomes. The primary scientific deliverable will be a rigorously validated model of how mesoscale organization contributes to cell-to-cell variability in phenotype among identical genotypes. Concretely, we expect to (i) identify a small set of mesoscale variables or modules that repeatedly improve prediction of cellular outcomes beyond molecular abundance, (ii) map putative causal pathways in which perturbations influence outcomes through mesoscale mediators, and (iii) characterize when mesoscale effects are conserved versus context-specific across organisms and cell types. A key outcome will be evidence-based “rules” describing organizational bottlenecks, nonlinear transitions, and conditions under which variability is amplified.

Methodological outcomes. The working group will deliver reusable synthesis methods for mesoscale biology: a harmonized data model bridging imaging and omics, feature-extraction pipelines with uncertainty propagation, multi-modal embeddings designed for interpretability, and causal discovery workflows tailored to heterogeneous public datasets. These methods will be packaged as documented, modular software and example notebooks that can be applied to new datasets without re-engineering.

Community-scale infrastructure. We will produce curated dataset manifests and metadata mappings that lower barriers to reuse of major imaging, spatial omics, and perturbation resources for mesoscale questions. Where gaps in metadata standards impede synthesis, we will propose minimal extensions and provide templates to encourage future deposition practices.

Training and workforce impact. Trainees will gain hands-on experience in reproducible, team-based data synthesis, including data curation, analysis engineering, and causal reasoning. Rotating trainee leadership will create tangible products (validated modules, tutorials) that strengthen career development.

Broader impact on molecular and cellular sciences. By establishing mesoscale organization as a first-class explanatory layer, the project will shift how variability is interpreted in contexts such as drug response, stress adaptation, and differentiation. The outputs will enable other researchers to test emergent mesoscale hypotheses using existing data, accelerating discovery while reducing redundant data generation and aligning with NCEMS’s mission to leverage public data, AI, and open science to reveal fundamental emergent principles.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-by-default products. All derived data products permitted by source licenses (feature tables, embeddings, harmonized metadata, dataset manifests) will be released publicly. All code will be version-controlled (GitHub/GitLab) with tagged releases and archived DOIs (e.g., Zenodo). Manuscripts will be posted as preprints and submitted to open-access venues when feasible.

Reproducible workflows. Analyses will be implemented as executable pipelines (Snakemake/Nextflow) with containerized environments (Docker/Singularity) to ensure portability across institutions. Each major result will have a “reproduce this figure” entry point that reruns the exact workflow from raw public inputs (or stable pointers) to final outputs. We will use continuous integration to test pipelines on small public subsets and to prevent bit-rot.

Transparent provenance and metadata. We will maintain machine-readable provenance records: dataset accession IDs, download dates, preprocessing parameters, and transformation steps. Metadata will be mapped to community ontologies (Cell Ontology, Gene Ontology cellular component, Experimental Factor Ontology) and released as a validated schema with examples. When imaging is used, we will store references in OME-compatible formats (e.g., OME-NGFF pointers) and document any preprocessing.

Robustness and bias reporting. For each causal claim, we will publish sensitivity analyses, negative controls, and alternative model specifications. We will report limitations due to missingness, batch structure, and selection bias inherent to public datasets. We will avoid overclaiming by labeling outputs as “hypothesis-generating” unless they meet predefined cross-dataset replication criteria.

Open training materials. The working group will produce tutorials, recorded workflow clinics, and “data sprint” playbooks aimed at trainees and newcomers. Materials will include guidance on ethical reuse of public data, licensing, and responsible AI practices.

Team science practices. We will adopt a written collaboration agreement covering authorship, issue tracking, code review standards, and decision-making. All meetings will produce publicly shareable notes when appropriate, and internal milestones will be tracked transparently to support distributed collaboration aligned with NCEMS expectations.
budget_and_resources:
Budget rationale aligned with NCEMS working groups. Because the project uses only publicly available data and generates no new experimental data, requested funds focus on enabling community-scale synthesis: convening a multidisciplinary team, supporting trainee participation, and providing the computational and data-engineering capacity required to integrate heterogeneous repositories.

Personnel support (major cost). Funds will support: (i) one part-time project manager/data curator to coordinate dataset licensing checks, metadata harmonization, and releases; (ii) one research software engineer (RSE) effort to build and maintain reproducible pipelines, containers, and CI; and (iii) trainee support (graduate students/postdocs) for sprint-based curation, feature extraction, and validation tasks. Personnel effort is essential because the integration burden exceeds typical single-lab capacity and requires sustained coordination.

Meetings and collaboration. NCEMS-style in-person meetings (e.g., 2–3 multi-day meetings) and regular virtual workshops will be budgeted for travel, lodging, and accessibility needs. Meeting design will include structured hack sessions, cross-training modules, and dedicated time for cross-dataset replication planning. Travel support will prioritize trainees and participants from under-resourced institutions to broaden participation.

Computational resources. While leveraging institutional clusters when possible, funds will cover cloud compute/storage credits for scalable image feature extraction and multi-modal model training, plus costs for data egress and long-term artifact hosting when required. Compute needs will be managed with cost controls: benchmarked pipelines, spot instances where appropriate, and caching of intermediate products.

Software and dissemination. Budget includes minimal costs for software services that improve reproducibility (e.g., managed CI minutes if needed) and dissemination (workshop materials, documentation hosting). No funds are allocated to wet-lab supplies or data generation.

NCEMS resource needs beyond a single lab. The project requires NCEMS convening power to assemble diverse domain experts, establish shared standards, and coordinate cross-institutional synthesis; NCEMS infrastructure will amplify impact through hosted events, community engagement, and alignment with center-wide open science policies.

title: From mutation to mesoscale phenotype: mapping variants to compartment disruption
abstract:
This working group asks how from mutation to mesoscale phenotype: mapping variants to compartment disruption can be understood as an emergent property that links molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcome. The scientific question is not simply whether particular molecules, organelles, or pathways are associated with a phenotype, but whether publicly available datasets can reveal rules by which many molecular parts collectively produce a new, system-level behavior at the scale between biomolecules and organelles. The project is designed for the NCEMS model because the relevant evidence is scattered across incompatible imaging repositories, omics studies, perturbation resources, structural annotations, and specialized literatures; no single laboratory is likely to have the biological breadth, data-engineering capacity, and methodological expertise to integrate them.

The group would synthesize existing public data centered on structural/sequence biophysics, prioritizing datasets with reusable metadata, perturbation or state annotations, and links to downstream cellular phenotypes. Depending on availability, sources could include public cell atlases, the Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, EMBL-EBI and NCBI functional genomics repositories, BioImage Archive or Image Data Resource collections, PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics datasets, public CRISPR or RNAi screens, AlphaFold/PDB-derived structural features, and curated pathway or protein-interaction resources. The core analytic strategy would be foundation-model representation learning: harmonizing measurements into a common representation; explicitly modeling uncertainty, batch effects, and missingness; and testing whether mesoscale variables explain cellular outcomes above and beyond molecular abundance alone. The biological scope would focus on human disease cells while deliberately including comparison cases that prevent the group from mistaking a narrow model-system pattern for a general law.

The novel element is the unit of explanation. Instead of treating mesoscale organization as an image label, downstream readout, or anecdotal mechanism, the working group would make it the primary object of synthesis: a measurable layer where composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion combine. The expected product is a predictive atlas that is open, versioned, and reusable, with transparent workflows, community-agreed metadata standards, and tutorials for trainees. The project would bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, imaging scientists, omics researchers, statisticians, machine-learning researchers, data curators, and trainees across institution types. Training would occur through hackathon-style data sprints, reproducible workflow clinics, and rotating trainee leadership of cross-dataset validation tasks. The anticipated contribution is both scientific and infrastructural: a defensible answer to a specific emergence question, plus a generalizable synthesis strategy that helps the molecular and cellular biosciences reuse public data to discover phenomena that only become visible when datasets, disciplines, and scales are brought together.
background_and_significance:
Many disease-associated variants alter proteins without obviously changing bulk abundance, yet they can precipitate striking cellular phenotypes such as altered organelle morphology, disrupted membrane-less compartments, mislocalized complexes, or aberrant trafficking. These phenotypes often manifest at the mesoscale—the regime between individual biomolecules and organelles—where collective interactions among many components generate emergent organization. Examples include phase-separated condensates, cytoskeletal networks, endomembrane contact sites, ribonucleoprotein granules, and multi-protein assemblies that spatially pattern biochemical reactions. Understanding how sequence-level perturbations propagate to these mesoscale structures is a central challenge in molecular and cellular biosciences because the causal chain is distributed: a variant can subtly shift binding affinities, conformational ensembles, or interaction valency, and only in combination with cellular context does a new system-level behavior appear.

Despite major advances in genomics, proteomics, and imaging, rules linking variants to compartment disruption remain fragmented across disciplines and data types. Variant effect predictors typically focus on molecular function (e.g., stability, catalytic sites) but rarely connect to spatial organization. Conversely, imaging-based phenotyping often labels outcomes (e.g., “Golgi fragmentation”) without mechanistic linkage to sequence biophysics. The missing layer is a quantitative, integrative representation of mesoscale organization that can be compared across datasets and directly tested as a mediator between molecular perturbations and cellular outcomes.

Public data now make such synthesis feasible. Large-scale variant catalogs (ClinVar, gnomAD), functional genomics perturbation resources (DepMap CRISPR screens, GEO/ArrayExpress transcriptomics), protein interaction/pathway databases (BioGRID, STRING, Reactome), structural resources (PDB, AlphaFold-derived features), and imaging repositories (Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource) collectively provide partial views of the same biological systems. Yet these resources are heterogeneous in metadata, measurement scale, and experimental context. The NCEMS model is essential because integrating these sources requires coordinated expertise in cell biology, biophysics, imaging analysis, machine learning, statistics, and data curation, as well as community-scale effort to harmonize identifiers, ontologies, and uncertainty.

This working group addresses a fundamental emergence question aligned with NCEMS’s mesoscale focus: when do many small molecular changes add up to a qualitative reorganization of cellular compartments, and can we infer generalizable rules from existing data? The significance is twofold. Scientifically, the project aims to identify mechanistic classes of variants that converge on mesoscale disruption (e.g., altered multivalency driving condensate dissolution; changed interaction topology destabilizing contact sites). Methodologically, it will develop reusable synthesis pipelines that treat mesoscale organization as a first-class quantitative variable rather than a qualitative label.

The proposed work is strictly synthesis-based: it will not generate new experimental data. Instead, it will integrate public datasets to build an open, versioned “variant-to-compartment disruption” atlas and predictive models that quantify how much mesoscale variables explain downstream phenotypes beyond molecular abundance alone. By focusing on human disease-relevant contexts while including carefully chosen comparison systems, the project seeks robust, general principles rather than idiosyncratic model-specific findings. The outcomes will enable the community to prioritize variants for mechanistic follow-up, reinterpret existing perturbation screens through a mesoscale lens, and accelerate discovery of emergent cellular behaviors that become visible only through cross-scale, cross-modality synthesis.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The working group will pursue a set of tightly linked research questions designed to test whether mesoscale organization provides an explanatory and predictive layer between molecular variants and cellular outcomes.

RQ1: Can mesoscale compartment disruption be operationalized as a quantitative, cross-dataset variable that is comparable across imaging repositories and perturbation contexts? 
H1: A small set of latent mesoscale descriptors—capturing properties such as compartment presence/absence, size distribution, spatial dispersion, boundary sharpness, co-localization topology, and organelle contact frequency—can be learned from heterogeneous imaging and annotation sources and aligned across datasets using representation learning with explicit batch and uncertainty modeling.

RQ2: Do disease-associated variants show convergent signatures of mesoscale disruption that are not explained by changes in expression or protein abundance alone? 
H2: For many variant–gene pairs, models that include mesoscale descriptors will significantly improve prediction of cellular outcomes (e.g., viability, stress sensitivity, pathway activation signatures) compared to models using only transcript/protein abundance and canonical pathway membership. We hypothesize that this improvement will be strongest for variants affecting intrinsically disordered regions, multivalent interaction motifs, and interface residues that modulate assembly dynamics.

RQ3: What molecular features best predict which variants perturb which compartments? 
H3: Structural/sequence biophysical features (predicted stability change, interface disruption scores, disorder content, low-complexity composition, post-translational modification site proximity, predicted interaction valency) combined with network context (protein–protein interaction centrality, community structure, pathway redundancy) will predict compartment-specific disruption. We hypothesize that different compartments have distinct “failure modes”: e.g., condensates are sensitive to changes in valency and disorder; membrane contact sites are sensitive to interface geometry and lipid-binding motifs; trafficking compartments are sensitive to short linear motifs and adaptor binding.

RQ4: Are there generalizable “emergence thresholds” where gradual molecular perturbations produce abrupt mesoscale reorganization? 
H4: In aggregated public perturbation datasets (variant series, graded knockdowns, drug dose responses), mesoscale descriptors will exhibit nonlinear transitions (bifurcation-like behavior) with respect to molecular-level predictors (e.g., interaction strength proxies, abundance), consistent with emergent phase or network transitions. We hypothesize that such thresholds are more detectable when integrating across studies than within any single dataset.

RQ5: How transferable are inferred rules across cell types, disease contexts, and measurement modalities? 
H5: A core subset of variant-to-compartment rules will transfer across contexts when conditioned on a small number of contextual variables (cell type lineage, stress state, baseline expression of scaffold proteins). We expect limited transferability for rules that depend on cell-type-specific expression of interaction partners, motivating explicit context modeling rather than assuming universal effects.

RQ6 (methodological): Can we build a community-reusable benchmark for “variant → mesoscale phenotype” prediction using only public data? 
H6: By curating positive/negative examples from imaging annotations, curated literature, and perturbation readouts, we can establish benchmark tasks with transparent provenance and uncertainty labels. We hypothesize that benchmark performance will improve markedly when models incorporate both molecular biophysics and mesoscale descriptors, providing a quantitative demonstration of the added explanatory power of mesoscale organization.

Together, these questions test a central claim: mesoscale compartment disruption is an emergent, system-level phenotype that can be inferred and predicted from public data through integrative, cross-disciplinary synthesis.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. The project will be executed as an NCEMS-style working group with coordinated data sprints and synthesis meetings. Subteams will focus on (i) data inventory and harmonization, (ii) mesoscale phenotype extraction and representation learning, (iii) variant/biophysics feature engineering, (iv) causal and predictive modeling, and (v) benchmarking, documentation, and training.

Data sources (public only) and inclusion criteria. We will assemble datasets with reusable metadata, clear experimental context, and linkable identifiers (gene/protein, cell line, perturbation). Candidate sources include: imaging (Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource); omics and perturbation (GEO/ArrayExpress, SRA-derived processed matrices when available, DepMap/Project Achilles CRISPR screens, public RNAi screens); proteomics (PRIDE/MassIVE); structure/biophysics (PDB, AlphaFold-derived features, UniProt annotations); interaction/pathways (BioGRID, STRING, Reactome, CORUM); variant resources (ClinVar, gnomAD, COSMIC where licensing permits). We will prioritize datasets with permissive reuse licenses and stable accessions.

Harmonization and metadata alignment. We will implement a reproducible ETL (extract-transform-load) pipeline that maps identifiers to canonical references (HGNC/Ensembl/UniProt), standardizes cell line names (Cellosaurus), and normalizes experimental descriptors using ontologies (e.g., Gene Ontology cellular component, Cell Ontology, OBI where applicable). Imaging metadata will be aligned to community standards (e.g., OME-NGFF/OME metadata fields when present) and extended via a minimal working-group schema for “mesoscale phenotype” fields with provenance.

Mesoscale phenotype extraction. For imaging datasets with raw images, we will use pretrained foundation models for microscopy (self-supervised embeddings) and classical feature extraction (morphometrics, texture, spatial statistics) to derive compartment descriptors. When only annotations/segmentations are available, we will convert them into standardized quantitative summaries. Outputs will be probabilistic: each descriptor will include uncertainty estimates reflecting image quality, batch effects, and model confidence.

Representation learning and cross-dataset alignment. We will train/finetune multimodal models that integrate imaging embeddings with omics/perturbation features. Key techniques include domain adaptation (to mitigate dataset-specific biases), missing-data-aware modeling (to handle sparse modality overlap), and hierarchical models that separate biological signal from batch and lab effects. Latent variables will be interpreted as mesoscale states, with interpretability aided by feature attribution and alignment to known compartments (GO cellular component, CORUM complexes).

Variant and biophysical feature engineering. For each variant, we will compute or retrieve features such as predicted stability/interface effects (from public predictors where outputs are reusable), residue environment from AlphaFold structures, disorder/low-complexity metrics, motif disruption scores, PTM site proximity, and network-context features (interaction degree, community membership, essentiality context from screens). We will aggregate variant evidence across clinical/pathogenicity labels where available.

Modeling strategy and evaluation. We will test whether mesoscale variables mediate variant effects using (i) predictive comparisons (abundance-only vs abundance+mesoscale models), (ii) mediation/causal-inference-inspired analyses with sensitivity checks, and (iii) context-conditioned transfer tests across cell types/datasets. Benchmarks will use held-out datasets and time-split validations when possible (older datasets for training, newer for testing). We will predefine success metrics (AUROC/AUPRC for classification tasks; calibration and uncertainty scores; transfer performance) and report negative results.

Training and collaboration workflow. Trainees will lead rotating “validation pods” that reproduce key results on independent datasets. Hackathon-style sprints will produce documented modules (data loaders, embedding extraction, evaluation notebooks) integrated into a shared repository with continuous integration tests.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific products. (1) A quantitative, cross-dataset atlas linking variants (and broader perturbations) to mesoscale compartment disruption signatures, with explicit uncertainty and provenance. (2) Evidence-based rules describing which molecular/biophysical feature classes (e.g., disorder/valency, interface geometry, motif disruption) preferentially map to specific compartment failure modes (condensates, trafficking hubs, contact sites, cytoskeletal assemblies). (3) Identification of candidate emergence thresholds—nonlinear transitions in mesoscale organization—supported by aggregated public perturbation series and replicated across datasets.

Methodological products. (4) A reusable synthesis pipeline for harmonizing imaging, omics, perturbation, and structural annotations into a common representation, including missingness-aware multimodal modeling and domain adaptation for microscopy. (5) Community benchmarks for “variant → mesoscale phenotype” prediction with transparent data splits, evaluation metrics, and baseline models, enabling future method development.

Impact on molecular and cellular biosciences. The project will shift mesoscale organization from a qualitative mechanistic narrative to a measurable explanatory layer. By demonstrating that mesoscale descriptors add predictive power beyond abundance and pathway labels, the working group will provide a concrete, testable framework for emergence at the mesoscale. The atlas will help researchers prioritize variants for mechanistic follow-up, reinterpret existing functional genomics screens through spatial organization, and generate hypotheses about why certain diseases show compartment-level pathology despite modest molecular changes.

Broader impacts and workforce development. The working group will train a cohort of trainees in data synthesis, imaging/omics integration, and open, reproducible science practices. Deliverables (tutorials, workflows, benchmarks) will reduce barriers for labs without extensive data-engineering capacity, broadening participation. By making all outputs open and modular, the project will catalyze follow-on community contributions and new collaborations, consistent with NCEMS’s mission to enable discoveries that are beyond any single lab.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-by-default outputs. All code, documentation, and derived data products produced by the working group will be released under permissive open-source/open-data licenses where allowed by upstream terms. The project will use public repositories (e.g., GitHub/GitLab) with archived releases (Zenodo DOIs) for each major milestone: dataset manifests, harmonized metadata tables, feature matrices, trained model weights when redistributable, and the final atlas.

Provenance, licensing, and ethical reuse. Because the project relies exclusively on public data, we will maintain a machine-readable “data card” for each ingested dataset: accession IDs, license/terms, allowed redistribution status, processing steps, and known limitations. For datasets that cannot be redistributed, we will provide reproducible retrieval scripts and generate derived artifacts that comply with terms (e.g., embeddings or summary statistics only when permitted). Human-related data will be handled in accordance with original consent and repository rules; we will not attempt re-identification and will avoid integrating any controlled-access individual-level data unless explicitly permitted and accessible to all working-group members under the same conditions.

Reproducible workflows. Analyses will be implemented as containerized, versioned workflows (Docker/Singularity) orchestrated with workflow managers (e.g., Snakemake/Nextflow) and executed with continuous integration on representative subsets. We will enforce deterministic runs where feasible (fixed random seeds, version pinning) and record compute environments. Each figure/table in the final products will be traceable to an executable workflow target.

Transparent uncertainty and robustness. The atlas will include uncertainty estimates and quality flags (image quality, batch confidence, modality completeness). We will preregister key evaluation plans within the working group (internal protocol documents) to reduce analytic flexibility, and we will report negative and null findings (e.g., compartments or contexts where models do not transfer).

Community standards and training materials. We will co-develop a minimal metadata schema for mesoscale phenotypes and contribute mappings to existing ontologies where possible. Training deliverables will include step-by-step tutorials, “reproduce this result” notebooks, and recorded workflow clinics led jointly by trainees and senior members, enabling reuse by the broader community.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support rationale. The project requires NCEMS resources because it is a community-scale synthesis effort spanning multiple modalities (imaging, omics, perturbation, structure) and demanding coordinated data curation, shared compute, structured collaboration, and open-science infrastructure that exceed the scope of a single lab. NCEMS convening power is essential to align domain experts, data curators, and method developers around shared standards and deliverables.

Major cost categories (illustrative, adjustable to NCEMS guidelines). title: A community challenge for predicting organelle morphology from molecular state
abstract:

background_and_significance:
Organelle morphology is a mesoscale phenotype: it emerges from collective molecular interactions (lipids, scaffolds, motors, tethers, chaperones, cytoskeleton) yet constrains higher-level cellular outcomes such as trafficking, metabolism, signaling, stress responses, and fate decisions. Despite decades of mechanistic studies, the field still lacks general, quantitative rules linking “molecular state” (gene expression, protein abundance/localization, post-translational regulation, interaction potential) to organelle shape, size, number, and spatial arrangement. This gap persists because morphology is controlled by distributed, redundant, and context-dependent processes; single perturbations often yield pleiotropic outcomes, and similar morphologies can arise from different molecular routes. These features are hallmarks of emergence, making organelle morphology an ideal target for NCEMS synthesis research focused on mesoscale phenomena.

Public data now make this problem tractable, but only through community-scale integration. Imaging repositories contain millions of microscopy images across cell types, species, and perturbations, yet are fragmented across formats and annotation practices. In parallel, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, proteomics, and perturbation screens provide rich molecular state information but rarely connect directly to morphology. Structural and interaction resources (AlphaFold, PDB, BioGRID/STRING, pathway databases) encode constraints on molecular assemblies that may shape organelles via phase separation, membrane remodeling, or scaffold formation. Each data modality captures a different slice of the causal chain; none alone is sufficient to infer generalizable rules.

A community challenge framework—shared tasks, standardized benchmarks, and transparent evaluation—has repeatedly accelerated progress in domains where complex, heterogeneous data impede individual-lab efforts. Here, the challenge is not merely to predict a label from an image, but to predict organelle morphology from molecular state and to identify which aspects of molecular state are sufficient, necessary, or redundant for that prediction across contexts. This reframes morphology as a measurable intermediate layer between molecules and cell-level outcomes, consistent with NCEMS’s emphasis on emergent properties at the mesoscale.

The proposed working group addresses long-standing puzzles: Why do distinct molecular perturbations converge to similar organelle morphologies? When does morphology add predictive power for downstream phenotypes beyond molecular abundance alone? Which features of molecular organization (e.g., interaction network topology, structural disorder, membrane-binding motifs, stoichiometric balance) best explain morphological regimes? Answering these requires integrating disparate public datasets, harmonizing metadata, quantifying uncertainty, and validating models across species and platforms—capabilities beyond most individual labs.

Significance extends beyond organelle biology. Establishing reproducible pipelines to link molecular state to mesoscale structure would provide a general synthesis strategy for other emergent cellular properties (e.g., condensate formation, cytoskeletal architectures, chromatin domains). The project aligns tightly with NCEMS priorities: it uses only publicly available data; demands multidisciplinary collaboration among cell biologists, imaging scientists, data curators, statisticians, and ML researchers; trains a data-savvy workforce via open workflows and community benchmarking; and produces reusable standards and resources that enable broader reuse of existing molecular and cellular data to discover emergent principles.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
RQ1: To what extent is organelle morphology predictable from molecular state across cell types, perturbations, and species using only publicly available data?
H1.1: Predictive performance will be substantially above baseline (e.g., cell-type-only or batch-only predictors) for multiple organelles (mitochondria, ER, Golgi, nucleus, lysosomes), indicating that morphology is constrained by molecular state rather than being dominated by imaging modality or laboratory artifacts.
H1.2: Cross-dataset generalization will be achievable when models explicitly represent uncertainty and batch effects, suggesting that shared mesoscale rules exist beyond dataset-specific biases.

RQ2: Which components of molecular state are most informative for morphology: expression levels, subcellular localization, interaction network context, or structural features?
H2.1: Integrating network and structure-derived features (e.g., predicted disorder, multivalency, membrane-binding propensity, complex stoichiometry, interaction centrality) will improve morphology prediction compared to expression alone, consistent with emergent mesoscale organization depending on collective interaction constraints.
H2.2: Morphology will be best predicted by combinations of features that capture balance among modules (e.g., fission/fusion, tethering/trafficking, lipid synthesis/transport), implying that relative coordination—not single markers—drives mesoscale outcomes.

RQ3: Does morphology provide explanatory and predictive value for downstream cellular outcomes beyond molecular abundance alone?
H3.1: In datasets with linked phenotypes (growth, stress sensitivity, secretion, metabolic readouts, drug response), morphology-derived latent variables will explain additional variance after controlling for molecular state, supporting morphology as an emergent intermediate layer.
H3.2: The incremental value of morphology will be highest under perturbations that rewire physical organization (e.g., cytoskeletal disruption, membrane trafficking defects) rather than purely transcriptional shifts.

RQ4: Are there conserved “morphological regimes” and transition rules across kingdoms/species, or are rules largely lineage-specific?
H4.1: A subset of regimes (e.g., mitochondrial fragmentation vs hyperfusion; ER sheet-to-tubule balance; Golgi dispersal) will recur across species, with conserved molecular signatures in orthologous pathways.
H4.2: Species-specific deviations will correlate with differences in organelle biogenesis strategies and cellular geometry, revealing where emergent rules depend on physical constraints (cell size, compartment scaling) versus molecular modules.

RQ5: What minimal metadata and representations are required to make morphology-from-state synthesis reliable and reusable?
H5.1: A community-agreed “minimum information for morphology prediction” (MIMP) schema—capturing imaging modality, segmentation provenance, organelle marker, perturbation annotation, and cell context—will measurably increase cross-study interoperability and model transfer.
H5.2: Harmonized representations (standardized morphological feature sets plus uncertainty estimates) will enable fair benchmarking and reduce performance inflation due to leakage, batch confounding, or inconsistent definitions of morphology.
methods_and_approach:
Working group structure and scope. We will run a 12–18 month NCEMS working group organized around a community challenge plus synthesis deliverables. Participation will span imaging repositories, omics/perturbation resources, biophysics, statistics/ML, and data stewardship. All analyses will use existing publicly available datasets; no new experimental data will be generated.

Data acquisition and inclusion criteria. We will curate a “challenge corpus” of studies meeting: (i) accessible raw or minimally processed images with organelle markers; (ii) molecular state measurements (single-cell/spatial transcriptomics, bulk/single-cell proteomics, or perturbation labels enabling inferred state); (iii) reusable metadata (cell type, species, perturbation, imaging modality); and (iv) clear licensing for reuse. Candidate sources include BioImage Archive/IDR, Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, cell atlases with linked perturbations, PRIDE/MassIVE, CRISPR/RNAi screens, and interaction/pathway databases.

Harmonization and representations. We will build a unified schema mapping: sample identifiers, cell context, perturbation/state, imaging channels, and organelle targets. Morphology will be represented at three levels: (1) classical features (size, number, eccentricity, branching, texture, spatial distribution); (2) learned embeddings from pretrained self-supervised image models; and (3) topology/graph descriptors for network-like organelles (mitochondria/ER). Molecular state will be represented as: (a) expression/protein abundance vectors; (b) pathway activities; (c) interaction-network features; and (d) structure-derived features (e.g., disorder, coiled-coils, membrane association) aggregated to pathway/modules.

Uncertainty, confounding, and missingness. We will implement hierarchical models and domain adaptation to separate biological signal from batch effects (lab, microscope, staining, segmentation tool). Missing modalities will be handled via multi-view learning (e.g., partial multi-omics factor models) and careful train/test splits that prevent leakage across batches or near-duplicate images. Evaluation will include calibration metrics and uncertainty-aware scoring.

Benchmark tasks (the community challenge). We will define tasks of increasing difficulty: T1 within-dataset prediction of morphology from molecular state; T2 cross-dataset generalization; T3 cross-species transfer; T4 prediction of downstream phenotypes using molecular state alone vs molecular+predicted morphology vs molecular+observed morphology. Baselines will include linear models, random forests, and simple neural models; advanced methods may include multimodal transformers, graph neural networks over interaction networks, and causal representation learning. All tasks will use standardized splits and metrics (R2/MAE for continuous features; F1/AUROC for categorical regimes; generalization gaps; calibration).

Mechanistic synthesis and interpretation. We will apply model interpretation (SHAP, counterfactuals, pathway enrichment on important features) to identify molecular modules associated with morphological regimes. We will test whether inferred rules align with known biophysical principles (membrane tension, curvature generation, phase separation propensity) and whether discrepancies point to new hypotheses.

Training and collaboration. The working group will run data sprints, reproducible workflow clinics, and trainee-led cross-validation teams. Outputs will be packaged as reusable pipelines (containers, notebooks, workflow managers) and a public leaderboard-style benchmark with documentation for community extension.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific outcomes. (1) Quantitative estimates of how predictable organelle morphology is from molecular state across contexts, including where prediction fails and why (e.g., missing modalities, confounding, true biological degeneracy). (2) Identification of conserved morphological regimes and the molecular modules that govern transitions between them, clarifying which mesoscale properties are emergent and general versus context-specific. (3) Evidence for (or against) morphology as an explanatory intermediate: we will report how much additional variance in cellular outcomes is explained by morphology-aware models beyond molecular abundance alone.

Methodological outcomes. (1) A validated benchmark suite for “morphology-from-state” prediction with standardized splits, metrics, and uncertainty-aware evaluation, enabling fair comparison of methods and reducing irreproducible claims. (2) A harmonized representation layer that connects imaging-derived morphology descriptors with multi-omic and perturbation annotations, including guidance on minimal metadata needed for interoperability.

Community and workforce outcomes. (1) An NCEMS-style working group network that bridges imaging, omics, biophysics, statistics/ML, and data curation communities, lowering barriers for new entrants and under-resourced institutions to participate. (2) Training artifacts—tutorials, recorded clinics, and example analyses—designed for graduate students and postdocs to learn reproducible multimodal synthesis.

Broader impact. By turning scattered public datasets into a reusable, open benchmark and synthesis resource, the project will accelerate discovery of emergent mesoscale rules and provide a template for similar efforts on condensates, cytoskeletal architectures, and chromatin organization. The infrastructure will increase the return on investment of public data generation, promote interoperability across repositories, and enable downstream method development in AI for biology grounded in rigorous cross-dataset validation rather than single-study performance.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-by-default products. All code, workflows, and derived non-restricted data products will be released under permissive licenses (e.g., BSD-3/Apache-2.0 for code; CC-BY/CC0 where appropriate for metadata/derived tables), with clear attribution to original data generators. We will not redistribute data with restrictive terms; instead we will provide scripted download/processing recipes that reproduce the corpus from source repositories.

Reproducible workflows. Analyses will be implemented as versioned pipelines using containerization (Docker/Singularity) and workflow managers (e.g., Snakemake/Nextflow) with pinned software versions and checksum-verified inputs. Each benchmark release will be tagged (semantic versioning) and archived (e.g., Zenodo DOI). We will provide “one-command” reproduction for core figures and leaderboard results.

Transparent benchmarking. The challenge will publish: task definitions, inclusion/exclusion criteria, data splits, evaluation metrics, and baseline implementations. To prevent leakage and overfitting, we will (i) hold out entire studies/labs for generalization tests, (ii) maintain a hidden evaluation set when feasible, and (iii) require method cards documenting training data usage and compute.

Data and metadata standards. A key deliverable is a community-agreed MIMP (Minimum Information for Morphology Prediction) schema describing required fields (organelle marker, segmentation provenance, imaging modality, cell context, perturbation annotation, units) and recommended ontologies (cell types, perturbations, species). We will coordinate with existing standards efforts (e.g., OME, BioImage Model Zoo conventions) and repository curators to ensure compatibility.

Governance and credit. We will adopt an authorship/contribution policy (CRediT taxonomy), open meeting notes, and a code of conduct. Trainees will receive visible credit through maintained contributor lists, citable releases, and opportunities to lead modules (baseline methods, metadata schema, tutorials).
budget_and_resources:
Budget rationale (NCEMS working group model). Requested support is primarily for coordination, participant travel, trainee involvement, and technical infrastructure required to synthesize heterogeneous public datasets at community scale—needs that exceed a single lab’s capacity.

Major cost categories. (1) Working group meetings: 2–3 in-person meetings at NCEMS (or hub sites) plus monthly virtual meetings. Funds cover travel, lodging, and per diem to ensure participation across geography, institution type, and career stage, including trainees and researchers from under-resourced institutions.
