(3) Trainee support: stipends or travel awards for graduate students/postdocs to lead sprint teams, develop tutorials, and maintain baseline models; support for accessibility needs to ensure inclusive participation. (4) Compute and storage: cloud credits or hosted compute for standardized preprocessing, feature extraction, and evaluation; storage for derived feature tables, embeddings, and benchmark artifacts (not duplicating restricted raw data). (5) Dissemination: costs for archiving (DOIs), workshop materials, and an open tutorial series.

NCEMS resources and justification. NCEMS provides convening power, neutral coordination, and infrastructure for open synthesis science. The project requires NCEMS support to: (i) convene diverse experts (imaging, omics, biophysics, ML, curation) not currently in a single collaboration; (ii) maintain a public benchmark/leaderboard and versioned releases; (iii) support community standards development (MIMP) with repository stakeholders; and (iv) deliver structured training activities.

Deliverables tied to spending. Each funded component maps to concrete outputs: curated corpus recipes, benchmark tasks and baselines, versioned pipeline releases, MIMP schema, tutorials, and a final synthesis manuscript plus a citable benchmark resource.

background_and_significance:
Aging is accompanied by widespread molecular changes—altered transcription, proteome remodeling, oxidative damage, and stress responses—yet many age-associated phenotypes are expressed at a higher level of organization: organelle fragmentation, altered organelle contacts, cytoskeletal rearrangements, changes in cell stiffness/viscoelasticity, and breakdown of spatial proteome organization. These phenomena occupy the mesoscale, between individual macromolecules and organelles, where emergent properties arise from collective interactions among many components. Despite extensive cataloging of age-associated genes and pathways, a central puzzle remains: why do similar molecular perturbations sometimes yield divergent cellular outcomes, and why do different molecular routes converge on shared aging phenotypes? A plausible answer is that aging is mediated by mesoscale “state variables” that integrate proteostasis capacity, organelle architecture, and mechanical constraints into a small set of organizational regimes.

Proteostasis decline is a hallmark of aging, encompassing chaperone saturation, reduced proteasome and autophagy flux, accumulation of misfolded/aggregated proteins, and altered phase behavior of biomolecular condensates. In parallel, organelles exhibit characteristic age-associated changes: mitochondrial network fragmentation and altered cristae, ER stress and remodeling, lysosomal dysfunction, peroxisome changes, and disrupted endomembrane trafficking. Cellular mechanics also change with age and senescence, including increased stiffness in some contexts, altered actomyosin tension, nuclear lamina remodeling, and changes in mechanotransduction pathways. However, these strands are often studied in isolation, with causal narratives inferred from single experiments or single data modalities.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to address this gap because the evidence needed to test mesoscale emergence is distributed across heterogeneous, publicly available datasets: high-content microscopy (organelle morphology, spatial proteomics, condensate markers), proteomics (abundance, PTMs, aggregation propensity), perturbation screens (CRISPR/RNAi, small molecules), structural annotations (intrinsic disorder, multivalency, phase separation propensity), and phenotype readouts (growth, stress tolerance, senescence markers). No single laboratory can reasonably harmonize these data, build uncertainty-aware integrative models, and validate generality across organisms and contexts. A community-scale synthesis effort can, and it can do so while producing reusable infrastructure.

The significance of focusing on the mesoscale is twofold. Scientifically, it targets the level where emergent behavior is expected: many-to-one mappings from molecular composition to organizational states (e.g., organelle contact networks, condensate material properties, cytoskeletal topology) that in turn constrain cellular outcomes (stress resistance, proteome stability, cell cycle arrest). Methodologically, mesoscale variables are measurable but rarely standardized across datasets; extracting them demands shared representations, metadata standards, and cross-modal alignment. This working group will deliver both: a rigorous, testable framework for mesoscale aging states and an open synthesis pipeline that the broader community can apply to other emergence problems.

By integrating proteostasis, organelles, and mechanics, the project aligns with NCEMS’s vision of emergent properties across composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion. It will transform aging research from lists of molecular correlates to predictive, mechanistic mesoscale models grounded in community data and reproducible analytics, while training a cohort of scientists fluent in cross-dataset synthesis and AI-enabled inference.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The working group will address a central emergence question: do aging phenotypes arise from a small number of mesoscale organizational regimes that mediate the effects of diverse molecular changes? We will frame this as a set of testable questions with explicit hypotheses that can be evaluated using only publicly available data.

RQ1: Are there conserved mesoscale “aging state variables” that summarize the joint organization of proteostasis, organelles, and cellular mechanics across datasets?
H1.1: Across species and cell types, high-dimensional measurements (organelle morphology, spatial protein localization patterns, proteostasis markers, mechanical proxies) can be reduced to a low-dimensional manifold representing discrete or continuous mesoscale regimes (e.g., “high proteostasis–connected organelle network–compliant mechanics” vs “proteostasis collapse–organelle fragmentation–stiffened cortex”).
H1.2: These mesoscale regimes are more predictive of functional outcomes (stress survival, growth, senescence markers) than molecular abundance signatures alone.

RQ2: Do mesoscale variables mediate the relationship between molecular perturbations and aging-associated cellular outcomes?
H2.1: For perturbations known to affect aging (e.g., chaperones, proteasome subunits, autophagy genes, mitochondrial dynamics factors, actin regulators), causal models will support mediation paths where molecular perturbation → mesoscale change (organelle architecture/condensate state/mechanics proxy) → phenotype.
H2.2: The same phenotype can be reached via different molecular routes but converges on similar mesoscale regimes (many-to-one mapping), consistent with emergence.

RQ3: What are the cross-scale rules linking protein properties to mesoscale organization in aging?
H3.1: Protein-level features derived from structure and sequence (intrinsic disorder, multivalency, aggregation propensity, predicted phase separation propensity, membrane association) will predict which proteins shift localization, become insoluble, or concentrate at organelle interfaces/condensates in aging contexts.
H3.2: Enrichment of specific protein-property classes at organelle contact sites or condensates will correlate with mechanical proxies (e.g., cytoskeletal remodeling signatures), suggesting coupled regulation.

RQ4: Which data integration strategies are necessary and sufficient to recover robust mesoscale signals from heterogeneous public datasets?
H4.1: Explicit modeling of batch effects, missingness mechanisms, and measurement uncertainty will improve cross-dataset replicability of mesoscale variables compared with naive concatenation or single-modality analyses.
H4.2: Joint embedding methods with biological constraints (e.g., known organelle relationships, protein interaction priors) will yield more interpretable mesoscale axes than unconstrained embeddings.

RQ5: Are mesoscale aging regimes general across model organisms, or are they context-specific?
H5.1: A core subset of mesoscale variables will be conserved across yeast, worm, fly, and mammalian cell datasets, while additional axes will be organism- or tissue-specific.
H5.2: Apparent contradictions in the aging literature (e.g., stiffness increasing vs decreasing) can be reconciled by stratifying by mesoscale regime rather than by age or genotype alone.

Together these questions operationalize “the missing mesoscale” as measurable, comparable quantities. The hypotheses are designed to be falsifiable using synthesized public data and to yield clear decision points: whether mesoscale variables exist, whether they mediate outcomes, and whether they generalize across systems.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will run an NCEMS-style synthesis program organized into three integrated aims, executed through iterative data sprints and analysis clinics. The team will include domain experts in proteostasis and aging biology, organelle/cell biology, biophysics/mechanics, bioimage analysis, proteomics, causal inference, and data curation. All work will use only publicly available datasets and will prioritize resources with permissive reuse terms and rich metadata.

Aim 1: Curate and harmonize cross-modal public datasets into a mesoscale-ready knowledge graph.
1) Dataset selection: Identify imaging collections (BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, Cell Painting-style resources), proteomics (PRIDE/MassIVE; including fractionation/insoluble proteome when available), perturbation screens (DepMap/CRISPR screens where applicable, organism-specific RNAi/CRISPR resources), and phenotype/aging annotations (GEO/ArrayExpress for transcriptomics linked to aging states; curated aging gene databases).
2) Common metadata schema: Define a minimal information model for “mesoscale aging synthesis” including organism, cell type, perturbation, age/stress state, imaging modality, segmentation level, protein identifiers, subcellular compartment ontology, and phenotype endpoints. Map terms to existing ontologies (GO, Cell Ontology, OBI) and record provenance.
3) Harmonization: Standardize identifiers (UniProt/Ensembl), align orthologs across organisms, and create a knowledge graph linking proteins, structural features (AlphaFold/PDB-derived disorder, domains), interactions (BioGRID/STRING), pathways, organelles, and phenotypes.

Aim 2: Extract and define mesoscale variables from imaging and omics.
1) Imaging-derived mesoscale features: Use open pipelines (e.g., CellProfiler, ilastik, deep-learning segmentation where pretrained models exist) to compute organelle morphology (network connectivity, fragmentation indices, contact-site proxies), spatial colocalization patterns, texture/organization metrics, and condensate-like puncta statistics. When raw images are too heterogeneous, leverage published feature tables where available.
2) Proteomics-derived mesoscale proxies: Compute proteostasis-related measures such as chaperone/proteasome module abundance, stoichiometric imbalance within complexes, insoluble/aggregated fraction shifts (when available), and PTM signatures linked to stress. Integrate protein property annotations (disorder, aggregation propensity) to derive “proteome material property” indices.
3) Mechanics proxies: Where direct mechanical measurements are absent, derive validated proxies from cytoskeletal organization features in imaging, expression/protein abundance of mechanotransduction modules, and nuclear lamina markers; explicitly label them as proxies with uncertainty.
4) Latent mesoscale state inference: Learn joint embeddings (multi-view factor models, variational approaches) that produce interpretable latent variables constrained by organelle and pathway priors.

Aim 3: Test mediation and emergence using causal discovery and cross-dataset validation.
1) Causal modeling: Build structural causal models linking perturbations (genetic/chemical), molecular modules, mesoscale variables, and phenotypes. Apply causal discovery with constraints (known directionality: perturbation precedes phenotype) and assess robustness via bootstrap and sensitivity analyses.
2) Mediation tests: Quantify how much of perturbation→phenotype effects are mediated by mesoscale variables versus direct molecular effects, using uncertainty-aware mediation analysis.
3) Generalization: Perform leave-dataset-out and leave-organism-out validation. Evaluate whether mesoscale variables learned in one context predict phenotypes in another.
4) Negative controls and falsification: Include non-aging perturbations and randomized mappings to ensure mesoscale signals are not artifacts of batch or annotation leakage.

Training integration. Trainees will lead cross-validation tasks, documentation, and tutorial notebooks, rotating roles across curation, feature extraction, and causal modeling to build full-stack synthesis expertise.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific outcomes. The primary scientific product will be a validated, quantitative model of mesoscale aging states that links proteostasis capacity, organelle organization, and mechanics to cellular outcomes. We expect to identify a small set of mesoscale variables—interpretable axes or regimes—that (i) recur across multiple public datasets, (ii) predict aging-relevant phenotypes better than molecular abundance alone, and (iii) act as mediators that explain why diverse perturbations converge on similar outcomes. A second scientific outcome will be cross-scale rules connecting protein properties (e.g., disorder, multivalency, aggregation propensity, membrane association) to mesoscale reorganization, providing mechanistic hypotheses that can guide future experimental work (outside the scope of this synthesis proposal).

Methodological outcomes. We will deliver a generalizable synthesis workflow for extracting mesoscale features from heterogeneous imaging and omics data, integrating them into a shared representation, and performing uncertainty-aware causal inference. This includes a reusable metadata schema, an annotated knowledge graph, and reference implementations for multi-view embeddings and mediation analysis tailored to molecular/cellular emergence questions.

The project will demonstrate the value of NCEMS-style working groups for problems that require broad expertise and intensive data integration beyond any single lab. By operating at the mesoscale, it directly advances NCEMS’s mission to understand emergent properties between biomolecules and organelles. The outputs will lower barriers for the community to reuse public data for mechanistic discovery, support downstream hypothesis generation for aging interventions, and provide a template for similar emergence studies (e.g., stress granules, organelle contact networks, morphodynamic transitions).

Workforce impact. Trainees will gain practical skills in data curation, bioimage analysis, multi-omics integration, and causal inference under open-science norms, producing a cohort capable of leading future synthesis efforts in molecular and cellular biology.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-by-default products. All code, documentation, and derived (non-restricted) feature tables will be released under permissive open-source licenses (e.g., MIT/BSD for code; CC-BY/CC0 for documentation and schemas) in a public version-controlled repository. We will not redistribute controlled-access human data; instead, we will provide reproducible pointers, accession lists, and scripts that operate on user-authorized downloads when needed.

Each major result will have an executable “research compendium” (environment + workflow + notebook) enabling reruns from raw public accessions to final figures. We will include continuous integration checks for linting, unit tests for feature extraction and identifier mapping, and regression tests to detect drift when datasets update.

Provenance and uncertainty. Every integrated datum will carry provenance (source accession, processing steps, timestamp) and an uncertainty/quality annotation (e.g., missingness mechanism, segmentation confidence where available, batch labels). Training and dissemination. We will run open workflow clinics and publish step-by-step tutorials (Jupyter notebooks, recorded walkthroughs) aimed at graduate students and postdocs. All meetings will produce public notes when appropriate, and we will release a public “methods and pitfalls” guide documenting failure modes (batch effects, annotation leakage, proxy limitations) and recommended best practices for mesoscale synthesis.

title: Microbial mesoscale collectives: emergence below the organelle scale
abstract:
This working group asks how microbial mesoscale collectives: emergence below the organelle scale can be understood as an emergent property that links molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcome. The scientific question is not simply whether particular molecules, organelles, or pathways are associated with a phenotype, but whether publicly available datasets can reveal rules by which many molecular parts collectively produce a new, system-level behavior at the scale between biomolecules and organelles. The project is designed for the NCEMS model because the relevant evidence is scattered across incompatible imaging repositories, omics studies, perturbation resources, structural annotations, and specialized literatures; no single laboratory is likely to have the biological breadth, data-engineering capacity, and methodological expertise to integrate them.

The group would synthesize existing public data centered on imaging + proteomics, prioritizing datasets with reusable metadata, perturbation or state annotations, and links to downstream cellular phenotypes. Depending on availability, sources could include public cell atlases, the Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, EMBL-EBI and NCBI functional genomics repositories, BioImage Archive or Image Data Resource collections, PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics datasets, public CRISPR or RNAi screens, AlphaFold/PDB-derived structural features, and curated pathway or protein-interaction resources. The core analytic strategy would be comparative phylogenetic synthesis: harmonizing measurements into a common representation; explicitly modeling uncertainty, batch effects, and missingness; and testing whether mesoscale variables explain cellular outcomes above and beyond molecular abundance alone. The biological scope would focus on microbes/parasites while deliberately including comparison cases that prevent the group from mistaking a narrow model-system pattern for a general law.

The novel element is the unit of explanation. Instead of treating mesoscale organization as an image label, downstream readout, or anecdotal mechanism, the working group would make it the primary object of synthesis: a measurable layer where composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion combine. The expected product is a predictive atlas that is open, versioned, and reusable, with transparent workflows, community-agreed metadata standards, and tutorials for trainees. The project would bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, imaging scientists, omics researchers, statisticians, machine-learning researchers, data curators, and trainees across institution types. Training would occur through hackathon-style data sprints, reproducible workflow clinics, and rotating trainee leadership of cross-dataset validation tasks. The anticipated contribution is both scientific and infrastructural: a defensible answer to a specific emergence question, plus a generalizable synthesis strategy that helps the molecular and cellular biosciences reuse public data to discover phenomena that only become visible when datasets, disciplines, and scales are brought together.
background_and_significance:
Emergent biological properties often arise at intermediate (“mesoscale”) levels where many molecular parts collectively generate organization and function that cannot be predicted from any single component. In microbes and microbial eukaryotes, mesoscale organization is especially consequential: cells frequently lack large, membrane-bound organelles typical of metazoan systems, yet still exhibit robust spatial patterning, dynamic assemblies, phase-separated condensates, cytoskeletal architectures, microcompartments, cell-envelope nanodomains, and transient supramolecular complexes. These structures shape core outcomes such as growth, stress tolerance, pathogenicity, drug susceptibility, and lineage-specific adaptations. Despite decades of molecular biology identifying genes and pathways, we still lack generalizable rules linking molecular composition to mesoscale organization and, in turn, to cellular phenotypes. This gap is a classic “emergence” problem: organization is not merely a label on an image or a mechanistic anecdote, but a system-level property that depends on collective interactions, physical constraints, and evolutionary context.

Public data relevant to mesoscale emergence has expanded dramatically. Imaging repositories contain high-content fluorescence microscopy, cryo-electron tomography, super-resolution, and time-lapse datasets; proteomics and transcriptomics repositories contain quantitative abundance and condition-specific profiles; perturbation resources provide genetic and chemical interventions; structural databases and AlphaFold-derived annotations provide protein-level physical features; and interaction/pathway databases capture known networks. Yet these sources remain fragmented across formats, metadata standards, and organismal scopes. Microbial datasets are particularly heterogeneous: different labs use different stains, reporters, growth conditions, and segmentation pipelines; proteomics uses varying quantification strategies; and phenotype definitions (e.g., “persistence,” “virulence,” “stress survival”) are inconsistently operationalized. Consequently, synthesis—rather than new data generation—is the limiting step. The central opportunity is to integrate these disparate public datasets into a coherent, uncertainty-aware representation that treats mesoscale organization as a measurable layer between molecules and outcomes.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to enable this synthesis. First, the scientific target directly matches NCEMS’s emphasis on emergent properties at the mesoscale and on cross-scale links spanning composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion. Second, the work requires community-scale coordination: no single lab can simultaneously curate imaging metadata, harmonize omics measurements, implement robust batch-correction and missing-data strategies, and develop machine-learning models that remain biologically interpretable across taxa. Third, the project will catalyze multidisciplinary collaboration among microbial cell biologists, quantitative microscopists, biophysicists, proteomics experts, evolutionary biologists, statisticians, ML researchers, and data curators. Finally, the project aligns with NCEMS’s workforce mission by training trainees in reproducible data synthesis, AI-enabled image/omics integration, and open-science practices.

The significance is twofold. Scientifically, the project seeks general rules: when do different molecular compositions converge to similar mesoscale architectures, and when do similar compositions yield divergent architectures and phenotypes? Methodologically, it establishes a reusable framework for integrating imaging-derived mesoscale descriptors with omics, perturbations, and phylogenetic context. The resulting atlas and workflows will accelerate discovery across microbiology, parasitology, and cell biology, enabling researchers to test emergence hypotheses using public data rather than relying solely on bespoke experiments. By making mesoscale organization the primary object of synthesis, this working group aims to convert scattered observations into predictive, generalizable knowledge about how microbial cells self-organize below the organelle scale.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will address a set of tightly linked questions about how mesoscale organization emerges from molecular composition and predicts cellular outcomes. We define “mesoscale collectives” as spatially and temporally organized assemblies (e.g., clusters, filaments, shells, condensates, nanodomains, microcompartments, and supramolecular complexes) that are larger than individual macromolecules yet smaller than canonical organelles, and that can be quantified from imaging and/or inferred from integrated molecular features.

RQ1: Are there conserved, quantitative mesoscale “morphospace” axes that recur across microbial lineages and conditions? Hypothesis 1A: Diverse microbes occupy a low-dimensional mesoscale morphospace defined by a small set of descriptors (e.g., clustering, anisotropy, surface association, compartmentalization, dynamics) that can be recovered from heterogeneous imaging modalities after appropriate harmonization. Hypothesis 1B: Positions in this morphospace are evolutionarily structured (phylogenetic signal) but also show repeated convergence under similar environmental constraints, indicating general physical/functional tradeoffs.

RQ2: Do mesoscale variables explain phenotypic variance beyond molecular abundance and known pathways? Hypothesis 2A: Mesoscale descriptors significantly improve prediction of cellular outcomes (growth under stress, drug response, infectivity proxies, persistence, motility, morphological transitions) compared with models using only transcript/protein abundance and curated pathway features. Hypothesis 2B: The added predictive power is strongest for phenotypes that are inherently collective (e.g., tolerance, persistence, spatially localized metabolism), consistent with emergence at the mesoscale.

RQ3: What molecular and structural features are most associated with mesoscale organization across taxa? Hypothesis 3A: Protein-level biophysical attributes (intrinsic disorder, multivalency, oligomerization propensity, membrane association motifs, coiled-coils, electrostatic patterning) derived from AlphaFold/PDB and sequence annotations predict membership in specific mesoscale collective classes better than abundance alone. Hypothesis 3B: Network context (interaction degree, modularity, pathway co-membership) moderates these relationships, such that mesoscale assembly is enriched in proteins with specific network roles (e.g., hubs in stress modules, scaffold-like connectors).

RQ4: How robust are inferred rules to dataset heterogeneity, missingness, and measurement error? Hypothesis 4A: Explicit uncertainty modeling (hierarchical models, measurement-error models, and multiple-imputation strategies) yields stable cross-dataset inferences and prevents spurious “emergence” claims driven by batch effects. Hypothesis 4B: When harmonization is performed with causal/graph-informed covariates (growth conditions, imaging modality, labeling strategy), inferred mesoscale–phenotype links generalize better to held-out studies and organisms.

RQ5: Do perturbations reveal consistent mesoscale “response motifs” that map to outcomes? Hypothesis 5A: Genetic/chemical perturbations induce a limited set of mesoscale response motifs (e.g., dispersal-to-cluster transitions, shell formation, polarity loss, filament thickening) that recur across organisms. Hypothesis 5B: These motifs mediate the path from molecular perturbation to phenotype; mediation analyses will show that part of the perturbation effect on outcomes is transmitted through mesoscale reorganization.

Collectively, these questions test a central emergence claim: mesoscale organization is a distinct explanatory layer—measurable and predictive—that links molecular parts to cellular outcomes in ways that are not reducible to single-gene or single-pathway effects. The hypotheses are designed to be falsifiable using only public datasets, with pre-registered evaluation criteria centered on out-of-sample generalization across studies and taxa.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. The project will run as an NCEMS Working Group organized into iterative synthesis cycles: (i) dataset discovery and triage, (ii) harmonization and representation learning, (iii) cross-scale modeling and hypothesis tests, and (iv) validation via held-out datasets and cross-taxon generalization. The team will include domain experts (microbiology, parasitology), imaging scientists, proteomics/omics experts, evolutionary biologists, statisticians, ML researchers, and data curators. Trainees will lead defined “integration tasks” with mentorship and reproducible deliverables.

Data sources (public only). Imaging: BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, EMPIAR where appropriate, organism-specific atlases, and literature-linked datasets with accessible raw/processed images and metadata. Omics: PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics; GEO/ArrayExpress/SRA for transcriptomics and functional genomics; public CRISPR/RNAi and chemogenomic screens (where available for microbes/parasites); curated phenotype datasets from community repositories. Structural/annotation: UniProt, InterPro, Pfam, AlphaFold-derived features, PDB where relevant. Networks/pathways: STRING, BioGRID, KEGG/Reactome (organism permitting), and curated microbial interaction resources.

Inclusion criteria and metadata minimal information. Datasets will be prioritized if they include (a) organism/strain, (b) growth condition and perturbation annotations, (c) imaging modality and labeling strategy, (d) replicates or quality metrics, and (e) linkable identifiers (gene/protein IDs). A “minimum metadata schema” for microbial mesoscale datasets will be drafted and iteratively refined with curators, then applied to all ingested datasets.

Mesoscale feature extraction. For imaging, we will implement modular pipelines (Napari/Cellpose/ilastik-compatible where applicable) to compute interpretable mesoscale descriptors rather than only deep embeddings: spatial clustering statistics, radial distribution functions, anisotropy/orientation fields, compartment boundary proximity, co-localization and segregation indices, texture/scale measures, and dynamic features for time-lapse (e.g., persistence, turnover proxies). When segmentation is unreliable across modalities, we will use weakly supervised and self-supervised approaches to learn representations, then map them back to interpretable axes via probing models and feature attribution.

Harmonization and uncertainty. We will harmonize identifiers (orthology mapping via eggNOG/OrthoDB where needed), units, and condition ontologies. Batch effects will be addressed using hierarchical modeling and empirical Bayes approaches, with covariates for modality, lab, and preprocessing. Missingness will be handled via multiple imputation and sensitivity analyses, explicitly reporting how conclusions change under different assumptions.

Comparative phylogenetic synthesis. To avoid overgeneralizing from a single model system, we will analyze patterns across taxa using phylogenetic mixed models and methods that partition variance into phylogenetic vs condition-driven components. We will test for convergent evolution in mesoscale descriptors under similar stresses or lifestyles.

Cross-scale predictive modeling and hypothesis testing. We will build predictive models for phenotypes using (i) omics-only features, (ii) mesoscale-only features, and (iii) integrated features (mesoscale + omics + structural + network). Models will include regularized regression, gradient-boosted trees, and calibrated neural models with uncertainty estimates. Performance will be evaluated with nested cross-validation that holds out entire studies and, critically, holds out taxa to assess generalization. Hypothesis tests will focus on incremental predictive value (ΔAUC/ΔR2), mediation analyses for perturbation→mesoscale→phenotype pathways, and robustness checks.

Deliverable-driven sprints. Each synthesis cycle will end with a public release: curated dataset index, harmonized feature tables, benchmark tasks, and a draft atlas. This structure ensures feasibility, continuous integration, and clear progress milestones within the NCEMS working-group model.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific outcomes. (1) A quantitative, cross-taxon “mesoscale morphospace” for microbial collectives, identifying recurring axes of organization and their evolutionary and environmental correlates. (2) Evidence-based tests of emergence: whether mesoscale descriptors explain phenotypes beyond molecular abundance and pathway membership, with rigorous out-of-sample validation across studies and taxa. (3) A ranked set of molecular, structural, and network features most predictive of specific mesoscale collective classes, generating mechanistic hypotheses about assembly principles (e.g., multivalency, disorder, membrane association) that are broadly applicable across microbes and parasites.

Methodological outcomes. (4) A generalizable synthesis workflow for integrating imaging-derived mesoscale descriptors with proteomics/transcriptomics, perturbation annotations, and phylogenetic context, including uncertainty-aware harmonization and missing-data strategies. (5) Benchmark datasets and evaluation protocols for mesoscale emergence modeling (study-held-out and taxon-held-out splits), enabling the community to compare methods fairly and avoid overfitting to particular repositories.

Infrastructural outcomes. (6) An open, versioned “Microbial Mesoscale Collectives Atlas” that links (where permitted) source datasets, harmonized metadata, computed features, and predictive models, with clear provenance and citations to original data generators. (7) Community-informed minimal metadata recommendations for publishing microbial mesoscale imaging and linked omics in a reusable form.

Broader impacts. The atlas and workflows will accelerate discovery in microbiology, parasitology, antimicrobial research, and quantitative cell biology by enabling researchers to formulate and test mesoscale hypotheses using existing public data. The project will also lower barriers for smaller or resource-limited institutions to participate in cutting-edge synthesis research through shared tools, tutorials, and well-scaffolded tasks. By centering mesoscale organization as a first-class explanatory layer, the working group will advance NCEMS’s mission to understand emergent properties and will provide a template for future community-scale synthesis efforts that bridge molecules to cellular behavior without generating new experimental data.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-by-default products. All code, documentation, and derived (non-restricted) data products will be released under permissive licenses (e.g., BSD-3/Apache-2.0 for code; CC-BY/CC0 for metadata/derived feature tables as appropriate). We will not redistribute restricted raw data; instead we will provide scripted download instructions, checksums, and provenance records that enable lawful reconstruction of analyses from original sources.

Reproducible workflows. Analyses will be implemented as containerized, workflow-managed pipelines (e.g., Docker/Singularity + Snakemake/Nextflow), with pinned software versions and automated tests. Each release will include: (i) a fully executable workflow, (ii) a machine-readable manifest of inputs/outputs, (iii) quality-control reports, and (iv) a “re-run on a laptop” minimal example plus an “HPC/cloud” profile. Continuous integration will run unit tests on feature extraction, identifier mapping, and model training.

Transparent provenance and versioning. We will maintain a public registry of ingested datasets with dataset-level citations, licenses, and reuse constraints. Derived artifacts (harmonized tables, embeddings, models) will be versioned with semantic versioning and DOIs via Zenodo or an equivalent repository. Provenance will be tracked using standardized metadata (e.g., RO-Crate/W3C PROV where feasible), enabling users to trace every atlas entry back to source data and processing steps.

Pre-specified evaluation and robustness. For core hypotheses, we will pre-register evaluation metrics and validation splits (study-held-out and taxon-held-out) to reduce analytic flexibility. We will report negative results, sensitivity analyses (batch correction, imputation assumptions), and uncertainty intervals for key estimates.

Training and community engagement. Trainees will receive structured instruction in reproducible research (Git, code review, data management, workflow systems) and will co-lead “reproducibility clinics” where participants reproduce a published figure/table from scratch. We will host open office hours and invite external community feedback on metadata standards and atlas usability, aligning with NCEMS community-created policies on open, team, and reproducible science.
budget_and_resources:
Budget rationale and NCEMS need. This is a community-scale synthesis effort requiring coordinated meetings, dedicated time for cross-lab integration, and shared computational and curation infrastructure beyond a single laboratory’s capacity. NCEMS support is essential to convene diverse expertise, provide neutral coordination, and sustain open, versioned releases.

Major cost categories (illustrative, adjustable to NCEMS guidelines). (1) Working group convenings: travel, lodging, and meeting costs for 2–3 in-person meetings plus regular virtual workshops, ensuring participation across geography and institution types. (2) Personnel support: partial support for a project manager/synthesis coordinator (to manage timelines, documentation, and cross-team interfaces), and limited support for trainees (graduate students/postdocs) to lead integration tasks, documentation, and benchmarking. (3) Computing and data infrastructure: cloud/HPC credits for large-scale image feature extraction and model training; storage for derived products; and costs for persistent identifiers/archival (e.g., DOI minting via Zenodo is free, but curation time is not). (4) Accessibility and participation: support for caregivers, accessibility services, and participation by researchers from under-resourced institutions.

Resource plan. NCEMS will provide convening infrastructure, facilitation, and access to center-supported compute where available. Participating labs will contribute in-kind expertise and existing tools (e.g., image analysis pipelines, omics processing scripts) and will designate leads for: imaging harmonization, omics integration, phylogenetic modeling, ML/AI benchmarking, and data curation/metadata.

Deliverables tied to expenditures. Each funded period will culminate in concrete public outputs: (i) curated dataset registry and metadata schema, (ii) harmonized mesoscale feature tables and benchmark tasks, (iii) predictive models with uncertainty and generalization tests, and (iv) a versioned atlas release with tutorials. Budget is therefore directly aligned with NCEMS priorities: multidisciplinary synthesis using only public data, open and reproducible outputs, and hands-on training for a data-savvy workforce.

background_and_significance:
Emergent biological properties often arise when many molecular components interact to produce new behaviors not predictable from individual parts. In molecular and cellular biosciences, this “more-than-the-sum” behavior is frequently expressed at the mesoscale—the regime between biomolecules and organelles—where macromolecular assemblies, condensates, cytoskeletal networks, membrane microdomains, and multi-organelle contact sites collectively shape cell fate and function. Yet mesoscale phenomena remain difficult to generalize because evidence is distributed across heterogeneous modalities (imaging, omics, perturbation screens, structural predictions) and across communities that use incompatible vocabularies and metadata conventions. As a result, many claims about mesoscale mechanisms remain anecdotal, system-specific, or untestable across datasets.

At the same time, the public data landscape is now rich enough to support community-scale synthesis. Imaging repositories (e.g., BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas) provide spatial context and phenotypic readouts. Functional genomics archives (GEO, ArrayExpress, SRA) and proteomics resources (PRIDE, MassIVE) provide molecular abundance and state changes. Public perturbation datasets (CRISPR/RNAi screens, chemical perturbation atlases) supply causal leverage. Structural resources (PDB, AlphaFold-derived features) and interaction/pathway databases (BioGRID, STRING, Reactome, GO) offer mechanistic priors. However, these resources are rarely integrated in a way that treats mesoscale organization as a first-class explanatory layer rather than a qualitative narrative.

This proposal advances a central idea aligned with NCEMS: curation itself can be a mode of discovery when it encodes evidence about emergence in a computable, uncertainty-aware form. We will develop an open ontology and knowledge graph of “mesoscale emergence evidence” that links (i) molecular composition and perturbations, (ii) mesoscale organizational variables (e.g., assembly, clustering, phase separation, network topology, compartmental proximity), and (iii) downstream cellular outcomes (e.g., growth, stress response, differentiation, trafficking efficiency). By representing evidence types, measurement contexts, and confidence, we enable systematic cross-study tests of whether mesoscale variables explain phenotypes above and beyond molecular abundance alone.

The significance is twofold. Scientifically, we aim to identify generalizable rules of mesoscale emergence—patterns that recur across species, cell types, and perturbations—thereby addressing long-standing puzzles about why similar molecular inventories can yield distinct cellular behaviors. Methodologically, we will create a reusable synthesis framework that makes disparate public datasets interoperable, enabling researchers to ask new questions that require integrated evidence at scale.

This work is well-suited to the NCEMS working-group model. It is beyond a single lab’s capacity because it requires (1) cross-domain expertise in cell biology, biophysics, imaging, omics, statistics/ML, and knowledge representation; (2) substantial data engineering to harmonize metadata and map entities across identifiers and species; and (3) community governance to establish standards and ensure broad adoption. By convening a multidisciplinary team and trainees, NCEMS support will catalyze both a high-impact scientific synthesis and durable infrastructure for mesoscale emergence research.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
The working group is organized around the premise that mesoscale organization is a measurable, integrative layer that mediates between molecular parts and cellular outcomes. We will focus on questions that can be answered using only publicly available data and that require synthesis across modalities.

RQ1: What is the minimal set of computable concepts needed to represent “mesoscale emergence evidence” across imaging, omics, perturbation, and structural resources?
H1: A compact ontology that distinguishes (i) mesoscale entities (assemblies, networks, interfaces), (ii) organizational attributes (size distributions, topology, spatial proximity, dynamics proxies), and (iii) evidence types (direct imaging measurement, inferred from perturbation, co-localization statistics, interaction/structure priors) will cover the majority of reusable public claims about mesoscale mechanisms. We hypothesize that explicitly encoding measurement context and uncertainty will reduce apparent contradictions across studies.

RQ2: Do mesoscale organizational variables improve prediction and explanation of cellular outcomes beyond molecular abundance and pathway membership?
H2: Models that include mesoscale variables (e.g., organelle contact frequency proxies, condensate propensity features, cytoskeletal network descriptors, spatial clustering indices) will yield significant gains in out-of-sample prediction of phenotypes (e.g., viability under stress, trafficking defects, morphology classes) compared with models using only gene/protein abundance and pathway annotations. We further hypothesize that these gains will be largest for phenotypes known to depend on spatial organization (e.g., secretion, polarity, mitotic fidelity).

RQ3: Are there cross-species “emergence motifs”—recurring mesoscale patterns that link diverse molecular compositions to similar cellular outcomes?
H3: When mapped through orthology and functional equivalence, distinct molecular components will converge on shared mesoscale motifs (e.g., stress granule-like assemblies, ER–mitochondria interface strengthening, actin-driven cortical patterning) that predict similar outcomes across taxa. We hypothesize that motif recurrence will be detectable even when individual genes differ, indicating mesoscale-level conservation.

RQ4: Which classes of perturbations most reliably modulate mesoscale organization, and are their effects context-dependent?
H4: Perturbations affecting biophysical parameters (e.g., charge patterning, multivalency, membrane composition, ATP-dependent remodeling) will show stronger and more transferable mesoscale effects than perturbations affecting single pathway nodes. We hypothesize that context (cell type, stress state) will gate these effects, and that our evidence graph can quantify context-dependence.

RQ5: Can contradictions in the literature about mesoscale mechanisms be reconciled by differences in measurement modality, metadata, and hidden covariates?
H5: A substantial fraction of apparent disagreements (e.g., whether a protein “forms puncta” or “localizes diffusely”) will be explainable by assay differences, imaging resolution, labeling strategy, and state annotations. We hypothesize that representing these covariates in the ontology will allow formal tests of reproducibility and identify conditions under which claims hold.

Together, these questions operationalize emergence for synthesis: not as a philosophical label, but as testable statements about when mesoscale organization carries explanatory power, when it is conserved, and how evidence quality and context shape our conclusions.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will execute a community-scale synthesis in three integrated workstreams: (WS1) ontology and evidence modeling, (WS2) data harmonization and knowledge-graph construction, and (WS3) cross-dataset benchmarking and hypothesis testing. The group will meet in NCEMS-facilitated intensive sessions (in-person/virtual), with intersession sprints led by mixed-discipline subteams and trainees.

WS1: Ontology of mesoscale emergence evidence. We will extend and interoperate with existing standards (GO, OBO Foundry ontologies, RO relations, Cell Ontology, Uberon where relevant) rather than reinventing. New terms will focus on mesoscale organizational attributes and evidence types (e.g., “assembly size distribution measured by microscopy,” “condensate propensity inferred from sequence/structure,” “organelle contact enrichment inferred from proximity labeling,” “network topology inferred from filament segmentation”). We will define competency questions, logical axioms, and minimal metadata requirements (assay, resolution, perturbation, state, species/cell type, confidence). Uncertainty will be encoded via evidence codes, quantitative confidence fields, and provenance links.

WS2: Dataset selection, harmonization, and integration. We will prioritize public datasets with (a) reusable metadata, (b) perturbation/state annotations, and (c) links to phenotypes. Candidate sources include BioImage Archive/IDR imaging collections, Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, GEO/ArrayExpress transcriptomics, PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics, DepMap/public CRISPR screens where licensing permits, PDB/AlphaFold features, and interaction/pathway databases. Harmonization steps: (1) entity resolution (gene/protein IDs, isoforms, ortholog mapping), (2) controlled vocabulary mapping to ontology terms, (3) normalization and batch correction within modality (e.g., ComBat/limma where appropriate, robust scaling), (4) missingness characterization (MCAR/MAR/MNAR diagnostics) and imputation strategies with uncertainty propagation, and (5) provenance capture using W3C PROV-compatible records.

Knowledge graph implementation. We will build an open, versioned graph using RDF/OWL for ontology alignment plus a property-graph layer (e.g., Neo4j) for scalable analytics, with synchronized exports. Nodes will represent entities (molecules, complexes, organelles, cell types, perturbations, phenotypes, datasets), and edges will represent relations with evidence and context. ETL pipelines will be implemented in reproducible workflows (Snakemake/Nextflow) and containerized.

WS3: Benchmarks and hypothesis tests. We will define benchmark tasks that quantify the added value of mesoscale variables: (i) phenotype prediction under perturbation (classification/regression), (ii) cross-dataset claim replication (agreement conditioned on context), and (iii) discovery of emergence motifs via graph mining/community detection. Models will include baseline (abundance + pathway) and augmented (baseline + mesoscale features) variants. We will use hierarchical/multilevel models to account for dataset and lab effects; causal-inspired analyses (e.g., instrumental-variable style sensitivity, do-calculus approximations where feasible) will be used cautiously and transparently. Performance will be assessed with nested cross-validation, calibration curves, and ablation studies. Robustness checks will include negative controls (randomized mappings), modality holdouts, and cross-species transfer tests.

Training integration. Trainees will lead “validation pods” responsible for one benchmark each, producing a reproducible notebook, a short methods note, and a pull request to the shared repository. This ensures workforce development while directly advancing deliverables.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific outcomes. (1) A defensible, quantitative assessment of when mesoscale organizational variables add explanatory power for cellular outcomes beyond molecular abundance and pathway annotations. (2) A catalog of candidate cross-species “emergence motifs” that connect diverse molecular compositions to convergent mesoscale patterns and phenotypes, with explicit confidence and context. (3) A framework for reconciling conflicting mesoscale claims by conditioning on assay, resolution, perturbation, and cellular state.

Resource outcomes. (1) An open ontology of mesoscale emergence evidence, aligned to OBO/GO where possible, with clear competency questions and community documentation. (2) An open, versioned knowledge graph linking molecules, perturbations, mesoscale attributes, and phenotypes across multiple public repositories, with provenance and uncertainty captured at the edge level. (3) Benchmark datasets and evaluation suites that allow the community to test new algorithms for integrating imaging, omics, and structural priors to explain mesoscale emergence.

Impact on NCEMS mission. The project directly targets emergent properties at the mesoscale and leverages AI/data science to synthesize a myriad of public data. It is intentionally beyond a single lab: it requires coordinated ontology design, large-scale metadata harmonization, and multi-modal benchmarking. The working group will seed a broader community of practice around mesoscale evidence standards, enabling future synthesis projects to be faster, more reproducible, and more comparable.

Broader impacts. By treating curation as discovery, we transform scattered public datasets into a reusable substrate for hypothesis generation and testing. The outputs will lower barriers for researchers at diverse institution types to participate in mesoscale science, support training of data-savvy biologists, and improve the return on investment of existing public data by making it interoperable and computable for emergence-focused questions.
open_science_and_reproducibility:
Open-by-default products. All code, workflows, ontology files, and graph releases will be publicly available under permissive licenses (e.g., MIT/BSD for code; CC-BY or CC0 where appropriate for derived metadata/ontologies), with clear attribution and compliance with upstream dataset licenses. We will not redistribute restricted raw data; instead we will publish derived, license-compliant harmonized tables and pointers (accession IDs, checksums) to original sources.

Reproducible workflows. Data ingestion and transformation will be implemented as scripted, containerized pipelines (Docker/Singularity) orchestrated by Snakemake/Nextflow. Each release will be tagged and archived (Zenodo DOI), with environment specifications (Conda/lockfiles) and automated tests. Analyses will be delivered as executable notebooks plus non-notebook scripts for batch runs. Continuous integration will validate schema conformance, ontology reasoning checks, and benchmark reproducibility.

Provenance, uncertainty, and auditability. Every graph assertion will carry provenance (dataset accession, processing step, software version), evidence type, and uncertainty/confidence fields. We will adopt community standards where possible (W3C PROV, RO-Crate for packaging, JSON-LD/RDF for semantic exports). Contradictory assertions will be retained rather than overwritten, with context annotations enabling downstream reconciliation.

Community governance. We will use an open governance model: public issue tracker, contribution guidelines, code of conduct, and a lightweight steering committee including trainees. Ontology term requests and mappings will be handled through transparent review, with periodic community calls to solicit feedback from imaging, omics, and cell biology stakeholders.

Training and dissemination. We will publish tutorials (short videos, written guides) on (i) contributing mappings, (ii) running pipelines, and (iii) using the knowledge graph for emergence queries. Working-group outputs will be accompanied by a “reproducibility checklist” and a public roadmap to encourage adoption and extension.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support rationale. This project requires NCEMS coordination, convening power, and shared cyberinfrastructure to integrate multiple public repositories, align standards across communities, and run intensive synthesis sprints. The scale of ontology development plus multi-modal benchmarking exceeds typical single-lab resources.

Budget categories (illustrative, adjustable to NCEMS guidelines). (1) Working-group meetings: travel, lodging, and per diem for 15–20 participants across institution types for 2–3 in-person meetings, plus support for virtual participation to ensure accessibility. (2) Personnel time: partial support for a project manager/data engineer (workflow maintenance, releases), an ontology/knowledge-graph specialist (schema alignment, reasoning checks), and trainee support (stipends or travel awards) to lead validation pods. (3) Computing: cloud credits or NCEMS-provided compute for ETL, graph builds, and benchmarking; storage for intermediate derived artifacts; CI resources. (4) Dissemination: publication fees for open-access outputs when needed; workshop materials; tutorial production.

Resource plan and roles. The working group will include: (i) cell biologists/biophysicists to define mesoscale concepts and interpret motifs; (ii) imaging scientists to advise on metadata, segmentation-derived features, and assay comparability; (iii) omics and perturbation experts to ensure correct normalization and causal framing; (iv) statisticians/ML researchers to design benchmarks, uncertainty models, and cross-validation; (v) ontology/curation experts to align with OBO practices; and (vi) trainees to implement mappings and benchmarks.

Deliverable-driven allocation. Funds and effort will be tied to quarterly milestones: ontology v0.1, first graph release, benchmark suite v1, and final integrated release with documentation. NCEMS facilities will host meetings, provide collaboration tooling, and support open-science compliance (archiving, DOIs, and community standards alignment).
